This game is something of a flawed gem.  But for all the issues I could gripe about, where this game truly triumphs is pure atmosphere. Imagine Call of Cthulhu meets Heart of Darkness.  I keep playing not so much for the gameplay (which is pretty basic actually) but just to keep puzzling out the glimpses I get of this dark world. The Long Dark throws you into a "frozen wilderness," in which the game challenges you to survive against all that mother nature can throw against you.
The eperience is wonderful and the view amazing as you wander the deserted landscape. Furthermore, even without zombies, monsters, ect. the game can still be very difficult.
Now for a list of likes and dislikes:
Liked:
-Very realistic simulation
-Beautiful scenery and artwork
-Seems to run well with few bugs
-The devs have been amazing with "bug fixes", "hot fixes", and large updates
-Many items and a variety of places to explore
-Very fun and challenging
There are not too many things to complain about except:
-The game does get slighty monotonous after a couple hours of play
Conclusion:
A very good game with great devs. I recommend "The Long Dark" to any who are interested in the survival genre.

The game is elegant and extremely well thought out. The experience feels real. As someone who grew up in rural America and who has hunted since a young age, I have to say the way hunting and trapping is handled feels quite convincing and real. You have to be pretty close to an animal to shoot it. It leaves a blood trail that can be tricky to follow, as well as tracks, and the animals are reasonably shy and hard to get close too- you have to really be patient and use your head.
The world is brutal. You will die, and often, until you figure out how to surive. Then, a simple mistake or a bit of bad luck will kill you anyway. This is a wonderful, harsh, unforgiving game, and it models real life survival about as well as any game I've ever played.
The graphics, while not perfectly real feeling, and always beautiful. The whole game is better than the sum of it's parts. I play a lot of games, in a lot of dfferent genres, and this, friends, is one of the very finest PC games that there is.

If you are ;eft wondering what this game is like, or what you do or how it works because of steams less than useless screenshots and description, then the good news is that I’m going to try and put into words just how great this game is.
Auditorium is a puzzle game, your goal for each level is to complete the music track,
You are given various different tools which affect your surroundings in various different ways. You use these to manipulate and bend the colour in the level to fill up a kind of "meter". For example, you bend the red light to the red meter, and if the flow of the light is constant enough (not just flicking it around), it will stay full.
Each meter plays a sound, and get increasingly louder as it gets fuller. Each colour makes a different sound when put into its place, you fill all of them in the level and each sound will work together to create a piece of music.
Every level and every stage is different and you are slowly introduced to more tools and more colours to play around with.
The music in this game is great, it’s calm and not to overpowering. The only downside in my eyes would be that if you’re stuck on a level, and I mean really stuck, it can get a little repetitive and annoying.
I won’t lie, a few points during the game I wanted to mute the game completely because hearing the same chimes over and over had really started to hurt my head. But then again, having the volume up fairly loud is no help.
It isn’t all that long of a game, but for me it was a good length, I didn't get bored before the finish and I didn't end up saying "that it?", seeing as there isn’t a storyline to keep me hooked. I think the length of the game was reasonable.
All in all, the game is great. Cipher prime really know how to make great puzzle games with wonderful visuals. I would recommend this to anyone.

Regency Solitaire is a fun little game. Its core gameplay is a modified version of solitare where you can stack cards in ascending or descending order, with some barriers put in place to make things more puzzling. It's not difficult, and you can repeat stages at your leisure, so it's very much a casual game. There's a small metagame in the form of winnings and the things you can purchase with them, but you'll have everything available long before the end of the game.
Story-wise, it tastes like a Jane Austin novel with modern sensibilities colouring the interactions; nothing to write home about, but not annoying either. The art and music are both good.
If it's on sale and you like card games, it's worth looking at.

Auditorium is a satisfying little puzzler. Its mechanics are elegant, and initially relaxing.
The difficulty ramps up pretty quickly, though. About half-way through the puzzle list, puzzle solving becomes less about having a moment of inspiration, and more about sliding the puzzle elements around the screen and seeing what happens. Sometimes moving a puzzle element just one or two pixels can dramatically change what's happening on screen. At this point, the game feels much less elegant, and more like a grind.
Still, auditorium has a certain charm, and memorable gameplay.

Apparently, concerning Auditorium I'm unknowing very LTTP.  The Store page promotes the game as "See why Auditorium has won countless awards and is considered the Second Best Browser Game of All Time."  I've never heard of the game but the grandiose description is not propaganda.
After spending sometime with Auditorium I can see why the game has won countless awards.  I'm going to classify Auditorium as one of those where did this come from works of genius.  The concept is amazing and demonstrates real imagination on the part of the studio (Cipher Prime Studios) and it's developers.
Auditorium is an abstract puzzler where you manipulate beams of light with and through constructs thus creating a musical score.  When the score is fully realized you've solved the puzzle.  If you haven't seen or heard of Auditorium I'll leave my description as is for Auditorium like another favorite puzzler of mine, Fractal: Make Blooms Not War (another Cipher Prime Studios work), is a puzzler where you discover the game's mechanics and once you start solving each puzzle and unearth the purpose of each of the game's constructs the feeling of satisfaction is immense and keeps you tuned in for the next puzzle.
Auditorium is worthy.  If you're a fan of rhythm or color based puzzlers or just have a passing interest then Auditorium should be in your library.

This is a shining example of how not to design a game.  The controls are fluid enough, and that's about it.
Limbo features simple, single-solution, direct puzzles.  One or two require lateral thinking:  video games have rules, and we forget to abuse physics behavior because we expect a simplistic physics subset.  Many are a matter of precision timing, rather than puzzle solving.  There is occasionally rapid death, giving you one-second experiments alternating with five-second load times to try again and see if you can't get the timing right without dying.
Allegedly, the game has a story; what it really has is an ambient motif of black-and-white, and a completely unexplained environment.  People, machines, and giant monsters?  Buildings, machinery, and wilderness?  Who built this, why are you here, how did you get here, who are these people, why are they doing what they're doing?  There is no explanation.  Even the ending is a cop-out:  it suggests a silent, visual, unexplained story resolution is about to happen, and then cuts to credits without actually playing through any sort of final cut scene.  You then wind up back at the title screen.
Limbo is more of a technology demo than a game.  With some dialogue, cutscenes, and more content, it would be an actual game.  As it stands, it's a set of procedural instructions which must be followed precisely, but they didn't give you the instruction sheet.

(The following review is mostly based on campaign/single player gameplay; I've yet to try the multiplayer portion)
I find that the opening menu of Tropico 5 sums it up perfectly. The amazing Caribbean soundtrack causes immediate deja vu for fans of the series, to the point where I thought they had recycled the same song from the previous games, yet something about the song feels better, cleaner, more refined. That's Tropico 5. Familiar ground that, on the surface, looks unsettlingly similar to previous entries, yet hides the game that Tropico 3 and 4 should have been all along.
I get the feeling that the majority of Tropico 5's target audience consists of people who enjoyed one or more of the previous four games. But, for the uninitiated, Tropico is one of the extremely scarce non-independant developed city building (aka management or simulation) games of the past decade. It centers around the idea of players taking the role as "El Presidente" of a Caribbean island, and building a small tropical society through agriculture, trade, tourism, and light-hearted political corruption. The first Tropico game was released in 2001 along with a sequel in 2003 and, though Tropico 2 was a major departure in theme from the rest of the series (a rather wonderful... piratey departure), both games gained something of a cult following. In 2009, Tropico 3 was released by a different developer and publisher as a 3D game, but by then most major city development games had vanished. The fact that Tropico survived was a pleasant surprise for fans such as myself. Though some would argue that the game lost a bit of its greatness in the transition, it stood on its own as a solid city builder in spite of its flaws. Two years and expansion pack later, Tropico 4 was released, and... it was Tropico 3. Though by no means bad, you had to dig quite deep to find additions that made it feel like a worthy sequel and not a copy. An overabundance of small DLC packs made it difficult for even the most diehard of fans to not feel cheated.
With that mindset, skeptical eyes turn to Tropico 5 and, if many of the reviews out there are to be believed, the knee-jerk reaction to this game is that it is yet another iteration of the same formula. However, I feel that these reviews are overlooking how the small changes make an all-around better gaming experience. So what's changed?
The most drastic change to the Tropico formula is the "era" and research system. Previously, Tropico focused primarily on the Cold War era, not-so-subtley hinting at the time and rule of Fidel Castro (he was even playable in earlier games), and only in the expansion pack for the fourth game did they try to shift the focus to 21st century society. Instead, the game now starts with Tropico as a 19th century royal colony, and El Presidente starts as a governer for the crown. Over time, you unlock new technologies, fight for your own independance, and establish new laws and decisions while new factions and global concerns crop up with each new era. Mechanically, this works brilliantly and fights off the biggest problems Tropico had with monotony over longer games. In addition to giving a perfect framework for Tropico's whimsical storytelling (more on that later), it adds a much needed sense of advancement to your society and promotes the use of strategies that would have been ignored in earlier games (such as how to deal with housing when you only have access to tiny houses and overpriced mansions). It all builds up to a much more refined modern era, complete with new industries like electronics and car production, as well as jabs at modern day political issues, which still fit perfectly into a banana republic setting.
Another change is a more refined economic system across the board. For me, this is Tropico 5's selling point. You can tell a lot of thought went into how the pieces of the game work together. Though Tropico is still a "butterfly effect" kind of game where the desires, opinions, and actions of every single AI driven person on the island effect the way things work, the chaos is controlled where it needs to be. For example, I haven't run into a situation where a ship misses a shipment because all the dockworkers were off at the tavern (a frustration in previous games). All buildings now also have an "effectiveness" rating, which acts as an easily understood percentage of how well a building does what it's supposed to do (a plantation with 100 effectiveness produces 100% of its crops, maximizing its budget gives +20 efficiency, whereas missing part of the workforce drastically lowers it). All buildings also fit together in a cleaner way than they did before (many are smaller), and things like the placement of a plantation's crop field is infinitely easier to work with. There are also two brand new features that make the economy more controllable, one being the addition of "managers" who are people with specific skills that you can assign to have special effects on individual buildings, and the other being a revamped trading system where, in addition to the traditional system of trade ships showing up at your docks and buying all your excess products, you can sign deals with foreign powers and send your own ships to them to get better deals on your goods, which both encourages specialization in your city and adds an extra twist to global politics.
The last, but least exciting addition is the idea of El Presidente's dynasty. In previous games, you had much greater control over the personality of your ruler, as well as his strengths and weaknesses. Instead, this concept is stretched out over multiple members of one ruling family who bundles their bonuses together. You gain new family members and increase their ranks through stashed away "Swiss Bank Account" money that you earn while playing (an interesting way to use the stolen money concept from previous games). Only one member of your family can be El Presidente at any given time, but the others can be deployed as managers in your city, or used in certain storyline-based events. It's an interesting system and it works well enough, but I can't help but think it didn't turn out quite the way it was supposed to. Ultimately, it ends up feeling less like a system of family and lineage, and more like a team of immortal El Presidentes for you to accumulate for their individual bonus effects. Fortunately, nothing about this system gets in the way of the game from anything other than an immersion standpoint.
((NOTE! - I cut out a portion of this review so it would fit on Steam's review system. My apologies for being so long-winded! This portion of the review can be read here
))
Overall, Tropico 5 is a very pleasant surprise. It's similar enough to earn criticism from some, but for those who felt the formula was strong and just needed some refining, the refinements are well worthy of a new game. It does fall short of perfect for some of the same reasons that previous Tropico games have, such as the lack of good explanations of some of the game's deeper concepts, its refusal to open the game up to any kind of modding, as well as clear signs that they plan to do a lackluster and exploitative DLC system similar to Tropico 4. But, for me, slipping into El Presidente's shoes may just feel better than it ever did before.

Only Tropico game that I've seriously disliked in the series.
Tropico 5 fails by effectively being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ stripped-down iOS-tier ghost of it's predecessors.  Important gameplay and ui features are cut away, while the UI becomes more bloated and inefficient.  Familiar concepts that set the series apart from other city-builder sims -- like being able to customize your presidential faults and qualities, which makes the game more dynamic, gives the player a wide range of gameplay styles, additional challenges and creates greater replay value -- have been removed or cut down to a micron of thier former strength.
The new concepts that are introduced (like FoW) are inconsistent with the genre, hindering that intrinsic creative value of city building.  The islands tend to be much smaller (in both campaign and sandbox) compared to the rest of the series.  The scale of buildings tend to feel bloated and awkward with few effective placeable locations.  Many of the 'new' elements are just disappointing replacements for previous staples, like cocoa being introduced but papayas being removed.  Dammit, I loved papayas...
In addition to the cumulative restrictive effect of these changes, the game tends to play carrot-and-a-stick with what little choice you have left.  The campaign (and even sandbox mode) essentially constantly micro-manages the player, which is an unpleasant if not ironic twist on gaming.  At times this is mandatory and oppressive, others it's simply and option one can choose to ignore -- however there is no benefit to attempting to do things your own way.  The player is basically caged in and asked to perform specific meanial tricks.
The UX is terrible and easily the worst-in-series.  I honestly felt that the Tropico 2 interface was cleaner, more usable and more efficient.  The Pop up build menu, which is ugly, bulky, and poorly laid out, interferes with with your world viewport inevitably blocking whatever it is you were trying to work on.  The overall design seems to be trying to accommodate touch interfaces, which in traditional iOS fashion means that your have to sacrifice detail and control for huge UI elements.  We've lost 2 degrees of speed control in Tropico 5.  The Overlay's have been turned into the ♥♥♥♥ing ugliest rainbow wire-grid that I've ever seen -- It's almost completely unusable.  The PiP viewport becomes annoying after 30 minutes, and takes up too much screen space as a non-interactive element.
All of the ui changes leave the player with less control and a more cluttered screen.  Useful elements like faction leader notices have been removed, as well as monthly/annual reports (like starvation and deaths from poor healthcare).  Mind you the game still internally wants you to build a new church, or improve healthcare, but you will be left in the dark to guess as to what the social problems are.
3/10.  Do not buy.

There is nothing quite like finding yourself in the middle of the wilderness on a snowy mountain pass with just the clothes on your back. I always like to think that I would be pretty decent in a wilderness survival situation because of my long background as an Eagle Scout and various outdoorsman skills. However, this game is just so great at pointing out at how laughable that feeling is.
Of all the survival games that I have played, this one takes the cake. I can honestly admit that I am constantly paranoid and scared while playing this; not because there are monsters or serial killers hunting you, but because just being out in the black of night while being snowblind is a feeling that I never want to experience irl. Also, there kind of are monsters. F***ing wolves.
At one point I was freezing and lost, when that was fixed I was being chased by wolves. Another playthrough I was freezing and hungry, I fixed the freezing by building a fire and found a deer being chased by wolves. Naturally, I waited for the deer to get cornered and killed, immediately chasing off the wolf with a flare. I died while harvesting the meat because I froze to death. This game is so amazing, but you have to be really careful about managing time more than managing your stats.
Time is the killer, not the wilderness.
Pros:
-Easy to learn mechanics
-Artistic landscapes
-Maintains interest due to actual challenge
-Plenty of opportunity to succeed
-Can only get better
-Music is beautiful
Cons:
-The video game logic can be limiting, mostly in the sense that you cannot build a campfire while indoors
Tips:
-Manage your time wisely, there are only so many hours of daylight available and travel alone can be what ends you
-You can rely on wolves to do the hunting for you; just make sure that you have a way to drive them off afterward
-Fire can hurt you. I know that sounds obvious, but jeez it can really f*** you up
-You can breakdown chairs, wooden crates, and cardboard boxes without tools to use as firebuilding supplies
-Check underneath shelves; I once found a bottle of antibiotics underneath that I could have easily missed (which I did and only discovered by chance)
-Tools are sometimes right in front of you; Keep your eyes to the ground (I found a hunting knife in the middle of the floor at the hydroelectric dam after finding a decent light source)
-Talk to yourself; probably not an actual tip, but it helped me to stay entertained and I've done it before to keep my spirits up when I got lost in the woods in real life
-The game is randomly generated. I walked into a warehouse that I thought I knew pretty well and instead got mauled by a guard dog. I did not even know that there were attack dogs
I definitely got what I expected from this game. There was certainly not a diamond-in-the-rough realization with this game. The best part was that it can be 100% in 2 hours.

This is my story of an experience which happened later on in the game, a few parts are fictional to provide more immersion.
One cold day I was traveling to a place known as the Desolation Point, the wind was howling and wolfs where strafing through the cold wasteland.
I heard about this place called Hibernia which was some kind of wale processing facility before the geomagnetic storm happened, I thought it might be worth a visit, maybe I would find some tools there, a saw would come in handy...
As I was making my way to Hibernia I saw a bunch of wolves and even a bear guarding it, maybe the smell of the wale meat was still hanging around. I really wanted to get to this place, I only had one bullet left and I had the feeling chances are of finding some more in this abandoned factory. As I came closer and started to walk slowly across the frozen sea, trying to make as little noises as possible, the wind turned and carried my scent towards the wolves. I pulled my gun off my back and as soon as I had my finger on the trigger I already heard paws and claws on the ice behind me, I turned around and looked the wolf right in the eyes, it was baring its teeth and growling. I slowly started walking backwards, the muzzle of the gun pointing towards the wolf but it did not seem that it wanted to attack me and my pulse started to normalize, but suddenly I ran into something, the chicken wire fence surrounding this place got me caught. More wolves where approaching in the distance and I had to make a decision, do I run towards and past the wolves or do I use my last bullet... The sound of a gunshot is incredible loud if you haven't heard any cars or planes for a few weeks, it made all the other wolves flee, perfect as I needed to gut the wolf because a man has to eat if he wants to survive in this cold hell. It took me almost two hours to skin this poor thing, I didn't want to shoot it, but it was hungry and it was either him or me...
My heart just stopped when I heard the breathing of something really big behind me, a big black bear stood not even 5 meters from me, I did not hear him coming because I was so busy pulling the pelt off this wolf, the smell of blood must've caught the bears attention. I slowly stood up, a mistake, the bear made a jump and his paws threw me to the ground, I was feeling his steamy breath in my face and I passed out...
Was it the 350kg of pressure on my lungs, the pain of the bear digging his teeth into my shoulder or the fear which made me pass out? I don't know. But as I woke up It took me a few seconds to remember what just happened, I had pain everywhere and my vision was blurred, I looked around and saw my attacker who was just a few meters away feeding on the corpse of the wolf, I was lucky he liked that better then me.
I dragged my body a few meters away as the bear noticed me and stopped eating and turned around and started walking towards me, with shaky hands I pulled out a flare and light it up. That was the best thing I could have done, the bear stopped and was afraid to come any closer.

I barely made it into the factory and blood is pouring out of my shoulder, luckily I've found this bottle of antiseptic which burns like crazy but at least my wounds wont get infected.
I can barely see anything because of the pain and its also very dark in here, it looks like a mattress is laying in that corner, time to rest a bit...
The few pieces wolf meat I was able to grab before the bear surprised me will be very useful to keep my stomach filled for a few days while I recover from my wounds.

I was quite skeptical when The Long Dark popped up in my queue so I checked the ratings and was impressed enough to make the plunge and have never regretted it. The Long Dark plops you down in a wilderness and immediately and brutally shows you how ill prepared you are for a life of survival in the bitter cold of the Arctic. With each death, however, you begin to understand how to survive starvation, dehydration, bone chilling cold, predation and your own stupidity.
There is no save, get killed, reload and try again mechanism. You die and you are dead, period, try again from scratch. It can be frustrating to pile up two months of survival to see it all wasted because you got cocky and attacked that lone wolf, only find out it wasn't alone, or to venture out with little food, water, no bedroll only to be caught in a blizzard and freeze to death. Death in this game is as final as death in the real-life Arctic.
It's on sale this Halloween so do yourself a favor and make the plunge.

When The Beginner’s Guide came out last year, I was intrigued by it. The trailer for it was odd and the connection to The Stanley Parable was intriguing. So, I gave it a go recently and I’ve got some thoughts about it.
TBG is a first person narrative video game in a genre that’s often described as a walking simulator. It’s about a player experiencing the narrative the developer wishes to share with minimal interactions. In this case, it’s mostly pressing switches, responding to a very basic conversation system and looking/walking around. It’s a pretty passive experience for an hour and half but there’s enough to keep the player invested.
The Beginner’s Guide’s narrative is about Davey Wreden showing off the many small games of an unknown developer called Coda.
but I did wonder for a second in the initial opening. I mean, it wouldn’t be the first time that indie creators came together on a game. But alas, this is a fictional tale. Davey is doing all of this because Coda quit developing games a while ago. So, Davey is showing the Internet these games and his perspectives about them in a bid to get Coda developing again. As Davey narrates, he talks about how he sees Coda through these small little games. That he thinks they give him an insight to who and what Coda is. However, as the game goes along, I start to get a disturbing sense of where this might be going. This was confirmed at a certain point. Davey talks about how he shared these once private works with others because he thought Coda was depressed and needed help to keep going. That Coda needed validation to pick them up again. As someone who is an introvert, I had a feeling that he had gone too far. Coda confirms my suspicions by breaking all contact with him after giving him a final game to play. In it, Coda states very clearly that Davey has a problem, a need to validate himself through Coda’s works and that Davey had taken things way too far by sharing it with others. That he is under the mistaken impression that he knows Coda through his games. Even worse, he had told others that Coda was depressed because of what he interpreted from a couple of games and had changed them through his own edits because he was unhappy with how the games played out. Even though it was distorting Coda’s work. However, it was a problem Davey must work through, not Coda. While all the time, Davey has been changing the work to suit himself and perhaps shows his own failings while doing so.
Upon finishing the game, I had quite a bit to ponder over. About my role in sharing other individuals’ work and how I review videogames. That maybe I do this entirely for my own selfish reasons of needing validation. Maybe a small part of me does, but it’s not the guiding force. However, I do think the more cynical interpretation that I’ve seen from others, of what is presented in TBG, is perhaps missing the point it's trying to make. It’s hard to say for certain, of course, but I do think the developer is trying to get the point across….see, it really is that easy to trip up and make the same mistakes Davey makes in the game. I think that this is a game best left up to your interpretation. What the dev may or may not have intended is for him to know. What I can say that I got from TBG is a cautionary tale. That pretending to know someone just based off of their works is dangerous. However, if the point trying to be made is a cynical one about reviewers and how they harm devs or profit off of them, I have one thing to say to that. That I’m in this to share videogames that are worth experiencing I am merely here to talk about and critique what I see as both good and bad ideas in said title. I like to think that what I’m doing is more of a net positive for the developer than myself. But, that’s how I view things. I’m sure some would disagree.
Running off of the Source engine, TBG has all of the expected video, audio and miscellaneous settings that are usually included. Honestly, this game is so short that it’s not really worth listing them all out for you. But if you’ve run a source game like Portal 2 before, then that’s what you can expect to find here. It has good performance and isn’t that demanding to run. I didn’t experience any bugs or issues to report.
Summing everything up, The Beginner’s Guide had given me something to ponder. This collection of short games narrated by a man who may have obsession and personal issues to work through is a different experience. It may be a little bit more cynical of reviewers if one particular interpretation of events holds true or it may just be a disturbing look into Davey’s mentality and personality. Either way, it’s a game that requires a pause to consider the implications of not just other’s actions but our own. And perhaps, that we shouldn’t so quickly judge that we know someone based on their works. The game runs well for it’s 1.5 hour runtime and is really only worth playing the one time. But what an thought provoking time that one playthrough is.

Immortal Redneck is a curious beast. Behind a name that certainly evokes thoughts of shovelware or joke game one can find a pastiche of the best elements in otherwise disparate games and makes them work surprisingly well despite not bringing anything new to the table in and of itself.
First, let's start with a pleasing presentation, with cartoonish graphics and enemies (sorta reminds me of Paladins), wherein the player needs to carve his way through a myriad of procedurally generated rooms, through mainly ranged combat. It is heavily reminiscent of Ziggurat in that sense, although the levels are, in my opinion better designed since they are more vertical, it relies less on melee enemies bumrushing the player, and the weapons make the combat more fast paced and, thanks to the ability to carry 3 to 4 weapons at the same time and the abundant drops the player will find room after room, more varied and tactical. The game is structured in three pyramids with 7 floors in each, the first ones being larger and as such having potentially more stuff than the latter ones, with a miniboss and a boss on each pyramid.
On the sound side the music is a nice mixture of guitars and banjos and drums mixed with what we could call "Egypt themed movie musical score", and the protagonist easily stands out, commenting on many of the enemies and weapons with quips that make him pretty fun and likeable.
There are several unlockable classes to the player's disposal, and each comes with a fixed loadout of weapons, a passive skill, and an active skill one can cast at no cost after a brief cooldown, some offensive and some defensive although imo of varying degrees of utility. On top of that there's the scrolls, which can contain power ups or power downs, some incredibly useful and some monumentally annoying. They are a point of contention along most reviews of the game, but overall they push the player to make the best of a given situation, and some of the good ones will cancel some of the bad ones so having a bad streak doesn't mean immediate death. But even if it was it's okay, because you're sort of meant to die anyway.
IR features a progressive skill tree one unlocks through the money they have accrued in past runs, very similar to Rogue Legacy's, where the player will gain access to perks as well as new classes, complemented by a shop that, while not as extensive as RL's, will allow him to further purchase starter scrolls and medallions.
What really makes Immortal Redneck a treat to play though, is a polished to a shine movement system, very reminiscent of the FPS games of yesteryear (or Doom '16), that will allow the player to zoom around the environment, ledge grabbing, double jumping and making the most out of every gun at their disposal, and their environments.
There's a few negatives about it, though. I found the classes rather unbalanced and generic since most if not all of them use perks that can be gained through scrolls, and some feel much more effective than others. The game is also rather short and a bit repetitive, and it's not something one will dump hundreds of hours into unless they just play for the hell of it, because the pyramids themselves are on the easy side most of the time.
Overall, I guess one could call IR a derivative game, but it's an example of why that term isn't necessarily bad. Albeit very few things about it are original, the game plays great, stays entertaining death after death and it's safe to assume one will easily get 15-20 hours out of it, easy, and every one of those hours will be thoroughly enjoyable. 8/10.

In short, Immortal Redneck is like the love child of Serious Sam and Rogue Legacy and I whole heartedly recommend it.
At it's heart is a first person shooter where everything is fast, fluid, and all around just feels great.  On top of that is the rogue-lite randomized levels, changing loadouts and collection of money to buy persistent upgrades after you die.
There are several gods to unlock to play as, which determines your starting loadout and skills for any run.  There is also a fun variety of weapons to pick up as you explore, as well as tons of scrolls that give you neat bonuses (and occasionally handicaps).  It all works together very well, and keeps each run fresh enough that you want to go back for more.
There are also small systems like every time you don't choose a god for your next run they get a small boost to attack, defense or hit points.  Over time that means you are gently prodded to try out the ones you were less fond of, and in turn end up realizing that they have their own perks once you learn to play them.  It's a great system that doesn't beat you over the head but encourages exploring the breadth of content as a nice bonus.
From the trailers I was worried that the overbearing redneck comments were trying way too hard and would quickly annoy me and turn me off.  Thankfully they are relatively sparse and if you really get sick of them you can turn them off separately.
As of the 1.2 update the weapons are even more satisfying to shoot, enemies respond more physically to getting shot, sounds are better, and several systems were tweaked or expanded.  It goes to show how responsive and dedicated the developers are to listen to the community and commit to further development to enhance the game in big ways post launch.
Run fast, shoot often, and support these guys if it sounds interesting at all.

I give Tropico 5 4.5 pairs of fancy El Presidente Brand Sunglasses out of 5. The other one got broke when El Presidente single handedly broke the noses of the Premier of the USSR and President of the USA with a swing of his beard.
Seriously, this game gets a 4.5 out of 5. Another of the great series of city-building dictator sims that made me fall in love with city-building sims again in the first place and have a personality that makes it so few people can turn away after beginning to play with them, it delivers much of what it promises, but there's tarantulas in those crates of bananas.
The first and foremost is that the voice acting has degraded, and things are less funny, than its predecessor Tropico 4. The storyline shares some mirrors to that game, ultimately, but is enjoyable despite this fact. The addition of tech research and a static continual build of your islands throughout the campaign (Which is something I greatly greatly missed in the Tropico 4 game, wishing it existed) provides a cohesive story and more believability, while keeping things humorous. Add in options like crafting your nation's constitution and it has plenty of playability, eve if your fun per minute might be lessened and ther's less commentary about your actions.
Sandbox mode remains solid, especially with the addition of a random generator for islands.
The multiplayer is a GREAT GREAT GREAT addition to the game, but that crate of bananas has a tarantula in it, too. What is that, you say? There is absolutely no save mode at all in it. So if you and your friends play 2 hours playing a multiplayer game? YOu'd better finish it because you won't be able to come back to it, you either have to devote a large chunk of time to it or play on small maps, in the end.
Finally, there are plenty of bugs and glitches, even now, including things like the menu stuttering (at least 30 people including myself had this problem, which was because an intromovie playing in the background had horrible frame rate issues) but there are easy enough fixes of these until official fixes from Kalypso come forward.
Over all? The game is a solid addition to the genre and the Tropico family. IT could have sailed higher, and it might still with DLC, but it's already far more enjoyable and far more playable for computers with lesser capabilities than its competitors in the city building genre, especially with very real trade, invasion, and competitive options in the multiplayer making an already deep game deeper.

Sickness and starvation can kill you as fast as the zombies. Well, maybe not as fast, but just as surely.
The world is huge and fun to explore and I genuinely was afraid to leave the safety of my house at the beginning and still feel a sense of dread everytime I'm opening a door.
It's still work in progress, so expect a lot of bugs and such other light annoyances (I couldn't get the bloody thing working at first and don't even dare get me started on those thrice-damned house alarms), but it already is a great game for those who like to survive the apocalypse as a mere human and not a demigod-like soldier.

I can honestly say that this game is one of my top 3 survival games I have ever played.
The atmosphere and the environment is amazing. The different weather conditions and the fact that the weather sometimes is so bad that you have to sit inside for literally an real-time hour and do nothing in-game is so realistic.
Haven't experienced any glitches and the updates that the developers have done have made the game even better and  more realistic than when I first started playing.
Pros:
+ You can choose the difficulty. If you want the exploration part more than the hardcore survival, you can choose that the wildlife will not attack unless provoked. Instead they will run away when you approach them.
+ Controls are great and everything goes smooth.
+ Crafting and repairing interface is easy to understand.
+ The open world is really big and you have to prepare real good before heading out for exploration which makes it even more exciting. (I needed to play for 14 in-game days to gather materials and food and make my gear to be ready for this)
+ If you die, you die. No saves. You have to start all over. Which also makes you more careful and tactical about how you approach things.
Cons:
- Weather can sometimes be bad for a longer time and there is nothing to do about it except just sit and wait. I'm waiting (hoping) for an update with books to read or something else you can do in cabins that will make it less boring.
- No map. You totally have to rely on your memory, where you have been and where you came from. I don't think this game should have a map beacause I personally like the challenge but they could at least give you a compass.
If you, like me, love survival and are looking for a good game this is it. It's totally worth the money.
Right now there is only sandbox mode but there will be a story mode soon.

This is an update of my previous review of The Long Dark.
I highly recommended it in my first review, and continue to do so now.
I'm old enough that I was a kid when the first gaming consoles were first hitting the market (Atari, Intellivision, etc.), and I've been playing games since then.  When PC games were just getting started, I got sucked into those as well.
There have been a lot of really good games over the years.  Some of those early ones (think:  Zelda) are still famous today.
For me, The Long Dark falls into that category of "historic" games.  Not because it's old, but simply because it's just that good and just that enjoyable.
It is, however, a single player survival game.  So if you're looking to run around on a multi-player map shooting, stabbing, and lauching grenades and friends and enemies with equal ease, well, this certainly ain't that, as I've yet to even find a grenade, let alone a friend!
But if you like survival games - just you versus whatever nature can throw at ya - well, here ya go!
There are no flesh eating zombies here, but the wolves and bears seem to be quite happy to play the bad guy.
I've been playing The Long Dark off and on since it first came to Steam Early Access.  Since then the Dev's have slowly and consistently been tweaking gameplay, fixing bugs, and adding content/maps.  They have an overall development roadmap that they're behind the power curve on, but they are and have been consistently and continuously pushing forward.  Updates are pushed through often, and they're incredibly good about communicating with the players - and that communication is a two way street with them.  They listen to player feedback and also communicate what they're working on and what their expected timeframes are.
As for the game itself, well, it is WELL worth the current $10 to check it out yourself.
But if you just have to have an idea of what you're getting yourself into, here's some tidbits for you:
- There are a variety of difficulty levels.  The easiest is quite easy.  The hardest - well, most players won't survive very long.
- Death is permanent and ends the playthrough.
- There are only a few games that I've ever played that I continually come back to time and again after taking a break from gaming.
- There IS a relatively steep learning curve where survival is concerned, but not so much where game mechanics are concerned.  The weather is your biggest adversary in this game, as it limits your ability to harvest food and water.
- I love the graphics.  They're not what I would consider HD, but the artwork is amazing.  Go outside on a clear night and look up.  It's really spectacularly beautiful!
- There are currently 8 different connected maps/zones.  Each map/zone has the potential for dozens upon dozens of hours of interactive/exploration gameplay, all while trying to avoid becoming a meal for local predators.
Of all of the games I've ever played, The Long Dark easily makes my list of top 10, and in reality it's probably in my top 2 or 3.
If you can afford it, plunk down the current $10 (it's 1/2 off right now) and find out for yourself if you like it.  The thousands of positve reviews certainly should tell you there is some survival gaming goodness inside!

I have nothing but positive things to say about this game.
I've played it off and on since it arrived on Steam.
The Dev's are incredibly active with the game and are regularly fixing bugs and/or adding content.  They commuicate regularly and are very accessible through both the Steam and Hinterland forums for help, questions, bug reports, etc.  They are also very receptive to gameplay feedback as they are always seeking to improve gameplay.
As for the game itself, it's simply excellent.  It's challenging and VERY replayable.  Once a player gets the learning/playing curve down, survival is not horribly difficult... as long as you don't make any mistakes.  And mistakes can be costly, sometimes resulting in death.  Death is permanent and ends the play through, which simply adds to the challenge because developing character resources that allow more in game freedom (from the weather) takes a lot of time.
The player is on a constant hunt for survival resources, which includes food, water, clothing while being on the lookout for predators such as wolves (quite common) and bears (fairly rare).  Depending on the game difficulty level chosen, play through goes from relatively easy to incredibly difficult.
The game graphics are not high end/high definition, but are quite nice, and a starry night sky in this game is phenomenally beautiful.
If survival challenge games are your thing, then I highly recommend this game.

There is nothing quite like finding yourself in the middle of the wilderness on a snowy mountain pass with just the clothes on your back. I always like to think that I would be pretty decent in a wilderness survival situation because of my long background as an Eagle Scout and various outdoorsman skills. However, this game is just so great at pointing out at how laughable that feeling is.
Of all the survival games that I have played, this one takes the cake. I can honestly admit that I am constantly paranoid and scared while playing this; not because there are monsters or serial killers hunting you, but because just being out in the black of night while being snowblind is a feeling that I never want to experience irl. Also, there kind of are monsters. F***ing wolves.
At one point I was freezing and lost, when that was fixed I was being chased by wolves. Another playthrough I was freezing and hungry, I fixed the freezing by building a fire and found a deer being chased by wolves. Naturally, I waited for the deer to get cornered and killed, immediately chasing off the wolf with a flare. I died while harvesting the meat because I froze to death. This game is so amazing, but you have to be really careful about managing time more than managing your stats.
Time is the killer, not the wilderness.
Pros:
-Easy to learn mechanics
-Artistic landscapes
-Maintains interest due to actual challenge
-Plenty of opportunity to succeed
-Can only get better
-Music is beautiful
Cons:
-The video game logic can be limiting, mostly in the sense that you cannot build a campfire while indoors
Tips:
-Manage your time wisely, there are only so many hours of daylight available and travel alone can be what ends you
-You can rely on wolves to do the hunting for you; just make sure that you have a way to drive them off afterward
-Fire can hurt you. I know that sounds obvious, but jeez it can really f*** you up
-You can breakdown chairs, wooden crates, and cardboard boxes without tools to use as firebuilding supplies
-Check underneath shelves; I once found a bottle of antibiotics underneath that I could have easily missed (which I did and only discovered by chance)
-Tools are sometimes right in front of you; Keep your eyes to the ground (I found a hunting knife in the middle of the floor at the hydroelectric dam after finding a decent light source)
-Talk to yourself; probably not an actual tip, but it helped me to stay entertained and I've done it before to keep my spirits up when I got lost in the woods in real life
-The game is randomly generated. I walked into a warehouse that I thought I knew pretty well and instead got mauled by a guard dog. I did not even know that there were attack dogs

It's possible that Sunless Sea could've been a very good "choose your own adventure" game in the style of 80 Days, but as it stands now, I struggle to think of a game in recent memory that I enjoyed less than Sunless Sea.

Sunless Sea has a beautiful gothic style and setting not often seen in games today. It's one that begs to be explored, and is the primary impetus of the game. Unfortunately, you can only do so very slowly, and if you die, you're going to start almost from nothing. You need a lot of money to explore the world, but the game right out says that the most obvious method of making money (running goods to ports) isn't profitable. You instead need to sell information, or ship unusual cargo, things that can only be found by exploring.
The story is the game's primary draw. Deep and dark, there's a fantastic amount of material. I almost feel it would be better told as an old school text based RPG (with art, this game's art is amazing). Do away with the resource management, and you could really plunge into the game's lore; this could very easily have been a game the people obsess over. But 75% of the game is money running, which is a realy tragedy.
That all said, do buy the game if you like a good story. One upside of the slow pace: it's a very peaceful game. Don't have many of those in my library, and it's nice to play something quiet every once in a while.
It's the perfect game to unwind with. Relaxing music and control over glowing lights. I imagine it'd be interesting to play whilst high.

You should watch the trailer for this game twice - once before and once after you've played it. Trust me - it's like watching two different trailers. And even if it doesn't work in your case than at least you've played the game and hopefully enjoyed it for what it was. So, is the game worth giving it a go in the first place? If you're a gamer who likes narrative-driven games the answer is: yes, yes it is. But if you're a designer, writer, artist, creator of some sort, and especially if you make video games, than this is one game you just can't miss out on, but not for the reasons you think of right now! Trust me.
***Rant about negative reviews incoming (minor spoilers). If you haven't played the game or simply don't care about me ranting just skip to the last paragraph***
I find it funny how people giving this game a negative review write 10-paragraph essays analyzing what the author intended to convey and pointing out where he failed to deliver on those intentions. Where they berate him for creating an "emotional confessional" and then trying to charge money for it. Where they accuse the game of being too disconnected, or too personal, too deep, or too shallow, or too confusing, or too simplistic, that you have to play The Stanley Parable to understand it, or that it has nothing to do with The Stanley Parable, that there's a clear message, or that there's no message at all. No joke, the most negative reviews are also the longest ones here, like the authors of those reviews are compelled to apologize for playing, to explain their motivations behind not jumping on the hype train, to express that they feel like they are the ones who have failed somehow... If you've already played the game you know where I'm going with this. Maybe they should write Davey Wreden an email. After all, he clearly stated his email address in the game.
But ok, let us not be the outcasts here - left out of the loop of people who have something substantial to say about this game. Let us try and do an analysis of the plot right here and now. In fact, let us one-up everyone and go extra-meta on this one: let us try and extrapolate the narrative portrayed in this game into the real world, Inception-style, and what we get is...
MASSIVE SPOILERS INCOMING!!! OMG!!! IF YOU HAVEN'T PLAYED IT DON'T READ ANY FURTHER THAN THAT VERY SENTENCE!!!
I WARNED YOU!
Seriously.
What we get is the realization that this game is... just a game. It's a piece of interactive media with a well defined narrative attached to it for dramatic purposes, and it relies on immersion to build an enjoyable experience for the player. This is why Davey Wreden opted to reveal his name and email address in the game. This is why he build this emotional attachment to Coda. Remember, this is Davey Wreden we're talking about here - the man who's sole purpose in life is to dissect a piece of narrative and turn it on its head in order to entertain you, to catch you off guard. The Davey Wreden in the game is not the same Davey Wreden who wrote the game. Coda isn't real. None of it is supposed to mean anything, beyond that what you make of it, and whether it provided 1.5 hours of entertainment for you. And even if that's your argument against it - that Davey doesn't do a very good job at immersing you in the narrative, than fair point - maybe you just weren't feeling it. We will just have to agree to disagree. But trying to analyze the game based on your assumptions of what is or what isn't real, how Davey felt or didn't feel when making this game, and whether he has or hasn't the ability or even the right to convey a hidden personal message of some sort, and then making a judgment call in a review based on that analysis is not only futile, it's... exactly what the game is about in the first place. The death of the author. Don't get me wrong, everyone has an opinion and some people even have interpretations (including me), and there's nothing wrong with that, but as soon as you make a judgment call on something that may or may not be there, you're digging your own hole to fall into and you're dragging others with you. Now, go watch the trailer again, but instead of Davey's voice, try and hear your own voice in your head.
***Rant finished. Closing thoughts follow***
So, does this game "do it for me"? Yes! I felt immersed and emotional while I played it and afterwards it got me thinking about some things for a while, specifically, how Davey can think out of the box in order to build this fantastic narrative, this illusion that leaves a lasting impression. To me, he's already looking to be one of the most influential writers/artists/creators of our generation. One who will be discussed in art and media schools for years to come. It's perhaps too early to call him the Quentin Tarantino of video games, but keep an eye on this guy because he's sure a hell headed in the right direction! Just google "Pleasurable You". Or maybe don't - I kinda feel bad for writing this now.

Auditorium is one of the best chill out games. It's a puzzler that can tax you intellectually, but still manage to feel fair and grounded in a consistent set of rules.
Ever played Orbient? It's a game in Nintendo's Art Style series, featuring gameplay that revolves around(excuse the pun) planetary orbits and gravity wells, singularities and the resulting trajectories of moving from one gravitational influence to another.
Auditorium quickly becomes the cousin to Orbient; At its best, ontrolling the path of the flowing lines across the screen becomes an entrancing kind of interstellar dance, with objects that attract or repel the flowing trajectories of sound. You create your own little solar system of music. Those moments? Sublime.

Pros:
- Incredible story that sticks with you forever and continues to make you think long after the game is over. Seriously, this is a standout even compared with books and movies.
- A thinking man's game. Knowing a little about Ayn Rand's Objectivism and libertarianism in general helps, but it's not necessary.
- Weapons have enough variety for me, and plasmids have lots of variety.
- You get to shoot lightning. Every game should have this.
- Enemies are reasonably diverse, and all seem pretty scary until you find out that *you* are a pretty scary guy too.
- Graphics are good, and art style keeps the game from feeling dated.
- Incredible aura and feel about the environment/sounds. It really draws you in.
- You feel completely alone. Even with your allies on the radio, you are alone in Rapture. Never played a game quite like that (though this is the first game I ever bought).
- Some of the best moments in storytelling ever are in this game, and I speak as a guy who as read thousands upon thousands of books.
Cons:
- Final boss is kind of easy, but not a big deal, I guess. Thematically, it's even justifiable.
- Like in Halo, you won't be aiming down the sight much. This is my one complaint about the combat.
- Good/evil dynamic could have been improved. Still, I liked how you got the choice whether or not to save the Little Sisters (I saved them all.)
Seriously though, buy this game. It's fun, dark, sometimes frightening, and has an amazing story and feel about I can only compare to the book Return of the King, the third volume in the Lord of the Rings. Rapture truly is Mordor.

Runespell: Overture is a near perfect marraige (or lovechild?) of Puzzle Quest and Poker (or Mythical Poker as the game calls it). It's a turned based RPG played with poker cards, where you must combine five cards in poker rules (pairs, royal flush, straights, etc) to attack. Performing attacks or getting attack builds rage points which are used for powercards that do damage, provide more turns, or cause personal buffs or enemy debuffs. It may sound confusing at first, but it's pretty simple after the game explains it to you, and it makes for a fun and interesting RPG, Single-player only, game+, 10-15hrs of gameplay (I finished in 12). I got it part of a bundle, but it's worth full price, especially if you like the Puzzle Quest series.

This is my story of an experience which happened later on in the game, a few parts are fictional to provide more immersion.
One cold day I was traveling to a place known as the Desolation Point, the wind was howling and wolfs where strafing through the cold wasteland.
I heard about this place called Hibernia which was some kind of wale processing facility before the geomagnetic storm happened, I thought it might be worth a visit, maybe I would find some tools there, a saw would come in handy...
As I was making my way to Hibernia I saw a bunch of wolves and even a bear guarding it, maybe the smell of the wale meat was still hanging around. I really wanted to get to this place, I only had one bullet left and I had the feeling chances are of finding some more in this abandoned factory. As I came closer and started to walk slowly across the frozen sea, trying to make as little noises as possible, the wind turned and carried my scent towards the wolves. I pulled my gun off my back and as soon as I had my finger on the trigger I already heard paws and claws on the ice behind me, I turned around and looked the wolf right in the eyes, it was baring its teeth and growling. I slowly started walking backwards, the muzzle of the gun pointing towards the wolf but it did not seem that it wanted to attack me and my pulse started to normalize, but suddenly I ran into something, the chicken wire fence surrounding this place got me caught. More wolves where approaching in the distance and I had to make a decision, do I run towards and past the wolves or do I use my last bullet... The sound of a gunshot is incredible loud if you haven't heard any cars or planes for a few weeks, it made all the other wolves flee, perfect as I needed to gut the wolf because a man has to eat if he wants to survive in this cold hell. It took me almost two hours to skin this poor thing, I didn't want to shoot it, but it was hungry and it was either him or me...
My heart just stopped when I heard the breathing of something really big behind me, a big black bear stood not even 5 meters from me, I did not hear him coming because I was so busy pulling the pelt off this wolf, the smell of blood must've caught the bears attention. I slowly stood up, a mistake, the bear made a jump and his paws threw me to the ground, I was feeling his steamy breath in my face and I passed out...
Was it the 350kg of pressure on my lungs, the pain of the bear digging his teeth into my shoulder or the fear which made me pass out? I don't know. But as I woke up It took me a few seconds to remember what just happened, I had pain everywhere and my vision was blurred, I looked around and saw my attacker who was just a few meters away feeding on the corpse of the wolf, I was lucky he liked that better then me.
I dragged my body a few meters away as the bear noticed me and stopped eating and turned around and started walking towards me, with shaky hands I pulled out a flare and light it up. That was the best thing I could have done, the bear stopped and was afraid to come any closer.

I barely made it into the factory and blood is pouring out of my shoulder, luckily I've found this bottle of antiseptic which burns like crazy but at least my wounds wont get infected.
I can barely see anything because of the pain and its also very dark in here, it looks like a mattress is laying in that corner, time to rest a bit...
The few pieces wolf meat I was able to grab before the bear surprised me will be very useful to keep my stomach filled for a few days while I recover from my wounds.

I was quite skeptical when The Long Dark popped up in my queue so I checked the ratings and was impressed enough to make the plunge and have never regretted it. The Long Dark plops you down in a wilderness and immediately and brutally shows you how ill prepared you are for a life of survival in the bitter cold of the Arctic. With each death, however, you begin to understand how to survive starvation, dehydration, bone chilling cold, predation and your own stupidity.
There is no save, get killed, reload and try again mechanism. You die and you are dead, period, try again from scratch. It can be frustrating to pile up two months of survival to see it all wasted because you got cocky and attacked that lone wolf, only find out it wasn't alone, or to venture out with little food, water, no bedroll only to be caught in a blizzard and freeze to death. Death in this game is as final as death in the real-life Arctic.
It's on sale this Halloween so do yourself a favor and make the plunge.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a point and click horror/suspense game. There's a bit of a story, and more of a hidden one if you care to look into it. All you need to know is that you're stuck in the security room of a kid-friendly restaurant at night, the animatronic animal mascots of the place are roaming around, and if they find you... you're dead. So you have a few ways to keep them out in order to keep your security job... and yout life. You can hover the mouse over the button on the bottom of the screen to bring up the cameras. You can look through the different ones by clicking on them in order to track the current positions of the roaming robots. If you think one is nearby, you can get out of that camera mode and check the doors on the left and right of you. Think one is in the hall? Hit the light button to turn it on and see. Want to look at the camera again but don't want to risk them getting in? Hit the door button to close it tight. So what's the catch? Everything you do uses power. There's a constant power drain. While look at the cameras, keep a light on, or keep a security door shut, it drains additional power. This is where the strategy of the game comes in.
You have to manage your power, your safety, and your sanity. The different mascots also have their own tactics. One will come in and kill you, one will disable a door and kill you if you use your camera again, one will come in without much warning, and one will try to physically run in if you don't put the camera on them enough. I may have that a bit wrong, but it seems to be mostly accurate from what I played. Basically, you have to find a good strategy for dealing with them. They get more and more active as the nights go on. Your goal is to survive for five nights, as the title would suggest. Wearing headphones to help track the noises will also be helpful for reacting to enemies that are in locations unknown or unsure to you currently, and that will help cut down on camera usage. If one of them gets to you, you die. If you run out of power... just hope you can survive long enough to run out the clock. You can still win, but it's a long wait when you don't know where the animatronics are or how much time you have left.
Five Nights at Freddy's does quite a bit with very little. There's not really music in this game, but the sound design is good. You only use a mouse to point and click on things in one room, and it's mostly a collection of still images for the most part. Yet this game, with the stylistic choices of darkness, grittiness, and the inherently motionless state of the clearly moving mascots, is able to create a convincing atmosphere that's genuinely creepy and a simple but effective premise to really let that fear and suspense sink in. Honestly, it's probably the best point and click game I've ever played.
However, it's not perfect. One super annoying thing is the randomness of the robots. I get it. It's scarier if you don't know what they're going to do and that also makes you think on your toes. But it also means that sometimes you'll be bested by a random action not going your way. You can play with the same strategy as many times as you want. Sometimes it'll work, sometimes it won't. I guess it'd be nice to have the standard five nights be in a set pattern so you could beat them, and leave the randomness for the custom nights you can do later. But maybe that's just me. Another problem I have is that... there's not a lot here. I mean, the gameplay boils down to a few things. Lights, camera, doors. It works well for minimalistic effect, but it's not super engaging if, like me, you're not scared by horror games. If the atmosphere and jump scares fail to make you really feel terrified, then you'll be left with an experience that gets more frustrating with each level rather than more intense.
Keep in mind I haven't completed the game. I still have yet to beat night 5. I haven't done so because it's past the point of fun for me on this night, and it doesn't run too well on my computer. Perhaps I'll finish it and edit this review when I get a better computer, but I think I've played and seen enough to make the review, as it's all generally the same throughout, only harder. Five Nights at Freddy's does the point and click gameplay very very well, and is definitely recommended for fans of horror games. If you want truly engaging gameplay, satisfying replayability, or if you're just not scared by horror games... then you might want to pass on this one. Still, if you're curious, it's only 5 bucks. It's not a lot to sink into it, and if you end up liking the game even as much as I did, then it'll still be worth spending those 5 bucks.
Five Nights at Freddy's gets a 6/10 for being a great point and click game, a solid horror game, and an aptly priced indie hit.

*On a whim, for my newest run of the game, i've been keeping a "journal" of sorts. If anybody is interested, check my screenshots.*
The single most terrifying game ever made. And not cheap terror like a teleporting white guy in a suit that magically kills you no matter what you do. Not random jump scares. Not even with a monster or killer. Your own mind scares you. You're alone. You don't really know why, but everybody is dead, covered in frost and dead. All of the wolves are rabid and deadly, sure, (9/10 deaths will be to wolves) but they arent the scary thing. the cold isnt the scary thing. Nothing in the game is scary, and yet it's terrifying. It's the isolation. You. Are. Alone.
After a few hours in a session if you've got a headset on and no distractions, every bookself becomes a serial killer. The creaks and groans of the old buildings are a monster creeping up on you. You know you are safe yet you are terrified. You set up your sleeping bag in the corner of a building so nothing can be behind you when you wake up. You waste matches or lantern oil to see in a building you've already looted and know the route of because the dark is scary. The isolation is simply torture, and i love to dread it. 10/10 for atmosphere.
As for the game itself... well, you're in northern canada and there's no electricity, and everybody is dead. Don't freeze. Don't starve. Don't get mauled by a wolf. Very decent point and click puzzle horror game. Really loved the atmosphere.
I also enjoyed the way key pieces of the story are revealed throughout each episode, but it felt strange that completing an episode kicks you out into a menu rather than continuing seamlessly on to the next episode. It was a little immersion breaking. The three chapters are distinct in that your inventory is cleared each time, and you are unable to return to areas in the previous chapter, but it would have been much more organic to throw up a title card and just let the game continue. I completed the first episode and honestly didn't even know there were two more until I looked at the achievements that described them.
That's not to condemn the game, though. It is genuinely spooky; a few of the jumpscares got me pretty dang good. And I enjoyed the puzzles overall but really wish they had been more difficult. There are a few somewhat challenging moments, especially in the excellent second episode, but often the hardest part was just trying to remember which room the clues were in.
Harder puzzles with complex components (i.e. more steps than just use item A in location X) and a more nuanced relationship with their environment would be a huge improvement. Simple puzzles work in the original Resident Evil games because they have combat and inventory management, but in a game like this puzzles are the player's primary interaction with the game. Great puzzles grow organically out of a game's unique logic, and horror puzzles in particular should contribute to an inscrutable sense of dread. Hopefully Shining Gate will hone in on that kind of development with their next title.

Banished is probably one of the most personal yet inpersonal experiences in gaming that I have had for a long time. I purchased the game before it even came out and was excited in the days before release. It turns out that my excitement was warranted.
The game offers you the chance to create and nurture a colony of banished people in the pre-Revolution era. You control (though not directl) the lives of men, women in children through their charming, fulfilling and dangerous existence.
Getting to grips with the basics of the game is not easy. There is a lot to think about and the balance of the game is so fine that one very slight change in its jenga like structure means that in the space of one season, you can easily go from 100 people to 10.
And thats one of the main features of the game, like Settlers etc, the season play a vital role in the game. You are literally struggling for food during the winters months, and abundent with it during the summer. If that does not offer the modern youth of today an opportunity to really appreciate what life is like out in the agricultural heartland, I dont know what will.
Resources are collected the same way as most other games, woodcutters, farmers, fishermen, miners, etc - But what sets this game apart (in my humble opinion) is the way that the work force tasking is controlled in a much more beaurocratic way. A Slide bar system gives you an easy way of transferring your working from say, farming to mining etc. Its good to be able to drop your farmers down to 0 in the winter months, and double your mine strengh, or stop fisherman sitting on their arses when the rivers have frozen over!
Faceless Beurocray aside, the game can hit you in the feels from time to time, for example, when one of the townsfolk I had nurtured from birth to adulthood died during childbirth I did get a swift kick in the moral and this does give you a passion to truly keep the welfare of the individuals in your town at the forefront - You want your people to survive, to work, to reproduce.
Being someone who loves military games, that seeks to be its only flaw - A lack of military, but then again it is a town building game and dare i say it, perhaps there isnt a place for the military in this game.
One of the best things about this game is the ability to mod it and download mods easily from Steam, it really does add a new dimension to your experience, giving it that endless feeling.
Pro's
-Great idea and concept
-Well executed
-Balanced to perfection
-The game can last you hours upon hours on a single town
Con's
-At times you want to zoom in more
-Is very difficult to just pick up and play
-Lack of military etc
-Islands are very samey

Story: To not spoil you of the very wonderful story, to put it simply is its about idealism gone wrong. A unique take on the human ideology of a utopia. Another plus is the twists and intricacies of the story will hook you from start to end. The audio logs scattered throughout the game do a good job giving the backstory to an already very elaborate plot. And the world of Rapture is very detailed and meticulously crafted that as you walk in its leaky halls it feels lived in and the unique atmosphere this game has created has never been rivalled by any other games of the same genre save for the sequel of this game itself. However, if you are expecting characters worth caring about you might walk away disappointed. They are more walking ideas than empathetic human beings. Not that its a bad thing, its just this is the kind of game that is more plot centric than character driven. One disappointing thing though is the ending is so abrupt that you don't get the payoff you deserve after battling through destiny.
Graphics: 7 years later and this game looks already aged. Not that it looks ugly, but textures are low res, water effects plasticy, and well its a last gen game. This is usually the problem with 3D games, especially ones that use a realistic art style. However, luckily this games uses a stylized approach and it has aged rather well in the art style side. The art deco 60s vibe w/ its neon-y glow is still great to look at. Character designs are very unique and disturbing. What could have been zombies in other games are what this game called splicers. They have a very distinct look to them that you won't find in any other game.
Sound: Music is great, Guns sound right, Little sister voices are scary, Big Daddies just make you want to run, and Splicers just make you euugghh.
Gameplay: FPS RPG nuff said. A variety of (9) weapns and (3) ammo types on each, about 5 enemy types, more than 10 plasmids which are fun to use, and many many augments (combat, engineering, physical) to mix and match. It's just a joy to play, and the shooting is very satisfying. The sheer amount of variety in combat strategy just keeps you on your toes for the whole duration of the game. You can hack machines to make them fight by your side, hack vending machines to get discounts, and so much more. The only downside though is although the hacking part is fun, it can sometimes put you out of the immersion. Especially, if things get hectic and you decided to hack in the middle of it, the transition is very jarring.
Overall, a very polished and well crafted game that deserves its plenty of awards. A gripping story, wonderful art, amazing sound, very fun gameplay. If you haven't played this game yet, then you are missing one of the crowning achievements of this medium. A must play.

A typical Golf Solitaire game that offers a relaxing aesthetic, nice art-style, a beautiful soundtrack and a mediocre story.
There is,
, nothing better or worse about this Golf Solitaire game than any others, they are all the same in nature.
They usually offer some sort of 'item unlocking' system, typically these are items relevant to the in-game story that you purchase using money/points you earn for completing levels.
Once an item is purchased it gives you a unique feature, like a 'click-to-use' ability that removes 1 or 2 cards, or a passive ability like 3 more cards show face-up at the start of the hand etc...
There are a bunch of other things that 99% of all Golf Solitaire games have, if you've played one Golf Solitaire game you'll immediately recognize the same
in the next Golf Solitaire game you play.
These,
, features is what keeps a Golf Solitaire game fresh 5 hours down the line.
The way you make a Golf Solitaire game good is by having a beautiful soundtrack, a beautiful art-style, a relaxing aesthetic/atmosphere with a good story.
The game has a mediocre love-story set in the Regency era of England, again, nothing state of the art, if you've read 2 or 3 stories like this before you will not see something new and mind blowing.
The game is not hard in the sense of skill requirement, it is hard in the sense that it's luck-based.
The small amount of skill needed to play Golf Solitaire is something you pick up after 1 or 2 hours of playing it and is forever remembered by you, I.E you carry it over to all other Golf Solitaire games.
The same way if you make a cake once or twice and you make it again 1 year later, after 1/3 way through you start to remember how the recipe goes, you enter the flow of making the cake with seemingly no trouble as if you've made that particular cake a thousand times before.
This game also is an easy target for anyone looking to get 100% achievements, although that is arguably not a good selling-point.
I recommend this game for anyone who is into Golf Solitaire games, and to any new-comers I recommend you check out
before and over anything else.
