Right, so, you've seen the glowing reviews, maybe even heard about it from your friends, and you're on the Store page thinking to yourself "what's the catch"? Well, the catch is that by itself the game mechanics are boring, skill in this game takes a backseat to luck, and speed is king. Allow me to explain. It's not hard to kill enemies in this game. And, save for a few cheaply designed monsters, it's not hard to avoid their attacks either, so how the game makes itself difficult as well as interesting (apart from the bosses, which I believe stand up on their own) is through scrolls. Scrolls can be broken down into four categories- the good ones that buff your character with no drawbacks, the wildcard ones that do something completely random, the tradeoff ones that give your character a buff in one way in exchange for nerfing another aspect of your abilities, and the ones that are, on the whole, garbage that at best are frustrating and at worst will ruin your whole run. How easy this game is is determined by speed and versatility; buffs, debuffs, multipliers, you can deal with those, but you get a scroll that limits you to one weapon, or halves your movement speed, or removes one of your jumps, and you're screwed. How fast your weapons reload, how fast they fire, how fast they kill an enemy, how fast your character is will all play into how far up the pyramid you go. So anything that kills your speed or your versatility, kills your character, and kills your mood. I couldn't tell you how many times I played this game, got to the miniboss or the boss of the first pyramid, and through no fault of my own get screwed out of completing the damn thing. All in all, it's a fun game, and I reccomend it. But if you're of the belief that games ought to be more of a matter of skill than a matter of blind chance, take a pass, because a game like this, lovely though it may be, will do little more than♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.

Loved this game. It may be a few years old, but I couldn't tell from the graphics, which were still stellar. The story is extremely well done and engaging throughout- you will be searching for every voxophone and going down every side corridor to learn more.
Gameplay was also very fun- I played on Normal difficulty, which was challenging enough that I was never bored, while not being hard enough that I was frustrated. There weren't too many weapons to choose from (and to be honest some just didn't seem that effective compared to the standard Wrench) but I never found myself bored or distracted by that fact. Same with the Plasmids (basically, magic spells)- I almost always used the standard Electric Shock, but the others were still interesting and the gameplay forced you to use some of the other Plasmids in order to unlock secret areas or find hidden voxophones which advanced the story.
In sum, I would give this game an 8/10, with a recommendation for people who want an engaging story to go with their gameplay.

Immortal Redneck is an FPS roguelite with superb platforming gameplay. The game starts slow but after warming up with your first runs you will be hooked by the frantic gameplay and the gorgeous visuals and atmosphere inside the pyramids, the crazy designs of the enemies, and a gameplay that demands some skills from the player beyond circle strafing.
Unlike other games of this genre, Immortal Redneck requires a degree of good aiming and mobility, and it utilizes that to create a platforming gameplay that is among the best I've ever tried in any FPS game, with an element of verticality that really spices up everything.
Random drops and different classes to play offer enough variety to keep you entertained every run, the game can be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at times with the RNG, though, but it only adds to the fun. There's enough content to spend dozens of hours on this game, I have never felt tired of repetition, because learning the rooms and making new strategies to clear them adds another extra layer. Actually I think there might be too many challenge runs, because I almost never get to repeat and practice them so after playing 20~ hours I still sucked at solving those.
The music is just incredible and pumps me up every single time, it's a perfect match to the fast gameplay and the great mood and visuals.
On the negative side, I think the sound effects could be improved and maybe the game starts too slow, it gets much better after the first couple of hours.
Last but not least, the developer Crema has been listening to the community and updating the game consistently since day1, improving on aspects that weren't that great at launch, but right now after a couple of revisions, the game is just amazing, even more for an $20 indie title.
In other words I love this game and you should buy it.

Reviewing at Alpha Stage: I took a quick look at the pictures and one video, noticed a demo was shared to us the consumer I decided to give it a shot.
Demo: The demo starts you off as a female hidden away, you're bitten which allows you to play for a couple of days before becoming a zombie, this is a tipical demo feature which stops you from playing the game for free and thinking that is all it. The demo gave me a strong impression on what it is capable of so I decided to buy it for a low cost compared to other indie games.
The Alpha: Bugs, glitches, crashes will happen in every single alpha so I tend to ignore these a little whiles doing a review unless it is a major issue which it is not and I am happy to continue this review.
The main menu is brilliant, the lightning flashes with the music kicking in that reveals a hidden dark secret to the two characters on screen, you have three game modes Survival, Last Stand, Sandbox.
Survival; As the game is meant to be, you create your character with its pros and cons, you start in  one out of two worlds which random generates items and your starting area which opens your eyes up and scares you from roaming too far in the early stage, you need to keep fed, watered, fit and infection free! If you're a zombie fan then playing this is logical, play it as a movie and real life scenerios for survival and you will not have a problem on keeping alive....until you meet zombies, they are slow, fast, weak and strong...some walk, some run, some crawls, they're all attracted to smell of blood dripping, sound and sight which creates or breaks hordes up.
Sandbox; just like survival but you're in control for a while on what the world can be like for zombies, make them weak or super hard.
Laststand: You're holding out aslong as you can before death, there is only one way to win.... stand and defend as long as you can.....Winning is death in my eyes.

This is a by-the-numbers, point-and-click, figure-out-which-object-I-need-to-get-me-past-this-dead-end adventure game. By advised that this does not use the Unity engine, so you are not moving in 3D space, but are instead presented with mostly static screenshots that you click between.
Steam is selling this for $10 regularly, which I think is an overall decent price for what you're getting which is about 3-4 hours of gameplay, but is an outstanding pickup when it's on sale for 99 cents.
The visuals are grainy and washed out, but this is likely an atmospheric design choice. Music was acceptable; nothing to write home about. There are some animated portions of the screens, including several effective jump scares.
As for gameplay, nothing you need to be agile about, it's merely point-and-click. The puzzles are medium difficulty at best, although the game does have the annoying tendency of creating artificial dead-ends until you've done something that is unrelated to clearing the obstacle. For example, one puzzle requires you to backtrack to areas you've already cleared, just to see a vital piece of the puzzle just magically appear for you to pick up without any real explanation of why the piece suddenly decided to show up, or any explanation as to why it was logical that you backtrack that way to begin with. Putting your players in a position where they can brute force their way through puzzles is bad enough; but incorporating this kind of design into your game intentionally - requiring your players to flail about without any rhyme or reason - is amateur hour. But then, this is an indie effort, and it shows.
As for plot...yeah, there is a fairly basic plot here; don't fret about it too much, because it has some massive holes in it and in some places, doesn't make a whole lot of sense. But understanding what's going on isn't mandatory to completing the game.
This is one of those games where you wish Steam had more than "Recommend" or "Don't Recommend" as options. Because really, I cannot recommend this game on its own merits, but will recommend it any way, because it accomplishes its task of entertaining you for a couple of hours for dirt cheap. So if you're in the mood for something atmospheric on the creepy, surreal side, and don't need to be dazzled for a buck, yeah, this is a decent enough time-filler.

Despite being early in development, I was really surprised by how addictive and fun the sandbox mode has been. This is definitely one of the best survival games I've ever played and the Gnu/Linux port is very well done. I haven't encountered a single bug and it's probably the best optimized unity 5 game on Gnu/Linux thus far.
Game Highlights:
Very good voice artist work, though it is minimal as of yet (until the story mode is added).
The audio production is top notch, makes all the difference having well produced audio and ambiance, snow crunches, flares sizzle, wolves howl to send chills down your spine, etc.
Art is stylized (not photo-realistic) but it isn't a negative, I think that only adds to the character and experience. Unique survival mechanism and so on..
Game play:
It can be brutal and punishing! Which I really like, the second time I played it started me in the middle of a fierce blizzard in pitch dark with only one flare to try and save myself - I did manage to find shelter in the Carter Hydro Dam (after a night in relative safety, I made my way to the Camp Office located on the western side of Mystery Lake).
Sometimes you get a nice easy start, sometimes a nightmarish struggle to survive what seems like the impossible! If you fail, there is no reloading a save you've simply got to try again (but you can quit any time and continue on another sessions if you have not perished - so a save of sorts).
I really like the change of pace from all the usual gaming fare, this one makes you think about what you need to do to really survive in the game. Supplies are always in the back of your mind, do you stay put in a comfy cabin with the supplies you have - or risk the outdoors to be proactive in your scavenging to prevent a situation where you could starve or freeze to death? There are no zombies, ghouls, or other such fictional monsters - just you versus the brutal arctic and occasionally a wolf or two (best to avoid them if possible).
Tons of fun if you love a challenge and an open world to scavenge up what you can to survive. I can't wait for the campaign story that will be added later in development - going from the current experience it should be amazing!
I can full heartedly recommend The Long Dark to all of you who are interested in the survival genre.

This is one of my favorite games.  I like slow-paced, intricate simulation-type games (SimCity, Patrician, Farming Giant, etc), so if you are looking for action and excitement, stay away.  If you are looking to really immerse yourself into a survival and city-building sim with a handful of people starting out with a wagon and some tools, then this will appeal.  You feel every birth and death as if you were the village leader shepherding his people toward a brighter future, and, at least early in the game, every decision seems essential.  I like that.
As others have commented, the mods really make this game.  The base game was built by one guy in his spare time, and he did a great job considering.  The mods take it to the next level, and although it seems like every version of mod left some bug unfixed, and it isn't likely the creator will go back and fix them, all in all its a very satisfying experience.
The weakest part of the game is late in the gameplay, where there just isn't much to do after survival is assured and your handful of villagers is in the 1000's, and the game can lag a bit on some systems.  But it is always fun starting over again in different climates (the frosty harsh climate, the arid desert climate), which brings a whole different feel to the game, and in the mods, new opportunities for different crops and growing seasons.
There are too few games like this for those of us who like this kind of detailed, down-in-the-weeds, slow-paced simulation style games.  Highly recommend.

A slow, stylistic and occassionally thought-provoking title ultimately bogged down by impenetrable lore.
Gameplay is simple and approachable, requiring very little direct interaction.  The pacing of the game is slow, and it is a grueling challenge to advance, especially as you start to run out of completable quests.  Some of the fun comes when having to make hard decisions to progress, and in these moments, the gameplay will briefly flicker with excitement before returning to its routine dullness.  Admittingly, the game hinges more on its story elements than gameplay, so to that effect, the gameplay is enough to service the story.
The style of the game is excellent for an indie title.  Many of the places hidden in the zee are diverse and appropriately Lovecraftian for those seeking that atmosphere.  Music and sound effects help to reinforce the sensation of being adrift in a hostile and alien world.
The story, however, is the issue I have with this title.  While the game is well written in regards to having an artistic style, the background and lore of this game do not convey well through the writing.  I often found myself reading paragraph after paragraph of dialogue based around histories, cultures and phenomenons I knew nothing about and for which there is little lore in game to explain.  I imagine that's the appeal of the game; the thrill of being thrust head first into an alien world that has little regard for your understanding or lack thereof.  However, without comprehension, there can be no investment, and I eventually found myself skimming the text of the game to get the gist of what's going on.  In a game all about text driven story, this is disasterous.
Not to say it's all painfully obscure.  There are genuine moments in the writing that get you feeling excited for what's about to come, typically nestled within the more grounded moments of the game.  There just are not enough to hold my interest past a free weekend playthrough.
For those people already immersed in the lore of Fallen London, this title is a must buy, and will likely appeal to players inclined towards Cthulian games.  For those not willing to take the time to learn and understand this world outside the game, I would recommend other titles.  Planescape Torment, the Witcher franchise and Pillars of Eternity, for instance, do a better job of plunging the player into an alien world while fostering investment.  For those attracted to the Lovecraft style, unforgiving decision driven gameplay and the low price point, Darkest Dungeon is an outstanding substitution.

I'm a little disappointed in this game. I DO enjoy it. However, I was lead to believe certain things about this game from the trailer and reviews that have turned out to be very different in reality.
1. It's a difficult game, and you will die. A lot.
I have yet to die once. Every single death-inducing element - terror, fuel, supplies - is easy enough to manage, even when exploring aggressively. Enemy units can be seen far enough away that it's generally simple to avoid engaging them in battle. I see no need to lose my Invictus charm, because there's no need to bother saving.
2. It's a survival horror game.
I guess this really kind of ties into my first point. There is no horror, and very little survival element (limited to resource management). At absolutely no point have I encountered suspense, because this factor does not exist. There is zero chance that you're going to encounter something entirely unexpected, and so the player has no fear of this happening.
Everything else I'm fine with. I learned from reading others' reviews that the game is slow paced, that earning money to advance is either difficult, or not intuitive. That it becomes tedious to play. That it's very well written, and has excellent story-driven plots. All this I found to be true, and for what the game is, I still enjoy it. Had it been advertised as such, I would recommend it.
However, some fairly important claims are made by the developers, claims that they simply do not deliver on.
I'm also disappointed that the game does not display snippets of text on the screen during events like it does in the trailer, because that would lend an extended air of significance and flair to the written element of the game, which in my opinion, is it's strongest point. However, this did not affect my review.

Cuphead is a fast paced arcade-style action platformer with a fantastic early 1900's cartoon art style and soundtrack. It sports single player & local co-op 2 player modes. Boasting some of the tightest controls I've ever felt in a 2D action platformer and subjectively some of the best looking authentic hand drawn animation in gaming, For me just the spectacle was worth the price of admission.  While difficult, the game consists of numerous boss fight stages and 6 platforming stages spread over the course of 4 worlds.  With the uber responsive controls, varied weapons, super moves and charms the player can purchase, the player is given all the tools needed to be succesful. Failure strictly lies with that of the player and not the game. It feels punishing but fair. So one must practice, practice and practice.
Besides the boss & platforming stages there is a small, linear world map to explore with NPCs, shortcuts and hidden goodies along with a shop to spend your gold coins in to purchase upgrades.  Once you've defeated the bosses of each world you're allowed to move on to the next ultimately facing off with the Devil at the end. There are special unlockable color & sound modes for completing hidden objectives, such as beating all the Run 'n Gun (platforming) stages without killing a single enemy. And for getting a perfect grade on all platforming and boss stages. There's even an expert mode if players complete the game on Regular difficulty. The achievements will also feel satisfying and well earned.
Is this worth the $20 USD price tag? I sure thought it was. My only regret was not buying the Deluxe Edition with the soundtrack. The game is short but sweet. Quality over quantity. That's it for my mini-review of Cuphead, thank you for reading.

I never expected Auditorium to be a puzzle game but rather a rhythm/music game. The screenshots made me think it was some kind of visual music player with gameplay elements added somewhere into the whole package. Like I said, I was wrong. It's a pretty game (windowed; it's looks extremely blurry in full screen) where you shift around dots with arrows on them to redirect a stream of grey colors. You can also increase the radius of the dots.
The idea is to get the stream across all colored bars at the same time, producing music. In order to do that, the stream has to move in circles, to the left, right, you name it.
It's beautiful in motion, but placing the dots is clumsy. I frequently moved around the wrong dot and eventually had to restart the level so I could see clearly again.
Also, like their other game Fractal, there's no tutorial. So it's up to the player to figure things out. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but - there's always a but - not for a casual puzzle game like this.

The presentation is top notch.  The problem is that there just isn't much to this game.  It looks nice, it plays nice, has good music etc.  But the target audience seems to be razor thin: Women who love Jane Austen, play Solitaire frequently, and actually have an use Steam.  Even then, the "Solitaire" in this game is basically just Pyramid, where you pick the cards that are one up or down from your current card, in a variety of layouts.  With power-ups.
Add more to the game.  Make it some real Solitaire varieties, like Klondike, Freecell, Spider, etc.  Don't try to lengthen the game with arbitrarily hard chapter goal requirements - then make them easy to bypass simply by retrying levels.  Power-ups are fine, but give us a bit more variety there too.
There's the backbone of a very good game here, and like I said, what IS here is extremely well polished.  But once you've run through the game once, which shouldn't take more than a few hours, there is zero reason to come back.  There's just too many other games vying for this same, tiny casual market.

One of the things I like about indie games is that they try out unique concepts that more mainstream developers would either never think of or be too scared to try. Runespell: Overture is a Norse themed RPG but is set apart from other RPGs by its unique battle system. You and your oppenent are given a deck of playing cards laid out solitaire-style and the idea is to build poker hands using the face up cards of you and your opponent. The better the hand, the harder it hits! Attacking and taking hits also builds up your rage meter which is used for activating spell cards similar those found in collectible card games to further give you an edge. Over the course of the game you will meet new allies, complete new quests, find new cards and further the story. If the idea of an RPG with poker-style battling and CCG elements appeals to you, get this game! You won't regret it.

Tropico 5 probably introduces the most new gameplay mechanics out of the franchise. It certainly is not just like 4 (which in turn was just like 3). The idea of advancing with a tech tree (of sorts) is an interesting change while a consistantly changing global environment can often catch you by suprise if you get complacent. Unlike previous Tropico games, putting all your eggs in one basket will be your undoing. I have also noticed that while in older instalments I could win ellections with ease, each election can often leave me with a nail biting victory (or twice so far defeat). So I would recommend reducing the difficulty when you first play as Tropicans in 5 will rebel almost 3 times as often as those in tropico 4 with the modifier Rebel yell on.
This Game still still retains the political satire and puns of the previous Instalments and on the odd occasion has made me laugh. It does how ever have a few flaws such as; a lack of customisation for EL presedente and his Dynasty (i feel like tropico 4 had more customisation options), the more clunky almanac (i much prefer the tropico 4 almanac) and the fact that you are only warned about a faction not being satisfied when they protest (often leaving you with little time to rectify the problem before some become rebels or you lose an election).

A lot of us will be familiar with the concept of enemies staying still until you’ve made your move in roguelike games such as
or Pixel Dungeon. But has it been done in a first-person shooter? If not, it has now! The SUPERHOT Team have put together an utterly unique piece of gaming unlike anything we’ve ever played. Not only have they managed to pull off a gaming experience filled with entertaining gameplay, but they’ve also combined it with an engaging and mysterious storyline.
SUPERHOT is a completely unique game, in that it’s a first-person shooter but enemies only move when you do. By standing still, you can pinpoint the location of your foes and plan which way to move so as to avoid bullets they’ve fired. After you’ve completed a stage, you are presented with a replay of your actions at normal speed, making your play look even cooler than the best quick-scoper you’ve seen on the internet.
Stun your enemies and steal their weapons by engaging in hand-to-hand combat, throwing objects at them such as vases and sculptures, or by swinging a baseball bat or katana at their extremities.
Get to the bottom of a mysterious story that’ll more than likely force you to quit. To help keep you occupied, play with and discover awesome ASCII games, artwork, videos and more in amongst the main menu of SUPERHOT.
Test your reflexes and awareness in the Endless and Challenge modes and upload your replays to
.
Overall, SUPERHOT is a great game unlike any we’ve ever seen before. The story is engaging and the gameplay is challenging and extremely quirky.

This game is a must-have you you are zombie survival games fan! The game touches on just about every aspect and difficulties faced during a zombie apocalypse.
Examples:
- hunger and thirst (well fed = increased strength and healing, hungry = reduced strength and healing)
- pain (more pain = less accuracy)
- fatigue (not sleeping can cause reduced awareness and can eventually cause you to pass out!)
- fear (the more scared you are the less accurate you are)
The game is full of surprises and the map is HUGE! There is also leveling which means you can improve abilites such as aiming, cooking, carpentry, stealth and sprinting!
If you are concerned about co-op, don't worry! The developers are hard-workers and it will be implemented in the near future. How awesome will that be? Surviving the Zombie Apocalypse with your mates!

I WANT to like this game so much I really do and there is a really a lot I admire about this game, but at the end of it lack of indepth game-play, annoying issues and replayability mean I can't recommend it.
What do I like?
SCENERY: Breathtaking and beautiful. I very often found myself sleeping in the day to look at stars at night!
REALISM: More in the mind. I found myself talking to myself during the game, double checking, reassuring, thinking and maybe even keeping myself company. Morale, oh how the heart sinks when you find a backpack when you are dying of hunger and it's -30 and it's EMPTY... The feeling inside of me was so intense and real... amazing and kudos!
MAP: Large enough to make it interesting and having to rely on your senses and remember way points.
MECHANICS: Drinking / Sleeping / Eating are all super interesting and reasonably well thought out.
In Summary - I loved the feelings this game gave me: scared, tired, drained, gutted, proud, not wanting to die - really incredible!
What did I not like - Why do I not recommend?
REPLAYABILITY: I am someone who wanted to stay alive a long time. I was in for the long haul. Sensible clothes, repairs, sleeping, drinking, stocking and never taking adverse risk. When out of the blue, I was walking along a hill from nothing it says, you died from massive internal injuries after a fall when I can see myself still standing was severely annoying and means I will probably not play this game again, because if that happens, there is really no point in playing a game that will randomly kill you with no reason. Exposure - yes / Famine/Dehydration - yes. Random unexplained death - NO. Secondly HOW DO YOU SAVE? I was playing a whole day straight because there is no apparent way to save and come back to it. I played it for a little while at first and got a bit bored as had a lot to do so just quit, when I came back I found I could "resume" however, many of the item's that I had already picked up were no longer in my bag and I had to go find them again so it's confusing as to how this works and as such annoying to start another longer game.
REALISM: 0.5Kg MRE = 1750 Calories / 1Kg Venison = 800 Calories... Not forgetting the effort needed to hunt, prepare, butcher and skin one!!! Can't store meat outside in "freezer" it spoils quickly despite it being -30... The fact that you starve very very easily... Yes, it should make you weaker, slower, tire more quickly but kill you no. Boiling pristine snow? Where and why is the snow so badly contaminated that I need to boil it? (Water you find - yes) Why when I just finished boiling water do I need to boil some more to make a tea?
How to improve (for me): Add more elements to the game - More things to scavenge / find naturally so you can try two ways: Live off only what you can find from man or nature... Add more natural things and make it realistic, more plant life tucked away. Berries that might / might not be poisonus (find a survival guide in a cabin and read it) More animals and better ways to hunt them (deadfall, spear, pit) More usage/crafting options for scavenged items. More realism than 8 mins to break down a simple crate with an axe... Why not be able to breakdown a ruined building. Add more interactability with surroundings. There should be a way to "mark" certain places or trails and surely a compass to be found/made and you should be able to make a "map". Add seasons, it's annoying that there is everlasting winter no matter how long you go. You should be able to live better in the warmer and prepare for the winter. More shelter options (fallen trees / tarps / snow caves...)
If you had this and you could reliably save ( meaning - up until that exact point stays the same unless you die "properly"...) I think I would not play another game again! But you don't and reading the Reddit section and all available info, it doesn't look like you are going this direction so I won't. 20 bucks for this or 50 for the Witcher, 20 bucks will give you about 20 hours of fun. 50 bucks will give you easily more than 100 on the Witcher therefore more bang for your buck! :)
Also apart from the "death by fall" incident, the game also crashed for me twice - once when heating peaches and the other when gutting a rabbit, so also annoying but fortunately I was only a couple of days in and not yet "comfortable".
All in all thank you for the experience but I feel like I wasted my money for a game that you will play for max 10-20 hours...

I came into this game not expecting a whole lot, I expected to get no more than ten hours out of this game. I was in for a pleasant surprise once I got into it. This game shares a lot of similar elements to games like theme hospital and Prison Architect. Still, it's worth buying if you've seen everything there is to see on the aforementioned games as it adds a neat twist to it with products and layers of roleplaying and logistical store specialization. The controls aren't incredible and lack hotkeys, but they don't kill the game. I spent my first run building up my first mall with stores with parodied names of popular brands. After ten hours I expected to get bored in, I've set up a nice source of income in the form of a moderately sized food store and completed the (frankly quite basic) tech tree, which seems to put me into midgame. I currently plan on setting up more specialized stores in my main area (which is only a dot on the plot is given) which I could easily burn another twenty hours into. After that, I plan to either expand further or restart with the knowledge I have about this game now. I certainly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a fun sandbox game.
Now that you know you should get this game, here's a few tips I hope to pass on. First, Specialize by category, in the beginning, my breadwinner (pun not intended) is a food store that sells primarily food and drinks, don't worry about it too much though, I also have other products I thought would flavor (again, pun not intended) well with a food store.
Another big thing is that builders kill rat infestations, not janitors, that almost ruined my mall the first time, as rats infested my entire food court and drove a lot of customers out.
Here are some flaws I hope to see fixed in the coming updates, First off, staff functions feel clunky, I hope to see an intuitive interface where I can follow, hire, and fire all staff in a single toolbar, as well as see staff numbers and filter through staff.
Storefront Windows; I mean no mall is complete without storefront windows. Could give a slight purchase bonus to shelves ajacent to it, or just decorative, I just feel my mall is missing it.
Coffee Shops: I mean, we have cafe tables, I just kind of want a starbucks knockoff in my mall

I'm writing this at the end of a free weekend.
After playing the game for 12 hours I've decided not to purchase. At least not until I can get it for 1 or 2 euros.
This game is strange. I didn't know a game could be so boring and so captivating at the same time.
What I like:
-The concept behind the game is extremely interesting
-The universe is fascinating.
-The character building is awesome.
-The music is brilliant.
What ruins the game for me:
-Exploring and traveling the sea is a repetitive, boring slog. This is bad because this is what you do 90% of the time.
-The rooftop perspective gets old fast. This is not 1995 guys.
-The font is too small. Makes me not want to read anything.
-The journal is almost useless because it doesn't list what I need to get to advance most quests.
-Understanding the stories and keeping track of what is going on is hard because of the slow pacing and the lack of a detailed journal. The journal should have every detail about every quest that I started. Specially what items I need to get and where I can get them.
-Why does the lamp require so much fuel to work?
Despite these issues, I still played 12 hours of the game and I have to admit I would play more if I could.
Why? Because of the game's universe. It's fascinating.
But is that alone worth full price or even half price? Not for me.

And it wasn't so absurd that it couldn't be taken seriously; it was a bit amusing, yes, but you're meant to care about the conflict and the characters and such. And they pulled it the hell off. How? I am asking you, how do you do that? How do you get me to read ~10 pages about rat slobs vs guinea pig snobs, and get me to care unironically?
This game is exceptional. It contains some of the best writing I've ever seen in any form of media, and literally every time I log on, I discover something new. This world is a horrifying, amusing, adorable hell, and exploring it has been my new fixation.
10/10. Would recommend if you don't mind spending all your time on this.

Playing Cuphead reminded me of that fact that I've never cared for the "Run & Gun" genre.
In over thirty years of gaming, I'd rented a few Run & Gun games  in the distant past (Contra 3, Gunstar Heroes, etc.) but had never actually bought a single one.  I've never been a big fan of "bullet sponge" bosses, either.
In regards to its gameplay, Cuphead embodies the "Run & Gun" genre to a T -- nothing more, nothing less, and replete with bullet sponge bosses.
However, I can't step away from Cuphead too long:  the art and animation are superbly done, a real pleasure to view.   The game's audio is equally great, featuring music and sound effects which truly capture the on-screen action and atmosphere.
Yes, anyone can say, "just watch it on youtube."   I'd say that the ability to interact with Cuphead's world is a gaming experience that shouldn't be passed up.

Immortal Redneck is a rogue-lite first person shooter along the lines of Ziggurat but with its own strengths and weaknesses. Keyboard & mouse are the preffered devices to play this with. I haven't tried it with a gamepad so I can't say how well it controls with that. Runs at a smooth 60fps with my current i5 & gtx 1060 rig in 1080p with settings on maximum. Probably will run pretty good on lower end systems too.  The music is a nice mix of southern themes mixed with egyptian ones with some metal thrown in there every now and then. It feels unique.
You play as a Redneck who somehow got captured and mummified after he was knocked unconcious from a dune buggy accident in a desert. You'll wake up in the hub area, which has 3 pyramids, one of them you can enter for now. The pyramid layouts are procedurally generated  and arranged differently with each new attempt and have quite a decent sized variety of room layouts and types. Most of the rooms will be arenas where you have to kill all the enemies to unlock the doors and proceed to the next room. Occasionally you'll find treasure rooms that have a treasure chest or two or three or challenge rooms where certain requirements must be met to open the treasure chest at the goal, such as not taking damage or reach the chest within the time limit. When you want to progress to the next floor you need to find a room with an ascending staircase. If the room has something special in it like a challenge or staircase, it will be marked on your mini-map for easier reference later in case you want to explore the rest of the floor.  In the first pyramid, there are a total of 7 floors. On the 3rd floor is a mid-boss while on the 7th you will fight the end boss of the pyramid. I've recently beaten the game and all 3 pyramids have an entirely different aesthetic with all new room layouts and enemies.
The Immortal Redneck gets plenty of help in this undertaking to clear the pyramids. There is an extensive literal skill tree that will look familiar if you've played Rogue Legacy. Every time you enter the pyramid you have to offer all your gold to the gods and go in empty. When you die you will bring the gold you earned back out to the hub and you can spend it on that skill tree to unlock stat upgrades, new Favors (classes), a merchant and other special abilities. Favors are class/playstyle oriented loadouts with their own positive/negative strengths and weaknesses, unique active and passive traits and starting weapons. An example, Apis, the God of Strength; high health and attack and comes with 4 powerful weapons and a temporary invincibility active skill. But he's slow and only able to jump once. Since there is a lot of verticality to the level design, you have to decide if his attack and beefiness are worth crippling your speed and mobility. There are plenty of classes that will fit your playstyle so hopefully you should find one that fits you. Once you start unlocking classes, at the start of each run you get to choose one of the 3 randomly selected classes you've unlocked, with the ability to reroll the choices if you unlocked the skill on the tree. The merchant you unlock sells medallions you can equip that have their own pros and cons however you need to find their blueprints within the pyramids first.
There are over fifty different weapons and knowing when to use each weapon is crucial. As crucial as it is to always keep moving and remembering to use your active skills. But not only do you get those, you can randomly find Scrolls either dropped from enemies or from treasure chests. Scrolls make a HUGE difference in how your run will play out.  There are three different tiers of scrolls, bad, neutral and good. Bad would be a scroll that makes it so you're stuck with one weapon until it runs out of ammo. Neutral being something like...your weapons now have less max ammo but they do a lot more damage. Good being a scroll with no cons to it, like being able to take no damage from poison or lava hazards. Sure, if you get a bad scroll you can just die and move on to the next run. But I learned it was also fun to play around that disability and see how much more gold I could squeeze out by the end, even if I didn't think I'd make it to the end boss.
The only negative thing I can say of this game is the gunplay needs some serious updating, which is currently being addressed by the devs. I've seen people complain that once you've played long enough, the room layouts can be repetetive but the way I see it, playing them enough to add to muscle memory just makes each run go that much smoother. But as I said, right now, the weapon sounds and animations don't pack that much of a punch. There is also much more being worked on and added which you can see in the Roadmap thread in the steam discussions for this game.
This is currently one of my favorite rouge-lites and I haven't had this much fun playing one since Binding of Isaac and Rogue legacy. With more updates on the way, I highly recommend this game.

We were both running around the map trying to find each other without shooting our guns. At that time, shooting your gun is suicide. Even if I did hear a gunshot that wasn't mine (the time my heart would jump), I'd think, "He's stupid!" We ran around for another 4 or so minutes. The suspense was killing me. I couldn't stand not looking in every direction, every nook and cranny, without feeling like I was being scouted out.
I was shaking terribly. "Oh god! I'm gonna lose this match!" I thought to myself as I was trembling.
Then we met at the Administration Hall. We were swinging our guns at each other as we circled the statue of Josef Stalin. Then I fired a dangerously lucky shot at his chest and won.
I rose my arms from the keyboard in victorious triumph, quietly chanting to myself "Yes!" My heartbeat slowed down. I felt less alert.
That, my friends, is the intensity of Red Orchestra 2

A lot of us will be familiar with the concept of enemies staying still until you’ve made your move in roguelike games such as
or Pixel Dungeon. But has it been done in a first-person shooter? If not, it has now! The SUPERHOT Team have put together an utterly unique piece of gaming unlike anything we’ve ever played. Not only have they managed to pull off a gaming experience filled with entertaining gameplay, but they’ve also combined it with an engaging and mysterious storyline.
SUPERHOT is a completely unique game, in that it’s a first-person shooter but enemies only move when you do. By standing still, you can pinpoint the location of your foes and plan which way to move so as to avoid bullets they’ve fired. After you’ve completed a stage, you are presented with a replay of your actions at normal speed, making your play look even cooler than the best quick-scoper you’ve seen on the internet.
Stun your enemies and steal their weapons by engaging in hand-to-hand combat, throwing objects at them such as vases and sculptures, or by swinging a baseball bat or katana at their extremities.
Get to the bottom of a mysterious story that’ll more than likely force you to quit. To help keep you occupied, play with and discover awesome ASCII games, artwork, videos and more in amongst the main menu of SUPERHOT.
Test your reflexes and awareness in the Endless and Challenge modes and upload your replays to
.
Overall, SUPERHOT is a great game unlike any we’ve ever seen before. The story is engaging and the gameplay is challenging and extremely quirky.

Holy crap, what is there to be said about this game? How on Earth do I explain how utterly mind-melting it is without spoiling the most freakish and complex components of the story?
Well, for one thing, the game starts you off with a very simple rules; Time only moves when you do, and red guys are the baddies... or are they???
Superhot, or, rather, SUPERHOT makes you question yourself again and again as you go deeper and deeper into the levels. Should I be doing this? What happens if I don't listen? Am I in control? What am I working towards? The game is uniquely frightening for the questions it, not only, makes you ask yourself but also forces you to ponder on.
There's not a great way to demonstrate just how odd the game makes you feel without giving away the ending, but it is absolutely worth a try if you're happy to dedicate a few hours to find yourself falling deeper and deeper into a rabbit hole that doesn't want to let go of you. And that's one of the key elements of the game that can creep you out; you are told to stop playing the game, but the game doesn't want you to quit.

More than any other game, Bioshock defines the essence of of a videogame: what it can do, and what it can make you do and think. The themes deftly explored throughout are never forced down your throat; rather, they are subtly represented to you through the game world itself. And oh is that world beautiful. The world of Rapture is hands down the most vividly realized, finely detailed world ever created. Creative brilliance oozes out of every little art deco detail found in its dimly lit, masterfully atmospheric underwater halls. The setting is perfect, and the technically astounding graphics greatly aid it in creating a unique, wholely original location. The gameplay is also a strong point, boasting interesting combinations of weapons, upgrades, and rpg elements in the form of the delightfully satisfying plasmids and gears. Trumping all that, however, is the story. The story grabs hold of you like a cold wrench from the very first moment of the game, and rides you along at an exhilirating pace all the way through to the poignant finale. In between you'll meet startlingly disturbed, yet immensely fascinating and meaningful characters, which with his own evil to personify. The connection between the big daddies and little sisters is perfect, and big daddies serve as the absolute scariest enemies I've ever faced. You have to play this game. It's my all-time favorite.

Despite being early in development, I was really surprised by how addictive and fun the sandbox mode has been. This is definitely one of the best survival games I've ever played and the Gnu/Linux port is very well done. I haven't encountered a single bug and it's probably the best optimized unity 5 game on Gnu/Linux thus far.
Game Highlights:
Very good voice artist work, though it is minimal as of yet (until the story mode is added).
The audio production is top notch, makes all the difference having well produced audio and ambiance, snow crunches, flares sizzle, wolves howl to send chills down your spine, etc.
Art is stylized (not photo-realistic) but it isn't a negative, I think that only adds to the character and experience. Unique survival mechanism and so on..
Game play:
It can be brutal and punishing! Which I really like, the second time I played it started me in the middle of a fierce blizzard in pitch dark with only one flare to try and save myself - I did manage to find shelter in the Carter Hydro Dam (after a night in relative safety, I made my way to the Camp Office located on the western side of Mystery Lake).
Sometimes you get a nice easy start, sometimes a nightmarish struggle to survive what seems like the impossible! If you fail, there is no reloading a save you've simply got to try again (but you can quit any time and continue on another sessions if you have not perished - so a save of sorts).
I really like the change of pace from all the usual gaming fare, this one makes you think about what you need to do to really survive in the game. Supplies are always in the back of your mind, do you stay put in a comfy cabin with the supplies you have - or risk the outdoors to be proactive in your scavenging to prevent a situation where you could starve or freeze to death? There are no zombies, ghouls, or other such fictional monsters - just you versus the brutal arctic and occasionally a wolf or two (best to avoid them if possible).
Tons of fun if you love a challenge and an open world to scavenge up what you can to survive. I can't wait for the campaign story that will be added later in development - going from the current experience it should be amazing!
I can full heartedly recommend The Long Dark to all of you who are interested in the survival genre.

It's hard for me to find a game that I like. I usually like building stuff that has some form of progression, without being too harsh in penalties when I mess up. I decided to write a review for this game - because it's a game that I fell in love with.
Another Brick in the Mall is about creating a thriving mall and combines a lot of things you learn and/or observe in every day marketing and economics. You need to understand how to create a layout for your customers to walk such that your cashiers aren't overwhelmed and that all customers check out in a sufficiently reasonable time.
You need to create a layout for the PRODUCTS so that the high end value items gets the most visibility, generating a greater return-of-investment (ROI) on your mall. You need to manage cleanliness because as your mall grows larger and larger, you are going to deal with A LOT of spills and stains. You need to determine whether to be 24/7 or run for 12 hours and how that affects your bottomline. You need to study trends and see which is the next most logical and cost-efficient step for expanding your mall.
I admit - not many players would delve that deep but if you truly pay attention to every facet of the game, you'll realize that it's an amazing game and you'd have plenty of ideas for how you can grow your business, and how the game can too. Forward your suggestions to the team, I'm sure they'd appreciate inputs as well.
For now, I hope you guys give it a shot and see whether you like it. I love the game, but I'll admit, the pace and the style, is not for everyone. But for me, it's a godsend; to find such a game is difficult for me.

Remember that old game "Commandos?" The one where you controlled a (small) squad of troops who would have to infiltrate Nazi camps and do stuff? But all you really ended up doing was staring at your computer screen for hours memorizing the Nazis' walking patterns?
Well, that's what Outlast is, only in a first person perspective. You sit and wait. It also has perhaps the least imaginative "no combat" system one could think of. Thief had no combat (okay, you could fight, but you'd lose real quick), but you still weren't passive. You could manipulate things to protect yourself (douse lights, blanket the ground, etc.). Not this protagonist. He just breathes real heavy to remind you that this is scary.
And the camera! Guy gets his fingers cut off, what does he do? Picks up his camera! Cuz, yeah, I wouldn't bandage my hands either, but grab my camera and scamper off under a bed to watch the story unfold around me. Which is what you do in this much beloved walking simulator. It's a haunted house walking simulator, which is neat, but it's still a walking simulator.

Playing as blindly as possible is the best way to go.
(But DO know beforehand that this is NOT another Stanley Parable-type-game, at least in terms of your influence!)
All you need to know going in is that it's a wonderful game that has multiple diverse maps to traverse, and it keeps you sufficiently engaged throughout the entire story. The narriative is wonderful, both posing questions and proposing answers while maintaining an air of innocent curiousity. If you seek answers, they will be handed to you in the form of an abstract world, or perhaps an artistic thought. In this way, yeah, it has some parallels to The Stanley Parable.
Something to be aware of when going into it, however; this game will make you feel a lot of things. Confusion, namely, but also relaxation, happiness, sadness, guilt... It'll make you think about things you don't understand. It'll make you think about things you WISH you didn't understand, or wish you did but cannot. Tears may occur, for reasons you possibly understand. You probably won't know what to think or feel a lot of the time, I know that's where I was at while playing. I also ended up thinking about the game for weeks afterwards.
I played this game in one session, with only a single break. This was half due to my determination to finish it all in one go, so I wouldn't be left hanging in the middle of it all, and half due to my growing addiction to it's ever-growing mystery: 'who IS this person?' (or, alternatively, 'WHO is this person?'). I highly reccommend doing this, as opposed to playing it over a long period of time. To me, it made it feel more like a movie, or a story book, and it made the experience all the more enjoyable for me.

Charming little solitaire game with some extra tricks and Jane Austen flair
This game was made by just 2 people and there's no denying they are huge fans of the Jane Austen novels. The scenery, themes, characters and dialog feel like they're straight out of Pride & Prejudice or Mansfield Park, down to the use of the word "beau" (for a good looking bachelor).
I hadn't played solitaire before, but it's easy to pick up with this game and there's some tricks which you can unlock such as being able to take away the top card of a stack taking a peek at what's below the top card of your deck. The animations, backgrounds and portraits are done well. Can't say much about the music because I mostly listened to my own during my playthrough but the little I heard sounded very fitting.
My biggest complaint with the game is that each stage simply takes too long. Playing 5 instead of 10 rounds at each stage would have kept the experience less monotonous. The objectives don't really help here since they are mostly stuff that you'll be doing anyways and complement each other. I had also purchased all the upgrades and was floating lots of gold near the end. As you can see I spend around 9 hours completing the story line, but doing so in 4 would have felt less tiring.
My other complaint is that the story is too much straight forward in the sense that there isn't really any internal struggle for any of the characters. Bella's (main character) friends and relatives even encourage her to engage with the right guy. I disliked the puny and descriptive names like "Mr Bleakly". The idea of gathering accessoires to furnish up your room fits very well thematically though.
Fortunately the game doesn't fall into the trap of having the story make up all kind of excuses to play solitaire. It would have been really lame if every other scenario was along the lines of "Fine, you'll get to have your ball on our premises, *but only if you can handle 5 perfect rounds of solitaire". Instead the devs wisely decided to separate gameplay and story in this point.
All in all a pleasant experience. As long as you know what you're going into you should be fine. If you've never read Jane Austen than all the references will be mostly lost on you. Watch a video of some gameplay if you're undecided as of yet.

First of all, I didn't find it to be really fun or enjoyable. I didn't hate my time with it, but I didn't feel like it was very worth it.
The whole premise of the game doesn't really make sense to me. I get that one of the themes of this game is that it's more about the narrator than Coda, but I don't understand why the narrator, who is ostensibly the one who put together this narrated sequence of games, would come to some sort of sudden realization/psychological breakthrough or have a panic attack while he's recording the narration for the game but still leave it in the actual game. It makes one think that the narrator is actually just hamming it up for the game itself, so that the whole game actually ISN'T about the narrator's personal struggle. It leads one to conclude that the narrator is actually just putting on an act for the game, since they obviously aren't really having some sort of breakthrough or panic attack - if it really was some sort of psychological event they could've just re-recorded or edited that stuff out. The fact that the narrator chose to leave that stuff in the game should make you think that it's intentional on their part. It prevents you from really buying ANYTHING the narrator says, actually. Maybe there really isn't someone called Coda. Maybe he made all those crappy boring little non-games himself. The truth of it doesn't matter - my point is, when the game gets you starting to think on that level (which you realize by thinking about the circumstances in which the narrator must've created the game), the whole experience just starts to break down.
I guess if you think about the entire game as a fabrication of the narrator, then the only thing it actually tells you anything about is the narrator himself - the fact that he structures the game in such a way and records the bits of dialogue that he does and things like that. But if you start analyzing it from that perspective, you're committing the same mistake that the narrator's character does in trying to understand Coda only by analyzing his games. The narrator clearly criticizes such behavior because the whole story seems to be about Coda being upset by Wreden doing just that. That little insight doesn't really make me appreciate the game. If I want to overanalyze something and think in circles around it, I don't need to spend 6 dollars to do so.
So what am I supposed to get out of this game? The gameplay isn't fun. If you try to appreciate it for its base-level aesthetics - art, sound, gameplay, the 3d environment, etc...it's nothing to write home about. You're not supposed to try to figure anything out about the narrator because he says that's bad (as indicated by the story). As a whole, as a game there just isn't enjoyment, aesthetically or otherwise, to be found here. If that's what it set out to do, to play at being something that can be analyed at a deep level but ultimately criticize that sort of analysis and so end up inscrutable while not even being fun from a gameplay perspective, well, congratulations, but I didn't enjoy it. Maybe some people are sufficiently amused by the simple "twist" of the game ending up being about the narrator more so than Coda, but it didn't do anything for me. Certainly didn't do anything worth even 6 dollars. For 6 dollars I could read a damn book.
Oh and one last thing: I also really disliked the song that plays during the credits. It strikes me as something that's just artificially trying to convey a sense of gravitas. "Oh it's so dark, deep, and moody, though! The feeling conveyed by this song proves that the game must be deep and complex and very very important!" No, screw that - there's plenty of topics much more important and dark then some game dev's neuroticism and social anxiety.  The singer's voice and lyrics were just grating to me and the whole thing felt cliched. I was browsing for a game on my favorite map, Barracks. Whatever game mode was available. It was TDM/Firefight. I joined the Axis team to play against the Russian bot Anton. I got 1 lucky kill on him at 43 meters. He "went away" and a human player joined allies (Russian team). I got a kill on him across a path 30 meters wide. We ran around for 3.5 minutes, then he got two kills on me. The time ran out. It said "SUDDEN DEATH!" At that moment, it felt more intense. A minute later, my heartbeat quickened. We were both running around the map trying to find each other without shooting our guns. At that time, shooting your gun is suicide. Even if I did hear a gunshot that wasn't mine (the time my heart would jump), I'd think, "He's stupid!" We ran around for another 4 or so minutes. The suspense was killing me. I couldn't stand not looking in every direction, every nook and cranny, without feeling like I was being scouted out.
I was shaking terribly. "Oh god! I'm gonna lose this match!" I thought to myself as I was trembling.
Then we met at the Administration Hall. We were swinging our guns at each other as we circled the statue of Josef Stalin. Then I fired a dangerously lucky shot at his chest and won.
I rose my arms from the keyboard in victorious triumph, quietly chanting to myself "Yes!" My heartbeat slowed down. I felt less alert.
That, my friends, is the intensity of Red Orchestra 2

Tight controls, varied levels, great visuals and audio.
If you've played Ziggurat it's a similar idea : run around randomly generated dungeons and shoot stuff, while collecting randomized powerups that make the game feel just different enough each time you play that things don't get stale.
It's fun and well worth the price tag.
I enjoyed my time with the game, but I would like to see more added onto it, either through more patches or through DLC.
In the future, I'd love to see more weapons, scrolls, enemy types, and rooms. While there are plenty of scrolls that can drastically change the way a run goes, (introducing moon gravity or reloading your weapons for you when you switch away from them) quite a lot of the scrolls provide simple stat-ups which do little more than make your run a little easier. I'd like to see more "game-changer" scrolls, such as ones that grant entirely new special abilities beyond the ones granted by your chosen deity each run.
A custom room generator for players to use and post up onto the Workshop would be fantastic and could provide a lot of extra variety.
All told, it's a great game and for the price of a movie ticket and a drink, the 40+ hours of entertainment I got from the game as of the writing of this review are hard to beat.

At it's current state, I can't really recommend this game (personaly!) because I simply don't feel like I got my money worth of content.
SPOILERS AHEAD:
It took me 11 hours to finish all of the 3 pyramids and in the end I had 3 deaths in total. ( Mostly silly deaths while testing game mechanics)
On my very first run I managed to complete the first pyramid without much effort at all, so I decided ( after spending some points on the skill tree) to continue to the second pyramid. For some reason, second pyramid actually felt much easier than the first one so after completing it, I naturally went to the third one (last) in hopes of it being a bigger challenge than the two previous ones. I will admit, it was more difficult than the previous two, but still pretty much a walk in the park (for me).
Now maybe it is because I have some experience in these types of games and I tend to play a lot of fps games (hence above average aim), but it all just felt very underwhelming once I was done with all the 3 pyramids. In terms of "end-game" there isn't much that the game offers CURRENTLY. All you can do pretty much is farm the same "random generated" pyramids for gold to spend on your skill tree or try to find all the blueprints for the shop so you can buy items at the start of your fresh run.
I did few re-runs and pretty much just by seeing the room layout I already knew what enemies there would be, which made the replayability (for me again) drop drastically. Now I know the game calls itself "rogue-like" but honestly after few runs I'm not really feeling it that much.
I tend to stay with the given default god guns, except if I lack a good Area of effect gun then I might switch out one of my starter guns since the default guns perform well in my opinion. (I finished the whole game with redneck default weapons)
I've also notice a lot of people complaining about now getting enough ammo, while I've not really had this issue so far. As long as you rotate between your guns and hit more than half of your shots you should be fine.
The reason why I am not recommending the game in it's current state is purely because I don't find it challenging and/or it doesn't seem to be fully rogue-like for me. There is not enough reason for me to use other than the default weapons and the rooms are predictable enemy spawn wise once you have done few runs in the pyramids. On top of that, the skill points just make it even bigger of a joke difficulty wise than it already is.
Currently I feel like the worth of this game is around 9.99€ TILL they add some sort of new game + or more randomized enemies in the room etc etc so the game feels like it's worth replaying. Don't get me wrong,
I really liked the game when I first started playing and I was hoping it would  get more difficult on the way, but as I went from one pyramid to another it just didn't increase enough to be challenging... The negative scrolls, while apparently being more rare than the good scrolls, still didn't really hinder my gameplay since you can easily adjust to the negative side-effects like explosive vessels and air is lava effects or fall damage.
So if you are looking for rogue-like shooter with good re-play value, I would recommend waiting a bit and see what will make it from the roadmap to the actual live game or just wait for a sale. Again, this has all been my personal opinions of the game and I will change the review if the issues I've mentioned get resolved in any good way.

So, Five Nights at Freddy's 3 has officially been announced! Choo Choo, all aboard the hype train! Final destination: your worst nightmares!
I already posted a review of FNaF 2, so you can go check that one out if you want. I figured I'd just talk about what could easily be my game of the year 2014 and the biggest indie horror sensation since Slender (though far more deserving in my opinion). So is Five Nights at Freddy's really that good, or is it an overrated piece of non-scary garbage after all is said and done? Eh, considering you already saw my recommendation, you probably know my answer in advance. Ah well, let's get to talking about it.
On the surface, the story of FNaF is very simplistic. You play as Mike Schmidt, a nightshift security guard at a family restaurant called Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria that's based on Chuck-e-cheese. The mascots Freddy Fazbear, Bonnie the bunny, Chica the chicken and Foxy the pirate fox are represented as animatronics, and though they appear innocent during the day, entertaining the children with songs and games, at night they roam around the restaurant and don't take kindly to any humans still around. Your goal is to survive five nights, from 12 PM to 6 AM (around 10 minutes in real time), avoiding getting your face rammed into an animatronic suit. Sounds fun, right?
The gameplay is refreshingly simplistic. Instead of moving around with a flashlight like in most indie horror games, you are stuck inside the security office. You can use the security feed to monitor the mascots throughout the restaurant, check the doorlights and close the doors should one of the aggressors get a bit too close for comfort. This would be a lot easier if you didn't have a limited amount of energy to manage. Everything you do uses power; using the cameras, keeping the doors closed and turning on the lights. When the power runs out, the building goes into a black-out, and it won't take long until Freddy gets his chubby bear hands on you. You can't close the doors all willy-nilly, you gotta do it when you really have to.
Balancing is of course very important in every game, and FNaF handles it well. Foxy and Freddy force you to use your cameras while Bonnie and Chica require you to check your doors. In short, if you only use your camera, Bonnie or Chica will kill you, and if you never check your cameras, Foxy or Freddy will eventually get you without warning. There's a fairly competent difficulty curve, where new animatronics become active across the first few nights, and become more aggressive during the later nights. Unfortunately, with some very simple tactics the main nights become kind of easy. Even on the bonus night 6 it's perfectly possible to prevent Freddy and Foxy from even moving at all simply by watching them frequently enough. Yes, my main complaint about the game is that it's perhaps a bit too easy. Then again, Custom Night 7 allows you to make it as difficult as you want it to, so you could say it's a moot point. I just wish the main nights were just a bit more challenging.
Now let's clear up a misconception I frequently hear about this game.
"In Five Nights at Freddy's you're just waiting for a jumpscare to happen."
This is a rediculous statement. That's like saying "Super Mario Bros is just waiting until you get hit by a Goomba".  Unlike a lot of horror games, Five Nights at Freddy's uses jumpscares as a sort of punishment for failing. A succesful night will have virtually no jumpscares. You could say that the sound that plays when an animatronic appears in the doorlight is kind of cheap and pointless (FNaF 2 removed this), but they're not THAT bad. I prefer a screamer as a way to accentuate failure over one of those fake jumpscares common in horror any day.
FNaF isn't all about jumpscares either. It nails other horror aspects exceptionally well. From the eerie dark ambient music that plays subtely in the background to the pitter-patter of the mascots on the move all around you. Weird circus music plays from an unknown source, mysterious knocking on the walls and children's laughter echoes through the halls. This game is filled with brilliant atmospheric sound design, and I'm a sucker for good sound in video games. I found the sequel lacking in this regard. Paired with the ominous dark rooms of the restaurant, the parts room being the most unnerving, and you've got yourself a highly immersive horror game that seems so simplistic at first glance.
The concept of having sentient animatronics as villains in a horror game is such genius I'm surprised it hadn't been done before. It plays off the irrational fear of mascots and animatronics a lot of people seemed to have when they were kids (and perhaps still do). I can't say I have the same sentiment for animatronics, since chuck-e-cheese is not a thing where I live, but I know mascots at theme parks unnerved me when I was young. I found Freddy, Bonnie, Chica and Foxy so fascinatingly terrifying from the moment I saw them, and they were the main reason why this game spoke to me, but Foxy sprung out to me. While the first three are designed to be creepy stalkers, Foxy is simply scary. With his sharp teeth and threatening demeanor, he evokes a more rational, primal fear, like you would fear a wild animal. Seeing him sprint down the hall towards you is comparable to being jumped by a rabid dog. His design and behaviour conveys it perfectly. He means you harm in more obvious way.
I would say Five Nights at Freddy's is more than a game, it's a psychological test. How well do you handle stressful situations? Do you easily panic under pressure? Because the game totally punishes you if you do. When you start freaking out you make mistakes and lose track of what is really important. It feeds off your paranoia and kills you when you start losing it.
Horror is extremely subjective, and not everyone will get scared by the same things. If it didn't scare you, that's a shame, but you can't deny that Scott Cawthon did a damn good job on this one, especially considering he did everything by himself. It's a game that has scared the pants off of thousands of people, reached cult status in mere days after its release, introduced characters that are already iconic, has a deep and dark storyline that sparked huge amounts of theories and has countless fans chomping at the bits to see more of Five Nights at Freddy's 3 in the near future. Oh, and it's fun to boot.
Five Nights at Freddy's is THE new IP of 2014 that by far had the biggest impact on me and I can't wait to get some more of that goodness.

Weaving together themes of objectivism, transhumanism and political ideology,
builds a coherent narrative that is engaging and thought provoking. On the surface it is a first person shooter with RPG elements, presenting a unique fusion of traditional weapon based combat with plasmid powers to take down enemies. But when the subtle thematic elements, inspiring art style and intriguing characters are taken together the result is a highly memorable exploration of human beings and being human.
What is the role of government? What are the rights and responsibilities of the individual? What does it
to be human?
In attempting to address these questions Andrew Ryan built an underwater city to serve as a fortress where unbridled creativity could flourish from the worlds intellectual and cultural elite. The city is called Rapture, and Andrew Ryan is its king. He envisioned an objectivist utopia whose citizens would be free to pursue self-interest, built upon free-market enterprise. He encouraged his citizens to abandon religion in favour of the will to be great. He encouraged scientists to conduct research without restrictive ethical guidelines; artists to express themselves without the fear of censorship; businesses to trade free of regulations.
The result is a society that quickly becomes fractured down class lines amidst a background of greed, corruption and an economic recession that hits when construction of the city ends. Rapture disintegrates, its citizens splitting into factions - Sophia Lamb espouses an altruistic collectivist philosophy that sets a background of discontent as she discredits Ryan in several prominent debates. Atlas leads the working class poor, bitter about the empty promises offered to them in Raptures halls. Andrew Ryan maintains the loyalties of most of Raptures wealthy and powerful elite. Civil war breaks out, made all the more horrific by the militarisation of recent 'plasmid' technologies which were initially introduced to enhance human abilities and provide novel solutions to first world problems -
The player enters this world accidentally, finding the smouldering ruins of a once great city being picked over by genetically enhanced 'splicers', as well as the little sisters that gather ADAM from their bodies. This substance is used as a currency for the purchase of plasmid abilities, but the sisters are guarded by big daddies - behemoths in reinforced diving suits that wield drills and rivet guns. In order to survive the player must defeat the daddies to obtain ADAM from the sisters. In doing so they must make difficult choices and live with the consequences.
The story, characters and dialog are fantastic. Splicers inspire terror, their deformed appearences and desperate voices giving credence to their ADAM addictions. Big daddies evoke caution and a great deal of planning on how to take them down effectively while managing the resources at your disposal. Little sisters are the embodiment of childhood innocence, their bodies turned into processing factories for ADAM as they consume the essences of the perished while humming nursery rhymes. The protagonists have complex motivations, emotions and agency. Combat is fast paced, improvised, always different and rewarding.
Raptures atmosphere is immersive and engrossing. Audio logs contain snippets of the lives of its citizens before and since the breakdown, highlighting the changes and practical effects that abstract ideologies have on people caught between two warring sides. Technically the game is brilliant. Excellent voice acting, atmospheric sound design, a great soundtrack from around the period, enough graphical polish to keep up appearences. The underwater setting, ambient soundstage, optimistic music, horror elements, and contrasting verbal testaments from lead characters combine well to create a truely memorable experience.
Overall, BioShock is an inspiring achievement of storytelling and must be played to be believed.
To get even more out of BioShock after playing it through on normal and hard difficulties, I recommend the installation of "Silvers Bioshock Mod" which is currently in its final version (Version 7.2 alpha). This amazing little mod represents hours of testing by its author (psikoticsilver) and aims to intelligently increase the difficulty, reduce the amount of loot, and in doing so make the BioShock experience require even more planning and improvisation. It consists of several config files which are extracted to the game directory and is customisable. Installation instructions can be found on its mod page at
while a summarised (and additional exhaustive) list of changes is included with the mod download.
To really get into the nitty gritty about development and the vision behind the game I highly recommend checking out the series of
created by the publisher 2K Games that documents game production. It features many key roles - art, sound/music, gameplay design and also Ken Levine the creative director. His thoughts are always interesting to listen to and shed alot of insight onto some of the background ideas that inspired the game.
