I WANT to like this game so much I really do and there is a really a lot I admire about this game, but at the end of it lack of indepth game-play, annoying issues and replayability mean I can't recommend it.
What do I like?
SCENERY: Breathtaking and beautiful. I very often found myself sleeping in the day to look at stars at night!
REALISM: More in the mind. I found myself talking to myself during the game, double checking, reassuring, thinking and maybe even keeping myself company. Morale, oh how the heart sinks when you find a backpack when you are dying of hunger and it's -30 and it's EMPTY... The feeling inside of me was so intense and real... amazing and kudos!
MAP: Large enough to make it interesting and having to rely on your senses and remember way points.
MECHANICS: Drinking / Sleeping / Eating are all super interesting and reasonably well thought out.
In Summary - I loved the feelings this game gave me: scared, tired, drained, gutted, proud, not wanting to die - really incredible!
What did I not like - Why do I not recommend?
REPLAYABILITY: I am someone who wanted to stay alive a long time. I was in for the long haul. Sensible clothes, repairs, sleeping, drinking, stocking and never taking adverse risk. When out of the blue, I was walking along a hill from nothing it says, you died from massive internal injuries after a fall when I can see myself still standing was severely annoying and means I will probably not play this game again, because if that happens, there is really no point in playing a game that will randomly kill you with no reason. Exposure - yes / Famine/Dehydration - yes. Random unexplained death - NO. Secondly HOW DO YOU SAVE? I was playing a whole day straight because there is no apparent way to save and come back to it. I played it for a little while at first and got a bit bored as had a lot to do so just quit, when I came back I found I could "resume" however, many of the item's that I had already picked up were no longer in my bag and I had to go find them again so it's confusing as to how this works and as such annoying to start another longer game.
REALISM: 0.5Kg MRE = 1750 Calories / 1Kg Venison = 800 Calories... Not forgetting the effort needed to hunt, prepare, butcher and skin one!!! Can't store meat outside in "freezer" it spoils quickly despite it being -30... The fact that you starve very very easily... Yes, it should make you weaker, slower, tire more quickly but kill you no. Boiling pristine snow? Where and why is the snow so badly contaminated that I need to boil it? (Water you find - yes) Why when I just finished boiling water do I need to boil some more to make a tea?
How to improve (for me): Add more elements to the game - More things to scavenge / find naturally so you can try two ways: Live off only what you can find from man or nature... Add more natural things and make it realistic, more plant life tucked away. Berries that might / might not be poisonus (find a survival guide in a cabin and read it) More animals and better ways to hunt them (deadfall, spear, pit) More usage/crafting options for scavenged items. More realism than 8 mins to break down a simple crate with an axe... Why not be able to breakdown a ruined building. Add more interactability with surroundings. There should be a way to "mark" certain places or trails and surely a compass to be found/made and you should be able to make a "map". Add seasons, it's annoying that there is everlasting winter no matter how long you go. You should be able to live better in the warmer and prepare for the winter. More shelter options (fallen trees / tarps / snow caves...)
If you had this and you could reliably save ( meaning - up until that exact point stays the same unless you die "properly"...) I think I would not play another game again! But you don't and reading the Reddit section and all available info, it doesn't look like you are going this direction so I won't. 20 bucks for this or 50 for the Witcher, 20 bucks will give you about 20 hours of fun. 50 bucks will give you easily more than 100 on the Witcher therefore more bang for your buck! :)
Also apart from the "death by fall" incident, the game also crashed for me twice - once when heating peaches and the other when gutting a rabbit, so also annoying but fortunately I was only a couple of days in and not yet "comfortable".
All in all thank you for the experience but I feel like I wasted my money for a game that you will play for max 10-20 hours...

This game seems unfinished, or unpolished, or both. It seems to have gone through some redesign cycles and the gameplay still isn't quite there. The story finds ways to surprise you with deleveling somehow based on "conversation" choices that you can make on land... It seems the economy is locked in, which makes it nearly impossible to participate in early on once your hold is full of "quest items," and not able to sustain you as you travel, without expensive new ships. The available ship designs don't really seem like they were thought through - a result of clear winners and clear losers and the time it takes to save up for these items. This applies to weapons as well and the item economy. The game seems to throw a full page of officers out at you and then mysteriously stop, some leaving without warning during other parts of the story. You have combat/utility and shore/utility options if you remember to change the officers before you take actions.
On the other hand the story itself and the actions you must take to survive enable you to do just that, but this is not a shipping/market/ports game. There is some combat, and you can grind on monsters to supply yourself as you travel, but combat is mostly by convenience, as searching it out will lead to the loss of your resources creating cost to outweigh your savings very quickly.  The simple and few combat mechanics lack excitement and don't seem to evolve. It is definitely frustrating to have to start over from the beginning after you sink well into the game - apparently I completely missed how to engage the inheritance portion of the story in my 12 hours, which allows you to leave more stuff to your heir when you restart.
The UI's small fonts/reading pages and lack of voice narration ultimately adding to my unwillingness to recommend or buy this game after the free weekend. A game I need to have a film or music on to play, as the in game entertainment is intermittent. This is like a book that I need my granny glasses to read unfortunately, as the hours melt away and I'm still wondering how I'm supposed to make money with all these stores and commodities. Maybe they're meant to be used later on as expense reduction...
If you're not here for the fantastic WRITING and the strange(ambitious?) multi-tasking survival/resource/grind dynamic and haunting emptiness... pass.

This is a game by people who love to tell interesting stories in an interesting setting, and they do a great job of that. They originally did this in a web game called "Echo Bazaar" (later renamed "Fallen London"), which had a wonderful setting and stories but was crippled by an expensive time currency.
In Sunless Sea they've ported this setting and storytelling to a "pay once" game, but unfortunately they've replaced the time currency with some equally problematic and distracting mechanics. Whereas Fallen London's storytelling was undermined by having to wait (or pay way too much) for the time currency, Sunless Sea's storytelling is undermined by spending even more time slogging back and forth across empty oceans at a glacial pace, desperately trying to scrape together enough money from a broken trade system that you can afford the next expensive thing you need to advance the story. In 90% of cases, that "expensive thing you need to advance the story" is just enough basic supplies and fuel to reach the next plot checkpoint.
Sometimes you fight bad guys in a brainless combat system that involves going toe-to-toe with them until one of you dies, but the rewards for combat are typically much lower than the unavoidable repairs for the combat will cost you.
So what could be done to fix it? The core problem is pacing, and there are two things that could be done to improve this: fast travel, and the economy.
If I had the option of "Fast travelling from Port A to Port B is a chancy use of your whatever quality", instead of spending a half hour slogging across an empty ocean I'd slogged across a hundred times before, that would be a big improvement.
I would also suggest fixing the economy so that the player isn't spending the majority of his time trying not to go bankrupt, and could spend more time focusing on the stories.
If your game's primary goal is storytelling, but there's so much slog between story snippets that your players forget the stories, and if they see the same text so often that they stop reading, then you're not doing yourself any favors.
This game is very highly-rated in general, so obviously these aspects don't bother other players as much as they bother me, but I think these additions could give the game broader appeal, and also improve the game for those who already love it.

This game in my opinion is not one of the greatest Rogue-like shooters around (that would go to either tower of guns or Ziggurat), however this game does have many strong points. Firstly the level layouts are rather nice, with many possible entrances and exits in every room (Minumum of 4 possible exits). The gunplay isn't the best but it definitely works well and the aiming feels fluid and responsive. The god alignments was a neat idea to make character selection both random and interesting, good touch. and in Individual run you can feel a smooth difficulty
there is one sin in this game that holds it back from being the best rogue-like shooter on the market, it has a leveling system very similar to rogue legacy. you can increase stats with in game gold that you pick up on your runs. what this does is make the difficulty curve go downwards and effectively slowly remove challenges from immortal redneck. This heavily hinders the feeling of progression later on in the game when you level tree essentially nerfs everything in the game.  It makes the progression feel less "earned" than if there was a challenge based unlock system instead. Although mostly solid, there are a few big cons holding this game back from being absolutely amazing.
I still had fun in Immortal redneck despite the one big problem I had with it. Immortal redneck gives me that "one more run" feeling I love from these rogue-like shooters. Immortal Redneck is a first person shooter with strong rogue-lite elements. In the settings of the ancient Egypt you, the mummified remnant "Redneck" are challenged to complete three different pyramid, each ones with their particular theme, with a mini boss every third level and a boss on the seventh floor. Graphics are vibrant, colorful and cartoonish, rooms are not procedural generated but carefully hand-crafted with an impressive good amount of variety, their positions are, though. The goal is to clear every rooms until you find the stairs to the upper level in a sort of old-school fps arena macth, like Painkiller. Perks are dropping in form of scrolls, they can be for the most part good but the bad ones are sometimes really bad, thus, with the randomized rooms position, the rogue-lite elements. You can buy permanent upgrades and unlock other "characters" (each one with a particular set of weapons and skills) in the skill tree with the gold collected through the runs. You beat the game when you complete the third and last pyramid.
While the action is frantic and really reminding of a fast paced old-school arena shooter, the guns feedback and the animation quality of the enemies are way below average, giving sometimes the impression to shoot at toys with toy guns, all cons of which the devs (who are really inclined to listen to the community) are already stating they're going to address.
Immortal Redneck is a first person shooter with strong rogue-lite elements. You begin the game at the main HUB as the "Redneck", a mummified farmer from Kansas who happens to be in Egypt to destroy malevolent entities known as "immortals".
The first step is to enter the first pyramid, where you'll be able to collect gold to unlock other deities, or"favors" in the skill tree, instead of having different character you'll going to be always the Redneck but stats, initial set of weapons active and passive skill are different depending on of which god you choose the favor.
To unlock those favors you need to invest a certain amount of gold to buy skills level upgrade of a certain stat. The main stas are as plain as they can be: damage, health, defense, crit chance and crit damage. Investing in them will eventually unlock other part of the tree like %gold drop, health recovered bonus, ammo found bonus and speed bonus. Really nothing special.
At one point you'll unlock the merchant, a guy with a really limited selection of items: you can choose to buy a random scroll, a guaranteed good random scroll or a map which locks the exact same map previously played but you won't be able to collect any gold in it. Also you can buy amulets, each one of them has a special effect but you need to find the blueprints inside the pyramid first and then spend some gold to craft it. Once it's done you'll keep the amulet forever and you just have to equip the one of your choice.
The game is divided in 3 pyramids, each one of them has 7 floors with a boss battle on the top, to access the second pyramis you have to beat the boss of the first one and so on. Every 3 floors you have a mini-boss room and every floor is divided in rooms, each one of them is basically an hand-crafted arena but their position on the floor are randomized at each run. To complete the room you have to kill every single enemy in. A gold sand bar indicates the amount of enemies still in the room, if you are having troubles to find the usual wandering loner, you'll be gifted with x-ray vision and it would appear as a bright-red shadow on your field of vision throught the walls.
Throught the floors you'll encounter chest-rooms, with 1 to 3 chests in it or challenges like time trial, don't get hurt, reach the chest without killing any enemies or simply find a way to get the chest. Failing the challenges will make the chests disappear.
Chests contains a fair amount of gold, health, ammo, scrolls and weapons so you definetely want to get as many as possible. Also they can be found in regular room and they works as a sort of "secret", exploring the rooms is always encouraged.
While you start the game with a prefixed set of weapon (or four, depending on your favor of choice) you'll stumble across some more inside the pyramid. You can carry a limited amount of weapons (usually 3) that can be expanded if you're lucky enough to find the right scroll. The more favors you unlock, more weapons have a chance to drop while playing.
Talking about scrolls, they're the perks you're gambilng on. They can be really good as double the amount of crit chance, or increase the gold collected or flat out increase all of your base stats but they can be also really, really bad as losing 20% of your collected gold, being unable to stand still and be forced to move perpetually or lose all of your weapons and replace them with random ones. Although there are definetely more good scrolls than bad ones, it's alway a gamble that can screw a really good run, which is a prerequisite for any game with some rogue-lite elements.
The gameplay is incredibly fast paced, controls are quick, responsive, a lot of jumping from side to side in some really well crafted level, each one of them enphasizes verticality, or have and open space kind of approch, corridors, floating platforms, elevators, lava pits, spike traps, fire vents, secret passages and so on, and the feel is really like playing an old-school are fps, especially when you unlock double jumps and maximixe the speed skill. You'll be able to jump from one end of the room to another while shooting flying enemies and avoiding flaming arrows coming from below and from above.
However it's not all roses, there are some flaw that can be a huge deterrent for some hardcore fps fans. Weapons feedback is really, really poor. While some weapons are really satisfying to use like the "4th of July" and the "Rocket Launcher" some others feels like toy guns, with a poor animation and sound feedback on them. And to add at the injury the animation quality of the enemies is sometimes abysmal so you're in a situation where you shooting a toy gun against toy enemies. No sense of impact at all, and that's really a shame because it's something that could undermine an otherwise incredibly well crafted game.

This game is much different from Tropico 1 and 4, with that so far it has its merits and a few things that I am missing from the series.
Some of the changes:
Much less banter like in 4, I really enjoyed some of the voice over work, made me laugh quite a bit.
You play as your own character, I really enjoyed playing as past dictators in 1 and 4, unless I am missing something.
Buildings unlock in 5 as you progress, in 4 you could place anything you could afford.  4 was a much more build oriented game with a nice story arch, there may still be a story arch in 5, but it is more multiplayer game than solo.
Solo scenarios go very, very fast to begin, I am sure those extend quite a bit as you move farther into the game.
I actually like the graphics of the building much better in 4.
I preferred the direct quotes on the save pages in 4 vs. the dictator "fun facts" on the save pages in 5...I know nit picking :)
Some of the things I do really enjoy so far with 5:
The whole trade system is a huge improvement, its fun to direct and agree where your goods go.
There are pirates, I like pirates.
Using exploration to discover portions of your islands make a lot of sense, but so far no natives have killed my tiny explorers...I would kind of think they risk getting boiled in a pot, but maybe I have just been lucky so far.
It does feel like I have to work harder to get my approval rating up and I have fewer choices to do so, especially early, I do like the challenge, but think more early choices would help the game.
New music...and yes I know that's the Squirrel Nut Zippers on at least one song.
I like that the building upgrades need to be researched and can't just be upgraded in 3 clicks like in 4, you have to work for those a bit more, not simply rake in money.
So far, Tropico 5 does feel like a pretty big departure from 4.  I have seen 4 described as a fun city builder game with good challenges.  5 feels like it is going to be much more unpredictable and interactive as long as you get a good group of people you know to play along.
My final recommendation on this is, grab Tropico 4, a great bargain now and a ton of fun.  I think Tropico 5 will continue to build on the series and this feels like the base of a new, evolving game.  5 is going to provide a lot of gaming enjoyment, but I think it needs more time to develop.  My biggest fear in buying the game was that it would be going online like Sim City 5 and have an EA-style launch disaster...it hasn't and so far as long as you have an up to date video card, Direct X 11 and a fast, newer machine, the game has not hit very few snags.  It is a good, positive launch, hopefully with much more to come.

The game looks like its predecessor's poorer cousin. There is less of everything - including building models, music or customization options - compared even to Tropico 4 without any expansions and DLCs. Quality of the existing content also seems actually worse than in the previous installation.
As for the gameplay, it seems more shallow. I'm not sure how happiness translates into popular support, because even with my Tropicans being pretty unhappy I never had problems with winning elections without fixing votes. You can rake serious debt without any repercussions and, with the amount of resources on the average island, it's easy to make obscene amounts of money without trying too much.
The new features are underwhelming. The consecutive eras don't change much except building models and the amount of available buildings and technologies. The only exception is the Colonial Era - you advance by converting people from Royalist to Independence faction. This sounds like fun but actually isn't - most of the buildings, edicts and other game features are locked, so you pretty much build the same thing several times and pray that the game lets you pass to its more interesting part before the time limit expires.
The family system also disappoints. From time to time, you get an another inhabitant of the island who happens to have the same last name as El Presidente. They can be sent to manage a building and may be useful during some events - and that's pretty much it. You can also let them run in elections instead of you, but you usually don't want to do that - most likely, your current president is more experienced anyway.
To sum it all up - Tropico 4 is simply better than its supposed successor.

Weaving together themes of objectivism, transhumanism and political ideology,
builds a coherent narrative that is engaging and thought provoking. On the surface it is a first person shooter with RPG elements, presenting a unique fusion of traditional weapon based combat with plasmid powers to take down enemies. But when the subtle thematic elements, inspiring art style and intriguing characters are taken together the result is a highly memorable exploration of human beings and being human.
What is the role of government? What are the rights and responsibilities of the individual? What does it
to be human?
In attempting to address these questions Andrew Ryan built an underwater city to serve as a fortress where unbridled creativity could flourish from the worlds intellectual and cultural elite. The city is called Rapture, and Andrew Ryan is its king. He envisioned an objectivist utopia whose citizens would be free to pursue self-interest, built upon free-market enterprise. He encouraged his citizens to abandon religion in favour of the will to be great. He encouraged scientists to conduct research without restrictive ethical guidelines; artists to express themselves without the fear of censorship; businesses to trade free of regulations.
The result is a society that quickly becomes fractured down class lines amidst a background of greed, corruption and an economic recession that hits when construction of the city ends. Rapture disintegrates, its citizens splitting into factions - Sophia Lamb espouses an altruistic collectivist philosophy that sets a background of discontent as she discredits Ryan in several prominent debates. Atlas leads the working class poor, bitter about the empty promises offered to them in Raptures halls. Andrew Ryan maintains the loyalties of most of Raptures wealthy and powerful elite. Civil war breaks out, made all the more horrific by the militarisation of recent 'plasmid' technologies which were initially introduced to enhance human abilities and provide novel solutions to first world problems -
The player enters this world accidentally, finding the smouldering ruins of a once great city being picked over by genetically enhanced 'splicers', as well as the little sisters that gather ADAM from their bodies. This substance is used as a currency for the purchase of plasmid abilities, but the sisters are guarded by big daddies - behemoths in reinforced diving suits that wield drills and rivet guns. In order to survive the player must defeat the daddies to obtain ADAM from the sisters. In doing so they must make difficult choices and live with the consequences.
The story, characters and dialog are fantastic. Splicers inspire terror, their deformed appearences and desperate voices giving credence to their ADAM addictions. Big daddies evoke caution and a great deal of planning on how to take them down effectively while managing the resources at your disposal. Little sisters are the embodiment of childhood innocence, their bodies turned into processing factories for ADAM as they consume the essences of the perished while humming nursery rhymes. The protagonists have complex motivations, emotions and agency. Combat is fast paced, improvised, always different and rewarding.
Raptures atmosphere is immersive and engrossing. Audio logs contain snippets of the lives of its citizens before and since the breakdown, highlighting the changes and practical effects that abstract ideologies have on people caught between two warring sides. Technically the game is brilliant. Excellent voice acting, atmospheric sound design, a great soundtrack from around the period, enough graphical polish to keep up appearences. The underwater setting, ambient soundstage, optimistic music, horror elements, and contrasting verbal testaments from lead characters combine well to create a truely memorable experience.
Overall, BioShock is an inspiring achievement of storytelling and must be played to be believed.
To get even more out of BioShock after playing it through on normal and hard difficulties, I recommend the installation of "Silvers Bioshock Mod" which is currently in its final version (Version 7.2 alpha). This amazing little mod represents hours of testing by its author (psikoticsilver) and aims to intelligently increase the difficulty, reduce the amount of loot, and in doing so make the BioShock experience require even more planning and improvisation. It consists of several config files which are extracted to the game directory and is customisable. Installation instructions can be found on its mod page at
while a summarised (and additional exhaustive) list of changes is included with the mod download.
To really get into the nitty gritty about development and the vision behind the game I highly recommend checking out the series of
created by the publisher 2K Games that documents game production. It features many key roles - art, sound/music, gameplay design and also Ken Levine the creative director. His thoughts are always interesting to listen to and shed alot of insight onto some of the background ideas that inspired the game.

The one thing I really like about Tropico 5 is that they really tried to make a new game. Anyone who's played the last 2 Tropico games knows that they're basically the same game with a little graphical touch up. Everything in Tropico 5 is different, from the apartments, to the power plants, everything has been redone.
A lot of mechanics have been improved to feel less redundant and more intuitive. Now you can clearly  see how much space plantations will require, and gone are the days were you can't figure out how to get rid of the "garage overloaded" message.
The campaign has changed in a big way. Maps from the previous missions are saved and you pick up where you left off in the next mission. No more having to start from scratch, the campaign is much more rewarding, and finally allows for building sprawling cities.
But my favourite thing about the campaign is that it is finally challenging. I loved Tropico 3, but some of the missions in Tropico 4 were so mind boggling simple, they were exhausting. Tropico 5 brings the challenge in a new way and actually encourages building sustainablitiy instead of suiciding your treasury for mundane mission goals so you can win and start over.
I haven't played the multiplayer yet, and I don't really plan to. This is the first time a Tropico game has really interested me with its sandbox mechanics, and when I'm done with the campaign I think I'll spend a long time trying to build the coolest island I can.

Goodness, where do I begin?
Grappling in Silver Grapple is as fun as it looks. The controls are tight and polished, allowing you to a large amount of control over your character's position and speed.
The level design in Silver Grapple is equally excellent. Paired with tight controls and satisfying grappling physics, the levels test both your skill and knowledge of game the physics. The levels are always fair to the player. Instantaneous respawns, generous checkpoints, and the ability to warp back to your checkpoint if death is inevitable all help keep the game pace very fast. Deaths are not punishing, but expect to fail repeatedly. When levels are properly executed, at it's best Silver Grapple makes you feel like a proffesional acrobat.
The story and lore in the game were deep enough to get me invested, although are completely optional and secondary to the gameplay. The ost in Silver Grapple is also worth mentioning, as the chiptune soundtrack accompanying the gameplay was very pleasing to listen to. On a visual standpoint, the game environments aren't the flashiest or most well developed. However, I don't believe this to take much from game enjoyability, as the player animations are smooth and satisfying to watch again and again.
Silver Grapple is the most suprising indie game I've seen released this year. If you enjoy difficult yet rewarding platforms like Super Meat Boy, or if the trailer interests you in any way, I certainly reccomend the purchase.

I just finished playing Just Cause 3 and realized that I never wrote a review for this awesome game.
Even though this game is 6 years old now, it has held up incredibly well. The graphics, while not anything special by modern standards, are still decent and the draw distances is still much better than 99% of the other games out there. The gameplay is still solid and plenty of fun.
What really keeps drawing me back to this game time and again is the world. The map is absolutely gigantic by the standards of any game not using procedural map generation, and because it was hand built it is chock full of interesting content just inviting you to get out and explore (and cause random chaos while you're at it).
Sure this game isn't perfect, the vehicle handling is pretty poor, the AI isn't anything special, the black market system has some issues (finite resources in game being the biggest one), chaos objects aren't shown on that map which makes finding the last one or two chaos objects extremely frustrating at times, and the story is barely passable (although it has some pretty epic set pieces), but these issues are forgivable since this game is simply so much fun to play, especially with the free multiplayer mod.
Given how cheap this game is now and how much fun it still is (I consider it to be superior to JC3 in that regard), it is extremely easy to recommend.

This top down sea adventure game takes me back to times of slower paced text-based games. It leaves most of the visuals of the world and happenings to the player's imagination.
The text isn't too long winded or flavored. But it is just enough to give the player a sense of the environment and the people around them. Some dialog options has elements of RNG based on player stats and other sources of networking. While other opinions are more linear paths of choices, using stats or item clears.
The sailing and combat is active real-time, you'll have to steer your ship and click on the enemy you wish to attack. There's a lower hit chance rate if you shoot before your crew finished targeting. As for dodging attacks, you can out maneuver pirate ships, but monster crabs might be impossible to out maneuver around. Mainly, the best strategy I've found was running away from crabs, and sneaking around pirates.
As for replayablity, I think it lies in what you want to accomplish. The world map does change to an extent, but the stories you've encountered seems to remain the same. What changes the most is your character and the win conditions you set for yourself.
If the game story and the world seems oddly familiar to you, this is the continuation of Fallen London, the free to play browser game.

Remember that old game "Commandos?" The one where you controlled a (small) squad of troops who would have to infiltrate Nazi camps and do stuff? But all you really ended up doing was staring at your computer screen for hours memorizing the Nazis' walking patterns?
Well, that's what Outlast is, only in a first person perspective. You sit and wait. It also has perhaps the least imaginative "no combat" system one could think of. Thief had no combat (okay, you could fight, but you'd lose real quick), but you still weren't passive. You could manipulate things to protect yourself (douse lights, blanket the ground, etc.). Not this protagonist. He just breathes real heavy to remind you that this is scary.
And the camera! Guy gets his fingers cut off, what does he do? Picks up his camera! Cuz, yeah, I wouldn't bandage my hands either, but grab my camera and scamper off under a bed to watch the story unfold around me. Which is what you do in this much beloved walking simulator. It's a haunted house walking simulator, which is neat, but it's still a walking simulator.

MY REVIEW
(MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS)
I played this during the three days it was out for free and frankly, based on my experience of the game, It's causing me to buy the game as it is.
WHAT IS THIS GAME?
Sunless sea is an open world, surviving Overhead POV game taking place in the late 1800s. You are the captain of a ship in an alternate world where the world has become sea-filled world and you virtually just....explore. You begin at London or at least, what's left of it and You are given some objectives in which you complete by traveling around and the way they do this is done right. There hasn't been a time where I stopped playing until I died. Immersion in this game is very heavy as you decide the best courses of actions or questioning how you strategically use your resources to maximize your usage of each of them. The "Zee" is full of mysteries that even I myself have yet to extensively find or solve. I wont go into too much detail on this, but I will say this, you will be busy....VERY busy and dont
PROS AND CONS:
+Frequently auto saves: Every decision you make, everytime you get to port, it WILL autosave and you are freely able to disable it and do manual saves (Though i wouldn't recommend it if you wanna play by the rules)
+Easy to learn, Hard to master: The game gives you the right amount of information to get started, but not engulf you with a lot of information that would cause you to lose interest. Spoonfuls rather than bowls.
+Immersion is intense: Once you start to travel from your home port, to the huge sea world out there, you'll start to learn how dangerous and unforgiving it is to be out there and how scary it can be to sail the dark depths of the "zee".
+Artwork and designs: Eye candy...the atmosphere and ambience of the "Zee" just fits well with the artwork and just adds to the creep factor of being out at see
+-Music: Music blends well with the game, it defines every place perfectly with a proper orchestral cue, though I put it as both a pro and a con cause you would be hearing the song cues A LOT.
+-Permadeath: This game has a bit of a permadeath feature included on it, but if you know how to work around it, it's not too bad of a feature to be included and it gives you more reason to feel more cautious on being risky.
-Money: Getting money can be a hassle. I didn't have that difficult of a time finding money after the 3rd time getting in it, but you will be busy starting out small and working up to getting higher amounts of money cause you need A LOT....of money...like A LOT....but the game gives you plenty of opportunities.
-Enemies: there are some easy ones, some REALLY annoying ones, and a very few neutrals. Some of the A.I.s can be cheesed pretty easily, and some are relentlessly hard (had like a power house ship with strong cannons, and i still get demolished) but they're aren't impossible. You'll see what I mean when you play it.
IS IT WORTH $20 ($18.99 if you didn't receive the weekend deal)?
At the current state that it's in, not really...but it is definitely worth getting when on sale and from what I've heard, they have more upcoming content. If you wish to keep the game for future updates then definitely buy it for whatever price it has, or wait for a deal...either way, this is a game you shouldn't just ignore.

Cuphead is one of those games that you can hardly put down, not only because it fills you with determination to pursue a perfect run, but because it's a charming piece of art, from the Jazzy OST to the watercolor backgrounds, the game's difficulty can be a bit harsh for newcomers, even the most seasoned of players can find a good challenge in the boss fights.
The Good: Cuphead brings some fresh ideas to the genre, the overworld map was a great addition and the unique boss mechanics were just great, add those charming cartoon graphics and the old film screen filter and you're set to roll.
The Bad: This is just my opinion but i think the game should use some more gameplay modes, like time attack or a boss rush mode, each boss fight takes about 1:50 - 2:15 minutes (varying from player to player) so a boss rush should take long enough to be enjoyable without feeling like an endless torture, that would add another layer of challenge for those hardcore masochists out there and it would be fun to see "how long i last on a boss rush mode".
The Ugly: "It may" scare some casual players out there, certainly this is not a beginner's game in my opinion at least, it demands a bit more concentration than your average platformer games, with so many things going on in your screen and at the same time, it dishes out a challenge that may bloat some of the younger inexperienced players. However i believe this is one of those games that get you "baptized on fire" like Megaman 2 was back in my days, so if you happen to be a videogame newbie, don't despair, the game will teach you the ropes and will provide you with some hardcore skills by the time you master it. Just keep trying, it will be worth it.

I never thought that solitaire, is the type of card game to which a new spin may be added. Then again, this title is far more than a simple solitaire game with a Regency Era (1795 – 1837) skin placed over it. Regency Solitaire is here to tell a story, one which isn’t half bad if you’re into Jane Austen’s style of writing (also known as “novels of manners”). Before I delve deeper into the card gameplay itself, I would like to point out that the beautifully drawn locations and characters would have surely benefited from some level of voice acting, which sadly isn’t present. That is the game’s sole con, as the rest of it is most pleasing given the small file-size. I admit that I seldom play cards and even less frequent have been my incursions into solitaire. I have to say, the game is wrongfully perceived by some as the bureaucratic time waster of choice. Regency Solitaire convinced me that there’s more to this card game than meets the eye. A progressive difficulty system and the presence of a tutorial, provided plenty of assistance. No glitches disturbed my gameplay and the inclusion of both Trading Cards and Achievements justify the price tag even more. If you’re into card games, Regency Solitaire shall not disappoint you.

+ Beautiful graphics and storyline.
+ Fully functional and competent card game.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
- Repetitive musical score and no voice acting.

I got myself in an odd position with this game. I watched the TotalBiscuit review, and felt like I had to avoid this game. At the same time, however, something in my head said I should give it a chance. Hell, I wanted a game like Ziggurat, but with guns, and this is exactly what this game is. So I decided to buy it anyways to test it myself. At first, I noticed that I disliked the gunplay a lot. Enemies have no reaction to your shots, most weapons are a bit weaker than they should, reloading takes forever, etc. I also disliked the scroll system at first, and noticed some other issues.
I then thought about asking for a refund, but then I noticed something: I couldn't refund because I already played 3 hours of it at that point. 3 hours, but it felt like 5 minutes or so! It was then when I realized I was having so much fun, I just didn't feel the time passage. The flaws ARE there, and they ARE noticeable. But the thing is: the flaws just didn't bothered me as much as I thought they would. Heck, they feel VERY minor while buried below the huge pile of good qualities this game throws at us.
And now I have to say it, and I'm gonna shout: THIS IS THE BEST INDIE ROGUELITE I HAVE PLAYED IN A WHILE! The game is just... too fun. It's challenging, frustrating at times. It DOES make me angry sometimes. But it's FUN. Just pure fun.
Just like most games in this genre, every map is randomly generated. But this game feels... different. The rooms are usually well made and fun to travel. I'm sure they are a pack of handmade prefabs, but after playing for quite a while, I'm yet to see a map that felt too similar to a previous one. The game has some Rogue Legacy elements, like the progress being mostly related to the money, a limited choice of characters to choose between all the ones you unlocked, being forced to leave all your money behind when you enter the dungeon again (forcing you to ALWAYS do better in every run), and that pleased me a lot. ^^
The gameplay is just great. Like I said, the gunplay is quite weak, but not gamebreaking. The areas you traverse are usually bigger than what we are used to ijn games like this, and feature lots of more vertical areas where platforming is needed. And just like the new Doom, you can grab on ledges and get yourself up when you jump, making the platform elements quite fun (instead of frustrating). And the controls are just perfect. It's easy to move around and go exactly where you want. If you fall on a pit of lava, it's due to your own mistakes, not due to the game's controls.
The RNG aspect is strong in here. And yes, sometimes you get unlucky to the point you WILL die in a few minutes due to random traits. But a Roguelite without strong RNG is not a real Roguelite, right? The randomness in here never bothered me as much as I thought it would. I died because I got horrible weapons before, I died because of a string of horrible scrolls. But everything felt fun anyways. I just restarted and got better stuff. Luck plays a big part in here, but I don't think this is a bad thing.
Lastly, the graphics are surprisingly good. There's nothing amazing looking in here, but the game IS pleasing on the eyes. The sand is beautiful, the reflexive tiles in some rooms are amazing, the weapons are... weird (in a good way, though) and very well animated. Enemies are weird and not very detailed, but are quite well animated. The first boss I fought, for example, has a VERY smooth animation and looks as menacing as a boss that's about to kick my♥♥♥♥♥should. There's nothing amazing-looking here, being an Indie game and all, but I also have nothing to complain about the graphics. And the game runs at a constant 60 FPS (at 1080p) in my not-so-good PC. I would say it's above average compared to other indies. The sound department leaves a bit to be desired, however. The musics are forgettable and there aren't many of them, and the sound effects are just... too quiet. Even a shotgun sounds more like a pea shooting gun in here. That's just a minor issue, but I hope they update it someday.
In closing, this game is just amazing. It's flawed, yes, but it's one of those games where the flaws are actually forgotten after a while due to how much FUN the game is. This is one of the best games I've played this year, even when compared with some AAA titles. I HIGHLY recommend it for fans of Roguelite shooters. ^^
EDIT: One thing that I also should mention is that this game is FAR from abandoned. It's clear that the developers are listening to the criticisms and patching the game surprisingly fast for an indie game. They REALLY deserve respect, and I'll GLADLY update this review acordingly.

Immortal Redneck is definitely one of the best roguelite FPS games available, right up there with Tower of Guns and Ziggurat.
How the game works is simple, but made complex by how random the game is. There are 3 pyramids that you have to beat in order and to beat a pyramid you have to traverse through multiple floors of the pyramid, fighting enemies and bosses on the way, along with finding chests and overcoming challenges in challenge rooms. Enemies and chests will drop new weapons or scrolls, which are mostly good, but sometimes also include neutral or bad effects. After you die or defeat a pyramid, you then go back to the outside where you can expend your money on new skills on the skill tree or buying things from the merchant.
You start with no "favours", playing as the Redneck, who has average stats, an average set of starting weapons, receives more ammo from ammo boxes and can temporarily increase his fire rate. As you unlock new favours from the skill tree, you'll then have access to these favours which change your stats, starting weapons, passive ability and active ability.
As mentioned, it's a simple premise, but due to the scrolls you'll find on your way, the game becomes a lot more complex and fun. Scrolls are mostly good and will give you varying benefits like an extra weapon slot, an instant ressurrect if you die, more HP, more max ammo or make you immune to environment damage, whereas neutral scrolls can replace your weapons with random ones or take half of your current HP to give you 2 other scrolls and bad scrolls will give you effects like removing your crosshair, making it so you never stop moving or taking fall damage.
How successful a run will be depends not only on the player's skill and the benefits gotten from the skill tree, but also on the effects of said scrolls.
But the thing is, even when you do get a bad scroll, it doesn't make the game any less fun - sometimes a single bad scroll can ruin your entire run, but it's still fun as hell to try to roll with the blows as your character never stops moving or has no crosshair to aim. Granted, there is some frustration level when you're doing well during a run and then suddenly that one bad scroll potentially ruins everything, but it doesn't make the game any less fun, specially when you keep on trying to go all the way up to defeat the boss at the top even while you have bad scrolls in effect. (actually, when I first defeated the first pyramid, I had two very bad scrolls in effect and still managed to do it anyway)
As there are a lot of upgrades and medallions to buy from the skill tree and the merchant, there are a lot of ways to improve your character, so even if the game feels hard at first, soon it'll feel a lot easier as you get used to the game and improve your character. That is, at least, until you then go to the next pyramid, when you're introduced to new enemies and a higher level of challenge...
As for the game's design, the interesting thing is that the three pyramids all look different from each other, each of them having their own style (or theme), so it doesn't feel like you're always seeing the same scenery. Not only that, but the two pyramids after the first one also include new rooms as well.
One very interesting feature the game has is a Twitch feature. When it's turned on, enemies and chests will no longer drop scrolls, instead your audience will vote for which scroll you'll get next from a selection of 3 scrolls, so whether you'll do great or terrible will be up to whether your audience wants you to succeed or want to get a chuckle out of seeing you getting screwed. The only downside to this is that it only works if you have at least some audience. If no one votes, you'll automatically get a &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; scroll (doesn't do anything). Also, if the game loses connection to the Twitch servers, it'll automatically return you to the main menu.
There is a lot of room for improvement and expansion in the game - more weapons, more pyramids with more enemies, new scroll effects, new favours... I'm really curious to see how the future of this game is going to be.

When you load up Regency Soiltaire for the first time, you will be almost overwhelmed by all the kitsch that literally slaps you in the face. It's not bad, however; it grows on you in a weird way and after the first few levels you won't mind the shamelessly ridiculous baroque atmosphere anymore. It's similar with the story - god, it's so simple, conciously archetypical and still you can't help to feel a weird sympathy for what's unfolding on your screen. You probably need to like the trashy kitsch-atmosphere or really love baroque, or you won't feel the same. Maybe it's just Stockholm Syndrome. All in all, it's not too bad and everyone purchasing this should already know what to expect after taking a short glance at the storefront.
Don't get fooled by the name - Regency Solitaire is not really Solitaire how you know it from your Windows-installations or Linux-repositories. There is no stacking of cards. Instead, you take cards from into your hand by clicking on it, but only if the card is exactly one value higheror lower than the current card on top of your hand. If there is no such card on the field, you draw one from a stack of cards. The game ends once the field or the stack is empty, the former is preferred. There a three abilities with a recharge and some special types of cards which bring a little bit of variety. Between sessions you spend the money you have earned while playing cards for powerups.
All of this is really relaxing, because you just click, and click and click without having much to worry about. Most of the time the next step to take is absolutely clear, it is very rare that you have actually a hard time deciding between two options. That is my main gripe with the game: You have almost no influence over what outcome the round will have. As I have said, you almost never have a real choice. If you win or not, is mostly a question of what cards are in your stack and on the field. There are games in which it is almost impossible to win, then you hit the retry-button and make it in two minutes. Three powerups bring a little bit of spice in the game, but they reload so slow that you can use them only once per round anyway, so they don't matter too much. In the end, it's just a game against your own time, when you hit the retry-button for so long until you got a good result.

After Spacebase DF9 I think the danger of Early Access is buying into a promise. The thing that one day may be is exciting, and can color the perception of what is right now.  I will never buy or recommend a game based on what it may one day become, but I can recommend this game on what it is right now. As it stands, right now, this is a game worth playing, but be aware that currently the minimalist art style is reflected in minimalist gameplay. There is just enough gameplay related content here, such as predators, pray, weather effects, and developed mechanics such as cooking, crafting, illness, injury and medicine, or "decorating" your home with your scavanged supplies to make it worthwhile.
(To the devs: The object moving and placing mechanic is extremly well implemented. A joy to use. Kudos!)
There is a great deal of area to explore, a compelling vista that at times can be beautiful, and atmospheric, but personally I believe breadth of game is secondary to depth of gameplay and at this point it is just deep enough to allow for some interesting emergent experiences. But just barely.

This is very solid Shooter Roguelite with a skill tree that presists between deaths. It's very easy on the eyes and runs well!
Movement is king in shooters and it feels great in IR; this game has verticality not seen in Ziggurat (probably the game IR reminds me most of) but it's not the the extermes of say, Tower of Guns. Being able to grab ledges REALLY makes first person platforming more enjoyable. A few runs gives you access to multi-jumping which is awesomeeeee.
People are comparing this game to Serious Sam, and while IR is an older-ish school shooter at heart I think they really only share the Egyptian asthetic. To me the gunplay is very different. Notably, many weapons recoil and have COF, so most guns in IR reward accuracy and use at correct range. Overall, this works and shooting stuff in IR is satisfying and skill based. The gun selection is very large with lots of fun and unique hardware to choose from.
FPS veterans will breeze through the first Pyramid, but I'd still recommend them this game. Anyone who's enjoyed the latest developments in the Rogue FPS genre will probably not regret the price of entry.
Edit: Oh, yeah: mummy pole-dancers too.

I just finished playing Just Cause 3 and realized that I never wrote a review for this awesome game.
Even though this game is 6 years old now, it has held up incredibly well. The graphics, while not anything special by modern standards, are still decent and the draw distances is still much better than 99% of the other games out there. The gameplay is still solid and plenty of fun.
What really keeps drawing me back to this game time and again is the world. The map is absolutely gigantic by the standards of any game not using procedural map generation, and because it was hand built it is chock full of interesting content just inviting you to get out and explore (and cause random chaos while you're at it).
Sure this game isn't perfect, the vehicle handling is pretty poor, the AI isn't anything special, the black market system has some issues (finite resources in game being the biggest one), chaos objects aren't shown on that map which makes finding the last one or two chaos objects extremely frustrating at times, and the story is barely passable (although it has some pretty epic set pieces), but these issues are forgivable since this game is simply so much fun to play, especially with the free multiplayer mod.
Given how cheap this game is now and how much fun it still is (I consider it to be superior to JC3 in that regard), it is extremely easy to recommend.

This is my second and updated review for Batman, lets get stuck in.
Unfortunately I still give this game a regrettable "negative", I want to give it a positive but just when I think they have finally fixed the performance issues they raise their ugly head again (in chapter 3 the lip sync is out by around 3-5 seconds for at least 10 minutes of gameplay), the stuttering is still present and seems to be caused by the engine just being unable to load all the "detail" in the game world (it looks like a game from 2010, cant be too difficult in 2016).
The performance issues aren’t a massive disincentive however, the real issue I have is with the story in general or rather the seemingly lack of "multiple choice", for instance in no particular order:
1) Characters keep telling you off for hurting or even murdering people despite the fact I have gone out of my way to be a "good guy" and not hurt or kill anyone (they try and push in the game its the media manipulating people, I think its them being lazy and not coding the events properly, case example a cop telling me off for seriously injuring a suspect despite the fact he should know I didn't).
2) Choices you make seem to always lead to the same outcome regardless, more so than other games telltale have made, it makes the experience very linear.
3) This is a big one and a *spoiler*, ties into point 2..... at the end of chapter 3 you have the option to give a good speech, political and not rise to the level of the penguin, needless to say the game ends with you going crazy due to a drug injection completely undoing all the careful political manoeuvring you did for the whole episode, showing how next episode you end up hated by everyone and put in an asylum for being insane... nice multiple choice their telltale, would love to see how you integrate my past choices into that one, why did I even bother?
Overall I get the distinct feeling to get the most out of this game you have to play as if batman has an existential crisis of identity and wants to go to the low levels of the bad guys, all the dialogue seems to point to that and I think if you enjoy that side of batman (eg not being batman at all) the game would make a lot more sense.
I will keep playing because its a good way to waste a few hours, I know my choices result in little but at least it is enjoyable.
Overall 6/10, ok but I would wait until its on offer.

This game is what Cave Story + Bionic Commando would look like.   You have the visuals, charm, and explorations of the first, and the swinging hook mechanic of the latter.
The game really surprised me on all fronts.  For starters, it was a much larger game than I was expecting in terms of the map, and it was much harder than I was expecting as well.   I'm a pretty serious advanced platform player, "I Wanna Be the Guy" is kids play to me, this game is pretty hard.  With that difficulty though comes really some amazing level designs that keep coming up with new and clever ways to tie the hook mechanic into the platforming pretty much all the way to the end.  You will die a ton, but respawn points are very plentiful and the game seldom makes you do too many manuvers in a row without a check point.
It's also worth noting that this game has no real combat in it.  Don't expect to to run into enemies really anywhere in the game, including bosses.   It's a straight up platformer with exploration.  I sat down to try this game for "a few minutes", ended up clearing it in one painful 9 -hour sitting.  It just grabbed me and didn't let go and I ended up liking this a lot more than I expected.  The soundtrack is pretty amazing with some pretty glorious chiptunes.
This game might be a little too hard for some casual players.  When this game gets going, it's a real man's game.  It takes the gloves off pretty quickly so if you suffer from low T you might want to proceed with caution.

I remember playing Dugeon Defenders on XBOX 360 when I was younger and how I rather enjoyed it. This... this game does everything Dungeon Defenders has... except BETTER.
For starters there are 7 new heroes to choose from with new tower types. These include creating a volcano to rain meteors down on the many goblins and orcs you will fight and summoning skeletal remains of the ones you kill.
Next, you can switch between 4 heroes DURING BUILD AND COMBAT PHASES. Something the first game didn't have. This is a very nice touch if you want to solo but need those towers from others or you need to take care of a certain enemy. For example, you are a Squire and Wyverns are approaching. Since they fly over defenses and go straight for the core, a sword would have GREAT trouble killing them, however you can switch to a hero that has ranged attacks and deal with them relatively easily.
Also, the hud from the previous game has been changed dramatically and looks much more cleaner and easier to see what everything is.
Lastly, there are MUCH MORE enemy types. There's enemies which heal others whilst also dealing damage and there's crystal beasts which run towards defenses and then burrow into the ground, reducing their defense whilst regenerating heath, making it easier for enemies to destroy your defenses and overwhelm you.
Oh, and the devs of Terraria joined up with Trendy Entertainment to collaborate and add the Dryad from Terraria into DD2, with Terraria enemies as the towers she can use.
Overall, a great game to play with friends (and even randoms)! Would definitely recommend to any tower defense fans!

So after sitting down and really devoting some time to this Ive decided to add a few things:

The Tropico series has always played it safe, never pushing too hard to renovate making sure people know what to expect each time. Tropico 5 is no exception, with the same infrastructure and demands those familiar with the series will know exactly what to expect. With that said, significant changes have been made to the economy, development and elections systems that Tropico 5 holds its own unique identity within the series.
One new feature is a redesign of the campaign, while in previous games each mission would start on a new island beginning with the basic building blocks each time. Now players are given the choice between two islands, once the player completes a mission on the choose island the player must then complete the next mission on the second island. Levels are not reset and any development on the islands remains throughout the campaign. This change allows players to watch an island flourish over time, crawling up from its colonial roots to its own independent metropolis. Each choice becomes a much greater decision as it will not only effect the player for that level but for later missions that follow. While it provides a much greater sense of accomplishment it's a system with many drawbacks. The greatest of this being put into an automatic lose situation.
After completing a mission I returned to a previously developed island which had a population of 900 before leaving. Once I came back I found my population had been almost cut in half to 500 however my foundations remained and continued to cost upkeep which left me with a drastically understaffed island. There was little I could do as I would almost immediately jump into negative finances and could never pull it back out. Restarting the mission left to the exact same situation every single time, an issue that needs attention. With some missions giving little time for a player to complete objectives, those starting in a bad situation can soon find themselves in impossible to win situations. With the current save system this could take you back numerous missions to repair.
While the infrastructure behind the game remains the same the countless economy changes significantly effect how you would approach missions. A major flaw with all previous games was that most players would soon find their own approach that would work in every environment. With your own approach that was guaranteed to succeed there was little reason to break that mold. In tropico 5 however a  much greater dependency on varied trade breaks that mold. Forcing players to constantly adapt to a ever changing economy and political struggles. Finance isn't the only major overhaul, as elections now become significantly more difficult. Factions will be tougher to please, often forcing the player to juggle edicts and votes between each election to keep the majority on his or her side. With most actions having an equally negative response as positive players need to keep a keen eye, balancing the books of finance with the cries of the population.
Sadly, with what Tropico 5 makes up in polish it loses in humor, failing to come even close to the witty comments, quality voice acting and wacky scenarios we were given in 4. It's still remains funny at times but fails to reach that unique charm that gives it such a unique identity we remember it by.
Pro:
+Well balanced economy
+Improved Visuals
+Increased Difficulty
+Islands continue to develop after completed missions
+Improved design of elections
+New well designed edicts
Cons:
-Less humor then previous game
-Generic voice acting replaced funnier voice acting from earlier games
-Some balance issues with builds, some produce little profit compared to others
-Campaign design can cause some missions harder then intended or even impossible
-Missing features, presume coming in as DLC for new buildings
Tropico 5 is a drastic improvement to early games but comes with many drawbacks of its own. With this in mind it's difficult to recommend or bash this title. Those who come for the gameplay and love a challenge will be happy with the changes. Those looking for a relaxed campaign with a humorous story may be left disappointed.  While i'm left with mixed feelings i'll still have to recommend it. It's well polished, well designed and exactly what most people asked for in this sequal it's just missing that cherry on the top to make it a memorable game.

Decay: The Mare is a horror point'n'click adventure game. Player embodies the persona of Sam - patient of rehab institution "Reaching Dreams" where he wishes to face his drug addiction. Sadly, as soon as very first night within the facility the place twists into the title "mare". Sam will have to face this world of nightmare in order to solve the dark mistery of "Reaching Dreams".
In terms of gameplay Decay: The Mare doesn't exactly shine. Game is a somewhat crude composition of heavily photoshopped still images. Animated elements are kept to a minimum and most of the game player "leaps" between pictures making transitions from one place to another not exactly smooth to say the least. Pictures in general are well made and game provides hints whenever player gets stuck. Regretably due to static nature of the game they are quite painful to watch whenever backtracking is necessary and at some points you have to run from one end of the level to another. Besides this "Decay" is a rather standard point'n'click game requiring player to look around for items to combine and utilize in order to solve numerous puzzles. Each of three chapters leaves a little freedom of order in which player solves the objectives but all of them have to be finished to continue the story.
When reception of gameplay might be a matter of opinion it's the horror elements that were the biggest letdown for me. It is commendable that Shining Gate Software tried creating more subtle and psychological experience. Especially nowadays when "collect "X" while running through a dim space for a jumpscare" appears to be a trend among indie horrors. Pictures witnessed in Decay: The Mare were succesful in creating an amtosphere of persisent uneasiness but nothing beyond this. I've spent most of the first episode almost waiting for some jumpscare to spice things up a little and when it finally came I realised that I started getting bored by the time it showed up. Decay fails to time its spook elements properly and atmosphere thins by the time they appear, stripping them of the impact they could make.
I could probably recommend the game to the ones who are easily frightened if they want to get used to the horror genre in small steps. Also point'n'click enthusiasts should find the experience enjoyable. Story, perhaps not the most thrilling, is the definitely the strongest side of the game. Regretably game is plain unrefined with elements like rotating items in equipment menu (used once in whole game) or mandatory scripts triggered by having a peek at a ladder. Decay: The Mare could be a quite good game but perhaps lack of creators' experience was the reason it failed to reach its full potential.

Outlast is a first person horror adventure with an emphasis on stealth. When I say, "Emphasis on stealth" I mean, "There is literally no combat at all, or any kind of defensive maneuver's for that matter." You can hide in and under things at times. But mostly you run and breathe heavily.
Outlast: Panting the Game.
The problem I have with this is that I've played Condemned: Criminal Origin. Similar premise: you're attacked by insane humans in ratty, delapitated buildings. Except in Condemned, you could pick up a pipe or four-by-four and use it as a weapon. In Outlast, the main character seems to have never learned how to swing anything at anytime in his life. The enemies are mostly just normal people. Hit them. There's plenty of debris laying around.
But. As stealth is the order of the day in Outlast, you'd think it would be taught and suspensful. Eh. The game breaks down like this: Enter new area. Realize you need X amount of Something to open The Other Thing. Run around blindly for a minute, dodging the marauding bad guy until you find those Somethings and run back to The Other Thing.
Now, the biggest issue with this cat and mouse gameplay is that 90% of the game is pitch black, leaving you to rely on your camcorder's night vision to help you see. Two major problems with this: 1) Your camcorder must be a model from 1994 because your battery life is butt. Every 20 seconds you need to replace a battery. And 2) Any cool environment or spooky atmosphere is lost to the player because the whole game is seen via night vision. I get what they were going for, but it just makes the game frustrating, not scary.
I won't mention specific enemies or moments because I don't want to ruin the story for anyone. It is interesting, albeit a little simple. The atmosphere is nice, the locale is large (though mostly the same crusty halls over and over and over with rain streaked windows), and the game does look really nice (when you can actually see anything.)
It's just repetitive. The game devolves from survival horror stealth to just holding the run button down and side-stepping bad guys. If you like horror and can find this on sale, check it out. Just don't expect it to blow you away.

Although billed as a "3D psychological horror adventure and homage to the Resident Evil and Silent Hill games," the game is more akin to Myst and their various clones. The game is played from a first-person perspective, but the movement is constricted to clicking directional arrows; i.e., you "move" through static screens and click on various objects to pick them up or interact with them. Essentially, it is a first-person point and click adventure.
That being said, it is a disappointing point and click adventure. The story is paper thin and offers few shocks and surprises. Although there is an ominous feel throughout and the music is appropriately creepy, the "horror" element simply falls flat; it simply isn't scary. Due to the very nature of Myst-like games, you'll often be confused directionally, especially since there's little variety in the environments. The puzzles are rather simplistic, requiring very little thought to complete once you have the requisite items. The lack of voice acting throughout is sorely missed; despite the fact that there are three other characters besides yourself, inexplicably, the only voiceover is for a short story and several newspaper clippings.
I want to call attention to the English text dialogue and descriptions, which suffer from poor translation, likely due to the developers being Swedish. Since the story is important in a game such as this, the awkward sentences and word choices drag the game down significantly. (I don't know why so many developers don't enlist native English speakers to fine tune their game; it would make a huge difference.)
For achievement hunters, I achieved 100% in 4.6 hours. The majority of extra time was backtracking to find coins and, for one achievement, hidden text revealed by the flash of a Polaroid camera. If you're not interested in 100% completion, the game could be blazed through in 2-3 hours.
TL;DR: In a word: disappointing. It's certainly not worth the $9.99 asking price, but if you see it on sale for a dollar or in a bundle and you can overlook its flaws, it can be a mildly entertaining time waster.

Until I got that combo, the chapter was a mess of grinding wild cards (power ups that spawn randomly), resetting, and near-misses. It's for this reason alone that I didn't recommend the game at first.
If you do decide to get this game and decide to play it on hard, wait until the last hand to get the combo in chapter 10. It's much easier than any of the others, and it is super gratifying to play.

As the game progresses, you will unlock various bonuses which greatly facilitate gameplay and in my opinion somewhat makes the game a bit too easy, even on the hardest difficulty.
To be honest, I have skipped 95% of the story and the game doesn't force you to care about its narrative, which is a great sign of user convenience.
The polish on this game is where it counts, menu navigation is smooth, the sound effects are all satisfying and never grate on the nerves.
If you're looking for a card-based "puzzler", give it a go and then you too can try to convince everyone that this is the greatest thing ever.

As it stands, right now, this is a game worth playing, but be aware that currently the minimalist art style is reflected in minimalist gameplay. There is just enough gameplay related content here, such as predators, pray, weather effects, and developed mechanics such as cooking, crafting, illness, injury and medicine, or "decorating" your home with your scavanged supplies to make it worthwhile.

So... After Faerie Solitaire and Chef Solitaire, this is the third game I'm playing that bears the name 'Solitaire' and is actually a variation on Pyramid Solitaire with power-ups. I don't know which came first (probably yet another game?), and in casual games it's common to re-use proven techniques, but I'm still not comfortable with that. Okay, it's a 'husband & wife game', even though they credit a ton of Russian artists for the (admittedly beautiful) graphics, so I won't complain too much. At least the game has the decency to be twice shorter than the excrutiating Chef Solitaire.
It doesn't have voice acting though, which would have been nice, if only to make the story slightly more interesting. I'm very much full of love for Jane Austen's novels (okay, a couple movie/TV adaptations of Sense & Sensibility and Persuasion, and I've also watched Austenland... Does that count?), but I couldn't help but roll my eyes with all the clichés I found in the script. Well, at least it's not about a reality-TV-cook-show, which is always a plus.
I didn't care much for the music either. Repetitive, uninspired, only one level (halfway through the game) has a seemingly original track that's more pleasing to the ears. The graphics, as I said, are beautiful. The heroine reminds me of an ex, I don't know if that was a plus or a minus for me, but I'm not going to take that into account for my recommendation. (Yes, I'm a serious man with a serious recommendation system. That probably explains why I have so few friends.)
What else, then..? I think that the 'pyramid solitaire with power-ups' system is great, but all three games I played suffered from similar flaws:
- Very, very long, with the game divided into chapters that require specific results to move on to the next chapter. Failing to reach these goals forces you to restart the chapter from the start (usually 10 levels, which can be finished in less than half an hour... Still, you don't want to restart that, do you?) Really, that's tedious. Why can't I select a specific level to redo inside a chapter? Only Chef Solitaire allowed me to do that, IIRC.
- Boring story! Don't blame me, this matters to most people of taste. Otherwise, don't bother to add a story, thank you very much.
- Ungrounded love for card combos. Yes, they're cool. But requiring people to achieve a certain amount of combos in each chapter is tedious, because it removes the fun of solving a game and forces you to be careful about one more thing. Plus, there are levels where it's easier to make a combo, but the game doesn't tell you that.
- In fact it doesn't tell you much... There's a would-be tutorial, but it never explains plenty of things, such as: what if you fail one of your goals? Do you have to restart from scratch? How are score multipliers calculated? Some requirements involve reaching a certain multiplier, but doing multiple small combos seems to increase it randomly (or even not at all). That's just an example. The game basically assumes that you've played this kind of game for years already, and that you don't need rules. Yes, you do. Not everyone is a pyramid solitaire veteran. Me, personally, I'm a Spider Solitaire veteran. Perhaps tens of thousands of hours on the record. Yet I'm not expecting everyone to know every possible strategy to win a game.
- A complete and utter disregard for balancing difficulty. Solitaire games are random by nature, so the difficulty level is determined by the card layout. Some layouts are just hard to read (upside down cards, really?), or even just tricky (multiple cards on top of one another without any visual clues, thank you very much), but what really happens is that hands are so randomized, the final chapter was by far the easiest to me -- I didn't have to redo any levels in my first playthrough, or maybe just one, as opposed to at least 5 or 6 out of 10 in previous chapters. I retried it in normal mode, which only lowers requirements to pass a chapter, and had to restart 3 or 4 levels in order to get a perfect score (which I wanted everywhere). Still easier than previous chapters, but really, it shouldn't be harder than hard mode now, should it?
Okay, I'm done with the complaints.
Overall I did finish the game, and enjoyed it a lot more than Chef Solitaire, so I'm giving it a thumb up. But please guys, if you ever make another one... How about trying to give a story mode with predetermined cards, and then a 'free-roam' mode where you get random layouts and random card orders? That way you could balance the game more effectively.

the sad thing is that there are only about 1 or 2 instances in every episode in which you get the option to go different locations. while that's great, the moment you go through them you immediatly go back  to the main line istead of creating a new one. instead of a game in which one single choice could change the outcome of the entire game (and thus provide reason for multiple playthroughs ) you have a game that makes you feel you're making a difference but in truth you're just doing what everyone else is doing with maybe 3 different lines of text.
An example for the choices being pointless would be the scene in episode 2 where you have to pick between saving Selina or saving Harvy.
Harvy is guaranteed to becomes 2-face, thus making "Save Selina" the default choice. what's the point in saving Harvy, fail and have him become 2-face just so you can rest assured that "Harvy will remember that"?
there is none.
In terms of graphics, the game has a very nice artstyle that provides a nice medium for a story based on a comic book.
unforutantly, the game is so bugged at this point in time that every 2 lines or so will lose context because the video and voice go out of sync or the game just completley decides to skip them.
The frame rate constantly dances around and was not stable what-so-ever.
As much as games of this genre usually get a pass even when performance is bad just because the story delivers, well,
the crashes, sound bugs, and entire sentances skipping themselves completley take away whatever immersion the game had.
If and when the bugs are fixed i will write a new review for this product sharing my opinions at that time.
