What to say about The Long Dark that does it justice?
Unlike most other 'survival' games out there in the market, do not be expecting to swing axes at Zombies and other supernatural beings. Your enemy in this game is the weather, wildlife (Wolves / Bears) , fatigue, thirst and hunger.
Simply walking around with no enemy in sight can cause your health to start deteriorating if you are being careless about how cold the weather is. When you are starving, the sight of even a small handful of herbs or a degraded packet of candy will get you excited.
Expect to build fires, evade wildlife, monitor the weather like a hawk, inspect every nook and cranny for food / water / medicine - expect to hurl yourself into a cabin with a wolf or bear on your tail like your life depended on it. (Which it does!) Expect to traverse up large mountains in the hope that there may be a shelter somewhere. Enjoy the beautiful sunlit and moonlit views of the Canadian forests whilst reminding yourself that you need to keep moving.
Expect to flounder in the darkness and traverse through mines with the kerosene in your lamp trickling away.
If you can plan ahead, if you can adapt to harsh situations and if you can handle doing as much as possible with as little as possible in your possession - you will relish this title.
This is an intelligent game designed for intelligent gamers. It is a true masterpiece and example of not only what a survival game should truly be about, but also how an Early Access title should be developed.
Hinterland Studios actively and consistently interact with their members on the forum and listen to inputs about any bugs and feedback about the game. And all along, they still remain true to their core vision of the game.
I cannot recommend this game enough. There is plenty of content in the game and it barely feels like an Alpha release.
------------------
Some key notes about the title;
* One life. When your game is over, it is over.
* Ammo is scarce.
* The weather WILL dictate how much you can explore at any given time.
* You can craft gear, which includes warmer clothing, weapons and food harvesting.
* There is item degradation. All repairable... if you have the materials.
* There is no "map". You learn by exploring and memorising.
* What you can carry is limited. Whilst you can go over your 'maximum' weight, be prepared for the fatigue, thirst, hunger and movement penalties.
* The game has a learning curve which would be considered steeper than most other titles - there is a bit to take in, there is no game manual - and it can be unforgiving. This is a game that intuitively makes you discover by yourself.
* You will be monitoring your four stat bars and your health bar a lot in this game if you want to succeed.
* There will be a lot of exploring where you do not get attacked for long periods. This is normal. (And to be honest, a welcome thing!)
------------------
The only things I would consider as "CONS" for this title is that it's in Alpha - so you naturally want more content and there are pockets of bugs you can discover. (I don't come across very many though...) Also, once you get proficient at surviving (takes a while to get there) it can be a bit lonely and repetitive if you aren't exploring around the maps.
Other than that - fantastic title. Do get it!
If you're a patient, planning player - then this acquired taste is more than for you. A hidden gem of a title that already has amassed a cult following.

STOP.  If you already own Tropico 4 you probably don't need this game and it will likely frustrate you.  I'm writing this review in the days after release so my gameplay time of Tropico 5 has admitedly been limited.  That said, I've played the Tropico series since the original back in the early 2000's.  I get that changes need to be made to keep the game relevant, but in my opinion Tropico 5 changed largely in the wrong direction.  However, if you're new to the series, you'll enjoy this game for what it has to offer.  Here's my initial breakdown.
Pros:
Beautifully redesigned buildings, everything just seems to fit together nicely when you're trying to cram a lot of buildings into one space.
The dynasty member function seems like a possible plus (haven't really fleshed that out yet).
I like the concept of having manager's in buildings, but it's not clear how they contribute to the overall expense of the building.
I like some of the new edicts like charging for healthcare!  Finally those lazy peasants will pay or die.
The addition of tanks adds a layer of badassery and battling rebels/other nations is more engaging.
Cons:
Can't set the exact wage for a worker anymore (it's done in an overarching budget system, so you set a budget for a building which somehow encompasses a salary for the worker and operating costs for the building).  You want to pay your farmers more than your doctors?  Sorry, can't do that...
You also can't set the exact amount for rent anymore.
The above two issues make it hard to become an uber-capitalist dictator.  I know it sounds ridiculous but they've dumbed down the economic system so much it's actually complicated.
Customizing your character is gone.  I don't care so much about what they look like, but who thought an astronaut suit should be 1 of the 5 outfits you get to choose?  I'm more upset you can't select negative and positive traits to create a more in depth character.  I always liked choosing flatulence even though the palace guards got double pay...
Am I missing the plants and shrubbery somwhere?  You basically have a large park and a small park, that's it.  No single palm trees to meticulously line your roadways...  Statues meant to glorify El Presidente's and intimidate your opponents are non-existent.
You have to pay to explore your island now which seems pointless.
Options like "paper plates" and "cloth napkins" that used to affect the quality of a restaurant are no longer options.  You adjust the budget of the building now to change service, but that raises the worker's wages.  What if I want to increase quality without raising wages...
El Presidente is pretty much useless.  He can't help rush construction or join in fighting the rebels like in previous games.  No option to sway election with speeches either.
Building progression through research/time feels poorly developed and arbitrary.  You earn research points through libraries and observatories which give you tech upgrades for different buildings.  Unfortunately, you can only build tenaments and country houses at the beginning so if you want to upgrade your citizens to apartments to improve housing quaility you have to wait until the Cold War era (and then destroy all your previous housing and try to make the apartments fit into your city layout).  I wasn't a fan of Tropico 4's purchasing blueprints, but I think it works better than this option.
You can no longer see who is actually visiting a restaurant, pub, doctor's office, etc.  You're just given a "number of visitors".
Searching in the almanac is painful.  All I want to do is find the least happy person and execute them, but you can't search by that.  You can find the person with the lowest approval rating, but they're not necessarily the most unhappy.
I know this is knit-picking, but I liked when you purchased a building upgrade in previous Tropico's, the physical improvement would appear (i.e. skylights in the cigar factory).  There's no visual changes on the buildings when upgrading now.
You can't toggle a dock to accept "tourists only" so I keep having my teamsters dropping export resources at the dock in my tourist area.  I don't want stinking peasants mixing with the upper echelons of society.
Only a handful of island maps to play.
One of the biggest negatives for me is the overall lack of buildings (where's the gourmet restaurant??? or El Presidente's childhood museum?).  I assume this is so we can be sold the inevitable expansion packs.
Suggestions:
The ability to choose the placement of our palace and dock at the outset of a sandbox game would be nice.
Consider reverting back to SOME, not all, of the core game designs from previous versions.  My big ones would be charging specific amount of rent and setting worker's wages (please change this back).
True roundabouts would be great for improving traffic flow.
Even with all the above, I'll still play it because I absolutely love Tropico, but just a lackluster delivery compared to past game versions.  Overall rating from me would be a 6 out of 10.

First of all, the game is very short, so if you're looking for something with a story-mode that you can play for 5+ hours, this most likely won't be it. I finished it in one session, probably around 2-3 hours, and I wasn't in a rush doing so.
But beyond that, it's such a enjoyable game and the most fun I've had with a FPS in a long while. The concept of time only moving when you do (including moving to look around, clicking prematurely and missing a shot/punch, and etc.) is very simple but done well. For those that care about the story, you'll find a strange but creative plot to follow, and for people that just want to shoot a bunch of red dudes, nothing is stopping you from just doing that.
The level design is unique for each stage, and for the majority of it, it seems fair and fun to move your way through it like a puzzle. A few levels did have issues with starting you too close to enemies and the randomness of their shots sometimes making it tougher than it should, but overall once you learn how to play with the mechanics it isn't too difficult for anyone that normally plays FPS games.
Importantly, just shooting things feels good, seeing them explode into a bunch of shards everywhere. Swords slice through enemies in a very gratifying way, shotguns feel good just to aim into a room and watch a ton of pellets fly everywhere in slow motion, and even throwing a pool ball across the room and smacking a guy in the head with it is an awesome feeling.
Overall get this game if you don't mind spending the cash for a short game, though the experience condensed in two hours is better than what you'd get for a lot of games in 10+ hours. There's replay value for speedrunning, finding secrets, and other modes unlocked upon beating the game, or just self-imposed challanges like melee only. I'd wait for it to go on sale personally or find somewhere cheaper (30$ is a bit steep in my opinion), but definitely pick it up at some point.
EDIT: Playing about 25 hours more, the game has a lot to play than I gave it credit for. Not all the challenges are different and unique, but most are fun and make you play the game in ways you hadn't before. Endless mode is also a cool mode, and there's a good variety of maps and gamemodes with that as well, but there's no motivation not to camp in a room with one entrance and play that way to get a good score, though that doesn't take away the fun of it. Speedrunning the game is really fun as well (not just the mode, but doing actual full-game runs) and the community surrounding it have been nothing but helpful when I've talked to them.

This isn’t something I thought I’d end up “playing” so soon, let alone write a review about. It isn’t a game. Games are closely linked to game theory. Someone looses, someone gains. Can we all gain? Sure, but it really hasn’t asked or answered, what if there was only yourself to play the game with?
This “game”, rather title, or art work, is not worth it. It’s not worth the $20 or the $10 or whatever it is currently listed at. Being a one in a life time experience, there’s no price tag to be placed on it.
Sure, someone, or a group of people had to come together, piece all the parts together, and that work should justify being paid. But pause for a second; is everything able to be placed under the cover of “monetary value”? Are personal experiences able to be placed under that very same cover? Is that a thing only humans are able to do? Distance and distinguish from “want”, “need”, and a completely different category that you can’t label?
I didn’t want to play this “game”. I’ll be honest. It was cheap because of a sale, it had some relation to the Stanley Parable, and it runs under the Source Engine. So it ticked all the right boxes, but I didn’t really “need” to “play” this “game”. I didn’t really “want” to “play” it either. It just so happened that I looked at in my list of games, and thought “hey, let’s play this game. I need to kill some time anyways”. Little did I know that I’d probably spend the rest of my life tinkering about with its ideas.
I wouldn’t be inclined to mention this “game” to others. Heck, even if I did, I couldn’t be in the same room as them. This is an experience you have to see for yourself and by yourself only. You might have looked at the “gameplay” on YouTube to see if paying money for this game is worth it. Simply put, you should come to your own conclusions while “playing” this title. In the next few sentences, I would usually be inclined to talk about the key ideas of the title or game. With this, I couldn’t. It would wreck it. Gameplay is not even a word I’d see myself using in this review.
That being said, you should probably talk to a psychiatrist before and/or after “playing” this “game”. If you would be unable to distance yourself enough, I think it could damage you. This title is dark, really dark. I am being quite serious. This is not a joke, or a pun on my name. You should prepare yourself, or know that you would be able to distance yourself from what you will see, and hear from the narrator.
While I’d recommend that any person could play Stanley’s Parable, you have to be a select few to “play” this title.
In the Stanley Parable, you could walk around, “play” and be done. You would completely miss the whole meaning of the game, the actual content to the game and still be ok.
Sure, what you see on the screen is a game, or something worth paying money for, but that is not why you should be there. There would be a lot of things I’d place in this review (like my many other popular ones), but I simply can’t. It just wouldn’t do the title justice. Perhaps you have finally picked up on that point. You shouldn’t be reading the reviews, just go ahead and try it.
What you will leave with after tinkering about in this title are the many questions left unanswered. One being, is the author of this title actually “Coda”, the person who makes the parts in the game? Why did it take this long to package this all together? Where is “Coda” now? What’s with the three dots? And… I should probably stop there. There’s a lot I’d be willing to talk about, but not before you sit down and “play” the “game” by yourself.
I will leave this review with this question: What does self actualization even mean, and what is it worth?

This is the start of a nice game, but it is not complete in my opinion. The designers made some strange choices about how the game would work. For example, a small village must have a building dedicated to cutting wood, and a person assigned to the wood cutting profession. IF not, the residents will eventually freeze to death. If you've ever been... anywhere... you know that if a specialist isn't available, people will make do. Villages and aboriginal people do not freeze to death because they are too busy farming or building or doing their **one job**. Rather, they go get some wood, put it on a fire, and live on.
The same problem happens with clothing. You must have a tailor. A tailor. Yes, a tailor. The resident of a house absolutely can not make or repair clothes. They will simply rot off their bodies. Never mind that for millenia, people have made clothes in their home. For some reason we are forcing industrial age specialization on these poor villagers. I don't understand why we want to do this.
It's a pretty game. You should watch a "let's play" of it. Then you can say you saw how pretty it was. But you can skip the frustration caused by illogical design decisions, pretty dumb AI, and seemingly arbitrary reasons for your town giving up and dying. Did I mention that building a mine on the other side of a hill from your town is a sure way to stop all childbirth? Yep, that too. So really, skip it unless you hear about some amazing update where they rebalance and rethink this thing.

I hate zombie games.
This blight on gaming, zombie games are popping up everywhere like mushrooms, or, well... the undead. No matter how many failures, developers still seem to think that they will succeed at making the new "Left 4 Dead." What they fail to understand is that Left 4 Dead was innovative at the time. You can't make a L4D clone and expect any kind of staying power as a game developer, because, "it's been done." Sure, some of the clones has done rather well for themselves, like Killing Floor for example. But looking at the mass grave of uninspired "zombie survival" games at their feet, you'd think most developers would stay well away from the genre. Apparently not so. The market is still flooded with mindless, uninspired, boring games.
This, however, is not one of them.
This game is still in early beta stages, and it already shows alot more promise than any other zombie game on the horizon. State of Decay? Pff, seen something like it, like, 100 times already. The Dead Linger? OK, they got a good idea going there, but so far, im seeing none of it's potential done justice. There are more obscure indie titles, but im drifting from the topic at hand.
I am a sucker for Early Access. I really am. And when this title popped up, I was apprenhensive at first. ANOTHER zombie survival game..? But as I read on, and looked up videos on youtube, and read about it, I realized I might be looking at a masterpiece.
A true zombie survival experience!
Hordes of zombies? Check! (Well, obviously)
Scavanging? Check!
Hunger, Thirst, Illness, Cold, Panic and Depression management? Check!
The feeling of impending doom? Check!
Believable setting and zombie lore? Check!
All of these combined in one game? You bet!
When you start your first game, you are greeted with a few options to consider, such as which part of the map to start in. This is followed by your cahracter creation screen, where you customize appearance, and add traits such as "Short Tempered", "Overweight", "Brave" or "Stout" among others. These traits work exactly like they sound! Overweight? Slower run speed, and bad endurance! Brave? Not as likely to get ravaged by panic or fear (the mind killer). You also get to choose previous profession, each with bonuses of their own.
The game then lets you customize your world. How long does it take for power and water supplies to cut? 2 weeks? 6 months? How likely is it that you find a shotgun in a closet? Are your zombies the fast sprinting type, or slow shambler? Do they rely on hearing, smell or sight to find you? Or all three? Do they know how to use doors? How long without seeing/smelling/hearing you does it take before they sod off so you can leave the closet with the shotgun you just found lying around (sadly no ammo though)?
When these settings are complete, you click start, and are greeted with these words, which set the mood for the entire game.
"These were the end times.
There was no hope for survival.
This, is how you died."
Because you will die... Oh, you will die! Haha! The corpses of your survivors will fill the streets! Unless you go easy mode in your settings, this is one of the games where you die a lot! But not in frustrating or unfair ways. Each and every death is your fault, and yours alone. Left your safehouse without bandages? Got careless and got jumped by a crawler in tall grass? Forgot to stockpile water before the water supplies cut? Stayed out in the rain and got sick?
All these are learning experiences. You will die alot, but for every death you will be one experience richer, and the next survivor you create will have a conciderably longer lifespan for it. Plus, if you keep playing on the same map you created, you can find your previous corpse to get back the loot you were carrying... And maybe put a round or two in the poor guy/girl's skull out of sentimentality, and/or the fact that they might be trying to eat your brains.
To help you survive, you have farming, building and cooking, three crucial skills that will keep your alter ego from death's claws (for now). And, ofcourse, loads of weapons. Some of them improvised, like forks or screwdrivers, or baseball bats, but also, if you are lucky to find both ammo and guns, you can pick the rotten ones off from a distance..! Remember though, sound attract more of them, and you will be eating through your ammo stockpile right quick if they gang up on you.
The style reminds me of oldschool games, like Sims 1, Fallout 2, SWAT 2, and and also some new indie games, like Shadowrun. It looks outdated, but extremely polished. And the world... wow. The world is huge! Huger than Xbox even! I almost died of thirst and cold weather treking through the woods to a distant diner and gas station in search of supplies, all the while cursing myself for underestimating the distances in this huge world, and not bringing enough supplies!
Speaking of the world, here's an interactive world map, to show you just how big this real world setting is:
Now, I could go on trying to explain the genious behind this title, but frankly, I have spent far too much time away from Westpoint as it is. I can feel this game consuming a conciderable amount of my spare time in the near future...

Someone managed to make bullet time interesting again (well i recently played FEAR but ya know)
"No reasons, just killing red dudes" as the game itself puts it. You get plopped into various locales and gotta kill all the red dudes. The hook is unless you make a move time advances extremely slowly - which makes this into a "puzzle fps" of some sort.
You can shoot of course, punch, grab and throw stuff (also jump). One bullet is enough to kill you or the enemy. Each action you take advances time to a certain degree. Moving advances it proportionally, throwing and shooting takes abit of time and grabbing a weapon for example takes the longest.
You face two dudes, one with a weapon. Next to you is a bottle. You grab the bottle. The armed dude fires. You dodge the bullet then throw the bottle at him. Meanwhile the unarmed guy advances, you punch him once. The bottle hits the armed guy, he recoils and his weapon flies towards you. You grab it out of the air and shoot them both. You hear a gunshot and turn around. You throw the weapon at the bullet hovering in front of you and the new dude fires again. Next to you is a pipe but is there enough time to grab it...
Stuff like that. One of the unlockable extra modes is a total timestop which allows for even more wacky matrix escapades.
Graphics are stylised and functional and it fits the game (the menues and such are retro ascii stuff, abit tired schtick but good enough and theres alot of funny useless extras in there). Same with the sound - dont think this has any music (in the main game) but the menues have bleeps and bloops and ingame theres the appropriate swishes and swooshes for time dilated matrix stuff.
The main "story" game is rather short but theres a few challenge modes (speedrunning, katana only and such) and endless arenas.
Following that the only thing one could object to would be the price, but considering all the sorts of garbage one throws money at nowadays its really not that much for this fine polished product id think.

Ah, Regency Solitaire: a simple casual game that's up-down solitaire matching, similar to Faerie Solitaire and others in the genre, but: it's polished to a mirror sheen. The devs got everything right in this game, so let's go down the list.
Design: The gameplay is rock-solid. You've got the scattered piles of cards that you clear by matching cards either up one or down one in the hierarchy. (i.e. if you have to clear a ten, use a jack or a nine.) You make chains for combos and multipliers to your score, and that's all simple enough. The game mixes things up by adding wildcards (you can have more than one in stock, too!) and three powers. There's the cupid (remove a card), the shuffle (as it sounds), and the phoenix (remove two cards). You're at the mercy of the RNG for a good layout in a given hand, so these tools help get you out of those situations, and getting through hard levels often just means hoarding them so you can use them at strategic moments. There are additional upgrades you can purchase throughout the game, for extra undos or a power-up that will randomly remove extra cards at the beginning of a hand.
Also, there are locks on the piles - you need to clear royalty cards to get rid of them, or find keys in the cards to undo them. I love this! Adds a little more complexity to the game without making it taxing.
The game is structured so you play ten hands in a level, and the challenge comes from trying to meet chapter goals, like getting two perfect hands or a combo of ten cards. Standard fare for this genre, competently done.
Visuals/Sound: It's all in theme with the Regency style. Everything looks good, everything sounds appropriately Regency-era. No complaints here at all.
Plot: It's presented in a visual novel style, with little scenes playing between levels. It's a bit thin, but amusing to watch the tale of the young lady trying to woo her beloved while her brother gambles the family fortune away.
Essentially this is a fantastic game to use for unwinding, with a gentle plot and sumptuous visuals and gameplay that's simple but addictive. There are oodles and oodles of levels, a normal and hard mode, and it's a lot of bang for your buck. Check it out!

A simple and forgiving solitaire clear-the-board game with a few extra additions. Reminds me a lot of Fairie Solitaire, though I haven't played that in a while. Story is mediocre, graphics and music are decent. You play as a daughter of a Victorian family and your brother Edward gambled away your family's money and you're also arranged to marry an unliked neighbor. Your story goes through how you marry upwards. It allows you to skip the story (via a button in cut scenes) if you prefer.
It uses the standard solitaire rule (you can only take cards from the playing area/tableau that are next in sequence to the one drawn from the stock/hand pile). Colors/suits don't matter. For example, if there's a 10 on top of the pile, you can only take a 9 or a jack. If there's an ace, you can only take a king or a 2. If you can't remove everything from the playing area before your deck/stock pile runs out, you lose.
There are two special blockers that stop you from interacting with piles in the playing area. Some piles have a lock card on top which you can't access until you find the key card (located somewhere in the playing area) and use it on the lock. There's a regal lock which can only be removed by taking a certain amount of J/Q/K cards off the playing area.
And sometimes cards in the playing area are tagged with a blue bow that show they need to be used twice to be removed from the board. The first usage removes the bow and the second usage removes it from the board as usual.
There are three special skills you unlock that can be used on a cooldown. One lets you remove a selected card, another shuffles the playing board, and the last randomly removes cards.
Wildcards are the 'Get Out of Jail Free' card of the game that allow you to brute force the game and combat bad RNG. You can randomly find them instead of regular cards while playing and then put them into your wildcard area (can store up to 11 for future use). When you use them, they take place of the active card on your deck/stock pile. So instead of waiting to draw the right card from the stock pile, you can use the wildcard to immediately start removing cards from the playing area. Since wildcards aren't refunded for retries you have to learn when it's better to go all-in for the high combo, when it's not worth using and when to cut your losses.
There are twenty levels. Each level has up to 10 stages and each stage is one 'game' of solitaire. You earn a maximum of three stars per stage for clearing all cards in a stage. You also earn gold based on how well you do that can be spent on items that make the game easier (better chance of finding wildcards, more undos, upgrading skills, etc.).
Goals for each level are to uncover an item (which is underneath cards on one of the stages), earn enough stars/perfect hands (max 3 stars per stage, 3 stars is a perfect hand), earn enough gold (based on how well you do & combo meter), and get a high enough combo/multiplier (which are linked). It's very forgiving because it allows you to redo stages so bad card RNG isn't so frustrating. If you take your time to clear every stage, the only difficulty is in getting a high combo which depends on card luck and usage of wildcards you've saved. There are little tricks you can do to make it easier to get a high combo (like going for it on stages with more exposed cards and setting up a long combo by intentionally removing/keeping certain cards on the board).
There are a couple quirks:
I found it to be a decent time sink that wasn't very mind-intensive. Because it's very forgiving in retries it's not especially challenging. However, any hardcore mode would just mean grinding levels until you save up wildcards and replaying levels hoping for great RNG. Not a very appealing idea to me. I think casual difficulty suits this genre. If you've spent time playing solitaire when it came with Windows before Steam existed, you might enjoy this version of solitaire.

Gave it a fair chance during the free weekend.
Pros:
-Beautiful graphics, music, tone, setting...
-Interesting narrative
-Option to play the game without permadeath and standard saving.
Cons:
-Tedious and repetitive mechanics (especially when you consider that you're going to die so many times before you get anywhere in the game)
-Lessons learnt after dying do not exactly help you the next time around because you're still going to have to repeat the same stories, and hire the same people, and visit the same ports, and sail for boring minutes on end. (FTL; while being a different game, does a better job at permadeath since each new attempt is a different game with an independent path and you never feel like you're repeating anything. And not having any boring navigation in between the action probably helps as well).
-Sailing from port to port is incredibly slow and boring. There's maybe a couple of battle-worthy enemies.
-Just finding one of the ports that the admiralty is interested in is enough to get you killed 2 or 3 times. North-East of London is just not enough in a map of this magnitude. Would have made the game way more interesting if you could ask for directions in ports along the way in order to plot a more efficient path.
There's also a game-breaking bug: if you decide not to choose your past at the start of the game, you'll get to do it at some point later in the game. Except that when the time comes for that, and you input your chosen name, you cannot confirm that selection and you'll be stuck in that menu. The only way out is quitting the game completely and reloading. At which point I found that some of my choices were corrupted, my player had no name, and I just went for another new game.
In short, it seemed really promising at the beginning but did not manage to win me over in the end.

Immortal Redneck is a Semi-Procedurally generated FPS Dungeon Crawler/Rouge-lite along the lines of Ziggurat and Tower of Guns. This time sporting the humorous (And occasionally a little tiresome) theme of a mummified redneck fighting his way to the top of the pyramids with the help of favors from various gods.
If you've ever played a rogue-like, such as The Binding Of Isaac, you'll be fairly familar with most of the concepts at play here; Death is permenant, but there is progress to be made across several lives. Each run will vary in some way, from how the pyramid is created by slamming together a layout of handcrafted rooms at random, to the passives and weapons you find along the way.
Immortal Redneck doesn't do a whole lot to set istelf apart from the crowd. It's pleasant to look at and the unique egyptian motif is nice, but it's more of a subtle refinement of the formula than reinventing the wheel. That said, it isn't without it's flaws.
The two main flaws most people will likely have with this game will probably boil down to it's ammo system and the room designs. You will be reloading. A lot. And it's a very slow process that breaks up the fast pace of the otherwise very frenetic and flowing combat as you dart around the room leaping from ledges at breakneck speeds. As for the rooms, there are some that are simply MASSIVE, or just plain long and maze-like. The problem being, there's often only one exit to these rooms, and once you've travelled all the way to the end to finish off that last pesky enemy, guess what? Time to walk all the way back. Some clever shortcuts on room completion are desperately needed here.
Having said all that, if you're a fan of the genre and are looking for the next Ziggurat or similar to kill hours upon hours on, this game is a fine addition to the growing collection of rogue-like shooters. As even with my 16.8 hours as of writing this review, I've only just made my way onto the second of three pyramids, all with their own unique rooms, enemies, and bosses. There's a lot of content here, and plenty of replayability. Worth a look for sure.

I deleted my chapter 1 review to put this one up (chapter 3 just finished) because my opinion of the game has totally changed.
More and more I'm seeing the choices not matter...for instance I took the high road the whole way through chapters 1 and 2, using as little force as necessary and not brutalizing anyone, and yet the police/Gordon still hate me because they think I'm a psychopath who tortures people.
Without spoiling anything, something radical happens at the end of chapter 3, this big f*ck you cliffhanger that is meant to steer the plot in the direction that the designers want it to go. They build this sense of immersion and RP and really make you feel like you're making meaningful decisions. Right up unil the last few moments that is, where they pull back the curtains violently. It's very clear Telltale has no intention of ever letting players have any amount of control.
It's so sad because the dialouge and story and character writing is so good...right up until the literal last minute scene that undoes everything. It could have been a really amazing game.
It would be one thing if the narrative was good, but it's absolutely riddled with plot holes and consistancy errors.
Moreover, as a dedicated Batman fan, I have to comment on the fact that they retcon the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the cannon on a systemic level. Characters have totally different allegiances/motivations that what we're used to. Almost none of the charming characters that you know and love are the same anymore. At this point, is it even a Batman game?
The tearing that was there in chapter 1 isn't a slight nuissance anymore...it's now very prevalent and annoying. Character models are glitchy, art assets are poorly coded, just all around this not a polished product.
Lastly, the gameplay is even more watered down now. The detective sequence in this chapter forces you to link evidence together so that you can "figure out the puzzle" even though it would be obvious to a simpleton what is going on. Then there's random uneccessary QTE when you're doing simple tasks (like not even timed, but just there randomly as if to check that you're not AFK).
Telltale is clearly running out of ideas and budget, and I don't have much faith in their products anymore. I may not even finish this game.

What we have here is a first-person shooter rogue-lite thing with cartoony artstyle and some nosense excuse plot about a redneck who is captured by monsters and mummified while on vacation in Egypt, only to break out of his sarcophagus and go on a rampage through some pyramids.

I'm enjoying it a lot, it runs nice and smooth, and it gets it's fast-paced retro-insipred shooting done well. Total package is well worth the money in my opinion.
Updates for version 1.2, since it includes significant changes:
- Gripes about weapons are now mostly non-existant. Updates to sounds effects make them feel more unique (and more powerful where appropriate), updates visual feedback makes shooting the various monsters in the face feel better too.
- Class randomization is out. You can now pick any unlocked class/favor at the game's central hub area, and favors that go unused eventually gain stat bonuses.
- There are now leaderboards to chase for daily & weekly challenge runs. (These challeges do use the same seed for the randomizer, so everyone gets the same floor layout, scroll & weapon drops etc.)
- Also, by now I've seen & beaten all 6 bosses, and only the 2nd boss in the 2nd pyramid is a bit weak. He looks cool, but he's really easy to beat compared to the others.
Original more in-depth review below:
If you're still reading, lets have a more in-depth look at what makes this tick:
- There's a persistent skill tree where you can spend cash you earn during your runs. As nice touch, the tree visibly grows in the game world as you buy things from it. Outside of a bunch of basic stat boosts, and favors from gods (this game's class system) it doesnt' offer too much though, which is a bit of a shame. There's a double-jump ability, a shop where you can spend more cash, but not much beyond that.
- Favors/classes do get randomized, and once you have more than 2 you'll get a choice of 2 at the start of each run. Each class has different starting weapons, and different passive and active abilities. It's  a pretty good mix, and forces mixing up playstyles. Unlocking a favor also means the weapons from it's loadout start dropping in the game
- The game puts a heavy focus on movement, weaving and dodging as you whittle down the opposition and in some cases. There are also parts that are quite platforming-heavy which I'm normally not too fond of, but which this game particularly does well - largely due to an effective ledge-grabbing mechanism that ensures small missteps don't turn into big problems.
It's the feel of this that makes me forgive the game's flaws really.
- Weapons have a nice variety, but do fall within FPS stereotypes - pistols tend to be low-damage but accurate, shotgun types scatter, grenades bounce and go boom etc. Weapon drops during a run aren't too common, so you do want to get familiar with the various default loadouts of the different favors/classes. There are some gripes to be had here in the current version: a few weapons just feel off, like the heavy-looking Rusty Revolver, which sounds like the average light pistol.
- Enemy design is varied enough both in mechanics and aestethics, and ranged enemies do not use hitscan weapons - anything that is being shot at you, you have a chance to dodge.
Still, here too there is reason to gripe: Sometimes the AI falters and enemies fail to engage when you expect them to, and all enemies basically react the same to getting hit - a small bit of stagger and that's it. That feels about right for some of he bigger, tankier opponents, but for others you would expect more effect - such as being able to interrupt enemy attacks with a well-timed shot of your own, or being able to scatter a pack of smaller, weaker enemies if you don't kill them outright.
- Scrolls are your main source of boosts, ranging from extra jumps and more defense, to being able to walk on lava without damage, big health boosts etc. and of course there's some weird ones (change gold drops into health drops - nice on the current run, not nice on the long term progression) and just awful ones (spend double ammo, lose all scrolls collected so far, get stuck with only a single weapon until you find new ones..). A bad scroll at an OK time you can usually survive but will still hurt. And a bad scroll at a bad time will make sure that "you did not reach the apex."
I really do advise disabling automatic scroll pickups in the options, so you can decide if you want to take the risk or not.
- Map randomization in this game is a bit basic - It's fixed rooms with mostly fixed enemy placement. And some speedrun/hazard dodging challenge rooms thrown in for variety. The individual rooms are mostly nicely-designed mini arenas though. On the downside, that does mean the surprise wears off relatively fast. But on the plus side, building familiarity is one way that makes advancing through the game easier.
Another nice touch is that you travel from the bottom of the pyramid to the top, and floors get smaller as you go along. This also plays into bonuses granted for exploring whole floors, and makes farming the lower, easier floors for more drops a viable tactic.
- There's also bosses - one at the halfway point of a pyramid, and one at the top.The 2 I've managed to reach and kill so far were pretty well designed.
- Another plus is that the developers are active on the discussion forums, and are working hard to improve the game further. So there are probably a few patches in the future which will hopefully improve the game further.

This game is basically FPS version of Rogue Legacy. You fight monsters and collect cash they drop, which you can then spend on upgrading yourself, unlocking new classes, etc. The money you don't spend is instantly removed upon starting new run, so it's advised to spend it all. What really caught my eye was the Egyptian setting, there isn't that many of first person shooters in this style. We need more.
Like in every good rougelike you unlock classes, which require different playstyle. For example the Redneck is the basic class which serves as an introduction to the game. Once you've unlocked other ones there's no reason to play as him. The other classes include Apis, Seth, Thoth, etc. You get the idea, each one is stylized after an Egyptian god. Each one has different set of starting weapons and a unique active ability.
If you watched the Totalbiscuit's video featuring this game, your opinion might have been a bit negatively colored by it. BUT, there were 2 patches since it's release, which resolve some of the issues he talked about- namely the drop rate of scrolls and weapons. Over the course of 5 hours I've seen about half of the items in this game, which I'd say is good ammount.
Now I've mentioned scrolls- these are the spice of your gameplay- they might be good or bad and will turn the tides in your favour or doom your entire run. It's not just stats up, stats down. I'm talking skipping floors, unlimited ammunition, one weapon limit, inability to restore health with food, etc. Also if you're really lucky, you might get a scroll which grants you the option to reject bad scrolls, effectively removing the "russian roulette" nature of the scrolls.
There is also plenty of creative weapons, which range from a basic redneck shotgun to more exotic stuff like electric flamethrower or a potato launcher. A crossbow machine gun is my favorite so far. The gunplay itself however is not too great, enemies don't turn into swiss cheese after being shot with hundreds of bullets, instead they flash white upon being hit and turn to sand when they die. But the guns will start to get more punch once you've upgraded a bit, so the gunplay actually gets better over time.
The pyramid is broken down to several levels. They consist mostly of randomly assembled rooms- arenas, where you fight monsters, treasure rooms and challenge rooms and of course, boss rooms. Also there appear to be 2 exits at every floor, so you don't have to worry about backtracking. Not every floor ends with a boss by the way.
In conclusion- it's not without it's share of flaws, but it's actually one of the better rougelike FPS games on the market.

This isn’t something I thought I’d end up “playing” so soon, let alone write a review about. It isn’t a game. Games are closely linked to game theory. Someone looses, someone gains. Can we all gain? Sure, but it really hasn’t asked or answered, what if there was only yourself to play the game with?
This “game”, rather title, or art work, is not worth it. It’s not worth the $20 or the $10 or whatever it is currently listed at. Being a one in a life time experience, there’s no price tag to be placed on it.
Sure, someone, or a group of people had to come together, piece all the parts together, and that work should justify being paid. But pause for a second; is everything able to be placed under the cover of “monetary value”? Are personal experiences able to be placed under that very same cover? Is that a thing only humans are able to do? Distance and distinguish from “want”, “need”, and a completely different category that you can’t label?
I didn’t want to play this “game”. I’ll be honest. It was cheap because of a sale, it had some relation to the Stanley Parable, and it runs under the Source Engine. So it ticked all the right boxes, but I didn’t really “need” to “play” this “game”. I didn’t really “want” to “play” it either. It just so happened that I looked at in my list of games, and thought “hey, let’s play this game. I need to kill some time anyways”. Little did I know that I’d probably spend the rest of my life tinkering about with its ideas.
I wouldn’t be inclined to mention this “game” to others. Heck, even if I did, I couldn’t be in the same room as them. This is an experience you have to see for yourself and by yourself only. You might have looked at the “gameplay” on YouTube to see if paying money for this game is worth it. Simply put, you should come to your own conclusions while “playing” this title. In the next few sentences, I would usually be inclined to talk about the key ideas of the title or game. With this, I couldn’t. It would wreck it. Gameplay is not even a word I’d see myself using in this review.
That being said, you should probably talk to a psychiatrist before and/or after “playing” this “game”. If you would be unable to distance yourself enough, I think it could damage you. This title is dark, really dark. I am being quite serious. This is not a joke, or a pun on my name. You should prepare yourself, or know that you would be able to distance yourself from what you will see, and hear from the narrator.
While I’d recommend that any person could play Stanley’s Parable, you have to be a select few to “play” this title.
In the Stanley Parable, you could walk around, “play” and be done. You would completely miss the whole meaning of the game, the actual content to the game and still be ok.
Sure, what you see on the screen is a game, or something worth paying money for, but that is not why you should be there. There would be a lot of things I’d place in this review (like my many other popular ones), but I simply can’t. It just wouldn’t do the title justice. Perhaps you have finally picked up on that point. You shouldn’t be reading the reviews, just go ahead and try it.
What you will leave with after tinkering about in this title are the many questions left unanswered. One being, is the author of this title actually “Coda”, the person who makes the parts in the game? Why did it take this long to package this all together? Where is “Coda” now? What’s with the three dots? And… I should probably stop there. There’s a lot I’d be willing to talk about, but not before you sit down and “play” the “game” by yourself.
I will leave this review with this question: What does self actualization even mean, and what is it worth?

Homemade Tortilla (for 8 servings)
Prep : 30 mins
Cook : 25 mins
Ingredients :
- 1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
- 3/4 teaspoon salt
- 1/4 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/4 cup vegetable shortening
- 1/2 cup hot water
Directions :
1. Whisk flour, salt, and baking powder together in a large bowl. Add vegetable shortening and work into flour mixture using a pastry cutter until it resembles coarse crumbs.
2. Form a well in the middle of flour mixture and mix in hot water. Work flour and water mixture together with a fork and transfer to a cutting board.
3. Knead until a smooth, soft dough is formed, about 3 minutes. Add more flour if dough is too sticky.
4. Place more flour on cutting board, cover dough with bowl, and let rest for 15 minutes.
5. Cut ball of dough into eight equal parts and cover until needed.
6. Roll out balls of dough either by hand or with a tortilla press.
7. Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Place flattened tortilla in skillet and cook until it begins to bubble, about 1 minute. Flip tortilla over and cook for an additional minute. Flip again and cook for 1 more minute. Repeat with remaining dough.

I heard so much about this game when it was released. I heard it was terrifying. I heard it was amazing. I heard it was a blast.
It is none of those things. It's not bad, not at all,  but it's not going to redefine what you know about horror.
Outlast is a first person horror adventure with an emphasis on stealth. When I say, "Emphasis on stealth" I mean, "There is literally no combat at all, or any kind of defensive maneuver's for that matter." You can hide in and under things at times. But mostly you run and breathe heavily.
Outlast: Panting the Game.
The problem I have with this is that I've played Condemned: Criminal Origin. Similar premise: you're attacked by insane humans in ratty, delapitated buildings. Except in Condemned, you could pick up a pipe or four-by-four and use it as a weapon. In Outlast, the main character seems to have never learned how to swing anything at anytime in his life. The enemies are mostly just normal people. Hit them. There's plenty of debris laying around.
But. As stealth is the order of the day in Outlast, you'd think it would be taught and suspensful. Eh. The game breaks down like this: Enter new area. Realize you need X amount of Something to open The Other Thing. Run around blindly for a minute, dodging the marauding bad guy until you find those Somethings and run back to The Other Thing.
Now, the biggest issue with this cat and mouse gameplay is that 90% of the game is pitch black, leaving you to rely on your camcorder's night vision to help you see. Two major problems with this: 1) Your camcorder must be a model from 1994 because your battery life is butt. Every 20 seconds you need to replace a battery. And 2) Any cool environment or spooky atmosphere is lost to the player because the whole game is seen via night vision. I get what they were going for, but it just makes the game frustrating, not scary.
I won't mention specific enemies or moments because I don't want to ruin the story for anyone. It is interesting, albeit a little simple. The atmosphere is nice, the locale is large (though mostly the same crusty halls over and over and over with rain streaked windows), and the game does look really nice (when you can actually see anything.)
It's just repetitive. The game devolves from survival horror stealth to just holding the run button down and side-stepping bad guys. If you like horror and can find this on sale, check it out. Just don't expect it to blow you away.

I am starting to write reviews for the games in my library and I declare this one as my first.  I will divide my reviews into three parts and a comments section to keep things standardized.  I will do my best to give candid and brief reviews.
Bioshock Review
(Story)
Do you have a choice?  This is the question Bioshock asks.  The game takes place in 1960, in an underwater city called Rapture.  The city is falling apart as civil war rages among its citizens.  As a nameless protagonist (who winds up in Rapture due to an accident), you meet and help numerous people as you learn more about what happened to the city leading up to the war.  There are good and evil choices to make and multiple endings to the main story that reflect your decisions.  The dialogue is well written and voice acting phenomenal.

(Gameplay)
Bioshock is a first person shooter with most combat taking place in close quarters areas.  You alternate between conventional fire arms and powers called "plasmids" that allow you to shoot electricity from your hand, throw objects, etc.  The weapons  have multiple ammo types/firing modes/uses that are acquired through upgrade stations.  Likewise, plasmids can be upgraded and all feel unique.  Multiple play styles are available: go in guns balzing, set traps for enemies to walk into, hack turrets so they fight with you, or take a stealth approach.  Ammo, health, and crafting supplies are acquired from looting or use of vending machines strewn about.  One mechanic the first two Bioshock games are known for is enemy research.  In Bioshock, research is accomplished through taking photographs of enemies and filling your research bar.  Every time you reach a new level of research, you gain a damage boost against that particular enemy.  Ammo can get scarce sometimes.
(Design)
The art-deco/1950's/1960's America decor are very well done here.  The advertisements, record player music, items, even the bottles all fit the time period. The game can get scary at times too due to the atmoshpere and noises you hear as you creep around.  Nearly every object has its own physics.  Glass bottles clink, suitcases float in the water, and fire leaves furniture (and enemies) charred.  The sound design is excellent, though I have an issue when gunfire starts where sounds cut out due to everything going on.
(Final Comments)
As the first in the series, Bioshock is a great game with good controls, great writing, and one-of-a-kind atmosphere.  The twist of the story is legendary in my mind and the dialogue will leave an impression on you.  Now, would you kindly stop reading my review and dive into Rapture.

It's very unfortunate that this game is only good for one or two playthroughs - because I absolutely loved playing through it.
Decay: The Mare is a spiritual successor to the Decay series that was released for XBox Live Arcade by the same development team at Shining Gate Software, and published by Daedelic Entertainment. It's a point 'n click tribute to psychological horror games, as per the description, and while it's not a survival horror game in the traditional sense, it's a solid story and has a thick atmosphere to share with all who play it.
The game itself is split into three episodes, all included in this one package. Unfortunately, the game is still short, which may be a blessing in disguise - the entirety of the game is chock-full of interesting, though perhaps easy, puzzles, and is visually enticing in a gritty way, much like classic survival horror games such as Silent Hill or Resident Evil. The gameplay is simple, as a  point 'n click, but there are some interesting elements that this game has, and just enough jump scares to periodically break the tension.
In the first two episodes, the story will be very confusing and probably not make too much sense overall - but in the third and final episode, everything is brought together into a big "aha" - arguably too well, although one of the two endings this game has presents just enough "what if" questions to leave the player with. It's a wonderful game with a very thorough and well-made conclusion.
If you're wanting a scary point-and-click adventure experience, I would highly recommend this game. If you can't really stomach the scare factor, there's enough playthroughs that can present the experience to you without you needing to do anything yourself. I'm not sure the game alone is worth purchasing full price, considering the length of the game, but the quality is top notch and I would love to see more from Shining Gate Software.
There is, of course, one question that is never answered. Why the horse?

In many ways, Sunless Sea is an amazing game. It's beautifully written, and the setting is rich and complex. There's so much content that there's almost always something new to see. And the soundtrack and art are just beautiful.
Unfortunately, the mechanics aren't so amazing. A lot of the game is spent traveling from one place to another, and travel is slow and tedious. There's not much to relieve that—you can evade enemies, fight them (combat is very simple, and not particularly interesting), and deal with the occasional issue that pops up. Otherwise you're just crusing along, trying to balance various stats and resources as you go. Even that doesn't require a lot from you: I spent a lot of my playtime reading a book and occasionally checking to see if my ship had reached port yet. I loved the idea of exploring the world, but there's a lot of downtime that the game offers very little to fill.
I'm recommending based on the strength of the writing, but I suggest players come with alternate things to do while waiting. Transit is a great time to finally clear your inbox!

I feel like if they would have added some more interesting characters and humour it would have helped to break the very dark atmosphere in the game at somepoints and provided the game with more balance to make the dark moments feel even darker. Now the game just feels like swimming in the sea of depression with no end. The more I played the less I cared what happens to my character as everything in the game is so dark and I ended up sailing reclessly which really took away the impact from the atmoshpere.
If I would compare this to Metro games, which I love for the same reasons, this would be like Metro, but  all the visits to the stations would be extremely melancholic with almost no light, no hope, no homour and no life. Even though the visits to the sations played a minor part in Metro games they really gave contrast to the dark tunnels and the dead city. They made you feel safe and happy in between the dark gameplay segments. Now that I think of it, I understand that that the visits to the stations and some of the friendly companions you meet on your journey make the darker tunnels feel darker and make you care for Artyom, humans and the gameworld much more and keep you interested and invested in the game until the end.
However I will recommend the game as it is very atmospheric, interesting, unique and has great gameplay. If the lack of humour does not bother you or you intend to play it for a short period at a time it is a great interesting game.

I really love all simulator games like this.  Yes, it does feel a lot like an early Prison Architect.  Yes, I was able to make my mall self sustaining within a few hours (felt like I "beat" it).
Things I would like to see done to the game to have a better overall experience:
Ability to name different stores
Highlight employees on the time sheet graph so you can tell where they are in comparison to the other employees (when you have one selected)
An overall employee tab, displaying all employees no matter what business they're attached to (to make it easier to move them from one business to another)
Break up the buildable objects into groups instead of having a long list of absolutely everything you can build
More options for aesthetics (more plants, floor choices, decor in general) to build
There were a few times my employees would come to work and immediately head home - turns out I had placement of their workstations wrong - but I only figued that out by rearranging things, would have gotten frustrating quickly if I were playing a game I thought to be fully finished.  Maybe have a dialogue box above an employee if they can't start or finish a shift?
All of my comments aside, I really have enjoyed playing this game.  Would like to see where it goes from here; the base game has a lot of promise.  I bought Prison Architecht in early access and definitely have not regretted that - I'm hoping it's the same for this game.

This may turn out to be a fine game, but I feel like it's got a long way to go before it should have even been opened for EA.
Here's why:
You make a building, stock it with products, and hire staff. That is basically the end of the game. You'll hire office workers to research more products, hoping that something cool comes along, but essentially you just stock the products you researched and hit the FFW button.
You can add restaurants, a bowling alley, and a theatre to your mall, but they feel like more of "tack ons" than anything.
There's no incentive to have a great mall design, or stock certain items together. I literally made one giant store with one entrance/exit and put fresh food beside laundry detergent  and video games. People still bought everything and within a couple hours I was a millionaire.
The staff statistics don't matter. A person with a high cashier rating seems to perform just as well as someone with a low cashier rating, and even if you force them to work 15 hour work days, they never quit.
Even if you read the customer logs, it doesn't make sense. "Customer A is looking for lingerie, can't resist buying DVDs, customer is leaving store." So they came to the store looking for lingerie, but were tempted to buy DVDs and left without buying their lingerie?  Again, counterintuitive to "tempting" people with great products, because they abandon the first thing they were interested in.
Overall, it's a really cool concept and might be a good game in a few years. As of now it's just a shell of a game that seems impossible to lose and offers no incentives or challenges. You will have seen everything the game has to offer within 3 hours.

Every Tropico released since 3 has felt like a refinement since, and that's not necessarily a bad thing. This series has always been right where it needs to be in terms of gameplay, humor and style; it's just been a matter of perfecting it. While Tropico 5 brings the series closer than ever to perfection in an absolutely beautiful iteration of the series, it's had to take some things that fans love away in the process. But I trust Kalypso to continue to refine the game in later updates and expansions. I'd wholly recommend this game to fans and newcomes alike. Viva El Presidente.
Pros:
- Graphic updates bring you a gorgeous, sun soaked Carribean.
- Difficult. In previous Tropicos I never had an issue getting elected with the majority of the vote. Now I'm constantly on the offensive trying to figure out what needs fixing.
- Fantastic little details crammed into every corner.
- A new sense of depth to the gameplay, new strategies to be brought out, and new ways to plan your regime.
- More of the fantastic humor that's always made the series a joy to play.
- New trade and political options.
Cons:
- Faction advisors gone, no more Sunny or Ms Pineapple to update you on the latest situation.
- Difficult UI, a bit of a hassle trying to sift through all the citizens to uncover the root of a problem.
- Buildings could have used more variety and height as in previous iterations. While the graphic updates are charming, there could have been more options.
- Seriously. I miss Sunny and Penultimo's banter.

There is a good game here. It is innovative. It is done extremely well in spots. As far as the survival genre, it has the potential to be in a class by itself. After saying that though, you should know what it is you are getting into. In places the game is exciting, immersive, and beautiful. It can actually give a jolt when a wolf drops in unexpectedly. The buildings that you find while exploring look beautiful. The landscape, when it is free of trees and the developer put some thought and design into it, is very beautiful and thought provoking. Walking into a clearing and seeing the sun rising while a flock of birds flys over you in a v formation is pretty cool, indeed.
Where the game does not do so well is what it seems to have the most of. The trees can span for what feels like actual miles. What seems to make that fact worse is there is single digit tree models. Therefore you go through literally hours and hours of looking at exactly the same tree. Take the fact that the encumberance mechanic makes you walk like you are carrying a gallon of milk with your sphincter, and you can see where this might get pretty boring and frustrating really quick. Also, no map function that I am aware of. The weather keeps throwing blizzards that leave you snow blind. Forget about setting a base and then exploring. Get ready to get lost, see the same thing and double back, see the same thing and double back, see the same thing and double back, etc for infinity. I'm sure with a little more investment you could possible set your own landmarks or drop food on the ground to make a trail. But dang, I just wanted to play a game. I found a perfect little base (Max's last stand). It was great. But I didn't have the rifle and needed a couple other tools. Went walking for a bit feeling confident I could find my way back. Next thing you know blizzard hits, walk for 2 hours seeing the same trees, sprain ankle by bumping a tree, become hypothermic, hit by blizzard again, weight limit decreases to 15, start walking like I'm keistering a pine cone, etc. No rifle found, never found my base again, found bow with one arrow, shot twice with no reticule, bow broke, could probably draw all three tree models from memory. Quit game.
I like this game. I would recommend it as I feel there is enough here for the twenty dollar price tag. But if you expect to have fun then you might be disappointed. Fun isn't necessarily what I felt I got out of it. It would be fun if there was more to find while exploring, and less trees. Or more variation. Also a map function is almost expected in this type of game. Not to have one really sucks. It wouldn't really break the immersion if where you had already discovered was mapped, a la minecraft. Setting up your base would be much easier this way, and would lead to prolonged gameplay/ greater enjoyment for the user. Traipsing through hours of trees to find more hours of trees just isn't fun to me. A reticule for the bow would also be nice. Also for the twenty miles of trees, is there only one dang rifle? I found so many rifle rounds. No rifle. I found a huge farm. I was like "This is it, no farm in the wilderness exists without a rifle". No rifle. Another cool base. Dropped all my gear into a bookbag lying around. Forgot to pick up my bedroll. Left. Remembered bedroll. Went back to find it. Never saw farm again. Wandered for hours till sleep deprivation. Weight limit decreased again. Testes attached to Mjolnir. Also work that encumberance out, please. My goodness, once you have close to the full set of tools, you are already at the limit. A few food items, some wood, and instant turtle.
It does have it's moments. With some improvements, could be best in class.

A Search-for-the-object game, and that fact alone will determine if you want it or not because there's not much else about it.  The gameshow theme is pretty good, some of the (rare) trivia questions are a bit hard, the rest of the difficulty curve is laughably easy (your score will probably be 80X the nearest NPC competitor's).  Unfortunately, the execution on the actual object-hunting part is somewhere between iffy and alright.
Clicking on small or partially-obscured objects can be a bit particular, and a good number of the objects were slightly hard for me to identify until I'd managed to get them once.  The hint interface exists and is fine for if you get stuck.  There are a few different game modes though -- either search for particular items, or for categories like "animals" or "office supplies", or for groups of items across multiple screens that you can go back and forth between.
The minigames are simple, pretty skippable, and change things up a little.

Overall, I'd give this game a 7/10. The gameplay is pretty mediocre and it brings nothing new other than it's atmosphere and setting. Where this game really stands out is in it's underlying theme. It's essentially a political commentary over one of Ayn Rand's novels which involves a lot of her political views and philosophies. Look into it if you are interested in that sort of thing.

UPDATED: 29/06/14
I've come back to this game again recently after taking a 6-month break or so (I find this is the best way to enjoy Early Access games) and I feel like it's improved markedly since my last review.
Project Zomboid is best described as 'DayZ meets classic Fallout' - if that's something that appeals to you (and it should!), then I can recommend this game wholeheartedly. In previous incarnations, the game was undeniably promising but very rough round the edges, meaning the absorbing battle against the environment and the monsters that inhabit it was punctuated with jarring bugs and glitches like falling through stairs, walking straight through walls and so on.
Many of the more troublesome gremlins have been zapped, and while there are still a few that pop up from time to time, the game is a lot less likely to do something utterly bizarre, and a lot more likely to kill you with cold, hard logic and survival elements.
The developers have handled the release fairly well, providing steady and worthwhile updates whilst continuing to listen to their community and prioritising the issues that matter most to the fans (stability and the addition of multiplayer). This has resulted in a game that I feel a lot more players would consider 'truly' playable and could sink many hours into, even in its current state.
There IS still a long way to go - NPCs seem like they're still a way off, and it's odd to see entire towns almost perfectly modelled, but without a single car in sight - wrecked or otherwise. These things will no doubt be sorted in time - the developers have proven over the past 12 months on Steam that they are happy to take their time working on things until they're ready rather than risking adding things too early and bringing in a host of bugs and issues.
Overall:
Fun?: Yes
Any Game-Breaking Issues?: Not really game-breaking, but it's not finished.
Worth the Price of Admission?: Yes.
============================================================================
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
First things first - I've been playing Project Zomboid since I first learned about it on Steam Greenlight way back when it was one of the flagship titles, so obviously the game-time in Steam doesn't really reflect that. Just for disclosure there. :)
Anyway, onto the game, and the first question you're going to want to know is 'is it worth it?'
And annoyingly, it's kind of difficult to answer right now. Let's get this out of the way right now - in its CURRENT STATE, Zomboid is bug-riddled and missing many key features. If you're buying it right now (November 2013), you need to understand that this is absolutely an Alpha - entire chunks of the game simply aren't there right now, in particular NPCs.
It's also clunky to control, has a learning curve that's almost Dwarf Fortress-esque in its steepness, and occasionally difficult to navigate.
But the one thing that keeps me coming back and that convinced me to part with my money in the first place is the potential. It's not the 'War Z' potential where the devs are making grand promises with absolutely no idea how on earth they're going to keep them - the basics are in there: the map is freaking enormous, and it's gloriously detailed. The zombie behaviour is excellent - individually they're not a threat, but make a loud noise or stumble into a horde and you're in a whole WORLD of trouble. The parts of the game that are complete show an attention to detail and that little spark of inspiration that give the player confidence that whatever's being promised/worked on is going to arrive, and when it does, it'll be awesome.
So to conclude, although it's often banded about these days, it's more true than most in the case of Project Zomboid - when you hand over your £9.99 (or regional equivalent, I guess!), you're buying the game it's GOING to be, not the game it is right now. If you're not convinced that this is a gamble worth taking, you might be better off waiting six months for the game to take a little more shape, but you should be aware that the price will likely creep up again slightly, as the developers have confirmed that they want to reward early adopters by offering it to them for less than 'full price', whatever that may end up being.
Fun to Play?: Yes
Any Gamebreaking issues?: Lots
Worth the admission price?: Depends on your patience.

Look, we are simple folk.
When I say "we", I mean of course my brethren, the Hidden Object Game people (or "hog people" for short).
We don't ask for much, just pretty-ish environments in which we can look around for misc. objects from a laundry list (such as: manacles, a whip, candles, an Xbox One console, heavy-duty plastic tarps, a wooden horse, tax forms, a ball gag) to click on. And that's enough to content us, really.
Sadly the art in this is pretty abysmal. Objects are resized in a way that does not make sense relative to each other; likewise, objects are fuzzy that should be in focus and conversely. The photos that the art is sourced from are pretty ugly/dull, and garish colour filters are applied liberally to make matters worse.
I understand that this was done in an effort to make the object hunting a bit more challenging, but the combined "eyesore power" of all these techniques used at the same time is just too much.
There's a game show conceit in
, and that's at least a novel way to frame the different environments. They bungled the meat of the game though, letting us hog people down.

I would prefer to give this a neutral rating, but Steam doesn't allow that.  Whether or not you will enjoy it depends on whether you expect the plot to make sense, or if you're only going to be reacting emotionally.  I didn't enjoy it, because I need plots to make sense to enjoy them.
The Good:
A plot that could have been written by a real paranoid schizophrenic.  Fitting for a game about a spooky asylum, right?
The spooky asylum atmosphere is pulled off well.
They bothered to include non-violent mental patients, which is a nice change from games that portray everyone in mental hospitals as cannibalistic sexual serial killers.  Some of these non-violent patients even become victims of the violent patients, making the whole thing more believable.
Jump scares are used, but not
.
All the settings PC users expect are provided.
The Bad:
A plot that could have been written by a real paranoid schizophrenic.  Math, science, technology, secret government projects, and the occult are mishmashed together in a nonsensical way.  This word salad portrays any field that the laymen doesn't (currently) understand as
, capable of doing anything (bad) that you can imagine.  The Lawnmower Man (movie) gave virtual reality the same treatment in the early 90s, and probably seems as laughable to most people now as this game's plot did to me.  It is often better to leave story elements unexplained than to give silly explanations.
The plot is very poorly integrated with the gameplay.  It is only revealed through documents you can find and notes the protagonist scribbles occasionally when you videotape certain things.  Perhaps this is for the best.  Some people may be happier ignoring the plot.
There are some serious believability problems:
Not only is the whole parkour thing ridiculous, it's also buggy.  When trying to sidle along eaves you will frequently move forward and fall when you are actually moving left or right with the controls.
There is no automap, and the game
needs one.
The puzzles are repetitive.  Someone at Red Barrels seems to have an obsession with water valves and fuses.
Outlast makes some mistakes common to almost every modern horror game:
Outlast, as its name might imply, feels unnecessarily drawn out.  I think it should have ended about 2/3 of the way through.  Maybe it was that I wasn't enjoying myself, but I think it was due to there being an excess of setbacks relative to the successes.  The experience felt unrewarding and full of filler.

I was skeptical at first, but this is a solid game. You'll die a lot as you learn how the game works, but that's just part of the fun. This is an exploration game with roguelike elements. I have heard people compare this to FTL, but I don't think that's a realistic comparison. The game is less linear, and the combat is more action than strategy. The gameplay isn't nearly as deep as FTL. In spite of that, it is a fun and challenging way to spend some time. Most of the game revolves around story, which you advance each time you explore a little farther without dying.
You are a captain of a ship in a semi-randomly generated map.  You pick a goal each game and have to meet that goal before you win the game and retire. In the meantime, you must keep your ship fueled and your superstitious crew calm and fed to prevent mutiny. The islands appear in generally the same section of the map, but in a different place in that section each time. Since so much of the gameplay is in the story, the drawback is once you've played through a few times, you already know what happens in each event. This detracts from the atmosphere of the game somewhat. Still, there is a lot to explore and, much like a book, you can pick it up and read it again from time to time. The writing itself is like something out of a twentieth century American pulp magazine.
Risk madness exploring far off islands with terrifying locales deep within the hollow earth. Hire a crew with strange and enigmatic officers and learn their stories. Build your reputation with the soldiers, scholars and criminals of Fallen London and nations far from home shores and become wealthy from trade. Spy on ports and sell your information to the highest bidder. Meet nomads, smugglers, exiles and villains in lawless ports like Gaider's Mourn and Khans Shadow and earn coin ferrying them from port to port. Romance men and women and have a child, or choose to adopt one together. Tattoo the memories of distant shores on your own sweet skin. Earn the favor of the gods of the zee or scorn them and risk their terrible wrath. Smuggle illegal goods. Hunt pirates and sea monsters. Earn stories from your adventures or trade the other captains of the zee for them with recent news from home. Become a wealthy and famous captain of the unterzee.
