An excellent solitaire game with a well thought out storyline placed strategically between "places" giving the gamer a mental break.  Set in the beginning of the Regency Period of England (1812) follow Belle through a matrimonial based societal season as she is pursued by one man but pursues her own dream of finding love and happiness with another man.  These short story breaks in the gameplay offer tidbits of what life was like during this period of history and the common places those of society went.  Bright and colorful artwork of each place added during gameplay as wallpapers.
Gameplay: Starts at three hands and increases to ten hands per place invited.  Every hand can be repeated, using retry, if the gamer wishes to achieve or needs to achieve a better score to reach the "local" goals. (Note: once the player moves on previous hands can not be repeated unless the player restarts that level.)   This particular retry feature comes in very handy when trying to achieve the 35 card combo, which as far as I can tell can only by achieved in two places (last chapter Belle's Ball, hand 7 or 10).  My best combo before Belle's Ball was 34 and I ran out of cards. So sad.
The player can have up to 11 "wild cards" and jokers can be used as any card which makes getting that elusive 35 card combo possible.  There are three "power-ups". 1) Cupid who shoots an arrow (2 when upgraded) to eliminate a single card on the playing field. 2) A fan used to shuffle the cards, and shuffle includes both the cards of the playing field and those remaining in stack.  Can be useful.  3) A fire phoenix that burns 2 (3 when upgraded) random playable cards of the playing field.  (Note: I do not recommend using any power-up when trying for the 35 combo since at most there are only 37 cards on the playing field.)
Just a few words on the card hands, some are very, very challenging.  One of the hardest hands I had only had about 16 cards on the playing field and about 28 cards in the stack.  The way the playing field cards were laid out overlapping one another and having multiple cards with ribbons (ribbons mean the player had to use that card twice) was quite the challenge to clear, and power-ups were certainly handy to have.
Overall, an addicting card game, that moves along rapidly though the levels, and becomes more challenging as the player moves through the story.

Sunless Sea is a unique indie game featuring London (the main city you start in) being taken underground by millions of bats. London is not the only location that has been taken undergroudn and as you explore you will find other cities that have been taken under from the surface as well. Surrounding London is the Unterzee, a subterranean ocean infested with monstrous sea life and adventure.
The Unterzee as opposed to the surface world is much closer to Hell. Devils/Demons appear constantly and show up  in various storylines as you play through the game; Some being outcasts while others being parts of society.
I've played 17+ hours of this game during the free weekend and this is my review.
Pro's:
-100+ hours of gameplay
-Dev team keeps adding more stories
-The games atmosphere is immersive, intense, and authentic. Its a mind trip. You will not play ANY game like this. Its a one of a kind. A diamond in the rough.
-If you do not share map charts with your heir after you die the map will change everytime. Like Diablo 3's random map generation this keeps the game very entertaining and fun everytime you leave port.
-Mysterious and compelling. Every quest offers atleast two choices but mainly 3 or more on how to proceed with a given mission. You often ask yourself what if i did this instead. It equates to more gameplay hours with more playthroughs. You will not get bored.
-Fear constantly keeps you on your toes. I've seen tentacles take crew right off my deck, one minute billy was sweeping the deck, the next he just wasn't there no more. At first I thought it was the whiskey, but after i took roll call I knew it wasn't just a bad dream.
Cons:
-There are some annoying money drains that really hinder echo generating progress; Such as sleeping in your London home for a night costs money.
-The Buying/Selling of goods from port to port is broken. For example in Irem i can purchase fuel and supplies just fine but if i want to sell those goods when i just need 5 echo to purchase an extra secret i literally cant. They will gladly buy my fuel/supplies but for 0 ECHO!!!! what gives? Furthermore only certain ports let you sell certain items. So you may have an item in your hold that you want to get rid of for a couple extra echo but cannot due to port buy/sell limitations.
Conclusion: This game is a unique, compelling, and immersive experience that took my mind entirely off everything else going on in my life. I have never played a game remotely like this in my 25 years of gaming. The stories are enthralling and unreal, the terrors of the Unterzee keep you on your toes everytime you leave port. It's the hapless Captains that don't pay attention that the drowned men take into the dark waters of the Unterzee.
However the inventory system is a pain to deal with at times due to fuel/supply storage limitations. The echo grind is insane and you will most likely never get to experience the might of the 30,000 echo dreadnaught ship.
Despite these flaws I have to give this game a 8/10. For a unique and rich plot and terrifyingly immersive enviroment that is actually quite hard to do in a top down view game. The dev team constantly brings updates and new content and I have a feeling the echo economy will be changing for the better with these updates.
Goodluck out there in the Unterzee Captains your going to need it, lest the black take you....

Unlike what the tags says, this isn't exactly an horror game, but more like a psychological horror/thriller game, which is way different. The only horror parts are a few jumpscares, which I find a cheap, very cheap, way to frighten the player, which don't work to me since when I was a kid.
The main point of the game, being a first-person adventure, is to go around and find clues to solve puzzles. I'm not really into puzzles because I find them boring unless they are done well, but I succeeded in completing this whole game in about 3 hours all by myself, except for one puzzle which don't have any clue around so it's pretty much a job of finding the right sequence, which I hate so I followed a guide.
If you get lost, there's a really nice help feature (the best part of the interface imo) which don't tell you how to solve anything, but just gives you directions about where to go and if you still have something to do in a certain place. It's a small "?" in the bottom-right corner, which seem to appear only when the game thinks you are lost and works pretty nicely, and is very useful since the navigation is so messed up.
In fact, navigating through this game is the worst part of it, and alone is the main reason why I didn't enjoy this game that much. Not the only reason, but an important one.
To navigate the game's map, you'd have to press some inexplicably small arrow buttons around the screen, but the direction you'll be facing is not really what you think it'll be, so you'll often wonder where are you looking at. To add to the frustration, some details of the game are repeated over and over, which will confuse you even more and not letting you find doors, which are obviously the only way for you to find all areas. For example, there's a place where you can press the right arrow to turn right and, when pressed, you'll be facing what looks like the corner of the floor and a door to the right, then you can press right again and you'll be facing the same exact door in front of you, which makes sense but not in this game, since these doors are actually two different doors.
The game is full of these navigation problems, and I found myself using the question mark to navigate through it most of the time, until I finally learned the map, and at about that time, the game will be finished anyway.
Yes, because even though it contains 3 chapters, these are very short, about 1 hour each, and the game will be over by the time you'll start to get into its clunky interface.
The puzzles are nothing new, and looks like just an excuse for the developers to make the game last that bit, and they don't add anything nor fit in any way to the story, except a very few. It's the same puzzles you can find in Hidden-Object games, only that here you'll need to interpret the clues around to be able to solve some of them.
I think the only redeeming factor of this game is the soundtrack, much better than the game really is for me.
At the full price I cannot recommend it. I got it from a bundle and yet I don't think I've really enjoyed the experience. It was barely worth the little time, efforts and money I've put into it, so I cannot recommend it for 10 euro.

An indie platform game that lets you explore a dark and myserious world filled with various creatures, deadly traps and some puzzles. It bets a lot on its atmosphere, but the gameplay is smooth and enjoyable, even if kept to a strict minimum.
It's not a very long game, count maybe 3-4 hours to finish the story, 5-6 if you go easy. Getting all the achievements will probably take you some time though (without walkthrough). Over-all, I would count 10-15 hours to finish the game 100% without help. I personally took a lot less time because I had already played this game without steam.
I really enjoyed the ambiance of this game, you really feel like you're "trapped" inside it. The fact that the human characters never speak doesn't hinder the game, it only adds to the morbid atmosphere you keep feeling around them. The sound effects are extremely well produced, it feels vivid and they contribute a lot to immersion. I strongly advise using headphones for this game.
The game-play is simple, but you never really feel like you miss something. Well, to be exact, the occasions where you feel that way are mostly when the character himself is also helpless. That's also a very good aspect of the game: it's very easy to empathize with the character and feel the world as if you were in his shoes.
The game isn't hard, even if you're not good with puzzles, you should finish it without much trouble. It's clearly not made for players who want a tough challenge, the adventure is its own reward.
Good luck and enjoy the game.

A few dollops of new paint has refreshened the series! Or has it...
To me as a fan of Tropico since #1, Tropico 5 has seemed to have thrown out all the old stuff that has been in the series since the Original Tropico. The Traits are now gone, alot of buildings from previous games have seemed to disappear, hardly any of the buildings look different from each other (Even Shacks look the same).
The concept of the time periods seems like an interesting idea at first but it is really poorly executed, around 80% of the buildings are locked in Colonial times, which is fair enough... Where are you going to get a Space Program in the Colonies? But what annoy's me is the fact that they didn't execute it like they did in the Modern Times DLC where you upgrade the buildings with the time. You can't even get a Medical building in Colonial times, or hardly any Entertainment buildings. And I'm pretty sure they were making Cigars and Rum before "The Great Wars"
The Gameplay can feel very dull and a bit of a drag at times. You feel like you've listened to the same song over and over and over, Done the same objective over and over and over. And you've gotten nowhere.
Also the customisation of the characters is appauling comparing to Tropico 4, which had limited options to say the least. The only costumes you can use in Tropico 5 limited to literally 5. And some of those don't even make sense, You can dress as an Astronaut in Colonial Times. This makes me facepalm very much so. They also slimmed down the traits to around 8. Considering Tropico's Useful and Humorous Traits from the past, these really aren't traits. Did I mention you can't have your own name? Nope, You got to have a name from this list. And going through the list is a grueling task as you have to go through each name INDUVIDUALLY by scrolling to the side.
The new characters also seem a bit... Bland and uncharacterful comparing to previous games. Even the Caricatures seem a bit lifeless. Also not having the faction figureheads stating what's going on really lets the game down.
It also is quite tough on the hardware, I would suggest using a beefy computer. But this could just be the early stages of the game.
On the brightside, It's pretty I guess. And Trading is a nice touch. But not much else has changed and had only really taken a step backwards.
I think Haemimont and Kalypso really need to get their act together, After that tremendous flop that was Omerta and now This. I don't understand why I thought this may have been better.

Honestly speaking, this is my first time playing Tropico series. I am truly intrigued. You are El Presidente, basically, a dictator of a tropical island nation. As a dictator, the entire nation is under your control. The historical period of this game ranges from the colonial era to its modern counterpart. For each period there is one or two particular types of economic activities that are lucrative and beneficial. You always have to change your construction plan over time. For example, in the Colonial Era, plantations and ranches generate money but as the time passes on you can't count on those to fight the Great War. After the Cold War the space program and internet become crucial as well.
It is not only a city construction simulation but a political one as well. You are the sole policymaker. You have to consider all aspects of your nation in terms of policymaking. Should I reduce the wages of the poor to gain public support? Should I use martial law to secure the position of my dynasty? Should I fight the Communists with the US or the other way around? This game is fancinating!

I picked this up in a pretty early state.  The idea is that you build individual stores, stock them with good, staff them, and then watch the customers arrive. You can build stores as standalone buildings, or as part of a larger mall building.   The challenges of building a mall are a lot of fun, and you can burn quite a bit of time on the project.
Pay attention to your needs chart.  As you grow, so do the needs of the community. You'll want to build stores to meet these needs. That, in-turn, creates needs in other areas as the community grows. Sometimes you might want to run a busy soda shop at a loss, especially if it helps draw customers to your high-profit camera store.  There's never enough fast food for these people, either, and that's a great way to make a buck.  Oh yeah, and don't forget to hire enough janitors to keep up with the messes those people leave everywhere. Mess attracts rats, and rats multiply.
I've had a blast playing this game in pre-release.  I can't wait to see how it develops further. I'm enjoying the replay value. Definitely worth buying.

Although I love horror games, I tend to get spooped and quit. For that reason I only finished the game recently.
It's a great game. The story is primarily conveyed through notes you pick up throughout the game, so without some reading you're not going to have a full grasp of what's happening. You don't get a flashlight, but a camera with night vision. Your job is to record anything interesting, but the camera is also used to see in the dark. However, there were areas in the game that were so dark that the night vision didn't help much. Plus, the night vision requires batteries which are picked up in the world, so if you use it too often you'll end up walking around blind.
The game is similar to Amnesia in that you can't fight back; you have to run and hide, and there are often parts of the game with a maze of corridors - some of which have dead-ends - which you have to navigate while being chased by a crazy man. Moments like those make it as much exciting as it is scary.
If you enjoyed the Amnesia games you'll enjoy this, and if you're a horror fan it's a must-play.

One of the most addictive games ever!  I love the survival genre but am so tired of zombies and guns, so having winter and lack of resources as the true enemies (oh, and wolves - can't possibly dismiss those as mere annoyances!) is a wonderful change of pace.
There are plenty of specific things I love about this game (crafting, the atmosphere, exploration, etc.) and even more elements that drive me nuts (how long it takes to walk anywhere, how tired you get, winter storms during the day, respawn rates of wolves, disappearing tracks and blood trails, save points only being in buildings, etc.).  There are a few things I feel would make the game better - for my style of playing, anyhow - including: a map, a journal where you can keep track of quests and personal goals (no, a real life notebook doesn't work for me), more variation in craftables, a better musical score, more woodland critters to interact with, just to name a few.
Can't wait for the story mode, but for now, this constantly-being-updated sandbox is a pure pleasure!

I stumbled upon PZ while browsing for a zombie rpg game back in 2011. I remember my eyes lit up once I viewed the features and played the demo. I was a die hard fan for PZ since then and have been waiting for PZ to become a zombie gaming hit. Those days back in version 1.4c were the best I could ever ask for and TheIndieStone has made my dream of a true zombie survival come to life with its great blast from the past graphics and ever expanding gameplay along side the modding community. I have met so many people because of this game and its great community and I hope PZ will become a even greater game in the future as TheIndieStone continues to develop their masterpiece.
This game has given me hours of fun and I'm sure any zombie fan like myself would enjoy it.
EDIT 2016:
Here I sit years after false promises or rerouting of the development focus. Still waiting for even a segment of story or at least the NPCs which were scoped some time last year (2015). Be it I'll be mocked by fans who still have the patience to wait or the moderators eager to argue against my opinion, I'm tired. I've sat here for several years now interacting with the community and even getting to be a part of the inner testing group until I was kicked out due to "certain views". Regardless I held my head high and no matter the conflict I enjoyed Project Zomboid and the select few who made my time feel productive and worth a damn.
I got to work with amazing people and discuss modding and even development with some of the devs. I can say I enjoyed PZ, but I don't anymore. The changes that have been put forward into the game have been minor to say the least. I like they're putting polish on many things but revising the look of the game three times that I can count is a bit much. Granted I know passion tends to die and it gets harder to continue projects but this has certainly been a long drought with only trickles of content making it's way into the game.
The Indie Stone has grown in size over the years hiring modders to be devs and turning the roadmap upside down making features that were not originally discussed with the community. To sum this all up I had fun but this game is dry and has been for years. Until I see the story or stories or even NPCs I would not suggest this game because it gets old fast. So hold tight if you still have any patience left, I know I've given up on this title but perhaps in some time it might get somewhere.

So far, I have had a lot of fun with this game. I'm glad to see a try/die/repeat game besides Dark Souls become this popular. Getting better at something until you finally get a high score on it is one of the greatest pleasures gaming has to offer. Even though Cuphead is difficult compared to most games, it is not particularly rage-inducing because of the shorter length of its levels and bosses.
The length and quality of this game really depends on how you approach it. Some might find it to be short. Personally, I am less than halfway through the normal difficulty with seven hours into the game. If I was playing the game just to beat the levels on the normal difficulty, I would probably be almost done with it. However, trying to get P ranks and A ranks has made me spend much more time.
Each of the levels and bosses feels incredibly fresh and varied. Game mechanics are introduced immediately, and then are never used again. In some games, this would be a problem, but it works well when you die a lot in each level. Moving and shooting are also very fluid. Bosses have enough move variety and variability to be fun after restarting multiple times.
I don't think I have to say the aesthetic style is great, but it is.
The only major con that comes to mind is that one of the run & gun levels won't let you get beyond a B score, unless you get a P score for some reason. I accidentally spent way too much time on it because of this.

This game may advertise itself as "Lose your mind, eat your crew", and yes, it is, in fact, a survival exploration game. But the strength of this game is in its comprehensiveness. Multiple involved parties, love life and upgrades to your home, occasional naval battles, resource management, slow paced long journeys - that's the whole life of a free zee (sea) captain. There is a lot of text - every port, every event, every character comes with a well thought out and well written story. Open world is fun to explore, and it gets generated slightly differently every game. Soundtrack is pretty nice but pops up rarely, making long treks across the zee more immersive, I think. Solid game.

Originally, I couldn't recommend this game due to its economy's quirks. But now, after the fifth life, I discover a few tricks and tips to survive at sea and the game becomes rather enjoyable.
It's imperative to take advantage of natural light sources and shores and know when to turn off the light to minimize fuel consumption. Hunger can be replenished at certain ports via certain recurring events (Light Chapel, Hunter's Keep, etc.) and via hunting zee-beasts (don't touch anything with three digit HP unless you're crazy strong already).
Combining the above with some net-positive trade routes allows a steady money income to fuel explorations. For example, a trip from London to Hunter's keep, Venderbright, Whither, Codex, Mount Palmerson, The Salt Lions, and Iron & Misery Co. yields 7 port reports, which can be traded at the Admiralty for fuel, coins and offers. More coins can be fetched by trading Mushroom wine from London to Venderbright and Devil's dice from Palmerson to London. A visit to Hunter's keep grants supply and replenish hunder. Same to the restaurant in Venderbright. There are bats on this path you can slay for supply.
If you do it right, you'll lose 5-7 supplies (100-140 echos, fuel is always a net-positive thanks to the Admiralty) for 7 port reports (worth around 180 echos) + 10% profit from wine trading + 5% profit from dice trading. A net profit of 90 to 40 echos depending on how conservative you are with the supplies + a bunch of exp + weird stories and artifacts you can sell to the university.
And once acquired enough echos to fill the cargo hulls with supplies, you can try the 22-port path north-east-then-south-west through Khan's shadow to Station III. Expect a guarantee net profit of up to 300 echos for a grand trip. And if you happen to find Strategic information or anything else of value, good for you. I once got 600 net echos out of one such trips.
It's still extremely tedious though and I still think hull upgrade is moot. But if you like Don't Starve and sailing, this might be the game for you.

Personally, I enjoyed this game. At a glance ro2 seems like another realistic ww2 game. But what makes it different is that it offers everything needed from an arcade shooter to keep balance (map, friendly nameplate, killfeed) while still having a punishing difficulty curve and damage model reminiscent of games like arma. Problem is. Whatever this game does, it's always a mixed bag of both good implementation and terrible implementation. Take the cover system for example: with it comes blind firing for good suppression to stop corner campers and you can lean slightly over/beside your cover to take pot shots at enemies. Downsides are that it's virtually useless as you always have a bit of yourself sticking around the cover for players to shoot you and you cant do anything about it. And this game is one of the few that somehow rewards campy attitudes. Teamplay is a big thing in the game so much so that without a decent pair of squad leaders throwing smoke grenades as cover you'll ALWAYS lose. Reasons why I don't recommend ro2 (or its rising storm expansion for that matter) is because everything and anything that's in the game is good in some aspects and generally clunky and terrible in most. Some would say this comes from it being "realistic" with how your character switches stances and runs like the tinman with autism. But that's just not the case. 6/10 play if you know you got friends with you or a good team don't play if you rather save on this frustration of a game.

So I've gotten about 5 hours into immortal redneck and I'm not going further.
When you first start you're given the default class of Redneck, it's got the worst startup weapons out of them all and it's abilities are alright but don't quite make up for the notoriously bad shotgun and pistol. It may be the first class and meant to teach you the game but it's in serious need of a buff to it's abilites and the shotgun.
The shotgun fires a burst of pellets with the same damage as the pistol shots, but it's super spread out right from the start, if you want to do any damage with it you need to be point blank to your target because it's insane spread makes it useless from any other distance. And for a lot of targets getting point blank means getting hit, so if you want to use the shotgun you're setting yourself up to get hit.
The starting class isn't the worst part of this game though, the class system is the worst part of this game.
As soon as you unlock your third class and start a new run the game slaps you in the face and gives you two random options for classes, and if you don't like them then too bad for you because you're stuck with them. What makes it worse is you have to pay about 8000 gold to unlock a re-roll on this stupid mechanic. And from what I've seen you still have a chance to get the exact same classes.
Now, there's a lot of good things about this game, the artstyle and music are amazing and by far my favourite thing about this game, when I first played I wasn't listening to music on the side or anything but instead listening to the game's soundtrack which is amazing.
The redneck's constant one liners actually don't really get annoying, they're not common and he tends to not really repeat himself. I infact really enjoyed the voice of the redneck. He actually managed to make rednecks sound badass with the opening line "Yeah you may kill me, but folks like me don't stay dead for long"
I'd say don't buy this game, but don't forget about it. Because I have trust in the devs. And I can see it getting fixed in the future.

I have been a big fan of city building / resource management style games since I first picked up Caesar II. However, I've never picked up a Tropico title until now and I am blown away by the wonderful game play and quirky humor found within.
Gameplay:
Players familiar with Sim-City style city building will be immediately comfortable with the Tropico layout. Similar concepts like connecting buildings via roads and strategic placement of buildings with resources are all present. Managing the economy is fairly straightforward although it took a few games to catch on to how the trade contracts enabled through docks affected the overall economy. Combat is thankfully mostly automated so it doesn't distract too much from city building and management and adds a slightly more dynamic negative event in addition to the random acts of God. The progression of a game through the ages and how the form of government evolves the criteria for success was a new concept for me and very enjoyable.
Sound
The sounds and music of the game pulls you into the tropical islander themed mood and is more than sufficient to emerse the player in the era of game play. Very well done.
Replayability
As with any game of this type, most players will run through a few guided campaign maps to familiarize themselves with the gameplay and then jump into true sandboxes. Thankfully a random map creation mode is readily available to churn out endless scenarios built to your liking. This makes replayability an easy checkbox to check.
Overall
Losing in Tropico 5 doesn't feel so bad. It seems the game can churn out any number of hilarious scenarios under which you will get booted from power. Accidentally import too much and go into deep debt? Oops...you got voted out and no your cheating didn't help enough. Didn't plan out your initial governorship very well? Man those 4 years flew by fast. This game will pull you in and hours will fly by.

Immortal Redneck boasts an impressive skill tree that has quite a few different things to upgrade and a lot of them can be upgraded A LOT, like 75 times you can upgrade certain things. The game has 9 classes which change your active ability, starting load-out, and passive ability, different passive abilites can also be obtained by collecting different scrolls throughout the pyramid, these can be both beneficial or detrimental. Shooting in Immortal Redneck often feels very good weapons sound good and shooting enemies feels very impactful, even if the actual death animation for the enemies is a bit weak. Immortal Redneck also contains a very large variety of different weapons and spells to use, at first i was rolling my eyes at the FPS box-standard, "Pistol, Shotgun, Grenade, ayy Macarena!" I was then promptly shut right up when the game started giving me Ankh's that shot other magic Ankh's, A electric pistol that bounced from enemy to enemy, and a sodding machine gun crossbow, A MACHINE GUN CROSSBOW!
Sound- The sound design in this game is brilliant, Highly reccomend you pick up the soundtrack. The enemies all sound like they fit their design, the music can be both exciting and ambient all while keeping reminiscent of the Egyptian theme. My only real complaint in this department is the voice actor for our protagonist the Redneck, as somebody who grew up in the American south I can 100% say this guy sounds NOTHING like an actual redneck. That said some of the quips thrown out are very accurate, others not so much. Speaking of quips, a small nitpick I had is that sometimes this game falls to the "Spider-man game" problem in that the constantly quiping character gets a bit annoying, but this isn't as bad of an issue thanks to the sheer variety of quips. Another samll bug bear of mine is that soem of the subtitles don't match the audio, a quick patch should take care of this pretty easy.
Graphics/Design- This is one of my favourite aspects of this game, the developers were very clearly going for a Serious Sam style desgin, and boy did they succeed. The mix of Egyptian style and Toony styles works very well, all the rooms look incredible, The weapons all look very unique going for a mix of styles, from wooden, almost hadn crafted looking weapons to futuristic lightining weapons. I'd like to give special mention to the enemy designs. All the enemies stand out and look very unique to each other. They almost all keep true to the Egyptian/Cartoon style and have almost a LoL and DOTA style to the design, and it works very well, once again highly reccomend picking up the artbook.
Misc.- As with most Indie fully-3D projects this game isnt without bugs, a few times i found myself clipping beside or through platforms or in some scenery, nothing a quick patch can't fix however.
Conclusion- Despite some slightly cringey lines and a few bugs here and there Immortal Redneck offers an addicting and satisfying old-school FPS wrapped in a nice Rogue-Lite package that can suplex you into next week and still have you coming back for more, all for 20 bucks.
9/10 - Must Buy

Regency Solitaire is a very good game.  I'm not going to bother describing the game, since its gameplay is obvious from the trailer and from other reviews.   I'll just list some positives and negatives.
Its core gameplay is similar to Fairway Solitaire's (originally made by Big Fish Games, but the PC version was made by Grey Alien Games, who also developed Regency Solitaire).  The addition of on-demand powers like the bow and arrow provide some strategic options lacking in Fairway Solitaire.   On the other hand, some mini-games like Fairway Solitaire's would have been nice.  However, I think it was a good decision by the developer to add powers instead of mini-games.  Mini-games did not add to the core gameplay of Fairway Solitaire.
There's something very addictive about finding long runs and continuing them with powers and saved cards.
It has a good amount of replayability because it has multiple difficulty levels and the items you acquire can change the way you play.
I liked the wide variety of scenic backgrounds, but I do prefer shorter scenes: having to play up to 10 rounds just to see a few lines of dialogue sometimes did not feel very rewarding.
I would have liked to see a way to compare scores with other Steam members, but I understand that this game is not just for Steam users.

I only recently was able to pick up a copy of FNAF on Steam (I also own the Desura version on Mac) and for what it's worth, it's a good horror game if you wanna just jump into it it, get scared a couple times and then start playing it like a strategy game.

In my opinion this is a standout among the releases so far this year. I'm really impressed this is apparently these devs' first PC game. Everything just worked right away for me. 21:9 resolution? No problem. Loads up right the first try. Tons of options in the settings menu. Proper FOV slider with a wide range. In terms of gameplay, the game does a great job of conveying a certain retro feel of a really polished shooter with tight controls, quick movement and frantic action. Interesting 3 dimensional level design that interacts with enemy types in smart and sometimes surprising ways. And retro in the sense of lacking any pretense of 'serious' context. The story is so simple it may as well not be there. No dumb cutscenes, apart from the super short one that sets up the intro. Just a cool and surprisingly engaging premise that gets out of the way of the super fun gameplay. Reminds me of games I played in the 90s, not at all a feeling I get very often anymore. And yet it also feels modern with well executed colorful graphics and nice lighting.
To be critical I'd say the guns sound and consequently feel a bit tinny, but honestly I don't really care when I'm having so much fun with the gameplay and exploring the levels. The progression system is engaging me so far and I'm interested to keep trying to get further in.
Overall I like this way more than I expected and it's already one of my favorite games this year so far.

Early Post Edit: Just finished Total Biscuit's "WTF is?" review.
This will be long as I want to give my opinion on what he's said. Some things I agree with, but most I don't agree with. Love TB and I've been enjoying his content for many years now. His reviews of most Rogue-Like games seem to always be coming from someone who doesn't enjoy the genre at all. So his opinion is fine, I just hope it doesn't hurt the sales of this game. Because of a few bad runs...
_____________________________________________________________
1 : "Unfun/Anemic Gun Play"

I partially agree with this. There are no decals, there is no blood, sometimes knowing if an enemy is indeed dead can take a second. These aren't a huge issue but true. However some of the weapons you aquire, as well as some scrolls, can drastically improve this. Just like Gungeon, there are guns that no one wants. But there are some really amazing and FUN ones you can find. The starting guns are under powered, but that's how it usually is...
He talks about unlocking additional classes, and how the first few runs can feel difficult or un-fun. I was able to unlock the first class after my first run... So yeah... And the first class is not that bad. His active can make quick work of bosses and tight rooms.
_____________________________________________________________
2: "Scrolls and Weapon Lock Scroll. Makes it boring."
I disagree with this. There are some really aweful scrolls that can really challenge your awareness and make you change your playstyle. Like taking damage if you jump while in air (double jump, or falling off ledge and jumping.), or jars/breakables explode when destroyed. Even one that turns all gold into health drops, which honestly ISNT A GOOD THING!. But there are also some good to ♥♥♥♥ing awesome scrolls as well. From his tree I can tell he didn't play much... And he hasn't even beat the first boss. (how I know I will address further down.) So critiquing a rogue-like off of a few bad runs is a bit unfair.
_____________________________________________________________
Most of these upcomming points are common in rogue-like games.
_____________________________________________________________
3: "Level Design: Never Rewarding."
There are rooms with "secrets" where you can find 1-2 chests hidden. I've found them in every floor. Which can grant you scrolls or weapons sometimes both. Making clearing and searching very rewarding.
_____________________________________________________________
4: "Never anything to point you in the right direction."
Being pointed in the right direction... What Rogue-like does... Seriously? There are items to point you in the right direction. Just like every other Rogue-Like...
_____________________________________________________________
5: "Cannot leave area till enemies cleared, and mindless enemy A.I. Hard to seek out remaining mobs. Making you endlessly hunt the remaining enemies."
This one is just silly. Yet again, what Rogue-Like lets you leave the area before enemies are cleared...? However there are some A.I. that will mindlessly run away/around. But that number is very few. And just like Ziggurat after a duration of time the enemies appear Red."
_____________________________________________________________
6: "Rare Meaningful Drops after fights."
This one I completely disagree with. Every enemy seems to have a small chance to drop a scroll or weapon. Again, I just think TB had a few bad runs... Each run I get around 4-8 new weapons before the first boss, and plenty of scrolls.
_____________________________________________________________
7: "No variety in scrolls, and too many negatives."
I know I already addressed this a bit, but he states it a few times. There are many different scrolls that do more than boost stats. There are a lot of negatives. Touched on this, but he states it a few times again. He had a few bad runs. Or he didn't explore. There are chest rooms with 1-3 chests in them. While also a few secret hidden chests on the map. I've had well over 15 different guns so far. Each completely different from the last.

I've have two challenge rooms on one floor. There seems to be at least on on every floor. Just like Ziggurat. Or just like seceret rooms in other games.

This game is pretty mediocre. The only reason I've spent so much time on it is because I really crave a city builder type game that's actually worth its price. This fits a niche that seems to be lacking any really good contenders but for 3 or 4 mediocre games.
What's good about Banished? The economy is reasonable without getting overly complicated. It seems to be challenging enough to come back to several times before you are able to get a knack for how the economy works best.
What's wrong with Banished? The terrains aren't very interesting. This is actually a 2D game. You can never build at any elevation. Everything is essentially flat and the hills/mountains are really just obstacles to build around or through. The square grid also kind of sucks. Certain buildings, such as the trader's post for example, are crucial to building a thriving town because it is the only way to acquire seeds and livestock. In fact those are about the only useful things to warrant the existence of the trader's post in the first place. Unfortunately, when you have a river that runs diagonally, it is practically impossible to place the trader's post since it can only be placed at orthogonal angles. Same goes for diagonal mountains and trying to place mines on them.
Its a good game I've enjoyed playing it, but it gets boring quickly and the minor annoyances become painful.

This is a zombie game like no other in the world. It doesn't have world class 3D graphics, or crazy melee dismemberment, so if that's what you're looking for, you ought to look elsewhere. If you're looking for a deeper experience; if you're looking to see what it would be like to try and survive the zombie apocalypse in real life, then you ought to pick this game up. As the Devs would tell you, try the demo first, but if you're still reading this with excitement, that you're probably the kind of person that will enjoy this game.
It speaks volumes to the Developers understanding of how a zombie apocalypse would actually play out that most of my deaths so far have been entirely plausible. It doesn't take a horde of a hundred zombies to take you down; just a couple of bad decisions. Forgetting that you left the stove on and going to sleep will have you burned alive. An untreated cut or scratch escalates quickly into a fight against disease. Hell, you can even die because you stayed out in the rain too long. Some people right now are asking, "Why in the world would I play something so abysmal?"
The answer to that question is emergent storytelling. Each death you experience in this game will leave you with something to excitedly tell your friends. In just a few hours of play in the alpha build of this game I've made more memories than in any of the last hundred some odd games I've played. What's so utterly astounding about this game is that the only objective so far is to just stay alive. The more I think about it feels more like philosophy than a lack of content.
You'll divide your time spent alive between cooking, sleeping, crafting, exploring and fortifying. There's combat here, and it satisfies it's purpose, but this game is often more about the survival aspects. I'm going to make an odd comparison now: Your   character is like a Sim. He has almost all the same needs, except for baths and showers. It is for this reason that the act of surviving is a little bit harder than avoiding the zombies. There is a finite amount of running water and electricity, so eventually you have to improvise when dealing with drinking, and preserving/cooking food. If you're into Minecraft style building there's plenty of that sprinkled in. Besides fortifying existing structures, you can build your own fortress which is quite rewarding should you be able to do.
Now lets get to the elephant in the room: This is in fact an early access game. It's impossible to know exactly where the game will go from here, and for some that will be a turn off. I will tell you this at least: there is a lot of game here in the Early Access version, and reading notices from the DevTeam on both their website and Steam make me think that the game is only going to get better. If you were hoping to tackle the zombie apocalypse with your friends, that feature won't be implemented until further down the road. Right now besides you and your audience of inumerable zombies, the world is quite barren. NPCs are also not implemented yet. The other promised features are just as great, as they pertain to the expansion of the world and the ability to hunt and survive in the woods. Right now the most viable options are to hunker down and start farming. It'll be interesting to see what these new elements add to the game.
There is a bit of a difficulty curve as well. Most basic things are explained in a series of tooltips, but as of the current release there is no tutorial. This isn't necessarily a gamebreaker, as many of the deepest games launch without a thorough tutorial. The game isn't easy, and it certainly isn't casual. You will die many times before you ever feel like you've got the hang of things. Like the Dev said, you should probably play the glorious demo, to see if it's your thing.
I guess the last bit I want to talk about is the pleasing art style, which reminds me of my earlier days of gaming. I grew up around games like Fallout 1 and Baldur's Gate, so I quite enjoy the isometric sprite based art. The dynamic line of sight system is ingenious, and manages to actually simulate it perfectly even though you can see the world around you with perfect clarity. The houses are pleasing well put together, and the dense forests are fun to marvel at. As of now the only hiccups in performance are due to the lack of optimization as of yet, rather than the nature of the game.
So what do I think about this game? In it's current state it's a wholesome, if a little lonely experience. If you feel a need to have a bullet list of quests and objectives you should turn elsewhere. This game isn't for those who think the zombie apocalypse is an action movie. It's for those who see it as a canvas for interesting storytelling. The roleplayers, the daydreamers are all welcome here. This is an amazing alpha, with a development team interested in deilvering on their promises. I believe that it's going to be an amazing game when it reaches it's final release. After I finish writing this, I'll probably play the game until 3 A.M., wake up for college, and play it all day afterwards. For those who can set their own sense of bearing in a game, this is the pinnacle of emergent storytelling.
Pros:
A realistic Zombie Apocalypse
Gorgeous retro isometric art style
Innovative Line of Sight system
Open-ended and infinitely replayable
The modding community is already budding
Walkers instead of Runners
Two beautifully rendered believable maps to explore
Very few bugs which is phenomenal for an alpha
Actually explores the possibilities of what living in a dead world would be like
Cons:
The Difficulty Spike will turn some off
It's still an alpha so it's not truly complete
You're alone in the world with a million corpses until NPCs are introduced
No tutorial for the uninitiated
Multiplayer has yet to be introduced
Score: 8.9/10

It's a great game. The story is primarily conveyed through notes you pick up throughout the game, so without some reading you're not going to have a full grasp of what's happening. You don't get a flashlight, but a camera with night vision. Your job is to record anything interesting, but the camera is also used to see in the dark. However, there were areas in the game that were so dark that the night vision didn't help much. Plus, the night vision requires batteries which are picked up in the world, so if you use it too often you'll end up walking around blind.
The game is similar to Amnesia in that you can't fight back; you have to run and hide, and there are often parts of the game with a maze of corridors - some of which have dead-ends - which you have to navigate while being chased by a crazy man. Moments like those make it as much exciting as it is scary.
If you enjoyed the Amnesia games you'll enjoy this, and if you're a horror fan it's a must-play.
Not really a bad game. But there's not much of an end game. After you've built a fairly self-sustaining community (which is pretty challenging), there's not much else to do.

When I first started in The Lone Dark I was focused on getting myself set up for the long haul. It didn't take me long to realize that this game is basically just a series of compromises. There's never a perfect place to stay for a very extended period of time, and each area of the map has its advantages and disadvantages.
In my first three hours I tried to traverse as much of the terrain as I could to get an idea of the map. After dying once getting stuck in a ravine, I started over with a much more reserved style of survival.
Fundamentally, The Long Dark is the perfect survival game. Surviving is a grind - between gather resources, hunting, fishing, repairing your inventory items, chopping wood, etc you're only left with a few hours a day to explore safely. There are environmental threats that if you are not prepared for, will result in a game over.
In my opinion this is the perfect player vs. environment survival. I'm excited to see what this game will be like upon the full release.

This is an AMAZINGLY UNIQUE game!! (But very hard to learn/understand at first! ^^) It's great in it's own special way; however, you have to like it's "type" of gameplay, otherwise it might be boring for you.
(It puts it's main focus on storytelling/questing/exploring, which is just textboxes with a lot of different choices which you'll have to click/choose. The bad thing is that the game seems to have no voice acting at all, while the good thing is that they are extremely talented at storytelling.)
All I can say is that it is clearly one of the most-unique and thus freshest games I have ever played!
Pros:
- Very weird/unique, mysterious story and economy.
- VERY challenging gameplay and complex economy with "random" elements; you have to try A LOT here unless you read guides, but even if you do read guides, everything is still "sort of randomised" and therefore takes a while to learn it. ^^
- Fun COMBAT! At first you won't even know there is real-time combat in this game, but there is. You encounter enemies while sailing and have to avoid their attacks and shoot in real-time; can be tricky.
- A big, partly-randomised map
- New updates for free! (Expect 1 old kickstarter stretch goal, they said, which - I guess - is not released yet?)
- Same setting as their free browser game "Fallen London" (which is amazing, too, but ~5 years old) and you can even come across cross-game quests and a big cross-game reward (appears only randomly) from it!! (If you link accounts.)
- More than 1 way to win the game, and all are quite hard.
Cons:
- Gameplay can seem confusing and unforgiving at first (you will die... and die again... ^^); you have to find out by yourself which stuff you should buy with which priority, in what you should invest your gold, how some attributes affect quests, which quest possibilities you should choose...
=> You might feel a bit "lost in too many possibilities", like I feel. :/
- Strange gameplay which is probably not suited for everyone; some may think it's boring.
- No multiplayer (obviously, but still I wanted to say it ^^).

To sum this review up very quickly, I have this to say.
The Long Dark is not a game. It's art.
Seriously, this one of the most beautiful games, if not the best looking game I've ever played.
No, it's not photorealistic or has a ton of pretty particle effects. Instead, the game features gorgeous environments that look like a moving painting.
And it's amazing.
Now, the game itself concerns a person trapped in the frigid Canadian wilderness after a solar storm devestates Earth.
There are no zombies, mutants, bandits, or anyone else for that matter. It's just you and nature. The gameplay can be challenging, but not frustrating. It encourages exploration and curiosity.  And even though its still in Alpha, the game fells very complete to me. I have encountered no bugs and everything feels fully fleshed out as is. Yes, there could be more items, wildlife, and locales, but I am more than content with what's avaliable right now.
There is not a ton of action to be found, but that's good. There's something peaceful about treaking through a snow covered forest and hearing only snow crunching underfoot and the wind whistling through the canopy. Or sitting in a cabin as a blizzard rages outside.
As I've said enough before, this game truly shines in the visuals category. There are many instances where I have had to just stop and admire the scenery (and take plenty of screenshots as well). Whether it be observing the sun rise from the top of a fire lookout or seeing the soft, red glow of a stove illuminate a darkened cabin.
10000/10. Get this game.

Decay really isn't as bad as it first comes off as, it immediately seems like some low-budget point & click, which has been super popular in the past handful of years. But Decay is set aside from the mumbo jumbo that floods the gaming market nowadays, as it's slightly unique in it's own way, though when it really boils down to the fundamentals, it's nothing special.
Decay is a point & click puzzle horror game, and the puzzles are the correct difficulty (some may be too easy), which is a huge step forward compared to most games of the same genre, which have incredibly specific puzzles which you will probably NEED a walkthrough for ("Scratches" comes to mind). The atmosphere is well established and you can get tied into the game pretty decently, though a lack of depth to the story/characters makes it hard to fully put yourself in Sam's shoes (the main character).
I completed all three episodes and it took me about 2 to 3 hours, and I took my time (took a couple breaks, etc.). It's a short game but I got it for like $0.49 on sale so I'm not complaining about that, also it adequately tells it's story (which is a pretty creative idea) in the correct amount of time so the length isn't a problem. There are a few dramatic cutscenes which explain more of the story which are pretty well-done and some are downright intense, which is cool because most games of this genre have super below-par animation and graphics, but like I said, Decay stands out because it's a bit better than the average point & click puzzle horror.
Though when looking at the theoretical side of Decay, even the good execution doesn't save it from being nothing more than an "above average" point & click puzzle horror. The story is incomplete, and the storytelling features are below par; the entire story is explained on newspaper snippets, which is the only time voice acting is present (and I don't know if it's just me but he reads WAY too slow). Voice acting isn't even present in the cutscenes, which is where I feel they should have allocated the talent, because I can read a piece of paper alone, but when I'm watching two people argue for example, I'd prefer to hear their voices rather than read it.
This is an ongoing problem for Decay: the developer just flat out made dumb decisions. The navigation is also difficult, given the fact that some rooms will start at the same orientation once you enter it no matter the angle you entered it from (the game is entirely "slide-show" style movement and looking). So for example, if you enter one of these types of rooms from the end of the hall, it will put you on the wrong side facing the door you just came through, making the buildings feel more like a labyrinth than a residential home. And some rooms don't do this, and will orient you correctly, making it just as confusing since you probably expected to be looking at the door you just walked through. It's all very confusing, but you quickly memorize the layout of the buildings in each episode since the maps are relatively constricted, so it's a short-lived con. The small maps aren't really that much of a problem though, as there's a good density of things to do in the amount of space they give you.
All-in-all, Decay isn't bad. It has a decently creative idea behind it, it's execution is above par, and the length is accurate-albeit short, if that matters to you. But the overall experience is what matters, and while at some points I was super invested in what was happening, and the game DID hold my attention for a good 2.5 hours (which is increasingly rare nowadays), it didn't have a lasting or any sort of serious impact on me. And being a dramatic horror game about murder and finding yourself and the answer to deep life questions, Decay should've made me feel way more.

Regency Solitaire is a very nice, relaxing, charming, yet challenging game.
The setting takes places during the Regency era in the United Kingdom - early 1800s. The Regency era is noted for its elegance, fine arts, and architecture. It also encompasses a time of social, political, and economic change.  This all is very nicely reflected in the game itself.
The game is centered upon a particular family within the Regency era, what each family member's role is, and how they handle, or mishandle, said role.  As the storyline continues throughout the game, the player learns a bit more about each family member.
The artwork is absolutely gorgeous!!!  The music very pleasant and reminiscent of that time era.  You do have the capability to turn off the music, if it distracts you.  There are two different settings, normal and hard. You can go back and forth if you like. If a level is too difficult, you can change the setting to normal ... or vice versa if you feel you want a more challenging game. Two of the Steam achievements involve finishing the game on the Normal setting and also the Hard setting.  [Note: If you do not want to play the entire game over on Hard when you have already played it on Normal, you can click on the last 'pearl' of the game and just play that last level on hard to get that particular achievement.]
This is not your typical Solitaire game. This game involves the playing of cards in an ascending and descending order on top of the faceup card to be played off of ... until all of the cards have been removed from the tableau (the board).  Within each level, there are specific challenges/goals you work toward achieving. By achieving those goals, you earn money to purchase power-ups, and to also decorate the main character's home.  They go hand in hand. Further clarifying that, each power-up has it's place as a decorative piece within the home of Bella (the main character), and also becomes integrated into the card game itself for the player to use when needed. The power-ups replenish over time -- not by the clock but by subsequent cards played. There are also random 'wild cards' that, once found, are kept in Bella's fan in the lower right corner, to be played when needed. The power-ups and wild cards carry over from level to level if not used.
If wild cards are used, you will come upon them again by continued play. Bella's fan can hold up to 11 wild cards -- from 'Jokers wild' to a specific card itself. There are no time restrictions, nor penalties.  The player plays at his/her own pace. For instance, if the player cannot complete the hand, has utilized the power-ups, and has used all the 'wild cards' they can use to keep that 'run' going, but cannot remove all the cards from the board by level end -- you earn no money, no achievements, but you are given an opportunity to retry that hand as many times as you like.  You also do not lose the power-ups, they simply replenish over time by each subsequent card played. However, if used, the 'wild cards' must be found again and will be displayed in Bella's fan for play.  The 'wild cards' are placed randomly throughout each hand.
There are several interesting additions in this game that I have not come across in other Solitaire games, which makes it that much more unique, challenging, and fun.  For example, some cards have big blue bows on them. What that means is that there are 'two' of that particular card on the board, right on top of each other and secured by that bow.  Sometimes, you will find that there are several sets of 'bowed' cards scattered about the board.  By clicking on the first bowed card in an ascending or descending order to be played off of the faceup card, that will utilize that particular card, leaving its double still on the board to be played when the opportunity presents itself ... but no longer 'bowed'. It has become its own singular card to be played. There is also a set of cards whereby one is a 'lock' and the other is a 'key'.  The player will find the key card through gameplay, click on it, drag it over to the lock, which then disposes of the 'lock and key' altogether, which in turn opens up that part of the board that was once blocked by the 'lock' card. Finally, there are also what is referred to as 'hidden cards' which I found even more challenging but fun, not a distraction at all! What happens is that on some of the boards, there is a card amongst the cards to be played whereby the player cannot tell if that is a 'stack' of cards or a 'singular' card on its own until it is clicked on to be played off of the face up card.
If you've played 'Golf Solitaire' -- this game is similar to that.  You play in an ascending and descending order off the faceup card.  It's the additional goals, types of cards, etc., that makes this game so unique and so much fun!!  Please remember, there is no time limit nor penalties.  You can take as long as you like to study the board and play accordingly.  If it doesn't work to your advantage, the devs have integrated a 'retry' capability ... again, with no time limits nor penalties.  This game does not have to be rushed through or become stressful. In fact, it is quite enjoyable!
And, yes ... the devs, Grey Alien Games, have also implemented Steam achievements and card drops!!!
I highly, highly recommend Regency Solitaire!!!!!

Playing Banished is like building a house of cards. Stacking each one in place, making a huge towering structure... hoping you don't do something to screw up that causes it all to come crashing down.

It could stand a bit more depth, as there really isn't much going on as far as "tech tree" research is concerned. Don't plan on ever really moving past basic medieval life. Nothing wrong with that, mind you, just make sure you're not expecting any real advancement in tech or living conditions.
There are mods that add a significantly deeper level of resource production, and I highly recommend checking them out. They turn a somewhat simple but fun colony survival experience into something that has the potential for a bit more depth of gameplay.
All in all, definitely worth the purchase price. There's a lot of fun to be had with Banished.

If you're like me, you've picked up RPGs from the 90's like Fallout 1 & 2, even the D&D classics and been able to appreciate an almost timeless quality at the center of them, beneath the dated (though I love them) visuals and at times wonky mechanics. To me, and I think many people besides me, this rock hard center is what we long for in gaming, but rarely get it. Project Zomboid, I think, has this. What's more, its classic, isometric perspective gives you the feel that this could very well have been side by side with those 90's RPG greats.
While the game in its current state has a long way to go and therefore any review should be taken with a grain of salt, there is no doubt that the core mechanics and systems of this game simulate a level of realism in this new Zombie Survival genre that I don't think any other in the genre has so successfully achieved.
You begin the game with the message "This is how you died." This immediatey strikes Project Zomboid as a game different than almost all others. Most games are about a hero or an invicible bullet sponge that goes up against the most extreme dangers and comes out a winner. In Project Zomboid you're an average person in a world of interminable dangers never able to escape the inevitable reality that you'll die alone and beneath a horde of soulless humuan husks gnawing away at your dirty flesh.
But while Project Zomboid is hard, it's logical in its difficulty. Surely you may rage quit the first 3 times you die, but you'll then sit back and realize the first death was due to hoarding too much loot, your second death was because you wandered too far away from the safe-house and became stranded without supplies, and the third death was because you really thought you'd be able to take out 5 zombies in a house with a frying pan and a pencil as a weapon. No, every death you'll die in Project Zomboid is justified and, to the persistent player, drives you to try again and play with better strategy. When you find that right strategy and finally survive more than a day or two with a character, the weight of the subsiquent satisfaction is real and keeps you coming back for more!
There's much that has not been implimented yet into the game, the largest of which is a fully functional NPC system. This makes the current game much more dark and lonely. I'm eager to see what continued development will bring to this game that is, at its core, so masterfully crafted to simulate a realistic survival situation.
Here at the end I'd like to mention that there are a few issues I have with the game, at least in its current state. Knowing that it's still in development, these things do not bother me much. There are many bugs and some can cripple some of you rsurvival tactics. For instance, the way the game handles the player's interaction with the enviornment isn't currently 100% dependable (though this isn't a game-ruining issue at all). With the isometric perspective, there are times with two items that you can interact with will overlay one another. Currently, and as far as I'm aware, there is no way to dependably interact with either items. The game will choose one of the overlayed items as primary and your interaction will always engage that one. This can be an issue when, for instance, you want to put a barracade on a window, but the game will only let you interact with the wardrobe that is aligned with the window in your isometric viewpoint. As it stands now, there would be no way to barracade that window. This might not seem like a huge deal to someone who's not palyed the game, but it most certainly could mean death for the player.
In any case, this is a game I HIGHLY recommend to those gamers who are patient and prodding with their games. Don't expect to jump in and become an instant-pro; this game asks you to practice and after 20 deaths to be satisfied with becoming "pretty good" at the game rather than "SUPER AWESOME NO-LOOK 360 NO SCOPE OWNAGE MACHINE" (or whatever, lol).
Grace & Peace to, peoples!

I bought the Dungeon Defenders Franchise Pack a few years back when it was on the Winter Sale, and can say that I absolutely fell in love with the series.
While I don't have many hours logged in DD1, I did enjoy the gameplay immensely. Though I didn't make it to the end game of DD1, I do plan to at some point. Now, DD2 improves on virtually everything that DD1 did. The only real difference I think is the end game content.
The graphics engine is FAR better, yet has options that make it work fine on older prebuilt computers like mine. Animations are well done, and the engine is capable of having large amounts of entities on it at one time. The maps are also well designed, and with the cell shading art style they're also beautiful to look at.
The gameplay has been improved upon by leaps and bounds over the games development. At first it wasn't much like DD1, but now at the full release I don't think I've seen a single thing that wasn't in DD1 missing in DD2. And unlike DD1, you can level infinitely in DD2 through the Ascension system.
The music in the game is pretty good, though easy to phase out. I personally love the soundtrack and frequently listen to it over my Spotify playlist. The sounds defenses make when they hit also vary I believe. If that is the case, then many kudos to Trendy for taking the time to gather multiple sound samples!
Overall I would recommend Dungeon Defenders 2 to anybody who enjoys tower defense based strategy games. It takes an interesting and fun approach to the genre with its hero based 3rd person perspective. Gameplay can get stale, but with friends could still be very enjoyable. The game itself encourages group play with the way its servers are set up. And to the DD1 purists who refuse to try this game at all, I have one thing to say; DD2 is a positive evolution on basically everything you loved about DD1 and I think you would enjoy it as much as the original.

Villagers working in food production are too stupid to just go to work to eat a damn squash when they are starving.  Instead they just sit around, presumably whining about how unfair life is, and meanwhile perfectly good crops go to waste in the fields.
Wool and Leather are not counted separately, instead lumped together as "Textiles", even though there's an empty slot for another resource in the UI.  This makes it almost impossible to gauge what your Tailors have the resources to produce.
The music is fantastic, the weather patterns are beautiful, and it's a fun city-builder.  But one little slip up and your people will just stop working, sending your civilization into an almost irreversible spiral of death and laziness.  Or laziness that leads to death.  It makes me wish there was a "murder" button on the citizens UI window so I could just kill people to save food for the people actually doing their jobs.  Maybe a "Kill them with fire" button.
Also, don't bother with the modding tools.  I downloaded it trying to fix some of this stuff, but couldn't get it to work because it's missing a necessary file.

The single greatest zombie survival RPG/sim I have played in ages. If you enjoy post-apocalyptic zombie-type games, I would definitely recommend giving this game a chance. I find myself thoroughly enjoying every moment I play, and even getting anxious when things like alarms go off or when helicopters fly over. Although early in development, I can see this game easily becoming an amazing finish product, and I already consider it a benchmark for all zombie survival games.
I absolutely love how there is no facade that you may get out of the situation alive; you play the entire game knowing that every single move you make is just leading up to your inevitable death! It sets almost a perfect tone for a zombie apocalypse, removing any base end-game goal like discovering a cure or finding a military quarantine for safety from the ever-shuffling hordes of undead. Your only goal is to survive as long as you can, to feed your needs and avoid becoming one of the zombies yourself.
If you enjoy zombie survival games or survival simulator games, I suggest trying out the demo as suggested by the developers (as amazing as the game is, there are still bugs which appear), and if you like what you see, pick it up!

The game does what it does very well.
And it is a testimony to just how good it is that I am going to complain about ... the snow.
You see, in a zombie survival game, nobody would as much as think about the snow, but in a game that is supposed to be "realistic" about survival in northern Canada, long, long before you would begin worrying about wolves, you would constantly worry about the status of the snow, how deep is it, is it frozen, will it carry your weight, are you going to cause a slide walking down that slope, you would invest titanic efforts into maintaining tracks, and hope they would not fill up with new snowfall, and your most prized possessions would be snowshoes or skis. Now nothing of this is going to happen in this game because their engine clearly does not support it, but I really hope they get rich from this and implement a snow engine in a later version!
Another complaint that would be more easy to address would be: more realistic astronomy! Realistically wheeling stars (navigate by the stars when the sky is clear), may be northern lights(!), and varying day lengths: for a game about winter in northern Canada called "the long dark", 12 hours of daylight seem long. Of course 4 hours of daylight would mess with gameplay, but they could have the game start at autumn equinox and make it your objective to survive into spring. This would lead to a natural progression of difficulty, and would add a long-term planning angle (stack up supplies), and you could also have the wolves behave more realistically, happy and careful at the beginning, but desparate and famished around midwinter.

This game is hard. Like, god damn hard. Almost too hard. And that's its main drawback.
It's almost too hard for it's own good. The bosses are challenging, and that's fine, but when it comes to the "Run N' Gun" sections (the only way to collect coins for upgrades like new weapons and passive buffs), it's completely ridiculous. I've spent about half of my time in this game replaying levels and tearing my hair out because of how cheap these levels can be. There's also the nagging addage that the only way to progress in the game is to beat each boss on "Regular" difficulty. They include a "Simple" difficulty setting which is a condensed version of the fight, but the only true way to complete the game is to beat all bosses on "Regular" difficulty. So, why bother include it at all? For replay value?
However, the game can really shine if you get into the groove. The big band recordings, the 1930s aesthetic, and the crazy impressive boss battles, while a bit gimmicky, can very much be enjoyable.

I don't know what to think of this game.
I honestly enjoyed the atmosphere the game was trying to convey, this creepy silent hill-esque vibe of the rehabilitation center, the uncanny graphics halfway between static and moving, but i don't know if it was intentional or simply a result of it being a point-and-click game.
It's been a while since I played a real point-and-click, the last one being Pajama Sam in the early 2000s when they came into cereal boxes, I enjoyed it greatly, but I was around seven years old.
I feel like the format took out the scary edge of the game. Sure, the narrative had potential, but I understood immediatly the limitations of the game. It's a point-and-click. Don't expect a fight scene, having to run away, hiding, etcetera.
It is all very straightforward. At first I was scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of the "thing" following me throughout the centre, but I noticed how it never really "came" for me. Thus the limitations of a point-and-click. No "real" action.
Still, I looked past this and continued with my exploration. The soundtrack was nice and unsettling, some of the characters (one in particular, if you played you know who im talking about) was fun to talk with and the puzzles needed exploration and some thinking, without being overly challenging. The coin-collecting is fun and unlocks some neat extras, I recommend collecting them, the game being pretty short.
To sum it up, I liked this game, even though point-and-click really aren't my thing.
I would give it a 6 out of 10. A nice, cheap way to spend time.

Ok, I never write reviews for games unless it's really good, or horrible. In this case, it was the former by far. I'll be honest, I epected some sort of Minecraft/Unturned rip off or something like that but I was pleasantly surprised. There is no tutorial, the game spawns you in the wilderness with a few basic tools and you're off to explore. What really surprised me is how massive the world is. It didn't occur to me in the beginning that all the regions would be connected, so when I came out of a cave and into a completely new region, I was amazed. I'm simply astonished at how pleasing the game is. It's peaceful, but at the same time, carries a subtle sense of danger *cough the Hydro Plant cough.*
And although it's not immediately obvious if you spawn in deep wilderness, the game constantly reminds you that it is set post-apocalypse by placing corpses in the least expected places. The game is perfectly paced to match the size of the world, and the way your resources fluctuate seems very fair and reasonable.
I'll say, this game surprised me. I can't wait to see what more Long Dark has to offer.

A Hat in Time is easily my
game of 2017, and that's saying a lot considering we had so many great
games, be it AAA or Indie developed. To put it simply: if you grew up with platformers like Super Mario 64, Banjo-Kazooie, or even Ty the Tasmanian Tiger, you'll
this game.
As simplistic as the facial animations are, the whole game is just beautiful to look at. Hat Kid is satisfying and smooth to control with no input delays (using an Gamepad, not sure about keyboard), and the abilities you can obtain later on are quite fun to mess with, even exploit in some cases. The game is split into five chapters (two more in the future), with each being different from one and another. Also the bosses are fun as all heck
.
As for overall plot, while I would have liked to see Mustache Girl a bit more during the adventure instead of getting little to no screentime outside of Chapter 1, I still enjoyed it. ..or rather the absense of one. The game's plot could be compared to the likes of Alice in Wonderland, as Hat Kid ends up traveling to various locations in search of the Time Pieces, with each location being unique in some way and have a story of their own.
The characters have quite a bunch of personality, and even the wit too. Yes, this game can be quite funny. I legitimately found myself laughing out loud at a couple of scenes. If the gameplay doesn't sell the game for you, the characters and clever writing most certainly will.
When it comes to the soundtr- y'know what, I'll make a seperate review for it another day. And yes, I think it's amazing.
Overall, I
recommend buying A Hat in Time if you're wanting to have a fun time, or perhaps sink your teeth into another platformer like the good ol' days. While there are the PS4 and Xbox One ports, I recommend getting this version as there's Steam Workshop support. You can make your own levels, paints, hats (with custom abilities), just about anything (and also play others' creations too)! ..of course, the game isn't flawless as I have ran into a couple of bugs as mentioned before, but the game as a whole was such a fun, childish experience.

Y'know, Just Cause 3 (Yes, I'm talking about 3 really quick, hear me out) had a much more refined game experience: the shooting controls were tighter, the grapple was far more versatile and useful, the parachute was easier to control, and the wingsuit was a blast to use and was a great addition to the game. The explosions were bigger, the voice acting was more tolerable, the weapons were crazier, and so on. I could list many more things that JC3 does better than JC2.
But you know what? Despite ALL of that, Just Cause 2 has a certain charm to it that 3 doesn't. JC2 is honestly just...I dunno. It's so much more fun to play. Maybe it's because it feels less generic and AAA-ish. Maybe it's because you didn't have to do little challenges and destroy the same boring props in every town to progress. Maybe it's because the world was more varied and interesting, and towns and bases felt like actual places instead of bullet points on a list of things to blow up. Just Cause 2, as unpolished as it is, ends up being the more enjoyable game in my opinion. And this is just vanilla; JC2 is stupidly easy to mod, and there's tons of crazy mods out there to really crank up the insanity. Naturally, it's also far easier to run than JC3. Even the craptop I keep in my room can handle this game at 30fps on low settings.
