Regency Solitaire is a totally charming take on the single-player card game by Grey Alien Games.  A variation on the golf solitaire play style, this fast-paced version of the classic game will have you addicted before you can say "tea and biscuits!"
Golf solitaire involves playing cards in ascending or descending order until all have been removed from the board.  There's a bit more to it than that, but it's a very easy to learn version of the game that will appeal to those looking for a more relaxing experience.  While there is indeed some thought needed in play, once you get the hang of things you'll be a solitaire pro in no time.
The game is divided into 20 chapters in which you have between 3 and 10 tableaus (boards) to complete a set of objectives.  These objectives get progressively harder with each chapter, but are never unfair in their requirements.  As you successfully complete each tableau, you'll earn money to purchase power-ups that will help you clear cards much easier.  You may also bank up to 11 wild cards which can be used to extend combos.  Chaining combos is the meat of the game play as bigger chains increase your score multiplier, thus rewarding even more money at the end of each chapter.  Of course, luck will play a factor in the draw, with particularly bad layouts often requiring several retries if you don't have enough power-ups or wild cards to get through them.  But that comes with the territory in solitaire.  At least there are ways to overcome it here.
While there are several different versions of solitaire out there, this is the first Regency era themed game I have come across, and it's absolutely charming.  Everything in the presentation has an air of gentility to it, from the beautiful hand-painted artwork to the elegant music and charming character dialogue.  The simple yet enjoyable story that plays out between each chapter feels as if it was pulled right from a Jane Austen novel, which is a compliment in its own right.  Altogether, it's a pleasant experience that  will transport you to early 1800's England when elegance and sophistication was prized above all else.
If you are a fan of solitaire, I cannot recommend Regency Solitaire enough.  Between the enjoyable game play, amusing story and lovely presentation, there's very little I can complain about here.  I only wish it were a bit longer, as playing through Bella's tale of courtship was an absolute joy that didn't last nearly as long as I'd have liked.
Bottom Line: Recommended to all solitaire and casual gaming fans.

A really addictive puzzle-ish card game. The objective is to get rid of (ideally all) cards on the desk, all of which are faced down except for those on the top. To do it, you start with a deck of cards from which you can draw. With the currently drawn card, you can collect a card from the desk that has one lower/higher value, making that your current card. By continuing collecting cards, you get combo multipliers and hence bigger score. The chain gets interrupted once you draw another card from the deck. Some levels also have special obstacles - locks for which you need to find a key-card on the desk, or royal-locks which require you to collect certain amount of Jack/Queen/King cards in order to unlock.
Simple enough to play in the morning, complex enough to wake you up :)
Each level consists of several desks you need to clear and has special goals. Those can be getting X perfect hands (leaving no cards on the desk), reaching a certain combo (chain of collected cards), getting high-enough multiplier (can be reached by multiple smaller combos), uncovering an item hidden under cards or getting enough starts throughout the level (3 stars for cleared desk, 2 stars for 1 card left, 1 star for 2 cards left, 0 stars otherwise).
To help with the goals, you can buy items. Those unlock by progressing the game, while you can buy them for your score. The bonuses vary from revealing certain cards on the desk to increasing the amount of Undo's to special abilities and upgrades. Special abilities consist of target-destroy (up to two) desk cards on top, shuffle all the cards and random-destroy (up to three desk cards on top).
Edit: I forgot to mention that there are also special blue cards, which you can collect and store. Those don't have any requirements to be collected nor played. You can use them in order to continue your collecting chain.
There're also two tiers of levels, easy and hard mode, where hard mode has higher challenges through the goals.
The art is nice and fitting, though the full-screen mode only stretches the game, making it feel... awkward.
There were some bugs forcing you to quit the game (and restart the hand), but I'm glad to say that those have been already fixed, and I didn't have to restart the game since. :)

You are in love with Henry, a man who loves ugly boys. Your brother continues to be garbage. You have a sister, Charlotte, who is much more attractive than you, but every one is too polite to mention this. Gameplay is seamless integrated with the plot. Someone will say something like, "We should throw a ball for Bella!" and then you are playing solitaire. Upgrades come in the form of decorations for your body (clothes) and for your ballroom that seems to travel with you. No one thinks that maybe the family's money issues could be solved by maybe not building a mobile ballroom and maybe not hiring piano and harp players because #yolo.
In all seriousness, if you like Faerie Solitaire (the gold standard of solitaire games that you're kind of embarassed to play) you'll most likely enjoy Regency Solitaire as well. It's basically the same game. You have a card and you need to click on a card that's higher or lower. You want to clear the board or come as close to it as possible. Each chapter has a set of goals you must achiever. Like in Faerie Solitaire, you can get wild number cards (however, you may not collect one of each, but you can get face cards and there are true wild cards which can act as any card), you can purchase upgrades and you can build up combos.
What's different? Levels have star ratings. A perfect is three stars, but if you're close you might get one or two stars. When a combo is over it is added to a gold multiplier that last the whole level (but not the chapter). You have three power-ups that do various things and are recharged by making matches. Also, in Regency Solitaire the cards are often at goofy angles like sideways or upside down. I'm sure this is a metaphor for emotions, but it's kind of annoying, especially with that whole 6 and 9 thing.
A great thing is in Regency Solitaire, you can retry individual hands without restarting the chapter. However, if you're OCD and feel compelled to get a perfect on every level you will have to find a way to cope with the shame of seeing the "NO STARS" ranking. Otherwise, you will be forever retrying and you will be trapped in the insidious Venus flytrap that is this game
Another noticeable different feature is that if you skip over a card that can be played, the card you could have used on the board will shake. This happens even on hard mode. It's kind of nice, but if you bought Regency Solitaire hoping for a hardcore challenge, then. . .I don't. . .maybe talk to a doctor, because you might be having a stroke.
If you like Faerie Solitaire and you're not ashamed to be playing an ugly boy-centric prequel to Downton Abbey, it's a fine game. Faerie Solitaire might be a little better, it has challenges, it has the eggs that will ruin your life if you want to 100% the game, there's just a little bit more. If you've had your fill, Regency Solitaire is more than adequate. Maybe get it when it's on sale.

If I could sum up Outlast in one word, it would be, uh, I dunno...one word? Hmm, I'm drawing a blank so I'll stick with...sticky?  Oh man that's a terrible pun...  I suppose that in the literal sense, the walls, and floor, and all the gore splattered surfaces of the inner chambers of the asylum are probably way sticky.  In the metaphorical sense, some of the more intense imagery has stuck with me weeks after I completed my playthrough of the main story.  Wait- that's the word, intense!
Outlast has the usual rising and falling of action you'd expect from a horror-thriller.  You'll spend most of your time on the run or hiding from the enemy AI.  The enemies are pretty decently varied, considering the setting being a locked-down asylum.  Red Barrels still manages to make a nice lineup of crazies trying to murder you without falling into the trappings of other horror games where the "fear" tends to dissipate from the enemy becoming too familiar to the player.  The saving grace for the enemies of Outlast is there's no question of their intent, if they get ahold of you they will beat you to a bloody pulp, and in some cases tear you to pieces.  So like any air-breathing human you'll be motivated to RUN.
Thankfully there's some breaks in the "omg omg, please don't let him catch up to me" bits to do a little exploring of the various sections of the asylum you tour.  Playing the role of a reporter, your goal is to document some shady stuff going down in the mountains of Colorado.  The plot exposes itself slowly via minor tidbits uttered from NPC's, and various notes scattered around the game, but the moment you enter the asylum you know something is wrong.  Red Barrels doesn't create a traditional horror atmosphere, instead opting for what I'm more inclined to refer to as terror.  Yeah, there's a difference and that's probably subjective, but I digress.  The graphics are gorgeous, especially for not being a AAA experience.  Outlast has almost set the bar too high for me, making other Indie horror titles seem kind of fake, or cartoony.
My favorite parts of the mechancics are the things that Outlast does that I haven't experienced in a horror game before.  The ability to pick a hiding place, under a bed, in a locker, etc. is a welcome change to the Amnesia-style "hide in the dark until the music stops", albeit that's still a perfectly valid strategy.  The thing is, the hiding spaces aren't always safe, and those moments where the bad guy enters the room hot on your tail, and decides to check the ONE bed you elected to hide under are terrifying and will send you running back out the door yelling "NOPE NOPE NOPE".  The other main defining characteristic of Outlast is the camera.  Keeping it running will expand upon the story by creating notes by the protagonist and giving their take on the events.  There's also a night vision mechanic that requires traditional resource management fans of Amnesia and Resident Evil will be familiar with.  If you run out of batteries, you won't be able to see in the dark at all, but thankfully neither can the baddies, making the pitch black areas a double-edged sword.  The only part of the gameplay I wasn't very in favor of was the reptition of certain sequences where I knew exactly what I needed to do to progress the plot (usually consisting of turn X valves or pull Y levers to unlock new area), but was having to constantly deal with the hassle of a big baddie trying to squish my head under his big thumping boots.
The story nearly becomes irrelevant later in the game because I just so desperately wanted the main character to escape and have a happy ending.  The plot stays competent to the end, though I can see some of the explanations of the more mysterious parts rubbing true horror fans the wrong way with its reliance on more traditional sci-fi tropes.  If you're looking for a more realistic, adrenaline packed NOPE-fest then Outlast is probably a good call.

You ever wake up in the middle of the night, look around the  bedroom where you've slept for years, and wonder for a moment where you are and how you got there? It's a creepy feeling, and "Decay: The Mare" manages at its best to be a creepy, creepy game.
This is definitely a "play with the lights out" game. The graphics aren't too sharp, which I enjoy in gritty, horror-themed affairs such as this. They're suitably dark, with haziness and shadows in all the right places. Little touches, like the art and photographs on the walls which occasionally change appearance, are quite eerie. The music plays well with this, predominantly consisting of forlornly beautiful piano pieces. The only thing on my wish list for "Decay" as far as the atmosphere goes is that some of the art unlocked as "Extras" was really spectacular, and I would have liked to see those insane ideas incorporated into the game itself. But this isn't a gory hack-fest, it's more of a spooky mystery/escape story with a few supernatural elements thrown in, so there's only so far it can go.
The gameplay is fairly basic point-and-click adventure, with some puzzles of mixed difficulty thrown in. Pay attention to details, because what you thought was simply a nifty scare tactic in one room may be the answer to a puzzle in another. While there's nothing too groundbreaking here, there are a few clever bits you can feel good about solving.
There are two big flaws to consider before playing the game:
1) There is no map function, and although the levels are small, considerable backtracking is required. "Decay" has an odd habit of both making the doors all look the same AND making a single corridor look completely different when viewed from another angle, which can be frustrating when you're trying to get back to the room you were in three screens ago. On top of that, sometimes when you go through a door, you'll end up on the opposite side of the room you're entering, looking straight at the door from which you just emerged. Yes, this adds to the sense of disorientation that your character would be feeling under these circumstances, but it also takes away the fun of exploration and replaces it with tedium.
2) The plot, as thin as it is, sort of falls apart at the end. Without giving anything away, new characters are introduced as late as the last five minutes of the game. The particulars of how everyone ended up there in the first place elude me, and the letters and newspaper articles found throughout the game don't really seem to foreshadow the final reveal. Sure, the main baddie's crimes and motivation are telegraphed early on, but everything involving the main character and his friends falls into the category of "AND THEN SUDDENLY BAD THINGS HAPPENED". I played through the endings several times to see what I might have missed, and was still flummoxed. So, pay attention! Be smarter than me and figure this all out. :)
I'm giving "Decay: The Mare" a thumbs up because it's a good effort. You might want to wait for it to go on sale, and you'll definitely want to use a spoiler-free walkthrough to help you find the tiny indistinct coins scattered about the levels so that you can unlock the extras.  But in the end, I got a couple of hours of enjoyment from it (both here and on Xbox), and the atmosphere it creates was enough to keep me engaged thoughout the game.

Deciding whether to recommend this or not was pretty tough. It's not that I didn't enjoy the game. It is, however, quite short - I completed all three chapters in one sitting yesterday - so if you're going to buy, I'd say get it on sale if you can.
On the positive side, the story was interesting, and some of the effects were pretty creepy. There's a good sense of atmosphere in this game. I also enjoyed the camera chapter in particular, as using the item to reveal secrets was an interesting element.
In terms of criticism...well, as I said, it's quite short. Also, the level design can be a little confusing. There were a few areas in the game where it wasn't always immediately clear which door to take, where you would find yourself facing a way you didn't expect and it was quite easy to accidentally double back on yourself.
Overall, I'd say this game is just okay. Worth a look if you have a few pounds to burn, but not wishlist material. Nothing awful about it, but then nothing great either. It's a good effort, but there are some much better examples of point and click horror out there.
Recommended with caution.

Cuphead is a run and gun side scrolling shooter/platformer with a focus on tough diverse bosses, the game immediately hooks you in with its 1930's cartoon style visuals, sounds and direction. It certainly is what captured my attention many years ago at E3 and I was very impressed with the final product.
Whilst I wouldn't really say there is a story as such there is a plot in cuphead, brothers cuphead and mugman have found themselves in debt to none other than the devil himself. Forced into a contract of debt the brothers must fight for their very souls whilst gathering the souls of those who are in debt to the devil in order to save themselves from a lifetime of servitude.
Which is where the boss fights come in, they are the main focus of the game and they don't disappoint. Each boss's soul is required to progress and each boss must also be defeated on the harder difficulty to access the final parts of the game which may be a throw off to some. The game has platforming elements but is mostly a side scrolling run and gun, enemy's attack in non stop waves and in many cases spawn infinitely never giving you a moment to rest. The game will give you 3 (upgradeable to 5) lives for each level, once they are lost its game over and there is no way to regain health or respawn (at least in single player) so skill and knowledge of each level is essential. There aren't many games that give me that wonderful sense of satisfaction and accomplishment upon defeating a boss like cuphead does and oh it feels good.....however. I would have to say I died well over 400 times throughout my playthrough (theres a counter) and it goes without saying that you will die a lot in this game. A lot. But endure through, push hard and theres a light at the end of the tunnel.
The biggest part of this game is the visuals and it does not let you down, each boss and area is completely different and unique and I can say that no 2 are the same. Theres a sense of modern wit combined with that classic 1930s technicolor film style and comedy that makes Cuphead stand tall. I can't imagine how much work went into each individual hand drawn watercolour paintings but it certaintly isn't something I've seen before, I would love to see perhaps another game by the same studio in the same style but a more traditional platformer?
Sound is all original jazz and swing recordings that is very pleasant to my ears, especially as a fan of the era and music of old and big bands.
In closing I highly recommend this game to all gamers not just those looking for a challenge or the hardcores, Cuphead is a breath of fresh life and deserves to be played.

Any 3D platformer is inevitably going to be compared to THE 3D platformer right?  And let’s get this out the way quickly, “A Hat In Time” is no Super Mario 64.  BUT, “A Hat In Time” is very, very good, borderline excellent in fact.  Here's why...
3D platformers (in this reviewer’s very humble opinion) should be like a good assault course.  They should be interesting and varied with a flow that keeps you moving and a difficulty that doesn't have you chewing on your controller, but does keep your skills tested.  Most of the levels in “A Hat In Time” nail the design, the flow and the difficulty.  The controls are tight enough that you don’t feel too cheated when you fail to pull off a move (though there were a few moments when the controls felt a little janky, these were few and far between).  I mentioned Super Mario 64 at the start of the review because when it gets it right “A Hat In Time” feels every bit as good as the greatest 3D platformer of all time.
The art style is big and bold and the music is listenable to the point you understand why you can buy the soundtrack separately (and you find yourself humming themes through the day).
The characters designs are original and fun and, coupled with an outright bizarre story, the whole thing combines to make a game that is just eminently charming.
A final couple of notes, these could be deemed as very minor spoilers, depending on your point of view.  I played through the game in about a week.  My playthrough was 95% complete and that took about 12 hours.  You might think this is a little short and I don’t feel there is much replayability beyond ticking off the Steam achievements and finding the final few secrets.  It’s a shame because I certainly found myself wanting more.  With a few more worlds and hats this could have been perfect but overall “A Hat In Time” lacks the depth of a Super Mario 64.  However I do understand there is mod support and a decent community so that could extend the lifetime of the game somewhat.  Also, despite the PEGI 7 rating there are some…very creepy moments in the game.  Personally I thought they were great but the tonal shift could perhaps disturb more sensitive kids.
So that’s a big recommendation from me then.  I hope that we see more of “Hat Girl” and Gears For Breakfast in the future because this feels like the start of something special.

A great, relaxing, addictive game, that feels like a cross between Project Highrise and a very very easy version of Rimworld. There is a lot of room for expansion, and I'm excited to see what they come up with. I got a good 15 hours of enjoyment out of this before I felt like I had experienced all the game had to offer.
Basically, once you get your research going and install an electronics or jewelry store you won't have any more cash flow problems, so there is very little challenge in that regard. It is slightly more difficult to manage your stores and employees, but once you figure out how to balance employee hours for one store, it becomes pretty easy to apply those same principles to the rest of the mall. Another challenge is to fulfill product demand on multiple tiers ("tier three" being speciality shops that feature more than 50% of one item - "women's shoes" for example). This feature is an ongoing struggle that gives the game a bit more longevity, but I didn't really feel there was much payoff when I actually started up successful tier 3 stores. It was slightly anticlimatic.
Areas for improvement:
-More input on customer needs/wants, and more engagement with the environment. For example, in Rimworld, your colonists will respond more positively to certain decorative features. In ABITM you can "decorate" with different types and colours of floor tiles, but this has no effect, so it feels like a pointless thing to do. Expanding decorative options that entice different levels of customers to different tier stores would be awesome.
-A drag to highlight or control and click feature so that you can set the stock for multiple shelves/fridges/tables. Right now you have to right click every shelf and set the product. For tier 3 stores this can get tedious.
-Being able to click on your stores and have the management screen come up. Currently, you have to click on the management toolbar and scroll until you find the store in the list. This gets annoying when you have 30 stores.
-A more intuitive "needs" screen. I kind of eventually figured out that the blue indicates the level of needs being met, and yellow indicates demand. Maybe include a short tutorial or legend for this? More information and detailed stats re: customer needs and demands would also be great.
-More variety in terms of restaurants and entertainment (obviously - I have no doubt this is on the way, but it kind of detracts from the game at the moment). Mini golf! Arcade! Day care! Dare I say, indoor water park?!
-in the vein of Roller Coaster Tycoon, a feature that allows you to set the area that certain staff take care of, so that you don't have janitors wandering around randomly and can assign them particular stores or spaces. And although your employees gradually improve their skills in whatever area they end up working, an option to spend money to train or discipline employees would be interesting.
-customer pathways, more options for outdoor decor and park spaces.

In its current state, Another Brick in the Mall isn't terribly deep.  It's a mall building simulation, where the only real challenge is at the beginning of the game.  You start spending money, and run out pretty quickly, and if you don't have a profitable mall, then its game over.  But once you're profitable, the game basically is over.  Profitability, lets you expand your mall, which almost always increases profits, which lets you expand faster, quickly making the game just an exercise in repeating what you've already done.  Before I've used up even a 1/4 of the map, I had already finished building all the "types" of unlockables in the game.
Often the game is compared to Prison Architect, but in its current incarnation, it isn't PA.  Nothing bad happens to your mall if you walk away and leave it running.  Shoplifters don't exist.  Disasters of any sort don't seem to exist.  The biggest disaster I've seen are rats from filth left in the mall, but with enough janitors, this is never a problem.  The only other disaster I've seen is not enough parking spaces for goods to be restocked in your mall.  It can reach the point where your stores aren't restocked quickly, but it still isn't death the your mall.
Of course this is Early release, and things are bound to change, but right now, I think I experienced the majority of the game in under 12 hours using two malls, neither of which had the "cheats" enabled where you have unlimited money or the research was already completed for you.  Neither game I came anywhere close to needing a loan.  So if I were to truly experience everything the game has to offer, I would probably need to experience the "loan" side of the game.
I'm giving this a begrudgingly don't recommend at this time.  I enjoy the game, but I'm probably not going to put in another 12 hours into the game until the next major update.

This game is pure genius.
I haven't gotten so emotional playing a game since To The Moon, which literally made me cry.
Let's start the review then:
FACTS
- 1.5 to 2 hours gameplay time for a run (not much replayability unless you want to revisit some chapters, clear doubts).
- add to that the time you'll be spending googling what the hell was that all about? Who's Coda?! And/or discussing the ending with your friends who've also played.
- truly unique experience for a game.
PROS
- great deep story, told in ways you've probably never seen before (most definitely not in a game. some alternative films might have similar structures - not mentioning names to avoid spoilers).
- very well polished, continuous experience/gameplay.
- easy and acessible
- The Stanley Parable worthy sucessor (related in a way, something entirely different too)
CONS
- You might not identify with this type of game. You will not be challenged, no puzzles will be mind-bending, there are no enemies to kill. The game is led by a narrator and what gets you hooked is the content of his speech, his ideas and thoughts, linked to what you're experiencing in gameplay. Enjoy-the-ride type of game.
- Short (man I wish there was more!)
- Sometimes you gotta be patient. And grind a bit. And be tormented, pure anguish. It's not really a con, just part of the experience. Be ready and do not give up. The game doesn't go easy on you, especially if you're a sensible person.
I'll stop there so to not spoil the experience anymore. That might be enough for people to get the picture and decide if it's worthy. If you're a game enthusiast in general, and like games about games, don't pass on this one. It's amongst my top 10 steam games for sure. And I'll be revisiting it very soon.

Banished is an extremely fun and unique game. While Banished is a city-builder, it is completely different from any other city-builder I've ever seen. You have to choice each building that is built, and I personally learned the names of many of my citizens and watched them as they worked and lived.
Also, this is a very challenging game. You can be doing really well and have plenty of food and firewood saved up, but one harsh winter can starve your entire city. This may not sound fun, but it makes the game very exciting. This game has a wonderful balance that the player has to maintain, and the smallest thing can tip your scales.
Furthermore, this is one of the most replayable games I've ever seen. Every city you make will be different, and that makes this game so replayable!
Banished really is a great game. It has a great look, the graphics are awesome, and it has such a soothing soundtrack. Most importantly, though, it's a very fun game that you can easily drop many hours into. I've gotten city-builders for double the price, and they weren't half as fun. GET BANISHED!

If there was a middle button, I would press it and here is why. The game is very good if you want to sit back and relax with some friends and play against bots. They are challenging and tough to play against as any faction, even if some of the factions are more powerful then the others, which I will get to in a second. I have played this game for 20.3 hours, some being with friends, some being with bots. I haven't done a competitive session but I will tell you this: The game is NOT balanced very well for some factions. Now I did say this game was pretty good right? That's only if you want to play against bots and have a bit of fun. Battles can stretch from ten minute skirmishes to full on battles with a bunch of units, artillery, support, etc. But I will give you an example of one of the most overpowered units and you can decide if it is to much or not. The session I was playing was a battle against bots. I was the Germans fighting the British on one of the desert maps. Great mapping and great use of terrain such as the hilltop allowed me to setup a damn good defensive line and build 88mm flak guns as well as entrench troops in dug out holes in the ground. Sounds awesome right?! Well....Thing is....One 88 flak gun can pretty much one shot anything that comes at you, from any direction, at any point, at any time...I had enough resources to build eight, yes I said it, eight flak guns, and if that was not enough, I could build the four barreled (Sorry the name slips my mind) flak guns that were able to rip infantry to bits. Now I know what your thinking... "Isn't that realistic?!" well yeah, it is....But keep in mind that I built these things in a couple minutes, got them crewed and whats worse is that even the 88 flak guns, the guns you would think only to be used really as a tank killer, one shots any vehicle they threw at me as well as any infantry unit in one shot. Vehicles? I can understand, it is an 88 mm after all. Tanks? Still understand but would at least do significant damage or break something. Infantry? Come on, maybe kill like one or two units in the squad but the ENTIRE squad? Thats a little to much don't you think? Ok, that was one battle. What about Bastogne? Americans vs Germans? While the Germans did do a number on my units as well as my AI counterpart, we ended up just pushing the enemies back to their bases and killing them after a while. And this was done with only a couple tank destroyers and some infantry. If you are looking for a mod that is PVP only, stay away. Sure you might be able to find a way to kill everyone but stay away from the desert maps with the german 88 gun. If you want just a relaxing game with your friends against AI on ther other hand, I say download it! It's free after all!

When this game launched it's early access they peaked at 18k players, nowdays it's like 3k players on a good day. Do you not realize that the game didn't have an issue with onboarding players, it has an issue with keeping players. This is besides the fact that the release has taken so long, but has actually done very little in comparison to their original promises from 2013.
TL;DR: Loot system was recently overhauled, but has major issues. Devs take too long to realize obvious flaws with the game. There is no end game; players can currently completely outgear the highest difficulty content, so much so that they can carry multiple players. Carrying people was recently made even easier as they nerfed the difficulty scaling for additional players. Endless mode was removed from the game and didn't make it back in to the "official release" of the game. Party play is also pointless now, as it makes more sense to farm your gear in a solo game.
In reality the game isn't finished. The devs have made repeated overhauls of existing systems over the last few years of development, some of those major changes have been within a few months prior to this "official release" date. These overhauls have come instead of actually ensuring there is a complte game.
Long version: So what's wrong with the game?
A recent change to the loot system means that if you don't do research outside of the game, you end up progressing INCREDIBLY slow. This is because the current loot system is contradictory to the way a typical person will approach the game. Many current players expected a "fix" for this on "release", instead it's all still a big guessing game. If the most recent post on "how loot works" is correct, it's even worse than expected.
Currently, loot works like this: If the difficulty you are doing can drop loot scaling from A to F, what drops is dependant on your most highly geared character. So if you are wearing C level gear, you will continue to get B-D gear until you raise your scaled tier and open up the next available tier. This means you can't jump to higher difficulty and get better gear as it still drops gear scaled to your existing gear.
This created two problems. The first is that skill means nothing now. You can't challenge yourself to do more difficult content and reap better rewards. Instead getting gear is just a slow grind and new content is completely gear dependant.
The second is it means you dump all the highest level gear onto a single character, regardless of optimization. Green rarity, blue rarity, purple, orange? Doesn't matter just pump that item level to raise your scaling.
Herein lies the second flaw with this system. Gear doesn't show the item's level (There used to be a ipwr stat, but they recently removed it just prior to this loot system overhaul). Most people are using higher base stat = higher level, others are using highest sell value = higher level. The latest post indicates that both of those are wrong. The latest guesswork that is making waves is this:
If you are in a difficulty that can drop upgrades for you, then wear whatever drops, regardless if it's a downgrade. The idea being that because of the way scaling works, the gear dropping is ALWAYS higher item level even if it has lower stats. Thus, if you put it on, your item level goes up and you contiually scale upward.
So now, instead of optimizing specific slots across your 4 heroes, you just dump all the "best" items onto a single character and trickle down the rest of the gear.
Obviously my biggest gripe is the loot system, but there are a myriad of other issues that just show how inexperienced the devs are.
For example, it took them 3-4 years to realize that core health should scale in some way with difficulty.
The new UI is just bad. They made a bunch of unnecessary changes. The new build phase and combat phase icons have aesthetics that look like they were stripped from Robot Entertainment; they don't match this game at all.
End game is nonexistent. Players can vastly outgear and outlevel the current content. Endless mode, something that was a big part of DD1 and previously existed in this game is not currently in the game. It's slated in a future patch, after the "official release" of the game. How does that make sense?
They made carrying players even easier. At this point in the game, it doesn't even make sense to play with people, or with friends. With the way gear scaling works and content difficulty being completely gear reliant, having an extra person in your game only really works one person is strong enough to carry building. There's less incentive to use teamwork and skill to beat content when you can farm the same gear in a solo game with less difficulty until you outgear and can carry people.
All in all this game is still a work in progress and far from a full fledged game, regardless of the official release. Keep in mind that the game was in development and early access for several years and changes have come slowly, with constant decisions to overhaul existing features instead of making a full fledged game.

Originally my intention for this review was to complete all of the challenge and endless mode, but after countless meaningless results and a loss of determination; I began to decide against it. This review is mainly based from my experience from the story mode. Also, a minor disclaimer. I have been waiting for this game for three years, ever since the 7DFPS challenge. So some bias is to be expected.
SUPERHOT is an FPS where time moves when you move (though you still breathe, so you can't completely stop time), and as of right now; is my favorite game of this year. SUPERHOT's main mechanic of time manipulation leads to what is easy and fun to get into, but is hard and challenging to master. But outside of the mechanic itself, the level design is also very well done (at least in the story mode). The weapons have just enough variety for it to feel different, and with the addition of the time manipulation mechanic; the difference becomes more noticeable. There are a few subtle things they added that really helped how much better the game plays, but I'll just leave them be to cut short on time.
The story of SUPERHOT itself isn't exactly very impressive, if not a bit lackluster. Some of the things it pulled simply did not work because of some pacing issues, but it honestly isn't worth dwelling on. If anything, the lack of length in SUPERHOT is a bit of a mixed issue for me. It's as short as it should be, sure; but there's this feeling that the game is too short. The length may raise a few eyebrows here and there, however for those who would like a strong new innovation; SUPERHOT wins a strong recommendation.
So in short, SUPERHOT is a game with some strong innovations (and a very beautiful aesthetic), with a somewhat lackluster length. And with the current price tag, there's obviously going to be some people who are against buying SUPERHOT.

Dude, this game is not easy. You think OK I can keep a bunch of little pixel people alive. Yeah it’s harder than it looks. Banished is a delicate balance between population control and food production and it takes time to master. Don’t be upset if your first few settlements go up in smoke (sometimes literally), this game is about what have you learned. You don’t fail with your settlements you learn new ways of what works and what doesn’t. There are some helpful guides out there that give you some great tips on making your life and the lives of your pixel people better. Here are some of mine.
~ Be mindful how many houses you build. But just enough to house your people but not enough to let them breed out of control.
~ FOOD! Food is your number one enemy in this game.
~Firewood, you don’t need it much in the summer. But don’t let your little people freeze in the winter.
~ If you have people die, take workers off things like mining, timber cutting and blacksmithing (if you have a stock pile of tools) and move them to food.
~ Trade, trading is a key backbone to this game.
~Chickens are your best friends. Cows and sheep take forever to grow but chickens are a good and quick food sorce.
~ AOE players, throw out everything you know from AOE it DOES NOT APPLY HERE.

Back when Flash first became a thing, there were a few websites that had little "adventure" games where you clicked on hotspots in heavily Photoshopped images to move through creepy scenes. It should surprise absolutely no one that they never stopped making those, and in fact started rammming them through Greenlight. I can only assume that's where Decay: The Mare came from, because not a whole lot of thought went into anything beyond the stitching of random scenes together.
You play some depressed kid at a clinic in New Jersey, which basically guarantees you're never going to recover from whatever's got you down. Wandering around at night, you end up in some nightmare series of decrepit hallways that you have to escape because... maybe it represents your depression? I beat the damn thing and I'm still not sure. Like I said, it's all static scenes linked by arrows at the edges of the screen, with no animations between them. Some of the transitions make sense, but others are so disjointed you'll have trouble figuring out where you just came from. That's a problem since the game is VERY heavy on backtracking, and there's little aesthetic consistency from room to room, or sometimes wall to wall.
Each scene might have one or MAYBE two interactables to fool with, either items to collect or puzzle boxes to open. The developers LOVE number pads, so get ready for plenty of four-digit codes (one hidden behind possibly the STUPIDEST puzzle I have ever seen). Aside from that there's basically nothing to examine, and no notes or files to collect. Oh, there are little collectable coins scattered throughout that unlock "extras", but they blend into the background and only help if you collect every single one, so eff that. For the most part, the scenes you navigate are devoid of interesting features and start to blend together very quickly.
The one thing you can look forward to are the infrequent and seemingly random jumpscares the developers decided to throw in. There's some corpse-looking thing in the area, and it likes to bang on windows and scamper past lights at just the right time to make you jump. This thing is never really addressed in the story, which is just as well because the story is stupid as all hell. There's a big twist to it, and some of the spooky bits get tied in, but most of the weirdness in the game goes unexplained, I guess just written off as you being crazypants. I found out the hard way that there are two endings, because I did the thing the game suggested I do and got the bad version.
I usually don't like to rag on games too hard, but Decay is just a really dumb game. I powered through all three episodes in about an hour and a half, but after the first twenty minutes or so I desperately wanted to be doing something more meaningful with my time. There are a few sparks of brilliance buried in there that helped keep me going, I admit. The camera in the second episode makes for some pretty interesting sequences, but that's one decent bit out of 90 minutes. If you're looking for a clever, challenging, or interesting adventure, don't look for it here.

It didn't occur to me in the beginning that all the regions would be connected, so when I came out of a cave and into a completely new region, I was amazed. I'm simply astonished at how pleasing the game is. It's peaceful, but at the same time, carries a subtle sense of danger *cough the Hydro Plant cough.*
And although it's not immediately obvious if you spawn in deep wilderness, the game constantly reminds you that it is set post-apocalypse by placing corpses in the least expected places. The game is perfectly paced to match the size of the world, and the way your resources fluctuate seems very fair and reasonable.
I'll say, this game surprised me. I can't wait to see what more Long Dark has to offer.

There are a rare few games that seem to be determined to make you lose and yet are still enjoyable. This is probably one of the best hardcore zombie games out there. In fact, it's probably the most hardcore I've ever heard of. Not only are you unlikely to ever even see any kind of firearm (usage of fire arms is a bad idea anyways in almost every case anyways) but you also have to scrape together enough food, find a secure place to sleep every night and also contend with your charater's mounting emotional distress. Staying a locked room with a years supply of beans might work in some games but in this game your character is likely to start going crazy by day five of the Beanocalypse.
Some other nice features are the ability to make a farm, build walls and barricades and, best of all for me, customise the zombies. You can have everything from 28 Days Later Sprinting Psychos to the classic Undead Shamblers. Or perhaps slow zombies with a superhuman sense of smell? The zombies may be coming for you slowly, but they never stop, drawn by the scent of your warm, succulent flesh. Terrifyingly awesome.
Most of all this game will give you some stories to remember. You won't survive long but you will have the time of your life.

Decay: The Mare is not the typical game I'd buy for myself. In fact, if I hadn't gotten a copy of it in a bundle, I'd probably never even consider in the first place. That being said, however, I decided to play it one night on a whim and found myself pleasantly surprised.
First off, this isn't the type of horror game that controls akin to Amnesia or the like (first person WASD control and all that). It's a point-and-click which brought me back to the era of old school horror flash games. It fits the game well, but not everyone may enjoy the control style.
Secondly, this game is not nearly as scary as I was initially expecting. The suspense, however, had me covering my eyes every time I walked through a door or clicked on an object as I was half expecting a cheap jumpscare which never actually came. Yes, there are some scares (keep your eyes out for the portrait in chapter 2, it's terrifying), but they aren't nearly as horrifying as I expected stepping into the game. This could be good or bad based on your preferences, but my tolerance for fear is low. If it had been toned up I probably would have quit the game before I finished it.
The music is phenomenal and sets the tone very well for the gameplay and the setting. The hallways and rooms you explore become tense in places where needed, puzzle areas provide a moment of clarity, and the moments of downtime in between are accompanied by slower, more deliberate and minimalist tone.
Finally, the story develops a lot more than I would have thought - what at first seemed like a simple method of dropping the player into a degraded, unkempt mess of a place and leaving the story at that actually gradually reveals a full-fledged and engrossing storyline, with a satisfying ending.
The game is a little short for its price tag - I'd wait for it to go on sale before deciding to pick it up -  but what I assumed was a game that would gather dust and never be played transformed into an experience that I enjoyed upon reflection, and I'd highly recommend making the trip yourself.

Outlast is a truely horrific experience.  From the very beginning, the warped atmosphere will leave you looking over your shoulder.
UPDATE:  I've now played Whistleblower, and my opinion hasn't really changed towards the main game.  See my whistleblower review for my thoughts on it.
Pros:
-The story is interesting.  However, it honestly isn't interesting
to make you really care.  (See this continued in cons).  I think this is because the game is more focused on gameplay.
-Night Vision Camera!  It's a cool take on the light-giving tool mechanic.
-The environment made me feel genuinely scared at points
-Less Jumpscares, more Psychological Horror
-You can look down and see your whole body! (Great attention to detail from the developers).
Cons:
-By the end of the game the story is, without spoiling anything, open to interpretation, I felt confused and wanted to know more.  Perhaps that's just me, but I think it could've been better.
-The game does at times feel like a rendition of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, with more annoying enemies.  In Amnesia, Enemies tend to permanently disappear after an encounter, not roam.  In Outlast, they roam.  This may be a pro to some and a con to others, but I mention it in my cons list because after a few times the game felt like hide and seek in the dark.
-The hide and seek parts make completing objectives while tip toeing around enemies annoying rather than scary or adrenaline-fueled.  Because of this, the game took me over a year to actually get around to finishing (I started August 11th, 2014 and finished November 7th, 2015), mainly due to being annoyed that after making so little progress, I had to stop and play hide and seek again.
-A very interesting type of enemy that could have been a nice addition to the overall game only appears at the end, which was disappointing.
I always try to list around the same amount of Pros and Cons, so don't take my opinion as too negative.  Outlast is definitely something worth playing if you're interested in the Horror Genre.  8/10 from me.

If you've ever watched/read a Zombie Thriller and thought that you yourself could do better than its characters at surviving a Zambo Apocanips, here's your chance. P. Zomboid offers what seems to be the most complete "Zombie Survival" experience (with graphics) there is by providing a huge amount of elements that range from putting yourself together on Day 0 and scavenging for supplies to stabilishing a fortified farm house months later, everything in between included. A sandbox mode allows you to create your own Apocalypse-to-Survive by permitting you to edit the Zombie Lore and behavior along with map conditions.
Despite being far from finished, the game is very much enjoyable in its current state and has a fair amount of big features yet to be impletemented - such as Online Multiplayer, NPC survivors & interactivity along with many more crafting options. While somewhat fun to dip into from time to time during 2011-2012, I can no longer recommend this game to the target demographic. If you're a fan of chaotic games full of hack, grief, and other assorted mischief like Rust, Gmod, Day Z, etc... you'll have a blast with this game. 10/10, buy it now, get copies for your entire ebin griff clan. However, if you came here looking for awesome war stories, PTSD simulator, and an in-depth experience full of teamwork, read further. (Also, nice job not letting people who bought Rising Storm before the F2P weekend write their concerns on the page everybody looks at with your new GotY edition that changes jacksh
t, Tripwire. Truly, indie developers are the light in the darkness that this industry needs. :^))
At launch, the game was riddled with bugs, and not the Bethesda kind. CTDs, server desync, all things that drove off most of the fans of the original mod, piled on top of the reduced realism and Cawadoody-esque maps and weapon leveling. It's worth noting that even in this state, there was nothing else quite like RO2 on the market, so it quickly attracted a new fanbase of people who enjoyed the depth of the tactical realism without the insane unnacessability of ARMA.
All was well for about two years. Most of the utterly gamebreaking glitches were fixed, stories of admin aboose and call-out threads were 99% obvious fakes, and those that weren't were investigated closely. It was generally a swell time to play the game. So, when we got word that the Pacific Front mod was getting officially picked up by Tripwire and was going to be given the funding of a full-fledged project, we were excited for new content.
And then the beta hit.
And there was RAGE.
Out of the gate, the U.S team was even more overpowered than it is now (everybody making threads to whine about the skillthrower these days never saw it in action during launch,) the maps were storage closets compared to vanilla's hallways, the Japanese team was crushed nine times out of ten, and it was painfully obvious that it had recieved nothing but a graphical makeover from the time it was a mod. Since the point of letting us buy into beta was to give feedback, we did, and were instantly shot down by what was a quickly growing group of yes-men that ultimately killed this game.
The fanboys.
Oh my god the fanboys
They're like every bad elitist nerd stereotype rolled into one big ball of grease and "nyehhhhhh!" Constantly bragging to anyone who brings up the blatant imbalances and terrible map design with "well you thee you only have two-hundred hourth put into thith game and I have ~3000~ tho you should shut up sc
ub," (< I guarantee that if you look on the first page of the forum right now you'll find a thread that has devolved into this,) and reasurring Tripwire on the official forums that the path they've chosen is the right one and anybody who says otherwise is from CoD and has no idea what they're talking about.
By the time the game was released, all that had changed was the range of the flamer (which could still overrun
on its own,) and the fixing of a few bugs, mostly thanks to the aforementioned yes-men. It was flooded by literal motherf
cking quickscopers concerned more with their K/D and weapon levels than teamwork, along with the occasional s
itlord looking to make a troll montage for Jewtube. This led to servers having to enforce stricter rules and hire more b& happy admins, the criteria for which was and still only is, "are you a member of our clan?" Stories of admin abuse began to gain more credence from people who had been playing since before Rising Storm, but, as always, they were drowned out by the TRU FANS.
It was worse than usual, but folks still managed. There were still enough intelligent people playing to pick off the run and gunners, and you only had to worry about your SL1 taking the class for the submachinegun about, oh, 60% of the time. And sure, the occasional free weekend brought the friendly fire and grief to an all-time peak, but those people left after it ended, so all you had to do was wait them out.
And then, out of nowhere, RO2 went completely free. And if you downloaded the copy, you got it forever.
In only a few days, hacks ground entire matches to a halt, commanders were threatened by their own riflemen for their automatics and were promptly gunned down if they didn't drop them, SANIC blared over the mic, and the chat was flooded by the navy seals copypasta. With the sudden influx of s
it, the admins couldn't deal with it all, so they retreated to teamspeak and only answered reports from clan members (a behaviour that still exists even after the majority of griefers left, and paved the way for absolute abuse of power and corruption.)
The game never recovered from this, and to this day it is the Day Z of teambased WW2 shooters. Use of cover and grenades is non-existent, and the commanders are too busy levelling their guns to throw smoke and mark arty. All of this, combined with the way Tripwire treats their community (paying money for inferior vehicle models when a mod team made ones with more detail for free, using Punkbuster, a system that scans every single one of your computer files and sends copies of them to their offices as DRM, adding "no cyberbullying" to their terms of service and only ever using it to silence criticism on the official forum, flooding the game with new content that only breaks it further instead of bug fixes, [s]heavy[/s] all but confirmed implications that the next DLC is going to be D-Day when everybody wants either Afrika Korps, Winter War, Italy, or the retreat to Berlin,) means that I can't tell anybody looking for a game with actual depth not to stay the hell away.
TL;DR: If you love anarchic games full of griefers, hackers, and circlejerking admins from a company that doesn't give a s
it about quality control, this is perfect. Anything else, run and never look back.

So far, I have had a lot of fun with this game. I'm glad to see a try/die/repeat game besides Dark Souls become this popular. Getting better at something until you finally get a high score on it is one of the greatest pleasures gaming has to offer. Even though Cuphead is difficult compared to most games, it is not particularly rage-inducing because of the shorter length of its levels and bosses.
The length and quality of this game really depends on how you approach it. Some might find it to be short. Personally, I am less than halfway through the normal difficulty with seven hours into the game. If I was playing the game just to beat the levels on the normal difficulty, I would probably be almost done with it. However, trying to get P ranks and A ranks has made me spend much more time.
Each of the levels and bosses feels incredibly fresh and varied. Game mechanics are introduced immediately, and then are never used again. In some games, this would be a problem, but it works well when you die a lot in each level. Moving and shooting are also very fluid. Bosses have enough move variety and variability to be fun after restarting multiple times.
I don't think I have to say the aesthetic style is great, but it is.
The only major con that comes to mind is that one of the run & gun levels won't let you get beyond a B score, unless you get a P score for some reason. I accidentally spent way too much time on it because of this.

I have always loved these sort of management games along the lines of Rimworld or Prison Architect. I admit I was skeptical upon purchasing ABINM due to its alpha stages and my history of not trusting Early Access games to come to finish. But I also determine the value of my games of being that if I spend at least an hour playing per dollar on a game it's well worth it. I purchased ABINM when it was on sale for 10 dollars. Coincidentally, my first playthrough of it over the weekend was just over 10 hours. I couldn't believe how much time I'd spent on the game.
It ran incredibly smooth for me on a GTX950 and an i3 6100 at over 200 FPS. If you're familiar with the games of Rimworld or Prison Architect, ABINM gives me a similar satisfaction akin to those games. In Rimworld, the fun is with building structures and homes for these little people that you get to take care of. You get to see them develop and hunt and grow. Another Brick In The Mall is not quite like that (or at least not yet ;D), but it offers a similar feeling of growth in that you are to build a mall, and satisfy the people that come to it, who may not be completely sure why they're at your mall. You may need more checkout counters or more space or a specific tier of product. It's a bit of a visual puzzle that I enjoy.
This being said, the game is very much so in Alpha. I'm giving it a recommendation right now simply because it's enjoyable as it is, and while skimming through the patch history I believe that the game will grow into something great.

This game actually achieves a good amount of game play depth for what it has. I found it enjoyable in learning to play and succeed. The main aim of the game is to achieve a functional balance so that your citizens may live. It's not so much of a game as it is a simulation, I'd say. The goal, or main objective of which is not to necessarily 'win', persay, but it survive.
And it does this very well. It's a very... methodically created game and 99% of the time, any and all city problems are player made, through a lack of understanding on how the games AI/script functions. Every issue has a solution. and every solution is findable.
It's one drawback, I find is in replayability. The base game, does not have a lot of raw content to it, even though the base game is also rather deep. There are, however a HUGE range of player made mods to choose from which can greatly enhance replayability, and the mod community content seems, rather endless. The gam was made with that in mind, as if the game designed just said... Ok, I'll give you all the basics, now make the game your own. Personally, I like that.

Where do I begin with Banished... With 120hrs on record, I haven't yet found a rhythm that can help me ascend to the greats and build a town that doesn't fall apart over a small span of time. One second I have more food than... Well, I have a lot of food, and lots of tools and resources and the works, the next minute my citizens are dying off and my town is up in metaphoric flames.
But I think that's the beauty of this game. I've played consistently on either easy/medium difficulty with disasters off, and I *still* can't exhaust the avenues of this game. There's such a learning curve, it's astounding. One day, perhaps when I have 300hrs on record, I'll graduate to turning on natural disaters, but we'll see...
There are some complaints that there isn't much to this game, and I suppose when you look at the 'tech' or the buildings you can produce, that's correct, but the very fact that the game can be so simple in concept and yet so complex in its gameplay and its outcome - shows this game for the gem it really is.
I will admit that some of the negative reviews on here that point out the sometimes frustrating AI have a fair point, but every game has its issues, and I think these downfalls are more than made up for by the beautiful style, gameplay, and concept. Couple this with a beautiful and relaxing soundtrack and you have a game that you can never stay mad at when it kicks you in the teeth and wipes out your town, because it was all down in the picturesque landscape with a soothing track to keep you distracted.
Another comment on here I think perfectly sums up why this game is worth every penny: you can leave this game for months/years at a time (I know, that's how I play it), but then you get the powerful urge/itch to play it, and nothing else will fill that void other than Banished. It is timeless, and I genuinely think it'll be classic in an age when we're looking at countless CoD sequels etc.
The playability is further boosted (if you could boost it any further) by the vast array of mods that open up the possibilities with more buildings and new mechanics. To name but a few, the mods by Redketchup will add at least another 500hrs to your gameplay.
So, I think for the mere price of £15, if you're thinking of getting Banished, think no more, buy it now!

A short and brilliant introspection on creativity and social interaction.
In The Beginner's Guide, you get to follow the story and train of thought of a man who desperately tries to help a friend, only to realise that not all who wander are lost, and that hell is paved with good intentions.
I've always been a huge fan of story telling in video games, and The Beginner's Guide has just set itself as a monument in the genre: It's profound, intimate, wise, and truthful. You share the narrator's every word and thought, following closely on his confidence, anger, disbelief, and eventually acceptance of what he did. A truly magnificent essay on a mistake we all made at some point in our life, and that will hit home for any creator out there.
It's short, and do not expect any form of gameplay besides walking and listening. Is the story even true? Probably not, but The Beginner's Guide will still teach you one of the most beautiful lessons there is: Learn to let go.

I'm really picky about my point n' click games.  With the right kind of horrific atmosphere, cool settings, characters, etc. I can get into it but other times it gets to be a real chore.  Decay interested me with its set-up, so I decided to pick this sucker up.  It took me about 4 hours to complete and it might appeal to you if you like the darker side of point n' click like Scratches, Lost Crown: A Ghost Hunting Adventure, Sherlock Holmes: The Awakening, etc.  It's probably better than the first two on my list, but not up to the third.
Anyway, you're Sam...a drug addict, a man on the edge, trying to get your life straight in this crazy asylum/rehab facility/group home etc.  From the very beginning it's clear things are not as they seem and the game takes you on Sam's journey through 3 chapters as you scavenge for items, solve puzzles to progress and try to figure out just what the heck is going on.
Decay is not a great looking game.  Serviceable.  Way better than Scratches which was hard to find anything because of the ugly, filthy rendering and graphics, but it's comparable.  Still, it's not too difficult to find what you need and the puzzles for the most part are pretty easy if you pay attention to your surroundings and all of the clues you pick up.  You'll  always have a couple of items in your inventory and it's pretty easy to figure out what goes where, what needs combined and what unlocks what.  About 2 puzzles stumped me for a bit but trial n' error is your best friend and even the casual point n' click gamer should be able to figure them out.
The game succeeds most in atmosphere.  Your environment undergoes several weird changes through the episodes, and  unusual things will happen in places you've already visited.  There's alot of achievements to get and I got most of them quite easily.  If you back-track and keep your eyes open, you'll find most of 'em.  Though the "asylum" setting is getting overdone at this point, it's well used here and there is a general sense that you're being followed and watched from the get go.  Like I said in my Dreadout review...Decay is a game that's not straight up scary, but rather weird, atmospheric and in your head.  I'll remember a couple of the weird characters I encountered forever.  Being unable to die ramps your courage level up for this one, so just keep pressing on.
Sound design was solid and the piano soundtrack was cool.  There's not alot of spoken dialogue but what is there is well-done enough and conveys the story, and as an old school game I don't mind reading text, so that was never a problem.  The puzzles were just challenging enough to give you some sense of accomplishment by figuring them out but don't expect a tough, daunting endeavor and you'll be okay.
Not everything is perfect here.  The interface can clunk around a bit.  It works alright but it's definitely not the most intuitive around and neither is moving around.  Sometimes when entering through a door, you'll be faced different ways than you'd expect to be facing which can lead to some stumbling around and doofusing your way into the wrong room or direction more than once.  A little more character development would have been nice.  You don't get to know Sam reallllllly well enough...enough to vest yourself in his adventure but I didn't find myself particularly worried or concerned about the character.  The same holds true with the protagonists.  Perhaps, a little more voice acting could have fleshed these parts out better and given a little more personality to the people and creatures that inhabit the asylum.  Although the weirder creatures (who I don't want to give away) were wonderfully well done and total WTF creations.  Play the game and you'll see what I mean.
Overall, point n' clickers with a taste for the macabre will definitely enjoy this.  I almost lean towards not recommending it because it's far from perfect, yet it's decent enough for a one time play through.  If you have a pretty free day off work you can beat it in one setting.  Decay is not quite a must have but I enjoyed and those with a taste for the macabre that enjoy classic point n' click should give it a try.  At $10...it's a "Hmmm, purchase," I'd say 5 or 6 on a sale would be the right price.  I'll break it down as I always do!
Pros:
-Good usage of an overdone setting
-Great sound design and soundtrack
-Creepy atmosphere throughout
-The story does just enough right to keep you going
-Fun puzzle solving that is just satisfying enough (very logic based)

Cons:
-Graphics are mundane at best.

-Despite the fun of the puzzles and their appreciable logic design, many are far too easy

-Story could use more emotional investment all around.

SUPERHOT:
~~~~~~~~~
Sitting down in front of your state of the art terminal (in the eighties, most likely) you are chatting to a friend about this game called, SUPERHOT! To play the game, you will have to download the exe. file and upon launching it, you will be killing SUPERHOT red opponents.
Superhot is a First Person Shooter with a time manipulation mechanism which make this game really fun to play.  You will be able to play a short story mode of approximately 2 hours and 30 minutes. When you successfully complete the story, you will unlock the endless and challenge modes.  The challenge mode is the story mode but you can only use a specific weapon all the way through and the first weapon is the Katana. In the endless mode you have to kill as many opponents as possible before your fall.
I really like the gameplay of SUPERHOT with the time manipulation mechanism, the whitish compact levels and the unmissable red opponents. Sometimes you will be harmed with a gun, shotgun, machine gun, katana, or maybe with nothing but your faithful hands, which can become tricky!  What you have to do is to dismiss all the red combatants to clear the level but remember, they too have the weapons mentioned above. As you spawn, you might or might not see one or several enemies. When you start moving, the enemies will move too, and will start shooting at you straight away. If you are fired upon and stop moving you will see the bullets coming at you in slow motion. In terms of ammunition they have a limitation for all firearms and sometimes the only way to stunt and acquire your opponent’s weapons is to throw your empty weapon towards them. If left with your bare hands, try to look around for tools or utensils to throw at them instead. On some occasions, you will be able to use the “hotswitch” ability, which is the ability to switch from your body to the enemy in front of you.  To be honest with you, I am very surprised how fast and frustrating some levels are. For me, it was the elevator levels where you have to clear three enemies armed with guns in the lift, with two other guys waiting with shotguns on the other side of the door. That was SUPERHOT AND SUPER HARD!
Graphically the game looks good and the animations are well done. I personally find the story very short but the endless and challenge modes give you good re-playability.  I would have expected more content for the asking price.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great concept with compact levels
-	Fun game to play
-	Endless and challenge modes
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Very Short Story mode
-	Needs more content, in my opinion
SUPERHOT is a fun first person shooter in well-designed compact levels.

The War of 1812 was a military conflict that lasted from June 18, 1812 to February 18, 1815, fought by the United States of America against Great Britain, its North American colonies, and its North American Indian allies. Historians in the United States and Canada see it as a war in its own right, but Europeans sometimes see it as a minor theatre of the Napoleonic Wars, as it was caused by issues related to that war (especially the Continental System). By the war's end in early 1815 the key issues had been resolved and peace came with no boundary changes.
The United States declared war for several reasons, including trade restrictions brought about by the British war with France, the impressment of as many as 10,000 American merchant sailors into the Royal Navy,[5] British support for Native American tribes fighting American settlers on the frontier, outrage over insults to national honor during the Chesapeake–Leopard Affair, and possible American interest in annexing British territory.[6] The primary British war goal was to defend their North American colonies, although they also hoped to set up a neutral Indian buffer state in the Midwest.
The war was fought in three theatres. First, at sea, warships and privateers of each side attacked the other's merchant ships, while the British blockaded the Atlantic coast of the United States and mounted large raids in the later stages of the war. Second, land and naval battles were fought on the U.S.–Canadian frontier. Third, large-scale battles were fought in the Southern United States and Gulf Coast. At the end of the war, both sides signed and ratified the Treaty of Ghent and, in accordance with the treaty, returned occupied land, prisoners of war and captured ships (though neither side returned the other's warships due to frequent re-commissioning upon capture) to its pre-war owner and resumed friendly trade relations without restriction.
With the majority of its land and naval forces tied down in Europe fighting the Napoleonic Wars, the British used a predominantly defensive strategy in the Provinces of Upper and Lower Canada. Early victories over poorly-led U.S. armies, such as in the Battle of Queenston Heights, demonstrated that the conquest of the Canadas would prove more difficult than anticipated. Despite this, the U.S. was able to inflict serious defeats on Britain's Native American allies, ending the prospect of an Indian confederacy and an independent Native American state in the Midwest under British sponsorship. U.S. forces were also able to make several gains and score victories on the Canadian frontier; taking control of Lake Erie in 1813, seizing western parts of Upper Canada. However, a large-scale U.S. attempt to capture Montreal was repulsed in November 1813. Despite the major U.S. victory at Chippawa on July 5, 1814, serious U.S. attempts to fully conquer Upper Canada were ultimately abandoned following the bloody Battle of Lundy's Lane on July 25, 1814. The U.S. then fell back roughly 30 km (19 mi) from Lundy's Lane to Fort Erie, where they withstood a siege for several months. The British eventually withdrew, but as winter set in, the Americans demolished the fort and fell back across the Niagara.
In April 1814, with the defeat of Napoleon, the British adopted a more aggressive strategy, sending larger invasion armies and tightening their naval blockade. However, with the end of the Napoleonic Wars in Europe, both governments were eager for a return to normality and peace negotiations began in Ghent in August 1814. In the Deep South, General Andrew Jackson destroyed the military strength of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend. In September 1814, the British won the Battle of Hampden, allowing them to occupy eastern Maine, and the British victory at the Battle of Bladensburg in August 1814 allowed them to capture and burn Washington, D.C. They were repulsed, however, in an attempt to take Baltimore and Fort Bowyer, and during their assault at Fayal. An American victory in September 1814 at the Battle of Plattsburgh repulsed the British invasions of New York, which, along with pressure from merchants on the British government, prompted British diplomats to drop their demands at Ghent for an independent native buffer state and territorial claims that London previously sought. Given that it took six weeks for ships to cross the Atlantic, news of the peace treaty did not arrive before the British suffered a major defeat at New Orleans in January 1815.[7]
In the United States, late victories over invading British armies at the battles of Plattsburg, Baltimore (inspiring the United States national anthem, "The Star-Spangled Banner") and New Orleans produced a sense of euphoria over a "second war of independence" against Britain.[8][9] The war ended on a high note for Americans, winning the final engagements of the war and bringing an "Era of Good Feelings" in which partisan animosity nearly vanished in the face of strengthened American nationalism. The war was also a major turning point in the development of the U.S. military. The poor performance of several U.S. militia units, particularly during the 1812–13 invasions of Canada and the 1814 defence of Washington, convinced the U.S. government of the need to move away from its Revolutionary-era reliance on militia and focus on creating a more professional regular force. Spain was involved in fighting in Florida but was not an official belligerent; some Spanish forces fought alongside the British during the Occupation of Pensacola. The U.S. took permanent ownership of Spain's Mobile District.
In Upper and Lower Canada, British and local Canadian militia victories over invading U.S. armies became iconic and promoted the development of a distinct Canadian identity, which included strong loyalty to Britain. Today, particularly in Ontario, memory of the war retains its significance, because the defeat of the invasions ensured that the Canadas would remain part of the British Empire, rather than be annexed by the United States. In Canada, numerous ceremonies took place in 2012 to commemorate the war, offer historical lessons and celebrate 200 years of peace across the border.[10] The conflict has not been commemorated on nearly the same level in the modern-day United States, though it is still taught as an important part of early American history,[11] and Dolley Madison's and Andrew Jackson's respective roles in the war are especially emphasized.[12][13] The war is scarcely remembered in Britain, being heavily overshadowed by the much larger Napoleonic Wars occurring in Europe
