Oddly enjoyable and a good bit different from the usual Arc System Works fighting game.
Battle Fantasia is an 3D animated 2D fighting game released in arcades in 2007 and consoles sometime later.
Then released in arcades again years later with new balance and thats what this version is based on hence the -Revised Edition-.
The game takes heavily from 80s/90s RPGs as its theme and art style and considering this game was apparently designed to appeal to a female audience that is a pretty damn nice thing to know. Since the taste for RPGs always came off as a sterotypical male nerd thing it is really nice to see something like this with a female audience in mind.
As much as the word progressive is terribly misused by fat, hateful, politically correct ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s this game can be considered progressive to a degree. Between the fact that the art style is classic RPG that was allegedly aimed at women and the fact that the all the ladies here are modestly dressed.
Moving on.
Music: It is nice though far less entertaining than other ASW fighting games. Considering the high standards of good soundtracks the developers have I am counting this as a big flaw of the game even if the music there is good if totally forgettable.
Characters: Most of the characters are done well enough. While none are absolutely amazing I'll admit they are all weird and do very well to stand out. I will say while I do not know what character counts as the default protagonist the game at least does not have one with as godawful a design as Blazblue's Ragna The Bloodedge and that is speaking as someone who is a big Blazblue fan. Come to think about it most of them also look better than Guilty Gear's Sol Badguy who is not terribly designed even if I am not a fan.  I want to add here that speaking of the "female appeal" the boss Ashley is, in all honestly, further proof of that in being a hilarious stereotype. He is the only really sexualized character constantly showing everything down from his horribly long leak down to his navel with a portrait looking like he is ready to pull "it" out. A character very obviously aimed at the "fujoshi" female audience being a flayboyant homosexual with a damn female name that just makes me laugh.
And finally
Gameplay: Battle Fantasia is a bit slower and more ground based than the usual ArcSys style fighting game so maybe this will appeal to the fans coming from the more KOF/Street Fighter games. Though like Guilty Gear its a weird case of a 5 button fighting game. One of those buttons is a parry button called the Gachi Button and while I am not a fan of button based parry moves and this game not helping the case I think it is kind of cool that pressing that button has a unique animation even if you fail to parry. Overall its a bit basic, but oddly pretty fun.
Verdict: Recommended! It is a odd one, a sort of standard 3D, with lack of full controller support and a small audience to ensure you will not get a lot of online fights. But its executed so well and this is an otherwise fine port based on the later arcade version from what I gathered. I enjoy the characters, and gameplay and it works as a game that served as an experiment from Arc System Works that although not hugely successful still got enough love and support to come all the way to PC many years later and is worth it because Battle Fantasia is a pretty good fighting game.
I look forward to maker's next

Just finished playing Episode 1.
It was amazing.
Stepping into the shoes of Batman has never been so real before. But make no mistake, this isn't just a Batman game. This is a Detective Comics game. It has everything you can ask from a Batman game - detective work (real detective work, not like Arkham Series' detective AI), lots of Bruce Wayne (yay for this!), the dilemmas and struggles of being Batman (like, really) and so on. So far, the script runs flawlessly and lines are great! It's an interesting story with some really good Batman moments. Although some lines (some of the answers of your character's) feel a bit sluggish, they are great in overall.
Storyline is intriguing but how about the other aspects of the game?
Well, controls are... You know, It's Telltale. It's pretty much point and click like all other Telltale games I know of. Nothing of really importance here.
Graphics are again, comic-ish style generally. Standard Telltale issue. But the art is really nice. I like how Gordon is visualized. I liked Gotham City. I have some mixed feelings about the Batmobile, but it's nothing of a big deal really.
Voice acting feels weird at first. Being used to Kevin Conroy has a part in that, of course, but sometimes the voice acting feels lacking in reflecting the intended emotion. But after playing for an hour or so voice acting gets it together and it flows fine.
I didn't like most of the motion-capture (if there is any) or animations in general. Most of the time the fights didn't feel real and the way Batman moves sometimes looks absurd. But these can be overlooked as the game is not about fancy graphics and action scenes.
One thing I do have a gripe about is the way Bruce acts. Maybe that's because he is portrayed as a "rookie Batman" but I do feel like Bruce Wayne, although a rookie in being Batman, is never a rookie in social interactions. He looks and talks like he is a 14 year-old beaten-up kid.
The soundtrack is nice. It doesn't really bother you as you play but also pique your interest. The game also doesn't give you so much room to let you appreciate the music. In overall, it has tunes from BTAS and '89 Batman and is satisfying to listen. It won't let you down.
Overall, I think this game is a must-buy for Batman fans and comic book fans in general. Also I believe this series have the potential to be better than anything Telltale have ever produced yet. It gives the feeling of Batman better than the Arkham games for me.

Since not much reviewers have been covering the Multiplayer, I'll take that for my account...
The multiplayer is what catched my eye first. I felt like I had to play the multiplayer first, and it's what I did
right after finishing the bootcamp. At first... It gave me the impression of the First Call of Duty game from 2003.
And now, it's not the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ kind of Call of Duty like now. It's that♥♥♥♥♥kicking bad moment you're about to
show the Nazi's a desperate last bit of what's left of mother Russia, and prevail, despite the heavy loss.
But as I said, I was about to cover the multiplayer, and I was now talking about the Call of Duty Singleplayer mission in Stalingrad.
In Red Orchestra 2, it'll make you feel like playing the first Call of Duty, but WAY better, deeper, and involved with the other players, because of the 64 player servers.
Also, the players are way more Mature here, unless you unfortunately ended up in a Russian-talk-only server.
You have the chance to decide what faction to play for (Germans or Russians), and what class, but as in real WWII, resources are very limited, so if 2 people already took the marksman class, good luck, but you'll have to stick with ironsighted longrifles and a handful of ammo like everyone else. The submachine gunners, can have a little more ammo, but then again, take care of your bullets and don't waste them. Your reserves are limited. But that is what adds charm to this game...
It's WWII.
They knew that if everyone would be marksmen, you'll get this pro sniper skills bulls*** as in the modern CoD.
What I personally liked myself is how satisfying one single kill with a longrifle can be... the longer the distance, the better.
This isn't a competetive shooter to show off how fast or how many you can kill, it's pure war simulation. Your character and other players' characters react very accurate on enemy contact and explosions or gunshots in their proximity... You really can feel the stress being put on you in this war situation. You can feel a morale ingame depending on what your win/lose situation is. There is no implemented morale system in this game, you just feel it. You and your team are have the upper hand in combat? You will feel the morale being held high. and the opposite when you're losing.
Although, You'll know the game's formula withing a short period o time, everyday is a new challenge. and you have a nice handful of maps, including a few gold rated community maps... My personal all time favorite is Winterwald. shooting down Russians with my Kar98k longrifle while hiding about 100 meters away in dense high grass, and a pack of trees surrounding the snowy hills. I don't know what else I could cover about the multiplayer, but it definitely is a MUST if you like playing WWII shooters.

My Original Review (A Thumbs-Up):
Hang tight until the NPC metagame is re-implemented.  It WILL be worth it.  Play it now if you need to scratch the zombie-itch, but it probably won't blow your mind until the NPCs return.
My Current Review (3 Years Later):
Soooo, about those NPCs?!?!
I'm not completely sure when Indie Stone stopped focusing on the NPCs, but if you've read any of the "recent" Mondoids posted by the devs, they've been silently swept under the rug entirely for at least the last 8 months.  PZ used to lay claim to the lofty promises of developing some of the most advanced NPCs gaming has ever seen, with unique AI behavior and the ability to perform many of the same actions players might, including banding together in groups based on need and circumstance.  However, the NPCs went from the forefront of discussion, slowly toward the background, and finally to the ether (where their development is assured, yet forbidden from question, and still entirely hypothetical... for years.  YEARS!).
Indie Stone, may I ask why your focus continues to shift monthly from frivolous pursuit to frivolous pursuit?  Why is it that each task you seem to undertake (animations, metal working, vehicles, weapons. etc. etc) gets to ~50-80% complete when you decide to transition to the next "absolutely necessary" addition that rarely actually gets implemented??  I'm personally riddled with ADHD, and believe me Indie Stone team, we know our own.
Know that MAYBE 10% of your player-base gives a hoot about new animations, which you've also "temporarily" shelved after several months of being your main development effort.  I hope at the very least you're learning from these events.  You either need to really weigh the importance of the features you'd like in your game before start you developing them, or at least make sure that what you claim you'll add is actually possible before drumming up the hype-train.  Many of us who've backed your game for years, praised it's development, and introduced our friends to the world of PZ really don't appreciate the snake oil treatment.  We're also the type of gamer that don't forget when we've been jerked-around and essentially lied to, and we'll certainly remember when it comes to the next game you develop.
TL:DR
This games development hasn't technically staled.  It's still being actively "worked on", it's just that most of the features being worked on never actually make it into the game with claims that they're being developed "behind the scenes" with no evidence in-game and dwindling reports on their progress.  This translates into a game taking MANY years to develop and what is tantamount to false promises about the finished product.  If during the development certain planned features are found to be unfeasible, just TELL US and stop dicking us around and teasing your player-base!

The amount of care put into the movement and camera alone makes it worth playing, but this game has charm for days to boot. Major Super Mario Sunshine and Wind Waker vibes, and little nods to many other titles (Banjo Kazooie, Psychonauts), but it holds up very well on its own as a brand new IP that gets a *lot* of things right. It would be lovely if this level of quality became the standard for similar projects in the future.
Pros:
-Controls are tight and movement abilities chain together very well, making the game quite forgiving of minor mistakes. That same moveset allows for some very creative speedrunning as well. You never feel like something is out of your control.
-The dialogue and general sense of humor are great, and really add to the game's style and charm.
-Most of the acts have several chapters taking place in the same explorable environment. This really lets you get to know the area and explore every nook and cranny without necessarily repeating the same chapter, and they're large enough to support this kind of exploration.
-Character customization via unlockable color sets and different hat skins.
-Remixes of the game's soundtrack were included as unlockables in the game.
-Menu includes descriptions of what various settings actually do.
-Two free additional chapters will be added later, per the kickstarter stretch goals.
-Workshop content to play around with in the meantime.
-Levels can be played mostly out of order, with the exception of a few requiring specific badges or items to complete.
-No unreasonable achievements.
-Cute-as-heck, of course.
Cons:
-If 3D platforming isn't your thing, this game probably isn't your cup of tea.
-A bit on the short side if you aren't keen to collect everything there is to collect, 100% the achievements, etc.
-If backtracking irks you, you will probably dislike that some early areas have hidden treasure that you will need from later on in the game to access.
-A menu option to restart a level would have made aiming for certain conditional achievements less bothersome.

First Impressions:
Tropico seems to suffer the reversed curse of Windows / Star Trek.
The even numbers are great, the odd numbers...not so much.
And why? It's the characterisation. Penultimo is competent and not the snivelling cowardly sycophant he needs to be and there's a Juanita replacement called Lucy - who is just as annoying.
While 4 had wonderful cariactures, 3 and 5 have "realistic" characters - who just don't suit the game. All across the game there are fingermarks of designers saying "But we should say this is bad" - which really hurt the immersion.
For instance, you can choose to have an Atheist Constitution while wearing a Fedora. While this is relevant in the 21st Century, the idea of Atheism would be far more abhorrent to the Crown than simple Independence - especially if you then join the Nazis.
A better option would be to have a choice between Catholicism, Animism (Witch Doctors) and Godhood (El Presidente is God himself) - same choice, far better game immersion.
Is it better than 4? No.
Tropico works best when it's lampooning reality - this feels like the FOX NEWS History Channel when it should always be the Muppets.
Secondary views:
Nope - this is plain awful. There's swathes of this game that are borderline offensive and it's removed everything that 4 took from 3. I can't recommend it in good faith. Just a badly written game.
TL;DR: A cynical pitch into brofist territory with pretty graphics and multiplayer hiding a fundamentally broken game.

Sunless Sea combines both the drudgery and the joy of rogue-likes in equal measure.
The Unterzee is vast, mystical and rife with interesting nooks and crannies to explore. The way the world shifts from game to game is also well implimented. Especially in terms of the varied legacy systems to you can use to preserve your Captain's accomplishments. The flavour for Sunless Sea is absolutely impeccable, the writing engaging, the world interesting and the combat...well sort of roundabout (literally), but servicible. This is a world that you'll sink hours into. Not to mention a fair number of lost souls.
Sunless Sea does atmosphere well. That's for sure. There's always a sense of mild fear when first heading for the Salt Lions. Will they be where I remember? Am I going to run into another questline that I'm unprepared to handle? The possibilities are exciting.
Sunless Sea's problem comes in two parts: a repetative early game, and the mid to late game transition. Often, players will find themselves traversing the same early areas with successive Captains. Heading to Venderbright is intersting the first couple of times you set sail. Less so after your previous Zee Captain has sailed off each corner of the map for nothing more than bragging rights.
The transition from early game quest structure into completing character specific storelines and tours de Zee is also a little bit sticky. Finding the cash to finance ships for these expeditions requires a little bit of mid-game mercantile tinkering. This is good fun the first couple of times you give it a shot. The problem arises when you have to keep running the same, profitible routes in order to pay for the equipment necessary for, just as an example, a grand adventure to save the souless apes of monkey island (Note: No grand adventures will be found. Burn the Zepplin).
Sunless Sea is a game that is very much worth your time. Just be aware that there'll be a surprising number of perfectly flat sections for a game concerned with sailing.

Five Nights at Freddys’ is a game about an employee who has to look after a pizza place that comes alive at the dead of night. As an employee of course you want to be paid so you're going to stubbornly stick to your seat and watch those monitors like a good lad and try to avoid dying. Surviving from 12 AM to 6 AM to get your paycheck sounds easy enough but it proves harder than it seems.
The animatronics start in the same locations every night, three of them in the furthest room and one in Pirate's Cove with a total of four animatronics to monitor it can become hectic when they start to separate. Though while I say there is four to monitor there is also goldy freddy to be careful of especially when the poster changes. Foxy the one from  Pirate's Cove is the most mobile of the four and will have you checking on him from time to time to make sure he doesn’t dash straight for you.
Management of your resources is utmost importance in order to survive the entire night, which also means not running out of battery. Battery is going to be your main weapon to fend off these animatronics. It’s used to not only lighten up the hallways to check if they are next to you but also to monitor their movement via cameras. This actually is well balanced to the degree where I had many close calls of nearly dying from running out but lasting just long enough to get the paycheck.
I died several times on the first night, if it wasn’t for the fact I died I would be fired quickly for just being overall bad at my job.. Having tools to fend yourself helps but in a sense its only there to “delay” the jumpscare unless you make it to 6 am, if you are unable to the tension will explode from the building climax especially when the music box starts to play at 5 AM. The game is basically relays on your mind to play tricks on you and to build up fear for the “one” moment you know can come at any time especially if you let your guard down.
Once you beat all the nights there is a custom mode you can play to increase the ai of the robots up to 20. Which allows you to try the most challenging part of the game. At this point however your less scared of the game and more in it for the challenge of it all. You will most likely already establish a routine like many others have that helps you keep control of the situation and power manage the animatronics properly, so that you won’t be killed.
The overly major problem this game suffers really is ultimately finding a good routine will diminish the tension you had when you first started. Going into this game without a clue is really the best way to get value of it. Figuring it out step by step really gives it a better experience however once you get there the only real fun thing that remains is beating the custom night with all the AI on 20.
The premise of the game and the simplicity really make it standout and is quite accomplishes what it set out to do. The mechanics handle fairly well and are balanced to the point where you will see many videos of others and myself barely surviving the night multiple times regardless how well we try to balance our energy usage. The game is great for the tension that leads up to the jump scares though this diminishes towards the end and ultimately becomes about the challenge I still found the experience well worth the money.

I have around 14 hours in this mod, and I feel like I’ve seen at least half of the content available in this mod, so i figured now i should review it in the form of a basic pros and cons list.
Pros:
Lots of varied theaters and large map quantity
The way the commander trees are done is theater based (with some exceptions), which further helps to give each theater/map a unique feel, and allows several tactics that really help make the game more true to its origins:
-  Operation Market Garden maps: America can only do para doctrine and their base is a glider
- Italy: Fallschirmjägers rain from the sky in gliders, allowing you to open up new flanks
- There's also some maps where you can do a 1 time landing of like 8 fallschirmjäger squads! it can really change the flow of the game and allow you to open up a flank far more effectively than landing 1-2 squads every 3 minutes would do.
- I’m not going to list everything because this is one of the few mods that says “we added a lot of new content” they actually looked up the meaning of the word a lot.
- The balance is pretty good, they’re are some things that are better than others, but it's a living process
- It’s on steam, effortless install and running, support if you have issues is phenomenal, i had an issue and within hours was contacted by an admin and had it fixed.
- There’s custom scripted missions which add some fresh elements to the game
- There’s a lot a lot of new content
- Units have different skins and weapons instead of just renaming a rifle squad.
- Game is constantly being updated and bugs ironed out
Cons:
As stated some things are a little unbalanced, and there’s some humorous bugs but the game is being constantly updated.
In conclusion, it’s free, friendly community and admins, and has a lot of new content, if you’ve grown tired of spamming volks in coh2 and need a fresh break, download it.

Your name is Sam and you have elected to enter a rehab clinic in New Jersey to get better. One night you take your usual meds and that's when things get weird. You are some how put into a slightly different world, where you will have to survive the night. Can you fin your way through, solve the puzzles, figure out the clues, or will you disappear, it is totally up to you.
In Decay - The Mare, developed by Shining Game Software, you are going to get to do just that. In this 3 episodes in one game you are going to have to solve the puzzles that block your path, and of course survive. Now there is no way of actually dying in the game, but there are a couple of jumpy moments that will make you wonder what will come next.
This is an interesting point click adventure game in which you are going to be interacting with rooms that a specific camera angle, and at times you will get to see different angles. This is actually one of the strange things about the game, its not that they have specific views of a room that you get to work with, its the fact that no matter how many exits to a room there are, and the views you have, you will always default to the first view of the room you see. This does make for a frustrating couple of minutes when you are trying to quickly move around an area, through different rooms, and you have to remember that you might automatically default to the view of the door that you just came through, instead of the view of the door that is defaultly behind you.
Another odd thing about this game is the episodes/chapters/whatever you want to call them. At the end of each one you're going to get credits, then you will be thrown to a chapter select which of course will take you back in game. You will then have to repeat the last set of actions you took right before the end of the last chapter to start the new one you are in.
To continue with the odd things about this game is that the second, or middle chapter, probably has the most to it. You are going to gain the use of a camera, a mechanic I really liked, to see what is hidden to the naked eye. There's also a slew of challenging puzzles in this chapter. The strange thing is that all of those mechanics disappear for the final chapter and you go back to the almost random clicking to figure out what to do next mode that I found myself falling back into from the first chapter.
The graphics for this game are not going to blow you away, but there is something about it that definitely gave me the vibe I was expecting to see in the game. That being said the inventory look was not my favorite. You are presented with a line of squares, each with an item on it and you have to basically move the squares until the item in the box you want is in the middle of the screen so that you can select it. I don't really understand why they couldn't just allow for more of a show all the squares on the screen in a different pattern look, and allow you to move the selection to the item you want to use, yes I know that the selection square allowed you a couple of options for the item, but you could have figured something slightly different to allow for that functionality (view, use, combine) to still be intuitive.
I am VERY confused by the voice acting in this game, there are times where you get a voice and other times where you're left wondering if someone is going to read the text on the screen, and you just end up voicing it yourself to keep the mood going. That to me felt sloppy, I've always been a firm believer in the all or nothing, preferrably all voiced, way of doing things.
So I guess we should talk about if you should check out this game, well the answer is yes, I still enjoyed the 2 and a half hours of gameplay it game me, and sure there were some strange things that I wish were done better. Is this a must have, by no means is it, but it is definitely something you should at the very least check out and see. It isn't for everyone, it doesn't feel completely polished, but it gets the job done. This game gets a 7.1 out of 10.

I liked this game to start. I didn't buy it for a sandbox survival game, I bought it for the promised story mode. The sandbox is entertaining but didn't keep my interest after exploring each map.
One of the big talking points about the game is that it's a survival game without zombies. The wolves behave exactly like zombies which pales fast for players who were hoping for deeper and more interesting mechanics.  The actual survival mechanics are ridiculous. Factors like weight, weather, animal behavior, calorie/water consumption, weapon functioning, and decay are all completely unrealistic.
Still, it was fun and interesting to see the changes and wonder what impact they would have on the future story mode. Also, the maps are large and well-designed and the art work is beautiful. The sound design is amazing.
Story mode seems like it will never be delivered. It's grown in scope from a few hours of simple 2D stylized animation and cut scenes to a mo-cap extravaganza with full facial animations.

This was an awesome game back in 2007, and it's still amazing.  With fixed graphical enhancements (not locked at 720p anymore) this is a treasure for the library.
Allot of people were mega butt-hurt on initial release because it didn't have air dashing/double jumping and the chain-combo/cancel/chain-combo/cancel option select rinse repeat system that ark sys is well known for.  The result of this were allot of short sighted reviews that were technically wrong.  The systems in this game are not simple or shallow in any way, quite the opposite in fact.
So, I’m not expecting to win anyone over with this review, certain people will buy this game no matter what.  To the fighter enthusiast that falls into this category, I would like to point to `some`  of the system features that will quick start you if you've never played Battle Fantasia;
First, it is a footsie game like street fighter, in fact it feels ALLOT like Street Fighter IV.  Combos take skill to do, like SFIV and come in the form of difficult link timings to special/super cancels.  The difficulties of the combos reward you with good damage.
Second, is the Burn System.  This is exactly like the V system of Street Fighter V.  The game uses LP, HP, LK, HK, Parry five button config.  You trigger the burn by pressing both punches or both kicks.  You then get an augmentation specific to that character (A dragon summon for one character,  souped up specials for another character, or super armor for another, etc.) .  I swear SFV stole the V-System from Battle Fantasia.
Third, a button parry system.  If you've spent time in Street Fighter III or Yatagarasu, you understand the complexity that a parry system opens up.  I love parry systems, but an unfortunate side effect is the huge gap between players that can parry and those that cannot, same as SFIII TS and Yatagarasu etc.
I'll leave it at that, there’s allot more to dive into, but if you actually purchased this game to play it, you’ll probably figure it all out.

I will start by stating I have never played a Telltale game before, so their formula was new and refreshing. The "game" plays more like an interactive "choose your own adventure" storybook, than an actually game. As a kid, I loved these types of books, so add Batman, and I'm pretty happy with the formula.
Be forewarned, while you do play as Batman and there are a few fight scenes, this story revolves around Bruce Wayne and a devilish plot that has been cooked up to discredit his family legacy. It was an interesting take on a Batman story that I don't recall ever reading in the comics.
The action moments are all controlled by quick time events (QTE) and while many dislike this approach, I was fine with it, considering this is more of a story than an actual game.
The first episode took me around 2 hours. While I always want more content in all the games I play, this actually felt like a nice complete time frame, since the majority revolves around dialogue and exposition. I am looking forward to the next episodes and the twists and turns this elaborate plot ends up taking.
Pros:
-Excellent story telling. Interesting plot.
-Dialogue at an outside restaurant between Bruce and Selina was phenomenal.
-Batman's detective mode was the best I've seen so far, and I'm a huge fan of the Arkham games.
-Choosing dialogue options felt like Mass Effect. The choices you make as Bruce and Batman were fun.
-The Batcave and Batcomputer. Finally we get to do stuff with the computer.
Cons:
-Would have preferred a noir setting along the lines of BTAS. This felt too much like the Arkhamverse when it comes to character costumes and some settings.
-Penguin's origin. I love the classic origin stories for Batman's vilains, and this one was way off.
-A few crashes.
-Ultrawide support shows up but does not work.
-Batman's voice work. I dislike that they went the "Arrow" path with it.
Overall I would recommend this if you really like Batman and you love story and exposition. There is a lot of it in this game. The choices you are allowed to make as Bruce and Batman really make you second guess yourself.

This is an apologetic review. I have to admit that my last negative review for this game was looking at it through the wrong scope, and after a long discussion with a friend and some research I can finally make a more educated analysis about the game. It will be long to discuss as many points as possible but I’ll make sure to add a TL;DR at the end.
First of all let’s take a moment to read my past review and see why didn’t I like the game, and how is it related to other opinions here on the store page for The Beginners Guide.
That’s it. That’s all I wrote on my first review for the game, and now we are going to discuss why I was wrong, and it all comes to this:
While discussing, my friend and I noticed that everyone was being harsh against the game for not being like The Stanley Parable, not living up to its standards. To be honest the trailer is a little deceiving, it made me have a perception of a more open-ended game. Even I fell for the trap that are expectations. When you expect something that is very much different product you are very likely to end up ruining the experience for you.
So what can I expect from the game may you ask? Well, I was right about that one point, don’t expect The Stanley Parable, if you need more specificity don’t expect a funny open ended storyline. I also said to not expect a “life changing narrative”, this is also true, but bear with me for a second. SPOILER ALERT:
Once Dave makes his GOTY awarded game, he went into a depression in which he writes in about here:
The point I’m trying to make is that the story you see on The Beginners Guide is a direct reflection of the developer’s emotions at a point of his life. The game is not aiming to change the way you think from now on, it’s simply asking for a little empathy, a little bit of understanding. If you start complaining about how the lack of gameplay mechanics suck on this game, you are completely missing the entire point of the game. It’s not about you, it’s about Coda, and it is about Dave.
I have apologize for my first review, I just didn’t knew… I also have to give credit to my friend Él Cabrony, which even after I convinced him that the game sucked, he agreed to played it anyways. To be honest I wanted him to play it, even when I told his it was bad, I think I subconsciously liked it and wanted to know his opinion about it. After that he apparently really liked the game and went on to have a discussion with me on what makes a game good, etc.
Going on a more general side on why you should play the game:
Honest opinion of what I did not like about the game.
TL;DR:
The Game is Good is you know what to expect.

Starting this out saying SPOILERS. SERIOUSLY. BEST TO EXPERIENCE THIS GAME FIRST. IT CAN BE COMPLETELY RUINED IN ONE FELL SWOOP BY READING THIS, OR MANY OTHER REVIEWS. YOU FOOLS WHO DARE TRAVERSE FARTHER HAVE BEEN WARNED.
Davey... is a master of unreliable narrators.
I was curious stepping into this game if there was, in any way, a connection to The Stanley Parable, because, well.... Look at my steam page at my hrs played for that game and you'll get it. And there is. Kind of. The narrator wants you to listen to their story and follow it, unquestioningly. Their story is what's important. But it's not the truth of the situation.
The games differ after that, though. Davey doesn't fight back once his story begins to fall apart, like the Narrator does. He, in fact, falls apart. And I can't stop thinking about that. What he says is.. both very relatable and very alien to me. I thnk that's why I feel like I relate to Coda, in his final part. I've been in that boat where someone who was once dear to me became toxic to me and my happiness, and the struggle to make them happy, their unhealthy "addiction" to me, and then turning myself away from them so I can actually live my own life and thrive. May be looking too much into what Coda said, but I've felt his side of the story before. Being a prize someone else shows off to others to make themselves feel better when you feel your relationship is, or was, more intimate and safe than that... It feels horrible.
Anyway, tl;dr, this is a good experience and can be related to in many ways, and omniscient narrators may not be as omniscient as they think.

Sunless Sea is an odd little beastie, to say the least.
If the idea of slowly sputtering from port to port, praying to the various gods you don't get eaten by creatures (or have to eat your own crew), with little to fight against except time, inertia, and your own lack of foresight, this is probably not going to be worth your time. The combat is rudimentary, as is the trading, and the arc quests could really stand to increment about twice as fast as they do, BUT, what it lacks in fundamentals, it makes up in world-building, and sheer creeping, clammy ATMOSPHERE. Don't think of it strictly as an RPG, think of it as Underground Boat Simulator 2015.
While a slow, vulnerable, leaky little dinghy makes for a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor fighting vessel, it is EXACTLY the right mode of travel for sightseeing in a world of creeping cosmic horror, and that world is easily Sunless Sea's biggest draw. Beautifully realized by the artists and writers, the Unterzee is filled with a menagerie of otherworldly weirdness that draws at least as much from the works of people like Mieville and Gaiman as it does from the great M.C. Lovehoney. Happily, there are enough of these crunchy little story-nuggets to keep an interested person busy for a good number of hours, but sooner or later you will probably hit the seemingly inevitable threshold where the awesomeness of your gear starts to seriously negate all the horror elements. Granted, I probably broke things a wee bit by strapping the biggest engine in the game into the second crappiest boat in the game and piling on every speed booster I could ifnd, but if the developers can't anticipate someone building a simple Miami Vice-style coke runner, then that's on them, frankly. Nevertheless, while the end-game can become a bit of a slog, especially with the aforementioned incrementation problem, the trip there is a rich and worthwhile one, and as Failbetter Games keep adding little content updates, the finale should become less sparse over time.
I never found my stupid father's stupid bones, but I did have a lot of fun exploring the Unterzee, and as an experience I thoroughly reccomend it, just not entirely as a game.

Decided to give DDII another try after over a year long break, ended up really disappointed for quite a number of reasons.
Difficulty curve is flat out broken. There are 3 map categories: campaign, incursions, chaos trials. Campaigns are an outdated introduction/tutorial, incursions are outdated content that no longer serves any purpose, chaos trials are the intended endgame, 7 increasingly difficult difficulty levels with special mobs spawning in each. At the point where you can easily do all campaign and incursion maps, you'll be struggling to clear any trial except chaos 1 and that's depending on your characters. After clearing chaos 1, you'll be struggling to clear chaos 2 or 3, until you grind your ascension level enough.
Trials themselves rely on cheap gimmicks and enforcing slow power creep via grinding instead of being tactically challenging for difficulty: they spawn mobs that render specific towers flat out useless, for example disabling traps and auras they walk into, or reflecting all projectiles, forcing to clear each trial in a very specific way. They also force you to play random maps, which can be very annoying when you repeatedly get maps you simply dislike playing on (for example because they're giant and setting up the towers on them takes longer than the actual map because you have to keep running back and forth before and during each wave).
Balance is nonexistent, Mage and Squire both have a barrier tower with the same cost, except Squire's both has more health and covers a bigger area. That's just one example, some other towers are also outright upgrades compared to another tower of a different class. One of the hero classes (gun witch) is unable to place turrets, being exclusively a dps class. Funnily, she's not the best dps and probably not even in top 3.
Inventory screen is by far the worst I've ever seen in any game. Instead of being a button that you press once, auto sorting is a toggled function. Except it's completely and utterly useless for 2 reasons: you can't manually put any new item in the tab that's being auto sorted and, upon disabling auto sort, all the items go back to their previous, unsorted positions. Can't even sort items according to stats or quality. Can't drag items to move them around either. Warnings when selling some items (low quality pets, purple quality gear) are also uncalled for in my opinion and just make inventory management that much more annoying. Lack of effective sorting means getting any information about items, besides quality, requires you to mouse over them.
With some exceptions that you'll only ever be running for the daily quests, maps only last 5 waves. There's no survival/endless mode. As far as I'm concerned, this means maps end roughly at the time I'm done warming up.
Upgrading turrets is, in many cases, meaningless. Some turrets do get significant bonuses such as roughly +40% stats when getting upgraded, others get +10% for upgrade that costs more than the turret itself. This feels like a lazy attempt at balancing, "we don't want you to use it like this, so we'll make the upgrades useless" style.
The way loot is rolled is questionable to say the least. Instead of each map dropping gear in specific stat range, maps only have an upper limit of gear they can drop, the actual dropped items depend on the gear you're currently wearing: they can only every be slightly better than your average, but not better than the max allowed for the map you're running. This prevents boosting, problem is the game doesn't calculate the actual strength of the gear correctly. To decide the strength of the gear you're wearing, it looks at a hidden property called iPWR or item power, represented indirectly by the item's selling price. Problem is, iPWR has only a very loose connection with the item's actual stats. Sometimes in order for the game to start giving you better loot, you have to equip worse gear just because it has a higher selling price/iPWR.
Also, I was playing the game with a friend whose pc is comparable or better better than my in all aspects except for the drives (I'm using all SSD, he only has 1 SSD for windows). I had no performance issues at highest settings. Friend's game however, had massive performance issues, with constant stuttering and freezes. Running same driver version too. Meaning the optimisation is terrible.
This game isn't ready for the official release which is coming in a week. It feels like a fresh early access product and even some of those are better.
Dungeon Defenders 2 is simply a major downgrade compared to its predecessor, I think there's no other way to call it.
It's boring to play. Feels unrewarding. There's no real sense of purpose. Interface is horrible. Grind is bad even for a F2P game.

Battle Fantasia is the first Arc System Works game I've played. I haven't played BlazBlue, Guilty Gear, or Fist Of The North Star so I can't say how this game plays compared to those, but what I can say is that this is a pretty fun game despite some issues. Don't get me wrong though, DotEmu's port job borders on atrocius. Starting with the launcher. You are given very few resolution options and no graphical options other than full screen. And you chose whether or not to use a controller from the launcher too. Speaking of controllers, the only gamepad I got to work was the Xinput (Xbox) controller I luckily just bought the day I wrote this review. My Dualshock 4 (DirectInput) didn't work properly.
Getting into the game proper, I couldn't do anything initially. It took me about 5 minutes to find the problem. Despite my controller appearing the dropdown box, it wasn't actually selected. Because I had set my controls to "Controller", my keyboard couldn't do anything except for killing the process in Task Manager. I didn't need to though, becuase it crashed. After I sorted that out, I finally got to play the game, and that's where it got good. The character roster is small, but it was a nice variety of characters with their own play style that is easy to pick up on. The visuals look a bit dated, as in they would look right at home on the PS2, but the style is enough to keep the game from looking very dated. The audio is pretty good, It has the standard fighting game modes. Arcade mode works exactly as expected and the Story mode is pretty neat. The AI is very brutal (Coming from someone who can play Skullgirls on Nightmare) even on the Normal setting. There is the occasional framerate issue, but it wasn't enough to disrupt the game, though that could just be me being used the 30 FPS of games like JoJo: All Star Battle. I haven't played online as the community seems to be barely there and I couldn't find a game open. It does have local multiplayer so you can play with your friends if they have Xbox 360/One compatible controllers.
Overall, it's a good fighting game, but you will have to look past the fact that it's a very dodgy Xbox 360 port.

I will start by stating I have never played a Telltale game before, so their formula was new and refreshing. The "game" plays more like an interactive "choose your own adventure" storybook, than an actually game. As a kid, I loved these types of books, so add Batman, and I'm pretty happy with the formula.
Be forewarned, while you do play as Batman and there are a few fight scenes, this story revolves around Bruce Wayne and a devilish plot that has been cooked up to discredit his family legacy. It was an interesting take on a Batman story that I don't recall ever reading in the comics.
The action moments are all controlled by quick time events (QTE) and while many dislike this approach, I was fine with it, considering this is more of a story than an actual game.
The first episode took me around 2 hours. While I always want more content in all the games I play, this actually felt like a nice complete time frame, since the majority revolves around dialogue and exposition. I am looking forward to the next episodes and the twists and turns this elaborate plot ends up taking.
Pros:
-Excellent story telling. Interesting plot.
-Dialogue at an outside restaurant between Bruce and Selina was phenomenal.
-Batman's detective mode was the best I've seen so far, and I'm a huge fan of the Arkham games.
-Choosing dialogue options felt like Mass Effect. The choices you make as Bruce and Batman were fun.
-The Batcave and Batcomputer. Finally we get to do stuff with the computer.
Cons:
-Would have preferred a noir setting along the lines of BTAS. This felt too much like the Arkhamverse when it comes to character costumes and some settings.
-Penguin's origin. I love the classic origin stories for Batman's vilains, and this one was way off.
-A few crashes.
-Ultrawide support shows up but does not work.
-Batman's voice work. I dislike that they went the "Arrow" path with it.
Overall I would recommend this if you really like Batman and you love story and exposition. There is a lot of it in this game. The choices you are allowed to make as Bruce and Batman really make you second guess yourself.

A survival game set in the wild canadian North (we sure have been getting popular lately, haven't we? :D), The Long Dark is still in early access but already has plenty of qualities to justify buying it right now. It's got atmosphere. It's challenging. And the biggest threat to your survival isn't always as obvious as you might think. Most of the time I died in this game, it was because of poor preparation and getting lost in a blizzard while trying to find my way back to a shelter. It's a game where smart decisions and patience truly pay off, and I can't stress enough how much I love games like that.
There are three difficulty levels right now. ''Easy'' allows you to play simply for the atmosphere and wild animals won't attack you, which makes the whole experience more peaceful, if ridiculously easy. The ''Normal'' difficulty is not a walk in the park by any stretch of the imagination. Every day is a struggle against time and the elements to procure food, tools and equipment, and fuel for fires. In fact, it's so tough and gritty I haven't bothered to try the ''Hard'' difficulty yet. I assume you just die of dysentry or scurvy as soon as you start the game. :P
The game can get a bit boring when you're starting to build up a good supply of stuff. It can also get rather stressful in the early game when you're trying to avoid overly agressive wolves while fighting against the clock in mad sorties across the wilderness to ''maybe'' find that tool you desperately need. Despite that, The Long Dark is a promising game that has a lot to offer and will probably have a lot more to offer as it develops.

I like this game it has potential but there are some issues with balancing etc.
The most prominent issue is the animals. on "Normal" mode, (putting normal in quotes because it's called something different in game), animals don't seem to live in the woods, bears just sully along on roads and frozen lakes, along with wolves and dear, it would be cool if there is a lone wolf or even bear in large buildings like the one that is in the damn but they're usually placed in villages and on roads and there are almost unrealistic amounts of wolves, I get it adds challenge but at the same time it would be better to populate deeper in the woods with wolves, instead of litterally out on a frozen lake, and then make going deeper into the woods more rewarding and challenging.
I think the fundemental problem is there is a vast open would but with the difficulty the game presents straight at the get go there is little oppertunity to explore before you die. The means to take on the challenges are usually few and far inbetween and then once you get them suprisingly ineffective, (The aiming needs a good bit of work, making aimming slow doesn't make things more realistic it just makes aiming slow.) Also something that really scares me is how slow progress is being made with this game, I think the assets seem to be all there, it's just game play that needs to be fleshed out.
So what's good about this game.
Well it's early access survival that isn't bugged out as♥♥♥♥♥♥ and is, well a game.
It's survival mechanics are also pretty good, you have to balance out staying warm, getting rest, drinking and eating. Dealing with temperature seems dynamic, this is the most interesting need to fulfill, there are multiple ways to warm up, finding better clothes and repairing the ones you already have, starting fires, eating warm food or drinking warm beverages, and just getting indoors, you also have to account for windchill along with just the temperature, some clothes handle windchill very well while others do well with temperature all in all a well done mechanic. The rest are simple, you sleep, drink, eat, not something to complain about, fundamentally they can't be as interesting as staying warm and thats okay, drinking and eating can still be hard to stay up on, they still provide challenge. All this contributes to your overall health, if one of your needs reaches 0 your health starts decrementing so you can't die of thirst directly but it makes sense to do that since animal attacks affect your health aswell. My only real complaint with this system is that it seems like the resting is 1 to 1, meaning 12 hours of sleep to be awake 12 hours, this needs adjustment as sometimes I hav ethe need to nap in the middle of the day.
The animal attacks are pretty well done and the recovery system is more thought out then "Put on a bandage restore hp"
You have to specifically treat the wounds you recieved and then wait for your health to slowly regenerate, treating alements ranges from sleeping to bandaging wounds, it makes a lot of sense and is a great addition to the game.
The graphics aren't as great as advertised, I'm on a low-mid range rig so this could be why but they are still awesome, the art style works so well and colors are vibrant they really pop and it's a nice get away from the 'psuedo realistic' graphics we get a lot these days.
The sounds well done, I'm not going to go into detail, nothing makes you cringe.
Crafting is good, you can't make structures or guns, anything out of the box. You can make what a normal person could in this situation. It works well, I'm not taping alcohol to a circuit board and getting a bomb, not gluing logs together to make a wall, etc. While these things can be fun, yes good games can be unrealistic, this one is in some places too but I can apprciate how the crafting is minimalistic and shifts the games focus more towards foraging and less towards crafting. It doesn't rely on crafting like a lot of other games do, you can be pretty succesful in this game without crafting (not counting harvesting raw materials and using thos materials to repair stuff as crafting, it's done differently in two seperate interfaces I feall that is justified.) This sets it apart from a lot of the sort of shovelware survival games out there.
So should you buy this game.
It depends really, you're going to have to have some faith that this game will get finished, it's been in early access for over a year as I'm writing this review and I still feel as though the game can be hollow in some places and defiantly needs adjustments in others. You're also gonna want to get this game if you're into more realistic survival or want a survival game that sets itself apart from others (keep in mind that while this is not totally realistic, it boarders heavely on the more realistic side). Also you have to be able to deal with the difficulty, normal is hard but easy mode is boring, bears litterally run away from you, this is just frustrating to be honest. While it's fun I'd honestly wait until it's more fleshed out,  or on sale unless you are really into more realistic survival or have a lot of moeny to blow. If I had to give it a number score 7/10 that could very well be a 9-10/10 with balancing and the story mode.

Telltale Games have created another tale for us to enjoy. This time, it is in the form of a Batman series. As a character, Batman has been sealed into many of our hearts as one of the greatest superheroes of all time. We know his backstory, what he is capable of, his strengths, and his weaknesses. So it begs the question, can Telltale Games create a brand new story within the world of Batman without treading old ground? Surprisingly, the answer is yes.
Gameplay
The fundamentals of Telltale’s Batman are in the form of a point and click adventure and gives you the ability to choose how the story plays out and define what exactly is Bruce Wayne and Batman is to Gotham City. Player actions involve participating in dialogue, interacting with objects in the environment, and through quick-time events.The combat set pieces rely heavily on quick-time events which is complemented by the outstanding choreography during these scenes. Overall, you will do a lot of watching during this episode, but what you see is like seeing a comic book come to life.
To be honest, controlling Bruce Wayne and Batman was great despite not having much direct input on his actions. What stands out in this series isn’t the great combat set pieces, but the various dialogue choices available for the player to choose. Defining who Bruce Wayne really is behind the curtain is just as engaging as defining who Batman is during the night.
What bothered about this episode involved the supposed consequences of your actions during one specific scene. Rather than having the story adapt to what I choose, I feel that the next scene of dialogue is decided without my consideration. This example involved me being chastised for actions that I had never committed, in fact my actions were the very opposite. And yet, the game decided the consequences were going to stay there, regardless of my input. Keep in mind, this problem has only arisen once during the entire episode. Regardless, such an error in storytelling breaks the immersion factor of the game. Despite the flaw, Episode One presents engaging gameplay in the form of choices in narrative as well as action set-pieces.
Narrative
So I won’t be spoiling any of this story, except for its premise, because I feel this is a unique take on Batman that everyone should see for themselves. We are presented Bruce Wayne and Batman during their first phase of their crime fighting career. And I feel the need to separate these personas into different characters because that is exactly how it feels to play these two. Batman comes across a crime that begins to develop into something greater and more terrible than anticipated. During the day, Bruce Wayne deals with his own set of problems involving crooked politicians, maintaining his social identity and secret, and understanding who he really is while having a nagging butler criticizing him every time he takes a seat in his bat cave. And this is riveting stuff every step of the way.
Overall, besides annoyingly recalling the death of his parents, this series presents a unique take on Batman as well the story told here.
Graphics
The visuals work well to sell you the feeling of seeing a comic book coming to life. Something to keep in mind is that this isn’t your kid’s version of Batman. This game earns its M rating more so than Arkham Knight ever could and this is only the first episode. Depending on how you play, Batman can be capable of great cruelty toward his foes and have everyone question how honorable is this version of Batman. Some instances of violence have a stylistic presentation and then are instances that can be downright brutal. The environment, the characters, and effects are all well done. Animation is mostly rock solid, however there are some rigid animations that could use some work.
Sound
I came into this episode not expecting much when it came to the soundtrack, but honestly it impressed me. During the moments where Batman takes on a group of armed thugs, the game really sold the intensity of the situation. Even during its more subtle moments, music plays a large role in the atmosphere of this episode and it is great. The voice acting too was well done. There was no line of dialogue to really praise, but Troy Baker as Batman definitely worked and so did the other voice acting.
Ending Execution
The end of this episode left me wanting more in the best way possible. While merely the beginning to a brand new story, the orchestration of Episode One’s ending will leave you with the feeling of satisfaction.
Originality
Despite this series slightly treading on old ground, Batman: The Telltale Series presents a unique take on Bruce Wayne and Batman. It really does feel fresh and aside from a few elements, I recommend any fan of Batman or someone who likes adventure games to pick this up and give it a try.

Snowkoban
AGSIHTB is an adorable block-pushing (ball-pushing, I guess) puzzle game. The premise is simple enough: Maneuver the snowballs around the playing field and push them into a stack. If a small snowball is rolled across a patch of snow, it will grow to become a medium snowball and eventually a large snowball. Snowballs can only be stacked in order of larger base to smaller top.
The puzzles are very accessible. There is a jump in difficulty in the late game, but it's not overwhelming or unforgiving. Many of the puzzles have multiple valid solutions. It's even possible to get an advantage by using each area's multiple entrances, but in order to get the "best" solution you'll want to stay inside the playing area. There is a rewind function, so you don't have to completely restart a given puzzle if you make a mistake on a long or elaborate puzzle.
Each completed snowman is presented with a name and some sort of hat or accessory to add character. Puzzles can be restarted and replayed at any time, so you can try to find alternate solutions to already-completed puzzles.
Ultimately it's a clever twist on sokoban puzzles and a very cute presentation.

SUPERHOT is by all means an utterly superb game. You can slice bullets out of the air, people! However, I'm assuming everyone already knows this, so instead in this review I am going to address the price point.
For a game that costs a quarter of $100, many people are complaining about how it has way too short of a story to justify its price. Now, it is entirely true that the story is short (it took me ~3 hours to complete and that's mainlly because I'm kinda bad at shooters in general), but the story was quite unique though quite frankly the story is not the reason you should buy this game. This game is about slicing red dudes in slow motion, not about spending hours on some sort of plot!
For $25 you get:
- A 2+ hour story mode
- 15+ endless arenas (which you unlock after story)
- 8+ challenge modes which let you replay the story in a UNIQUE way (I've unlocked the first few and they reall change things up)
- Incredibly fun and unique gameplay
- Basic replay editor
- Speedrun modes
In all, this is a great game to pick up and play, especially if you're a completionist, and is totally worth $25 if you're looking for a game that is simply entertaining and highly replayable. 'Nuff said.
Well, I also forgot to mention that...
... It's the most innovative shooter I've played in years ;)

Cuphead has been a highly anticipated release for the better part of three years now. The publisher/developer, StudioMDHR Entertainment, launched the game's campaign initially in January 2014, and at the time set a release date expectation of 2014. After numerous delays that pushed the title into 2015, then 2016, and finally 2017, gamers were understandably beginning to wonder if the difficult 1930's cartoon inspired platformer would actually see the light of day. Without a doubt, the patience of the public has finally paid off, and Cuphead hit the market on September 29, 2017.
The story is not one that is overbearing, and there are only a handful of cutscenes throughout the game; all of which can be found after beating one level and moving on to the next. Cuphead and Mugman have found themselves at the Devil's Casino, and they're on a big winning streak. The devil appears and challenges them to one last roll of the dice with a catch; if they win they take everything he owns, but if they lose their souls are his. Of course the devil wins, but when Cuphead and Mugman plead for their souls, the devil sends them out around the Inkwell Isles to gain soul contracts from various other characters.
Inarguably, the aesthetics of Cuphead are extremely pleasing to the eye to anyone that has a nostalgic soft spot for the look and feel of 1930-1940's era of animation. The backgrounds are all lovingly handcrafted with soft, yet gritty,  pastel colors. While the characters and enemies are rendered in the same fashion, they have a cartoony brightness to them to make them stand out dominantly against the mix of stagnant and scrolling screens. The two progagonists, Cuphead and Mugman, are comprised of simple shapes and colors, leaving your eye to comfortably explore the landscapes and foes rather than focus on them. Additionally, the soundtrack is nothing but complimentary to the retro style, bringing a mix of upbeat swing jazz, orchestra, and classy noir soundscapes; I should also mention, it's all performed by real musicians using live instruments, not synthesizers. Every composition is unique only to the game, along with a few tracks that feature a singing quartet. All in all, you will have no problem feeling like you are back in the golden oldie days while playing this title.
The controls are, for the most part, very smooth and fluid, although the buttons are not rebindable at the moment. This is definitely a game that is best played with a controller, so keyboard + mouse elitists be warned. Of course you have your standard jump and shoot buttons, but you're also able to parry objects that glow bright pinks by double jumping on them, as well as use special moves to deal extra damage to foes. You can also duck and jump-dash as well. There are several upgrades that can be purchased from an in-game shop, using in-game coins that are collected from a handful of levels, many of which come with new attacks that range in both power and reach, along with charms that have various effects. At any time while on the map screen, players are able to interchange attacks, special moves, and charms, in which finding the right combination is crucial to advancing within some levels.
With all of that being said, Cuphead is not a game that will appeal to everyone. This is primarily due to its perceived difficulty which has been rated to the levels of old school Megaman titles. Though I personally did not find the game to be that difficult, it still does present a devilish challenge; especially to those who may be used to the comparative ease of modern gaming. It will, however, appeal to those who enjoy a more hardcore platformer/side-scroller/shoot 'em up, along with those that enjoy a good co-op title. Be forewarned, though, that this game only comes with local co-op, which can be an unfortunate downside for gamers with long distance cooperative buddies.
For all of the good that it possesses, this title still has areas where it can improve. For anyone going in to Cuphead thinking that it will be a side-scrolling platformer akin to Megaman, throw that idea out the window. The majority of levels are simply boss-oriented, meaning that you will find yourself on a stagnant screen, fighting a boss through its various phases. There are only a handful of "run-and-gun" platforming levels, and each one of those has their own mini-boss at the end. Therefore, you will spend the biggest majority of your time facing one-on-one bosses. Additionally, if you're playing solo, you only have the option to play as Cuphead and you will never see Mugman unless you have a local friend to play with. It would be nice to have the option to switch between the two characters, but alas that is not the case.
There's also no incentive to do your best. Cuphead grades you at the end of each level by your remaining health, how many super move slots you earned, your total time, and if it's a "run-and-gun" level also by how many coins you found. Unless you're really in to achievements, there's no reason to stress yourself to get that perfect A+/S ranking, as there are no unlocks of any kind to be had. The only thing that comes close is unlocking Expert difficulty after beating the game, but even then there is little point unless you're die-hard. This is much more of a disappointment than not being able to freely play as Mughead, as many older games did provide unlockables or alternate endings to some degree.
Though Cuphead does come with its share of hits and misses, it's still an outstanding adventure through the long forgotten, yet still wholly beloved, era of a simplier time. The inclusion of things that are banned in cartoons of this day and age, such as cigars and gambling, are a really nice touch that just add to the nostalgic factor. With a little bit of hope, the developer will listen to feedback and hopefully include more platforming levels in the next installment, if there is one, rather than an over-abundance of one-on-one boss levels. If you enjoy difficult titles, then Cuphead is for you, but do not believe all of the reviews that compare this game to Megaman or any other game of that nature, as this beast is a monstrosity entirely its own.

The game seems so simple but it is surprisingly addictive. As the name subtly suggests you basically build your own mall, manage the various stores in terms of stock, hire and set staffing levels, and try an maintain customer satisfaction and the profit that goes along with this. Sunless Sea is a mixture of a book and a game. It is deeply flawed as either of these but at the same time there is something about it that makes me sink lots of hours into it.
Book part plays when you are in a port. There you’ll find stories that are available depending on your skills, items and whole lot of behind the scenes stuff. The stories are well written and the world of Sunless Sea is truly a strange place. These stories have a lot of text to read with some options to change the course but it’s basically like clicking “next page” until you get to the ending. While the writing is praise-worthy, it’s really hard to read a book that is scattered around a game world that takes hours to see. The rewards from these range from gaining supplies to losing crewmembers and it’s often nearly impossible to predict what happens.
Everything in this game is an item that can be used. You have your fuel, supplies and such, but also items like “Latest news”, “Memory of a distant shore”, “Zee story”, “Tale of terror” and so on. These are rewarded from quests and can be used to buy stuff or open new quests. It’s an interesting system but not flawless: Some ports only use one of these as a currency and without a guide it’s a monumental task to remember which uses which. Giving up is really close when you finally have five “tales” you need to buy something and make a long and expensive trip to somewhere, only to find out that they only accept “stories”. It doesn’t help that sometimes the journal doesn’t record any of the vital info and sometimes it does.
Outside of the safety of harbour is a vast zee that you travel with a miniscule steamboat. It is rough out there with gradually diminishing supplies. Then there is terror, which builds up constantly and can lead to the crew losing their minds. Monsters lurk in the darkness but avoiding them is really easy. I’m sure you can finish Sunless Sea without firing a shot. This is a good thing since combat is definitely the weakest part of the experience. You can buy a better ship and the costs are astronomical, but it’s actually not necessary. The ship you start with can easily sail to the other side of the Underzee and back. Traveling takes a lot of time with very little happening. Talking to crew members and such always pauses the game so be prepared to just stare at the screen for a long time with nothing to do.
If (and most likely when) you die, you’ll lose your progress. Some of the items you gathered are given to your next captain but you’ll have to start again. Islands in the game switch places so you really have to do everything again. Stories stay the same so a lot of the beginning is just mindless clicking around. With that said, my first captain survived 4 hours of real world time so this doesn’t happen very often.
The UI could use some work. I’m on ultrabook with 13” screen and 1080p native resolution. On this screen the text is really small and hard to read. Windows screen scaling options do affect the ingame assets but it’s less than ideal to do this every time you boot the game. On a bigger screen or one with smaller native resolution this would not be an issue, but it’s worth mentioning since modern ultrabooks go way higher than 1080p. Downloading more stories in the main menu leads almost always to crashing and it’s a matter of luck to get them. This doesn’t lead to loss of gameplay progress and the game boots quite fast but is annoying anyway.
I’m sure I’ll never finish this game nor will I ever understand all of its secrets. For once in my gaming life I’m happy for that. Not knowing in itself is rewarding. Sailing in Sunless Sea is slow and what I’d normally call boring and tedious but it somehow manages to make nothingness into something special in a way that is at the same time calming and scaring. Atleast for the first few hours. I’ll recommend Sunless Sea as unique and interesting but flawed and glacially paced experience.

This review is being reposted now because Trendy used skeevy tactics to prevent reviews marked "early access" from showing.  Specifically, early access reviews older than a specific point were treated as though they were for a different game, resulting in them no longer showing up.  As a result, Steam would not recognize my old review and would not show it.  I am reposting it now to ensure that my voice is heard.  Keep in mind that despite the date on it, this review dates back to just after Dungeon Defenders 2 left Early Access.
Dungeon Defenders 2 is a game with so much potential to be good, hamstrung by a developer that does not know what they're doing with it and cannot keep the promises they made to those who backed them.
The Trials update was a mixed bag.  Some of the things it introduced were good.  Others were incomprehensibly bad.  The Shard system and Ascension powers were good ideas, as was the separation of Hero and Defense stats (finally, you don't have to choose whether to fight OR build, you can do both on the same character!)  but they came at the cost of the functioning and well-balanced Sphere mechanic and Stat Allocation System.  The handling of converting everyone's spheres into shards was done abysmally - they gave you
, a currency earned relatively easily through playing the game, as a refund for spheres that cost
, a much, much more difficult-to-earn currency.  Honestly, a straight wipe would've been better than a mishandled conversion, because at least that would've been done properly.
Even within the Shard and Ascension systems, mistakes were made.  With the loss of SAS, most players lost a vast amount of Defense Range on their towers, a stat heavily relied upon to make towers useful.  Rather than increasing the base range of towers to compensate, or offering an Ascension power that increased range, they offered Range Gambit ascension powers - bonus range at the cost of power.  The problem?  Taking range gambit too early can gimp you.  A Chaos-1 Medallion has a Defense Power under 1,000.  Maxing out a defense range gambit for a given tower will cost you 1,500 defense power.  You can *utterly destroy* your tower's offensive abilities by attempting to correct their lack of range.  The only viable means of increasing range without risking gimpage is the Deadly Strikes shard, which, at the time I last seriously played, was rare and difficult to earn, and naturally required a shard slot on the defense you wanted to increase the range of.
As a result of these poor decisions, and Trendy's adamant refusal to fix them, the game wound up a lot less fun.  Offensive towers became much less useful, with only anti-air towers and barricades being genuinely effective.  This is a far cry from what the game once was, where your hero could support towers, but also rely on them to handle enemies on weaker lanes while you're away.
TrendyEnt, when this game was first announced and put into Early Access, promised a lot of things to players.  Among them, split-screen local co-op.  Now the game is launching on June 20th, and this promise is still not met.  TrendyEnt cites their failure as an issue with Steam disallowing multiple concurrent Steam logins on one machine, a feature that Steam has expressly stated that they will not permit due to security concerns.  Who designs a feature reliant on
feature on another program that the other program's developers have flatly stated
That's quite frankly insane.
For me personally, the biggest broken promise is the promise that the game will never be pay-to-win.  Anyone remember
?  That DD2 will make its money entirely off cosmetics and conveniences, never by selling power.  Well, that ended somewhere in the last couple months, because now they're selling Shard Packs in their cash shop.  Yes, shard packs.  The very same shard packs you play Chaos Trials to get.  Shard are a huge force-multiplier.  Many towers aren't even viable without a defense power shard and a defense range shard in them at a minimum, unless you have hundreds of Ascension Levels to beef them up with.  Selling shard packs is directly selling power, which is the one thing I won't tolerate given their promise.  If they can sell shard packs, then it's only a matter of time before they start selling equipment or other forms of power.
I am so intensely disappointed with this game, and its developer.  TrendyEnt, I expected better from you, and had such high hopes.

Ah, BattleFantasia.
Back in the day, this was just about the only game that every member of my FGC enjoyed. Everyone from the Street Fighter players, the Tekken crowd to the - then new and coming - anime players.
The game is a cartoony, fantasy themed fighter which is very easy to pick up, with a small roster and easy to grasp movelists for the characters. That's not to say the game is simple, this in an Arcsys game after all. Sure, the small roster makes it easier to learn match-ups so players can focus on their gameplan rather than having to grind out 63 different character specific punishers in advance, but every characters also has a whole host of little tricks and traits that you can brush up on the continually expand your repetoire over an extended period of time.
For example, the charge character Cedric can combo off of his regular throw in a variety of ways, the catgirl Coyori can mix you up with sweeps, overheads and even crossups during her rekka chains and the big guy DeathBringer can sacrifice start-up speed on certain moves to give himself a point armor and mess up trigger happy opponents. And that's just the basics, every character can also activate heat mode, which gives them completely new and unique abilities. Overall, if you have strong foundations, you'll have the basics down in a jiffy, but it'll take a long time to fully master a character.
BattleFantasia also features a parry system, similar to Street Fighter 3, Garou and the recent Yatagarasu. At the press of a button you can parry an attack and punish immediately or even get a big combo opening with extra juggle opportunities that are not normally possible, but in this game a mistimed parry has a lot of recovery that can easily be punished so it requires a lot of finesse, practice and timing to use properly.
The game features the basic arcade, survival and practice modes as well as a lengthy story mode for players who like a solid single player experience. And there's also an online mode with the usual ranked and player matches.
If you've already played BattleFantasia previously, here's a small list of changes to expect.
- Improved visual effects. You will notice that textures are sharper, making background details such as the signposts much easier to make out, the background during supers looks a lot better with more depth to it, and KOs now have a fancy shockwave effect that makes them more dramatic.
- Improved online. While it doesn't seem like the new online is better than the average for this type of game, it's still a massive improvement over the original console release.
- The latest balance patch. The game was already pretty well balanced with the vast majority of match-ups coming down to which players is actually better, but this release comes with the infamous Ashley infinite already patched out so now he has to earn his wins just like everyone else.
The game runs silky smooth on my computer at the default settings, which is actually surprising considering how often ports like this one has to be patched to stop crashing and lagging at certain resolutions.
