This is the second game I have ever returned in my entire life for a refund.  I enjoy TellTale Games other works - Tales from the Boarderlands and The Wolf Among Us are some of my favourite works of fiction.  I love the Batman: Arkham series (until Arkham Knight, which is the first game I ever returned for a refund) so you can see where this is going.
I played through the first episode, and it was horrifyingly bad in two completely different ways.  First was the technical faults.  Mouse lag, graphical stuttering, frame tearing the works.   I'll be the first to admit my nVidia 760 isn't the greatest graphics card ever created, but it handles all the other TTG games at max graphics.  Even set to its lowest settings, the lag made QTEs difficult, the mouse lag made aiming sections (and sometimes dialogue selection) nearly impossible, and the jitteriness gave me severe eye strain.
Yes, I did try what was posted in the forums to try and fix it, but no dice.
Secondly, the story is just BAD.  Generally speaking, the first episode of most TTGs is the worst of the series, but without getting into spoilers, the set up for the story is just a mess.  Utterly predictible, occasionally tedious, and disingenuous - it promises to reveal Bruce Wayne's psychological turmoil within by falling back on everything you have seen before.  The only way the story would have provided a new angle on Batman is if you have never ever seen a Batman story before.  There seems to be exactly one reasonably meaningful "choice" in the entire plot.
I could have forgiven the technical issues if the story was grand.  I could have forgiven the story if the game was stunning and innovative.  Having both issues is just crude.

A pleasant little game, if a tad frustrating at times. Albeit, in those moments, it may have been best to set it aside on my part, but I was determined to roll through this in a single sitting (unaware of the achievement, mind). Nevertheless the game utilizes some captivating ideas that other games have arguably used to better effect (environment rotation and gravity manipulation, for example) yet still uses them in clever ways.
The narrative is intentionally ambiguous, without a word uttered, yet there are some fascinating themes told through unusual imagery and events in the game, as well as your (and other characters') actions. It never explicitly comments on these, leaving it up to you to interpret, which may leave you disappointed or frustrated, but it creates a more fascinating tale than it may otherwise have told had it been more direct. That in itself could be a mark against it, however I think it's a mark for it, despite some misgivings with how some of the puzzles pan out (some being a little finicky with physics or timing).
I think it may be best played twice for full effect (given its short length, that's not a major problem), since once you know the puzzles, you might be able to gather more from it upon a second playing. Certainly suggest giving it a try if you haven't, and I'd keep an eye out for Playdead's next games to see what they get up to.

By now,  everyone has had a chance to have a take on Batman.  That Telltale is able to give us a good story is a minor miracle really.  And, despite being familiar with the characters, the story is interesting and moves along well.
I personally don't have a problem with the Telltale version of gameplay.  There may well have been major revisions to the engine and gameplay from past games, but it seems similar to me.  Neither the artstyle, the graphics, or the game mechanics take away from what is an engaging story.
The art definitely is in the Telltale style (cell shaded outlines), but it looks beautiful and the Batman armor looks and moves great.

If you are expecting action gameplay like in Arkham Asylum, or, alternatively, want a completely unique story based on your individual choices, you will be disappointed.  This is a good Batman story that, while influenced by your choices, still stays true to the logic of the plot and characters.
One quick note about Gordan.  Though early in his career (he is a Lt.) he already seems somewhat beat and at the end of his rope.  It is an interesting choice.  Rather than the action Gordon who can ninja fight like the best superhero, this guy is closer to a heart attack over whiskey at a local dive, or over a tv dinner.  I like it, and I hope they develop him more

If you are a fan of shmups, leaderboards, cute graphics, and solid mechanics give this game a whirl!

Let's begin this review with a spoiler.... 'YOUR GOING TO DIE!!!'
Also let me next begin to decalre to all those that have played this game and have an opinion as to it's meaning, you are all WRONG!
Sorry it had to be said, i'm merely trumping the hundreds of opinions circulating around as to the games true meaning with each one of them contradicting the opionions of the one before. So I thought i might as well get in on the act. It's understandable really why there are so many idea's floating around, as the game was purposefully designed to be vague. Other than the word 'Hotel', no other written or spoken word is mentioned in the entire game. The game and it's contributing story is entirely acted out in visuals and it's many, many, many death scenes.
This has even led many gamers to dismiss that there is any hidden meaning at all behind this game and that it is just a game, but for those that have done a bit of research on the matter and watched some interviews, will no doubt soon discover that the Lead Developer behind this game Jensen openly admits that there was a clear indistinct meaning behind all the inspirations discovered in the game and was kind of personally shocked how close the fans had got to that original concept. He has never admitted openly that anyone has it correct and now with all the millions of guess framework layed out, it is very unlikely that he will ever do so, as that is a further added attraction to the game.
So let me personally dispell a few of the erroneous down right wrong idea's floating around and give you some more things to think about. Personally I don't think this information will ruin anything, but rather enhance the beauty of this game for you.
The biggest clue to the game is it's title 'LIMBO'. Limbo is a doctrinal place made up by the Catholic Church. There is no mention of it in the Bible, yet there are many rules about it as set out by the Churches traditional theology. Basically in a nutshell it is a waiting place which some people go to before they are called into Heaven or Hell.
The other things that you need to keep in mind is that there are several different Limbo's. There is the Limbo of the patriarchs (Abraham, Moses etc) and Limbo of Infants. This game's main character is a young un-named boy who for the purpose of this review we will call him 'Mr Bright Eyes' and his sister. There are several other children in this Limbo too. So evidently common sense dictates that we are in the Limbo for infants.
Do all children go to Limbo? No... Only those that are not baptised. Evidently Mr Bright Eyes and his sister, neither of them are baptised. You also have to be dead to enter into Limbo, comatose states do not count as Limbo.
The next big clue about this game is when it was released which was in 2010. For several years just prior to this there was quite a lot of hot debate as to the teaching of this doctrine and the need of some clarification on it. One of the biggest questions raised which caused a great ruckus was if it was possible to be 'tested' while in Limbo?
Eventually after many arguements back and forth it was determined that it was possible to be tested within Limbo and from there your fate could be further decided. Let me give you a hypothetical situation where testing in Limbo might be required....
There is a young boy who for one reason or another gets angry and pushes his sister out of a tree house the fall which basically nearly kills her/ or does in fact kill her. He then feels remorse for what he has done and goes off to find help. On his way he is bitten by a poisonous spider. As the kid continues in his frantic search for help, the poison rushes through his system and kills him before he is able to get any help. In this following hypothetical situation the boy would be tested in Limbo as to his sincerity.
Sounds an awful lot like the game doesn't it...
One more thing you need to keep in mind about Limbo is that two people can have a completely different experience in exactly the same place, at exactly the same time. For instance a Cruel boy in Limbo will not have the same experience as a sweet girl does have in Limbo. The Catholic church has never really defined how this is possible other than stating that there must be some type of 'barriers' in Limbo.
So while Mr Bright Eyes gets to play with saw blades and brain bugs, his sister gets to play with butterflies and all things sweet. Therefore any crashing at the end of the game could be attributed to breaking through that barrier which seperates a good kid from a bad kid. Since both brother and sister are in Limbo they are both dead, but which one died first? It seems little sis did. He is aware of her and where she is and is looking for her evidently he already knows she is dead, while on the contrary little sis has no idea that her brother is in limbo too and is startled when she eventually finds this out.
It is a bittersweet game from start to finish and though it only takes 55 minutes in a perfect run or thereabouts, with the constant deaths and respawn system you will be at it for days. As you journey through it, concentrated on the backgrounds and the places that you are and think about the hidden meaning. It is quite fun to do so. Did Mr Bright Eyes get out of limbo and enter heaven. Well it all depends on how much money his parents gave to the church though. Maybe we will find out in Limbo 2...

One of my favorite under the radar surprises in a while, this horizontally scrolling shooter takes inspiration from the classic Defender and its left/right mechanic, and adds a very compelling weapon system where you have one basic weapon and three specials, and the only way to use the specials is by killing enemies and collecting their energy. It's very well balanced -- all four weapons are needed and useful against specific enemies, yet you can't rely on one over the others. The basic gun isn't strong enough to kill some of the nastier bad guys, but you can't just spam special weapons, you'll run out of energy. It's a constant back and forth, split second decision making in the middle of a fire fight.
The game starts out easy but the difficulty ramps up nicely by the second planet. Online leaderboards, achievements, trading cards, cloud saves -- this is a high quality title, well worth the price if you like shooters.

Wow! This is an incredibly tight shooter that is a bit of Defender in a modern style. It’s definitely channeling the spirit of a young Eugene Jarvis. I have nit-picks, but I don’t think they’re worth mentioning because the more I play the more I find that each tiny flaw feels deliberately designed to make the game more fun.
I played with keyboard, which feels pretty natural, but I’m sure it would be at home on a game pad. Basically arrows move, space flips you from left to right, shift dashes, and WASD is 4 different weapons. There’s a main weapon that overheats and the other 3 come from a pool of ammo refilled by dead enemy pellets. Really simple and definitely gets you into a state of flow.
The audio and art are just ok, but unique and easy to understand. Sometimes it gets a bit cluttered, but again this feels like an intentional choice, especially given the title of the game. If you like frantic shooters give this a try.
UPDATE: I've finished the game now and have a few additional thoughs.
The introduction of new enemy types throughout the game really keeps things fresh! None are particularly difficult on their own, but each has a unique pattern that combines within the swarm to create a huge variety emergent situations.
It also took me a while to pay attention to the combo system. It's very simple, but really adds an extra layer of challenge if you're trying to keep the combo going.

I can see this being viable as a multiplayer game; but if you are looking for a solo experience then I found this game woefully lacking for one reason only, the AI is absolutely awful.
The main criticism is that it has absolutely no concept of urgency at all.  It's only tactic is to form a cage and then run the ball in.  If it is turn 8, and the Elves have the ball (in a cage of course) in their half and they have catchers with the potential to score a TD, they would sooner reinforce the cage than make any attempt to pass the ball down field.
It is so intent on making a cage, that if the ball were in a square next to both a Thrower with Sure Hands and a Lineman, it will pick the ball up with the Lineman and use the Thrower in the cage.
The only fun to be had is by having a bashy team and by beating the cr*p out of everything you face.
Aside from that, the visuals are nice, the commentary is good, the game has depth in the form of its league.  It's just the bad AI that spoils it.

Nice little shoot em up game, first played it on the Nintendo Switch, then I heard its coming to Steam and the PS4 so I bought it again.
It's a game about controlling your little "ship" and shoot up a variety of enemies in a restricted space, there are a few different weapons/moves you could use and they work really well so you wouldn't be smashing the main cannon all the time. Actually you can't smash it all the time because weapons cost energy and you need to balance the energy of your ship by collecting the crystals dropped by the enemies. There are 4 planets with about 10 levels each, seems a little short for a $13 game but the difficulty rise up quickly and chance is you wouldn't beat them on a single run. Overall this isn't classical shooter like Striker 1945 or Dodonpachi, it's more like a top-down beat em up game trapped in a alternative view angle, or Resogun in a panic room.
I really like the game, so despite the following flaws I still give it a thumb up, I hope the developers could address them in future updates.
So about the a few flaws I had with the Steam version of the game:
1. The default control scheme for keyboard sucks. You got arrows keys for movement and A/S/D/LShift/Space for weapons/dash. It needs to be made configurable ASAP, maybe change the default scheme to be WSAD movement based.
2. (update) This might not be the developer's fault, but the game has vsync problem with my laptop. According to the developer the game always run with vsync on, yet the frame rate caps at 120 instead of 60 on my 60hz laptop, and occasionally the graphics tears up a little while the game loses the ability to recognize my control for like half a second. Forcing vsync ON with the nvidia control panel didn't solve the problem. Capping frame rate at 60 with RivaTuner Statistics Server makes the game skipping a lot of frames like running at 30fps (but displayed as 60fps). I've yet to find a working solution to this particular problem.
3. (fixed in the 1.1.2 update) Support for Nvidia Optimus needs to improve a bit. The game defaults to integrated graphics which made my laptop 10C hotter than it should be, forcing discrete graphics with nvidia control panel solves the problem, but I think the problem deserves to be mentioned and should be avoided by the developers in the first place.

Sunless Sea is a mixture of a book and a game. It is deeply flawed as either of these but at the same time there is something about it that makes me sink lots of hours into it.
Book part plays when you are in a port. There you’ll find stories that are available depending on your skills, items and whole lot of behind the scenes stuff. The stories are well written and the world of Sunless Sea is truly a strange place. These stories have a lot of text to read with some options to change the course but it’s basically like clicking “next page” until you get to the ending. While the writing is praise-worthy, it’s really hard to read a book that is scattered around a game world that takes hours to see. The rewards from these range from gaining supplies to losing crewmembers and it’s often nearly impossible to predict what happens.
Everything in this game is an item that can be used. You have your fuel, supplies and such, but also items like “Latest news”, “Memory of a distant shore”, “Zee story”, “Tale of terror” and so on. These are rewarded from quests and can be used to buy stuff or open new quests. It’s an interesting system but not flawless: Some ports only use one of these as a currency and without a guide it’s a monumental task to remember which uses which. Giving up is really close when you finally have five “tales” you need to buy something and make a long and expensive trip to somewhere, only to find out that they only accept “stories”. It doesn’t help that sometimes the journal doesn’t record any of the vital info and sometimes it does.
Outside of the safety of harbour is a vast zee that you travel with a miniscule steamboat. It is rough out there with gradually diminishing supplies. Then there is terror, which builds up constantly and can lead to the crew losing their minds. Monsters lurk in the darkness but avoiding them is really easy. I’m sure you can finish Sunless Sea without firing a shot. This is a good thing since combat is definitely the weakest part of the experience. You can buy a better ship and the costs are astronomical, but it’s actually not necessary. The ship you start with can easily sail to the other side of the Underzee and back. Traveling takes a lot of time with very little happening. Talking to crew members and such always pauses the game so be prepared to just stare at the screen for a long time with nothing to do.
If (and most likely when) you die, you’ll lose your progress. Some of the items you gathered are given to your next captain but you’ll have to start again. Islands in the game switch places so you really have to do everything again. Stories stay the same so a lot of the beginning is just mindless clicking around. With that said, my first captain survived 4 hours of real world time so this doesn’t happen very often.
The UI could use some work. I’m on ultrabook with 13” screen and 1080p native resolution. On this screen the text is really small and hard to read. Windows screen scaling options do affect the ingame assets but it’s less than ideal to do this every time you boot the game. On a bigger screen or one with smaller native resolution this would not be an issue, but it’s worth mentioning since modern ultrabooks go way higher than 1080p. Downloading more stories in the main menu leads almost always to crashing and it’s a matter of luck to get them. This doesn’t lead to loss of gameplay progress and the game boots quite fast but is annoying anyway.
I’m sure I’ll never finish this game nor will I ever understand all of its secrets. For once in my gaming life I’m happy for that. Not knowing in itself is rewarding. Sailing in Sunless Sea is slow and what I’d normally call boring and tedious but it somehow manages to make nothingness into something special in a way that is at the same time calming and scaring. Atleast for the first few hours. I’ll recommend Sunless Sea as unique and interesting but flawed and glacially paced experience.

is basically a reflex game where each level is a massive boss fight. There are 7 bosses with different stage events that require a unique strategy. For combat, you only have a dash, rifle attack, and a super attack. Controls are simple but they require hitting a timing window to deal any damage. If you have competent reflexes it should take about 5 hours on the lowest difficulty. My death count ranged from 3 to 48 deaths per boss. Some of them are more fair than other but overall it takes a lot of skill. It is easy to dislike CrownFall do to unrefined feel but I enjoyed the challenge once I understood how to fight.
Controls are a little weird and you can't change them. Game settings only have volume bars. Gamepad works but I find it extremely hard to use just because the game does not give you much time to aim with analog. You are welcome to try but I am using the mouse for this one. Also if you have gamepad in a port it will probably hide the mouse cursor.
Combat is not complex but the game focuses on reflexes so much that it becomes ridiculously hard. When using the rifle you have to hit a timing window that deals more damage and generates power for a super attack. Aiming locks you in place which puts you into a danger territory entire fight. Even though you only have 3 moves the bosses are so different that it does not feel repetitive. However, there are no RPG elements or any sort of power progression. It is pretty self-explanatory but figuring out the timing is where the skill comes in.
It is not a terrible looking game for $3. Quality tends to go up and down depending on which boss you fighting. I got to say that Lava Shark boss might take the cake for my favorite boss in any video game ever (**** hilarious, one of those things you should see before you die). There are a decent amount of unique animations on bosses like the Golem who keeps losing his limbs and changes how he attacks. Overall not too bad, I expected less, to be honest.
The music was great though. If it was made specifically for the game props to the composer.
It is not a great game but the price of $3 is very fair for the experience. This is actually the first time I ever played a Boss focused game which is a fresh concept (from what I hear Fury is a much better example of that) All of the fights feel different and I think it is the best part of the game. Skill requirement is very high so some might enjoy the challenge.If you looking for a polished game with a good difficulty progression you should skip this one. But that LavaShark boss, you do not know what you missing.

I don't usually write reviews, but after completeing this game I felt compelled to do so. I grew up on Nintendo games, specifically the gamecube and wii eras. As a kid I was never really into shooters or racing games or sports games or whatever, but platformers were always a good time. Its been a while since I sad down and played a 3-D platformer, but when I saw A Hat in Time and read some of the positive reviews, I didn't hesitate to buy and launch it up.
Within 5 minutes of launching the game the plot had been established and I was jumping around in Mafia Town. I won't go into details for the sake of spoilers, but the plot is very simple, yet compelling enough to motivate the player to complete the game. In terms of atmosphere, this game hit the nail on the head. The art direction is fantastic and apealing without being too demanding. Each of the game's four main levels (or chapters, as the game appropriately calls them) are brilliantly eye catching and unique, and really encourage exploration with little to no use of invisible barriers. Each chapter is split into several acts, similar to Mario Sunshine. Despite the recurring scenery, each act brings something new to the table and I never got tired of any of the chapters. The NPCs are filled with cheesy humor and memorable character design. The fact that 99% of the dialogue in this game is voice acted just adds to the charm.
In terms of mechanics, this games plays very smoothly. Hat Kid's moveset is simplistic yet varied enought to allow for plenty of unique gameplay. What sets this game apart from other platformers are the inclusion of Hat abilities. There are a total of 6 hats in this game, each allowing for slightly different gameplay mechanics. You can swap between each hat quickly and seamlessly, which really adds to the immersion in the game. I never felt like Hat Kids moveset was limiting, and really enjoyed how quickly you could move through the non-linear stages with optimized movement. While there were a few instances where wall jumps would be a bit wonky or where the camera wouldn't exactly do what I wanted, these were essentially non-issues and didn't take away from my enjoyment of the game at all.
The fact that this game was developed by such a small staff (albeit a long development period) is incredible; the polish of this game is akin to lots of AAA titles. The main story took me around 10 hours to complete at a leisurely pace (I took time to explore every nook and cranny of every level), but I will certainly be dumping more time into this game to 100% it.
Overall, I would say this game is a fantastic revival title for a long forgotten genre, and would highly recommend it to anyone, whether they grew up on platformers or if they are newcomers to the genre.

So I received a bit of flak for my original review and to be fair I probably hadn't played enough of the game so I thought I'd play it a bit more and watch some videos online. Here is my "revised" review. I've left my original review below.
++Pros++
+Story mode
The scenarios are fun to play through and characters are likeable and have strong personallities. I really like how the characters interacted with each other in combat and also in the story mode
+Combat
After actually trying everyone out, watching some videos and playing through some more of the game modes I have to say the gameplay really grew on me. It's easy to pick up and each character is actually very different. Some are more fun to play then others and you can do some interesting things when you really know how to play the game, my original comment that the gameplay was boring was unwarranted.
+See my original points below
--Cons--
-Dodgy Port
The game still runs smoothly on my system, but I've had some weird issues with the sound looping and one or two random crashes. It could be my computer but I've not had this happen on any other game I've played so far.
-Online
I couldn't find anyone playing this game online so I dragged a friend to play a bit. However I still encountered the same issues with dodgy connections and underwater gameplay. Considering I can play other fighting games without the issues I had in BF I still believe the netcode is trash. Without playing other people I can't say this would happen all the time.
-Lack of game modes
The game has a pretty good story mode, but other then that there is only Survival, Arcade Mode and Time Attack. It would have been nice to have a challenge mode or some other unique game mode such as Abyss mode in Blazblue or something like the towers mode in MK. Maybe thats asking too much but I still feel the game is lacking in game modes.
If there was a "maybe" button for recommending this game I would probably choose that. The gameplay is quite fun and I really enjoyed the different scenarios. However I want to play fighting games against other people at the end of the day. The online felt sluggish and choppy, and thats when it wouldn't just disconnect in the middle of a match or desync. Even if it was working better the online still lacks a lobby feature which makes it hard to get a group to play together.
Buy this game if you don't really care about fighting other people online.

Alright, let's establish what Banished is NOT.
It's not a city builder like Sim City, it's not a life sim like Sims, it's not a survival/crafting game like Don't starve and it's not an econ sim like Industry Giant. It's a little bit of everything, but Anno on a micro scale might be a pretty fitting description.
You basically start the game with a few settlers and various resources/buildings established. You do not have ANY goals, your only goal is to survive and thrive. To do that you're going to build houses, establish an economy and "produce" new settlers.
That means cutting wood, gathering/hunting/harvesting food, so your citizens won't starve to death, creating building materials, chopping firewood, so your citizens won't freeze to death during winter, and carefully establishing houses and increasing your population, so your city won't simply die out. Blacksmiths create tools for your citizens to work with, trade posts let you trade materials, etc.
All in all there is a lot to do. You need to balance your need for expansion with a sustainable economy. If you have too many citizens and not enough of them producing food, then your city will simply starve, which will usually lead to a chain reaction of you losing the game, since dying citizens can't produce more food, but if you take too many citizens away from other production like fire wood, hunting, tailoring or anything concerned with blacksmithing, you will have other issues to contend with. The game can spiral out of control quickly, which is what makes it appealing, I guess. The larger your city grows, the more sprawling your infrastructure becomes, the more challenging the game gets.
I would also definitely recommend the Colonial mod, which opens up the game immensely with new buildings.
Not so great stuff: The UI could need improvements, several buildings share "jobs", so it's a bit finnicky to assign citizens to a specific building. It's also very hard to see dependencies of buildings. You want to build X, but you don't realize that you need to produce Y first...only having icons is not so great. Apart from that I don't have many complaints.
Now the obligatory game report:
Started my city, everything went pretty well, produced food en masse, unfortunately did not realize that my citizens were getting too old, so my 40 peeps city went down to below 30 pretty quickly. Thankfully my Banished were still in a happy mood and procreated happily. Still that took over 10 years or so, then my food supplies started dwindling, all the while my old guys kept dying, and I still could not make all my children work...damn it. Vicious cycle. After having burnt through about 6,000 units of food (a lot) I almost got back on track, but then my city was ravaged by a disease. I was able to erect a hospital in time and got that under control as well. After that things started to go smoothly again. I played for about 31 years, then I got "bored".
Banished is a great game, but lacks longevity, unless you are content to just simply sand box your way for hours upon hours. Still, I liked it and getting 5 hours out of it for a product on sale makes it worth it to me :D

Gameplay Review:
this comes from a CoH1 expert i am playing COH since 2006 and i took part in 4 tournaments so this is my opinion about this mod:
it is a lot better than COH2 ( i do not even count COH2 as a competitive game because it is typical pay to win and it is only based on spam not skill or flanking) this game is mix of CoH1 and CoH2, suppose in CoH1 mechanics you have the entire CoH2 features. The tank damages are so crazy that you nearly can one shot kill a panther if you hit it in rear armor and same about panther vs sherman it can also one shot kill a sherman even in front armor. tanks cost less, unlike coh2 where tanks are so pricey but they are totally useless (unless we are talking about ISU 152) so it is not a big deal for me to lose a tank like that because the cost is not that much. you have to play a bit different in EAW because it is not exactly like CoH1 (sadly) unfortunately it is a little bit designed for comp stomping, units come in super large numbers (9 men riflemen squad and 9 men volks squad and 6 men fallschrimjaegers etc) and almost every commander has off map reinforcement which sends at least 3-4 really good tanks to the field for just manpower and nothing else and it basically always leaves a chance for comeback.
Balance review:
I think the weakest factions in this game are panzer elite and british forces because every other army has increased squad size but PE and Brits are same as before, i would say wehrmacht is strongest at the moment because you just build one grenadier squad in T2 they can be upgraded to MP44 + LMG 34 + Panzershreck at same time. so one 9 men squad has access to everything and it is anti everything.
defensive doctrine is extremely over powered because not only you gain defensive advantage but you also get super offensive advantage too because it has access to super large number of off map reinforcement (3-4 panzer IVs for 1400 manpower and 800 manpower for flak anti infantry tank + panzer IV + howitzer supported with 4 fallshrimjaeger squads and two halftrucks).
sadly gameplay is so much based on spamming because no one bothers to make tanks in base it is better to call in reinforcement for just manpower and save fuel for something else.
Sniper is totally useless in this mod becuase not a single smart person spends 360man power for ONE sniper against 270manpower 9men squad they have enough time to get close and kill him, and that 270manpower 9 men squad can be upgraded to become anti everything but that poor sniper for 360mp is only anti infantry (not even anti-inf).
Gamebreaking issues:
too many options for building and almost you have 2-3 type of same featured buildings just with different names (medics+ammo points) and there is just too many second abilities just like in CoH2 for units which is wrong in my opinion.
M26 pershing has been removed from the game and it is replaced with some sort of off map armored reinforcement which sends 4 super anti tank shermans and 2 halftrucks which increase their range, so just call this group for 1200 man power and ♥♥♥♥ a tiger in less than 1 second. each of these shermans should shoot it once and it is down, in original coh1 you need to micro your heavy tank to be able to survive and win the battle but here since you have too many tanks just rush in front of the tiger and u shoot it down in no time. sadly just like coh2 it is spam encouraging instead micro and skill encouraging.
If you need visual proof of how this mod is broken in terms of balance have a look at this yourself:
it is the replay of 1v1 between me and a friend, and enjoy the power of "off map reinforcement at the ending"
the most bad feature of the game is the unit marker is removed, you never know what squad you have chosen because they dont get highlighted by those blue circles, this really annoyed me in game because i had no idea which one of my fallschrimjaeger squads are moving forward since they just come in large numbers i was confused as hell.
overall it is good mod (at least it is free and not pay to win like coh2) and for a change it is not bad but for competitive play it suffers a lot, new maps are fun to play and there is too much to do here but only if you seek comp stomp orwhere not much skill is required. it is sadly spam encouraging like CoH2 and i hope developers reconsider this idea of sending too much off map reinforcements.

Let's begin this review with a spoiler.... 'YOUR GOING TO DIE!!!'
Also let me next begin to decalre to all those that have played this game and have an opinion as to it's meaning, you are all WRONG!
Sorry it had to be said, i'm merely trumping the hundreds of opinions circulating around as to the games true meaning with each one of them contradicting the opionions of the one before. So I thought i might as well get in on the act. It's understandable really why there are so many idea's floating around, as the game was purposefully designed to be vague. Other than the word 'Hotel', no other written or spoken word is mentioned in the entire game. The game and it's contributing story is entirely acted out in visuals and it's many, many, many death scenes.
This has even led many gamers to dismiss that there is any hidden meaning at all behind this game and that it is just a game, but for those that have done a bit of research on the matter and watched some interviews, will no doubt soon discover that the Lead Developer behind this game Jensen openly admits that there was a clear indistinct meaning behind all the inspirations discovered in the game and was kind of personally shocked how close the fans had got to that original concept. He has never admitted openly that anyone has it correct and now with all the millions of guess framework layed out, it is very unlikely that he will ever do so, as that is a further added attraction to the game.
So let me personally dispell a few of the erroneous down right wrong idea's floating around and give you some more things to think about. Personally I don't think this information will ruin anything, but rather enhance the beauty of this game for you.
The biggest clue to the game is it's title 'LIMBO'. Limbo is a doctrinal place made up by the Catholic Church. There is no mention of it in the Bible, yet there are many rules about it as set out by the Churches traditional theology. Basically in a nutshell it is a waiting place which some people go to before they are called into Heaven or Hell.
The other things that you need to keep in mind is that there are several different Limbo's. There is the Limbo of the patriarchs (Abraham, Moses etc) and Limbo of Infants. This game's main character is a young un-named boy who for the purpose of this review we will call him 'Mr Bright Eyes' and his sister. There are several other children in this Limbo too. So evidently common sense dictates that we are in the Limbo for infants.
Do all children go to Limbo? No... Only those that are not baptised. Evidently Mr Bright Eyes and his sister, neither of them are baptised. You also have to be dead to enter into Limbo, comatose states do not count as Limbo.
The next big clue about this game is when it was released which was in 2010. For several years just prior to this there was quite a lot of hot debate as to the teaching of this doctrine and the need of some clarification on it. One of the biggest questions raised which caused a great ruckus was if it was possible to be 'tested' while in Limbo?
Eventually after many arguements back and forth it was determined that it was possible to be tested within Limbo and from there your fate could be further decided. Let me give you a hypothetical situation where testing in Limbo might be required....
There is a young boy who for one reason or another gets angry and pushes his sister out of a tree house the fall which basically nearly kills her/ or does in fact kill her. He then feels remorse for what he has done and goes off to find help. On his way he is bitten by a poisonous spider. As the kid continues in his frantic search for help, the poison rushes through his system and kills him before he is able to get any help. In this following hypothetical situation the boy would be tested in Limbo as to his sincerity.
Sounds an awful lot like the game doesn't it...
One more thing you need to keep in mind about Limbo is that two people can have a completely different experience in exactly the same place, at exactly the same time. For instance a Cruel boy in Limbo will not have the same experience as a sweet girl does have in Limbo. The Catholic church has never really defined how this is possible other than stating that there must be some type of 'barriers' in Limbo.
So while Mr Bright Eyes gets to play with saw blades and brain bugs, his sister gets to play with butterflies and all things sweet. Therefore any crashing at the end of the game could be attributed to breaking through that barrier which seperates a good kid from a bad kid. Since both brother and sister are in Limbo they are both dead, but which one died first? It seems little sis did. He is aware of her and where she is and is looking for her evidently he already knows she is dead, while on the contrary little sis has no idea that her brother is in limbo too and is startled when she eventually finds this out.
It is a bittersweet game from start to finish and though it only takes 55 minutes in a perfect run or thereabouts, with the constant deaths and respawn system you will be at it for days. As you journey through it, concentrated on the backgrounds and the places that you are and think about the hidden meaning. It is quite fun to do so. Did Mr Bright Eyes get out of limbo and enter heaven. Well it all depends on how much money his parents gave to the church though. Maybe we will find out in Limbo 2...

Anybody who has ever passionately tried to create something owes it to themselves to play this game. Whether it be game design or any other artistic venture, if you are a creator at heart and have acted on it, the story will reach you. It's perhaps more accurately described as an experience than a game. It took me about 84 minutes to complete being particularly thorough in what little exploration there was. The gameplay consists mostly of walking around and listening to a disembodied voice (oddly familiar...) The stages consist of unreleased experimental games that the narrator gives his thoughts on as you progress through them.
The Beginner's Guide relies on reaching the player's thoughts and emotions. It's rare for something to reach me in that way on the same level that this did. If you end up not really feeling anything, you'll probably figure it was a waste of time. That's why I recommend this game only to people who have tried to create. It's not an experience that tries to cater to everybody, it's for more specific types of people. That's what makes it effective. Many things try to appeal to a large spectrum and end up not deeply speaking to anybody in particularly. When it's more focused, the people the messages do reach really hear it.
If somebody puts their soul into their work and doesn't feel validated by other people's opinions, they can spiral. Is that wrong? Overdramatic? Vain? Whatever it is, it's human and it happens. Deep down, most people crave recognition for what they really care about doing. At the same time, people can be reluctant to share their work with others, even after all the time and effort they've put in. When they're sharing something they put their soul into creating, then it is like sharing a part of their soul. A lot of people are desperate to see more creative work they can identify with. Something they can see themselves in, feel something from.
Immediately after playing this, for the first time in over a month, I actually went to work on my story... then after only 190 words I stopped. My creative energy is still held down. I still feel I don't have anyone recognising my work. At the same time, I'm afraid to show my work to too many people. However, even a brief time of having the creative energy return in some force is so rare these days and so precious. The game made me feel less lonely in what I was experiencing. I could see so many things I could really identify with. The simple thing of seeing something I'm experiencing reflected in someone else's creative work is reassuring. Knowing that on some level, I'm not entirely alone. Doing this so masterfully in such a short space of time is really impressive. Usually I criticise any storytelling medium that is not at least several hours in length due to not having enough time to develop character and emotion, yet this game did it better than most, in a length shorter than most modern movies.
The game explores both creative fronts beautifully. The need, yet lack of energy, to create. The oftentimes needy desire to see a creative work that can be identified with, that a person can feel a real connection with. As a person familiar with both things, it's fortunate for me that the game addresses both as well as it does.

Blood Bowl 2 by Cyanide Games is a wonderfully faithful adaptation of one of my all time favourite tabletop games by miniatures game company Games Workshop. The world of Blood Bowl is a zany parody of the classic Warhammer Fantasy universe, in a reality where a god of chaos named Nuffle (a reference to the NFL) prefers to be worshipped by the playing of the ultimate game of Fantasy Football, Bloodbowl.
The Blood Bowl sport is similar to football with a few key differences. The first major difference is ordinary games of American Football don't feature elven, orcish or undead players on the pitch. The second, more important, difference is that Blood Bowl doesn't have any rules forbidding the killing of players on the enemy team (A reality that set in for me rather harshly when three of my poor goblin players had to have their corpses dragged off the pitch in a single game).
The objective is, of course, to carry the football across the field to the opposing team's end zone. The game plays as a turn bases strategy game, where players take turns controlling their entire team. In a standard match, you have two minutes to move all of the players on your team, unless your turn is interrupted by a turnover, which is an event that interrupts your turn to pass it over to the enemy team should one of your players fail an action. Every action that a player takes short of moving short distances carries some sort of risk, and this is where the game gets very unpredictable and wacky. Every player action results in the rolling of dice, either six sided or special "block" dice. The more skilled the player, the better their odds of rolling the required number (a less skilled player will need a 6 to succeed while a more skilled player will need a 5 or a 6). If a player makes a block action against an enemy player (think of it like tackling another player), they will need to roll the special block dice, which have symbols on them that mean various things to the game rather than numbers (knock a player down, get knocked down yourself, dodge, both-down and push). The stronger the player, the more dice they will get to roll, choosing the best result. Coaches are allowed to spend gold, the currency they use to manage their teams outside of games, to purchase dice rerolls should they fail an action critical to the game, such as fumbling the football just outside the end zone,  or failing to tackle an opponent blocking your ball-carrier.
Coaches will spend the better part of a Blood Bowl game rolling dice, and every coach is going to watch their beautifully laid out strategies fall apart because of bad luck. You will watch your dice roll badly, spend a precious reroll and cry salty tears and you roll the same result again, while your opponent giggles at your misfortune. This part of the game is a lot of fun for more tabletop oriented players, as the unpredictability can force coaches to adapt their strategies, and allows for a level of excitement that games without chance just don't offer for me. However, competitive minded gamers more used to a video-game environment might find this part of the game frustrating, as inevitable bad luck ruins the game for players who play to win.
My advice to anyone who buys this game: Don't play to win. Try to win for certain-do your very best. But by all means, no matter how prepared you think you are, never go into a game expecting victory, as even the best player and lose a match to sheer bad luck. Instead, try to have fun with the zany, unpredictable nature of the Blood Bowl universe.

It's finally out and it was worth the wait! Cuphead is a challenging 2D platformer with a lovely 1930's cartoon art style. The majority of the game is fighting bosses; there are a couple of platforming stages but they aren't necessary to finish the game. Most of the difficulty lies in learning the different attacks each boss uses. Some bosses take just 10 minutes to learn while others could take an hour or two- one of the later bosses took me a couple days to beat. The game can be very frustrating at times, but the satisfaction when you finally overcome the challenge is huge.
The only issues that stick out in my mind:
-The default controls suck. You'll need to change them.
-A couple of bosses have RNG that can make them much harder. You can still adapt to this though.
-There's a couple of bugs, but nothing game-breaking.
-Spoiler regarding one of the bosses:
Everything else about the game is fantastic. If you like games that are hard, if you think this game looks interesting, I highly recommend you check it out. It's a little bit short, but it's well worth the $20 for how much fun it is.

I've played the game for a couple of days now and I love it. It's easy to figure out and understand once you get the hang of it. I enjoy the micromanagement involved, and it isn't too overwhelming and nit-picky to the point where you're micromanging every tiny thing, while retaining control over business hours and employee pay. I like the amount of detail that has already gone into the game, such as the stock rooms, the necessity of restrooms, and staff-only parking/loading zones.
As of Alpha Update 0.2.0.3, I am a bit confused about how the tier system works and I do find the demand/supply menu difficult to figure out. I may figure it out with a bit more playtime.
I would love to see seasons and weather implemented into the game, which would affect sales and scheduling. Higher traffic during the holiday season would be amazing, and possibly something resembling the American Black Friday shopping (although not quite as crazy). I'd also like to see a difference between weekdays and weekends, which could also play into the sales. A rainy Saturday might not generate as much traffic as a sunny Sunday, for instance.
It would also be fun to be able to have special sales on items to hopefully increase traffic for a certain day. Something like having a sale on, say, appliances, and then stores could plan accordingly.
I'd like to set the prices of movie tickets as well-- having a cheaper price point for a matinee versus a night showing.
Also, while the sales graphs and sorting employees by starting time are helpful, I find myself writing down which cashiers are coming in and leaving at which times for my large grocery store, which has 10 registers and will need more soon. I would like an option where I can click on a specific store and see everyone who is coming in and leaving and at what time. This will also be useful when/if the developers are able to implement staff breaks. It would be nice to be able to send employees home early or call employees in to work if the business needs call for it. Some nights I'll have too many people working and other nights I'll have too few. And my poor employees work 7 days a week... they could use a day off!

I have been following this game for a couple of years after inadvertently discovering it on
. Being farily young and with an all-too-apparent shortage of money, I couldn't back a game that advertised itself as a collect-a-thon akin the famed Banjoo-Kazooie (of which I was born too late to play legally). I found myself coming back to it time and time again to look at the various builds of the game. I saw footage of Hat Kid swimming, being able to go into the giant geyser in the middle of Mafia Town. I saw artwork for an older Hat Kid, with a mechanic of traveling back and forth through time. It had true sandbox environments.
All of those mechanics are removed. You cannot swim, you cannot experiment, you cannot push the boundaries of the game in any sort of way possible—which is extremely disappointing. The levels are like those of Mario 64, where you select the Time Piece you're looking for, and the one "Free Roam" level is quite restrictive contrary to what its name implies.  Comparing the enironment to actual sandbox areas in the recent Odyssey makes them feel hollow and underdeveloped.
The game is fantastic if you disregard the last 2 paragraphs. I found very few flaws in my entire playthrough of the game, and there are plans to add more content through strech goals on Kickstarter. As it is right now, however, I don't recommend the game at its $30 price tag for the amount of content that it has. I would suggest that you wait until it's on sale for at least a third off, as I feel like that is a good price for what you recieve.
I will update this review in the future when/if need be.

A very fun zombie sandbox survival game that pits you agianst hords of zombies while you try to survive for as long as possible. There is no hope. There is no cure. This is how you die. It reintroduces ideas of zombie games such as farming and healing your own wounds, but it brings to the table new ones such as if you get bit, to prevent from getting infected you can cut off the limb thats bitten before the infection takes you over. They are also working on npc survivors that you can befriend and use to help defend your base. By the way you can build your own base. That's right, but good luck finding the fire axe to chop down trees to get wood, the nails, and a hammer to put it all together. Yes there are some glitchs, but compared to what they were years ago when I first started playing it, they went a long way from where they started. They are also planning to add muiltiplayer so when that comes out, that's when the game will get really good. Some gamers might not like it because they're times where its enraging to find an area without zombies to make a safe spot, but if you start playing enough, you'll come to understand that where ever you start, thats what you are going to get, unless you kill most of the zombies in an area you want to make your base. They orginally had a story mode where you took care of your injured wife, but it isn't in there anymore and it's what the title screen is based off of. Lastly the one thing I learned from this game is that GUNS ARE A BAD IDEA, not only are they loud, this was proven on mythbusters, but the time it takes to aim, shoot and reload, is enough time for them to over run you and kill you. So yeah, to the people who think the shotgun or the chainsaw is the best weapon againse a zombie you are dead wrong... Well... undead wrong I should say...

Project Zomboid is a game I have seen evolve over time. In its current state it is a brilliant game, though it will improve more in the future. PZ is unlike any other zombie survival I have ever played. The goal is to survive as long as you can. When playing the standard free mode you must create a character to your liking. After this, you will be dropped into a random house with randomly generated supplies. From there you must go house to house breaking and entering to find more supplies. As you collect supplies you must also watch out for status conditions. Your character might be feeling hungry, thirsty, sick, tired, etc.  The game has skills which level up as you play such as combat with blunt or sharp weapons, or even cooking and construction The two current maps are decently massive and I haven’t completely explored either of them yet. I highly recommend this game if zombie survival is your style. I believe multiplayer will be coming in the future so prepare to play this game with your friends.

First off, I love The Beginners Guide but I also think that it won't exactly be much of what anyone would expect. This game is one of those games that might be controversial to actually call a game. There isn't much interactivity in it and what little there is seems to just be there to complete mundane tasks and not really anything else. The game's story seems to be fairly bare and often confusing.
I realize it now sounds like I'm hating this game which is why I started the review by saying that I do indeed love it.
Most of the game is simply a narrative guiding you through a story but the gameplay in question comes from the mystery the game provides in it's story, the clues you piece together  and exploring the environments while listening to the narrator.
The game doesn't really lack anything as much as it just chooses not to provide certain elements and while that might sound pretentious it's the lack of these elements that makes the narrative work in the story the game tries to tell.
It's hard to say much else without spoiling it a final thing I could mention is that unlike The Stanley Parable (the developers previous game) this game doesn't seem to have any replay value. Once you have completed the game it's over and it might be a bit short when factoring in the price for some people.

The bleak, lonely atmosphere made the game more depressing to play than dying repeatedly already is and didn't do anything to draw me into the game. The puzzles are creative, but can be overly frustrating at times with the timing requirements. The game is also rather short, which was a relief for me (I try to finish all my games at least once even if I don't particularly enjoy them) but would be a negative for someone who paid full price for this game and was expecting more.
Overall, this game is great from a technical and creative standpoint but completely failed on the fun and enjoyment aspects for me. Given the game's age and short length, if you do fall in the group of people who might enjoy it, wait for it on sale.

Pros:
-Compelling story
-Some cool levels
-Very relatable themes and message
-Intersting concepts
-Well narrated
-Good comentary on life, people relationships, and game design
-Something that has never been tried befroe
Cons:
-Very short (Took me 90 minutes)
-No replayability
-Extremely linear
-No difficulty, No death, no puzzle solving (except one really obvious one)
-Player choices are rare and have literally no effect on the story or anything
-Kept freezing when loading voice over lines
-Levels are short and mostly filled with empty content
-Game self referencing is heavy handed (narrator tells you how to feel about what you are seeing)
-Hard to suspend disbelief that a real person made these games, they feel extremely manufactured.
-Repetetive and becomes shallow at times.
-No Achievements or Easter Eggs (That I found, other than the 3 dots)
-Nothing interesting to see in the levels except what you are supposed to for the main story (wandering off the path yeilds nothing of interest)
-$10 (This is the big one, If this game were $5 I would give it a positive review, but it is too little for the price)

Pretty good little puzzle game. The general gyst of gameplay is you push balls of snow around in order to build a required number of snowmen per level. Similar to an Increpare game, you're given a rewind button that lets you quickly backtrack on mistakes and focus on the puzzle without distractions. Although there's only a couple core mechanics, the developer did a good job of exploring their possiblity space and presenting the more elegant findings.
Controls are just simple enough and serviceable but I wish it had been more refined. Too often I found myself grabbing onto bushes when I meant to turn a corner, for example. Not a big issue, but with such a small amount of mechanics in play you would expect it to be more refined.
The whole game, post-campaign content included, will amount to roughly maximum of 6 hours of play, so it's a rather pricey game for its content. At full price it's a bit of a tough sell, but discounted I think it's a great experience that puzzle game lovers will get a good kick out of.

*'Save As' button. Saving it and typing in a name takes too long when all I want to do is save over that file.

*The Research seems too easy to get, even with the amount hours it takes. Maybe you have to complete a challenge...for example, you have to have a store sell a certain about of a item before you can unlock something else.

This is a difficult game to recommend to just anyone, and there are a few things you should consider before you drop $20 on this beautifully animated and composed platformer.
First thing to mention is it is rediculously hard. A player of average skill will struggle with the first few stages of this game, and if you don't handle repetitive deaths well and starting from the beggining each time, then you will want to reconsider buying this. If you are below average at games, or just platformers in general, you'll for sure want to look elsewhere as you simple will not get much value for your money.
Second thing needed to know is it is "heavily focused on boss-battles" according to the steam description. I feel more needs to be said about this because it's pretty much a boss-battle game, with a very small amount of platformer levels throw in. Essentially you begin a majority of level fighting the boss and that's it. If you're expecting something like Megaman, this is not that.
After all that being said, if you're still interested, then I recommend you buy this game. It brings the same sort of challenge you would expect from games like Wings of Vii, IWBTG, and Boshy. All the bosses are very unique and bring new challenges, and the controls are spot on. The parry system takes some getting used to but is very fun to use and feels great when you land them properly. There is a rating system which brings simple, classic replayability that old school gamers will enjoy, aswell as 2 player coop.
My only complaint so far is how the difficulty scaled during my normal playthrough. I found that the difficulty went up very sharp towards the end of world 2, which is ok, but it dropped off at the end of world 3 and all the way towards the end of the game. Based on some world 2 bosses taking me an hour+ to beat I was expecting the final few bosses to take me days to beat, but instead they took me maybe 20 minuites each. I'm hoping expert difficulty is different.
Super fun game though.

The writing in this game is amazing. The variety in the stories spread across the islands is captivating. Playing Sunless Sea is not dissimilar to getting hooked on a really good book, with the addition of atmospheric music that matches the mood and feel of the game perfectly. Add to this the agonising decision making and the continuous, tempting gambles the game seduces you into (and probably requires) to make progress, and you begin to understand the call of Zee.
Is it a bit grinding? In all honesty, yes, it takes a while to re-reach the same place in the/a story after the death of a Captain. That said, the game would lose a lot of the trepidation that makes it so enthralling if the permadeath had no consequences.
On a more personal note I am a HUGE fan of the Victorian Gothic styling of the game universe. I don't think this game could have worked as well in any other setting.

Like a good sequel should, Call of Duty: Ghosts doesn’t ignore the formula of fast, fluid gameplay that has made the series famous, but introduces a unique new premise, unprecedented player personalization, and sweeping changes that breathe new life into the multiplayer experience. It’s over-the-top and at times unnecessarily complex, but serves both current and next-generation consoles with ambitious new ideas and tremendous replay value.
Despite sharing a name with one of Modern Warfare’s best-known characters, Ghosts takes place in an entirely new Call of Duty universe set in the not-too-distant future. In a genre overwrought with antiquated Russian conflicts and ambiguous Middle Eastern terrorist threats, Ghosts takes on a refreshingly unique premise in which the threat comes not from the east, but the south: a federation of oil-rich South American nations rises to take over the hemisphere, pushing north and coming to blows with the U.S.
The prelude establishes a harrowing vision of a United States homeland that's broken but not beaten – not quite Red Dawn, but not Fallout 3, either. It’s a space not often explored by modern shooters, and its mood is heightened by missions set in a besieged Santa Monica and the wasted remains of San Diego, to the tune of an excellent, somber score from David Buckley (The Town, Metal Gear Solid 4). But ultimately, time on the poignant homefront is short lived as the story goes behind enemy lines in Caracas, the Andes mountains, and other exotic locales.
Those might lack to familiarity, but the variety of environments keeps the campaign fresh, not only in terms of visuals, but in gameplay as well. Instead of just fighting waves of enemies through a linear stage at ground level, you’ll find yourself rappelling down skyscrapers, flying helicopters, having firefights in space, commanding tanks, scuba diving through shipwrecks, playing as a dog, and evading shark attacks. Each requires new strategy, acute situational awareness, and – in the case of the space and water missions – special consideration for verticality and physics.
Of course, it wouldn’t be a Call of Duty game without elaborate setpieces, fierce shootouts, and tense stealth missions, and Ghosts delivers some of the most memorable experiences in the series. I felt genuine dread as the ground and buildings collapsed around me during orbital weapons strikes, the zero-gravity spectacle of the Federation’s space station ambush is awe-inspiring, and bursting through a highrise window as the entire building crumbles during the Federation Day mission is exhilarating.
But like previous CoDs, the story of Ghosts struggles to remain in focus amidst the fray of explosive cinematic moments and relentless firefights. Narrated loading sequences with stylized story animations push the campaign forward, but only last for one or two minutes before launching back into the action. It’s there, on the front lines, that much of the plot progression is presented and oftentimes lost.
It's by no means an achievement in dramatic storytelling — it's more about dumb fun — and it lacks the player-choice element introduced with Call of Duty: Black Ops II, but when given time to breathe Ghosts actually offers some interesting human drama. The story centers around two brothers, Logan and Hesh, their father Elias, and yes, their dog Reilly as they fight the Federation as part of the battered remnants of the U.S. military, and later as the elite Ghosts squad. The family ties, specifically the relationship between Logan and Hesh, made me care about the protagonists in a series that's habitually made its characters a dispensable commodity. The voice acting is decent overall, though there are periodic moments of cringe-worthy dialog, like one superfluous moment when Elias reveals he’s a member of the Ghosts. And then there’s Riley. Though the subject of many a meme at this point, Riley not only acts as a useful tool for recon and silently dispatching enemies, but is integral to several dramatic sequences, saving your character on more than one occasion.
The story stumbles in the second act when it strays away from the more evocative character focus in favor of a long stretch of back-to-back missions driven almost exclusively by guns-blazing combat. While not poorly done, this visually arresting, action-packed, but ultimately hollow middle stands in stark contrast to the effective first and final acts. On the bright side, that padded out my play time to roughly 10 hours, making this campaign one of the longest CoD single-player experiences.
The Verdict
Call of Duty: Ghosts isn't a reinvention of the franchise, but proves there's still room for innovation within its existing formula. Though at the risk of overcomplicating things at times, its robust multiplayer gameplay, surprisingly fun co-op modes, and lengthy, challenging, and varied campaign makes Ghosts one of the best Call of Duty games to date.

I played the first Blood Bowl years ago and despite it being a clunky mess I found it very enjoyable when it wasn't just providing growl-inducing frustration, so I was quite hopeful this game will provide me with more hours of campy fun.
Boy was I wrong...
While there are a few improvements over the last game, mainly in
better graphics and maybe one or two innovations but it's otherwise pretty much the same game, only with a couple more annoyances bundled onto it.
The biggest issue with the game is that it is heavily RNG-based, with so much depending on literal rolls of the dice. Almost everything comes down to dice rolls and those are so often only minimally influenced by a player's stats.
The RNG can be in your favor as easily as it can screw you and I cannot emphasize enough
the RNG can completely ♥♥♥♥ you over and cost you a match.
You can get the worst possible results several times in a row and botch simple but crucial actions while your opponent gets the gods' personal blessing and breezes through what should have been impossible odds.
You can get demolished by a random event that strikes at the start of a drive and knocks out half your team while the opponent remains unscathed.
You can charge a weak opposing player, roll three dice, see those dice all turn up "Attacker Down" results and use your last re-roll
.
You can knock down half the opponent's players without so much as stunning them, while the opponent somehow outright kills or completely debilitates several of your players on the first five turns... And then you try to use your Healer to save a choice player,
.
If you think that's just hilarious and this game is supposed to be a barrel of laughs anyway, wait until you get that stuff happening to you for a whole match. The laughs tend to run out pretty fast and frustration starts to kick in on the third time you have your hulking Chaos Warrior gets counter-punched to the ground by a stunty Halfling. Funny as that may be the first time you see it, it gets less fun to watch when you are then forced to see that same Halfling scoring a touchdown against you where he should have been a red smear on the field.
See, unlike a game that is designed to be pure camp and humor, Blood Bowl is an actual game that cares about how many points you had (and you get nothing for having had comical misfortune visited on you) and who won the match. It also keeps track of who got injured (and
are the
who suffers from that♥♥♥♥♥♥if you're playing Solo against AI).
So seeing a player you struggled to level up and develop gets the♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of them and outright dies on you isn't so much fun, as it would be in any other game.
Speaking of leveling up - yes, there are totally levels and levelling up in this game as those were in the previous one, and yes, it is still a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
To earn points for levelling up you mainly need to have a specific player score touchdowns or inflict injuries on an opponent (which, remember, is completely up to the RNG - you can have your mutated Minotaur plow through half the opposing team with Horns and Claws and inflict no more than a stun, meanwhile a vanilla Lineman from the other team casually kills that same Minotaur by tripping him once) - and you have to do all that several times with the same player just to level that player up.
Your other players get nothing for whatever else they've been doing if they haven't also scored touchdowns and killed other players.
On a lesser note, the narration from the commentators (Jim and Bob) is still depressingly juvenile (which is fine if you're under 20, I guess) - and by that I mean, "sounds like it was mostly written for very small children", which makes you feel like you're playing something that's supposed to keep a toddler busy or something.
Even if you like them, they get extremely repetitive and you'll be forced to hear them say the same two or three lines over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over
.
Some of their comments are completely detached from anything that actually takes place on the field and instead delve into nonsense like a
factoid about some fictional nonsense that has nothing to do with your match. Some of it just recycled from the previous game.
Also, Multiplayer has gotten more focus in this game - which might be a plus for you - but if you're mainly interested in just having casual fun on your own, you might wonder why you can't name your team whatever you like because the name you had in mind is taken. You want to play Solo and name your Chaos team the Southside Slashers like you did in the last game? Nah, that's used by some other player somewhere, so you can't use that on the team you have no plans on playing in a multiplayer because there is no mechanic to just have a team specifcally for Solo use.
I still sometimes get a bit of casual fun playing the game - until the RNG gods rear their disgusting head - but I would not recommend it for others and frankly, I'd have refunded it if I could.
Blood Bowl is the kind of game that you might either enjoy very much or not at all, but will have to deal with a lot of frustration as well as fun moments.
To me, the frustration simply overweighs the fun.
