This game is just amazing. I was skeptical at first of buying it but after i saw overwhelmingly positive reviews for this game I ended up buying it on boy am I glad I did. I'll go ahead and list the pros and cons of this game:
PROS:
- Fantastic Soundtrack
- Art Style is fantastic
-- This game has amazing music, I love the boss fights songs especially as they always seem to fit so well into the frantic and hectic battles that are underway.
- Incredible movement/Excellent Controls
-- I kid you not, probably the most fluid and smooth movement in any 3d platformer i've ever played. It took about 30 seconds of controlling Hat Kid to realize I was going to enjoy this game so much because of just how tight and responsive the controls are. Something that always makes or breaks a good 3d platformer and A Hat In Time really nailed it.
- Skill Floor and Ceilings for all kinds of players
-- Yeah. level design is incredible. It allows players of all kinds to enjoy the worlds available. Newer or less skilled players at a 3d platformer type game are still able to enjoy the levels in a comfortable manner while high-caliber and hardcore players that like to play with a challenge are certainly able to blitz through the levels sequence breaking left and right as well as certain badges attainable making the game from a laidback and chill experience to a brutal and challenging fiesta with the 1-Hit Hero Badge. It basically removes a badgeslot and sets your health to 1 making the game way more challenging for those who like a tough challenge. Like I said, A Hat In Time caters to all kinds of players so that no one is left feeling out when playing this game.
- An enjoyable Collect-A-Thon
-- Normally Collect-A-Thons are pretty dragged out and feel like a chore after the novelty of the game wears off for players who have played it for a while. I have accululated 21 hours at the time of this review and im still replaying chapter 2  levels grabbing everything I can because it doesnt feel like a chore. Its so much fun exploring different routes of each level and see how fast I can get to new objectives because of how tight and responsive the controls are. Nothing feels like a chore, It has level selection similar to Super Mario Galaxy, a central hub in which you access the worlds from, then individual Acts within each world that each one feautures the same themeatic feel of each level but each Act offers a different experience such as chapter 2 in which 2 acts for one of the characters involves you traversing his train seraching for clues as to who murdered a passenger, a much slower paced and mysterious exploration based level. Then the very next act in his storyline involves the same train but instead requiring the player to speedrun through it while its about to explode with buzzsaws and acid pools and rockets and explosions all pillaging the exact same train in order to save all the passengers at the very end by deactivating the self-destruct sequence. Each level is so unique and fresh that you will never feel as if you are being forced to run errands.
- Boss Fights
-- Oh my lord are the boss fights incredible, the soundtrack with them makes them all the more epic. This game does 3d platformer's boss fights some justice. Very hectic and fast-paced boss-fights that are certainly no jokes, the enemies in the game tend to be fairly weak and feel more of an environmental-hazard than an actual enemy with threatining abilities but the boss fights are the complete opposite. They are incredible and very well done. Easily the best boss fights in any 3d platformer I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing.
- Abilities
-- Your hats for the most part are not even manditory. Though you certainly will be using them because they are so much fun to use and make the game way more enjoyable. A lot of different routes throughout each level are available through the use of hats alone. Not only this but badges in combination with hats allow for some incredible skips and sequence breaks in terms of platforming that are always extremely satisfying when they work out. My personal favorite is the sprint hat and the scooter badge. Regardless, The hats are unique and satisfying to use.
- Bonus Levels
-- Within the game, Such things known as time rifts will appear in levels already beaten allowing you to go back and replay a level you beat in order to find them based on a picture given as to where it was. If you manage to find the time rift, you can access it permanently from the hub and they serve as a bonus platforming level with a very laidback and relaxing environment that you can of course choose to take slow or sequence break the hell out of and speed run that course. Personally my nit-pick with them is that they are very easy but they are still fun.
- MANY MANY MORE
CONS (few and far in between):
- Length
-- This game unfortunately is pretty short, I had finished half of the game in about 16 hours which is still descent. However, in perspective its just fine when you consider its offered at the price of half of a AAA title game at only 30 bucks so its length is fine. Still bittersweet as I would definitely pay for this game at a price of a AAA title if its length were that of one. I guess its a great sign that I wish it was more expensive because that just shows that I want more of this game. It's so good but so short that it just leaves you wanting more, if any dlc drops for this game im grabing it asap becasue holy hell do I love this game.
- Hat Kid Customization
-- I will say the customization of Hat Kid could have been done better, Im not really a fan of random chance based loot in cosmetics. I'd prefer if we could use some of the in-game currency you start to accumulate a large amount of after you get all the badges in order to buy pallete swaps that I actually like. Also, it would be nice to have actually different outfits instead of just color swaps. Also the alternate Hat Flairs shouldn't be locked to individual hats in my opinion. Especially when you consider how little you use 2 specific hats, Kid's Hat and the Dweller Hat, I feel that the flairs for those hats should be allowed on any of the other hats. I don't have anything to say on the track remixes because I frankly didn't care for them to actually try to get them, I just re-rolled for anything but them. I wanted the pallete changes first then the flairs.
-  Certain Badges, Some of the badges feel useless and unnecessary like the mumbling voices one for 800 pons. I don't even remember hearing anything different when I tried it. Others like the Hook or Dive-Bump badge felt like they should have been part of your kit from the moment you obtain them instead of taking up a badge slot. It isnt that bad considering that you can change badges on the fly by the press of the start menu so its not too annoying.
- Performance
-- Not really a con because its actually really great. I get decent frames on this game with the graphical settings maxed on everything and only a few frame dips in certain spots and even then the best part is it only lowers frame rate rather than large spikes and stutters which are far worse than just consistent low fps. Eitherway the game runs great for the most part, only in certain areas and events it acts up, like in Chapter 2 Act 4 after you complete train rush, for some reason the end result screen that counts your points up for those acts starts lagging like crazy, like about 10 fps. Its not a big deal since it only lasts for that countup screen and isn't during any actual gameplay but still, certain weird things the game will act up on and they add up over the course of your playthrough. My setup isnt complete trash but its not anything special. Definitely a budget setup with a gtx 960 and a crappy AMD Athlon X4 860K processor. I get averaged around 45-50 fps on this game at max settings so its definitely playable while not sacrificing any quality whatsoever.
CONCLUSION:
Buy It, Its GOTY worthy.

This is a unique puzzle game combining a mutated form of Tetris with tower defense.  It has a great personality that will make you smile, and it's $10 right now.  If you're one of those unfortunate souls that paid $60 to preorder No Man's Sky, here's your chance to redeem yourself.
Gameplay:  Here we have Tetris with enemies, a story, and more freedom.  The game eases you into the concept and mechanics without coddling you.  The controls are easy and intuitive enough, freeing you up to master the game.  Once you are confident that your base can handle the waves of monsters, you can fast forward which is a nice feature.  The developer obviously took great care to test the game before releasing it on Steam.  All I've found so far is a typo and that you can't change your screen resolution in the settings.  Whoopdie Doo.
Graphics:  Simple but fun.  The visuals are very colorful and almost childlike, but in a good way.  The monsters are very original.  They made me laugh.
Sound:  For me the sound was the most redeeming quality.  The music is great and a perfect fit for this game.  The sound effects seem to be vocal, as in someone made them with their mouth a la Michael Winslow from Police Academy and ran them through effects.  They're awesome.  The menu item select sound effect will take you back to your childhood.  The developer clearly played a lot of console in the 90's.
Content:  The dialogue is funny and well written.  Menubot is adorable.  The story is silly.  The number of planets is limited but will increase.  In our current age of early access where we are getting used to buying games and watching them grow I have no problem with the current level of content.  The game is hard enough as it is with what it has.
I can drink $10 worth of booze in seconds.  Throw down and support this game.

A Hat in Time is honestly one of the best 3D platformers I've ever had the pleasure to experience. It's like a mix between various Mario 64/Sunshine/Galaxy/etc.. with the cel-shaded art style that The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker uses, which is my personal favorite game.
Let me start by saying I knew literally nothing about this game. Never watched any playthroughs/gameplay/trailers or looked at anything about it whatsoever as far as the game and news of the game goes outside of looking at the it's Store Page on here. I thought the art style stood out to me and it looked charming and fun but I don't believe I was very interested until I saw a screenshot of it in the Community page. In the screenshot was one of the rift stages and it had a rotating rectangular platform on it that was straight out of the Mario Sunshine special stages. I lost my♥♥♥♥♥♥and slapped this game on my wishlist and picked it up during the winter sale and my god was I enthralled by it the whole way through.
The story pretty much goes like this; You're a kid with a hat and while flying through space in your ship, a member of the Mafia busts a window on your ship open after you shoo him away which causes your fuel (Time Pieces) to zoom right out the vault and outside into the vacuum of space and of course, you've gotta get em back to make it home and you do so by platforming your way through various wonderfully built worlds with all sorts of charming things and characters to see. Which brings me to my next point, the world-building in this game just feels so wonderfully done. You start out in Mafia town and pretty much everyone is part of a "Mafia of Cooks". The level is sunny, the music is wonderful, some Mafia members will play patty-cake with you and wallop you in the face or one will even trip you just while walking by. Then in the later levels you're greeted to a darkened sky with soothing music, a calm rainfall and HAT KID EVEN WEARS A DAMN PONCHO DURING ALL OF THIS IT'S SO PRECIOUS. Then at one point the whole town is literally flooded with lava and I just can't even begin to express how much I love these things. The levels then take off from there and you visit a place called "Dead Bird Studio" and the chapter is split between two movie directing birds who are in a constant conflict between whose the better director and you dash through levels associating to their genres or character traits, dark forests filled with spirits who want to die, talking nooses, ghastly minions, and probably one of my favorite characters due to the events near the end, the Snatcher. You sign your soul off to some contracts and each serve as a mission for the level. Then one world, Alpine Skyline, is literally an open-world level where you do things in the order that you please and that level was honestly such a blast but I can't ramble too long with limited review space, sadly. Then there's the final world which currently hosts one chapter:  the final chapter and ooooo is it amazing. It's one of those final levels that made me feel giddy and teary-eyed and ugh, it's just too great. Each chapter has a boss fight or two and they're such nice big changes of pace from your usual jumping and parkouring you typically do in this game and they're just super well-done, I won't spoil them. Plus there's even levels that require a stealth approach which throw in stealth mechanics similar to MGS which is even referenced in one stealth level on a TV screen. The whole game is voice acted and the voice acting is honestly really really nice. I was pretty surprised and I'm baffled as to why some negative reviews list this as a con as if it takes away from something but I think it makes all the characters memorable and aids to presenting them and their personalities.
As far as gameplay itself goes, Hat Kid is honestly really fun to play as and control. You get a double jump and a dash that's cancelable to make platforming as precise as you need it to be. Then throw in the addition of what makes Hat Kid unique which are, you guessed it, hats. Each hat has it's own ability. Your main hat allows you to target the goal or goal related items, serving as a hint/help giver. Then there's the sprint hat which lets you run faster than you normally walk. A brewing hat to chuck potions at enemies and blow up various crates and barrels and get pons (the currency) or even yarns to make new hats! Then you also can have up to three badges on these hats that open up for more things or change up gameplay or features. Take the Mumble Badge for example. The characters are all voice acted but with the Mumble Badge, it turns their speech into garbled mumbles like Banjo-Kazooie. Or how about the Magnet Badge to attract pons to you from a small distance. Or even a Camera Badge to take screenshots with ease and apply depth of field and even filters while adjusting the angle for your Steam screeenshot gallery.
Lastly, the music. The music is just so overwhelmingly wonderful that sometimes I just felt myself standing there listening to it. Nothing is too loud or too quiet or in-your-face. Level themes perfectly fit their overworld counterparts and boss fight themes kick complete♥♥♥♥♥ It's hard to put how I feel about the music, let alone the whole game, into words. But it's all charming.
**Also, for you platformer speedrunners out there, you can enable a few options such as a timer and a no-save feature. :)**
A Hat in Time is now up there in my list of my favorite games of all time. I loved every minute of it and I can't wait for the free DLC and to also start up my next playthrough. The worlds are crafted beautifully and every moment and character were most certainly memorable to me. Every single second of this game had me with a smile on my face the whole way through and even teary eyes at the end because of how I really just didn't want this beautiful game to end. 100%ing it was a blast too because of going back to past levels with new items to open up more to explore. It's a cute and pleasant throwback to older platforming collect-a-thons and  definitely a HUGELY FRESH installment to the genre and I love it to death and highly, highly recommend it.

First off - this game is hilarious. All of the little sound effects, and the way that the robots in the intro talk, help give this game a light-hearted, approachable feel right off the bat.
But man, after the tutorial level, and subsequent first/second planets, this game can get difficult in a hurry. After having played through the first set of 4 planets, I would love to go back and play through in a different order to find an easier path. It kind of reminds me of playing any of the MegaMan games on NES -- the order of which you choose to play the levels is not set, and you could easily debate which path to take for sake of ease or challenge. To help explain this: for each planet you beat, you are then expected to survive 1 night longer on the next planet. So if you survuved 1 night on planet A, you now need to spend 2 nights on planet B. You get to choose the order of A, B, C, and D, but no matter which path you take, the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th nights become more difficult to survive. I barely beat the 4th night.
I enjoyed having to consider the unique obsticles present on each planet, and expirimenting with my base to best suit what was being thrown at me. It could sometimes be a bit overwhelming to search for the proper piece, create stacks of discarded pieces, work to build new bots, and maintain units to fight off the monsters - but that said, it can also be very satisfying to complete a robot's build at the last second, and send the little yellow dudes in to power your stuff and save you from certain death.
Honestly, for an Early Access game, this is really fun. I'm interested to see where the developers take this game in the future. I would say money well spent, especially if you like tower defense or puzzle games.

Despite only being in Early Access I have to say that I was impressed with Robots in the Wild.
The basic premise of Robots in the Wild is to create a base of robots around the heart block to prevent the hostile alien creatures from destroying it for a given number of days. To do this you drop blocks onto the planet in order to create robots. These robots are created when you create the shape that represents one of the robots.
The thing I was most surprised about was that the game has a surprising amount of strategy to it. You need to wisely use your blocks since you only receive a limited amount of blocks in the level and then have to wait to get additional blocks. In order to prevent wasting blocks you really need to plot out which robots you want to build and where you want to build them. While there is a little learning curve as you figure out how to play the game, I like how much flexibility the game gives you.
While the game is going to add a lot of content throughout its time in Early Access, there is actually already quite a bit in the game. It is quite polished and there is already quite a bit to do in the game. The levels alone should probably take around 6-8 hours to complete. Outside of a couple small bugs here and there, if I didn't know it was an Early Access game I probably wouldn't think it was one.
If the game's premise doesn't really interest you it probably won't be for you. If the game looks interesting to you though I think it is worth picking up Robots in the Wild.

I hate to be one of the few negative voices here, but I want others to be aware that this is a somewhat niche game. If you love puzzle platformers, get this game.
For everyone else, consider what you want out of a game. Do you like a challenge and a dark atmosphere? If not, then you might want to reconsider.
The game for what it is isn't that bad, but I don't happen to particularly enjoy platformers so my perspective on this game is rather negative. The bleak, lonely atmosphere made the game more depressing to play than dying repeatedly already is and didn't do anything to draw me into the game. The puzzles are creative, but can be overly frustrating at times with the timing requirements. The game is also rather short, which was a relief for me (I try to finish all my games at least once even if I don't particularly enjoy them) but would be a negative for someone who paid full price for this game and was expecting more.
Overall, this game is great from a technical and creative standpoint but completely failed on the fun and enjoyment aspects for me. Given the game's age and short length, if you do fall in the group of people who might enjoy it, wait for it on sale.

I managed to beat SUPERHOT in four hours, and I have to say it's honestly one of the most intense games I've ever played. In SUPERHOT, you start just by mindlessly killing Red Dudes from being told to do so. Story starts to shift throughout the game, however. It quickly becomes creepier as the System makes you one of them.
No, I will not use the phrase the game told me to use. I will say however that it has one of the most interesting mechanics of any game I've ever played: time control. The speed at which you walk around and look with your mouse determine how fast time goes, and you learn to use this control to your advantage as you dodge bullets, jump over cars, and even throw katanas into lines of Dudes. The game isn't a very long one, but I feel like I can go back and visit it when I want to do the endless mode.
-Time-control mechanic
-
-Artstyle. The enemies shatter into crystal shards, and they're the only colors in the level aside from the onyx-colored guns/weapons.
-Hotline Miami-like gameplay. Everything kills you in one hit, and you can do the same to enemies. Think HM but in first person.
-Internal messages. To me, the game tries to make a point about how we as gamers are somewhat controlled by machines.
-No soundtrack. While there doesn't really need to be, I like listening to music while I kill. Having only an odd ambience kind of detracted a bit.
-Frustration at times. It's near-impossible to beat some of the later levels without shifting into bodies.
I rate this game an
. This is definitely one to pick up next time it's on sale (I got this from a friend).

A Good Snowman may be Hard To Build, but it's an immensely satisfying endeavor.  There are a few relatively simple and highly intuitive mechanics that allow the game to ease you in to its puzzles before ratcheting up the challenge by subtle tweaks of the configuration.  The puzzles are simple enough in design that if one has you stumped, you can roll it around in your head while you go do something else for a bit.  And then just when you think you've mastered the game's last challenge, they find a clever way to turn those mechanics inside out...and now you realize you might be 50% done.
The presentation is perfect for a reflective puzzle game - soothing soundtrack, subtle sound effects, crisp and simple (yet utterly charming) visuals, and while solving a puzzle could be its own reward...well, there's an undeniable sense of contentment that comes from hugging a snowman.
This game should be more popular.

What makes Just Cause 2 the best open world game in existence? You get to enjoy complete freedom in the z-Axis, too!
The ingenious mechanic of grappling hook and infinite parachutes allow you to instantly fly any place you want. In a second you can be up in the sky enjoying the view. And boy are there varied views to enjoy: Snowy mountaintops, lush forests, deserts, beaches, small towns, big cities.
The story is completely ludicrous and dumb in an immensely fun way. And so are the physics. A childish smile on your face is guaranteed the first time you tether a car to an airplane, take off, climb out of the plane mid-flight, jump into the car and then release the tether. You can blow up almost anything and drive every type of vehicle. It's one map, no loading times, and the size of it is simply mindblowing. I have spent well over 200 hours exploring it all.
Car steering is frankly terrible (there is a racetrack on one island) and you cannot enter buildings.
These seem like minor quibbles for a game that has given me a feeling of freedom unlike any other.

Banished is a city-building strategy game developed and published by Shining Rock Software LLC. It was released in February 2014. In Banished, you control a group of individuals that want to start a new life by developing a new city. You develop your city by increasing your population, gathering resources, and constructing buildings. The game embraces simplicity as trade is the primary currency and not money. This review will cover the gameplay, the integrated Steam Workshop, and the performance and graphics.
Banished presents strong and complex gameplay as game mechanics heavily alter the game. You will learn some mechanics as you play the game whereas other mechanics such as average health and average happiness are presented on the UI. For instance, average health represents an average of all your citizens health. The worse health your city has the less productive they are and the higher chance they have of dying. Furthermore, couple worse average health with the dynamic weather seasons and expect them not to be productive in Winter. As you continuously learn the game you will learn how to strategise and manage your city while incorporating the various game mechanics and the weather seasons, which all seasons have an effect on your city. Other mechanics have long-term implications. For instance, when children turn 10 they can enrol into a school until they turn 17. If they don't enrol you can use them as workers. If they enrol, you cannot use them as workers, but educated citizens will be much more productive long-term compared to uneducated workers. So by and large, these game mechanics emphasis strategy and they showcase the challenging nature of Banished because it is a very difficult game.
Also on gameplay, the game incorporates randomly generated maps that have different amounts of water, hills, and so forth. These affect your plans for your city, but there is a very useful and very informative UI that is customisable. It allows you to add different data to your screen which constantly updates. Specifically, if you want to keep your storage house information box on the screen, you can move it to the top left corner. Overall, the game teaches you about strategy, understanding the mechanics and their consequences, and to assist you allows you to customise your screen with informative UI to help you manage.
Banished uses Steam Workshop. Briefly, Steam Workshop allows individuals that own the game to tweak it, improve it, and mod it. I will admit for the majority of my play time I used Banished Plus, a large mod that provides more balance to the game by tweaking mechanics to reduce the fast-paced length of the game and increase realism. There are an abundance of other mods that once you download the game will inform you of any compatibility issues, which is a nice and handy tool. I use Banished Plus because I think the vanilla game is basic and fast-paced because there are not many buildings in the game are citizens can be very stupid and lazy. Furthermore, add these with the lack of long-term objectives showcase the need for mods to help improve the behaviour of your citizens and expand the amount of content. Therefore, using mods drastically improved my experience of the game. And as a side note, I generally think the developers should have made DLC to expand the content to give more replayability.
Technically, Shining Rock have excellently optimised this game. I can play it on max settings and achieve a constant 60FPS on x10 speed. Features like the weather system and the large amounts of population usually would hit the game in performance, but for the most part I did not experience that. At 110 population on x10 speed I stayed at 60FPS. At 220 population, I was managing a solid 50FPS with the drop due to a larger city and more population. It is evident the six patches in Banished helped improve the performance of it. Graphically, the game is gorgeous. Buildings and citizens are very detailed and the weather system adds a layer of realism to it.
Banished is a very good game. I love the complex gameplay through the variety of game mechanics and their effects on other mechanics. I absolutely adore the beautiful graphics as the buildings are incredibly detailed, the seasons are highly realistic and the scenery is just superb. Banished has excellent performance as I managed to sustain 60FPS for the majority of my play through. It was only at 200+ population I started to see a small dip in FPS and performance. At USD$19.99, I recommend purchasing Banished because overall, it has high replayability.

Sunless Sea is a hard game to review. On one hand it’s one of the best written interactive experiences you can find, but on the other hand it’s also on of the most slow and tedious ones where most of the game mechanics are actually artificial padding in disguise.
In the almost 40 hours I’ve invested in the game I’ve not even come close to finishing all the quests and usually that would be a great show of a rich game. But with Sunless Sea most of those hours are spent empty, slowly traveling to and forth, collecting the required pieces to progress the story. It also doesn’t help that the economics system is as convoluted as the traveling, making the trading almost impossibly slow to progress from.
That’s not time well spent in my opinion and I very much would have wanted a much denser experience.
It’s also a very rich game world that completely lacks any overview to make sense of it as you progress through the narratives. The journal that is kept is so minimal that each occurrence is only given a few sentences each, making it impossible to keep track of what you are doing or what you should do next without writing it all down.
I would recommend it to anyone willing to take comprehensive notes by pen and paper, as well as having an oversight with huge amounts of time spent transiting between the different story points.
The writing and the lore is of such excellent quality that it could almost be forgiven but for most players the artificial padding will be to much to overlook.

This masterpiece is a lesson that should be taught to every game developer involved in the FPS genre. I could save a few compliments and shorten this rather passionate, but humble, homage. But no. When talking about BioShock, one should let the words flow, just like the essence of its beautiful concept flows richly and vividly through every character's line, every thematic poster hanging on a random wall, every bit of Art Deco reconstruction, and every trace of Andrew Ryan's infamous personality.
When I first played this game, back in 2009, I couldn't believe my eyes. The compelling and psychologically deep story that I was witnessing should be in a book or something "narratively more complex". Back then, with all my ignorance and prejudice towards the potential of videogame storytelling, I hadn't realised what sin I was carrying on my mind. The way I've come to think is: BioShock should've always been what it is: a story-driven, linear first-person shooter that touches the deepest veins of your perceptions on notions of compassion, violence, regret, love, and themes such as mindless obedience, civil disorder, despotic leadership, dystopian lunacy, transhuman monstrosity, and other rather shocking motifs that this game courageously explores. Images of fear and perdition that make us cringe, but also touching scenes of sacrifice and loyalty.
Troubled and oftentimes scary characters are all over the place (including the player-character). It's as though journeying deep into the sea brings a progressive loss of sanity and grasp on common sense in virtually all the individuals involved. Coming back to the surface would be their only redemption (cleansing), not only salvation (rescue).
On top of that, there is the addictive gameplay, with the clever and concise variety of weapons that respond directly to specific situations and areas, enemies and game frenzy. The plasmid feature dialogues with the game's spiritual ancestor, System Shock, as do most of the dystopian themes here represented. The enemies and their classes also adapt excellently to the progression in the game, making the contention *difficulty vis-à-vis enjoyment* close to perfection.
The emblematic setting, and a unique steampunk atmosphere in the depths of the ocean. It's an eschatological drama in videogame form. The oneiric visions of mankind crushed by its own mental abyss.

I don't know what I was expecting when I picked up this game. A professor recommended it to me...followed by a friend...followed by Extra Credits. And then it went on sale. So I bought it.
And it wasn't until today--probably three weeks later--that I decided to finally sit down and play it. For the sake of spoilers, I can't say anything. This is a game that is best experienced with fresh eyes. Also, it's a game best experienced in one playthrough--approximately an hour and a half. And for anyone who's crying, "BUT LITVAC, THAT'S SO EXPENSIVE FOR SUCH A SHORT GAME. OH, HOW MY WALLET ACHES. OH NOOOOOOOO-", you can stop that. Right now. This game is so...so impactful. It tells a deep and emotional narrative not just through actual dialogue but through playing the game itself. And it's sad. It's really sad. But it makes you think about games. It makes you think about the people who create them. And, most importantly, it makes you think about the way we individually consume them. That's why The Beginner's Guide is so great. After playing this, I would've still bought it if it were at an even higher price...because you won't find a narrative like this in a 60+ hour AAA game.
The Beginner's Guide is special. Please play it.

A great horror title that scared the crap out of me.  I've been liking this trend of horror games that give you no weapons or means of defending yourself, instead relying on the player to run and hide from the threats that are lurking about.  To me, being defenseless in a hostile environment really makes you feel that much more vulnerable and the world of Outlast more palpable.  There is a certain rush I got everytime I heard an enemy get closer and my characters heartbeat and breathing quickend, not knowing if your hiding spot is adequete.  Even then, your attackers will often-times check hiding spots for you and you best hope you're not there when they check.  More tense still is the moment when you have to leave your cover to move on, knowing that your attacker may only be just a few moment away from you.  The moments when you have to run for your life are just downright terrifying.
The graphical presentation of the game is great.  The real-time lighting and environmental effects do a lot to pull you into this world.  There is a lot of attention to small details as well, like walking through a pool of blood and leaving bloody foot-prints on the ground.  Audio wise is where I think the game shines.  The creaking floors, the distant footfalls of a would-be attakcer, the nasty sounds of insane patients doing insane thing all make the experience feel more genuine.  The musical cues also help bring tension to the game by changing depending on the situation.
The only negative I have about this game is the mission structure in that, it doesn't do anything different (or better) than most other horror games.  Most of the time it's either find a key to open a door or find and push button A then find and push button B to activate a console, system, or generator located elsewhere; it just feels so uninspired.  It especially gets tiresome towards the end because the amount of times the game tells you to go find a key or turn something on ramps up in frequency.  Luckily, you don't have to back-track often and the game does a good job of moving you to new areas.
All in all, it's a great game.  Despite the uninspired mission structure, it's still a must play for any survival horror game fan.  Play it in the dark with a good sound system or pair of headphones.

Dungeon Defenders I was such a great game. I have incredibly fond memories of playing it with my friends. Everything there was so simple, easy to understand, well constructed, and it just felt like a normal game. During the creation of DD II, it's almost as if the devs said to themselves "how can we trash the Dungeon Defenders name and line our pockets?" There is so much wrong with this game I don't think I can write it all down, but let's start with the most obvious.
It's pay to win. Anyone who says otherwise has absolutely no idea what they're talking about. At all. There is no argument. This is the definition of pay to win. As far as I know, there are at least FOUR different types of currency in this game. There's gold, discolored "retard" gold, gems, and some BS shop-specific currency. Pretty much everything worthwhile does not cost gold. It costs retard gold or gems, which aren't that easy to get. Yes, you get retard gold at the end of levels and by doing other♥♥♥♥♥♥ but you can't even save it up past a certain amount. Yeah, you can't save up one of the major currencies in the game. Ridiculous.
Anyone with a functioning brain can tell something is wrong with this game the second you create a character. You can only choose between two: Squire and Apprentice. What about the other's? They're there, you just have to PAY for them. First, you buy the game. Then you have to buy the characters in the game. Then you buy more stuff with real money because if you don't your characters are horribly underpowered and suck. Everywhere in the tavern there are displays of costumes and skins and other BS that costs actual money. It's basically showcasing a bunch of cool items and saying "yeah if you want these you have to pay real money." Pathetic. You even have a limit on how many heroes you can create! Want more slots for heroes? Pay us!
Then there's the problem of the characters themselves. There is separate "mana" for using skills and placing towers. OK, I guess that's understandable. What's not understandable is why there are only four towers for each character. You start out being able to use all 4 towers, so that takes a lot of the excitement out of leveling up your character. Playing as the squire was an outright horrible experience whenever I would want to do melee damage. I was terribly underpowered, even fighting against basic monsters at low levels when I had decent weapons/armor. I had to strike even the weakest monsters for a good 3-4 seconds straight to kill them. And the tougher ones? I'd take me a solid 10-15 seconds just to kill 1. Just get better armor you say? No problem!
Except that when you look at the items that are on the ground you only see the stats of that item. So you can't easily compare them to what you have equipped. Going through dozens of dropped items this way is just not possible since you'd have to open your inventory every single time. Why don't I just pick everything up? Great idea! But then I'd run out of bag space (which is pretty limited to begin with). Want more bag space? Pay us more money!! Are you seeing a trend yet?
Then there's the maps. I don't mind the layouts of them, but dear God the logistics are absolutely horrible. I don't know why, but some maps I can only open ONE chest, even if there are others that haven't been opened. In multiplayer, if someone opens a chest, that chest does not appear as open for you, it just appears greyed out. The idiot who thought that was a good idea needs to be executed. Chests do not show up on the mini map. Neither do dropped items. Now, if I want to find strong items, I have to weed through every single little piece of trash on the map every single round. There's no guarantee I'd look at everything either without missing anything. What more can I say besides absolutely horrible?
The menus in the game are downright horrible. Everything is literally a showcase of what you can buy with your real money. It's teasing you with all these skins, and these bonuses and packages and extra features. It's absolutely riddled with this sort of crap and it's ridiculous.
The tavern itself is much too big and has too many useless junk spaces that don't even have any interacting capabilities. NPCs are just outright painful to talk to, and there's so many people and so much going on it's an absolute pain to keep track of who sells what BS.
This game is quite literally a 1/10, and that's being generous. It's an absolute shame that this is the direction DD has taken. Absolute and utter trash. It's a disgrace that they call this a "better" Dungeon Defenders. There is absolutely nothing better about it. The only thing it does is drain your wallet and your spirit. If you want to experience DD in its purest form, stick to the first game. This is an absolute nightmare. I haven't enjoyed a single second of this trainwreck of a  game.

First episode was great. I was originally inspired by the artistic approach Telltale applied to the game which I must say is incredible and also being a Batman fan how could I say no?
Of course the graphics aren't the only thing to appreciate about this game. Telltale offers a unique and refreshing experience on DC's story. Although we revisit a few plot points, the game still has a degree of mystery to it which is more than I can say for most games that just rehash everything off the original source.
The game gives you a bit of leg room with your choices. As we know Telltale, the choices don't usually matter in the end because the outcomes are very limited. What's different with Batman is that it's not so cut and dried. In Batman, every choice leads to something bigger. Every decision you make will shape how the people of Gotham perceive you.
While the game is nowhere near perfect, it's interesting and straight to the point. Here's to hoping that the story picks up it's game next episode.
7/10
The first episode is never that great when it comes to Telltale but this episode definitely made up for it. Telling a genuine Batman story is pretty much a long shot but Telltale has somehow pulled it off in spades.
One of the biggest things this episode focuses on is Oswald Cobblepot. Oz is an old childhood friend of Bruce Wayne, but his family lost it's wealth. Eventually his father committed suicide and his mother went insane. Oswald left Gotham City and grew up to become the infamous adversary that we know as "The Penguin". When he returned to Gotham he spoke of a revolution, the intentions of that revolution become clear in episode two.
Of course, the second episode isn't all about Oz. We also learn more about Bruce's father, whose dark secret rises to the surface for everyone to see. But this comes to no surprise given what we learned about the Wayne's "criminal history" at the end of episode 1.
We also witness some pretty awful events unfold which is a pretty big move for Telltale but not surprising for anything Batman related. Along with this, we face some pretty difficult choices but being Batman is quite challenging and putting you in his mindset benefits your experience that much more.
Children of Arkham is a fantastic addition to Telltale's Batman and I'm really looking forward to the future episodes hoping that they'll get better as they go on. Needless to say, Telltale has me sold.
9.5/10
Now..where do I even begin?
Episode 3 is definitely a slow paced episode that has high promise for a lot of interesting plot points later on. In Episode 3 we get to focus a lot on Bruce Wayne's side of the story and his relationship with Harvey Dent and Selina Kyle. There are also a lot constant twists and turns throughout the episode that will leave you on the edge of your seat.
There is only so much I can say about the story without spoiling it but it's definitely given the series some footing as the end of Episode 3 sets us up for a very compelling next episode. The only negative thing about this episode was some lagging during the driving scenes which put me off a little bit but nonetheless its another great addition to the series!
This episode builds a lot on storytelling and dialogue. Despite the fact there wasn't much action, I rather enjoyed the thrill of it.
7/10
Stellar episode!!
Guardian of Gotham starts from where we left off after the cliffhanger from Episode 3. We discover that Bruce Wayne has been locked up in Arkham Asylum. Because of this, Bruce finds himself in a unreliable situation. We also bump into a familiar face during our stay in Arkham. Of course, this is very short lived as this "friend" conjures up a plan to bail Bruce out of the Asylum. When this happens, be ready for the episode to start getting back on track because, to no surprise, the episode gets much more amped up.
While we are still hanging around the Asylum, we learn that Harvey had Bruce committed to Arkham because he's apparently "too dangerous" but we learn after this chapter that this is a more personal vendetta. With that being said, Harvey has become a bigger threat towards Bruce Wayne AND Batman so it becomes difficult to play the hand we've been dealt and with so much stuff going on in one episode, it becomes really hard to keep up with so I can't help but notice it feels a little forced. In retrospect, the storyline, characters and even the Jokers voice and design are quite solid! Hopefully we'll be seeing more of him *fingers crossed*
The last fight between Harvey and Batman was quite a lot of fun! The combat for this game is worthy of praise because its so immersive. Episode 4 definitely lived up to that affirmation. Guardian of Gotham had me very emotionally invested in the story and although it's not the most exciting of the series, that doesn't mean it should be overlooked as a great standalone episode.

Red Orchestra 2 and its buddy Rising Storm are without a doubt the best quality FPSs out there. I've played shooters of all kinds, from Halo to Gears of War to Call of Duty to Battlefield and even once to Arma. This one is a gem, this one is the best. The biggest fault with the game is that not enough people are playing it. I can not recommend this game enough.
RO2/RS is a World War II-based shooter, which makes many people roll their eyes because the WWII genre seems to have been "played out" in the eyes of many. In Red Orchestra 2, you take the sides of either the Red Army or the Wehrmacht, fighting for control of the area surrounding the city of Stalingrad. In Rising Storm, which can be purchased seperately or with the RO2 multiplayer mode exclusively, you get to pick from the United States of America or the Empire of Japan, fightng for control of islands in the southwest Pacific. Neither of these are particularly original locations, but that doesn't take away from the game.
There are two basic modes: a single-player and a multiplayer. Single player...well...I've never played it, but people tell me it is glitchy and not that fun, although it is a great way to get used to the mechanics of the game. Multiplayer is a very team-based experience, with hoardes of soldiers on both sides vying for control of some of the largest maps in FPS history.
The mechanics are incredible, combinding the best aspects of the best shooters. In harcore mode, which is the only multipalyer mode that gets played, where a bullet strikes the body deritmines if you live, die, or are wounded. Most of the time, it's a one-hit-kill, and this is true of all weapons. Bullet damage mechancis do not vary as they do in most games. Bullets also drop, forcing you to consider the velocity of roudns flying out of your rifle and the beaten-zone created by them hitting the ground. This makes sniping very difficult, and snipers in the game generally are actually the best shots in the community. You can adjust your sights and check your ammo (you have to in hardcore mode, since there is virtually no HUD). Your soldier gets tired, and he also gets afraid. He will paralyze with fear if you do not take care of him, and you will wear him out if you run him too far. Every gun has it's own feel; no two guns, even upgraded verisons of the same gun, are alike.
This is truly war at its worst. And for a video game, that means at its best. Struggling to make it to the front lines, commanding or taking out tanks, clearing buildings, withstanding artillery barages, cowering in trenches, and capturing points of strategic importance is all of what this game is about.
You have a variety of classes to choose from each game, but you will not nessecarily get the one you want. Like in real war, there are only a few machine-gunners, snipers, demo-men, and officers. RO2/RS makes this reality by limiting the slots availible for certain classes of soldier, which means most of the time, that bolt-action piece of junk is your best friend. And you will appreciate its range and accuracy, which are still unmatched by the so-called "better" weapons (like SMGs, MGs, Pistols, Automatic Rifles, etc.) Plus, you only get the weapons that your chosen nation used in that theate of war. In Rising Storm, this gives the Americans a certain advantage weaponry-wise, but it is countered by the special abilities of the Japanese, which include portable mortars, booby traps, and the most effective bayonet-attack of all nations: the dreaded Banzai charge (which is surprisingly effective, don't knock on it 'till you've tried it)!
Hours of fun and excitement await you if you purhcase this game. I recommend getting the verison that is RO2/RS. You only get multiplayer, but the game still comes with training missions, and besides, you are really getting a whole extra game with RS. More maps, guns, and fun.
That being said, there are a few problems with Red Orchestra 2 that I have to discuss, in order for this to be a fair review:
-1) Victory often goes to those with the best graphics. If your computer can't handle some of the most acturate physics and graphics, then don't bother getting this game.
-2) It almost never lags or glitches, but when it does, boy, hold on to your ♥♥♥♥ing hat.
-3) The community of players is generally rude and unforgiving, but you will find certain pleasent folks if you play enough. But the game has a steep learning curve that can be hard to overcome thanks to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that lurk around every corner.
-4) The upgrade system for weapons is not at it's best, I'm not sure exactly how to deescribe it...
-5) Soldiers in RO2/RS throw grenades liles♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Yes, you can't throw across the map like in COD, but jeez, they can never throw more than three strides away from them, and that's just too damn close for reality or comfort.
-6) This isn't a problem for me, but many people have trouble identifying opponents in hardcore mode. This reults in lots of TKs, which occur all the time and everyone is in denial about. You are guarenteed to TK a bunch, I do it too, everyone does it.
None of the afore-mentioned problems outweight the glory and wonder that is Red Orchestra 2, though. And because this is a WWII based game and not a more modern war, you get to focus less on the problems (and infinately more bullets) around you and deal with yourself and your teammates and enemies one-on-one a lot more. If you like shooters, and you like realistic, then this is the single best game you could possibly buy. I guarentee it.
Red Orchestra2/Rising Storm gets a whopping 9 out of 10.

is a great sokoban styled puzzler that while short, is also very
. This game has perhaps the most aesthetically pleasing visual style of any puzzle game I've played. This game has also got some good spirit, each snowman you build get it's very own name and clothing style and you can even hug your frosty creations. If that doesn't spell out FUN then I don't know what else does. Perhaps a fun twist to sokoban style puzzles will do it instead?
The main twist from standard sokoban puzzles is that anytime you push a smaller or medium sized snowball across a snow patch it will increase in size until it grows to the large size. You are only given three snowballs (of varying initial size) per snowman (or snowwoman) you have to make. Each snowman is comprised of one large snowball, one medium sized snowball, and one small snowball. As you can tell, it takes some care and attention to make sure end up with the right sized parts...if you push the only snowball through a snowmatch, your future snowman is now headless (and you'll have to restart). This makes for some pretty fun and interesting puzzling, you definitely have to think things through on some of the harder puzzles. The better you can make sense of your spatial layout, as well as the how and where of how each snowball will end up the easier it is to solve the puzzles. The last puzzle really exemplified this the most. I pushed around the snowballs a bit to get some ideas but really had to think critically about what I was trying to achieve and what problems I would encounter by pushing the snowballs in certain directions/patterns. I didn't find any single puzzle to be too difficult (in the "IT'S WAY TOO DAMN DIFFICULT" sense not the "meh, it wasn't too difficult" sense) and I was pretty happy with the progression in terms of difficulty.
I will say the game is on the short side. I beat the "base" game in around an hour and a half. I will say that I found that the final puzzle was really well made, it was difficult but satisfying and it really made me think. While it was a great last puzzle, other puzzles like that would have been a great bonus. Also worth noting that there is apparently some hidden content, but I'm not sure what it all involves as I have yet to find it. If you are a budget gamer or if you prefer games give you a lot of playtime for their buck, I'd caution you towards getting this game. It is a great game, and I do recommend it, just keep the game length in mind before purchasing. Despite all this, I was still very pleased with the game. I'm not exactly someone who can throw money around, but I would not have been upset with what I got out of the game, even if I had paid full price for it. It's a very memorable game and it's something that I wouldn't mind replaying in a year or two once I forgot all the solutions just for the enjoyment of re-experiencing the game.
p.s. I've been shoveling snow for the past five days up until I wrote this review, and I still think positively on this game all about snow!

I managed to beat SUPERHOT in four hours, and I have to say it's honestly one of the most intense games I've ever played. In SUPERHOT, you start just by mindlessly killing Red Dudes from being told to do so. Story starts to shift throughout the game, however. It quickly becomes creepier as the System makes you one of them.
No, I will not use the phrase the game told me to use. I will say however that it has one of the most interesting mechanics of any game I've ever played: time control. The speed at which you walk around and look with your mouse determine how fast time goes, and you learn to use this control to your advantage as you dodge bullets, jump over cars, and even throw katanas into lines of Dudes. The game isn't a very long one, but I feel like I can go back and visit it when I want to do the endless mode.
-Time-control mechanic
-
-Artstyle. The enemies shatter into crystal shards, and they're the only colors in the level aside from the onyx-colored guns/weapons.

-Internal messages. To me, the game tries to make a point about how we as gamers are somewhat controlled by machines.

This game is really cute, but deceptively tough. The concept is simple: You have to build a snowman. How do you do that?
The game is laid out like an "open-world," where eventually you can tackle diverging snowmen/women in any order you like. The "levels" within the world are separated by hedges, and you're given a small space to make your snowman by stacking small, medium and large snowballs together. Most puzzles begin with three small snowballs, which you roll into the snow to make larger. Grass patches are left befind as you roll your snowballs, allowing smaller balls to move over them without fear of becoming larger. You can also pass a smaller snowball over a larger one (i.e. medium/small over large, small over medium) in order to solve some puzzles.
Once you complete a puzzle, your snowman magically grows clothes and has a name (don't forget to hug them afterward)! Each completed puzzle is signified by a butterfly. But beyond simply completing the puzzle, there is much to this game than is on the surface. It's a game about exploring, so go find it for yourself!

Games like this don't come around often. SUPERHOT makes you feel like a badass, while having fun doing so.
The 'main story', per-sé, are the 34 levels included with the game. Where the game really shines, is in its extremely fun and challenging 'Challenge mode'. Challenge mode includes 13 (maybe more) sets of the 34 levels where modifiers come into play. For example, there's a 2013 challenge mode where the game plays like how it did in 2013, with the graphics of the time. This includes punches killing, no melee weapons, no throwables. There are other challenge modes like 'Barehands', that only allow you to punch enemies to death. It gives the game a real challenge, and completing a level is a real accomplishment. You WILL die and you WILL have to learn from your previous runs. Luckily, you never feel like your death was a cheap one. I see some of the challenge modes as an extremely futuristic version of chess - where there are many different ways to play a level out, but each time you make a move it will change your level run drastically. There is an endless mode, that can be played on several different maps.
SUPERHOT is something revolutionary, with great level design and an interesting aesthetic. Challenge mode gives those who want to dig deeper tools to do so, and that's great. I still haven't completed all of the levels on some of the more challenging challenge modes, but it's something I look forward to doing.
There's a fine line between difficulty and cheapness, in many games. SUPERHOT plays with this fine line with such finesse, it's impressive. That being said, you never REALLY feel like you've been cheated out when you die. You'll simply press R and go again, this time knowing more than you did before. Watching your replay in real time after victory is one of the most satisfying things I have experienced in gaming, in recent time.

Let me preface this by saying that Sunless Sea is not a game for everyone, and that I have not played Fallen London.
Sunless Sea isn't so much a game as a very well written naval trade economics simulator. A very slow, grindy simulator . You start off with a ship, a crew, and a meager sum of money. There are multiple ways of increasing this sum of money, but all of them revolve around sailing from one point on the map to another. Occassionally you must dodge underground sea monsters and insane pirates, but most of the time you'll be watching your fuel and supply gauges slowly tick downwards while the terror creeps up.
Sure, you can fight sea monsters, but good luck doing so with the basic ship and weapon, because those barely do squat against even the weakest of monsters. And if you do manage to kill them, the rewards won't pay for the repairs you will need to make for your hull. If you want to fight monsters, or do any of the fun missions in the game, you will need to copious amounts of money. Unfortunately, money is extremely hard to come by, especially at the start when you have no idea what you should be doing.
I don't usually turn to online guides to figure out how to play a game, but for Sunless Sea it's pretty much essential as the game does an exceptionally poor job at telling you what you should be doing. On just about every level, Sunless Sea moves at a glacial pace. In order to make enough money, or raise your stats high enough, in order to accomplish the more fun things the game has to offer, you will need to bide you time and grind.
Port reports and quests will only get you so far, as the main source of income comes buying resources in one port and selling them in another for incremental profit. While there are a few ways of making lots of money in a short period of time, you will be cut off from them after a while, often times with little forewarning.
The combat itself is nothing to write home about either, and is pretty lackluster. Even with some of the more powerful weapons, fastest engines, or bigger and better boats, it is a pretty bland structure of 'keep the enemy within firing range'.
So given all these pretty damning statements, why am I giving it my recommendation?
Well, what the game does right, it does phenomenally well. The writing is utterly incredible, painting a tapestry of this world and your place in it with evocative prose. And the world itself equally stunning, suffused with an air of mystery that becomes ever more expansive the more you dig into it. There is truly a sense that everyone you meet, and every where you go, has a deep an intricate backstory that ties into the greater narrative of this strange underwater sea and its equally bizarre denizens. The visuals themselves are simplistic, but tell entire stories through appearance alone. For that reason and that reason alone, I give this game my recommendation.
Like I said at the beginning, this is not a game for everyone. It is boring, repetitive and a grindfest, but its an eloquently written grindfest with excellent worldbuilding. If you don't mind doing a lot of reading, then there is a lot to get out of this game. If not, than this isn't the game for you.

Bioshock 1, the spiritual sucessor to System Shock and keeping most of the creepyness of its forefather intact. *SPOILERS PRESENT*
Lets talk about the first thing we see in the game, the Graphics, the game just oozes with atmosphere and detail, when you walk around rapture you can see how people would live their lives, theres no randomly placed gap which would make you wonder how people got over it or why its there its modeled in a way that you'll walk around a place the same way you would if Rapture was real, and not falling apart, or have crazed looniees trying to kill you.
That said there are a few low points about the graphics, some stuff feels VERY Copy and Paste, like i never enjoyed going into the bars because they felt too similar to each other, I might just be oblivious since I don't go to pubs in the real world but I would assume at least SOME differance also while I get this is meant to be a city that is collapsing from the inside but I think there is way too much grey around, its a typical gripe with FPS games in the last 10 or so years bit I still belive it to be a valid complaint
Next the sound, Honestly I didn't find the music that good, thats not a bad thing though as the lack of music or the sound of old style music playing from old radios helps add to the atmosphere, I don't know if this is a glitch though but sometimes when there was alot of shooting and such random audio bits would cut off, a prime example would be when I fought the first "boss" of the game (not the Big Daddys) I had 2 Flying guns (Buzzers I called them) and a turret shooting at him, with an alarm going off and him shooting my buzzers, during the entire fight the turret and one of the buzzers would be shooting with no sound coming out, other times when grenades were thrown the Wistle sound would keep cutting out and starting back in, as I said it might be a glitch but still, Minor gripe, The voice acting is pretty well done as well though the lines are repeated a liiiiittle too much which can make the fighting a little grating to the ears
The Gameplay is your pretty solid run and gun kind of shooting game I played it on the hardest difficulty and I'm going to say right now, its too easy, the reason is because it is impossible to Game over unless your at the final boss, Got killed by a Big daddy? don't worry you respawned and the big daddy is at the same health it was when you died! it kills alot of that fear the game could have as your being hunter by a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off diversuit man and your down to your last sliver of health and EVE, While we're talking about Big Daddys and Difficulty its pretty dissapointing that on the case you have the Driller Big Daddy (Bouncer) but on the hardest Difficulty you face primarly Rivet gun Big daddys (Rosie) it doesn't help when actually the Rosies are easier to kill then the Bouncers, sure you can get two shotted by a Rosie but at least you can keep your distance and snipe them while dodgeing the bullts, I honeestly found fighting the Rosies the worst part of the gameplay and fighting the Bouncers one of the best, because your constantly back peddling from the Bouncer while he is slowing you and charging at you, one of my fondest memories in the game is when a Duel between me and one of the Few Bouncers in the game ended with us both killing each other when we charged at each other in Melee, Fondest memory with the Rosies? eh, taking control of them.
So I'll talk a bit about the Plasmids too, to be honest they seem like a mechanic that wasn't fleshed out in time, I only ever used 3 Plasmids (except when the game forced me to use other ones to progress or for plot convinience) Shock, Big Daddy Hypnotise and the Swarm, Shock just so I could hack turrets, Big Daddy Hypnotise because it was fun and Swarm just so I could yell out "NOT THE BEES!" The Plasmids are just "there" I never had a reason to use them except of course For Fun, Hacking or Quoting Nicholous Cage (all of which worth it in my eyes, especially the last one) Outsid of that I pretty much felt there was no real use for them, No enemies weak to a certain Plasmid no Deus Ex style of using a Plasmid to get through a place. As for the Passive Plasmids again there was no real point in some of them, the only ones I generally wanted more of was the Hacking ones because as the game went on Hacking got so hard to the point where it was literly impossible to hack without a few hacking plasmids.
So lets move onto the Hacking...Honestly it stars fun but it gets boring, like REALLY boring This was basically how my Hacking excitement went
*Start of game*
Sweet! i can hack these Buzzers and turrets to fight for me!
*1/4 through the game*
Well Lemmi hack this Vending Machine, Cause why not?
*1/2 Through the game*
urgh.....Boring
*After the 1/2 point*
Screw this, Autohacking tool!
It just becomes so very dull that I was using my huge amounts of cash (Again because the game is too easy so i always had alot of cash) on Autohacking tools, and on the final chapter I just stopped Hacking the vending machines all together because it was so very very dull
Finally the Story *AGAIN, SPOILERS*
Honestly its a little bit all over the place but in a good way and ends mostly with closure, ok well except one, why the hell did your plane crash? but I digress the game does a good job at pacing the story up to the big Shyamalan style twist and makes Atlus a very beliveable friend which is all the more suprising at the end, Atlas as a character is a rather well developed character...untill near the end when he becomes Fontanie, he then spends the rest of the game mocking you from your com system and to degrade him even worse during the last hour I kid you not about an hour before you face him he suddenly becomes a spliced up looney, Personally that was weak because all it didn't feel like I was faceing the guy who set me up, i just felt like I was facing another Splicer Alibet a newer one, I would of liked a good ol fasion Gun duel and before you beat him he THEN pulls out a new plasmid he made to turn him into what he is to try and get the edge.
Overall Bioshock is a well made game and has alot of atmosphere, gunplay, and likeable characters, the things I don't like about it though is how the main villian becomes a Splicer loony like the rest of Rapture, The hacking gets VERY boring and because you can only game over at the final boss its very VERY easy

Yet another Kickstarter success,  this game is just awesomely bizarre from a lot of angles:
1).  The world is a alternate universe ancient London and nearby areas that fell from above ground to a great giant, underground sea
2). That world, the Unterzee, and Fallen London, is inspired by Cthulthu mythos stuff, and is in a Mythos-esque universe
3).   The game is a naval adventure that puts you at the helm of an ancient and hoary steamboat.
4).  You fight against other creatures in the Unterzee by maneuvering around and firing at them.  With weapons.
5).  You collect a variety of allies and NPCs for various roles on your boat, and some of them are....well to say seedy would be fluffing them up a bit.
6).  You choose a destiny at the beginning of the game and then try to fulfill it.
7).  In traditional RPG style gaming, you gain stuff, money, and crew.
8).  You choose the game you want to play.  There are a few runs you can do to make some money running cargo from one place to another.  But fuel, repairs, and food for your ship and crew can be pretty pricey.
9).  The game is pretty hard on you, and has perma-death normally enabled.   (You can turn it off).  There have been times I have done a cargo run, purchased a bunch of stuff, finished a quest and gotten my quest reward, and then only to have
after refitting and repairing my ship
10).  This game takes its time.  It's not some quick and fast game.  You move and fight with enough time to get things working and to prevent issues.
That's a pretty odd set of stuff for the game.  And it's a fun game.  The flavor for this game is just outstanding.  Sunless Sea has some of the best writing of any game I've ever played period.
And Flavor?  It's oozing with it from every single tentacle.  From the squid like humanoids to various eldritch additions to your crew, and yourself, it's good.  In various ports you have people, quests, exploring, allies, enemies, and more.  From stores to upgrade your ship or to purchase new ones, to buying and picking up some stuff for your crew and officers, there's a lot to do.  Make sure to keep your terror levels as low as possible too, by the by...
Get ready for a creepy, fun, slow-paced, game that really pushes Roguelike games to the next level in my mind.

Bioshock has now become essentially a household name in the realm of gaming, and you probably don't need my word on it, but here it goes.  Once upon a time there was a game called Bioshock that was a beautiful, disturbing, wonderful take on the dystopian effects of true freedom as it relates to anyone doing any type of work without moral or lawful restraint. Science, industry, firearms and more have created a havok-ridden world for you to explore, and what a dark, disturbing, beautiful and thought-provoking world it is.
Honestly, I only have one issue with the game, and explaining it in full would create some very unwanted spoilers for the late acts of the game, but suffice it to say that when the story is nearly at an end, they stretch it just a bit more, and it is this stretching, this needless extension of an otherwise tight and complete story that mars the presentation somewhat.  But this is a rather small nitpick in what is a compelling and entertaining shooter.  And make no mistake, it is a shooter, so if that isn't your bag, you might not enjoy the game.
However, I don't really dig “First Person Shooter” type games, and I am heartily recommending this game for all the people, so take from that what you will.

Anyone who's looking for a real 3D platformer should defenitely play this game. If only for the fact that it's something new we haven't seen yet because it's a new franchise. It plays less like Super Mario Odyssey and more like Mario 64 but is nonetheless a ton of fun. You can tell the developers really cared about this game. Sure it has some animation issues here and there and sometimes the camera will glitch out a little, but keep in mind the developers didn't receive as much money as say Yooka-Laylee did. The levels are all fun, the voice acting is brilliant (I actually adore hearing everyone's voice without skipping forward), a protagonist who you simply can't resist but to call cute! The soundtrack is on point as well. It's fitting for a platformer but has a lot of tunes where you just put the volume high up because it's so catchy. I haven't played it to the end yet, but so far I discovered three worlds and each world feels like a new thing without just copy pasting from other worlds. Those who are looking for difficult platforming sections will also get their piece of the cake as the game lets you play levels called "Time Rifts", scattered throughout each world where you'll really face some difficult platforming. Note that those levels are difficult, but not on Cuphead difficulty, so it still feels like a great and doable accomplishment to finish them.
To sum it up: if you're into platformers like me and miss traditional 3D platformers from the old days, there is no way you cannot buy this game. For everyone else, if you're on the blink of deciding Do I wanna get this or not, I can assure you, you get your money worth. A Hat in Time is brilliant, fun, charming and a memorable 3D platformer that understands what people want from a 3D platformer, whilst staying modern and fresh instead of focusing on nastalgia! I do not regret getting it in any way!

Playing through A Hat in Time made me realise that 3D platformers are rare nowadays. It's not an innovative game, and it's definitely not a long game but the game is both charming and highly enjoyable. Playing through this game gave off the same sense as when I played Super Mario 64: a bright and fun game that begs for you to explore it. The worlds are your playgrounds where you run around to look for stars or time pieces. There are only four main courses but each course is widely different from the previous one: a town, a movie set, a forest and the sky. Each world is unique, complete with collectables, challenges and boss fights.
This game is a celebration to one of the best era's of gaming while still feeling completely original and extremely refreshing. What's impressing about this game is that 3D platformers aren't easy to make at all. So for a small indie studio backed by Kickstarter supporters to deliver something of this quality is amazing, and there still working on adding more levels as free DLC. A Hat in Time is such a joy with its bright, cute, happy feel to it. It doesn't try to deliver a big story or do something groundbreaking. The game wants you to have fun, and it does this perfectly as every single minute of this 15 hour game has been fantastic.

You're a naval captain and along with officers of your choosing and a crew, you explore the stygian wonders of the sunless sea to unravel its mysteries. When the 'zee' takes you 'unter' you inherit your captain's fortunes and your next captain gains additional starting attributes and items if you fulfill certain requirements.
It's intriguing in its exposition-heavy yet understandable storytelling, prodigious in its textual output, ever-so lovely in its art design and mystical in its sound design. While enthralling in the aforementioned, it severely lacks in gameplay. It's not odious or bad but merely somnolent. If you're a strict gameplay centric gamer then I’d stay away from this. If you hate reading in your games then I’d stay away from this. If you can manage those two things and find intrigue in creative, fleshed out (Lovecraftian inspired) worlds then I'd totally recommend this... just don't get mad when you die half a dozen times in the 1st few hours.

A good snowman is certainly hard to build. This is a precious little puzzle game that successfully executed what it wanted to accomplish. Roll snowballs around and build them on top of each other to make a frosty, new pal (and don't forget to give them a hug!) The best part by far though is that each level allows for anyone's creativity to shine; there's no one way to build each snowman, and can be approached with multiple solutions. Not only that but the simplistic graphics are done exceptionally well, and there is much attention to detail with everything your character does, it's a real treat to see played out in the game.
My only one qualm is how cryptic the dream world can be, as it takes quite a bit of trial and error and lengthy guesses to figure out what works, but the dream world merely serves as a sort of bonus area so it's not required in completing the game. Overall A Good Snowman is a wonderful puzzle game that eases the mind and is perfect for anyone to pick up.

I enjoy this game very much, but i must say, if you don't play on easy, this game is gritty and challenging and instills real instinctual fear into you, something most games lack. The overall graphical design is beautiful in my opinion. The devs knew they couldn't make everything hyper-realistic, so they went for a cartoon-like design, which, you don't really notice unless you pay close attention to things.
There are some flaws to the game, mine being that you can't improvise weapons, i.e. swing your hatchet at a wolf unless it is already on top of you, and you can't hunt anything until you find a rifle or craft a bow, you can snare rabbits but i haven't bothered with that. I often find myself complaining about how often i feel fatigued so quickly and how a couple hours can't do much to restore yourself in the long run. But i then think that these factors that make me (irl) able to operate on 5 hours of sleep, couldn't be possible in a survival situation, let alone subzero temperatures.
But my favorite aspect of the game is the weight and pressure of risk that goes into nearly every decision you make. Such as, you may plan to go out and get firewood the next day, but tommorrow comes and a blizzard rolls in, and you know that if you dont get firewood you could freeze to death or dehydrate. I once choose to go out and gather a couple logs just to last me, and what seemed like 30 meters away from my home felt like a vast tundra. The weather can make it impossible to see, you can get lost, and wander into a wolf, and what was planned to be a simple run for wood, turns into a nightmare. Starvation leads to some pretty tough risks too. You may decide to go out to fish, and then get snowed in a fishing hut, with no wood and you freeze. Or you may take the chance of attacking a wolf in order to take its fresh deer kill, or even try to kill the wolf.
Every action has consequences, and those consequences can instill legitimate fear into you. But it is nonetheless beautiful and stunning and it brings you somewhat closer to mother nature, despite her relentless effort to kill you. It's gritty and real and I highly recommend it.
