Definitely one of the best Zombie games that i have ever played. It was also one of the first Indie games that I ever purchased. The game challenges you to survive for as long as possible, At first, the world is very similar to how it would be without zombies, only they are roaming outside. But as you survive, the electricity shuts off, lights no longer work. You must roam with a flashlight to cut through the dark Mudlraugh wilderness. Then the water shuts off, you must collect water bottles, pop bottles. Or construct a barrel to store some rain water. All while evading hordes of zombies, and risking infection in all of your close quarter battles. You are a regular survivor, every scratch and bite has a chance to turn you into a moaning, bloody mess. Sometimes a frying pan isnt enough to save you when zombies are breaking in through every entrance of your shelter. The game is definitely worth the $15, as i have far more hours on it than almost any commercial game if you count desura time, and the moaning of zombies is calling you to fight or die. However, a warning, when you get insanely addicted to this, and want more zombies, you will be disappointed by the other games.
Visuals - 9 for what its meant to be and an Indie
Sound/Music - 10, scary moaning and awesome soundtrack
Story - Not back in place (maybe never it seems)
Gameplay - 10
EDIT: While most of my review from Nov 2013 stands true, since then the indiestone team have implemented a full world decay system so buildings/roads Crack and break or grow over with grass and bushes (originally by a modder that joined the devs), implemented seasonal tiles (now there's snow!),  have redone the whole game in double resolution for when you zoom in, added a bit of the world meta events,  and added a great multi-player mode and expanded the map with a major expansion. However, game is still lacking the most requested feature of NPCS, and I feel underestimated the difficulty of adding such complex AI interaction. However, that is supposedly there current focus but if that's a deal breaker for you it's still not in...
Basically, If you can handle the isometric view this is probably the best zombie survival game that you will find and it does go on small sales  periodically.  This is what started my addiction to Early Access/Indie games.
EDIT: 3 Years later and they're still talking about adding NPCs but all we've really seen is their brain storming chart for interactions. Kind of sad this and Kenshi were one of the first Indies I ever got and 5 years later it's halted development. Honestly I don't think developers do anything anymore and it's just the modder they hired on carrying the project. Still a great game and I recommend it but it's jsut sad to see them working on easier stuff the community doesn't ask for because they don't want to release the challenging stuff like a story or NPC characters. I understand before they wanted it to be perfect but when Kenshi (a solo dev until the last year) is faster than a team, we got problems...
Basically its still an amazing survival game and really is one of the best zombie survival games. If you've ever watched zombie shows or movies and been like hm I wonder what I would do, buy this game for sure. But don't buy it for future content of vehicles or NPCs, buy it for once in it now. Still one of my favorite indies. Kenshi is very different but an amazing indie that's come so so far. Subterrain is another survival game that is great if you like Doom atmosphere.

A walking simulation personal journey that touches upon aspects of humanity that I imagine almost everyone can relate to at some level or another.  The game doesn't so much challenge the player's perspectives as The Stanley Parable did, but instead focuses on walking the player through experiences that might touch upon the player's own lives, thoughts or memories.  I naturally cannot speak for the sprawling mass of humanity, but I sincerely believe there's something in this game that will connect with you, whoever you are.
Gameplay is about 90 minutes, and as you'd expect, beyond re-experiencing the sensations the game attempts to deliver, there's no reason to come back to it upon completion.
The game gets a little ham-handed at times when delivering its narrative.  Those who cannot suspend disbelief may struggle to immerse in the experience being delivered.  Despite this, the game will leave an impression on you that will leave you thinking about it after you've shut it down for its one and likely only run.
As painfully cliche as it sounds, to say more is to say too much.  If you're interested in exploring a unique take on a "Slice of Life" interactive experience, if you are a fan of games like The Stanley Parable or Dear Esther, or if curiosity has simply gotten the better of you, purchase this game.

This game is really a lot of fun. Well, it can me. You see the game has some major flaws that are just virtually impossible to get around. The game has a good amount of working elements that let you build up a thriving city or town but the problem really is the massive amount of micromanagement when your town starts to expand.  It makes the game almost unplayable once the town starts to grow.
For example, you have a good area to your east that is ideal for fishing, you have set up a nice little area to your south for some early game hunting and gathering for food, herbs and firewood, have some farms up to your north and some hills which you are using for mines to your west. City in the middle. Now you manage to run out of your natural resources in your immediate area, so you need to get a bit more which of course means further away. Now you can literally have people starve to death or freeze to death while walking the road. You can build houses near the new resources but then you need to micromanage every person. Which person(s) live in a house, where they work etc. Now that is doable with a small population, but once you get to 50 odd people, the life/death rates means that at any given time, a person working in a quarry may die. Then the game automatically picks a new person to take that job, he might be on the far side of the map, he starts walking over, his home is on the far side of the map, so he will almost certainly freeze or starve to death. That just makes the game really hard to enjoy when the AI is so stupid. There is no way to create city/town zones. Like for example assigning an area a town name which makes only units from that town work there.
I really enjoy the game nonetheless but after a while, you just start modding it to death. New buildings, houses, everything but there is no progression. You can build everything from day 1. Most people say you need to stick with wooden houses at the start but I tend to have everybody living in their best accomidations within a year or two in game which then just means I am trying to keep a bunch of freakin ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI units alive by preventing them from following the actual AI. Makes it relatively fun to set up a village but then once you get over that initial hump and it becomes a game of sustainability it really just means you are now fighting against the AI of your own units instead of the environment and the resources.
So this game is really fun, it is hard to pick up and you might want to watch some tutorial videos on youtube first but once you get the hang of it, you should have a lot of fun for a while.

This is a fun little game similar to the Sim City 2000 of yore, with a tiny element of The Sims as well; you manage a town or city, and you have little people with names, and education status, and families. They have to eat food, wear clothing, sleep, and all those goods thing that little people do. You balance their needs with resource growth and development, harnessing the power of the land, your workers, and trade with the outside world.
Pros:
- When it's on sale, it's definitely worth the price.
- It's fun a lot at first, and then fun again in small doses after the novelty has worn off - it does have some replay value with randomized maps and assorted achievements.
- You can disable natural disasters, making gameplay pretty purely fun and non-stressful if that's what you're after.
- There are pretty much lots of ways to play, and it's easy to pick up as you go along.
Cons:
- The AI that controls your people is kind of dumb; if they live on one side of the map, and they work on the other side of the map, they are probably going to die in the winter.
- Rocks will crush all the wrong people to death.
- Lack of population control method; if you want to free up homes for new couples, you sadly have to evict old couples by shuttering their house and waiting for them to freeze to death (which is difficult to accomplish if you have good clothing and food diversity), so someone else can move into their house, instead of having ritual sacrifice, or possibly just living quarters for old people. (You need young people to move out of their parent's house to make babies and such, so this poses a real problem on maps with limited space and resources where you can't just make houses all willy-nilly and you end up with a large non-reproductive population.)
- $20 is kind of a lot if you don't love this kind of game/genre.
- Only 2 kinds of natural disasters, and they are wayyyyy too devastating to really enjoy.

(Note: I have barely touched this game on Steam, however, I have played it before, off of Steam - mainly the demo, which you should check out).
Gimbal is a cool little top-down (mainly) Multyplayer Spaceship Combat Game. Using a nice creation suite, you create your own little Fighter by dragging and dropping, rotating and such of individual modules - pieces of steel & armor, wings, weapons, energy/engine related parts... You have a lot of freedom to create various designs this way, both simple and complex, and thus create your own personalized Fighter - it may be good for long-range bombardment but thus be frail or slow-moving, it may be good for dogfighting, it may be good all-around... Lots of choices! Yes, of course, you can totally screw up too and make a barely functional ship, but doing that and then learning from it is obviously part of the fun!
The gameplay itself is somewhat simple: You control your own ship and, along with your teammates, battle opposing ships in various game modes. When it comes to the gameplay itself, you move your ship either by keyboard, controller, mouse. Movement and combat are quite difficult at first, especially if you didn't make the best of ships - but thankfully, it is still easy to learn and improve, and you will eventually become an experienced pilot - which is ever so satisfying.
Some important things to note: You can zoom out *a lot*, you can use your radar to detect enemies and allies (teamkills *will* happen), ammo is limited (or you risk making your ship too slow if you overload it with ammo) and a lot of the fighting can be relatively long range, since taking damage is easy - and it cause modules of your ship to fly off, thus, making it harder for you to control it and continue fighting. Obviously, this means that you will be smart to play it safe.
To summarize gameplay itself, I'd say that, for starters, you should play regular Deathmatch, with loads of bots (due to map size) and that you should use the 3 preset ships available to you at Rank 1. Given that constructing a proper and fully-functional ship can be tricky, this is the best way to learn.
It is also very important to mention that the game has a progression system, meaning that you will have to grind for a while until you fully unlock all customizable parts *and* increase your Ship Budget (similar to Call of Duty!).
Game modes, from what I recall, are mainly focused around your team and you fighting the opposing one in a simple Team Deathmatch - the kicker, though, is the fact that both teams have large Motherships/Capital ship. Depending on game mode, these are either your target or they are mainly an obstacle to deter you from diving in deep. There are a few more modes, all based around eliminating enemies, their Capital ship or Capturing the perennial flag. There even seems to be a "Race" mode of some description.
When hosting a game (online or offline versus the AI) there are a lot of options to tinker around with - the basic being, of course, score limits, respawn timers, as well as more game-specific stuff, like limiting the upper-level of Ship Value or - more interestingly - editing the weapons that the Mothership/Capital has. It is also important to note that the maximum number of players is very high - 64.
The game has simple but detailed and well-drawn sprites for the ships, as well as very nicely made particles and other assorted effects for ship movement and combat - it is satisfying to watch your ship "drop in" (I assume from hyperspace) and watch it glide into the battlefield, with nice little visual details emphasizing the speed at which it enters - and then later, once you actually start flying it, admiring everything from the thruster and weapon effects to the pretty (but simplistic, it's space after all) backgrounds.
I am not much of a music guy (don't pay much attention to it), but I don't remember anything particularly bad or good about the game's music. The rest of the audio is fine - I'd single out the satisfying sound effects that you can hear from some of the heavier weapons as well as from the destruction of (enemy, heh) ships.
The game options are fine and you can, of course, customize things like resolution, graphics, audio (note: No Audio Sliders, only a separate On/Off for both Sound and Music).
The game, unfortunately, has two (related) issues:
1. It lacks players for Multyplayer
2. It lacks a true and long Singleplayer mode to make up for it.
As it happens with small indie games that don't get exposure (If only someone *cough* TotalBiscuit *cough* had covered it), the playerbase is small or non-existent. The potential to organize a playtime via the Steam forums or something is there, but, still, you can't just jump into the server browser and play a game.
Thus, you are left to play versus the AI, which aren't of noteworthy quality. All of this means that, of course, the game doesn't have a lot of time to offer you...
For the end I'd say that this is a fun little game which is "ruined" by the lack of people to play it with. The aesthetic, graphics and audio are good, the gameplay is challenging and satisfying, the customization is present and very important, like any good Multyplayer game there are a lot of options to make your own personalized game server... But basically all of this is for naught given that you won't have anyone to play it with. As of right now, there are 3 people online!
Still, you can potentially have some fun with it if you just screw around with the bots. It's still really charming and satisfying to glide into the battlefield with your own customized Space Fighter, awkwardly fly around your teammates and try to shoot your enemies - and, as your mighty cannons utterly annihilate a teammate of yours by accident and as the silly AI bots shoot you and destroy your steering modules and/or thrusters, you can then revel in the silence and loneliness as your ship slowly drifts away from the battlefield into the nothingness (since the AI failed to finish you off), thus forcing you to suicide and redeploy. The pretty aesthetic and relaxing, minimal sounds only at to this weird calm feel.
Cool game, pick up if you want to screw around with it a bit or if you happen to have 10+ friends ready and willing to revitalize it.

I came home to a dead lover and a dead son.

It's like Amnesia: The Dark Descent with some of the flavor of F.E.A.R., and none of the puzzles or interesting physics. The mechanics are pretty simplistic but it's decently scary.
At least until you nail down how the AI acts - it doesn't seem to vary between enemies, similar to Amnesia. But whereas Amnesia only had three different enemy types (and only two of those even had models), this game has three distinct and interesting recurring villains (not including the final boss), complete with some personality and unique kill animations - as well as a smattering of mooks with minor visual variation and different voices and lines. So while their AI doesn't exactly keep you on your toes, there's at least enough there to keep them from being monotonous. However, the lack of any female characters whatsoever seemed pretty lazy.
Usually the stealth sections are a simple "Collect X number of keys to unlock the door to the next area," which they try to disguise by making the keys electrical generators that need to be powered to open a unpowered gate, or pumps that need to be engaged to get the water out of the room you need to go through. However, there were some parts that were legitamately interesting, such as wading slowly through a pitch-dark, flooded sewer while a giant clad in clinking chains that can move unimpeded searches for you as you hide behind columns and pipes you can't even see until you're within ten feet of them. I can't fault the game for its atmosphere.
I tried playing it on a harder difficulty than Normal and all it did was make it so I didn't have enough batteries for my nightvision, which is completely necessary in most parts of the game, at least at the recommended Gamma setting. Amnesia avoided this problem by making your lamp oil not your only option; you could light wall sconces or just see in the dark at a slow sanity drain. Technically you
see with no battery left but your vision goes to basically a foot in front of you if there's zero ambient light (aka most of the game), which is unplayable even when you're
in a stealth section with enemies. On Normal, I found the battery consumption/find rate to be a good, suspenseful balance.
I'm guessing higher difficulty is also supposed to increase the damage you take and the speed enemies chase you, which would have been nice things to be able to turn up independantly since after a while I figured out that they're all noticeably slower than you and getting "caught" and hit by most enemies on Normal often didn't do enough damage to really be a big deal. That was basically the end of being scared for me, but I still enjoyed the basic stealth mechanics. This is coming from someone who thinks the stealth sections in The Last of Us were fun and interesting (except for the lack of a quicksave), though, and most critics didn't seem to agree.
Also, the final boss is a D&D monster.
Overall, I give it a spooky/10.

I'll never forget how incredible the first 30 minutes of game play was to me when i first got this. It had been out for a few months by this point and incredibly i had heard nothing of the game other than a vague report from a friend it might be alright (months before it's release). The events of those first thirty minutes (trying not to give anything away here) quite literally had me sitting on the edge of my seat mouth open wide. It wasn't just the story, it was the immersion effect it had on me. Had a console version back then and played it through a few times.
Now owing a pc version i decided to have another wander through Rapture. Boy am i glad i did! Lots of things i remembered, plenty i forgot. But what really had me was how well it has stood up to the test of time. I just plain enjoy everything about this game. Graphics and animations are beautiful with creative level design coupled with dynamic lighting that really gives the sensation of being on the bottom of the ocean, even if it is a little dated. Yes there is a bit of backward and forward grinding to be done mission wise, but the story/tapes you uncover along the way i feel are worth it and help the overall story. All in all Bioshock is a classic and a fantastic 25-35 hour adventure.

One of the most scariest games I've played. I haven't been this happy with a horror game since the first few moments of Dead Space back in 2008. I nearly gave up 15 minutes into this game because the first hour is so damn scary but if you power through that one hour, the rest is easier on the psyche. I don't know how this game affected me overall but it did depress me quite a bit.
That said, if you really want a gaming challenge, play the game a second time in Insane mode where you can't save the game nor are there any checkpoints. If you succeed to the end in Insane mode, you're awarded the fittingly titled LUNATIC achievement. I got this achievement and it was probably one of the most mentally affecting gaming challenges I've undertaken. I'm not in any hurry to get to OUTLAST 2 but I will say I'm looking forward to RED BARRELS' future work. This game was a thoroughly enjoyable masterpeice in my opinion. However, it is possible that I feel so for not having played other horror games like Amnesia, Penumbra or the more recent Alien Isolation.
The DLC is also fabulous. It can be argued that the most monstrous character you encounter in the base game is Dr. Trager and I went into the DLC thinking that there is no way that the developers can top themselves in that regard. But they did. Eddie Gluskin aka The Groom took up it several notches. Dr. Trager only cut off your fingers but the groom wants a whole lot more of you. Just play the DLC too.

Clans is an old school hack and slash action game similar to Diablo. After playing for a while i managed to complie a list of good and bad points which i shall list, i shall point out the flaws and leave the good bits to the end to leave this review on a happier note;
Their doesn't seem to be any stratergy involved. There are three warrior classes and the "elf" class which is the wizard. and while i enjoy the idea of different fighting styles, there is the Warrior, the Barbarian and the dwarf, which is less cliche more boring when selecting a character, people who prefere long range only have one class and that is the elf class.
The lack of items. The game seems to try and make it out that there is challenge when really its just unfair, you get two lives and they go quickly as you get surrounded by more and more enemies, i got down to about half health when i encontered a mini boss. I thought he was some form of boss as he was hiding behind the statue so he got the first hit, and he did the most damage out of all the other monsters I fought, this lead to my death and i respawned and killed him, this rbought be down to four hit points left and he dropped a potion which brought me up to 11, i was thent asked to clear out a cottage (so my first real quest) where i found myself swarmed with no healing of any kind and i died again losing my last life and going back to the main menu.
The controls. The controls for moving are straight forward but attacking is the right mouse button which is odd and i was not told this so i had taken a few hits before i figured it out, there are interactable items within the game but there is little to no clue apart from a slight light up of the item. weapons do not have any sort of indication as to whats better or what it requires, there is an axe for example which requires two hands, i didnt know this untill i saw that i didn't have my sheild equipped anymore. There are also items in the game world that dont seem to have any use, left clicking (which is used for moving and item management) does nothing and the right mouse button swings your weapon.
the writing: this is a minor point but the spelling and wording could use some work it isnt bad but it doesnt scream "in your face bioware"
Now onto the good points which im pleased to say, what this game does well it does -very- well so lets get started:
Sound. The music and sound effects are brilliant and you get the right atmosphere that some games simply cannot achieve.
Introduction. the opening introduction is fully voiced (and voiced quite well i will add) and gives a very retro feel which made me feel quite excited to play this game.
Function. The game downlaoded quickly, had no problems getting it to run, and it ran smoothly with no obvious bugs or glitches, it seems this was a main focus of their time and it shows.
so i have listed three bad points (not counting the spelling and writing becuase what do you expect from a hack and slash diablo clone?") and three good points so its time to give my final verdict.....
I would -not- recommend this game on its own merits.

This game is really a lot of fun. Well, it can me. You see the game has some major flaws that are just virtually impossible to get around. The game has a good amount of working elements that let you build up a thriving city or town but the problem really is the massive amount of micromanagement when your town starts to expand.  It makes the game almost unplayable once the town starts to grow.
For example, you have a good area to your east that is ideal for fishing, you have set up a nice little area to your south for some early game hunting and gathering for food, herbs and firewood, have some farms up to your north and some hills which you are using for mines to your west. City in the middle. Now you manage to run out of your natural resources in your immediate area, so you need to get a bit more which of course means further away. Now you can literally have people starve to death or freeze to death while walking the road. You can build houses near the new resources but then you need to micromanage every person. Which person(s) live in a house, where they work etc. Now that is doable with a small population, but once you get to 50 odd people, the life/death rates means that at any given time, a person working in a quarry may die. Then the game automatically picks a new person to take that job, he might be on the far side of the map, he starts walking over, his home is on the far side of the map, so he will almost certainly freeze or starve to death. That just makes the game really hard to enjoy when the AI is so stupid. There is no way to create city/town zones. Like for example assigning an area a town name which makes only units from that town work there.
I really enjoy the game nonetheless but after a while, you just start modding it to death. New buildings, houses, everything but there is no progression. You can build everything from day 1. Most people say you need to stick with wooden houses at the start but I tend to have everybody living in their best accomidations within a year or two in game which then just means I am trying to keep a bunch of freakin ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI units alive by preventing them from following the actual AI. Makes it relatively fun to set up a village but then once you get over that initial hump and it becomes a game of sustainability it really just means you are now fighting against the AI of your own units instead of the environment and the resources.
So this game is really fun, it is hard to pick up and you might want to watch some tutorial videos on youtube first but once you get the hang of it, you should have a lot of fun for a while.

This is a fun little game similar to the Sim City 2000 of yore, with a tiny element of The Sims as well; you manage a town or city, and you have little people with names, and education status, and families. They have to eat food, wear clothing, sleep, and all those goods thing that little people do. You balance their needs with resource growth and development, harnessing the power of the land, your workers, and trade with the outside world.
Pros:
- When it's on sale, it's definitely worth the price.
- It's fun a lot at first, and then fun again in small doses after the novelty has worn off - it does have some replay value with randomized maps and assorted achievements.
- You can disable natural disasters, making gameplay pretty purely fun and non-stressful if that's what you're after.
- There are pretty much lots of ways to play, and it's easy to pick up as you go along.
Cons:
- The AI that controls your people is kind of dumb; if they live on one side of the map, and they work on the other side of the map, they are probably going to die in the winter.
- Rocks will crush all the wrong people to death.
- Lack of population control method; if you want to free up homes for new couples, you sadly have to evict old couples by shuttering their house and waiting for them to freeze to death (which is difficult to accomplish if you have good clothing and food diversity), so someone else can move into their house, instead of having ritual sacrifice, or possibly just living quarters for old people. (You need young people to move out of their parent's house to make babies and such, so this poses a real problem on maps with limited space and resources where you can't just make houses all willy-nilly and you end up with a large non-reproductive population.)
- $20 is kind of a lot if you don't love this kind of game/genre.
- Only 2 kinds of natural disasters, and they are wayyyyy too devastating to really enjoy.

The creator of the Beginner's Guide is also the man responsible for the Stanley Parable, one of the most interesting games to come out in the last five years. I will try not to spoil the Stanley Parable or the Beginner's Guide here, but to me, the Beginner's Guide just didn't resonate with me the same way Stanley did. There may be some mild spoilers ahead.
The best way I could describe the Beginner's Guide is the video game equivalent to Oscar Bait. It has all the makings of a unique indie title, but yet for me fails to deliver that unique experience. Whereas the Stanley Parable was a clever and witty take on game design, the Beginner's Guide would be the Stanley Parable without the funny narrator, witty writing and world interaction.  Even though I hate this term, it is, by all definition, a Walking Simulator. Is that unfair? Maybe.
Perhaps it is unfair to compare the Beginner's Guide to the Stanley Parable. They offer completely different experiences with completely different goals. Perhaps the blame is on me. I was expecting remnants of what made the Stanley Parable so great in this game, but they were nowhere to be found. What the Beginner's Guide offers is a short play through, clocking in at an hour and a half, that involves you walking from level to level while listening to the narrator talk about his very personal story. The story can be touching at times, but it feels as if the levels have a "look, don't touch" type of feel to them.
The Beginner's Guide is not the Stanley Parable. If you go into with that mindset you might like it more than I did.

In all these years hence recovering from Catholicism, a little game called Sunless Sea has almost convinced me to take up prayer again.
To understand how something like this could ever happen, let me spin you a little shanty of perma-death at sea, cannibalism, and the bracing agony of bungled quartermastery that would make Melville, DeFoe, Conrad, and Edgar Rice Burroughs either die of exhaustion from relentless sphincter-clenching or ejaculate to the point of death by dehydration. One of those.
I took a shiny, spanking-new Corvette-class ship out to the furthest reaches of the Underzee and surveyed a colony of ape-men building a zeppelin. Something about that must have whipped my crew to an existential frenzy (powered FLIGHT!? We have wandered far from God!) because the next thing I knew I was staring down the grimmest version of a Monopoly opportunity card I've ever seen: a mutiny that, if failed, ends the game, with two choices for quashing it--fighting it out tooth and claw (30% chance to succeed) and administering negotions (18% chance to succeed).
Somehow, I survived the rebellion, only to find that the mutineers had a lot of good reasons to die for what they tried to do. I hadn't brought nearly enough supplies to feed even the three surviving, misguidedly-loyal crew members, and no cash to buy more in any nearby port on this bleak♥♥♥♥♥end of cavernous ocean. At this point, the recent purchase of my new ship was looking a little more like a sunk cost for a literal sinking. We crawled back west, toward home, without the crew to move at more than half speed, with the light out to conserve engine fuel despite the roaring dark all around, and were soon forced to stoop to the indelicate task of eating one of the crew to keep what little remained of our wits about us.
It became a matter of judiciously choosing where to port next, either at a port I had intended to visit on the first draft of a long-dead travel itinerary to trade a ship component for supplies, or chance a detour that would guarantee one fuel and one supply item for the crew to eat. I chose the latter, unrepentantly brave as always. We coasted into port on fumes and were greeted by the wharfsmen with a single ration for the crew to split, and we cruised in relative half-starved comfort to the next port and took a sweet $250 for the resold ship component, and my horrifying gamble and only day as a competent ship captain was looking pretty good.
With restored provisions, we drifted southwest two days, cursing breathily and repeatedly as we desperately steered wide berths around pirates and abyssal crabs, finally chugging into our home port with a fresh salty scent, weeping scars, and ageless nightmares of eyes staring out from the infinite black above, muttering in unpronouncable jargon all the apocryphal horror a gaggle of human craniums could hold before eating a buckshot breakfast.

I dont know how to do reviews so here a good recipe for banana bread
2-3 very ripe bananas, peeled
1/3 cup melted butter
1 cup of sugar (can easily use 3/4 cup, or drop it down to 1/2 cup if you want it less sweet)
1 egg, beaten
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 teaspoon baking soda
Pinch of salt
1 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
METHOD
Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C), and butter a 4x8-inch loaf pan.
In a mixing bowl, mash the ripe bananas with a fork until smooth. Stir the melted butter into the mashed bananas.
Mix in the baking soda and salt. Stir in the sugar, beaten egg, and vanilla extract. Mix in the flour.
Pour the batter into your prepared loaf pan. Bake for 1 hour to 1 hour 10 minutes (check at 50 minutes) at 350°F (175°C), or until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean.
Remove from oven and cool completely on a rack. Remove the banana bread from the pan. Slice and serve. (A bread knife helps to make slices that aren't crumbly.)

Note: Review is fully completed
Telltale had it's ups and downs, but after they announced Batman I was incredibly excited by what Telltale could do to one of my favorite super heroes of all time and boy did they deliver.
Story wise the game follows more on Bruce Wayne than Batman and what happens to him when the caped crusader takes control of his life. It follows on how broken both of them are in ways and it's interested seeing what happens to Bruce Wayne when Batman takes control.
The first episode delivers on the thrills and exciting action you would expect from a Batman game. Also the game has some puzzle solving, where you have to put together details to solve a crime which was very fun.
Graphically the game looks alright. Telltales comic book style translates well for Batman and gives it a decent look which translated both well for The Wolf Among Us and Tales from the Borderlands.
Audio is strange, I had a few times where in the action scenes the sound would cut off, but overall it's pretty good.
Now for a few negatives I had. The story is a bit weak, but it's still enjoyable. Hopefully the other episodes are better.
Overall Batman Telltale Series is a great title and is worth it purchasing at full price.
Episode 1 Rating 8.5/10
Episode 2 Review:
Episode 2 Picks up almost as soon as Episode 1 wraps and again fallows on Bruce Wayne more than Batman.
We start to learn that Bruce's parents weren't the people we were lead to believe they were and we start digging deeper to find out the past of Bruce's parents.
So as Stated at the start of the review this again follows more on Bruce than Batman and how he copes with all the things crashing down on him while people accuse of being a criminal like his parents and it's really interesting.
This episode unlike the first one has even less Batman segments until the very end, which is rather disappointing since I really wanted to see a lot more of Batman kicking♥♥♥♥♥
In the end I can say this telltale series is still really strong and I can't wait to play through the other episodes.
Episode 2 Rating: 8.5/10
Episode 3 Review:
Episode 3 also begins right after Episode 2 wraps up and Batman now has to investigate what the Children of Arkham are planning for Gotham after he finds out that they stole a bunch of chemicals that could kill a lot of people.
Episode 3 is so far not as good as the previous episodes as the story kinda falls flat and both Bruce Wayne and Batman don't really feel like the character, especially Bruce Wayne who acts like a different person entirely from the first two episodes.
The action is again once you play as Batman, but this is the least you play as Batman which is again sad and I really think it should have a lot bigger emphasis on Batman, but Bruce Wayne again takes the reigns.
Overall this episode isn't really that good, but the plot twist at the end of the episode is what saves this from being straight up bad.
Episode 3 Final Rating 6/10
Episode 4 Review WARNING SLIGHT SPOILERS:
Episode 4 begins after Episode 3 and Bruce Wayne is placed in Arkham Asylum. With everything crashing down and Lady Arkham's plans coming together and Penguin taking over his life Bruce has to make difficult choices to save the day and any cost.
Episode 4 is rather good as it finally passes the spotlight to Batman which two great scenes and this episode is rather dark in content as the drug that injected Bruce at the end of Episode 3 shows his darker side emerging.
Also Episode 4 has a great, but rather small cameo from the clown prince of crime himself JOKER. He steals every scene he's in and it's absolutely great and I really want him to appear in the final episode or in Season 2 if that ever happens.
In the end this penultimate episode is great and I can't wait to see how everything wraps up in the final Episode.
Episode 4 Final Rating: 7/10
Episode 5 Review:
Episode 5 begins as soon as 4 wraps up, after the events leading up to the ending of episode 4 Gotham is turned into a war zone between factions and as Batman/Bruce Wayne you have to make tough choices to save the day.
This Episode is great, but it has one massive problem, which I will talk about later.
First of all the episode has great action scenes as Batman, where you kick major♥♥♥♥♥ This episode also has great segments for Bruce which up to this point I felt he was quite boring and his best segments sort of bland. This episode founds a great mixture of both of them showing everything you want to see out of both of them.
Story wise it wraps up almost every loose end, but this is where my problem comes up. The ending is a big middle finger if you hoped for a satisfying conclusion and it ends in the generic telltale way where there's a cliffhanger and it's probably never gonna get resolved like Tales from the Borderlands, Minecraft and The Wolf Among Us.
Episode 5 Rating 8/10
So now I'll go over the entire season:
Overall the season is good. The characters and story are interesting enough to warrant a couple of playthroughs.  Batman is bad♥♥♥♥♥and Bruce is interesting enough you want to see how he deals with being Batman.
Is it the best telltale game ? Hell no. It's probably the best telltale game since Tales from the Borderlands. Hopefully if telltale make season 2 it won't have a cliffhanger ending.
Final Season 1 Rating: 8/10
Pros:
+ Batman and Bruce Wayne are both fantastic characters
+ Story is insanely intriguing
+ Graphically looks great
+ Joker
Cons:
- The ending of Episode 5 is terrible
- Pace issues through the entire season
- A lot of visual bugs

A Hat in Time is the closest we have gotten to a sequel to Super Mario Sunshine, thats including Oddessy. The hat power ups remind me of the different flood nozels, it has secret levels that have much more geometric and challenging platforming, The levels tend to have a strong feeling of being a 'place' and not just a bunch of platforming objectives. The Different missions within the levels drastically change the layouts and what you need to do. All of this is just Amplified by how funny and original the game is. World Two in Particular, Dead Bird Studios, was more interesting and varied than many full games. It goes from being a stealth mission, to a murder mystery, to a celeberity fame tour, to a race against the clock on an exploding train, to shooting a musical, to undercovering a conspiracy to rig an award ceremony. If this sounds like its absolutely nuts; it's because it is.
Don't even get me started on the bosses either. I think AHIT has the best bosses of any Platformer i have ever played, they honestly remind more of World of Warcraft raid bosses than the traditional " hit the red spot 3 times" bosses you usually see in a Platformer. They have multiple phases (the second boss has like 5 or 6), tons of mechanics that you need to dodge, and are just generally engaging.
As a side note I also want to say the voice acting in this game is entertaining to say the least. The main antagonist of world 3 in particular made me crack a smile every time he started on one of his tirades.
I really only have two criticsms of AHIT and they are that the character models are a little PS2 era looking, it's a kickstarted indie game so i am not too bothered by this but a few of them are really rough looking (Cooking Cat comes to mind). Thats not even saying the graphics as a whole look off, the environements / effects are very good looking and detailed. Its just the character models that are a little off. The Other complaint is its also a little on the short side. With only 4 worlds (and a 5th that's just a boss fight, Think Carona Mountain in SMS) the game goes by pretty quick. Once again its a kick started indie game thats $30 and the worlds we did get are pretty large and are full of interesting different subzones, so i can't complain. But a true 5th world would have been very welcome.
I couldn't reccomend this game more, I ussually don't binge through games anymore but I more or less played this one in all of my free time until I beat it. I am just so happy that 2017 had this massive revival in 3D platformers. Yooka-Laylee, Super Mario Oddessy and A Hat in Time were all Great additions (ok ill be honest Yooka-Laylee is too much of a nostalgia trip and needed to focus more on being fun and less on being nostalgic but thats neither here or there). And on top of that there was also the Crash Bandicoot Remakes and even some not so good games like Knack 2 and Super Lucky's Tale. I hope this continues in the future because i missed this genre so much in the last 10 + years when its was completely dead.

Very dated but surprisingly good.
Dont be fooled by the description, this game has nothing in common with Diablo.
You move by mouse clicking. The map is divided in small isometric areas (rooms) and you move from one to another by clicking on the red arrows at the edge of each area.
The rooms/areas can contain enemy mobs, treasure, npcs...or nothing at all.
These areas form a sort of maze that you have to explore in order to find treasure, key items....or a fast death.
There are puzzles that have to be solved in order to advance, and these puzzles are quite nice, a little bit in the style of point and click adventures.
Surprisingly the graphics look nice because of the decent filter (scanlines), something that is rare nowadays when it comes to re-releases of old games.
The game is very tough at least in the begining, but you can save anytime.
It was an odd game when it was released 15 years ago and its an odd one now, you have to burn the music from the game folder on a CD and have that CD inserted for the game to use the music. Quite a pain by today's standards, but the neat gadget is that you can use any music Cd and the game will use the music from it.
This game is not bad at all especially for the price. If you can look past the antiquated controls and interface and past the harsh difficulty level, you have a nice old-style rpg with a rather unique concept.
Matter of taste of course, but i was pleasantly surprised by this title.

First, I worked for Origin, developer of Ultima and Wing Commander series, plus more, in the early to mid-90's. Love old-school games, so the age of this game, 1999, is not relevent. :f2_happy:
I was a beta-tester on several old-school games, having an eye for such games. I also did tech and hint support. With the responsibilities of hint support, I played many of the earlier, early to mid-80's, games which most, if not all, other fellow employees had no experience. Some of those earlier games kinda bit it as far as being good games.
I have played MANY games from other companies. Many were good to great, quite a few were awful. I have played some of those not-so-good games seeing that they were just that after playing for a short span of time. Continuing to play some of those, I backed up my initial impressions.
As far as what I had seen of this game was extreme small grids for the character to traverse. There are limited number of grids to a location, and approx 1/2 in a "random" pattern giving the impression of a large area.
And, using the age of this game, 1999, this is pitiful when compared to other games definitely from that time period and earlier. Just to put a comple games up for inspection: Ultima VI (1990), VII (1992-3), and VIII (1994) -- each with completely separate game-engines; Baldur Gate I (1998) and II (2000) -- same game-engine; the two Crusader non-FPS shooter-games (1995-6) -- same engine; more I could look up if I was so inclined.
The games listed above were either top-down (U6) or isometric (the remainder) game-engines. None of these games relied on grids similar to what Clans used. Yes, Baldur Gate games used seperate areas but in a more playable format.
Combat is OKAAAY, but should be better, again looking at the age of the game. One problem with combat, the availability of health potions.
If you want further reasons why I dislike this game for your edification, ask. :happycthulhu:

Bioshock is one of those games that is eerily difficult to forget. I think that the next genration will look back and say it is was classic.
Bioshock is a story driven first person shooter with slight RPG and survival horror elements. You must navigate the underwater city of Rapture, which has become run down and dystopian due to the widespread use of addictive genetic enhancement drugs.
The atmopshere is one of the best things about Bioshock. For a game where you posses the ability to destroy your enemies, it is quite creepy. This is pretty much owed soley to the atmosphere. The world of Rapture is opressively quiet and dark, and dead bodies splattered with blood warn of doom. Sometimes, the enviorment tries to scare you: perhaps a body falls from the ceiling right in front of you or splicers (drug adicts who try to kill you and the games' main enemies) whsiper at you from the shadows.
Even the awesome atmosphere takes a backseat to the story. Bioshock's narrative is much more complex than your average shooter which will keep you engaged and make you actually care about what happens next. There will be epic plot twists that you won't see coming. And the main villian, Andrew Ryan, the creator of Rapture, is one of THE most charismatic and entertaining villians of all time. This really adds polish to an already amazing narrative.
The gameplay is really unique for the genre as well. While it is a shooter for sure, it has small bits of other genres too. Exploration has a big importance, similar to old-school shooters. If you need more ammo, you have to go and look for it very methodically. If you don't conserve your ammo well enough, well that's too bad, and you may die because of it. You will also feel alone and vulnerable the entire time. In this respect it is like a survival horror. However, there are RPG elements as well. You will encounter little sisters, which are girls that have been experimented on to produce ADAM, the genetic enhancement drug that the people of Rapture have become addicted to. You can cure them, or kill them and take their ADAM, which will determine how much ADAM points you get. ADAM will allow you to make genetic modifcations to your character, increasing stats, adding tonics (which function like passive bonuses), and learning new powers called Plasmids. The combinations of upgrades are limitless, thus making Bioshock a step above almost all other shooter games. No two playthroughs will be the same.
Lastly, the setting is particularly creative. Dystopian cities have been done before, but never underwater, and never with this type of subject matter. The technology has a different spin than typical sci-fi games, in the way that the technology is a mixture of futuristic and 1960's. It reminds me of Fallout, but Bioshock puts a bigger emphasis on the "old school" aspect. And the genetic enhancement theme is creative and hasn't really been done before either. I find Bioshock's setting and style to be really captivating.
Bioshock is cross-genre and doesn't hold your hand. It is a difficult, but rewarding game to play. Its game mechanics are one of the most creative and interesting you can find in a game, and we haven't seen anything as clever since. If you love horror, survival horror, shooters, or even just like a good narrative, Bioshock will exceed your expectations. It is a game that is unforgetable. 10/10, no doubt.

BioShock is one of those games that is still enjoyable to play despite its flaws. Like System Shock 2, BioShock takes place after things have gone south. It does a great job of establishing this eerie and disturbing world by revealing what exactly happened through audio logs strewn across Rapture. The combat is fun, but the aiming personally feels inaccurate and the gunplay is a bit wonky. The sheer satisfaction, however, of using Plasmids helps compensate for this and the severe lack of enemy diversity (there's really only three enemy types in the game).
BioShock is worth playing just for the story alone. It isn't as grandiose as BioShock: Infinite, but it is still very well told and many of the characters you come across are insanely fascinating. This is a great game. Don't hesitate to buy it.

Blood Bowl 2 (Vanilla) is a solid game for the player looking to learn Blood Bowl. While the AI can be brutally and entertainingly stupid, it still does a solid job of emulating a board game through a video game. While luck can sometimes never be on your side, it still is an enticing game to play.

Positives: This is one of the best WWII games. It gives you a real war experience. At first it is quite frustrating because you get killed quite a lot without even seeing anybody from the enemy team, but as you work your way through the game mechanisms and learn how it works it becomes a huge fun. And as a bonus the devs are really making their best with updates, even bringing new things into the game like armored transporters and weapons.
Negatives: Not much to say really, maybe some minor bugs and flaws which occur from time to time but the devs are always up to the task repairing those issues. One of the drawbacks may also be that if you are new player its not that easy to play at first, you really need to learn the basics and I certainly recommend to play the tutorials in order to do so.

This game really is a love letter to the GameCube-era 3D platformers of my youth. Being inspired by some of my favorites like Super Mario Sunshine, how could I resist?
A Hat in Time is literally cuteness and fun incarnate. Every chapter and every act is colorful and filled with personality, and the levels themselves are huge too (Alpine Skyline, my god). I found myself spending an enormous amount of time speaking with NPCs and searching around for hidden collectables, and was rewarded basically every single time. Finishing the acts were merely an afterthought considering how much fun I was having just exploring.
The game controls just fine, and it's as basic as you can get. Think of it as a more lightweight Mario with far more midair mobility. Hats and badges do add more to diversify that though, like the Hook Badge which can allow you to swing in midair in certain places and the Dweller Mask that lets you turn some nearby objects into solid platforms to find secrets. It's very easy to pick up and play, and you'll quickly get accustomed to the upgrades. My only small complaint is the camera being a bit obnoxious sometimes, but it actually doesn't get in the way that often.
For the most part, the bosses were relatively easy. The patterns were incredibly simple and I felt like these might've been the weakest part of the game in that regard, but they had enough personality to keep them just as enjoyable anyway.
The soundtrack, well, yeah. It's really great. My personal favorite is the Snatcher's boss theme.
I had a ton of fun with this game. I highly recommend it if you're into 3D platformers, or platformers in general. It reminded me why those games got me into gaming in the first place.

Or skip dialogues, in which case you'll mess up your character's future pretty quickly. For your travels you need fuel, supplies and a crew, whose fear level is constantly increasing while you're at sea. This means that you can only be away from the starting location (Fallen London) for a very limited time, before you have to return to resupply and lower fear levels. You can do all of this outside of London but it will be considerably more expensive and getting money is very slow and very grindy.
Others have said that the easiest / most effective way to acquire money is to do stories and explore but so far this hasn't been true for me at all. I've explored whenever possible, did all the stories I could, visited ports many times and the main part of my income stems from delivering reports to the admirality and doing smuggling runs, both of which are easy but very repetitive and uninteresting.
Combat is somewhat tedious and not rewarding at all, as you'll just get your ship damaged, which will cost you money to repair, and hardly ever get anything good out of it (mind you that I am not very far into the game however).
The story and quests are surprisingly well written and manage to turn ridiculous-sounding stuff into an actually compelling universe, that just begs to be explored. The atmosphere is great as well. It's dark, eery and at times macabre. It unfortunately also tries very hard to be PC, which doesn't exactly suit it well but it still works for the most parts. Unfortunately the sheer amount of text, despite being well-written, tends to get annoying as it further slows down a game that already progresses at snail speed.
Now, I honestly wouldn't mind the game's being so slow if I knew that my progress actually meant something. The thing is, it's a roguelike (or -lite, I guess) and you can die at any time, pretty quickly and lose pretty much everything you've done in hours of creeping the Underzee. The game tries to mitigate this with a system that lets future captains inherit some of the things your - now probably dead - previous captains possessed, which in itself is a great idea. The problem is that it's far too limited and requires ♥♥♥♥♥ons of effort to even get anything useful to the next game. To get any sort of money to your next character you have to craft heirlooms and write a will, the former requiring lots of materials that are hard to find. The heirlooms are also limited and in terms of stats only a very limited amount of selected stats will be transferred. It all makes sense in game and is fairly well thought out but it still doesn't make up for losing hours upon hours of progress and having to start all over again, reading the same texts, facing the same challenges, having to grind money again and so forth.
Eh... Maybe I'm just being a crybaby over all of this. Honestly, if I were in a different mood I might actually enjoy this game quite a bit. It's basically an overlong, interactive book (a quite decent one at that), I just wish the gameplay parts would make up for the massive amounts of text and not slow the game down even further. If you want stuff to happen in your games, see your character's progress and actively do stuff, don't buy this game. Or bring a lot of patience, because if it actually changes mid- to late game, you still have to get through many hours of slow grinding before you get to the actual cool bits.
If you are up for a book in disguise, that lets you do stuff sometimes and don't mind repetitive tasks, this game is for you. The atmosphere is great, the world is interesting, the game is well-written, it looks nice, it sounds nice and is basically a romantic sailor's dream (or nightmare) come true.
Can't really give a recommendation or not, it simply depends on what you're looking for in this game.
Oh, also the soundtrack is absolutely brilliant. Unfortunately it doesn't play all that often.

Okay, let's get this out of the way - I enjoyed this. You're going to have trouble believing it if you read this review to completion, but I did enjoy it.
That doesn't mean I recommend it, though. Maybe if it was free, or only $2 or so, but ten bucks is steep for such a short and odd experience. I'm not sure how else to explain it. I got it on sale over the holidays, and I feel fine with the price I paid.
Since this sort of thing seems popular on Steam, let's cover pros and cons:
PROS:
+Interesting ideas and presentation
CONS:
-Much of it is plain ugly to look at
-It's flat-out pretentious
-There's virtually no player interaction, which would be fine at this price point if it weren't also...
-Very short and...
-Has absolutely no replay value
This is, at it's heart, a so-called "Walking Simulator" - a description I use without rancor or intent of dismissal/insult. I like walking simulators when they're well done and expansive. Gone Home is one of my favorite experiences, where every step takes you deeper into the story. In that game, even the littlest details (like rejection letters and shopping lists) add verisimilitude to the experience. The Beginner's Guide? not so much.
The game is presented as a tour of a "game" designer's past, private work. I put game in quotes because most of the presented work can only generously be described as a game. "Slightly Interactive Art" is a better description for most of it... which would be fine if  could understand the narrator's fascination with the stuff. I can't.
With only a few noteworthy exceptions, the presented levels are mundane and unintersting. At best, they are pleasently weird. The narrator's insistance of deeper meaning doesn't mean it's there. The eventual outcome of the story isn't well foreshadowed, and therefore seems to come out of nowhere. Furthermore, once you've experienced it once, there's no reason to go back for more - you pretty obviously got everything the first time you played through.
In short: PLay The Stanley Parable, Gone Home, or Dear Esther instead - they're all much better than this.
**SPOILERS - TURN BACK NOW**
So, the narrator is the unreliable sort. The Unreliable Narrator is a trope in fiction, and while it's not overly common, it it common enough to have a specific name. There's nothing particularly interesting in it's use here, and it winds up just feeling weird: with almost no foreshadowing, it comes out of nowhere, but it still manages to be completely unsurprising. The so-called "door puzzle" in the game isn't a puzzle at all, but the developer was so proud of it it's repeated four or more times... which is kinda "whatever," if it weren't for the pretentious attitude of the narrator, portaying it as some deep metaphysical statement. It's not. It's a switch hidden on the back of a door.
Essentially what I'm saying is that I liked the experience, but it's not worth ten bucks. It's not even worth five, really. From the guys who brought us the Stanley Parable (a magnificent game with an almost shocking level of hidden depth and a wonderful story), this is dissapointing.

A Hat in Time - A Timeless Classic.
This isn't a cheap nostalgia trip down memory lane, there is something special about this game, something magical.
A Hat in Time is a loveletter to the 3D platformers of old, Super Mario 64 and Super Mario Sunshine in particular. But not only does it pay homage to Mario in a charming indie package. It goes beyond your expectations and delivers an experience that in some ways rival the classics!
The game starts of in your spaceship which serves as a sort of hubworld, much like the Castle in Mario 64. From there you can choose from four distinctively different worlds, each with many levels, or acts as they're called here. Your objective is to collect enough Time Capsules to go back home. The journey begins with a fairly limited selection of powers and powerups for you to choose from, which come in the form of hats and badges. However, as you play you unlock more until you soon have a large inventory, somewhat reminicent of Zelda games.
Speaking of Zelda, the game looks an awful lot like a mashup between Mario 64 and Zelda: Windwaker. It's very bright and colourful with beautiful lighting. You even get a camera to take pictures with if you so desire. The music is deserving of a mention as well. It is gorgeous and packs a large array of genres to fit all sorts of stages and scenarios. I felt like it took inspiration from all sorts of games but in the end it's definitely its own thing. The game also features voiceacting which is well-acted and fits the characters well, the writing is very comical and doesn't take itself too seriously. If you prefer not to understand what they're saying (although you can still read their speech bubbles), there's even a nod to Banjo Kazooie with a badge that replaces all the voice acting with incoherent mumbling reminescent of the dialogue in those games.
I cannot go through the whole review without mentioning the controls. And I can happily say that I felt they were damn near perfect. You have a large amount of movement like in the 3D Mario titles, running and jumping feels fluid, and airdashing and doublejumping feels intuitive and natural. The only thing that really felt missing to me was being able to move sideways while hanging of a ledge, but I understand why it's not possible because the levels were not designed around allowing for it.
The camera almost never felt like it was a hinderance which is often the biggest flaw in games like these. I only had one part in a windmill in the fourth chapter where the camera didn't move exactly how I wanted it to, but other than that I had no issues with it. You can configure it quite a bit as well, so if you have any problems they should be easy to fix.
I could go on forever about how fun this game was, and how much it felt like playing a classic platformer for the first time again. So instead, let me simply reassure you one more time that this game is well worth your time and money.
I said at the very beginning that A Hat in Time has something special, something magical. And although it may sound cliche, I believe that extra something to be love. It is blindingly obvious to me that the whole team behind A Hat in Time poured their heart and soul into its creation, and they made something special. I think we should reward them for that, and play this Timeless Classic they have created.

Just cleared the game. The visuals and music are great, but just about every review will already tell you that.
The boss designs are very well done. It's a game of trial and error as you discover how to handle each boss mechanic. Being able to only fight the boss rather than trudging through a level each time really helps lower the frustration when mashing your face against a wall.

Also don't go walking into this game thinking it's going to reach the same difficulty as "Wings of Vi" or "IWBTG". Yes it's difficult, but I believe the community is overblowing it a bit.
It took about 5 hours to complete with around ~125 deaths, so it's a short game. This can obviously be extended by playing through the additional difficulties such as expert mode but the main experience for me was seeing all the bossess and the amazing visuals.
$20 for 5 hours of enjoyment is starting to brush the line, but I leave that for you to judge.

If you enjoy atmospheric platformers, challenging - yet intuitive - puzzles, and a grim/dark style, then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are great - although they are simple, the dark artstyle is very good at creating a desolate atmosphere during your journey through Limbo. For a 2D, black-and-white platformer, the death animations are plentiful and fairly gory - I was very impressed with the variety of deaths you can encounter. The sounds and ambient music are also good and help add to the vibe of the game. The way the chapters flow together is well-done, so nothing seems too ridiculous or crazy.
The controls are simple to learn. There isn't really a tutorial, as you learn everything slowly (the pacing in the game's difficulty is very well done, like Super Meat Boy). The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with puzzle platformers. A lot of the solutions are intuitive, and will eventually reveal themselves to you in a moment of insight if you just keep persisting and applying trial and error. The checkpoint system is very fair and well-plotted out - you will not have to repeat entire puzzle segments often.
The variety of puzzle types is fantastic, always added in at a reasonable pace. Many include item manipulation like moving boxes, carts, etc. Eventually, you will also have to plan around momentum - for example, you may have to push a cart down a two-way slope so you can climb jump off of it onto a higher platform. There is a fair amount of timing-based puzzles, but the windows for error are always good. An interesting element is this leech-type animal that sometimes implants itself on your head. When this happens, it will keep moving your character in one direction - you can still jump, slow down your pace, and push objects. Any beams of light will cause the organism to turn you around, and the only way to remove the pest is to reach a hanging animal that will eat it.
For achievement hunters, the extra collectibles are fun to look for, and trying for a no-death playthrough can be intense and satisfying if you manage to complete it.
Overall, the game is a lot of fun for anyone into the puzzle platforming genre, and the execution and presentation delivers a very nice final product.
Recommend!

Five Nights at Freddy's is a game in which you have the job of a night watchman in a pizzeria, what could go wrong? Unfortunately for you the animatronics seem to get a bit quirky during the night and roam freely around the pizzeria to prevent their servos from locking up. Make sure that these animatronics don't get into your office as they assume you are just a bare endoskeleton without a suit and will attempt to forcibly stuff you into a Freddy Fazbear suit, which wouldn't seem so bad, but the suits have all kinds of wires and crossbeams, and the only body parts that would ever see the light of day, would be your teeth and eyes.
In the game you must survive all five nights which increase in difficulty per night. You must stay in your office and use your monitor to check where those pesky animatronics are, and how close they are to your office. Use your hall lights to see if any animatronics are right outside, and if they are, use your doors to stop them from getting in. Also remember to frequently check pirate cove, the animatronic in there always was a bit different...
This game is truly a horror game, the creator has made an amazing job of making yourself on edge with all the tension that you get from the music and the creepy looks of the animatronics up until the point that they are right in your face screaming. The tension makes the jump scares even scarier and even if you see them coming, they will still be scary as hell. My only negative comment about this game is the fact that once players figure out a correct strategy, the game becomes incredibly easier, and the game does get a bit repetitive after a while, but apart from that, this game is truly one of the best, if not THE best horror games out there, and I would completely recommend this game to everyone.
Overall rating: 9/10

I'm sure you've all heard about how great Limbo is and that it is a excellent example of video games as art.  I can honestly say that those things are no ecsagetation.  When I first played the game, it left a lasting impression that not a lot of games have done already.  It's dark, depressing, and it makes you think about how far a person will go to protect the one he cares for.
The game is a puzzle platformer, but it mostly relies on environmental puzzles.  They are all set up so that you'll die a few times before you find the correct solution.  You have unlimited lives, so don't be afraid to expirament.  An interesting thing about the puzzles is that the character always dies a violent and often grusome death for every wrong move you make.  This discourages the player from making the same mistake over and over again and believe me, you do not want to see the character mutilated a hundred times.
The gameplay is smooth and simple.  All your character really does is run, jump, climb, pull, push, and utilize certain objects.  It's how you go about playing the game that counts.  Some puzzles will take many tries to solve, but they become a bit easier once you figure them out.  The art direction is hauntingly beautiful and the presentation looks like something out of a black and white horror cartoon.  There's barely any music in the game, which adds to the unsettlty.
The only problem I had with the game is the story.  You have no idea what's going on, other than that you're a boy looking for his sister in a hellish world.  Everything is told through gameplay and there nothing there to explain why you're here or why you're sister is missing.  The ending is very confusing, and it's up to you to interpret the game's meaning.  The story isn't really an issue for me, since the gameplay is all that matters.
Overall, I would recommend Limbo to anyone who likes puzzles and platformers or someone who likes dark and creepy games.  The gameplay is solid the puzzles are clever.  The art is amazing and the sound is unnerving.  The only downsides are the short length (you can beat the game in about 3 to 5 hours) and the confusing story, but other than that, a trip to Limbo is definatly worth it.

I want to like this game, but it's making it really hard.
The game is slow. Like, really slow. Everything in this game is slow as ♥♥♥♥. Your ship. Your character progression. Getting money. Everything takes ages. A lot of the time you'll be staring at your screen, while your ship slowly makes its way to the next port, where on arrival you'll do the second major thing this game has to offer: read. Or skip dialogues, in which case you'll mess up your character's future pretty quickly. For your travels you need fuel, supplies and a crew, whose fear level is constantly increasing while you're at sea. This means that you can only be away from the starting location (Fallen London) for a very limited time, before you have to return to resupply and lower fear levels. You can do all of this outside of London but it will be considerably more expensive and getting money is very slow and very grindy.
Others have said that the easiest / most effective way to acquire money is to do stories and explore but so far this hasn't been true for me at all. I've explored whenever possible, did all the stories I could, visited ports many times and the main part of my income stems from delivering reports to the admirality and doing smuggling runs, both of which are easy but very repetitive and uninteresting.
Combat is somewhat tedious and not rewarding at all, as you'll just get your ship damaged, which will cost you money to repair, and hardly ever get anything good out of it (mind you that I am not very far into the game however).
The story and quests are surprisingly well written and manage to turn ridiculous-sounding stuff into an actually compelling universe, that just begs to be explored. The atmosphere is great as well. It's dark, eery and at times macabre. It unfortunately also tries very hard to be PC, which doesn't exactly suit it well but it still works for the most parts. Unfortunately the sheer amount of text, despite being well-written, tends to get annoying as it further slows down a game that already progresses at snail speed.
Now, I honestly wouldn't mind the game's being so slow if I knew that my progress actually meant something. The thing is, it's a roguelike (or -lite, I guess) and you can die at any time, pretty quickly and lose pretty much everything you've done in hours of creeping the Underzee. The game tries to mitigate this with a system that lets future captains inherit some of the things your - now probably dead - previous captains possessed, which in itself is a great idea. The problem is that it's far too limited and requires ♥♥♥♥♥ons of effort to even get anything useful to the next game. To get any sort of money to your next character you have to craft heirlooms and write a will, the former requiring lots of materials that are hard to find. The heirlooms are also limited and in terms of stats only a very limited amount of selected stats will be transferred. It all makes sense in game and is fairly well thought out but it still doesn't make up for losing hours upon hours of progress and having to start all over again, reading the same texts, facing the same challenges, having to grind money again and so forth.
Eh... Maybe I'm just being a crybaby over all of this. Honestly, if I were in a different mood I might actually enjoy this game quite a bit. It's basically an overlong, interactive book (a quite decent one at that), I just wish the gameplay parts would make up for the massive amounts of text and not slow the game down even further. If you want stuff to happen in your games, see your character's progress and actively do stuff, don't buy this game. Or bring a lot of patience, because if it actually changes mid- to late game, you still have to get through many hours of slow grinding before you get to the actual cool bits.
If you are up for a book in disguise, that lets you do stuff sometimes and don't mind repetitive tasks, this game is for you. The atmosphere is great, the world is interesting, the game is well-written, it looks nice, it sounds nice and is basically a romantic sailor's dream (or nightmare) come true.
Can't really give a recommendation or not, it simply depends on what you're looking for in this game.
Oh, also the soundtrack is absolutely brilliant. Unfortunately it doesn't play all that often.

Overall I would recommend Blood Bowl 2 as it's one of my favorite games, but I can see where the disconnect would be for other people.  What I mean by that is:
-Individual team DLC's are
Just don't do it.  Buy the normal edition, or buy the legendary edition.  The prices of individual teams is rediculous and I don't know how they think ONE TEAM is worth over 1/4th of the ENTIRE GAME.  Or another way to look at it, 1/8th of the LEGENDARY edition, that includes all like 25 races and mixed races.
-The game is heavily RNG based, and ultimately you are trying to use your abilities and positioning to
that RNG into your favor...but ultimately it is still RNG.  You can roll two 1's in a row when you only needed a 2, and your opponant can then turn and roll two 6's in a row when he needed a 6 minimum.  Because of this, losing a game because of pure bad luck on dice rolls can leave you with a headache and sour taste in your mouth.
-The game has a lot going on, and throwing the turn timers into the mix it can be frustrating for new players.  The campaign tutorial will teach you the basics, but there are a LOT of abilities effects you need to understand and play around, as well as making your team correctly for the type of competition your playing in.  Add in the RNG from above, and it's really easy to get frustrated and blame the dice for everything, when you may have just missed an ability a unit has that is making it harder to make that roll.
-Getting into the game without friends who play is rough.  There aren't very many populated ladders besides the main XXL tourny, but you could be facing people much better than you.  Besides that, there isn't much else to do besides the campaign which was fun to start with, and fighting AI.  With friends in a custom league with them is the way to go, as well as the best way to learn if they are explaining everything.
Ultimately, if your someone who gets frustrated easily I would avoid the game.  But if you can handle it, taking the time to learn it is really fun, and watching a play you saw in your head unfold in front of you is so satisfying.  I know I put a lot of negatives up there, but I want to make sure you know what your getting into up-front.
