School of Dragons, at its core, is a very simple game to learn and to enjoy. While it doesn't have many features, and the ones that it does have seem very unpolished, I still seem to get many hours of enjoyment out of this game. (I would just like to clarify that I have had this game for two or so years, and I have had it before it became available on Steam, so the 30 or so minutes that it says I have is not accurate.) I can sit down with friends and enjoy this game in short sittings, but any length of time playing this game and it become very stale. Now, let's get into the actual features of the game, the good, the bad, and what should be added.
To start with, the game does have a few features that I really do enjoy. To start with, you can, of course, train your very own dragons. There is no limit that I have found yet to the number of dragons that you can train, but you must buy stables with in game currency, while it is premium currency, to keep your dragons in. The game gives non members one free stable that can hold two dragons, and after that you're on your own. Hatching and owning dragons is a very cool feature in this game, as it should be, because that it what the game is based on. You can color the dragons as you want and name them what you want (To some extent). You can create some pretty cool, unique patterns with the dragons along the way, as you gain more dragon eggs, a feature we will get into later. Dragons, like your character, level up with XP gained, but in this case, certain XP specifically for dragons. The dragons start out as baby when they are hatched of course, and once they get to level five you may turn them into a teen. This allows them to glide, but not yet to fly. They can fly once you reach level ten and turn them into an adult dragon. Speaking of leveling up, that leads us into the next positive feature of the game.
Stable quests is a phone-like feature that allows your dragons, besides the one that is currently active and walking around with you, to do quests in order to gain the non-premium currency (gold), dragon XP, and tamer XP. The tasks and time vary, as do the dragons that are actually able to do the tasks and the dragons that perform better in the given task. While it's simple at its core, it can lead to some very promising rewards, such as the premium currency, gems. Now, there is a catch. You can only send up to four dragons on each quest, sometimes less, and you only have a certain percent out of 100 to complete the quest. You don't have to do anything except order them to go out and do the quest, however, so no real complaint here.
Next up, we have the farm. The farm is a very raw feature that allows you to...well...farm. Simple as that. You can grow crops, feed animals in order to get produce, and decorate your farm however you like. Not much else to note here, except that you can grow crops to raise your dragons happiness, which affects how fast they go in races, and food, which gives the dragons energy to race. Speaking of racing....
Racing is the pinnacle of this game. It is the prime feature, and, while its not the best and could be better in some aspects, it's actually very good. It's as simple as it sounds; you hop on your dragons that you have trained up to the adult stage and race. There are some other factors that go into racing, however. Each dragon has their own unique stats, unique to the species not the individual dragon, which directly impacts how a dragon does in a race. The stats are acceleration, pitch rate, turn rate, max speed, and fire power. Fire Power doesn't really apply to races, so ignore that for now. Acceleration determines how fast your dragon starts out, and, if it gets bumped or you run into a wall or something of that nature, how fast you gain speed from losing all of your momentum. Max Speed determines the fastest your dragon can go at any given point, usually the higher the better here. Turn rate is pretty obvious, and pitch rate determines how fast your dragons go up and down. There are hoops to go through in racing, the normal brown ones which give you a significant speed boost, and ones that have green in the ring, which are checkpoints that MUST be passed through if you want to actually have any chance of winning the race, as, if you don't pass through it, you will have to turn around and go through it for your laps to actually be counted. There are, as in most racing games, mystery boxes, which can have shields that protect you from fireballs, fake mystery boxes, fart clouds, or speed boosts in them. Racing is the most polished aspect of the game, and is very enjoyable. However....
While racing is very, very good, one thing cannot keep people occupied forever. The game lacks anything outside of missions and racing, and has very little content if you are not a member or do not pay in any way. I'm not saying that this stuff completely ruins the game, as it is still very fun to play without paying, thanks to that of the battle event, an event that happens every two hours that allows you to get great rewards to keep progressing in the game, but other then that battle event, there is very little motive to play this game. A couple of my friends and I hop on every two hours in order to get the loot that is obtainable when you beat a battle event, but find very little else to do in that game. Racing is fun, but it does get boring after a while, as does everything. Also, like mentioned before, if you don't pay, there will be a LOT of grinding in this game in order to get much. While you don't have to pay much to get a lot, and while the membership isn't the most expensive thing in the world, it is still tedious to almost have to pay if you don't want to grind long hours. Like I said before, stable quests and battle events do help quite a bit with that.
This closing here is more of a plea to the developers, which I doubt will ever see this, but I really hope that you guys do, and, if you do see this, I very much hope that you guys listen to this. Your game is very fun. It is. But it lacks content. That's just the honest truth. While you guys have many dragons, with very good models, which I praise you for, I can't personally play this game for hours on end, and neither can many of my friends, which I would personally love to. There should be more types of minigames of sorts. I don't mean minigames as in the ones found within the expansion "The Secret of the Leviathan", either. I mean things such as actually being able to battle your dragons, so those that are useless in races aren't so useless here. Things like that could, and would, really spice this game up and allow for more hours to be spent enjoying this game. All in all, this is a very fun game to play in short sittings until more content is added, and I do recommend it.

Project Zomboid has been in development for a very long time and have endured a series of hardships such as a burglary and failed backup plan which caused a setback of many months. Bioshock.Well,i played BI first and then i tried this one,and i can clearly admit that i enjoyed this one way more than Bioshock
plot,strongest gameplay.I loved every second of my playthrough.I couldn't stop pressing F12,i took like 60 photos,because in every room,there was something interesting.A corpse,a painting,a quote,you know,these kind of things.Plus,this game got its creepy moments too.For example dead corpses which are not really dead,Or rooms with creepy stuff like,toilets with not-so-much-light,or weird statuary.Anyway,lets continue on the details.
1960, and you're flying over the Atlantic Ocean. One mysterious plane crash later, you're floating in the water, apparently the lone survivor, surrounded by the flaming wreckage of the aircraft. But there's a lighthouse on a tiny island just at the edge of your view.Your only chance is to get there.and so you do.inside,you find a submersible called bathysphere,which only purpose is to get you into the void of the sea.You don't have a choice,so you pull the trigger,the door closes,and you get down...down..There you find a secret city,underwater,named Rapture.An underwater city created by Andrew Ryan,with her own rules,her own freedom.However,everything has gone completely wrong.The city is vandalised,destroyed,and deadly lunatics roam the paths of Rapture.Apart from the phreaks,little girls named ''little sisters'' who contain the corrupting substance called ADAM move through the city with their ''protectors'' ''Big Daddies'',some people with a huge armor.
Character Customization.nope,i dont mean you can change your appearance,however,you can find ''magical powers'' which can be shot out of your fingers,elemental powers such as electricity,Ice,fire,wind,even BEES (no,not the bees).Those powers consume EVE(mana).You can use your powers to control your enemies against your other enemies,you can use them to gain control of machines such as turrets.
Also,you got a variety of purchasable talents,which variety from Engineering,Physical,and Combat talents.each kind of talents got a different use,for example there's a physical talents which makes you swing your melee weapon faster.You start with 2 slots for every category of talents,and you can purchase more from a Gatherer's Garden .
There are 8 types of weapons,1 melee,6 guns,and a camera,which doesnt deal any damage,however it is used to take photographs of your enemies,so you can learn more about them and find new methods of dealing with them.There are 3 types of bullets for every gun,the normals,the armor penetration ones (against machines and big daddies) and the Antipersonnel ones which are useful against lunatics etc. You are also able to find weapon upgrade machines,which will make your weapons more powerful.
You can hack vents,safes,or even turrets to help you defeat your enemies.There are 2 types of ''money'' the normal money,and the consumable ADAM which give you new powers or slots or even higher health.ADAM can be used on a different kind of vent,the Gatherer's Garden.You can consume ADAM from the little sister,by either saving them(you will earn less,however everytime you complete a series of 3 ''rescues'' you will earn a surprise),or killing them.Finally,You collect audio logs which help you understand more whats going on.
I cant say i went crazy about the graphics,however Bioshock got some nice atmosphere.
Easy Enough,however at the begining i got a little confused.
Incredible voice acting,making the game stick greatly with the plot.Great soundtracks,but the thing i loved about the audio,is the music which plays when you rescue a little sister.its both beautiful and cute.

Banished is a city building game wherein your responsible for the construction and survival of a small medieval village.   It's pretty typical in its mechanic: A set of buildings to construct, resources to gather, and a growing populace that needs things like food and clothing.  What I find sets Banished aside from the others in its genre is the emphasis on survival and basic human needs.
The gameplay and options are streamlined to focus more about trying to keep your villagers alive than it is about building up a huge beautiful city.  Basic needs like food, clothing, and tools are emphasized over civic projects and monuments.  Careful monitoring of your populace and their evolving needs will be mandatory since notification of a need usually means you are too late to address it before negative consequences arise.  For example, when the little food icon starts to appear, be ready for the bell to tole the death of a few villagers before supply lines can be properly restored.  Every choice has consequences.
In summary, the game is an extremely fun and highly streamlined village builder that feels more like a survival game than it does a civics game.

This game desperately needed a character hot-swap for what they were trying to do (turn the metroidvania gates into character specific obsticles). Instead you end up doing a deeply tiring amount of backtracking.

Excellent game with excellent writing. The levels are a mix of open worlds that give you a goal and let you figure out how to platform there, and more linear levels where there's really only one path you can take. The real magic however comes from the major differences between the various worlds you'll visit: their storylines and characters, and how the levels are incorporated into these. In one world you'll be doing chores for an evil forest spirit after you sold your soul to him, in another one you have to help two director birds who both want to win a movie trophy. The music is absolutely top-notch, Your Contract Has Expired can compete with Megalovania in terms of catchiness.
Unfortunately the game suffers from Super Mario 64 syndrome: your greatest enemy is the camera, which is constantly trying to reposition itself and gets in the way with the more trickier jumps. More than once I've had to make a leap of faith because the camera decided to move while I was in the middle of a hard platforming section and didn't have time to readjust it. Fortunately the game has much more to offer than just pure platforming, so this problem is not as bad as it could have been.

Metal Slug is a great, side-scrolling action game that plays a lot like Contra. The graphics look superb, the animation is very nice, and there are even some 3D effects. The game doesn't need 3D effects to look impressive, but given that this game was originally developed for Neo Geo hardware, the fact that 3D effects could be executed as well as they were is quite an accomplishment.
This port of the Neo Geo title is very good, but there are some instances where the game experiences slowdown that shouldn't be present on a PC. The slowdown isn't severe enough to ruin the gameplay, but it shouldn't be present and is a sign that the developers didn't go out of their way to optimize the game for the PC. However, the menus that were created for this port are all very nice, there is excellent gamepad support (I can use an original Xbox gamepad without having to map gamepad buttons to keyboard keys), and playing online in co-op mode seems incredibly easy. I say that netplay 'seems' easy because so far I haven't found anyone else waiting to start a game in an online lobby, but it's nice to know that this feature is available. I hope the netcode is reliable, because I'd like to play this game with a buddy one day.
Other than the aforementioned slowdown, my only gripe with this game is that there is a delay between the time you press the D-pad to turn around and your character actually turning around. Your character sort of walks backward for a second before turning around, which sometimes leads to death.
If you like action games and/or enjoyed playing Contra on the NES, I recommend playing Metal Slug.
ADDENDUM: Not that it detracts from my enjoyment of the game, but since Metal Slug is old, I think the developer should have ported all of the Metal Slug games together as an anthology rather than releasing them as separate games.

An extremely solid indie game in a genre I love, Magicians & Looters is a pretty easy game to recommend. At its core it's a platformer with (small-ish) sprawling, fully backtrackable levels (all the better to go hunt for any missing treasure) and lots of combat and exploration. The levels start out pretty linear but they start spread out as you unlock traversal abilities like wall-running, rolling and tall jumps (but weirdly enough, no double-jumping or dashes).
I... guess that's a long-winded way of saying that yes, this is a metroidvania game.
You play as one of three apprentices of varying skill with weapons and magic, which you can switch between in special rooms. They each have customizable equipment slots and unlockeable abilities - I actually needed to plan their builds for different bosses in my playthrough, and that's something I don't remember from other Metroidvania games, at least to this extent.
Most of the combat is weapon-based. Magic is important, but unless you equip some very specific items the energy regeneration is so slow as to keep it supplementary. The game handles very well (except for Brent's Wall Jump) and doesn't overstay its welcome at a breezy five hours or so (for me, at least and  that's exploring every nook and cranny for secrets.)
Finally there's a surprising amount of dialogue-based story to go through. The tone is unrelentingly goofy and even if the jokes don't always land, it remains likeable.

The game that started it all.
Based mostly on the Humble SNK Bundle (DRM-free) release of Metal Slug, so don't take my Steam stats too seriously.
To understand Metal Slug's place in gaming history, ya gotta travel back to the mid 1990s, when SNK rivaled Capcom in the arcades. In my late-teens and early twenties, I'd find myself bored at the local laundromat in St. Pete, Florida. To aleviate said boredom, it was a Neo Geo arcade machine to the rescue. Aside from Capcom's 2D fighting game offerings, there was SNK's multi-game cabinets featuring King of Fighters, Fatal Fury, Samurai Showdown, and...Metal Slug.
While consoles had the likes of Contra and Gunstar Heroes, the 2D side-scrolling shooter king of the arcades was Metal Slug. While Metal Slug's action was on par with Contra III (SNES) and Gunstar Heroes (Sega), it's artwork was iconic. At home Gunstar Heroes kept my ol' Sega Genesis arockin'. In the Neo Geo multigame arcade cabinets I grew to admire Metal Slug.
Fast forward to 2016, when Steam carries Metal Slug 1, 2, 3, and X. Most of these games have been ported to every platform from the Sony PlayStation to the PS2 to the GameBoy Advance to XBLA to Nintendo's Virtual Console to the Android App Store. With the Steam release featuring Achievements, Leaderboards, multiplayer, co-op, cloud saving and XInput gamepad support, there's no reason to not own Metal Slug.

This is the Metal Slug game that tends to be forgotten in light of its showier sequels. Though every video gamer probably deserves to experience at least one Metal Slug game, any will do, and this probably isn't the fanciest package. Still, this is a master class in sprite animation and enemy design. The generic thugs, given that they make up most of your foes, are given massively exaggerated personalities and exaggerations, from terrified screams when spotting you to hanging out around a fire. Tanks bounce on their suspensions, buildings collapse, point awards shimmer, and so on.
However, it's also a lot more "fair" (not actually fair, but more fair) than its sequels, and is generally friendlier about not putting the player(s) in bullet-filled corners. Mind, it's still extremely hard if you want to beat it without continues. It's also the basic gimmick that the others build on- the sequels usually have twists on the basic run and gun formula from this game. You die in a single hit, shoot in four directions, pick up weapons with different advantages, carry ten grenades, etc. Every so often you get an get into the titular "Metal Slug", a tank with a machinegun that can take up to three hits. Bosses are large affairs, though nowhere near what you'd see in later games. It's not long, being an old arcade game, but the game tries to beef stuff up with some extra mission modes. I see some talk of emulation issues, but I honestly don't think most of them are going to get noticed save by emulation enthuisasts; I don't notice them myself.
It's worth experiencing one Metal Slug game, and if you like that, pick this one up too... when it's on sale. SNK tends to overprice their old games at $8, unfortunately, but are worth it when you see it on Steam Sales or Humble Bundles.

It's wierd, but for the last several years, I have felt that there was a void in the gaming market where business/tycoon games are concerned. When I was a kid, I adored SimTower, The Sims 2 'open for business' (Yes, two Sim titles in a row, sue me), Zoo Tycoon, and (God Forbid) The original Mall Tycoon.
As an adult, I found each of the above titles neigh impossible to locate/run on modern systems. It really bothered me that no-one was releasing the old classics, or making a new generation of my kind of business managment sims.
Now we have Prison Architect, Project Highrise, and finally Another Brick in the Mall.
Understand, this game is in early access, as Steam should make you well aware. It's not finished. There are things that are ugly, things that are not terribly intuitive, and things that clearly need varying levels of polish.
But, by God, it works.
I can see that the developer(s) has the framework laid for what could easily be an epic business management sim. It's great to be able to design, manage, and oversee a retail/dining facility. Something I always wanted. I also connect with it, because as much as I love Prison Architect and Project Highrise, I'll never (I'm pretty sure) design a maximum security detention facility, or a skyscraper. But I have had plans for opening a retail outlet and a restaurant at different phases of my life. That being said, it has some elements that are inspired from the mechanics of both Prison Architect, and even RimWorld. And after a basic tutorial, it's not hard to pick yourself up and move forward on your own.
Theres no reason not to go ahead and pick this up and enjoy what you can. I like experimenting with different things, and am anxiously waiting for the big updates down the road!

Quite possibly my favourite game of all time.
BioShock puts you in the shoes of a man named Jack, his plane crashing in the middle of the ocean.  With nowhere to go, he spots a lighthouse.  Going inside, he takes a Bathysphere into the underwater world of Rapture, a city where the brightest sparks of society have gathered.  Quite quickly you begin to notice that, while looking pretty on the outside, the city isn't what it seems to be; non-existent morals and a civil war have turned this city into an abandoned mess, its inhabitants becoming addicts and constantly searching for the wonder drug ADAM.  Having to defend yourself with weapons made by man and superpowers developed by the citizens (fueled by EVE) you'll have to protect yourself as everyone comes after you.  The rest of the plot is more enjoyable to experience yourself so I'll just stop here.
This game is simply amazing.  The graphics still look great to me after SEVEN YEARS, Rapture itself still being nice to look at.  The atmosphere is fantastic and, for once, I actually gave a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the collectible items; the audio diaries you find are interesting and enjoyable to listen to, each one being a treat.  Combat is cool, the enemies are fun to fight, the characters are all extremely interesting, everything is a treat.  What the best feature was for me however was definitely the story of Rapture itself; a city gone mad, its leaders going crazy for power, a war tearing it apart, it's truly phenomenal.
One can only ask how a game can be made as a spiritual successor yet still define itself in its own way.  Then you get BioShock and you understand.

Banished is a city building game wherein your responsible for the construction and survival of a small medieval village.   It's pretty typical in its mechanic: A set of buildings to construct, resources to gather, and a growing populace that needs things like food and clothing.  What I find sets Banished aside from the others in its genre is the emphasis on survival and basic human needs.
The gameplay and options are streamlined to focus more about trying to keep your villagers alive than it is about building up a huge beautiful city.  Basic needs like food, clothing, and tools are emphasized over civic projects and monuments.  Careful monitoring of your populace and their evolving needs will be mandatory since notification of a need usually means you are too late to address it before negative consequences arise.  For example, when the little food icon starts to appear, be ready for the bell to tole the death of a few villagers before supply lines can be properly restored.  Every choice has consequences.
In summary, the game is an extremely fun and highly streamlined village builder that feels more like a survival game than it does a civics game.

An absolutely gorgeous game that is just spewing with style that no run and gun game's got. The vast majority of the game consists of fighting bosses in their own levels, with a few standard "get from point A to point B" levels (which are NEVER a walk in the park), this game never stops for a moment to throw another punch at you. Each boss has so much personality, it's absolutely iconic. Successfully beating a boss takes one to three minutes each (after finishing the first dozen), making failure an embarassing memory you sweep under the rug as you try and try again.
The controls are SUPER slick, super smooth, and very satisfying. Even the small range of additional weapons and passive power-ups you bring to each boss are great, helping you deal with a boss that positions itself in awkward tight spots.
My only complaints are bosses have randomized attack patterns, meaning muscle memory takes a lot more time to adapt to. This makes replaying the boss over and over yields different results, which can be good for difficulty and mix-ups, and bad for innexperienced players to intense platforming and bullet hells. This is of personal opinion, and not a fault of the game.
Overall, this game is an instant classic. I can't believe how far this game has come over the years in development. Absolute dynamite job, this game hits it way out of the park.

I made a mistake.  I clicked on an ad. The ad in the Steam sidebar said "Lose your mind, eat your crew." So, I clicked.

They wanted to tell me a story, and I wanted to drive a tugboat.
There is no "story", but an immense atmosphere. Nowhere else will I feel like a possibly-undead Victorian subterranean steamboat captain, on nodding acquaintance with devils.

So I start from Fallen London, with a flimsy vessel and HULL, FOOD, FUEL, SANITY ticking down as I fill out a procedural map of stopping points where I get "story" and "storylets" that I can't complete until I return to London, or cross to the other side of the map, roughly ten minutes.
Success in any challenge is based on stats which return to next to nothing on each playthrough.
Unless I’m super lucky, I’ll never be able to break the early game stat barrier.
Progression is painful, death is expected. The point is to keep dying and losing everything until you slowly gain enough to fail less.
I think the developers used everything from Echo Bazaar/Fallen London to make Sunless Sea; and could not separate from the “keep clicking and wait” model of browser games.

some quick pros and cons:
pros:

cons:
-Lots of micro/macro managment
-feels like you are running a town
-actually hard on normal
-no hand holding you have to figure the game out through trial and error
-the layout of the controls are a bit odd and it would be nice if you could change them around.

i really enjoy this game. for the first 30 or so minutes you have to be on top of things and the micro managment is very real. as the town grows though the game becomes more macro then micro once things are stable. dont stop growing the town though or it can lead to problems down the road but you can slow down the growth by a lot.
somethings i recommend:
-get an (12X12) orchard as soon as you reasonably can, i recomend the second spring time period to plant it. after it starts growing build a tavernand have it produce ale then stock 500 ale in the trade post when you get one. 500 ale is equal to 2500 "trade points" which is enough to get just about anything from most traders.
-when setting up a wood cutters hut build a hunting cabbin and either a herbalist or a gathering hut and one house around it. build them very close together later when you have the materials build one or two more houses there as well.
-always have at least one 5X5 (or bigger) stockpile and barn near your wood cutters outpost for quicker rescource gathering.
-dont stop building houses.
-dont ever build more then 4 wood houses in the early period of the game. the only reason you should ever build wood houses outside of the initial 4 should be for cosmetic reasons in the late game.
-build 3-4 wood houses and 2-3 stone houses when the game starts and clear the area around the start of rescources.
-never build a farm in your first year.
-build a fishing dock if you are close to a body of water in the begining of the game

The story is great.
Your ability to participate in the story... Not so much.
Telltale gets criticized for "choices that mean nothing."   I've never thought the critique was very fair.  Ask any English major: a story is more than plot points-- it's about characters, mood, style, i.e. the manner of telling. In the best Telltale games (Walking Dead season 1, The Wolf Among Us), your choices never dramatically change the plot, but they absolutely effect the tone.  You define your character in those games within a web of social interactions, and by the end of the story, the protagonist is yours and yours only, a hero created meticulously through hundreds of responses to different characters and situations.
(My Bigby was a forgiving guy... Who ripped some arms off here and there.)
Alas, "Batman" is not one of the best Telltale games.  It looks, sounds, and feels like Batman should.  The story twists and turns in all kind of satisfying directions.  The Rogues Gallery is big and, for the most part, well deployed.  It's an ambitious and well-presented narrative, and that might be the problem.  Telltale is so devoted to telling their complicated story that they forget to include you, the gamer, as a teller.
To reiterate, I don't expect to drastically alter the narrative arc of a Telltale game.  (Harvey is gonna turn into Two-Face, and there's nothing anyone can do about it.)  What I do want is choices that change who I am, choices that effect the way I am perceived by other characters.  You'd think that you'd have plenty of opportunities for such choices in Telltale's Bruce Wayne-centric version of Batman.  A game finally about Bruce Wayne's public image ought to afford many chances to shape it, right?
Unfortunately, your choices as Bruce are limited.  Of the four primary characters you interact with-- Harvey, Alfred, the people of Gotham, and Selina-- three consistently and stubbornly stick to the Telltale script.  "I'm a good man!" you scream... It falls on deaf ears.  "I'm a very bad man!" you yell... Again, no response.  Not that it'd matter, anyway: the spectrum of options you have rarely deviates much from that sort of black/white, good/evil dynamic.  You have two choices as Bruce-- good or bad-- and most of the time, no one cares.
As Batman, you have even less control.  A dark red herring occured in Episode One.  During the game's only sequence where your behavior as Batman can dip into true vigilante ruthlessness, you can choose to refrain from torture.  I did.  And what did the police of Gotham say in response?  "Batman!  Why are you torturing that man?"
What the ♥♥♥♥, police?  What the hell, Telltale?  The good/bad thing here is that such a failure to give a care never happened again.  You're typically doing two things as Batman: fighting through QTES, and performing "detective work" at crime scenes.  Neither of these scenarios is particularly engaging.  The fights look great-- again, this is a well presented little game-- but they don't require any skill to complete (unless, of course, you're running the game pre-patch, and every fight is a choppy, glitchy mess) and they never put you in the action the way Wolf's fights do.  In the Wolf Among Us, a missed cue did not simply mean an annoying sound effect or an instant death, the way it does in Batman: it meant a usually great moment of Bigby temporarily getting his♥♥♥♥♥handed to him.  As for the crime scenes, well, you're linking stuff.  You're drawing lines between things that are similar.  Don't get the right combination of lines going?  It's okay: this game won't let you fail.  You're at the scene until you "solve" it in the precise way Telltale wants.  Wowwee, it's fun being Batman!
Telltale's "Batman" truly has an impressive, compelling story, one that touches on classic Batman themes.  But I feel like a simpler story might have worked better as a game.  A story that wasn't so dead-set on certain twists being twisted might have given gamers the chance to craft detailed public personas for both Bruce and Batman.  A story that didn't have fights and action sequences going exactly one way might have offered gamers a chance to fail, and to thus create a character that wasn't quite as seasoned as the Batman of yore.
Alas...
Oh yeah, and the game is short.  Really short.
Still recommending it though.  I'm not sure if I even know why, anymore...

What to say about this game? I could be negative and list all the things that could use some improvements or are missing in this
game, but what good would that do to you or the dev? Nothing!
Look, this game came out on steam a couple days ago and is in a very early stage of development. So the game would have some serious issues, bugs or missing content. I don't care and you shouldn't either if you like building and management games.
I see a lot of people posting negative reviews about the game missing depth or content or even functions and I do agree with some of the list items I saw. But the thing is, the game is very new and for this stage it’s a wonderful game. You have complete freedom in your builds and management style. Is it fully functioning like other building and management games? No! It has some issues. But instead of complaining about those issues and saying it’s a bad game, send in your ideas to the dev.
I hope the dev is reading the reviews and doesn’t become unmotivated to work on this game. Because it has potential and is already fun to play. I hope the dev would see the negative reviews as feedback and an opportunity to improve the game.
Like I said, the game gives you complete freedom in building and management style already. Things that could use some improvements are rotating or moving the objects or overwrite an existing build (like the parking spots from customer to employee without deleting the parking spot first). The UI is something you need to get used to. It’s not all that obvious or user-friendly. After a while you will get the hang of it for sure. It’s just a bit different than you’re probably used to in other games (like prison architect).
On the other hand, the cartoons are funny. Have you seen an upset person? I have a cook who comes in every day completely unsatisfied. He has a red face! As soon as he’s behind his stove, he’s happy again and sometimes looking at his phone. I think he has no internet at his house or something.
I’m thinking that this game has a great potential and if we support the dev(s), it could become something amazing. But they need our support for that.
So let’s be clear. This game, in its current state, is a simplistic but entertaining game. You would be through the hard part of management within an hour. You can build wherever you want (on the provided plot of land that is) and you design your infrastructure as well. The UI needs some updates but is manageable.
I like to see where this game is headed. Maybe some funny storylines or some events that could happen. It’s early access after all. Wait to see what the dev(s) are planning.
Don’t buy it if you only want to play finished games or if you want games with tons of functions and possibilities.

After hyping up BioShock for a long time, expecting it to be System Shock 3. I was VERY dissapointed.

So I stopped playing it, and left it for about 6 years (not even kidding).
I returned to it last year with a fresh pair of eyes, knowing it has nothing to do with System Shock and is it's own thing.
The gameplay was not as bad as I thought and is quite in depth. The enemies are varied and interesting. And a fair amount of weaponry is available to dispatch them. Each one can be upgraded and can be used in unison with plasmids and tonics to create deadly combos.
But where it really shines is the story, characters, setting, art, lore, concepts and atmosphere. It is AMAZING. It all comes together to make a truly immersive and terrifying experience. And should be considered to be an artistic masterpiece.
I can't recommend this any more. Play this in the dark with headphones and soak it in.
However the ending leaves something to be desired.

An amazing survival game that is constantly updated and worked on, with plenty of content to keep you busy. Here are some pros/cons:
really, I'm sick and tired of this cliche that plagues this genre.
apart from wild animals you will only fight nature and your needs.
even if you know there's no zombie to jump on you, you'll still get uneasy feelings when going through an abbandoned place
there are very few other games that emulate real survival so well. Everything from hunger to weather or wildlife behavior is spot on.
this is clearly not one of those alpha/EA games that is abbandoned after the first cash grab
the game is designed in such a way that you cannot jut bunker down in a cabin and live there indefinitely. You NEED to explore to survive and it's alaways a hard choice to leave your cozy "base" to brave the unknown.
one moment your condition is 100%, everything is great, then you make 1-2 mistakes like you decide to butcher a deer even if it's frozen and there's only 1 hour of sunlight left, then a wolf attacks you and you're maimed and can't find your way to your precious shelter.  The cascade/butterfly effect can kill you even after 30-40 days of survival
- No HUD to display the hunger/thirst/energy levels. While this is intentional (for immersion), I'd like to have it as an option.
- Needs a bit more wildlife variety and more crafting recipes.

I'm very mixed on this game...it's got way more faults than it has positives, for sure. Btu it does has SOME things that are actually really nice...it's just a shame those few nice thigns aren't good enough.
Pros:
-It's got okay graphics (even though it's dated still and could use a lot of improving)
-The music and sound-work is actually pretty good (they repeat some sounds too much too, liek the dragon grunts)
-Some of the mini-games are pretty fun (Racing and Flight Club are the better ones).
-The flying mechanics are not bad. Probably one of the better flying mechanics out there that isnt' a simulator. (dragon slows when flying up without boosting, picks up speed when divebombing, and they aren't THAT slow)
-Dragon species have their own stats, making them unique and making different species useful for different stable quests or the battle event.
-Battle event is fun, and it's nice that the rewards are pretty good for it.
-The learning part of the game is okay I guess, if you even pay attention to it (at least it's there and I can't say no to someone trying to be educational).
Cons:
-It's a kid's game. Sadly this is what holds it back the most, since most of the cons in here are a result of this fact.
-The questing is terribly easy and boring. It's all just fetch quests and the world is so small that there's no sense of adventure or satisfaction.
-The rewards for the story quests and the Johaans trading post are completely crap. You only get a marginal gain, and if you do too much spending with what little you get, you will have no coin VERY often.
-It has not enough in it to keep you occupied for hours once you've gone through all the quests or get stuck on one because your farm is too low a level to grow what someone needs. And you don't have the coin to buy seeds for said reason above.
-Most of the mini-games stink or just arent' fun (Fireball Frenzy, the Lab game for example). Even the science-y lab work is just boring.
-Getting both coin and gems in this game is terribly hard and limited. Other than the tiny amount you can get from quests, you can only get coin by doing the johaan jobs (which rewards CRAP amounts for what you put into them), or you get lucky with the RNG from the battle event (about the only reliable way to get them, and even it is luck-based)...even the minigames reward you to crap unless you play it for hours to get a high score, and even that isn't worth it. Even the stable quests aren't reliable until you have a large assortment of dragons at high levels.
-Leveling a dragon is not easy. Exp is only gotten through the battle event (adult dragons only), stable quests (only consistant way), and story quests (which are too limited)
-There are not enough story quests to keep you playing. This is an MMO...I've nearly run out of story quests to do and I've only played for 20 hours? This is not good for an MMO...
-Getting new dragons is 98% luck-based. You'll get 2 starter dragons at first, and maybe 2 more from quests. All others are bought with gems or you get lucky with the RNG of battle event. In a game where having a variety of dragons is plus, this is a huge hinderance to people who want to collect them all...
-Toothless is frikkin behind a membership wall...no Night Fury for you unelss you shell out the cash.
-90% of the cosmetic items you get in this game are bought with gems...if this is a kids game then it's clear they are banking their hopes on whiners begging their parents to shell out money. This is a terrible mentaility...gems are best earned with cash, and some of the faster dragons are also only via gems (or again RNG that isn't in your favor ever).
-You WILL encounter bugs...I ran into about 6 in my 20 hours of play (earned rewards wouldn't redeem, the quest arrow wasn't pointing the right way until you were flying, invisible quest items on the map, quest recipients not being in the right location or in multiple locations on the same parts of the map, random GUI disappearances...there's more but those were the big ones)
-Oh and apparently trying to make an account for the forums to report these bugs requires you to wait a week and counting for an admin to approve
So overall I am very disappointed with this game...I know it's for kids, but the good parts to this game have so much potential...and the developers are clearly just using it as a cash grab. It's an overglorified app game disguised as a kid's MMO that lacks so much content to do for replayablility that it's just sad. I hope this game improves, but it doesn't look like it...

Came back to the game after a 9 month hiatus, staggered by the amount of updates added to the game (the way EA should be!). Restarted my game for a fresh start, some nice changes to the interface definitely (fires,gathering,inventory,crafting) but my favourite is the addition of the hunting bow and the new area "Pleasant Valley".
Actual Gameplay Story follows (may contain spoilers):
After the usual heart-pounding death by Fluffy that most new sojourns into Mystery lake end abruptly with, I started a new game and everything was going well 10 days in, but food was starting to run low, so I decided to head to the new area of Pleasant valley. Survival is a real struggle and death will take you when you least expect it if you let your guard down for even a moment. Truly a unique gem, Sunless Sea is a game like no other.
Its setting is deceptively calm and serene, hiding a truly brutal and fantastic universe of stories that will have you coming back to discover all there is to know in the Neath. Even if it means dying a few times.
While the naval combat is basic and quite easily exploited, the game really isn't about that. It's about exploring a well-developed, living world that will be shaped by your decisions. Rob Pigmote of its scintilliack? You're locked out for good. Side with the Anarchists? The Admiral goes into hiding. These are fairly tame compared to what awaits you further East.
The mechanics support this main theme. You level your stats with Secrets which are made by accumulating Fragments, which you gain every time you discover a new island or landmark. Various interactions also provide Secrets, but nothing replaces the rewards reaped from fully exploring the Sunless Sea.
While it does have a slow start, this is deliberate and creates an impressively immersive experience. The soundtrack is great, and the art captures the mystery and dread the devs want you to feel. Some reviews point to how it eventually becomes a grind, but that has far more to do with the player than the game. In near 50 hours of gameplay and with all legacy items unlocked, I have yet to run a single grind.
Regular updates mean I've returned multiple times and enjoyed the game once again. The recent Christmastide storyline was a lot of fun. And with the Zubmariner expansion around the bend, they're will be a lot more to explore (AN ENTIRE OTHER SEA!)
RECAP
The writing, art, music, and general atmosphere are great. The game rewards you for exploring and seeking out opportunities. While it has a fairly slow start, it is nonetheless very enjoyable as each island presents something distinct and new.

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad is one simulation that really simulates war. It's not one of those americanistic-patriotistic "Realistic" Shooter, no it's what I call near to reality. There are plenty of soldiers on the field, every one can be dead in less than one second, killed by one cross flying bullet. Laying in a trench, covered by mortar and MG-fire, the game creates an Athmosphere as I never have seen or experienced before. Well, I have to admit that the graphics aren't that good, but the game really knows to use it's potential.
But enough of athmosphere or graphics and all this useless stuff. When it comes to an MpFPS, the gameplay, the structure is most important, especially when it comes to competitional gaming. From my point of view, there isn't any actual problem considering the gameplay so far. You can pick of a punch of classes, which number depends on the map. You don't need AT, when there is no tank. The classes are limeted. Depending on the number of players and bots, there are e.g. 1, 2 or 3 snipers avaible, thats a really good thing. If you are too slow, you have to pick the standart rifleman class, which can provide cover, but isn't really effective. As mentioned, you die fast. Really fast, so cover is most important. There is a function for that, but I strongly recommend you not to use it. It may bug, or your head is visable. That brings me to the next point: The Hitboxes are realistic. It's  not possible to hit an enemy 2 cm left of is head.
I think I described the game enough and I really appreciate that you read so far. Red Orchestra 2 is a really good game, you can buy it, if you want, but for that I have a little tip: Buy the Rising Storm DLC. Doing that, you can play the maingame multiplayer without restrictions as well. The singleplayer isn't integrated, but you can ignore it anyways.

The last part of the game has some puzzles that either make absolutely no sense (2 large boxes, anti-gravity, magnet) or are frustrating. The very last puzzle of the game takes the cake. It requires a precision of about 0.2 seconds in order to complete, even if you know exactly what to do. You can only do it through trial and error or by using a stopwatch. The ending isn't either something to write home about. I got this during a Steam sale for 66% off, and I am glad I didn't pay more for it. I finished the game in about 3 hours and it can probably be done faster. There is little replayability value unless you want to get the achievements (one of which is to do the game with less than 5 deaths, which would probably take several hours and failed attempts).
Avoid unless heavily discounted to the price of a bag of chips, because you will get pretty much the same time and enjoyment out of it.

My only complaint is that there are sometimes where you reach a grind, just needing to do repetitive tasks to raise money, but with a little creative navigating, every trip can be an adventure, and even with that complaint this is still easily one of my favorite games.

If you consider the story mode as training for endless mode, then this is a fantastic game. Indeed, it seems that every level is made to introduce another element to the game, whether it is dodging bullets or effective use of melee. It is just like Portal in this sense, where the story is actually mostly clever tutorial. Story mode is also very interesting where there is more going on than is initially apparent. I won't spoil but it is cool.
That said, many complaints say that story mode is short, with about 25 levels and under two hours of playing to complete the whole thing, but I think it is a good amount and there are plenty of challenges and endless modes that make up for it. The challenges are special limitations on the different levels, and they are fun. I am currently enjoying the first challenge, the katana only run. There are also about 7 different arenas in endless mode that you first unlock by completing the game and then by killing dudes in endless mode. These test your skills to the fullest and once the bad guys finally get to you, you get a real time replay of your run and you can see all your awesomeness like it an awesome action movie. I think the developers plan on making a way to share your good runs but at the moment their killstagram thing isn't working very well.
Still, great game. I really enjoy it.

You don't just walk into the battlefield, explosions left and right, and expect everything to be sweet. You don't even have convenient vision overlays to tell you how many more steps to take until you win.
Combat is vicious, it's the real deal. One bullet will either drop you on the spot or cause you a world of trouble before giving in to shock and blood loss. The level of detail is astonishing: projectiles are affected by ballistics and require both leading the target and sighting in/aiming higher.
There are multiple classes available to play, each suited to specific roles: the Sharpshooter is given a scoped rifle to pick off high value targets like Commanders, who can send in airstrikes and lead teams, and Squad Leaders, who can use smoke grenades for covering their advance and work as mobile spawn points.
You even have Tanks, but not in the revolutionary "One-Crew" format: you start with a Tank Commander, a Driver, a Cannon operator and a Loader. All are necessary for the tank to work well, otherwise you'll have to constantly switch seats, which takes time. Tank shells have believable physics as well, and can either punch through side/rear/top armor or deflect harmlessly.
But all classes are heavily restricted, usually no more than 4 of them on most maps. The only general exception, the Rifleman, is both the cannon fodder and the most important asset of the team, much like Chess.
Despite looking fairly drab and brown most of the time, the game looks very pretty - Scenery Gorn runs amok in the heavily bombed areas of Stalingrad. With a hellish warzone as this, what would you expect?
The audio is amazingly immersive, for both good and bad. Native voice acting compliments this, in addition to giving you a good chance to not understand most of the chatter.
Finally, your (many) inevitable deaths at the hands of other human players will be accompanied by gurgling of vital fluids, breathless gasps for one more lungful of air, or heart breaking cries from your stricken soldier to see their loved ones before expiring in a dirty trench. That is, if you're lucky enough not to get killed by an explosion, which tears off your limbs and leaves you a bloody mess
in pain.
Stalingrad wasn't a victory for one side and defeat for the other.
Thankfully,
of Stalingrad is a very, very good multiplayer first person shooter set in the Eastern European Front of the Second World War.

Will you love this game too? If you meet the following critera, I believe so.
-You love reading. The writing in this game paints an otherworldy abyss where life still finds a way. Your choices are impactful on the world. Exploring the evolving enigma of the Sunless Sea is an unmatched experience.
-You enjoy survival. Fuel, supplies, crew, and terror. These are your diminishing resources. When you set out on a voyage, preparation is key. The Sunless Sea will tax you at every turn. Your crew will go mad with terror, be devoured by monstrosities, and otherwise claimed by the unknown.  Fuel burns quickly, even moreso with your bow lamp blazing away, fending off the terror inducing abyss. Supplies dwindle, Canabalism is an option, but not a welcome one. Each port is a risk to your resources, but one that must be made.
-You appreciate art. The world of the Sunless Sea is hauntingly beautiful. Every new area uncovered is exuding character. Exploration for the thrill of discovery is it's own reward.
-Depth- There is much to do on the Sunless sea. Once you have mastered the ways of the waters, you will be able to sustain and indeed profit from your voyages. Purchase a better vessel, more powerful equipment, and attempt the expansive quests of the endgame. Death need no longer herald the end of your legacy. I'll not spoil, but the replay value is definitely here.
REASONS YOU WOULDN'T ENJOY SUNLESS SEA
-You don't like reading. If you pick dialogue options without reading, You are going to have a bad time. A simple line of text can have far reaching implications.
-You don't like a slower paced game. The game is slow and methodical in pace. It's boh tense and relaxing simultaneously.
-You aren't down with the Lovecraftian style. I'm not sure why you are reading this review at this point. This game is dripping in Lovecraftian style.
I believe you are now well equipped to judge wether you would enjoy this game.
If you are still on the fence, pick it up anyway.

Let me just say this: I do not see the fun or hype from this game...I have completed the demo, and played this game thoroughly enough. I am not hooked by the premise, and the game is truly just one big rage fest to me. Do I think it has an artistic form? Sure. Is it something dynamic or out of this world? Hell no, nothing that hasn't been done before in other games, just a bit differently. Do I think the mechanics are interesting? Sure...if you want to rage over a simple f*cking level that you end up spending almost an hour to beat...yeah. Me? I do not play games to get mad at them: I play them to have fun. This, although has its moments, has a lot of fixing to do, particularly throwing objects around corners.
Overall, I rate this game 5/10...a -1 from a 6/10 only because the slow-time thing is not all that impressive, really...Its so dumb that the premise behind the game states that "Time Moves When You Move", and yet when I want to take a sec to analyze the scene, I am literally taken away from it because time does NOT move when I move, rather, time speeds up to NORMAL pace when you move...not stopping it completely...perhaps adding a new mode would fix this? A difficulty setting? Idk...it's thoroughly frustrating when I am let down from such a well-spoken title from other peeps who liked this game. All I see is a super-simplistic game lacking any real reason to make me play this again if all I do is get mad when I die everytime. Now, maybe if I take more time and play more, get the better ryhthm of the game, I may find a different opinion on the game, but for now: I am thoroughly unsatisfied that I spent 25 bucks on a game that makes me nothing but mad.
On the bright side, I do like the implementation of a clever "Killstagram", and hope they add more features to the replay sections, such as replaying a level to try and make an even cooler clip, and playing with the timecode/timeline more, adding music, and so on...If they improve this mechanic, this will definitely make me want to play this more, and ignore all ragefests...even bump my rating up to a 8/10. But sadly for now, I can only give this a 5/10...its nothing too crazy, but definitely challenging to play, which is both inconsiderate to people new to FPSs, but smart to those who really want to have a blast and challenge back-to-back.
Edit: After going back and playing through this all the way, and being patient, I found this game to be suprisingly addictive, and acceptionally challenging. Initially, I was frustrated beyond understanding with the mechanics, and some bugs, but once you understand fully how to engage the enemy, you can safely call this a simple, yet interesting shooter!
I still think it has some improvements to make, but overall a solid game. Not really worth 25 dollars, IMO, but I am still content with my purchase.
Also, something else to suggest: allow a sandbox/level creator! THIS WOULD INITIALIZE SO MUCH IMPROVEMENT, AND SO MUCH CREATIVITY, IT'D BE MIND-F*CKING-BLOWING TO THE FANS, MYSELF INCLUDED!!! :D

The thing is, the AI is really poorly made. If you have a team with high strength values (like the human team in the campaign where you have an ogre and get 2-3 free star players), you will have absolutely no problem. You can easily knock down the opposing team and win comfortably.
But if you play a team like Dark Elf, where the players are expensive and don't have many skills and everybody have STR 3, you will soon realize something is seriously wrong.
The AI is absolutely useless at the game. For example I have played 20 hours vs. AI, and I have only ever seen them do ONE (yes ONE!!) pass on normal mode. The AI only has one playstyle -
picking up the ball and making a cage around it
You will still have a very tough time winning with the mentioned STR 3 team. Because the AI team will never fail a block or do anything to make a turnover. 15 out of 16 turns, the AI player will occasionally use a reroll or a skill after a failed block, dodge etc, but it will always avoid turning over the round.
It is redicoulously easy to make a touchdown the round you recieve the ball. But if you're like me, the AI team will never, ever score. The AI player will then be in offence 4-5 times during a game, where you will be in offence once. With the STR3 team and the AI never failing a block, you will have at least 4 players lying down, knocked out or worse after every touchdown and one of the halves (Minimum 3 players on line of scrimmage plus the blitz).
This gets so frustrating, it nearly drove me insane during my last session.

All in all, bad game unless you want to play it for the online part only. I don't want that, I play enough online already, and I wanted to play this against friends or to take a break from online games (people are poisonous online).

TL;DR: I usually can't be bothered to beat a game without several endings twice, let alone speedrun it. I did both of those things with this one. I can't think of a higher praise.
Magicians & Looters is a metroidvania, basically a nonlinear action platformer. You can switch between three characters, all of which get several unique abilities needed to bypass obstacles. They also fight in different ways – one is focused on all-out DPS and blitzing (which is basically filling a rage bar and getting buffed for a limited time), one on mobility and special moves, and the last one on defense and spellcasting (however, mana regen is quite slow, so you will be hitting things with his sword a lot anyway).
I have found the gameplay to be fun, with just the right amount of challenge. I also like looking for secrets, and this game is filled to the brim with them. Exploration is rewarded with experience orbs, which level up and improve your characters, items with many unique properties suited for different playstyles, and money, which you can spend to buy more items at shops or to utilize one of several "Toll-a-Warp" quick travel stations. The variety of moves each character has isn't too big, so combat can become a bit repetitive. The number of enemy types isn't too high either. However, the game is well-paced with combat interspersed with platforming, so none of those become too much of an issue. A special mention goes to bosses, several of whom I have found to be quite original and fun to beat.
The aesthetic is simple and functional, but pleasant to look at. The soundtrack won't blow you away, but the tunes are relatively catchy. The highlight of the game is its writing – while the story isn't deep or complex at all, there is a huge amount of absolutely hilarious dialogue and banter between the characters. The game pokes fun at many different fantasy and videogame cliches. You can choose to switch on an "Abridged mode", which makes the dialogue less verbose, but keeps some of the fun. There are also 3 randomly chosen beginnings with different dialogue and I recommend you play all of them. I have been playing many "serious" games lately, and this was a welcome breath of fresh air.
The technical aspect of the game is quite solid. It runs well and I didn't find many bugs. The only issues that I did run into is that an enemy once teleported behind an unbreakable locked gate which required me to beat all enemies in the room to open (I just had to run out of the room to reset it), and a few times the game got stuck mid-room transition. The only solution I have found for that is restarting the game, which results in lost progress. Fortunately, the game is very generous with the amount and placement of save spots, and the issue itself only happened two times in my 10 hours of playing.
Overall I recommend Magicians & Looters to anyone seeking a light-hearted metroidvania with just the right amount of challenge. However, even if you aren't a fan of this genre, there is a lot to like in this game.

I recommend this game, but with some caveats.
It gets a lot right. The atmosphere, the graphics, the 'culture' of the game all feel right. There's no stated time period or location which probably helps with not having to think 'why don't I have this' or 'why are these people here'. The 'background story' is one line - some people are 'banished' and now have some open countryside in which to live. The developer himself has admitted that the 'banishment' plays almost no part in the game, so the fact that it's named 'Banished' is odd, but probably more fitting than 'Sim Colonial Town'.
It's challenging but fun to learn how things work - and most of the time your intuition is right, which is what makes it an enjoyable 'simulator'. There are different ways to succeed but none of them seem outlandish or 'gamey'. Keeping your population alive is enough of a challenge at the start that the lack of any particular story or events isn't noticeable. The first 10 hours, then, is probably the most enjoyable.
Where things start to go downhill is after this. When you've got the hang of the game, it becomes pretty easy. The environments don't really vary that much, so the main difficulty or variety is your starting wealth. This means you start growing pretty big towns, and that is when some of the cracks in the 'simulation' begin to show. Your people only 'breed' when they have houses to move into, meaning that if you build a lot of houses, you get the dreaded 'death wave' (also seen in games like Cities: Skylines) when that new generation of people all born at the same time die at the same time. It makes sense within the game's simulation, and you can plan around it, but it feels like a 'gamey' aspect.
Eventually, you get the hang of that too, and now it's just a bit of a slog. One large town looks pretty much like any other large town, so the unique problem solving aspect diminishes. Without much of an 'end point', it feels a little aimless and eventually you just don't feel like carrying on. This is when you might turn to the many, many mods for this. It's a great feature that it is moddable - some of the packs feel like they have more content than the game itself.
The game is definitely worth your first 10 hours, especially at a sale price. If you enjoy economic games or city builders, it's a nice little pre-industrial twist on that genre. However, it may feel a little stale after a while and the replayability isn't as great as some others. I think the developer could have chosen to expand the game a little - even some DLC could have given new life to the later game, through events or technological progression or something. But I enjoyed the game, it is the best of its niche, the mod community did some great things it it, and it's nice to come back to it every year or so.

Full disclosure beforehand: I played through 22 minutes of this game, which is supposedly about 1/4 of it, before I decided to submit a return ticket to Steam support.
It was recommended to me that I play this game blind, having read no reviews or watched any videos covering this game, and I have to say that I'm very disappointed that I followed that advice. This game was made by the author of The Stanley Parable, and so when I started it, I expected more of the same.  I expected a deep narrative with multiple story paths to follow and secrets to discover.  However, while the depth of the narrative could be argued, the game was incredibly linear. There wasn't much else to do but walk around and enjoy the scenery while Mr. Narrator spoke at you.
When I submitted my refund request, I had to choose why I wanted to refund the game.  "It wasn't fun" was one of the choices.  It could very easily be argued that this game isn't
to be "fun." It's meant to deliver a story to you and to move you emotionally.  However, The Stanley Parable was also this way.  The Stanley Parable wasn't meant to be "fun." You may disagree with me here, but it was designed to convey the meaning of choice in video games, or the lack thereof, and get the audience to think about their own, personal choices.  Despite the lack of gameplay, The Stanley Parable may not have been "fun," but at the very least, it was an enjoyable experience, unlike The Beginner's Guide.

So far I have tried 3 different store layouts and have enjoyed the game greatly.  I found that in it's current state it is very difficult if not impossible to make a big box store.  My best and most profitable setup was a bunch of very small stores with only a couple different products in each and around 3 registers.  This would basically be a typical strip mall.
Pros:
-Fun game if you like building and management sims
-Lots of different products to sell even this early in development
-Simple graphics that don't make it confusing (some games try to be too pretty and it ends up being more difficult to build)
-Easy to pick up but hard to put down.
-Lots of potential with future updates that are already apparent looking at the framework that has been layed
Cons:
-Scheduling system is a nightmare for anything with more then 5 or so employees.  We need horizontal blocks showing who is working when. Look at something like Kronos that is used in real world scheduling.
-Impossible to make a large store that functions efficiently
-One storage per store
-Can't rotate anything (this needs to be a priority)
-Shelves can only be stocked and filled from below (see above)
-Build menu needs a complete revamp before more is added
-No ability to select multiple shelves to assign product to them
-Can't move objects you have placed, which forces you to remove and place new ones
Overall I think this game will be really good with another year or so of development.  If you aren't into watching early access games grow as you play them, then I suggest waiting a while to pick it up.

Gimbal, to me, is first sand-box game that also features great space combat.  The 2D visuals are very appealing, but offer a welcome retro look reminiscent of space shooters from an earlier gaming era  The similarities end there, however, Gimbal has realistic physics, a large arsenal of guns, thrusters and upgrades, and really allows you to make it whatever game you want to be with different player modes like capture the flag, racing or traditional team vs team combat.
The most iconic portion of Gimbal is the ship builder.  Depending on your player rank you can build varying strengths of ships.  It's a humbling experience meticulously placing parts onto your deathball just to launch in a game and find that someone else in the community has already thought of something better/stronger.
Some features that I think made this game stand out: tethering to enemy/friendly ships; player controlled +/- gravity fields; ship modules that can control thrusters, aiming and more; stealing enemy ship blueprints after a kill and the well designed ship explosions.  This is a great game for any age that encourages and rewards your creativity.  Highly recommended.

This game is an incredible combination of fast paced combat and detailed ship design.
Combat:
Combat is fun and, at times, thrilling.  Some imbalances exist, especially on the "newb" servers-but there isn't anything that       skill and design can't overcome.  The design of your ships will have a major impact on how you fight.  Build a hulking tank?  You won't be moving much, and will probably need a turret to hit anything.  Build a lightning fast missle boat?  You'll be darting in and out of combat, tactically choosing when to strike, and when to retreat for repairs.  Controls are 100% customisable and never hinder gameplay.
Design:
Ship design is deep, although slightly restrictive.  You start by choosing an airframe, essentially determining your base stats (a "class" if you will).  Due to some imbalances, the larger airframes are rarely used, but eventually this should be fixed.  On this base you can attach weapons, thrusters, structures, machines, and more.  Realistic(ish) physics mean the interactions between parts and the locations of your thrusters will play very important roles.  Other components are simpler, but still require careful contemplation on how to balance the monetary and spatial constraints, while maximizing combat output.
Progression:
As you play you progress through four ranks, increasing your budget with kills and wins, and unlocking new technology each rank up.  Reaching max level is not difficult, and can easily be achieved in a single day-perfect for those with less time to sink, but who still want to compete.  On the other hand, it is possible to reset your rank, gaining "cool points" and rejoining the newbs.  While this provides no tangible advantages, releveling can be quite fun.  You can design ships for every price range, and master flight of the weakest platforms.  Additionally, its sometimes more fun to fight with weak ships than powerhouses, as skill becomes even more important.
Multiplayer:

Gimbal, is a nice looking 2D space shooter that has a lot going on underneath the hood. At first glance it looks like one of many ordinary space shoot'em up games, but as soon as you unlock the so called hangar option a new dimension opens up.
Within the hangar players are able to construct their own personal space fighter to do battle on one of the many maps. With each level progression the player unlocks new parts which become available at the hangar screen.
Much, if not most, of Gimbal's power is due to this feature and sometimes you're spending more time construting and tweaking your ship than actually playing a map.
The maps which are at your disposal are okay and look nice. Each map comes in 2 versions: normal and mini.
Another good thing about Gimbal is the option to host your own server, add bots to it (This allows for Co-Op and solo play) and to adjust almost any setting to your liking.
Controls are another league of their own. I haven't seen that many games that allow for just "You got a key, button or axis to use? press, jiggle it." That's a very nice feauture, because with the many weapons and construction options at your disposal, controlling that killer ship can become a science of its own.
But, it's not all sunschine with Gimbal, it actually has one huge flaw. And that's the level cap. First of all there're just a hadful of levels/ranks you can gain: about 4. And as a result you're pretty soon done gaining ranks and earning parts. Which is another downer for Gimbal. Although the hangar is just the thing to use, you soon realise that it's not perfect. There're not enough parts. With a game as Gimbal you want 1000 and more parts, 200+ weapon choices and so one and so one. You don't just want to build fighters. You want to construct a Star Destroyer... Not gonna happen, not allowed.
True, it's a lot of work to creat a game with such options, I won't deny that, but a game like Gimbal needs at least some modding support so players can add their own parts and designs. Without that option its life span is rather short.
On the other hand, with the low price tag you can't go wrong with Gimbal.
All things work just perfect, no bugs, just not enough construction parts in the end.

This is another World War 2 First Person Shooter, but with a few key differences: it's set in the Eastern European Theatre, and you're not the badass mobile sentry you're regarded as in other FPS games.
You don't hide behind cover, waiting for your Eagle-headed God to provide technical long-term immunity from lead poisoning. You don't just walk into the battlefield, explosions left and right, and expect everything to be sweet. You don't even have convenient vision overlays to tell you how many more steps to take until you win.
Combat is vicious, it's the real deal. One bullet will either drop you on the spot or cause you a world of trouble before giving in to shock and blood loss. The level of detail is astonishing: projectiles are affected by ballistics and require both leading the target and sighting in/aiming higher.
There are multiple classes available to play, each suited to specific roles: the Sharpshooter is given a scoped rifle to pick off high value targets like Commanders, who can send in airstrikes and lead teams, and Squad Leaders, who can use smoke grenades for covering their advance and work as mobile spawn points.
You even have Tanks, but not in the revolutionary "One-Crew" format: you start with a Tank Commander, a Driver, a Cannon operator and a Loader. All are necessary for the tank to work well, otherwise you'll have to constantly switch seats, which takes time. Tank shells have believable physics as well, and can either punch through side/rear/top armor or deflect harmlessly.
But all classes are heavily restricted, usually no more than 4 of them on most maps. The only general exception, the Rifleman, is both the cannon fodder and the most important asset of the team, much like Chess.
Despite looking fairly drab and brown most of the time, the game looks very pretty - Scenery Gorn runs amok in the heavily bombed areas of Stalingrad. With a hellish warzone as this, what would you expect?
The audio is amazingly immersive, for both good and bad. Native voice acting compliments this, in addition to giving you a good chance to not understand most of the chatter.
Finally, your (many) inevitable deaths at the hands of other human players will be accompanied by gurgling of vital fluids, breathless gasps for one more lungful of air, or heart breaking cries from your stricken soldier to see their loved ones before expiring in a dirty trench. That is, if you're lucky enough not to get killed by an explosion, which tears off your limbs and leaves you a bloody mess
in pain.
Stalingrad wasn't a victory for one side and defeat for the other.
Thankfully,
of Stalingrad is a very, very good multiplayer first person shooter set in the Eastern European Front of the Second World War.

Limbo is a beautiful looking puzzle platformer, whos biggest appeal is its art style and ambience.
3-4 hours
7/10
Limbo is a fairly simple and straight forward puzzle platformer. You play as a young boy, traversing through limbo to rescue your sister. You’re simply thrown into the game with no real indication of what is going on, and the story doesn’t really develop past that.
But let’s talk about the gameplay itself, as a platformer it’s pretty simplistic, there aren’t a whole lot of tricks to master, nor do you really even need to master any. It’s not a game about pixel perfect platforming. Nay, it places greater focus on its puzzles. While there are a few tough puzzles throughout the game, most are able to be solved in a fairly reasonable time frame. Long enough to make you think and feel satisfied once you do solve it, but not so long as to become frustrated with the game. More importantly the puzzles are fun to solve, and the platforming is enjoyable.
Now for the main attraction of Limbo, the wonderful looking art style and it’s excellent atmosphere. Limbo has a simple black and white art style that frankly looks fantastic. It’s nothing fancy, but it’s a pleasure to look at.	The art style plays a large part in helping create the wonderful, bleak, atmosphere of the game. There’s a general sense of loneliness, despair, and death hovering in the world of Limbo and pervading throughout the game. Music is used sparingly, occasionally flaring up to indicate danger and heighten the tension, and it helps contribute to the ambience of the game.
My main criticism of the game is the lack of anything useful in the options menu. Limbo is a fairly simple game, so it’s not like it needs a bundle of configurable settings, but it lacks options to adjust anything but the brightness. The main thing I would have liked is to have been able to remap the controls, as I much prefer using WASD to move than the arrow keys. Thankfully the controls and gameplay are simple enough that this ends up being a fairly minor complaint, but it would still be a nice addition. (One can also use a controller to play, but as I don’t own one at this time I obviously haven’t used one).
Nonetheless, Limbo is a rather fun puzzle platformer with a wonderfully bleak and depressing atmosphere to it.
