Staggeringly wasteful of your time.
This game has an incredible aesthetic, and very unforgiving gameplay, which is fine.  It's basically a roguelike.  howEVER.  Sailing from port to port takes an incredibly long time.  The sea is almost empty of things to interact with, which is good because they are mostly punishingly overpowered, but bad because if you actually want combat, it can take 20 minutes to find some.  You can spend an entire day playing this game, and have not advanced yourself enough to have moved up from the baseline boat you start with.
The game is set such that there is almost no value in trading early on.  Seriously.  Your inital boat has a hold capacity of 40.  One item that you can buy, wine, costs $21  The most it can be sold for normally is $23.  That's $80 per run, when a new ship costs 2000.  You will also need to pay for fuel and food, which runs to about $30.  Also that fuel and food needs to be stored on your boat, further cutting into profits.
Ok fine.  We've all played these sailing games before, what about combat, can you make money doing that?  Sure.  After a bunch of trial and error, you will find that there are two boats (The pirate destroyer and the crack pirate destroyer) that are both weak enough to be destroyed by a new player, and reliably have food and fuel to make up for the 5 minutes you spend chasing their tails, as well as some cargo.  The rest?  Well there's a crab that can be killed for 1xp (takes about 200 for a new 'level') or a free, non-transportable meal.  Your crew just ate?  Well, that xp is the best you can hope for.  Bats can be killed for a transportable meal, to be eaten when you, you know, need it.  That's worth about $20, actually a lot of money considering how much you are scraping early on.  Other sea monsters you will find are much too hard to fight. Other pirates have either nothing, or are so high level that instead of food and fuel, you get bolts of silk.  Which can be resold at an eye-watering discount for less than the food and fuel found on a destroyer.
Exploring?  Each port you visit will net you a usually small amount of money, and one fuel when you give a report to the admiralty on returning in London.  Generally getting from one port to another requires more than one fuel.  Additionally, the money you make will go to supplies.  So exploring is almost always a net negative.
So basically your only hope is missions.  There is one character who will send you on fetch quests, basically trading, but with an actually worth-your-time profit margin.  Then there is the mob smuggler, who will give you missions than can lead to instakills, since he sends you out to sea with contraband to a place you may not know how to find.  If you can't find it on the supplies you packed, and return to London you'll have it confiscated (there's equipment for smugglers, but it doesn't fit on the initial boat, and you WILL NOT have a better one at this point in the game).
And hey, I get it, resources can be scarce.  There's tons of games like that, from the first Resident Evil to Don't Starve.  But this game plays out so damn SLOWLY.  You boat barely moves in the water, and everything is so far away.  Getting a few hundred dollars together to buy a new gun for your boat can take, and I am in no way exaggerating, HOURS.
If there were twice the monsters, at half the danger, and the boat moved twice as fast, this would be an amazing game.  As it is, I spent a few days on it, always with the promise that if I stuck out the lame slow start, I'd get to the good stuff.  My hold would get big enough to start trading, my weapons would get good enough to start fighting.  Instead all that ever happens is you slowly burn all your fuel and food, occasionally doing a fetch quest to inject a little more cash into your operation, but always dwindling, until you die.  I die a lot in Super Meat Boy, but that game doesn't make me play three hours for the privilege.
Basically this game smacks of an unfinished alpha, that is somehow inexplicably considered finished.  The early game seems wildly unbalanced, the pace of the game is super slow, and there's not enough things to do and interact with, especially since interacting with things usually involves money you don't have (either pure cost, fuel, food, crewmen that need replacing or hull repairs)

If you're looking at this and thinking oh my God it's H.P. Lovecraft's Pirates!, don't. Turn right around and go play Pirates! or Sea Dogs or something free-form and piratey. Would-be buccaneers are going to be eaten alive by giant crabs and living mountains, and aspiring privateers are going to be trading in arcane secrets and still-warm lifeblood. This one is nothing like those liberating high-seas adventures, no matter how interesting what I just typed sounds. If instead of swashbuckling you want a mysterious, story-rich world to explore and never fully master, keep reading. Much like the people and creatures you'll meet in this game, Sunless Sea is not at all what it seems.
The game sets you up as a zee captain in the unique and storied Fallen London setting, a Victorian-era underground sea full of cosmic horrors. In creating your character you choose a background and a goal, and then prepare for your first journey. Every port is presented as a series of journal pages, with you choosing actions based on the resources and stats available to you. Everything is abstracted as cards, from cargo to terror to snippets of news, which makes it clear to see what you need to access or complete a story but hard to tell what is actually valuable before you find a use for it. It's a strange system held up by the quality of the writing, which never becomes tiresome in its quirky melancholy and ominous reveals.
Between ports you sail the sunless seas in real time from a bird-eye view. Your ship has three major resources to manage during voyages. Fuel powers your engines and your deck lights, supplies feed your crew, and terror measures how stable your crew actually is. There's a lot of interplay between these resources that will affect how you sail, helping to liven up otherwise dull (and occasionally tense) trips. Running your deck lights burns almost three times more fuel, but sailing in the dark ramps up your terror faster. You can sail past natural lights and coastlines instead, but your crew will be consuming supplies at a constant rate, making long trips costly.
Odds are that mismanaging one of these resources is going to be what kills you, because you burn through fuel at an alarming rate and terror mounts quickly without clear methods to alleviate it. It'll be that or one of the sea's monstrous inhabitants, which are almost all more than a match for your sad little starter ship. And when you die, you lose pretty much all of your progress. There's an heir system where you can pass on one item or a bit of money, and once you start an estate you can create a will to pass on more resources. As far as stories and quests go, however, it's back to the beginning and this is where the game starts to really come apart.
At some point playing Sunless Sea, you're going to realize you're not really making any progress. You're learning the systems and uncovering stories and accumulating... things, but every time you die, and you WILL die, most of that gets wiped out. You can do things faster on the next captain, but the goals in the game are so long-term and require so much work that they come to appear almost impossible. It might be that you need seven of something from the opposite side of the world that you can only get once per trip, or you need one of something that you had and then lost and have no idea how to get again. And the sailing is so slow and the resources so strained, that soon the oppressive and mysterious atmosphere will turn to tedium.
You're not going to beat Sunless Sea, I'd wager, and frustration or boredom will claim you far before that's even a possibility. So why do I recommend it? Because despite all that, I keep coming back to it. Part of me still wants to puzzle out the stories, find new ports, and maybe someday mark down a victory, even if it's with permadeath turned off and the wiki open the whole way. The stories don't get old, and a dozen hours in there are still more to discover. As long as you understand that you're getting a nigh-endless choose your own adventure book where you sail (and very possibly die) instead of turning pages, there's a good chance you'll become as enraptured as I am.

Magicians & Looters is a deliciously crafted Metroidvania that is true to itself. It's full of soul and full of detail. Your attacks feel like they matter, and there are quite a few of them for each of the three characters you can play.
You can decide who to play as, but ultimately, as you explore for the opening to the next area you'll be forced to take the character with the ability required to progress. You're made to experience each character's abilities and move set, and made to adapt. Morgopolis have made the transition seamless.
The items and weapons you can collect throughout the game serve to test your play style, making you synergize and re-experiment for every boss. The leveling system is based on exploration, but doesn't punish you should you withhold its progress. The abilities provided through leveling up are quite nice, and unique to each character, which helps to make item synergies for each character based not only on their default stat values (such as attack speed or aerial strikes), but on whether they've got extra resources to a certain pool.
Magicians & Looters really got me. It's witty, charming, difficult, and tasty as ♥♥♥♥. Any Metroidvania fans out there would be missing out if they passed this game by.

I recommend this game, but with some caveats.
It gets a lot right. The atmosphere, the graphics, the 'culture' of the game all feel right. There's no stated time period or location which probably helps with not having to think 'why don't I have this' or 'why are these people here'. The 'background story' is one line - some people are 'banished' and now have some open countryside in which to live. The developer himself has admitted that the 'banishment' plays almost no part in the game, so the fact that it's named 'Banished' is odd, but probably more fitting than 'Sim Colonial Town'.
It's challenging but fun to learn how things work - and most of the time your intuition is right, which is what makes it an enjoyable 'simulator'. There are different ways to succeed but none of them seem outlandish or 'gamey'. Keeping your population alive is enough of a challenge at the start that the lack of any particular story or events isn't noticeable. The first 10 hours, then, is probably the most enjoyable.
Where things start to go downhill is after this. When you've got the hang of the game, it becomes pretty easy. The environments don't really vary that much, so the main difficulty or variety is your starting wealth. This means you start growing pretty big towns, and that is when some of the cracks in the 'simulation' begin to show. Your people only 'breed' when they have houses to move into, meaning that if you build a lot of houses, you get the dreaded 'death wave' (also seen in games like Cities: Skylines) when that new generation of people all born at the same time die at the same time. It makes sense within the game's simulation, and you can plan around it, but it feels like a 'gamey' aspect.
Eventually, you get the hang of that too, and now it's just a bit of a slog. One large town looks pretty much like any other large town, so the unique problem solving aspect diminishes. Without much of an 'end point', it feels a little aimless and eventually you just don't feel like carrying on. This is when you might turn to the many, many mods for this. It's a great feature that it is moddable - some of the packs feel like they have more content than the game itself.
The game is definitely worth your first 10 hours, especially at a sale price. If you enjoy economic games or city builders, it's a nice little pre-industrial twist on that genre. However, it may feel a little stale after a while and the replayability isn't as great as some others. I think the developer could have chosen to expand the game a little - even some DLC could have given new life to the later game, through events or technological progression or something. But I enjoyed the game, it is the best of its niche, the mod community did some great things it it, and it's nice to come back to it every year or so.

Still, great game. I really enjoy it.

So, the recent changes made quite an upheveal and I would like to have the other side's opinion out there too.
The game has became much harder with the Chaos and shards system. It became somewhat more grindy, which most of these people would not care about, if it wasnt for the fact that their precious AFK simulator has been taken away.
Essentially, Trendy is making an effort to reduce people's ability to AFK throught content that rewards the best gear and shards so that people actually have to PLAY A GAME! How audicious of them.
They took an AFK simulator, balanced it around so you actually have to play a mixture of fighting the waves and tower defense instead of having a tower defense game with loot in it.
On the con side you have the RNG involved in Shards, but the game is still in development so such things can be skewed.
EDIT: After having played at C7 for a while and reading some criticism, ill add a few more points.
Pros:
-The game is headed towards a more choice oriented system (I remember the skeleton archer only era). Options are still limited, but the direction is there.
-Heroes are actually more than walking loot machines / hitboxes, and things that actually have stuff to do during waves.
-Shards allow you to keep the same passives in a slot regardless of stat which provides a much less RNG based gearing once you actually have the shard you need.
Cons:
-Despite the direction its taking the number of viable tower choices is still way too limited.
-Shard RNG makes it painful to advance to higher difficulties if you get unlucky.
-Goblin rollers are the only things players actively have to engage, although the devs promised more similar enemies to come soon.
-Balance is out the window in some cases, both for defenses and heroes.
TL;DR: The game is heading in a much more enjoyable direction, not one where one person builds it all up and the rest runs around to collect the loot (nm4 onslaught im looking at you).

PLZ READ THE ENTIRE REVIEW FIRST BEFORE JUMPING TO CONCLUSIONS: I DO NOT DESPISE THIS GAME IN ALL ITS ENTIRETY!!! :(
Let me just say this: I do not see the fun or hype from this game...I have completed the demo, and played this game thoroughly enough. I am not hooked by the premise, and the game is truly just one big rage fest to me. Do I think it has an artistic form? Sure. Is it something dynamic or out of this world? Hell no, nothing that hasn't been done before in other games, just a bit differently. Do I think the mechanics are interesting? Sure...if you want to rage over a simple f*cking level that you end up spending almost an hour to beat...yeah. Me? I do not play games to get mad at them: I play them to have fun. This, although has its moments, has a lot of fixing to do, particularly throwing objects around corners.
Overall, I rate this game 5/10...a -1 from a 6/10 only because the slow-time thing is not all that impressive, really...Its so dumb that the premise behind the game states that "Time Moves When You Move", and yet when I want to take a sec to analyze the scene, I am literally taken away from it because time does NOT move when I move, rather, time speeds up to NORMAL pace when you move...not stopping it completely...perhaps adding a new mode would fix this? A difficulty setting? Idk...it's thoroughly frustrating when I am let down from such a well-spoken title from other peeps who liked this game. All I see is a super-simplistic game lacking any real reason to make me play this again if all I do is get mad when I die everytime. Now, maybe if I take more time and play more, get the better ryhthm of the game, I may find a different opinion on the game, but for now: I am thoroughly unsatisfied that I spent 25 bucks on a game that makes me nothing but mad.
On the bright side, I do like the implementation of a clever "Killstagram", and hope they add more features to the replay sections, such as replaying a level to try and make an even cooler clip, and playing with the timecode/timeline more, adding music, and so on...If they improve this mechanic, this will definitely make me want to play this more, and ignore all ragefests...even bump my rating up to a 8/10. But sadly for now, I can only give this a 5/10...its nothing too crazy, but definitely challenging to play, which is both inconsiderate to people new to FPSs, but smart to those who really want to have a blast and challenge back-to-back.
Edit: After going back and playing through this all the way, and being patient, I found this game to be suprisingly addictive, and acceptionally challenging. Initially, I was frustrated beyond understanding with the mechanics, and some bugs, but once you understand fully how to engage the enemy, you can safely call this a simple, yet interesting shooter!
I still think it has some improvements to make, but overall a solid game. Not really worth 25 dollars, IMO, but I am still content with my purchase.
Also, something else to suggest: allow a sandbox/level creator! THIS WOULD INITIALIZE SO MUCH IMPROVEMENT, AND SO MUCH CREATIVITY, IT'D BE MIND-F*CKING-BLOWING TO THE FANS, MYSELF INCLUDED!!! :D

This game gave me A LOT to think about. I wrote many iterations of this review talking about what it meant to me and what I learned from it, but I'm deciding to save that for me, and just talk about the game for what it is. While some games are like novels, this can be more equated to a series of poems that symbolize an artist's constant internal struggle. Our creator, Davey, takes a look back at games created by what he calls Coda, and by taking a look back at them he understands what they truly mean to him, and how trying to help Coda, began to destroy Coda's voice and ultimately silence it. If you are a creative and/or internally struggling person I strongly recommend this game.
I will just say this one more thing. If you are creating out of expression and not impression, you cannot be driven by other's opinions, you can only hope that they understand you. I hope that Davey finds Coda again, a way to work in tandem with it, and a way to expose us to its work without it being infected by our opinions.

The Beginner's Guide is more a piece of narrative art than a game. It takes you through a series of source-engine made levels while the narrator talks about his relations with the "game's author" named "Coda". The game invites the player to think about human pitfalls, mostly regarding the compulsive need for self validation. It can be a tiny bit deppressing towards the end, but still thought provoking. In contrast to the Stanley's Parabol, which has a funny and curious approach to narrative gaming, the Beginner's Guide is much more serious. Also, unlike the Stanley's Parabol, the Beginners Guide does not seem to encourage free roaming, and opts to give you a single, hard set path with a single outcome.
If you're into thought provoking narrative games though, this is a game worth trying.

As much I like this game, I'm not recommending it because you probably won't.
I actually have many more hours on this game than my Steam account says, because I used to play this a lot about 2 years ago, and it's not because I quit, it is because I ran out of things to do.
So, prepare for several of the things this game has to offer from the eyes of someone who has actually played this for more than 20 minutes 3 years ago.
In the beginning, you start with a quest which in the end earns you a fully grown version of one of four species of dragons. Back when I played this for the first time, this wasn't a thing, but I'm glad it's in place now, since you don't have to walk everywhere for the first few hours of the game. In the time I played it two years ago, I had cleared all the base quests and the expansion pack available at the time, as well as become the leader of my clan. When I returned, I have completed all but one of the 5 expansion packs available. I'm not one to play a game for 20 minutes and then write a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ review on it.
Now, let's take a look at what some fellow Steam users have said about the game, and we'll see what an experience player has to say about it.
"It's pay to win."
In a lot of ways, yes, it is. Gems in this game are purchased with real money and can be used to by dragon eggs, saddles, warpaint, and some other items. However, they are very hard to come by and come in small quantities unless you buy them. But, with the quest at the beginning of the game to get a fully grown dragon right from the start and the new Battle Events to earn expensive items from, like dragon eggs, warpaint, expensive farm items, and even gems, it has improved a lot since December 2014 when most of these review were written. You also get gems a few days from your daily reward, so if you keep playing it you should get a remarkable stash of gems.
"It lags too much."
Expecting something to run well from day 1 of it being on a new platform is childish. It has improved a lot, and I think that it runs fine. I haven't had a single crash.
"The dragons fly too slow."
Maybe, but I've still found I can get where I need to go in a timely manner. There are plenty of dragons I've found through expansion packs that fly pretty fast.
"Membership is ridiculously expensive."
I do not have a membership, and I agree with this statement. Pro tip: You can compete easily with members. I've beaten plenty of members in Thunder Run Racing, which is the actual dragon racing. It's rediculously expensive, and doesn't really give you anything that's worth that much money.
Closing thoughts: I really like this game, because I loved the movies and the books, so it feels like I'm living it. Despite this, I can see where many of the negative reviews are coming from, and I'm going to have to agree with them. I'm not going to stop playing this, because I really do enjoy it, but you probably won't. But, as Drago said in How To Train Your Dragon 2, "By all means, great dragon master, Try."

A very different take on the survival genre, The Long Dark really pushes you to consider risk and reward and for me that is the biggest focus of the game.  For example you'll find many risk/reward scenarios on a regular basis- should i shoot the bear, or can i get around it? is it too cold to collect wood? do i use my bullets to hunt or for defense? and even sometimes have i been here before and am i wasting time scavenging here? these scenarios although a little monotonous in aesthetics really carry an impact on how your game plays out and thus make for a tense and very cagey affair.  the art style of the game is also very refreshing and makes the environment feel a lot more harsh and unforgiving (also it allows for a bigger player base with very low minimum spec requirements) although i do keep wondering what would it look like if it had the art style of some of the snowy scenes in `Until Dawn`.  basic game machanics are all there and stable which is very rare for a pre-alpha these days and i'm looking forward to see some of the new features and content that is coming our way.  As it is i'd say 7.5/10 for the price, when you add in the fact that its a pre-alpha and that the devs are releasing updates often i'd say 8.5/10 on the basis of great mechanics, stable gameplay on low-end systems, and a great atmosphere to the world.

Basically a game that captures the fun essence of 3D platformers with all the charm that should come with them.
A Hat in Time is a game that revels in giving you a variety of challenges to tackle in an effort to reclaim all your lost time pieces. Whether you're hunting for vault codes to open a safe, sneaking around to find evidence of a murder, using a scooter to deliver mail to underlings or using various tools at your disposal to ascend to the top of a giant windmill. Each challenge in the core worlds is a joy to tackle and the variety ensures things never get old. For the platforming challenges naturally many of these stages will test your leaping skills, but special note to the time rift stages - bonus levels akin to the ones in Super Mario Sunshine where the focus is entirely on platforming your way from A to B.
Hats and badges form the core of your powers to assist you. Hats grant powers like sprinting, throwing explosive potions or using dimensional powers to alter certain platform's solidity. These hat powers really help to shape the adventure by requiring players to switch around as necessary. As new hats are obtained new areas in old locations open up. Badges are more optional (with the exception of the grappling hook, which is needed to access many areas) and offer perks like preventing fall damage or letting you charge up a beam attack.
Aside from the 40 time pieces in the core game you have many other collectables to acquire. Yarn balls are needed to craft the hats to progress, although there are more of them than needed to craft all hats, leaving the rest just for fun. Artefacts open up new time rifts for some of the time pieces, while rift tokens can be exchanged to play a slot machine which rewards cosmetic items like clothing dye, music remixes and hat styles. Even if this sounds a bit short to you then fear not, because this game also has Steam Workshop support. Currently the feature is in beta so requires players to actively sign up via the game's properties to the beta, but once done you have a wide variety of additional content. Some of this is even more cosmetics, yet you can also find entire new levels within the workshop.
Did I mention the charm this game has? Hat Girl, for being a mostly silent protagonist (outside of a few general shouts) exudes personality. Even just leaving her idle shows her dancing on the spot or playing with dolls. During play you can play patty-cake with certain mafia goons, see her hiding scared from a monster that puts even the resident demon to shame or play the lead of a marching band. Other characters don't slack here either. The mafia goons are hilarious with their dialogue, the contract demon of the third world is a riot from start to finish and we certainly can't forget Moustache Girl's rebel antics.
Admittedly, like with any 3D platformer, the camera can get a bit wonky in places (most notably if it has to go up against level geometry). However, this has been a magical adventure, and with Workshop support there's plenty more to do even after finishing all the official content. This is definitely standing out as one of my most memorable experiences of 2017.

Limbo is a beautiful looking puzzle platformer, whos biggest appeal is its art style and ambience.
3-4 hours
7/10
Limbo is a fairly simple and straight forward puzzle platformer. You play as a young boy, traversing through limbo to rescue your sister. You’re simply thrown into the game with no real indication of what is going on, and the story doesn’t really develop past that.
But let’s talk about the gameplay itself, as a platformer it’s pretty simplistic, there aren’t a whole lot of tricks to master, nor do you really even need to master any. It’s not a game about pixel perfect platforming. Nay, it places greater focus on its puzzles. While there are a few tough puzzles throughout the game, most are able to be solved in a fairly reasonable time frame. Long enough to make you think and feel satisfied once you do solve it, but not so long as to become frustrated with the game. More importantly the puzzles are fun to solve, and the platforming is enjoyable.
Now for the main attraction of Limbo, the wonderful looking art style and it’s excellent atmosphere. Limbo has a simple black and white art style that frankly looks fantastic. It’s nothing fancy, but it’s a pleasure to look at.	The art style plays a large part in helping create the wonderful, bleak, atmosphere of the game. There’s a general sense of loneliness, despair, and death hovering in the world of Limbo and pervading throughout the game. Music is used sparingly, occasionally flaring up to indicate danger and heighten the tension, and it helps contribute to the ambience of the game.
My main criticism of the game is the lack of anything useful in the options menu. Limbo is a fairly simple game, so it’s not like it needs a bundle of configurable settings, but it lacks options to adjust anything but the brightness. The main thing I would have liked is to have been able to remap the controls, as I much prefer using WASD to move than the arrow keys. Thankfully the controls and gameplay are simple enough that this ends up being a fairly minor complaint, but it would still be a nice addition. (One can also use a controller to play, but as I don’t own one at this time I obviously haven’t used one).
Nonetheless, Limbo is a rather fun puzzle platformer with a wonderfully bleak and depressing atmosphere to it.

A Hat in Time is
.
Let's start with options. I always say that the quality of the main menu and available options speaks volumes about the quality of the game itself. There is a surprisingly detailed assortment of options available here. Hell, motion blur is even separated into per-object motion blur and screen blur (because who likes screen blur?). Every option is accompanied with a description of what it does. In terms of essential options, you have all the ones you'd expect from a decent PC game: FoV sliders, individual audio sliders, wide array of FPS locks, and plenty of graphical options.
Performance wise, I get a consistent 120 FPS on a i5-6600K and GTX 1070 with every option maxed (except screen blur, of course). Seems fairly optimized for my particular build, but your mileage may vary.
Controls are tight. You never feel like you're fighting against the game.
Level design is, well, good. Not great, but good enough that you certainly don't notice its shortcomings while playing. When you step back and think about it though, the level design really isn't anything to write home about. In general I found the levels to be too busy and lacking cohesion. They're not very memorable in the sense that if you were to drop me in a random part of a level, I'd have difficulty identifying exactly where I was.
There's a ton of little details in the world that are just delightful. There's an adorable little roomba that roams your spaceship! But the one thing that really stood out to me is the 4-piece band you have in your spaceship. You can tell this band to play you some tunes, and get this: the members of the band only start playing at their corresponding parts of the song! If there aren't any drumbeats, the drummer doesn't drum. The trumpet player doesn't start playing until the song has trumpets. That's an incredible attention to detail.
Which I guess brings me to the soundtrack. It's phenomenal. At the time of writing (with a -20% discount), the deluxe edition is only $4 extra, and is well worth the cost. Gear with Breakfast has also put up the full soundtrack on YouTube, so go check it out!
The platforming is solid. It's not hard as nails; there's some measure of difficulty but not frustratingly so.
There's a lot of collectibles. Typically you get cosmetic rewards for your efforts. The platforming is satisfying enough that I had no qualms in going out of my way to collect 'em all.
Overall A Hat in Time is an exceedingly good game. I think it's one of those games that are greater than the sum of its parts. While each aspect of the game is good in and of itself; put together it's just a work of art.

Cuphead is a lovingly crafted tribute the cartoons of the early 1920s and 30s, complete with faithfully created animations and original music of the era. But not only is Cuphead aesthetically pleasing and atmospheric, the controls and gameplay are extremely tight, and it's one of the more challenging modern platformers that i've played. I usually ignore people who compare games to Dark Souls because it's difficult, mostly because I've never played Dark Souls, but Cuphead is actually a difficult game, and I'm no Dean Takashi either. However, Cuphead's difficulty makes every level and boss fight extremely rewarding and not frustrating, and adds an element of replayability to the game. Cuphead clearly was made with love, and while being unforgiving, it is definitely not unrewarding.

A Hat in Time is absolutely beautiful concoction of new and old that has since rocketed to one of the most memorable games of 2017 for me. It is able to effectively emulate the wholesome charm of old-school games like Banjo Kazooie, whilst still feeling differentiated. It also captures the fluid and polished movement of more recent titles like Super Mario Galaxy and the like. Being separated into four worlds with only 40 time pieces to collect may seem on the shorter side, but the way the game takes an utterly unique premiss with each world means it keeps the punches rolling and the gameplay changing.  This all culminates in enjoyably cheerful experience that honest to god warmed my heart while also leaving me challenged.
Overall, I would recommend this to anyone look for a bit of personality in their game (old or new). Fantastic writing, heart-of-gold charm and amazing originality - 9/10

What draws a man to the sea? I haven't the foggiest, but the zee is another story. Do you desire to conquer her? It is a fool's errand; the most you can hope for is the chance to win and keep her favour as she menacingly surrounds your vessel with a glassy void. Do you seek adventure and exploration? You will soon see things unimaginable; things which you will wish remained undiscovered, things whose very existence you will dismiss vehemently in every tavern in every port, if only to convince yourself that such things do not exist. Do you seek answers? Expect more and more questions.
So what draws a man to the zee? It's hard to put into words. Maybe I am just a glutton for punishment, perfectly content to be at the total mercy of the zee. Perhaps the prospect of smuggling sunlight through a zee of ever-shifting islands is too much of an intriguing opportunity to pass. Or maybe, the steady rhythm repeating the word "NORTH" is a compulsion and an obsession that only the zailor's life can satisfy.
I can only say what draws this man to the zee (as I surely durst not speak for the other men, women, or anthropomorphic squids who may aspire to the calling of a captain). The first voyage changes a man, filling him with the appropriate yearning and fear preceding each ever more ambitious venture; the thrill and actual terror felt as madness sets into your crew; the joy and regret of neglecting your carefully planned route as chasing a phosphorescent light draws you through ever direr straits.
The zee does not forgive.
The zee does not disappoint.

Though a bit rough in small places, Magicians and Looters is a thoroughly rewarding little metroidvania.
The combat is simple enough to pick up and play: each of the 3 characters have their own bonuses and styles that range from special movies to boosted stats. There is some magic, a rage meter, and some interesting equipment options, and it all feels solid. The platforming is also well done, which makes reaching new areas quick and fun. The 3 characters all feel distinct in their playstyles and tweaks so that one never outshines the others (too much... Vienna was probably my most used character)
The leveling up mechanic is interesting in that it is based of exploring (to find level up orbs) rather than grinding. This really goes a long way in keeping the pacing fresh for the game. Not only that, but grinding tends to cheapen the experience and spend more time on a game that is not necessarily fun after 20 hours of grinding. This mechanic is probably the most deserving attention because it highlights what the game does right: juggle characters and explore the environment.
The story is not to be taken seriously, but in a good way. The humor was more hits than misses, and that is quite the accomplishment given how subjective humor can be. I laughed a few times, snickered more, and grinned through most of the game. The characters were all likeable and I am ready for the sequel.
Magicians and Looters is a quite the hidden gem: great mechanics and lighthearted fun with excellent pacing. This a great, if a bit short, metroidvania that deserves a look.

I hate to say it, but as much fun as this game looked it really was a flop for me. The turnover mechanic is a terrible mechanic that can't be toggled on or off, but totally wrecks the game by giving brawling based teams a serious advantage every time. Turnover's are a mechanic where if you fall to a tackle, theres a high probability you will lose the rest of your turn. Which is a huge turn-off for a strategy buff like me. It basically eliminates the trade-off's inherent to most stragety game where you make certain sacrifices to gain certain advantages. For instance, placing a player into a blocking position even though I know he will lose his tackle roll simply to slow down a ball carrier for example. The result is often a turnover, and with my turn gone the other team just sails right on past me. It's not a fun mechanic and I can't recommend this game. I really can't Which is sad. But...the developers are the ones who make the rules here. They could have made the mechanic have a toggle switch for player's who hate it. And judging by a lot of community forum posts, I'm not the only one!
It's a highly devisive mechanic and a lot of new-blood such as I are seriously turned off by it. Making matters worse, long term fans of the game are often toxic in the community forums and frequently naysay or bash new player's when we point out that it's a terrible mechanic without an "off" switch and we aren't enjoying the game because of it. Teling us to "suck it up" isn't the way to build a strong community base.

If you're a fan of open world sandbox games and zombies, look no further than Project Zomboid. Drawing inspiration from games like the Sims, Crusader Kings 2, and many others, Project Zomboid manages to create a living, breathing world. Search for food, weapons, nails, seeds for farming, and eventually find a source of water once the water works is turned off. Fresh food like fruit or bread can expire so eventually you'll be down to canned goods or you might even have to make the descion to eat the rotten food and risk getting sick if you have no other options.
Only in alpha, the game already has more gameplay than a lot of completed games out there and this is without the most important part of the game, NPC's. Once NPC's are added, you will begin to see your world change and react to many things you can't see on screen. This is very much like Crusader Kings 2 in that each character in the game have their own goals and their own needs. NPC's will have traits very similar to Crusader Kings 2 which will make each one react to the world in a different way. They'll form their own groups based on these traits, and you might even have someone in your group that is a detriment to everyone else. The game is still in development so there are a few minor bugs (mostly cosmetic and not game breaking at all). Getting the game now is a great opportunity for you because you'll be able to communicate with developers or modders on what you want to see in the game. There have been many things suggested by the community that the game developers are now planning on doing. This game is replayable beyond belief and I'm sure it will provide you with more playing time (hundreds of hours) than a lot of triple A titles.
The more people that buy this game, the more will be added to it. So please, buy the game, I know you'll enjoy it!
Some more features planned (but not guaranteed) to be added:
Hunting
Trap making for zombies and for animals. This includes things like sound traps that generate noise in order to attract zombies away from you or your safehouse.
A complete meta game experience involving numerous events that momentarily change the game world or change it completely. Some examples that are already included: Water and electricity shutting off after a couple months, helicopters flying over thus making zombies restless and likely to move in herds, gunshots that attract zombies to a certain location. Right now the things like gunshots and helicopters are just sounds that play, but in the future, they will be connected to real physical things in the world. For example the gunshot you hear will be an NPC in distress or the helicopter will crash somewhere and you'll be able to track it down and loot it for ammunition or whatever it might be carrying.
In short: If you like playing games however you want, in whatever manner you want with no structure, this game is for you. I consider it a zombie survival "simulator". All those times you've talked to your friends about what you'd do in a zombie apocalypse? well now you can test those theories and see how long you'd last in a world gone mad.

Zombie survival has exploded in the last couple of years, and this game just does what it needs to. Even though the Early Access is buggy( not gamebreaking though ), you can still enjoy the game, either alone, or with friends.
The story of the game is about how you died, how you struggled to escape hordes of zombies, build your base, resist the environment. There is no scripted ending, you die, game over.
You start off customizing your characted, not many customizing options yet, but, the most important thing in the game are the traits. The traits of the character help you a lot, like giving you strength, running speed, etc. After finishing your character, you spawn most likely in a house, zombie free of course. You must scavange for food, materials, tools and whatever you can find to survive. Once you have found enough tools and materials, you should start looking for a place to make into a safehouse, or, building yourself one! Be aware, there is no safe place in this game. If zombies find you, you are screwed. Farming, trapping, fishing, carpentry, all of these are available. Also, based on your actions, your character will improve, awarding you with skill points you can assign, helping you further on.
The game features a single-player mode, also multiplayer, and, local Split-Screen Co-Op, up to 4 players, by using PS3 or X360 controllers.

The Beginner's Guide is more a piece of narrative art than a game. It takes you through a series of source-engine made levels while the narrator talks about his relations with the "game's author" named "Coda". The game invites the player to think about human pitfalls, mostly regarding the compulsive need for self validation. It can be a tiny bit deppressing towards the end, but still thought provoking. In contrast to the Stanley's Parabol, which has a funny and curious approach to narrative gaming, the Beginner's Guide is much more serious. Also, unlike the Stanley's Parabol, the Beginners Guide does not seem to encourage free roaming, and opts to give you a single, hard set path with a single outcome.
If you're into thought provoking narrative games though, this is a game worth trying.

It's like the Contra revival we've been waiting for, not to mention the outstanding sound design, tight controls, excellent level composition and the wonderfully refreshing 1930s art style.
I've just reached the game's third island and while some boss encounters have been immensely frustrating, it's not due to cheap or unfair level design, it's moreso that this game simply demands a lot out of the person playing, yet the feeling of conquering a boss never ceases to be gratifying.
Despite the difficulty however, Cuphead is also relentlessly charming, with expressive, bouncy character designs and animations that are incredibly pleasing to the eye. Even the setup of a cup and mug having to pay back a debt to the devil himself by taking the souls from others is highly original and inventive, and leads to a story that is actually far more interesting than your average platformer.
The soundtrack is similarly fantastic, with loads of fun jazzy tunes and some great vocal tracks, it's all very pleasant and much like the visuals, it offers something unique from the average platformer.
The controls are incredibly tight and responsive, making the fast paced run and gun platforming stages, which while being quite challenging, also a joy to blast through, and the parry system is a really fun mechanic that helps in making the gameplay of Cuphead stand out from the crowd. As for the bosses, they generally have three phases, and ramp up in difficulty as they progress, some of the harder ones so far for me have been the clown, the bird and especially the dragon.
While the run-time of Cuphead is not insanely long from what I've heard(although it's taken me a bit over 5 hours to reach the third island),the game's ranking system in the levels, coin collectables and expert difficulty are great additions that add to it's longevity, making Cuphead a very replayable title.
To put it simply, Cuphead has absolutely been worth the over three year wait, and I can't wait to see what StudioMDHR will make in the future.

Metal Slug, or as some might know it as, Super Vehicle-001, is an arcade shoot’em up, 2D side-scroller that requires quick reflexes and precision aiming. For those that haven’t been into the arcade scene much, or didn’t play these in their prime, Metal Slug is a pillar in the arcade arena. Smooth controls, hand-drawn animations, detailed levels and overall solid gameplay help to make Metal Slug a timeless classic, even after all these years. With that being said, let’s take a look at both the game itself for those who might not be as familiar, and the quality of the port itself.
Over the years Metal Slug’s formula and gameplay hasn’t changed much. You’re given the option of choosing between four characters, whom, aside from cosmetic differences, are widely the same and you’re told to kill everything in your path, solo, or with a friend. While the story can be completely ignored, for those wondering what plot the game has, let me explain.
You’re tasked at stopping General Morden from building an army and completing/deploying a new form of tank, code name “Metal Slug”. With world powers crumbling at the might of General Morden, two members of the Peregrine Falcon Strike Force are deployed with nothing but a handgun apiece and a handful of grenades to stop him, destroying any and all Metal Slug tanks and save the world in the process. A solid plan!
During the course of your risky adventures, you’ll encounter hordes of General Morden’s henchmen, monsters, excellent boss battles and a cache of weaponry at your disposal. Much of the scenery is destructible, giving off a feeling of immense power, as you carve your way through waves of enemies on your way to defeat General Morden, but remember one hit from enemy fire and you’re dead.
With the thinly veiled plot out of the way, Metal Slug was never about substance of story, but substance of gameplay and blowing things up, which is does so wonderfully. For those that have played the original versions of Metal Slug, the port does it a deserved justice.
The game can be played with either mouse & keyboard or a controller and mapping the keys to either is easy to do. During single play, co-op and online multiplayer I had no issues with lagging, disconnections, desync or anything of the sort. The port runs smoothly from beginning to end, over and over. I know the word “port” has often been vilified lately in PC gaming, but not here.
However, the quality of the port isn’t what I’ve felt keeps Metal Slug so beloved by fans. When you truly watch the game, examine the terrain, the level design, the fluidity of gameplay and what I feel is most important: the enemies. What you don’t see often in bullet hell games of this genre is a sense of human contact and subtle humor and
Metal Slug does an interesting job of portraying that. When you encounter groups of soldiers, you’ll often find them engaged in conversations, laughing, warming themselves over a fire or even sunbathing; it puts a face on the enemy, which is usually hidden by scripts that mold the game into a very “you vs them”, but the enemies in Metal Slug will often flee, try to run away and it’s your call whether you gun them down for those delectable points, or let them go [we know you just shot them, you monsters].

This sense of humor adds a lot of value to the game, shaping it into far more than just killing everything that moves. It gives humor; it gives atmosphere. It’s a small addition, but not something I’ve not seen since, which helps to really give Metal Slug a unique charm that other games haven’t been able to recapture, even after all these years.


Overall, if you loved Metal Slug in the past, love bullet hell games now, or think you might enjoy it, I would highly recommend it. This port keeps all the nostalgia and charm of the arcade coming, combined with a solid, well-crafted port to keep the experience going. Just remember, no quarters required!

Guppy is a poetic game, which lets you control a fish by moving its tail left and right.
No other control is used; and every movement of the tail is propelling the fish in the direction of the movement. Used alternatively, left and right movements allow the fish to progress forward, or any way you so desire; by gauging how much of each movement to produce.
Both the left and right sticks can be used; but the game really shines when shoulder controls are used, epecially the analog ones. I am unsure as if the game is using them in an analog fashion (I think not), but using them feels most natural to me.
The premise of the game is simple: collect (eat) flies while avoiding to be eaten by the predator (the large black fishes), by escaping them and/or hiding under water lilies.
While simple, the game is surprisingly challenging, demanding agility, wits and audacity to succeed. And maybe a bit of  learning too; as the movement logic, while somehow surprisingly natural, is also very original and definitely unconventional.
The art of the game has a raw but elegant touch. Playing with the original soundtrack; or better yet, with Debussy's Preludes, Nocturnes, or "suite Bergamasque"; fits really well.
Guppy is certainly not a game in which most of us will put hundreds or thouthands of hours, but it is definitely worth a buy and a try at its full price, if nothing but for its refreshing gameplay and originality.

Growing up throughout my life I knew  that there was something different about myself compared to everyone else. I can remember back to the first day off school, everyone has to wear a costume. Some kids went as pirates, some as football players and some even went as those white armour guys from that Star Wars movie. Not me though, I went as a fish. I was the most glorious fish in the school and everyone was amazed at me for being that fish. That first day at the time was the best day of my life.
All the kids came too school in their uniforms that day, however I chose to stay with who I truly am and continued to wear that fish for the rest of primary school. High school was a bit different though, they wouldn’t allow me to wear that fish around. I kept begging and begging because it was who I was, I didn’t fit in being a human, I was more so a fish. We came to a compromise and they let me paint myself with scales too fit in. I also got gills put in either side of my neck too let me breathe like a fish.
Throughout my whole younger days, I have owned many fish, and have dreamt about joining them as part of their families. I watch in jealousy as I see them swimming around together enjoying each other’s company, struggling as I know I can’t be with them. I left out one very important detail from my story... I can’t swim.
For someone that wants to be a fish, struggling to swim is not very helpful. I thought it would come to me naturally since I am part fish, but it did not. I struggled with the thought in and out every day that I would never be able to join my scaly friends in the ponds or the tanks, until I saw the project thatninjadodo have been working on. Then my life changed...
Yesterday was one of the best days of my life, thanks to Guppy I can finally live my life as a fish with all its friends. The game is a perfect simulation of how a fish survives in a lake and has a very in depth hunger system. It is clever because it includes a score system along with the hunger system that allows you too determine how well you are doing.
It also has a very real combat system too, with bigger fish chasing you down until they defeat you, and you have to use your wits and knowledge too out manuever them just like in the Amnesia series.
This game has changed my life and any people that have had the same condition as myself in their life should pick this game up. I was lucky to get it on sale, but it is well worth the $3 price. Stay safe my fellow fishies, I’ll see you all in the pond.

Don't buy it if you're looking for a fast-paced or even medium-paced game, it actually feels really slow:
-Your ship is slow:
As much as I hate it, an "exploration" game would feel kind of shallow if you could navigate the whole map within 10 minutes, making the map larger accordingly doesn't really solve the issue if you think about it. Game is hard and unforgiving as it is, lengthening the distance to London, your home port, would make it even harder. Maybe if combat would be more profitable/complex, it wouldn't feel so tedious, which leads to my next point.
- Combat is really simple:
It comes down to pressing a button whenever your weapon is ready to attack, or a bit earlier for a faster shot with a slight miss chance, kiting sea creatures, and staying behind enemy ships. Furthermore, early through mid game engaging in combat is not worth the fuel, resources and risk involved given how little profit you can get, and is really only usefull to reduce your crew's terror while at sea.
-Earning echoes(in game currency) is slow:
I see a lot of people complaining about the grinding. I must say, you're doing it wrong. Most quests don't yield a single echo, instead, they usually pay you with merchandise, which you can sell, trade, or use for further quests. This is were it gets controversial. If you sell these quest/special items, you can earn a really quick buck, usually enough to get a really good ship relatively fast. However, if you want the best ship, this is really not enough, and the grinding game starts, usually with trade routes, and given that merchandise value does not fluctuate with time, or even between playthroughs, they are always the same routes, which gives the "grindy" feeling.
-Reading the game story is slow.
And its really what makes the whole exploration thing worthwhile, its amazingly well written, and really pushed me to try and find every story in the game. However, after 66 hours, I think I've found most (so technically, feels like I have finished it), and given the earlier points I wrote, it gets boring, but every single-player game does after a finite amount of time after you finish it, eh. :v
Tl,dr: Buy game if you're patient and  like: -> reading <-, so if you just skipped to tldr because you're impatient or lazy, its probably not a game for you, lol.

At a glance, you could mistake it for generic fantasy fare, but it's actually out to lampoon the setting, and unlike so many games that make an attempt at humor, it manages to be amusing. If the game did nothing else well, it might be worth playing just for the laughs.
You wouldn't be wrong to show some degree of skepticism towards a satirical video game. Games that parody other games have become dime-a-dozen, and frequently, their devotion to sending up their target leads to the would-be satirists committing the same crimes that they're supposedly critiquing. Magicians & Looters, however, backs up its parody with solid design of its own that usually manages to cleverly side-step the issues that it mocks. It draws liberal influence from Castlevania: Symphony of the Night in particular, with several direct references that will make any fan smile, but despite wearing their fandom on their sleeves, Morgopolis have just enough ideas of their own to keep their game interesting.
The gameplay mostly sticks to the tried and true formula for Metroidlikes with the player exploring a series of caverns, forests, and castle interiors while gaining new abilities and fighting enemies with melee attacks and spells, but it's very adept at this style. Little things bring Magicians & Looters into its own, such as the inclusion of three distinct characters with unique play-styles, balanced leveling that makes it impossible to grind, and a Lightning mode that increases the player's speed and power, making them almost invincible. The power-ups, with one or two notable exceptions, are the reliable staples of the genre such as the slide, wall jump, and high jump, and the selection of items is not nearly as vast as what we've seen in the various Castlevanias, but the items that are featured all have their own advantages and disadvantages that cater to different play styles in a manner of which Castlevania really only played lip-service. The level design is also very good with backtracking being kept to mostly a minimum but also with enough to explore that you never feel led by the hand. The only major tweak I would have made to this aspect is to give the player the ability to change characters at any time as you can only do this in save rooms and certain routes require a specific character's abilities. This may have been done to increase the difficulty or to simplify the action, but considering that the game fails to make it clear when to use which character, the necessity of returning to the nearest camp to switch between characters significantly slows the pace of the game.
As strong as some aspects of M&L are, the game falters considerably in its production values, made all the more stinging by how much the Castlevania and Metroid games have excelled in this category. Now, I would be the last person to write off a game for not having state of the art visuals, but the art design is, to be frank, ugly. The drawings look very amateur, and the color palette is ghastly, full of shades of brown, yellow, gray, and orange. Furthermore, the characters, most especially the common enemies, lack distinctive visual characteristics, looking rather crude and generic. This game may have been low budget and farcical, but that's no excuse for such a bland style. Some people have suggested that ungraceful visuals were deliberate, and the even more rudimentary concept art that can be seen in the game's credits lends support to that theory, but if this was done for humor's sake, they should have realized that bad artwork is not necessarily funny artwork. Whatever the reason there may be for the poor style, this area of the game feels rather sloppy and does not live up to the pedigree set by others in this genre. The animation is slightly better than the art but still not great, and the music, while more adequate than the visuals, won't be remembered for long once the game is finished.
With games like Guacamelee, Valdis Story: Abyssal City, and Cave Story, there has been no shortage of decent Metroidlikes for PC in recent years, but even if it is lacking polish in certain areas, Magicians & Looters more than earns its place among them with its unique sense of humor and enjoyable gameplay. If you've never played an adventure-platformer in this vein before, it may not be the greatest place to start, but seasoned fans shouldn't hesitate to dig in. This love-letter to Castlevania is a real treat to behold.

Banished is a simple but very unforgiving game. More often than not, you won't know you made a mistake until it's too late. When you think your food reserves are enough, and that unforeseen baby boom happens and half your population ends up dying to hunger; it's  unfortunate. But now half your population dies again to old age, because majority of the surviving half from the previous catastrophe is much older than the new generations that followed. Ok... Not enough workforce between the old men and the toddlers to forge and distribute clothing, firewood, and stone houses(opposed to wood houses) for warmth.
You have to micromanage every factor, every citizen, every need for survival on a grand scale to build the ultimate utopia. Balance is the name of the game. Banished is a highly polished, enormously engrossing game with a hugely unsatisfying (re: none at all) payoff. I don't for a second lament purchasing it, but I regret every minute I devote to it.
Why is this?
Because there's really no point. Ultimately, like Sim City, even the smallest town can be self-sustaining, provided that you achieve the proper balance (for example, with tiny villages, you can get away with not having a blacksmith if you build correctly; you need not worry about replacing wood houses with stone, etc.). But the thing about Sim City is that the endgame, has, for a generation, built in tempting rewards: higher order buildings, airports, seaports, etc. that push players to drive as hard as possible for the top.
By contrast, nothing unlocks in Banished as you go - if you desire, you can foolishly thrust towards a town hall from day one (note the use of the word 'foolishly'). And while you can expand your tiny settlement into a bustling outpost and even colony, the experience never really changes - you harvest, you fish, you gather, you hunt, you build more houses, and every so often winter comes early and kills half your crops, leading to famine. It NEVER. CHANGES.
The developers could have addressed these shortcomings in one of two ways:
1) Go more personal. All your villagers have names; all of them, being heterosexual (I'm not making any comments here - it's a game mechanic) hook up with members of the opposite sex and produce offspring. However, when a spouse dies, leaving a parent struggling to feed their children amidst their grief and the harshest world imaginable, we don't experience any of their anguish or eventual triumph... all we see are little pixelated 'dudes' on a screen, of which there is one fewer. Moreover, because the replacement rate is so high in Banished, within a few minutes of game time, you've completely forgotten that daddy dearest ever existed - the hole he should have left in this tiny community is almost instantly plugged by some welp coming of age.
The point is, Banished really could have gone down to a smaller scale than it does, where people aren't completely disposable; where the loss of a blacksmith or a doctor or a tradesman means the elmination of years of professional experience, which, in the short to middle term, is irreplacabl... and where screwing up really does kill off your entire town in a snap.
2) Explore more of the backstory of these characters. I mean, the game is called friggin' Banished - the implication is that these people were tossed out of somewhere, either over religious beliefs or goodness knows what else. Is someone hunting them? If your town became successful enough, would a vengeful lord invade, seeking to stomp them out? When nomads show up at your town, why can you simply dismiss them without causing a riot, or risking that they return to the mother land to sell out your location?
Banished doesn't have combat, and, I guess, doesn't really need it (though some wooden palisades might be a nice touch to ring your cities with)... but it would be nice if there were some kind of political or even localized consequences for your being on not-so-friendly terms with wherever it is your folks arrived from. Intead, it's just town building. And famine. Lots of famine.
8/10. If it's on sale, give it a whirl.

I really enjoyed playing this game. Probably the best part about it was the atmosphere the developers were able to create. The art style, lighting, sound effects, voice acting, and setting all molded together into one of the best atmospheres I have ever experienced in a video game. This is shown brilliantly in the first level which was also my favorite part of the game. This introduction to the world of Rapture just felt so dark and mysterious and it really compelled me to want to push on and unravel its mystery.
As far as gameplay is concerned BioShock was a lot of fun. I love how they keep this game relatively non-linear and allow players to explore and approach situations in a variety of ways. The combat is really intense and the wide range of player abilities make the game really stand out from other shooters.
I feel this game also did a good job mechanically and with its balance. I played through on the hardest difficulty and I felt it was tuned perfectly for this game. The ratio of enemy difficulty to player strength is just right and it scales really well as you progress further in the game. Although I feel the difficulty is at its best in the early game when ammo is scarce, and you have to rely more on planning and stealth.
My biggest problem with this game is the plot. The first half of the game I feel is written very well and is extremely engaging. However, later in the game it seems to almost get stagnant. For example there’s a boss in the middle game that just feels out of place and like it doesn’t fit into the story’s plot very well. I feel some of this could have been rethought and adjusted to allow for better pacing.
Overall this was a great game that deserves a special place in its generation. It isn’t a perfect game by any means, but I feel the world Irrational Games was able to create in Rapture is genre defining for story driven shooters. I give this game 8.5 out of 10.

There are some very good aspects to the games design here, but unfortunately they can all be credited to Games Workshop in the 80s and 90s. Or, put another way, the good part of this is that it implements the Blood Bowl boardgame, and the boardgame is excellent.
Negatives:
- Buggy and highly prone to crashing (more so than any game I've played in the last couple of years). This game has been out for 2 years, come on. According to Steam, I've played this for 14 hours now. I'd say about 80% has been replaying crashed games.
- Premium game price for basic components (a fairly short roster of teams, which you need to buy as add ons). This game has been out for 2 years, come on.
- Single Player doesn't permit autosaves, despite high crash rate; only in "campaign mode" (a lengthy tutorial season which throws in scripted events, so that you never get a proper game) is there a save option during games. Even then, it's only "Save and Quit". I don't mind Iron Man modes, if a game wants to be bloody minded. But this is crazy - to save a game (and bear in mind a match takes 30 mins plus to play) you have to Save and Quit, then restart, going through the same idiotic commentary every time.
Next time, I suggest the developer do some user (and for that matter, system-) testing before releasing and continues to do so each time it releases a patch.
Really, cannot recommend.
===
EDIT:
- as a user below points out, I continued to play the game (so sue me).
- I completed the campaign. The game crashed at least once *every* game (but seldom more than once). The save/quit/restore continued to be infuriating, as was the constant bombardment of new rules (in one game, the weather changes maybe 4 times) and additional victory requirements (you can win a game, but not fulfil the other requirements - you're then made to replay from scratch - same if you lose).
- Some friends and I started a league, 3 real players and 7 AIs, playing Round Robin (I think you all need Legendary Ed for this). 4 games in, none of the games have crashed. It's a fairly faithful reproduction (apart from the implementation of star players) version of the board game. It's great fun. Though I'm not sure how random the results are when AI teams play one another; from obvservation, I'd say "very".
So ... have switched my recommendation. The campaign's worthwhile as a tutorial, but needs some significant quality control attention. Multi-player's great though (with friends. From what I've read if you get more competitive and play with random players, many of the games get conceded before they've finished). And the league games against the AI are decent. The AI is better than a lot of the reviews seem to imply, although at the end of the game it will keep trying for touchdowns - even if there aren't enough moves left - rather than just randomly battering players, as I would do.
I love going back to this game for some city building. Not the game I've played the most, sure, but I still would recommend it to friends.

The Story Mode is really short (did it myself in 4 hours) but there are loads of challenges and new Levels in Endless Arena Mode so THE CONTENT IS THERE. I still have about 60% of the game ahead of me after having put quite some time into Challenges and Endless Mode.
For the Story:
I really liked it and how it even made me turn off the game as a part of the Plot. It's got a pretty dark athmosphere and breaks the 4th Wall which is always a plus in my book. The only bad thing I can say about it is that they've wasted a lot of potential by ending the Story so early and that they assumed the player to be wearing a VR Headset which kinda took a bit away from the immersion.
The Gameplay:
Unique but Awesome. What else did you expect here? After you are done with story mode you are still far from done with this game. Try unlocking all the Arena Modes and Challenges. In my opinion that is the actual core of the game.
The Graphics:
I like how they used the Red, White, Black theme throughout the entire Game. Keeping usable objects and People as rough Polygons with one colour assigned to them really gave it a nice touch and kept it simple but intriguing whilst having the surroundings a bit more detailed by smoothing the surfaces and applying textures. Also using triangles instead of blood really gave it a cool look.
Overall the graphics are not too demanding or "next level" but it adds to the game in my opinion.
Some Animations need fixing though: When i pick up an item I already have it in my hand, even though it is still flying towards me.
Secrets:
There are quite a lot of secrets hidden in the in-game file browser so search through every single folder and open every single file. It's worth it.
Things I'd still love to see:

A very clever fiction wrought of truths; an impressive analysis of the relationship between creator and audience, and what happens when the audience begins to thrust too much of themselves into the work - reading what isn't there, and through perception and demand, possibly changing the nature of the work.
Also, on a slightly more objective note -
* Very nice architectural work. You can really see how far this guy has come since the humble mod version of The Stanley Parable, with all its HL2 prefabs. It's also very nice to see a developer make use of such raw architecture, instead of littering his maps with generic, high-detail props.
* Very nice sound work. The music and ambient sound is all at once subtle, but really effective.
If you play this, try not to get too caught up on the question of whether or not the story is "real". If you've played the original Stanley Parable, or know anything about game design/map design, you'll know almost as soon as the game starts, and you'll know *why*. But with any luck, you'll also understand why it's no less true, despite not necessarily being real.

In Superhot, your every move costs you precious fractions of a second. Every time you walk, every time you pull the trigger or just look around, the game goes from extreme slowmo to a real time. Ironically, you don't have time to just stand and look around. There's no room for wasting time on unnecessary actions, because there's always a bunch of trigger-happy red dudes nearby. So yes, Superhot is indeed an FPS, but it plays more like a turn based puzzle game. There's a great deal of strategy involved. It's more about predicting one's movement, and less about landing headshots.
Now, this may sound exaggerated, but it's true: it's one of the most fun, most satisfying videogame experiences I've ever had in my life. The thrill when trying to literally dodge the bullets, and that extremely rewarding feeling when you actually manage to do that, is something that very much reminds me how I felt when I played through Hotline Miami. It's addictive, intoxicating and cathartic experience.
Because of that, I see Superhot as a very important game: it's an FPS, that let's you experience those extremely cool MLG moments, even if you suck at FPS's. For those brief moments, you are the biggest action movie badass ever. Everyone can be badass in Superhot. I think that's wonderful.
There's a lot of people complaining about how short the story campaign is. And sure, it really isn't that long. But frankly, if you watched a trailer for this game, seen all the cool stuff happening on the screen, and then said to yourself "I'm buying this because it maybe has a story campaign", then you're a dumbass. For ♥♥♥♥s sake, this game let's me slice a bullet with my katana as it is about to hit me. I couldn't care less about how long the story is.
No, I won't tell you Superhot is a flawless game, because it isn't. It could benefit from more levels, maybe even a level editor or some daily/weekly challenges. But I had to ask myself: "Does that matter? Do I enjoy the game less, because of those things?" And my answer to that is no. I think there's enough content to justify the price. There are already different challenges and endless modes, and there are secrets to find there as well…and that's more than fine by me.
I've already played for more than 14 hours (campaign took me like 2 hours btw) and I'm still having fun. It's one of those games I can start up every day, play for half an hour and just unwind. I honestly think that punching a guy in a face, grabbing his gun in mid-air and watching him shatter as he gets hit by his own bullet will never get old for me…at least not anytime soon.

Okay, so I don't usually like to write bad reviews, I just tend to brush over games that didn't quite scratch my interest or had little flaws that make them less than optimal, but still, games. This product however barely qualifies as a game I am afraid. Based on the screenshots you would believe you are getting into a block placement based puzzle game that will challenge your wits and makes you think in new and interesting ways about 3D spaces and whatnot.
This game however offers none of that. It actually is a more sluggish version of Minecraft's find the button custom games. You basically spend all of your twenty or so minutes of playing this game (if you are a completionist) hunting down the red blocks you can place and after that you just do the same thing you did since the begininng, which is either building a bridge with two cubes or building a stair with two cubes. There are levels where you have to catch the cubes mid-jump, get them from hidden places, and the final level is putting the blocks literally behind the spawn, in plain sight. There is nothing puzzly about this product, only looking for red blocks in an uninspired 3D environment.
The controls are sluggish, there are no control options whatsoever, the video options are lackluster to say the least, I have encountered a bug where all sound would just go away, probably due to alt+tabbing out of the game, and there are popin issues when you look out from behind pillars while moving. But at least you get a sandbox mode where you can place any color of block in infinite numbers (unless you fill the available space in of course) and build your Mario pixel art in 3D or something. If you are looking for that, this game can offer it, no problem. If you are looking for a puzzle game, stay away from this.
TL;DR: Wants to look like Qbeh-1: The Atlas Cube, but does not provide any of the sort.
