A Hat in Time is one of those games that, right after completion, you wish you could re-experience for the first time again. From its title screen to the first cutscene, the game feels… alive.
I like-a-me some 3D platformers. [i.e. Uber biased] Several games that A Hat in Time’s are some of my all-time favorite and it’s great to see that legacy continued. 3D Platformers (especially, triple A ones) are becoming less and less predominate with only a few significant releases for the genre in 2017. It’s heartwarming to see people vote with their wallets to fund passion projects and to then see those games become successful.
Enough rambling. Hat Kid controls smoothly. Most jumps are composed of combination of a single jump, double jump and dash [with a small cancel]. There’s also one long jump that the sprint hat uses (same distance, not as much height), wall momentum (double jump gets you way higher) and wall jumps. There’s not much complexity [that I know of] here for, say, the wizards of Mario 64 speedrunning to utilize, but for us mortals, it’s plenty. The double jump is forgiving and you can easily recover from most slightly over/underestimated jumps. You’re not allowed to switch directions with the dash, but that’s pretty fair considering how that might be abusable. Wall jumps felt a little off a times, despite their rarity. There’s no way to cancel sliding down a wall into a straight fall so I found myself instinctually pressing A out of impatient to get off a wall resulting in a tumble into the abyss. More than anything, the fact that I felt obligated to mention these moveset hiccups both displays my involvement in Hat Kid’s movement and the potential for even more subtle mechanics that might allow for a higher skill cap.
A Hat in Time orchestrates a beautiful aleatoric soundtrack where leitmotifs and unique instruments breathe life into and give a signature feel to both characters and chapters.. Tunes, like the Main Theme, appear in numerous situations, branding the aspects of the game as connected adding to their memorability. There are plenty of great examples of this. The way the music in purple time rifts fades between instruments or how an overworld melody changes between biomes or how boss themes ramp up during battles, to name a few. It’s something you were and think, "Once I'm done with this game [avoid spoiler tracks] I'm going to listen to this stuff over and over". [Although it should be noted that the music always sounds better when you’re enjoying it as a part of the game]. Parts of the OST also fulfilled my chiptune element quota :3
props to Pascal Michael Stiefel for capturing a brilliant sense of adventure.
A few technical problems did show up here and there but it wasn’t anything unforgivable. Sometimes collision errors appeared when the game had tricky geometry or struggled with apply wall jumps. One instance forced me to return to hub after getting caught falling above ground endlessly. The way this game handles circular objects can be a bit off sometimes as well. Grabbing nonexistent ledges and generally being afraid to hop onto round surfaces also hurts the game’s otherwise polished surroundings.
Chapters feel like toy boxes and have a good density of little secrets/intractables. Chapters not only change up visually but have an assortment of unexpected variety (hallway sprints, races, stealth segments, parades etc.) that have you wondering what they’ll come up with next. Nothing ever feels like that game has failed at trying to contain too many types of gameplay, a common trap for other platformers. Outside of Chapter 2, areas have a central act that let you explore and choose what objectives you want to complete first. Personal choices like where to explore, what Acts/Chapters to do and even what Hats/colors you wear make for an adventure of your very own.
Secrets, in the form of token/relics [for time rifts]/yarn, foster spatial awareness that turn landscapes into memorable play-places. Finding and playing the bonus time rifts, with their somber music, were some of my favorite moments.
A Hat in Time is filled with frienemies who, plot-wise, are on your side but seem to be okay with a few murders here and there (perhaps in acknowledgement of Hat Kid’s god-like superiority). The personalities of NPCs are across the board silly and enduring. For example, Mafia Town hosts some Mafioso that are both aggressive and a few that just want to chit-chat or play patty-cake. I also love Hat Kid’s lovable and confident nature. Detail in the animations for walking have her stomp around like a superhero and extras like that are topnotch. Collectively, A Hat in Time has too many little moments to count. It feels like love and care went into bringing these areas to life.
Thankfully, completion is forgiving, there no achievements about getting every token/yarn. 100% means you’ve seen every mission and done a few goofy extras. Going all out and getting all the yarn or tokens to grab hats/colors is your choice. Some of the harder achievements are all something I spent a decent amount of time on before becoming too frustrated to continue. I’m a little disappointed in myself for diving into them knowing my typical response to ‘beat with one health’ challenges. Through my drive to pointlessly acquire achievements, I ended up hurting my last few experiences in a game I enjoyed. For Steam’s in-game overlay, this has been its final nail in the coffin and I’ve chosen to disable it from now on and learn to savor games in the moment more.
A Hat in Time has been, and will continue to be, a fantastic escapade. It’s a great reminder of why I love video games and there’s plenty more I could discuss. There’s always an element caution when shouting praises at a game in this manor so it’s good to try to stay real. After all, the worst way to recommend something to someone is to completely overhype it. In the end, A Hat in Time blew me out of the water and it’s something that I hope others can enjoy as much as I did <3

In a generation where many developers try to coast by on nostalgia value, it's nice to see a game that captures that giddy platforming delight I had back when I first gave Super Mario 64 a spin. Though not without its faults, A Hat in Time is an exciting 3D-platformer romp with quite a bit of love and charm backing it all up.
Marooned in space on the way home from.... Something, the protagonist Hat Kid must retrieve the Magical Hourglasses used to power her ship. The stakes are high--however, as once people find out these trinkets have the power to reverse time, all bets are off. In typical 3D-platformer fashion, Hat Kid has a wide range of moves, powers, and gadgets to maneuver the jump-heavy worlds and plenty of goals to achieve. Missions range from challenge stages to races, and while many of said challenges aren't particularly challenging, they still offer an enjoyable time. The levels are backed up by a distinct artistic vision reminiscent of Wind Waker and Paper Mario--a cutesy, almost storybook world with goofy characters. The soundtrack evokes the orchestral pieces from Super Mario Galaxy along with newer, groovier tunes, and the voice acting ranges from excellent to somewhat annoying. Thankfully the developers included a special item to turn most dialogue into the jibber-jabber made popular by Banjo-Kazooie, so nothing grates too much. As for the script itself, it's simplistic, but fun. You won't find yourself laughing at every joke, but there are definitely ones you will laugh at. The game doesn't take itself too seriously, nor does the plot. In conclusion, if you find yourself weighed down by a few extra dollars and you catch this on sale, give it a shot. Even if you don't love it you'll get a good amount of mileage!

If scary first person stealth games are your poison, you'll find much beefier sustenance in Amnesia and Alien: Isolation. Conversely, if you have played either of those titles, Outlast will seem like a walk in the park by comparison. The atmosphere is solid, but immersion is hamstrung at every turn by the simplistic AI. Enemies follow rigid and easily observeable paths when trying to track you down (though maybe that's better on "insane" difficulty?) The worst part is the storyline, which pilfers liberally from the great cliché trove of Western Horror, with absolutely no idea how to piece all the disparate tropes together into a coherent whole. Just when the plot threatens to get interesting, you're whacked over the head with some ridiculous "twist" that seems ripped straight from Resident Evil, Bioshock and even Wolfenstein. I still played it through to the end, so something apparently kept me going, but I'm not sure what. It's trite and predictable throughout, but there's a certain charm to the ambience. I think it reminded me of Condemned. Yes. There you go. Play Condemned instead.

Just Cause 2 is not a game that let's you slow down.
This action-packed, explosion-fueled, frenzy of a game has a very simple premise. Destroy as much as you can as stylishly as you can. The games B-movie story is here merely to provide context to all the destruction you will be causing.
A bond-esque supervillian/dictator is terrorising the island of Panau. As wise-cracking, special agent Rico Rodriguez - you must infiltrate the island, team up with allies and factions to take down the villian. The several campaign missions you can play through are designed to showcase the games best setpieces and locations. One mission has you infiltrate a heavy defended military base that is destroyed up as you escape. Another has you battle three seperate bosses on the roof of a hotel. The campaign missions offer a nice amount of diversity and variety in their structure. Just don't go in looking for a groundbreaking story or voice acting. The game is intentionally cheesy but also very humourous.
Outside of the campaign there are multiple faction missions you can partake in to increase your standing with a given faction. These can range from simple tasks such as delivering a vehicle to a waypoint or escorting an NPC. One standout mission has you crash land on strange island that houses a mysterious weapon that you must destroy before you can leave. The best missions from factions are the stronghold takeovers. Strongholds are heavily defended complexes that you must siege with your faction allies in order to gain control over a region of Panau. These missions showcase the best parts of Just Cause 2 - destruction on a massive scale, intense gunfights, relentless enemies and tough encouters. Your reward for taking strongholds are new faction missions and racing/time trial challenges.
The racing and time trials are decent and mainly serve as a means for players to earn extra money in game. What I will commend is how creative and challenging some of them are. Trials use the games cars, boats, helicopters, planes and base/sky diving and each takes advantage of the mode of transportation. You may be tasked with driving trucks across beaches, boats through rivers and planes through cities. The base jumping in particular requires a lot of skill from the player.
Outside of all these missions, the player will be exploring Panau for faction related collectibles or upgrades from vehicles and weapons. Players are also encouraged to 'sabotage' (see: blow the hell out of) government property and infrastructure. This can range from small power generators to enormous gas silo's and cranes. Needless to say, the destruction is relative to the property being destroyed - the aformentioned generators spark and fizzle while gas silo's explode into enormous balls of fire and cranes come crashing to the ground. The destruction is immensely satisfying given how much of the world can be interacted with.
So how can the player achieve such destruction? The game provides a plethora of weapons from simple pistols to more extreme options such as grenade lauchers and C4. Weapons are easy to use - in fact perhaps a bit too easy. Just aiming at an enemy and firing away will send them to the ground or spinning in the air. The games enemies mostly serve as fodder rather than strategic opponents. Some will use jeeps or pilot helicopters but even these are easy disposed of.
These options aren't limited to enemies however as Just Cause 2 has an even greater number of weaponised and passive vehicles. The range of offer here is IMMENSE - Sports Cars, Trucks, Motorcycles, Tanks, Speed Boats, Patrol Boats, Transport Helicopters, Airliner planes and massive fighter jets. My personal favourite is the enormous 'C-130' inspired cargo plane.
Just Cause 2's greatest tool is Rico's grappling hook. Acting as both a mode of transport and a weapon, the grappling hook adds a dynamic not seen in many other comparable games. Enemies can be grappled to walls and vehicles to create some creative kills. Using the grappling hook you can access hard to reach places, hijack vehicles and use in combination with your parachute to sail across the landscape.
All of this action takes place across the beautiful islands of Panau. There are snowy moutains, vast deserts and thick jungles to explore. The game is stunning and runs flawlessly.
Just Cause 2 is great game to invest your time in. Whether on sale or at full price, you will definitely get your money out of this one.

Magicians and Looters is a really solid Metroidvania style platformer.  Exploration is the name of the game, and exploring MAL's levels, packed with secrets, shops, items, monsters, and some light puzzles is a real joy.  The game consists of three playable characters, each having a unique set of abilities and its own play style.  New abilities can also be acquired by exploring the map.   The player can freely switch between the characters and recover health by visiting camp sites.  Each section of the game is punctuated by a fun set piece boss fight.  The game's story isn't particularly serious, but is full of goofy humor.
The graphics in this game are serviceable, but not as pretty as some of its contemporaries.  The game is a bit shorter than I would have liked (my original playthrough of the Desura version took around 10 hours).  Overall, I found it to be a lot of fun, and I can definitely recommend it to fans of the Metroidvania genre.

I'd first like to say that I don't play metroidvanias, but this game stuck out like a sore thumb to me, in a good way of course. Ever since I saw the trailers on greenlight a few months back, I knew this game would be awesome because of how different it looked from other metroidvanias I have encountered. Once MAL came out, I instantly bought it and boy did it deliver.
The game is a breath of fresh air, from the story line to the VERY SMOOTH controls. The game reccommends you play with a controller, but the keyboard works perfectly fine just because how accurate the movement is. Everytime I died was only because I was being too reckless.
MAL's storyline is cliche, but it is very well executed. I've always had a saying that cliche isn't bad, as long as it's well done and solid. The dialogue is well placed and the timing is perfect. It definitely made me laugh the whole way through. Also, I really liked how thee's a chance to see funny interaction between the three heroes when you go into camp.
The combat is solid, very easy to pick up and difficult to master. There's no super heavy ultra super sayian combos, but it gets the job done, especially if you play Vienna :D. Boss fights are very challenging and not some monster with a lot of K.O. moves. Enemies are fairly tough, you can't just run and there and expect to wreck everything. Recovery items are almost nonexistant, but that's a good thing because I don't like games holding my hand. Besides, you can always go back to camp to heal if you really needed to.
Level design in this game is great, as expected of a metroidvania. The secrets are moderately spread out and not too hard to find. All the maps seem to flow together seemlessly. I do often times get lost, but that's half the fun. I also really liked how
this game utilizes ALL THREE heroes, instead of just making one do all the work. The maps require you to use all the characters in order to find all the secrets and access different areas. However, one very minor grip I have is that aside from regular secrets, I wish there were like super hidden secrets. I know you guys are trying to make it completeionist friendly, but a few super secret loot wouldn't hurt :3 (unless there's super secret loot and I just havent found it yet. I'm on to you developers!! Just kidding).
The music in this game is great. It's not the best, but it definitely fits with the atmostphere of the game. Very mellow and ambiant. You don't really notice it being there, but without it the stages wouldn't be the same. But, if you do decide to stop and listen, it's well made and pretty darn catchy.
Art style and animation in this game is subjective in all honestly, but it is, however, very solid and gets the job done. That's all that matters. Long as it doesnt look like I'm playing a game at 2 FPS when the actual FPS is 60 or Vienna looks like a burly man XD.
I highly reccommend this game. 10/10

Wait for Legendary Edition to come down in price and then buy that; regular version is missing most of the teams (including ones that were base in BB1, like Amazons).
Compared to BB1, League customization is a LOT better, but finding matches can be a bit more awkward (the UI also makes it difficult to challenge someone directly). Game HUD is more sparse, but it's also customisable, so eh. The game is a lot smarter about activating skills now; it (usually) intelligently checks for if you might not want to activate a skill (like Wrestle), rather than you having to set it skill-by-skill as in BB1. There is a very slight change to the interface (r-ctrl now cycles pitch info, including grid, player skills, etc.), and in particular you have to click outside the player's movement if the interface gets 'stuck' asking if you want to blitz. Also, passes/handoffs can no longer be declared as part of the same movement action in which the player picks up the ball (you have to finish the move - say, just move them to the ball - and then move them once they have the ball. This doesn't interfere with gameplay, but is different from BB1 and may catch you out).
Regular BB2 gives you a new team, Bretonnians, who I was initially pretty unsure about since they're not based in the LRB, but they're actually pretty fun (they're a very sticky human-esque team with some unusual starting skills). Legendary gives us back pretty much everything that was missing from the base release, adds in Slann (in the guise of the Kislev Circus), and gives support for multi-race teams based on the Chaos Pact team (haven't tested these much though). Also adds an eternal league single player option, and the AI has been pretty seriously improved (it's still garbage compared to a human, but much better than in BB1).
The commentary is generally a fair bit better now, but it does tend to suffer by only having so many lines per team (especially for DLC teams). It also responds by cutting off dialogue for new dialogue if there's a sudden change in  situation on the pitch, although the logic can be a bit dumb (i.e. Bob may apologise for talking over himself).
Realistically Legendary Edition IS worth the full price it's asking for, but fifty bucks is still a big ask, especially for a game where a game can take an hour to play (so it eats a lot of your time), so wait for it to go on sale.

Double Cubes - The name says it all - To solve most of the levels, you simply need two cubes.  The hard part, especially on the latter half of the levels, is finding those pesky cubes.
Is it a complete game?  No - people looking for more than what you see in the store video would be disappointed.
Does it have potential?  Yes.
Why do I like it?  I'm running this game off a GTX 970 SC and it's smooth.  The sterile environments and mouse movements give me a nice Zen feeling as I move through the levels.  For the $0.49 I picked it up for on sale, it was worth the 90 minutes of play time.
Controls:  Move with WASD, no run modifier.  Right Mouse Button brings up the cube editing mode, scroll wheel changes between add/remove cubes, Left Mouse Button performs the Add/Remove Action.  That's it!
Pros:
+ Animations are smooth (Mouse movements, turns, Blocks being added / removed).
+ Sandbox is HUGE.
+ Has a unique artistic style that I can appreciate.
+ Ambient music is nice.
+ Restart a level at any time.
+ No need to save, the game tracks your level progress automatically.
+ When looking for the red blocks, they really stand out, even if they are far away.  There's no worry that you are overlooking a block due to darkness / shadow issues. (Though some are cleverly hidden).
Mixed:
~ You can add / remove blocks from any distance.  If you can see a surface, you can access it with the edit function.  Not sure how I feel about this.  The mechanic for far away block retrieval is used in the later levels, which makes it work well in those circumstances.
Cons:
- No real story - intro and final cut scenes are nice, but don't add much.
- Only 15 levels.
- The 'two block walk*' severely limits the game in terms of challenge.  If the dev could figure out how to come up with another mode that limits the (repeated) use of blocks, it would make it much more of a puzzler.
- Nothing such as timer or info that lets you know what level you are currently on.
- No control descriptions other than 'tutorial' as you start.
- Sound effects / Music randomly don't play.
- Music was so low by default, I almost didn't realize there was any until I visited the options.
- You don't feel as the character really exists (no shadows are cast from you as you move around / you don't see any arms or legs where you'd expect them to be). - minor gripe!
- Level 12
- Level editor / Sandbox has no save / export / import functionality.  Steam workshop + adding the editor could make this game something special with community levels.
- Can't free-roam the sandbox (you walk around and start at the bottom of the editor instead of being able to float around to place blocks).
So, yes, I'd reccomend this game for something to do while relaxing, even with the negatives.  I hope there's more to come!
*Two Block Walk - Place 1st Block, jump on 1st block.  Place 2nd Block, jump on 2nd block.  Remove 1st Block.  Rinse, repeat.

Very charming, possibly-incomplete (see Cons section), light-hearted platformer, bringing back memories of N64 platformers.  Think along the lines of Mario 64, Banjo-Kazooie, and Donkey Kong 64.  Thoroughly enjoyed my playthrough of this little gem; A Hat in Time is a fine example of what someone can make utilizing Unreal engine.  You collect yarn to unlock a variety of hats which contain special powers.  Each power allows you to reach new areas or unlock new stages.  You also collect gems as currency to purchase ability badges that either upgrade your hat powers or give you some abilities.  3 badges and one hat may be worn at a time, so learning to switch when needed is essential (but not that difficult).  A few takeaways:
Well-funded.  Wonderfully textured environments that fit the cartoony feel.  Whoever the main artist is, there are tons of in-game "artwork" and illustrations to be found.  Kudos to whoever the artist(s) was/were, as well as the director for investing to have so many illustrations done.
This is the main difficulty and focus of the game.  While not impossible or requiring mastery levels of practice, there are some solid challenges to overcome.  Hopefully you, the reader, understand when I describe a "pooper retracting up your spine" feeling, yes?
Like the Art Style, the various worlds shine brightly.  Each are beautiful in their own way and are full of life.  Besides your main spaceship (think Peach's Castle), you have 4 themed worlds to visit.  Each world has distinct zones to visit that differ, but fit in with the theme of the world.  Most are open worlds while one is instanced.  Puzzles mix between fighting bosses, scavenger hunts, difficult platforming, and even stealth!
Suitable, non-cringy dialog.  A few adult-nudges for any parents that are playing with kids.  No obnoxious, Eddie Murphy sidekick.
Surprisingly smooth.
Subjective, but very well done.  Original songs that fit the game, with the exception of two.  One is a mixture of two Zelda OoT songs and the other... I swear it is a remake of Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence.  Not complaining though, MCML is one of my favorite songs.
Custom fun!  Players are creating their own levels and designing their own hat skins.
The game ends.  You don't have to grind, buy loot boxes, or whatever online nonsense.  Strange to think one would get excited about something ending, but its >current year+1.
Story is free of any of that nonsense.  There is onneeee small political joke against capitalism tucked away in a level.  I'm guessing whoever owns Gears for Breakfast likely believes differently now that this game is a hit.  Funny how that works, huh!
You will likely not reach the [$1 / 1 hour] quota on you first playthrough.  Mario 64 had 120 stars and cost $70 at launch in 1998.  This game has 40 "time pieces" (same as stars) and costs around $30.  I managed to collect them all in the course of 18hours while not exactly speeding through levels (taking screenshots, eating meals, looking around the levels for fun).  In addition, did not use any guides.  More time will be invested to collect the achievements.  the Achievements call for beating a certain number of stages without losing a life or beating a boss without taking damage.  If you dabble in user-created levels through Steam Workshop, you will likely cross the $1/1hr threshold.
Once you know the main use of each ability, there's very little "creative applications" for them.  The game is very straight forward.  When originally starting the game, I was speculating if one could further upgrade their hat powers with extra yarn (items needed to unlock the ability hats).  Turns out they don't.  There's a badge that powers up one hat, and another that reduces cooldown for two others.  That's it.  Additionally:
Don't sweat like a thick, elephant cup, elf milf in a sinkhole when you suddenly realize you have no more coins to use the cosmetic-item-giving slot machine.  Also, don't scratch your head when you end the game with 100% and still have hat-creating yarn leftover.  This is working as intended.  You can obtain additional slot machine coins by playing user-created levels.  As for the leftover yarn, no idea what (if anything) is planned for them.
Boss fights are challenging and very entertaining.  However, the normal rank and file enemies are extremely limited.  Once you observe the one way they attack and the easiest counter, that's all you need to know.  The challenging aspect of this game is platforming, not fighting.   Puzzles do repeat, however.  None are overwhelming difficult or elaborate.  No Zelda 64 Water Temple, but also no Skyrim spinning totems.  While more focus is placed on platforming, doing the "throw the bomb" puzzles became dull after the 10th time.
You will know from the art style and hearing "N64 platforming" whether or not you will want this game.  I found it to be an extremely enjoyable, light game and enjoyed every minute of running around.  Wondering now if there will be any updates / DLC that add anything.  Its a bit interesting that the game ends with excess yarn in your inventory.  I certainly do recommend A Hat in Time to friends.  If by some remote chance a member of the development team is reading this, please consider these for the next DLC or game in the series:
~ Ability to power up hats with a currency/yarn.
~ More relics to hunt.
~ Sidequests with NPCs.
~ Some sort of a final hat to spend excess yarn with.
~ Collection notebook/menu that shows progress of everything collected and numbers that are missing.  This includes Purple Time Rift photos, R.K. notes, relics and yarn.

A Hat in Time is a game that borrows from Super Mario 64, Super Mario Sunshine, Super Mario Galaxy, and Banjo-Kazooie, featuring 3D platforming mechanics, collecting things for the sake of collecting things, and multi-objective large open areas with wacky yet not out-of-place designs (perhaps a bit of Psychonauts?)
That said, AHiT is worth much more than just nostalgia: it's cute, humorous, challenging, and a lot of fun, while also meeting modern standards with high-quality graphics and fluid, precise controls. There's also modding support with a bunch of well-made mods already available on the Workshop (currently in an opt-in beta).
Also, you can ride a Roomba.
(Note for OSX users: Modding support beta is currently only available on Windows. DirectInput controllers - most notably DualShock (PlayStation) controllers - are not recognized properly by the game at the moment, so you may have to use keyboard controls.)

This is an amazing game that probably shouldn't be purchased in this incarnation. You should absolutely play it in some other way, no doubt; it's run and gun nirvana. It's a crazy fever dream of World War 2 with big bosses, big explosions, and lots of dying unless you have super good arcade twitch reflexes (and even then, man, those little flashing orb shots will get ya!). The later games in the series would be bigger and wilder, but the first one remains an unfiltered heavy metal, chunky, explosive masterwork in its own right.
This port by DotEMU is pretty shoddy, though...more slowdown than the arcade original, surprisingly blurry visuals, and unresponsive controls. And on top of that, they are asking for 8 bucks for this. If this was a perfect, flawless 1:1 port made by a team like the retro wizards at M2, ok, I'd be willing to see it, but with the state of this port as it is, the price is really overblown. There are many other and much cheaper ways to play this game, including numerous collections and anthologies released over the years on a wide variety of consoles. Unless Steam is your only way to play video games, you can easily track down a better way to play Metal Slug.
So yeah, in conclusion, I certainly recommend the game but not this version...play it, but not like this or for this price.

I grew up playing 3D platformers, so after my disappointment from Yooka Laylee’s supposed mediocrity (still haven’t played it), my interest was sparked by A Hat In Time. I finally got to give it a chance, and after I started I couldn’t stop, the whole time with a smile on my face. The devs know exactly what their game is in terms of game design and it shows, in other games I would consider it too ambitious to switch up level design so much but A Hat in Time does it with a lot of tact, and I actually welcomed it. Whether it was the short vignettes of the movie studio or the vast, beautiful expanse of the mountains, this game made me smile at every turn, it was infectious, and I couldn’t help but see the love and care put in by people who actually care about video games.
Pros
------
-Change in level design from act to act was done well and was actually welcomed
-Adorable story and characters
-The controls felt great, and the tutorialization was fun
-Kept gameplay fresh with badges and other missions
-Some of the visuals are absolutely amazing in this game, and some of the visual experiences left me audibly saying “WOW!”
-Exploration was fun
-Surprisingly deep amount of customization for the main character
-Great music!
-Made me laugh constantly

Cons (minor complaints, just little things I think the game could have to make it better)
------
-Lack of free roam after completion of worlds/ levels (you can practically free roam in most 	levels, but it would be nice to have a dedicated feature for free roam on all levels that 		have collectibles.)
-Sometimes it felt like a map was needed to navigate, and I think would be useful to younger and/or more inexperienced players who have a trouble with landmarking in games (I’m thinking mainly in the forest level)
-Graphically there was a lack of polish, but no game breaking bugs, and totally understandable for an indie dev for a game of this scale (this seems contradictory to my pros statement, but this game was on a spectrum graphics-wise).
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall this was one of the most pleasant experiences with a game I’ve had in a long time, and it was good from top to bottom. There was a lot of good games to come out of 2017, but A Hat in Time is definitely in my top 5 this year.

Sunless Sea doesn't initially seem to offer much. Until it does. The game is set in across an underground ocean, where current and tides shift the islands and landmasses around every once in a while. You're the captain of ship amongst many others, in a world of Lovecraftian piracy where smuggled sunlight and spirit-infused honey are contraband goods.
It's not a game for the wilfully illiterate. If you are annoyed by reading paragraphs upon paragraphs of texts on the sidebars, Sunless Sea probably isn't for you. After all, the game derived from a browser-based game called Fallen Londoni consisting of large swathes of text to go through.
As you create your character, you also designate your aspiration, which may be retiring rich or perhaps making a great discovery. You're then set with a rickety ship at the Wolfstack Docks in Fallen London. Through trading, piracy and other quests, you're going to make money, improve your ship and recruit a crew.
Sunless Sea mainly features a bird's eye view of Unterzee, the abovementioned underground ocean. You navigate these waters and find your way around by deploying a Zeebat, which scans a large circle around your ship, allowing you to explore the map. For what is essentially an animated map, Sunless Sea looks spectacular. The artworks in some of the islands are simply things of sheer beauty to look. Many islands feature some sort of trading post, which you should manipulate, so to speak, and buy cheap to sell dear. When you learn how to manage your fuel and supplies, and remember the price rates in varipus ports, making decent amounts of money becomes manageable.
During your voyages, you're accompanied by a crew. These are divided into "named" characters and anonymous crew. Anonymous crew consists of the "brute" force of your ship and they determine the efficiency of your speed and maneuverability. In other words, fewer crew members, the slower you'll sail and turn. Then, there are the named NPCs, which you can recruit and assign to posts such as Chief Engineer, Chef and so on. These characters come with certain benefits and improvements to your ship, not to mention their specific quests and backstories. These quests sometimes lead to further improvement of their traits, which makes them worth following through.
While out there in the Unterzee, your Insanity meter will crawl up. Darkness is a major factor in this - if you stray from the buoys dispersed across the Unterzee, the darkness will slowly madden you and your crew. This leads to nightmares, which may exacerbate the situation, and at really high levels, you may end with a mutinee. Of course, these lamp-mounted buoys are not particularly linear in their positions - straight sailing from one to the other will deplete your fuel unduly, while ignoring them altogether will cause undue Insanity. This is one of many micro-management deals in the game.
The soundtrack of the game is often pleasant and sometimes particularly beautiful. As it doesn't loop often, the sudden introduction of the background music adds to the eerieness and tension, whereas returning to the Wolfstack Docks will almost always be matched with one of the more warmer tracks to emphasise that homecoming feeling.
Sunless Sea nevertheless skirts around the niche category. Its long texts, necessary for the its intricate stories, do not speak to all players, neither does the micromanagement of scarce maritime resources promise joy to everybody. Yet, for those who do enjoy such features, as well as those who have liking of Lovecraftian themes, Sunless Sea is a satisfactory title.

If you're wondering whether or not to buy this game, then the answer is this: YES, ABSOLUTELY !
Now, I don't normally like shooters and scary games, where your enemies jump at you out of the blue but the trailers and screenshots from BioShock have always appealed to me and I finally decided to go through with the purchase. This turned to be one of my best gaming-related decisions so far.
From the intro, the game had me captivated. I immediately loved the atmosphere of Rapture, with its amazing art-deco architecture, and various locations (after all years since its release, the game still looks great), I could almost feel how it must have felt to walk in the shoes of the protagonists. This feeling was further enhanced by the music... Ohh yes, the music. Nothing builds an eerie atmosphere better than hearing a pleasant old-shool song, played as if from a vinyl disc, while exploring a blood-stained, ruined city.
The game mechanics? Here, there is little to mention apart from the fact that it's a solid, well-balanced shooter with some RPG entwined in it. You;ll have plenty of weapons, plasmids and genetic upgrades along the game but when all is said and done, you will end up using your three favourites. Hacking mini-games get a tiny bit boring after some time, but you can easily skip some of them with the help of items found along the way.
As far as graphics are concerned, I can only say that Irrational Games made wonders with Unreal Engine 3 and even now, even with almost minimum level of details, the game looks great.
Storywise, as far as video games are concerned - it's a masterpiece. If you don't play BioShock, you're missing out on a great story. and that's notwithstanding the fact that after the main plot twist (somewhere aobut 3/4 of a game) the plot loses its momentum a little.
Quick summary of advantages:
+amazing design and atmosphere of Rapture
+great soundtrack (music and voiceover alike)
+easy to master, entertaining combat with many possibilities to take down enemies
+brilliant storyline and memorable characters
+the game graphics did not age much
Some disadvantages:
-rubbish map, unintuitive journal (although you won't use the latter too much)
-if you don't like it - can give you a jump sometimes
-only a few types of enemies
-some artificial limitations - money cap, no plasmid+weapon combo...
One additional thought. If you're anxious that BioShock might be too scary for your tastes: don't worry. Just pluck up the courage and force yourself through the first two locations (like I had to :D) and from there, it will go al lot smoother. There are much fewer scary moments in the further part of the game and when they do appear, you will be able to predict them with ease.
So, coming back to the start: play BioShock, enjoy the story. You won't regret it and the memory of Rapture will stay with you for long.

A very fun game, provided you are a fan of turnbased games.
Basically this is turn based american football, replacing the people with all kinds of races from the Warhammer franchise, and adding cool skills and rules.
We are talking about chainsaws, fireballs, ko's and deaths.
One important thing about my review is that I only play pve (in most games). So I haven't even tried the pvp and don't plan too either.
* Since the legendary update there is a very wide diversity among the teams. More single race teams, but also the chance to create mixed teams. This is really great and adds more depth in tactics on how to build your team.
* Turn based. For me that's a huge plus, There is no stress you'll forget anything, you can easely pause the game too or you can change the time each turn takes so you have plenty of time. It's turn based strategy really.
* Humor, it has plenty of humor in it.
* The single player campaign is great and funny. It's a tutorial really, in a very entertaining way. After that you can create your own leagues.
* Since the legendary edition, there are also more options in creating or joining leagues. From the eternal league to a tournament, your choice. Create it, or join it.
* RPG aspect! This is what keeps you going. You get to level each player individually. After each injury they deal or touchdown they score you get points. After a certain amount you get level up, and you can give 1 skill to that player, untill his next level up. This is very exciting and allows you to build up a strong team from scratch, and also as you see fit.
* Choices. It's really fun to create a mixed team as you want (almost), and then progress it towards what you want. You want a bashing team, or an elegant team that passes etc? perfectly possible.
* Deaths and injuries are permanent. You can replace a player between matches, but you'll have to rebuild him and level again. And at one time, your favorite player WILL suffer an injury or death... It adds value to each player :)
* RNG. Everything is decided by dice. From how much money you win each game, towards the pool of skills you get to choose from when a player has level up. The attacks, passes, blocks during the match: all dice and RNG. This isn't necessarely negative, but after the 5th match where the AI picks up every single ball and you can't pick up a single one without a reroll, you can get irritated. I know people state it's true RNG, but I'm telling you it isn't. the ai has 80% more chance of picking up the ball then you, same goes for dodging out of enemy zones. It's something you can take into consideration during the match though, but tbh it can be infuriating.
* Slow. Because it is turn based, you can expect almost 1 hour per match. At least between 30 min and 1 hour.
* Inducements. This is my only real frustration, and it controls the entire game. If you are thinking about making an uber team, levelling all your players and become the most OP team in the game world, you can forget that. Whenever a team is pitched against a stronger team (teams are rated based on level, powers, money) the weaker team gets inducements. This is a ton of money to buy incredibly strong "powerups" and/or star players (very strong players) for one match. Hence, if you power level everything, all your opponents will get a ton of inducements and trust me, they will faceroll you every single time. Thus, the key is to keep your rating low, sometimes by handicapping yourself. I find this extremely counter intuïtive and often irritating. It also negates a large chunk of the rpg part, why level up huh?
* Last negative is that some teams are unbalanced. For example: the undead are OP. Especially the mixed undead. Whereas the halflings are so weak, it's a bonus round. Expect to have knocked out/killed the entire team during 1 match if you are pitched against them. Fun as that is, being pitched against undead will turn that around.
All in all, I love the game, loved the first version too. And I can't stop levelling my teams and see how far they get. It is very much fun either way.

The version of Battleship that's on Steam has three different modes: classic, salvo, and nuclear.
Classic mode is what we're all probably used to seeing. You fire, and hit or miss, it's the opponent's turn.
Salvo allows you to fire as many shots as you have ships available. In other words, if you have three ships remaining, you can fire three individual shots anywhere on the board during your turn. It's in Salvo mode that keeping as many ships afloat is crucial, as serious advantages or disadvantages can occur based on fleet size.
Nuclear is a made-for-video-game mode only. In here, you have special weapons (such as torpedoes, mines, air strikes, etc) that are unlocked as you progress through the game. While the additions in Nuclear mode are neat, the problem is that the AI does not have the same restrictions you do, so it has immediate access to all weaponry. Unless you've unlocked enough weapons, you'll be at a serious disadvantage.
While playing there are cutscenes when you attack with any weapon. If you miss, your shells fall harmlessly into the ocean; however, if you hit, you see your shots doing damage to whichever ship you hit. These cutscenes include special weapons in Nuclear mode, so if you launch an attack helicopter, you'll see that particular cutscene instead of the standard "turret aims and fires" scene.
The graphics aren't great, but they aren't absolutely hideous either. I like that the cutscenes differ depending on weapon fired and which ship you hit. Also, the weather can change, so in one game it can be bright and sunny, and the in the next, it can be dark and stormy.
So far, this is sounding like a pretty good adaptation, but there's one MAJOR problem: it's single-player only.
That's right, there's no multiplayer at all. You can't play against anyone online and apparently there's no local multiplayer (aka "hotseat") available either, despite the store page specifically stating "sink enemy battleships in hotseat play."
This means that whoever wrote the store's description either had no clue what they were selling or outright lied. Both possibilities are inexcusable.
Battleship is meant to be a multiplayer game. Playing against the AI is okay, but most people (myself included) would've liked to play against other people and probably bought it with that assumption in-mind because the store page says there is hotseat gameplay.
Fortunately, I bought this game during the Winter Sale, so while I'm still annoyed at the errors posted on the store page, at least I didn't waste money purchasing it at full price.
Due to the incorrect information presented — through either carelessness or dishonesty — I'll have to give this game a NO recommendation.

This review is in Early Access and was posted 1/7/2017.
Double Cubes tries to be a puzzle game, but seems to forget any puzzling elements to it.
The mechanics are simple, you can pick up and put down red blocks that can be found throughout the map. These are then used to make it to a portal at the end of the map. Along with jumping, that is it.
In terms of actual gameplay, this game breaks down into searching the map to find the red blocks, in other words a hidden object game, and then a simple matter of usually making a staircase. The only thing that's at all difficult about the game is finding the red blocks, which only presented itself as a challenge on one map (I walked by it approximately 4000 times. I'm dumb).
As an Early Access game, I don't see potential in the gameplay mechanics at this point. There needs to be major changes to make it a decent puzzle game. New mechanics need to be added such as buttons to trigger events or additional player abilities beyond placing blocks. I hope that'll come to be, but I can't recommend the game until I see the potential.
Even for $3 I can't recommend the game. I spent more time annoyed at the game then enjoying it. To the devs, I hope that you can work on this game and make it a great one. I'll keep an eye on it as I hope I'll be able to change this review to a recommendation.

If you're looking for a simple, but still cool, single-player Battleship game, then Pop Cap made the perfect one right here. Not only does it show the use of white and red pegs to give an authentic feel to it, but also some animated radar cosmetics. You're shown some eye candy animated cutscenes with every shot for either a miss or a hit, and the background graphics comes complete with random weather and ambient sound effects. You can easily immerse yourself into the game and play for hours while trying to increase your rank. It's a very pleasant "chillaxing" type of game where everything is point-n-click super easy.
I like all 3 modes of Classic, Salvo, and Super Weapon, but Super Weapon is my favorite mode. Super Weapon is probably everybody's favorite.
In Classic mode it's your basic Battleship game where you and the computer take turns destroying each other. Not that much to it.
In Salvo mode it's a Ship-turn-Shot game. If you have 5 ships, then you get 5 shots on your turn. Lose a ship and you lose a shot for only 4 shots per turn. Then 3, 2, and 1, if you're having a bad game. Trying to maintain 5 shots is really hard to do, but not impossible. Salvo is Salvo, that's all there is to it.
In Super Weapon mode it's a Weapons-charge-Shot game. You only get 1 shot per turn, but you can really make that shot count when your weapons charge up. With one shot you can fire upon 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15+ coordinates, depending on what weapon you have loaded into your arsenal. There's bombers, gun-copters, shields, satellite laser beams, mines, decoy's, and a bunch of others I haven't even unlocked yet. Yes, you have to unlock most of the weapons by continuing to play the game and keep sinking enemy ships over and over, round after round. You also have to rank up to unlock some of the weapons too.
The graphics are not superb, but it's good enough for this type of game.
The sounds would be what you normally expect with clicks, explosions, turret effects, and other sounds matching their device or purpose. Some of the ambient sounds can get a little annoying and repetitive, but still tolerable.
Now let's talk about the A.I. - It starts out rather easy and appears to be dumb at first, but after you play the game and start ranking up, the A.I. appears to match your rank and gains intelligence. It also uses a multiple random seed to pick coordinates and this is reflected with the multiple decisions you see the A.I. making before taking a shot. Seeking your ships is completely random, but after it gets a hit the A.I. will concentrate on sinking that ship with similar human intelligence. You will notice the A.I. behavior by the time you reach Captain and your usual ship configurations that used to trick the A.I. does not work anymore. That's how I know this Battleship game has an advanced A.I., and is a worthy opponent.
I would recommend this game to anyone who likes board games.

Sunless Sea doesn't initially seem to offer much. Until it does. The game is set in across an underground ocean, where current and tides shift the islands and landmasses around every once in a while. You're the captain of ship amongst many others, in a world of Lovecraftian piracy where smuggled sunlight and spirit-infused honey are contraband goods.
It's not a game for the wilfully illiterate. If you are annoyed by reading paragraphs upon paragraphs of texts on the sidebars, Sunless Sea probably isn't for you. After all, the game derived from a browser-based game called Fallen Londoni consisting of large swathes of text to go through.
As you create your character, you also designate your aspiration, which may be retiring rich or perhaps making a great discovery. You're then set with a rickety ship at the Wolfstack Docks in Fallen London. Through trading, piracy and other quests, you're going to make money, improve your ship and recruit a crew.
Sunless Sea mainly features a bird's eye view of Unterzee, the abovementioned underground ocean. You navigate these waters and find your way around by deploying a Zeebat, which scans a large circle around your ship, allowing you to explore the map. For what is essentially an animated map, Sunless Sea looks spectacular. The artworks in some of the islands are simply things of sheer beauty to look. Many islands feature some sort of trading post, which you should manipulate, so to speak, and buy cheap to sell dear. When you learn how to manage your fuel and supplies, and remember the price rates in varipus ports, making decent amounts of money becomes manageable.
During your voyages, you're accompanied by a crew. These are divided into "named" characters and anonymous crew. Anonymous crew consists of the "brute" force of your ship and they determine the efficiency of your speed and maneuverability. In other words, fewer crew members, the slower you'll sail and turn. Then, there are the named NPCs, which you can recruit and assign to posts such as Chief Engineer, Chef and so on. These characters come with certain benefits and improvements to your ship, not to mention their specific quests and backstories. These quests sometimes lead to further improvement of their traits, which makes them worth following through.
While out there in the Unterzee, your Insanity meter will crawl up. Darkness is a major factor in this - if you stray from the buoys dispersed across the Unterzee, the darkness will slowly madden you and your crew. This leads to nightmares, which may exacerbate the situation, and at really high levels, you may end with a mutinee. Of course, these lamp-mounted buoys are not particularly linear in their positions - straight sailing from one to the other will deplete your fuel unduly, while ignoring them altogether will cause undue Insanity. This is one of many micro-management deals in the game.
The soundtrack of the game is often pleasant and sometimes particularly beautiful. As it doesn't loop often, the sudden introduction of the background music adds to the eerieness and tension, whereas returning to the Wolfstack Docks will almost always be matched with one of the more warmer tracks to emphasise that homecoming feeling.
Sunless Sea nevertheless skirts around the niche category. Its long texts, necessary for the its intricate stories, do not speak to all players, neither does the micromanagement of scarce maritime resources promise joy to everybody. Yet, for those who do enjoy such features, as well as those who have liking of Lovecraftian themes, Sunless Sea is a satisfactory title.

Okay so over an hour in and a few things you will be sure to notice:
(Please note that the game is still in Early Access and I'd imagine a lot of the 'cons' I list are likley to be addressed)
Pros:
It's very fluid, easy to grasp and all in all quite a casual Mall/shop builder/managment game. Everythig that is in the game makes sense and is very basic in terms of gameplay. You can manage everything from what is on your shop shelves to opening hours and your staff at any given point of the day. If you enjoy shop managment games then this is a quirky but a great addition.
Cons:
The micromanagment can quickly become tedious if you look to build on a large scale or have lot's of stores running. Where you have to individually hire lots of staff and pick what each shelf holds, the game is definatly meant for starting out small and taking things slowly so I wouldn't dream of having a massive mall any time soon, which is a con based on your intended play style.
There are obviously few objectes in the game for you to use/build with (which makes sense considering it is early access).
In all I'd reccommend it based on the potential it has, it has great building blocks in place and the idea is clearly there. Makes me think of Mall Tycoon meets Prison Architect. It is very playable and I'm likley to put a few more hours into this build of the game at least. However it will take time to get a big mall up and running.

Words can't describe how much i love this game. So i'll just give you the lowdown of my favorite playthrough (Of dozens of great ones)
Day 1:
Plane crashed somewhere in the woods near a frozen pond and a hunting blind. I found (much to my joy) two granola bars and a bottle of water. Walking through the cold, i picked up a few sticks and some lichen just in case i needed to start a fire. After about 5 minutes of walking i found an old logging camp with three trailer houses. I scavenged a promising amount of food, got some matches, and even found an out ski jacket to wear over my sweater. Exhausted, i spent the night.
Day 2:
I wake up rested and thirsty as hell. I pop open a soda and head out. It's early morning and freezing, but i need to find a suitable place to bunker down, and those little trailers werent it. Following the snow covered trail through the woods, i pass a forest overpass. It's a long hike up in freezing weather and deep snow so i decide against, moving further down the trail. Right as i start to wonder if i had made the wrong choice, i hit a small frozen lake full of Ice-fishing huts. I dot through them and find a good set of stuff before i decide to bunker down in one for a little rest. After a few failed attempts i get the fire in the furnace going. I hear the wind picking up outside, but thinking nothing of it. I lay out my bedroll by the fire for a few hours sleep.
I wake up to what i was sure to be my death.
That light pickup of wind was a precursor to a blizzard. A bad one. The little hut was shaking and creaking in the storm, the opening (there was no door) let in frigid air and snow, putting out my fire and freezing me to the core. I gather my things in a panic. The storm is so fierce it's picking up snow that had settled on the ground, whiting out everything. I culdn't see five feet in front of me. Knowing staying in the hut would be my end, i blindly push into the storm, assumingly towards some camping lodges i saw when i first arrived. The wind cut straight through my clothes and the snow soaked my jeans, shoes and socks. My body trembled uncontrollably as heat was quite literally ripped from my body. After a few minutes the ice of the lake gave way to snow and i was sure i was close to salvation. I keep walking forward, waiting to see a beautiful log cabin any second.
Then i walk straight into a rock wall.
Panicking and wondering how the hell i got so turned around, i follow the wall, hoping beyond hope to find something to keep me safe until the blizzard gave way. I wasn't going to die yet, not here. I willed myself on, even when i felt so tired from the powerful wind i was ready to just drop. Eventually the rock wall gaveway to a some kind of house. Nearly collasping from relief, i get inside and fall asleep immediately, no energy left for anything else.
Day 3:
Apparentely this used to be a park ranger station. It was obviously abandoned in haste, as plenty of things were still left over. The blizzard is still raging, but im safe inside, with a decent supply to last me a few days. I cut up some furniture for wood with the hatchet i found in the closet and get the fireplace roaring. A get some snow quickly from outside and boil it for water, then i eat a hardy meal of beef jerky and a candy bar. I stay up a bit to assess my gear. Somehow i don't have hypothermia, but my pants looks a little worse for wear. I pathc them up with cloth then call it a day, i'm still exhausted from yesterday.
Days 5:
I'm stuck in the ranger hut for another full day. Finally, on Day 5 since my crash, the storm lets up to beautiful weather. I pack my things and head out, the Ranger station now depleted of useful things for me. I crunch along fresh now and a warm sun for a while, reminded of why i used to love skiing in New Mexico. After a while i find train tracks and few wrecked cars. It must of been carrying aid to somwhere becuase scattered amongst the snow i found antiseptic bottles, bandages, a bottle of painkillers and 3 flares. I rest for a bit and have a snack and a sip fo water, and move on. A little past 12ish i find what looks like an old hydrodam. Knowing there could be emergancy supplies and food inside, i make a beeline towards it and walk in, shutting the old iron door behind me.
The place is pitch black. I have to light one of my flares just to see. I look around for a bit, find a prybar and some other useful items including some workers old scarf (My new scarf now), and decide i'm going to spend the night here.
Wrong decision.
As i preparing to set my bedroll down i hear a growl behind. Spinning around, the light from my flare provides me a eerie and terrifying look down the nearby hallway, where a wolf is looking right back at me, growling dangerously. Slowly, i begin to back out towards the door, and he charges me. I panic and throw the flare at him, which seems to scare him long enough for me to fly out the door and across the snow as fast as my damn legs could carry me. I run into the train tunnel and slow to a walk, trying to catch my breath, thank god the weather was still nice. I come out the other end just as the sun begins to set, and find myself in a massive ravine.
After some hopping and skipping and a scary balancing act on a tree that feel across a 50 foot drop, i find a sheltered area behind a old train car and set up camp. I start a fire and give it enough wood to last the night. As i eat dinner i watch the sun set over the horizon. The light reflecting on far distant snow creates a beautiful allusion of fire, as if the horizon around me was burning briliantly. When it sets i am treated to freezing tempertures and a starry sky. I crawl into my bedroll and shut my eyes, hoping to god the weather treats me well.
Day 6:
I was lucky, i woke up to a light snow and nothing else. Hardly any wind. No wolves dragged me away last night so that was also a positive. Thanking my lucky stars i pack up and begin my journey west, to the coast. From there i planto keep heading down south to warmer weather. After traversing a particuarly large and rickety wooden train bridge (And almost falling to my death twice) i go through another tunnel and break out into the coastline.
It was a beautiful sight. The sun glowing over all that sea ice. I would have watched forever if i wasnt freezing. Crawling down the mountain, i find another small trailer house (For the train unloading crew, i presume) and rest there. It felt nice to be inside again after almost 2 days in the wilderness.
Day 7:
One week after my crash. Woo... Anyway, i woke up to howling this morning. More wolves. I headed further down the hill, another flare at the ready (I didnt even bother wielding an Axe, im not a swordsman). Sure enough, i run into one near the highway. It circles me before charging. I throw the flare at it and it runs away. Relieved, i walk over to pick up the flare when suddenly another wolf turns the corner, running after me full speed. I turned and ran like hell towards a cabin down the road. But right before i got to the door he grabbed my leg and i tried. In moments he was on top of me, ripping at the arm i threw up to defend my body. I hit him over and over until he finally let go, running away and barking angrily. Bleeding and hurt, i crawled into the cabin to treat my wounds, sure this was the end. I treated my wounds with antiseptic, bandged them up and took some painkillers. Then i slept.
I survived, and made my way to a cabin on a small island across the frozen bay. On my way, a white out struck. I couldn't see anything yet again. Walking slowly in hopes of not opening my wounds again. I pressed forward. Little did i know i had long past walked by the island, and was on thin ice.
As the whiteout cleared, I looked up. It was as if every star in the universe was looking down at me. Somewhere in my mind, as the cold enveloped me, i wondered if anyone was out there...
Then I fell through the ice.

This has to be one of the best games I have ever played. Yet, action-wise, there is very litle. This is all about survival and survival depends on the tactics you employ within the game. There are no 'buddies' to ask for help. No one you can telephone. Make a wrong turn, wonder off into the forest with night falling, and you are dead. Simple as that. It's all about decisions and making the correct one at the point you are at is the essence of the game.
There are no real spoilers in the review - but there are a few tips that could be useful for beginners. Be warned.
...
...
...
...
In fact, the first few times you play, you are likely to end up dead very quickly... There is no real game help, as such, and it is a struggle to understand what is required of you. However, give it time and it starts to make sense.
When the game first starts, you are dropped in a random location and it could be day or night. I suggest starting on the easy level as wolves don't attack you. In some respects, this is more accurate as wolves tend not to attack humans.
The first thing to do is find shelter. You are unlikely to survive the cold of the night (or the day) if you are out for too long. This can then be used as a base.
There are buildings scattered about to scavenge and hidden caves where you can find a few scraps.
Journeys need to be planned. Never, ever, go out with just a couple of hours of light left. Darkness comes in rapidly and you are liable to get disorientated and die of hyperthermia. Also, weather can change rapidly and you need to know that you can make it back. Pay close attention to your surroundings and make a map ( I count steps).
Explore each area thoroughly to find the exit. Carefully time when you leave the exit area.
This is the beauty of the game. Everything needs to be calculated carefully to survive - just as in real life.
Another nice feature is the lack of other people. Clearly, they were there at some point but for reasons not given, you could be the only person alive on the planet. To meet other people would spoil it and wisely, the developers know this.
After all, what is more terrifying than being totally alone in a hostile environment? And that is the cleverest part of the game - the shear lonliness.
So why is the game so compelling if there is no action, as such? Well, you live and die by your own actions and there can be no excuses if you do die. Therefore, everything is down to you the player and we all want to survive, right?
I treat the game as a real life simulator. Should the big freeze ever come, I fancy my chances. Well, maybe a little bit more than most.
Buy this and enjoy one of the most beautiful and yet scariest games ever written (without a monster - or is 'cold' the monster?).

Important note on realism: Hinterland does not aim for the game to be completely realistic, but rather a game that is balanced between game-play and realism. Some elements are therefore not in line with the real world (for example the degradation of items goes a lot faster). There is (currently) no intention of making a separate game mode that is as realistic as possible, although there are talks of mod support to enable this by the community.
I bought The Long Dark because I have been searching for a realistic survival game / simulator for a long time. Even though it is not meant to be entirely realistic / simulator, it comes very close. So close that I can state it is the best game I have ever played. I have played a lot of games for many years (a lot outside Steam) so this is quite impressive considering it still is in early access. The game-play is fantastic and is a must for any gamer that is into survival games and crafting. I don't want to spoil it for you, but there are times where I am trembling of fear and excitement. The immersion is so great that I sometimes forget I am playing a game. It is visually stunning and the sound is even better.
The game is constantly changing and new content is added regularly (big update each month and smaller ones in between). The developers are enthusiastic and committed and are willing to listen to the community, while maintaining their own vision. While there is currently only a sandbox, story mode is planned for release at the end of this year (which includes great voice actors like Jennifer Hale). The price will probably go up at that point, so buy it while it is still cheap.
The Long Dark will not hold your hand and there are no tutorials. It is very intuitive, but you have to use your intellect. There are three game modes. One which is forgiving and primarily to explore (Pilgrim). One that is exactly in line with the vision of Hinterland, challenging but fair (Voyageur) and my personal favourite, brutal and unforgiving (Stalker). I love the challenge in the game (or any game) as there is nothing better than to recover from your near dead experiences. Most people will die, some a lot. As it is permadeath you will lose your hard work. If you don't like dying or to lose your progress, I would suggest waiting for story mode (but be ready to pay more if you don't buy it now). I however love permadeath and (almost) impossible games, which is why I play games that have this (Faster Than Light, XCOM, Don't Starve etc.). Always on the highest difficulty and with permadeath on if this is possible. The Long Dark has a difficulty mode for every kind of player, which is a big plus.
To conclude, this game is so amazing that I bought a new Xbox One just to play The Long Dark. I bought the game for my low-end laptop, which was below the minimal requirements. Surprisingly I could play it extremely well until last big update. I felt so sad and empty when I could not play any more that I just had to do something about it. It is all worth it as I am 100% sure it will be a huge success (unlike other early access games). If there are any doubts or questions, feel free to send a message or post on the forum. Hinterland, me and the community are happy to help.

This is a game worthy of praise. Bioshock is an example of a game that does not get repetitive in story. The setting itself is quite original from most shooters to start with. This game also gives you a diverse range of ways to kill opponents and a lot of back story, which is not common for most videogames. The fighting is fairly simple, with a flair for dramatic deaths and a way to make quick allies. The fighting is very satisfying and new players can catch on quickly. The story is so well written and dialouged with excellent voice actors that you are drawn into it. The silent protagonist makes you sympathize with his situation from the very start. The plot twist could not have also been better delivered. The Plasmids also make fighting enemies an extremely creative process, I dare say an art form. No two people may choose the exact same plasmids as another person, making this game very fluid in its ability to offer many ways to combat enemies in the game, not just limited to run and gun. Stealth is also an important component in this game when you are low on ammo or are surrounded by numerous enemies and big daddies, often outting you at a disadvantage. The layout of the levels are also very condusive to the atmosphere and the the music score was flawless. The last thing is that though this game may not be known as a horror title, it definitly has its moments that frighten you. This game is so well made that I would dare recomend it even to people who only like playing sports games. This game whould be labled in my opinion the best well rounded, because of all its attributes and pluses. I can't even really think of anything bad or negative to say, though then again, I never really say anything bad because I always look for what is best in a game. This game has my full confidence. If you are planning to buy, you should have full confidence that this game will give you the best time for your money. ever.

This is going to be an unpopular opinion, but that's okay.  Its just my opinion.  I do not think this is a good game.
The game presents a story of the narrator interpreting the creative work of a friend who ultimately cut contact with him over his interpretation of the works and mis-assumption that creative works are necessarily a reflection of their creator.   Not enough information here is presented to know if the story is true, or what parts of the story may or may not be accurate.  As such, I am taking the game on face value, just the story as it is presented.
The game presents no real meaningful discussion on its premise, just imagery and an emotional narrative about how the narrator felt about the 'games' his friend made and how it caused a falling out.  These games are not games, it is more accurate to say 'interactive creative works absent of themes of play structure.'  The problem is that the story just seems to boil down to two people who did not really agree or understand each other about one of their creative expressions, and nothing more.  You are not given enough information to make any sort of reasonable assumption on what transpired, or gain insight about how the two interacted.  The Beginner's Guide presents no meaningful discussion of its own on the topic either.  Its 1.5 hours of someone saying 'this inspired me then I♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the guy who made it.'  Does it seem like I'm repeating myself?  I can't think of how else to say it.  Theres nothing else to the story but that.
The 'games' made by the narrator's friend are shown to you in game and you are free to poke around them, but they aren't particularly meaningful or thought provoking.  Maybe its because I don't identify with the presented themes of idolization, creative burnout, drama, social anxiety, or whatever else people seem to see in this game.  Maybe it's because the presentation is too shallow.  The narrative states that the 'games' made by the narrator's friend were never made to be shown to other people.  This probably explains why.  Maybe its because the themes seem to be the struggle of an immature person who isn't very good at figuring out his life or approaching things logically, perhaps why the game is titled 'The Beginner's Guide'.  This isn't a jab at the creator if the story is true.  Young people are immature because they are inexperienced, emotional relationships cloud logic, and so forth.  Thats just how things are, and that's not a character flaw on anyone.  But its not a situation that appeals to me.  I see it and on top of the narrative and presentation being too thin, it just does not appeal to me.
So overall, I don't recommend it.  I bought the game at $6 and felt like the narrative presented was so lacking that my time was wasted.  I requested a refund.  I cannot believe that he would ask $10 for this title, and I don't even think it would be worth your time at $5.  The value of your dollar is up to you, and my opinions often run contrary of popular ones.  Feel free to dismiss my review, and if you buy The Beginner's Guide I hope that you enjoy yourself even if I did not.
I want to put this last because it is somewhat tangential to my review.  To top off the rest of what I have said, the non-fictional potential of the narrative puts the game in a possibly negative light.  The narrative says that the games presented in The Beginner's Guide are ones that the narrators friend
the narrator from sharing and that he put them in the game as a cry out to the friend who severed contact.  This puts the act of putting them in this game into moral and legal question.  Obviously the narrative is, once again, incomplete.  The narrative states information about events that occured at just one point in time, and that may have changed in events not included in the narrative.  I can only assume that permission was given or legal concerns accounted for, because otherwise The Beginner's Guide shouldn't be on steam.  If it was the creator's intent to evoke this reaction with the story, it seems strange.  Am to assume that the narrator's story is true and the creator of The Beginner's guide has done something reprehensible and immorral?  If not, why is it trying to make me think it is?  It seems underhanded, and just underscores how the game is so badly lacking.

A hat in Time feels like a throwback to old school golden age of platformers. It takes insperation from the collectables from Banjo Kazooie without making collecting everything feel like an outright requirement. Super Mario Sunshine with the various amounts of ways you can travel, jump, run and pounce your way through the game along with some level ideas. And even physchonauts of all things from its original and very funny humor. To memorable characters you meet while progressing through the game.
The Story of the game is pretty simple, there isn't much that happens spoiler wise. The main character Hat Kid is trying to get home but while doing so she lost all of her Time Pieces which is fuel for her ship. If she wants to return home she needs to collect them. You don't need all of them to beat the game but its nice to play extra levels and it feels great when you complete and gather everything. The controls for the game are great! you can use a keyboard or controller to play the game. You can unlock different abilites by collecting yarn and turning that yarn into hats. Each hat acts differently and can bring something new to the table in regards of movment, combat, or ultility.
My few complaints about the game is the camera doesn't feel like it likes to cooperate in tight spaces, which can make certain jumps pretty tricky or annoying to deal with. Another complaint I have is that I've had Hat Girl's collision when dashing into certain objects getting her stuck in certain objects or places and having me to restart the level. Its nothing game breaking and its mostly nit picks, But for a game that was on Kickstarter its a great game to play. It can feel a little short towards the end of the game but all the levels were memorable and there wasn't one that I hated.
All in all its a solid kickstarter game that made me enjoy playing and collecting everything I could. I'd give it an 8/10

A Hat in Time - a bright and upbeating action-adventure platformer that will surely bring you back to the times when things were much simpler.
The game follows a simple story: a kid with a hat heads home with her spaceship that uses hourglass-shaped entities called timepieces as fuel. But all things goes so wrong when she passes through Mafia Town. Now, in order to return home, she must retrieve all the timepieces while meeting all new friends and foes.
The game features multiple levels, called "Chapters". For each chapter there would be multiple "Acts" for specific scenarios and activities. So level diversity is something that's definitely not lacking. Activities can be racing, fetch quest or going into special levels called timerifts. Players are dropped into a Chapters and they can either follow that scenario or just go around and explore freely without time limits.
As Hat Kid, you are aided by your trusty umbrella as a weapon and a collection of Hats with special abilities to overcome obstacles. This can be a simple default Hat that locates the main object of interest, or a time-stop Hat, or even a Hat to see the alternative world. Keep in mind that a Chapter may feature obstacles that is impossible to do until you get the right upgrades in later Chapters, but these are usually not game-stopping, so no worries. You can still progress through the stories normally from collecting enough timepieces.
The overall tone of the game is amazingly diversed. It's upbeat, funny, a little bit spooky and maybe sad. But there's no noteworthy cringe moments so people can watch you play without feeling awkward.
It's no suprise that the game is inspired by other 3D platformers such as Super Mario 64 or Banjo-Kazooie, and for these games, music has always been a great part of them and it's no exception for A Hat in Time. The music definitely gives me a lasting and positive impression.
The game is my personal GOTY for 2017. I would wholeheartedly recommend this game to you if you find joy in exploration, platforming and CUTE things!
