Welcome to the Unterzee, captain.
Here, amongst the people of Fallen London, you will sail out into the vast unknown, making your way. You will have goals and ambitions- they may not be satisfied. You may not survive. You may eat your crew. One simply never knows, and that is life on the Unterzee.
My advice, from one captain to another- don't fight the zee-beasts. It is unlikely to end well. Also don't fuss too much with upgrading your ship- you'll want most of the echoes you save to go towards fuel and supplies, which are the life blood of any running ship.
Of note- the Unterzee is a big place, and your ship is slow. It will take time to go where you would like to, and often more time when going somewhere you'd rather not like to. But there is so much to see here, so many stories to hear, that the journey will always be worth it.
Beware the zubmariners, as well- they can spin yarns of a thousand sights beneath the Unterzee's surface, magnificent stories to light up the eyes of any youthful zailer. Unknown dangers and terrors lurk beneath the murk, however, beyond the wildest imaginations of any poor London soul.
So go on, explore, and see the wonders and cultures to be found on the myriad shores of the Unterzee. Just keep a wary eye open- life is never simple here, and so often dangers lurk unseen in the darkness.
Good luck.

Another Brick in the Mall is a top-down sandbox mall construction game. You start on a massive plot of land and your first order of business will usually be to construct a small general store. As you do research you unlock new things - some are simple and straightforward such as fresh fruit and ice cream, and others unlock entirely new possibilities, such as opening a fast food restaurant or a cinema.
This makes every Mall different. If you want to make a massive megastore that sells everything from diapers to soy sauce you can. If you want to make a giant cinema complex that sells overpriced popcorn and candy you can. If you want your mall to focus on fashion, you can. If you want to make a mega-mall that has everything you need, you can. Just make sure to provide enough parking space - your mall is in the middle of nowhere, and all your customers and employees arrive by car.
Speaking of employees, each and every one of them has their name, skills, and traits. If you're trying to sell soup you don't want a grumpy employee working in the front. Keep in mind that people are not robots and they will only work 8 hours per day - make sure to organize your shifts properly and always have someone as backup, just in case your best chef gets stuck in traffic.
Early Access games are often plagued by poor performance and lack of optimization (I'm looking at you, Prison Architect). This is not the case with Another Brick in the Mall - I've never had it go below 1000 (yes, one thousand) frames per second even on a massive map brimming with people.
Another Brick in the mall already has more than enough content to justify its price, and it's only going to get better over time.

Oh where to begin?
The usual quick time event rubbish that has serious latency issues, only one scene where any kind of detective work is done - and it's slowly done at that, Batman has lost the ability to run or walk without a stick up the proverbial and yes...the origin story is covered AGAIN.
Worse is the origins of other characters like The Penguin, who is this living-on-the-streets sort-of revolutionary. Think Anarky and The Penguin combined and a poor take on Nolan North's cockney Penguin voice from the Arkham games, it really doesn't gel and as it's established Bat-fans who'll be buying this game? Come now Telltale, if this is the best you can do...walk away now.
I mentioned the detective work, which is confined to a single area (warehouse) where you link various bits of evidence together to form a theory. Well that's fine...in theory (ahem!)...but in practice, it means you are really just playing pairs (as in the card game). There isn't any room for error in the overall reconstruction or the ability to come to the wrong conclusion, except via dialogue choices later in the game.
And yes, just like with Back To The Future way back when and right the way through to The Wolf Among Us, expect your choices to not be remembered properly. I, for example and not to spoil anything, chose to give a quote to the press that was both noted in-game itself via dialogue and in the "choices you made" screen at the end of the game...but in the Codex? That says I didn't provide a quote at all.
Moving on, the graphical fidelity is so-so to oh dear. The characters are detailed well enough, as they were in The Wolf Among Us, but the areas and props - such as an item taken from
at the beginning of the game is decidedly low detail in both polygon count and skin. Almost as though it was a reject from the Sam & Max days...
Additionally, there are some backgrounds that are very clearly low resolution and random frame drops to 15fps during cutscenes (and potentially other areas of the game) where normally the game is at 60fps at 1080p. That's another thing, when you first launch the game it will default to windowed mode at 1366x768 (aka 1080i) on a monitor whose native resolution is a true 1080p. Easy enough to configure, but it shouldn't have had to be done in the first place.
Finally the mouse input can be extremely slow to overly sensitive, very annoying and no menu option to tweak that.

Ragna May took my attention on the first glimpse, because of it´s unique art design. I couldn´t determine wether I like the graphics or not, but it somehow drew me in.
So how do I like the game so far ? I have only 1 and a half hours in by the time I write this review, but there are some things that stood out:
Cons:
- Controls:
The controls are narrowed down to W,S,A,D, and / ( or # on some european keyboards ) and left mouse-clicks   This means, you really can´t go back in the menus or during a combat with the ESC-button or right-click.
You have to use / or # to get back. If you don´t know the mapping you likely won´t find a way back or out of a submenu
- No Settings:
There are no settings regarding graphics, sound etc.
- Balancing:
I just went 1 hour into the game and the encounters don´t only seem random in terms of enemies, but in terms of difficulty. I just left the bear to continue the story and I encounter enemies that often one-hit-kill me and theres not much I can do about it. I am very experienced in hardcore games and also very difficult RPGs, so I´m sure it´s not because of the lack of skills
Pros:
- Despite the strange graphics, the game has a very unique atmosphere and even though it´s not open world or packed with npcs, it fits to the lore that expands itself.
- I like the soundtrack so far and I get nostalgic feelings when winning a fight and 8-bit-sounds are played afterwards, while collecting items and xp
- the mechanics are kind a like unique. The system is very interesting and I´m sure that it unfolds during further plays.
For instance: When you attack with a spell, not only the HP gets drained, but MP, too - also something that is similar to your defensive stats. Or, Debuffs negate Buffs, while most Buffs don't negate debuffs ( there are exceptions)..which is a very very interesting approach.
This is of course, due to the lack of more playtime, just a first impression, but I´m sure that there are many gamers like me out there that have an eye on this title and ask themselves if it is worth the price / time.
I got the code from the developer so I didn´t pay for the game. I really can´t tell right now if the price is worth it. From my view the game is more in a early access state than a 1.0 stable version. It´s not bugged, but the mentioned cons are signs of a unfinished game and reminds me more of - at least beta state. It has huge potential and I think if the dev is putting some hard work of coding hours into it, it could maybe surprise us all.
I will recommend the game though, as I think it has huge potential for a indie-game, but read my advice below.
If you are a hardcore RPG-Fan, that needs to touch every RPG ever made, get it! or wait on a sale.
If you are uncertain and don´t like to deal with flaws and unbalanced and unfinished contents, wait for future versions, as this version right now is still unpolished and early access-like.

Legend of Mysteria is a prequel to Labyronia RPG, but the style of gameplay is very different. There are only a handful of battles (some of them quite difficult), and the game centers mostly around exploring, finding necessary items, and using them appropriately in the right locations to progress your way through the game. It's fun for the first hour or so (of a 6 hour game), but there are many things you have to discover, and they aren't always obvious. The remaining five hours are spent consulting the walkthrough at every turn.
The premise of the story is that, after a leading wizard apparently is murdered, and you are implicated and imprisoned, you must disguise yourself and gather evidence to find the real culprit among 12 suspects. There is such a large cast of characters that it is difficult to keep track of the different stories of who's who and who did what, and unfortunately, this is crucial to figuring out which of the dozens of notes and diaries to use in front of which characters, which again, requires consultation with the walkthrough.
Aside from a painful reliance on walkthroughs, there are few things to complain about. The game is rich in content, and the story, while too broad at first, wraps up nicely towards the end, and the ending itself is very satisfying. Overall, it's a fun game.

LONG LIVE JRPG GAMEPLAY!
First things first, I've been following this game since it was first posted on greenlight last year, so I know how different the quality is compared to when it was first made public. Honestly, at the time, I loved the synopsis since it drew me in, but the gameplay footage at the time and graphical quality was quite questionable. However, with this, with the final product, I'm glad I followed it.
The game can be better in several areas, but overall, the gameplay mechanics make it a game worth buying.
Nearly 3 hours into the game, I've nearly cleared the 1st of 7 floors of the Labyrinth of Razuri. The field gameplay follows retro-type jrpg games where exploration of the floor can lead the player to treasure chests, random battles, and optional battles. Battles can occur as the Dullahan explores the floor, but the twist with this game is there are optional battles where additional rewards can be earned. The field camera reminds me of Resident Evil where if the player enters an area, the camera is moved to a fixed position. Also, like Resident Evil, the positioning of the camera can hide certain explorable areas and you'll miss certain items and battles. This must be where the "retro" of the game's retro-modern comes from.
Now, the best part of the game, BATTLE GAMEPLAY AND CRAFTING
Battle Gameplay is pretty much Final Fantasy X style, and I LOVE IT. BUT, what makes this game's battle gameplay really shine are the Mirages and Damage Factors. Mirages can be created by the Dullahan's servant, Miria, and they are your party members. To create a Mirage, first you'll have to get an Akasha Fragment of the Mirage you want to create (these drop from enemy Akashas), and once you have one, go to a data terminal (Save Point. You could also save on the pause menu but you can only create a Mirage here.) then create a Mirage. And here's the fun part, lets say you have a level 10 mirage in your party and it dies in battle,
However, you can create a mirage again at a save point BUT the mirage will go back to level 1. Oh and by the way, the Dullahan can only be revived 13 times the whole game!
There are alot of Damage Factors in the game, the main ones are the attributes, STR DEF etc. like in all RPG's. Then there's the Vulnerability Guard(VG). The VG is just great, the simplest comparison would be.... FFXIII's Stagger Guage but without the staggering. With each attack, the VG can increase or decrease. If you're the one attacking, your VG will increase and you decrease the damage you take, and if you're the one receiving the attack, your VG will decrease and you'll increase the damage you take. Interesting right? But there's more, Elemental Fragility(EF), each character in Ragna Maya has an EF, and the higher the EF, the more damage you take from that element, and vice versa. Cuphead is 1930s cartoons stylized boss battles platformer. You take control over the titular character (and if you have friends, like I don't, you can play local coop mode with your buddy Mugman) and you try to defeat a bunch of bosses, because you need their stuff :P
Now, I was waiting for this game for years, I was afraid that it might end up being poopy like some other games in the past with infinitely long development process (cough cough, Duke Nukem Forever, No Man's Sky...), but I'm happy to report that Cuphead is just awesome!
Everything is great about it. Crazy, hand drawn (!) animations, beautiful soundtrack, hilarious cartoonish sound effects, fluent controls, insane multistaged bosses with the most over the top goofy attacks, upgrades to your loadout, special powerful attacks, dash/parry system and so on and so forth :P
The difficulty is high and you can adjust it before starting each boss battle. It's based on patterns recognition and your reflexes, this way you rarely feel like you've been screwed by RNG. You're going to die. A lot. But I just can't get mad at this game for killing me mercilessly when everything is so cheerful, colorful and cute :P It definetely has 'just one more try' syndrome and it's great. You want to kick the enemy's butt and when you do you feel amazing! And then you go to the next beautifully animated boss battle and you get the crap kicked out of you again, the cycle never ends and you're happy to be a part of this pandemonium :)
So Cuphead. Unique, super fun game! I highly recommend checking it out!

SUPERHOT is unlike any FPS you've ever seen. This is one of the most innovative shooters of our time and I was overjoyed when I saw that it had finally made it to steam. I had played the early online version of this game many years ago when it was just an idea, and was blown away at the concept. The premise of the game is that you have to kill a bunch of red dudes through a variety of different settings in a world where time only moves when you do. You also unlock a bunch of new content after completing the main story. I'm extremely satisfied with this game and it's definitely something you should try for yourself.

Just Cause 2 is an open world/sandbox action game that highly encourages Exploration. In this game you play as a man named "Rico Rodriguez" who is air dropped onto the fictional "Island of Panau" in order to find an Agency operative (the same Agency Rico is in) who has defected and gone rogue. You are freely allowed and encouraged to cause as much chaos and destruction on the fictional Island as possible, in order to spark a civilian resistance against the Island's ruthless Dictator, a man nick-named "Baby Panay".
In JC2, you earn "Chaos points" for causing Chaos (destroying buildings, killing enemies, sabotaging pipelines, assassinating military targets, or in general destroying anything that belongs to the Panuan government), which you can then use to unlock Main Story missions. Most of the Gameplay revolves around either exploring the Massive 400 Sq Mi island, doing missions, or in general causing chaos and/or destruction. You are given a small variety of weapons, including pistols, shotguns, assault rifles, machine guns and sniper rifles. You are also given a grappling hook that you can use to hook on to things, tether things together, or for use as a melee weapon.
The game has a faction system; there are three different factions you are allowed to join and become a member of. You can partake in Faction missions (which usually involve doing miscallenous tasks, such as hijacking a truck for example). The first Faction, named the "Ular Boys", have the eventual goal of turning Panau into an isolated nation, free of any and all government oppression/influence. The second Faction, named "The Reapers", believe Panau should be a controlled, communist nation. The third and final Faction, named "The Roaches", are a criminal syndicate and consequentially the most crime-oriented faction of the trio.
The game's graphics are very eye-catching and still hold up today. You can see the sun's light rays shine through the trees, every tire track on the highly detailed textures of the dirt roads, and every individual ripple in the very aesthetically-appealing water. With the game set to max, you wouldn't be able to guess this game was released in 2010. Gaming standards have really come a long way. Long gone are the days of "Half-Life" and "Rainbow Six", when the graphics were blocky and slightly unbelievable (but still great for their time). Game developers now focus on the graphical qualities/abilties of their video games, and it really pays off in the long run. However, I still believe the Gameplay aspect of any video game should be its primary focus, because thats where most of the heart and soul should go into.
Just Cause 2 is a very detailed and rich video game, that is not only very attractive, but also significant in the amount of general things to do. Some could argue that the game can get repetitive after the Main Story has been beaten and most of the Side Missions as well. This can hold true for some, however (even though I still have yet to beat the Main Story), I strongly believe this game can stil stay as fresh and vibrant as your first playthrough, solely due to the fact that the game is a giant, living Toybox just waiting for you to come and play. I find it immensely satsifying to use the grappling hook to board a plane mid-air, or tether an Enemy to the back of your car as you go for a ride, or even just in general exploring parts of the Island you either haven't seen before or haven't seen in a while (which will most likely be common, as the Map is really huge, it's hard not to miss things). In general, I highly recommend this game if you are a fan of Open-World Sandbox videogames.
My Final Rating: 8.5/10

I was behind this on since it’s days on Steam Greenlight. Sunless Sea is dark, rogue-like exploration RPG from Failbetter Games. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
Sunless Sea features a delightful plethora of Lovecraftian themes. This alone (assuming you’re a fan of Lovecraft) should be enough to make you want to play the game.
The initial combat system left a lot to be desired, but those were the days of the beginning of early access. Since then, the combat has been streamlined into real time and allows for constant movement and maneuvering. Needless to say, it is a vast improvement over the old system.
Exploring the Unterzee in your vessel is always a good time. Whether your dumping a few hours into the game or just looking to kill a few minutes doing something other than beating your head against the wall in boredom. You’ll always find something out around Fallen London to entertain (or frighten) you.
The artwork is outstanding. It was the first thing about the game that really made me fall in love with it. You can see for yourself in the trailer. Everything has had a lot of detail and care put into it and it really shows through in the finished product.
The soundtrack is, likewise, awesome. From sea shanties to pleasant melodies, there is always a tune to accompany you on your voyaging through the Zee.
The developer is one of the best out there in my opinion. They provide regular updates to the game (even now that it has left early access), the listen to their fans, and they are passionate about making their game the best that it can be.
Did I mention that you can cannibalize your crewmen or make your crewman cannibalize their fellows? Yeah, that’s a thing. And it’s brilliant.
The Bad
The old combat system is about the only bad thing I can think of when it comes to Sunless Sea. But, that is long since a thing of the past.
The Meh
Once again, I’ve got nothing to say in this category.
Verdict: Yea
If you haven’t played Sunless Sea, you should very much consider picking it up and sinking some serious hours into it. It’s well worth the price and, in my opinion, can quickly become one of the best games in any collection. I’m pretty sure it is on sale right now for the Steam Halloween Sale too. As always, thanks for reading.

DAY 15, DUSK: I'm getting really low on food. I only have thin clothes, my trusty hatchet and a few granola bars to get me through the run i'm going to attempt. This is gonna be a leap of faith ; Tomorrow, I'll venture into the freezing forest in search of food. I'm enjoying a last cozy night in my cabin, slowly falling asleep next to a fire with an empty belly.
DAY 16, MORNING: I got lucky ; I woke up to an unexpectedly warm dawn. Fully rested and ready to go, I leave the safety of my cabin to venture into he woods, filled with courage.
Hours later, the weather gets colder and forces me to stop to warm up next to a fire. I find a spot behind a hill to start the fire and protect me from the chilling wind. I eat my last food supplies, then decide to climb the hill.
What I see on the other side is pretty interesting : a frozen pond. A wolf. And the best part : a frozen deer carcass being eaten by the wolf. Quick, I snatch a flare from my bag, light it, then run straight at the wolf, yelling with the courage of a starving man. The wolf turns around, but starts to back away when he sees me. When i get closer, I throw the flare at him, and that's it: he runs away on all four, scared. The snow stopped falling, the sun is going down, and my surrounding is incredibly silent. I might freeze to death if I harvest this meat, but a moan from my belly convinces me to proceed with this choice.
DAY 16 , DUSK: Oh god. I'm in for trouble now. As I finish harvesting all the frozen meat from the deer, a strong wind starts, followed a few minutes later by such strong snowfall that I can barely see 5 meters in front of me. I'm stuck in a blizzard. My low quality clothing instantly shows it's innapropriateness to the situation: I start being cold. I take out a storm lantern from my bag and light it ; It's warmth is going to be insanely useful. Exhausted from my day of traveling and starvation, I start walking back to my cabin, one slow step at a time.
I'm not going to make it. This reality strikes me hard an hour later, when I can no longer feel my arms and legs, frozen like I've never been in my life. I was following my footsteps back to my house, but they have long vanished. I'm getting slower and slower. At some point, I just drop on my knees. I start recalling my best life moments. I remember my wife, Laury, and pull out a photo from my bag with my icy fingers. It depicts her and my son, playful, with a smile on their faces. A tremendous spark of courage strikes me to the core. I can not die in this frozen hell. I get up and walk with renewed courage back to my cabin.
DAY 17, 2 AM: I stumble upon a hollow tree. My know my cabin is near this landmark. I'm almost there.
My vision gets blurry, but I see the faint outlines of my cabin in front of me. It takes me every last bit of willpower I have to get back inside, but I make it. As soon as I close the door behind me, I drop on the floor, uncouscious.
DAY 17, 1 PM: I wake up, frozen to the core, hungry and thirsty. I'm shaking uncontrolably. I grab some Fir firewood and light a fire. I then cook my meat and quench my thirst with some warm green tea. I might be more dead than alive, but...
I made it another day.

Spoiler-Free Review: The game was cute and entertaining. The only thing that I didn't like about it was the lack of direction and the story. I ended up looking up a guide to get through the game because it wasn't always clear what I was supposed to do. The combat was decent, the hidden puzzles/clues here and there were clever. I would recommend this game for anyone that wants a quick game to play or an easy game to get 100% achievements for.
SPOILERS FROM HERE ON:
The story was way too bloated. It felt like 4 people all had different ideas on what the game's story should be and all tried to write it in. The conflict made sense (head honcho murdered, then having to collect clues in a town of magic-fearing people) but the romance (if you could call it that) felt very last minute and rushed. The clues were fine but I felt like there were too many of them, too many specific ways you had to use them and specific people you had to give certain items to. On top of that, you have to translate some spells. This would have been fine if the translation would stick. Everytime you want to use a certain few spells, you have to re-translate it.
As I said above, this game is entertaining at best. If you ignore certain parts of the story and information-overload, this game is actually pretty enjoyable. It's clear that the developer had a good idea here, but it got too crowded with other elements that were seemingly forced in (the whole entire religion speech, the over-explaining how things in the wizarding world work, the too-long diaries or notes, etc).
If the story had been left at "Head honcho Wizard is killed and you're being framed. Now you have to go into hiding and collect clues to prove your innocence and find the real culprit!", then this game would have been a lot better. Even keeping in the romance would have been acceptable if the story had just focused around ONE idea, not 5.
TL;DR - They tried to put a Skyrim-sized story into a game I only spent 5 hours on because I kept getting lost and ended up looking up a guide to get through. (A speed run on YouTube only took a little over an hour, if I'm remembering correctly.)

Note: This IS NOT a "Flatout" sequel (even if it's by the same devs); this is a bangers-style derby game. A lot of people buying Wreckfest seem to think it's another Flatout style game; with ragdolls and crazy jumps and NITRO!!! This game is more similar to Destruction Derby, with detailed physics and handling; but lots of destruction.
There's plenty of options to customize your driving style, but in the end it's always the same: Destruction! I'm more of a casual driving\racing gamer; but I loved the old Destruction Derby and Flatout games so I gave this a try. Instantly you'll notice the physics and particles from almost every object in the level. 90% of objects can be manipulated in some way, usually resulting in spectacular displays of destruction and mayhem.
MP is a blast. The MP community is small, but dedicated, and there's usually planned events to join every several days\weeks. But as with most MP games, it's best to find a friend\group just to weed out the random trolls. Even racing a buddy H2H can be some of the best fun in a racing game; and it gets even better with a group.
The SP is still fun and challenging; with the AI able to put up a decent fight most of the time (you can change their difficulty if needed). There's also mod support that has already produced some great addons like more tracks, cars, parts, objects, etc. to keep things fresh while the (albiet slow) development continues.
The main "con" with the game is that it's been a slow development process; but each update improves and refines the game into what the devs envisioned.

I don't know what's going to happen with this thing after the first scene, but I'm ready to review.  Even though it feels like we're going into things which have been done before, I love it.  For the most part, I enjoy Telltale, and I love Batman, so it seems like a good combination.
First off, I have to complain about the only complaint I have:  graphics.  I'm miffed that I can play a game like Arkham Asylum on a 5-year-old laptop on lowest graphics with less lag than a Telltale story-based adventure game on a newer laptop...  I hear everyone's having some kind of graphics issue, so I'm going to look into it.  As it stands, the opening fight with Catwoman was incredible, even though I don't know if the fight went the way it was supposed to because the lag didn't always show me whether my choices hit...  I'm getting tired of every new game feeling like it has to compete graphically with every other game out there, regardless of genre.  If the graphics to this game were as simple as even the older Sam and Max games, I'd be happy.
Now, I want to see whether my choices really affect much.  I believe (unlike in The Walking Dead) I won't care too much if my choices don't have a big impact.  It's a Batman story, and I want to see it played out.  Life is Strange ruined me with its twisting of making my choices matter while at the same time making them completely irrelevant.  ^_^  Based on the opening of this game alone, I recommend this game.  If this is our "gritty" Batman of modern times (and it's looking like this will be somewhat based on the latest installment of our movie Batman), I look forward to seeing all of my favorite characters and watching them develop.  It looks like we'll have a nice mix of action in combat, pulling us into the Arkham vibe, drama in dialogue, and hopefully some detective work between the scenes.  We deserve to see  the "world's greatest detective" go back to figuring stuff out.

This game has some of the most flawless, dark, and interesting writing of any game I've ever played. Through the writing alone, it drew me into its world and ate me whole.
The problem is, that's all it has. Combat is rudimentary, even at advanced stages of play, and never really changes, and the economic system is an economist's worst nightmare.
The standard unit of currency is the Echo, but it's almost never actually used ;some items are bought for entirely different items, most items are only sold and never bought, and many items can only be acquired in one location. You'd think that having such a small supply pool would make for great profits, no? Actually, no. You generally make something like a 10% profit on any particular commodity; that's BEFORE you account for fuel costs, supply costs, the cost of keeping Terror down, and the chance you'll get randomly attacked by a Lifeberg or have a stalagtite fall on your ship or any number of other terrible things that can happen purely at random.
But there you go; you've made a dozen trading trips, accumulated a tidy thousand echoes; you can now afford a 20% increase in engine power and a weapon that does 4 extra damage. Congratulations, for all your effort, you've achieved nothing.
Not even the quests you can get are particularly effective, as they tend to reward you in strange, symbolic ways, or with stat increases that help you succeed at further quests that give further stat increases; I kid you not, one sequence of quests is simply a check against a stat, a roll of a die, and if you win, it increases that stat and gives you a few echoes. Then you do it again, with a slightly higher skill requirement (handily provided by the last quest!)
But none of the quests are good for the progression of your character; the best quest will maybe give you 500 echoes, after you sell off all the strange and bizarre items it rewards you with - of course, after you pay for the fuel, supplies, and crew that you've lost finishing that quest, you'll be lucky to come out in the black at all.
This ultimately results in a game with a massive quantity of theoretical content, with more advanced ships, equipment, and weapons, but with almost no way to actually get them. Even worse, there is almost no reward *for* getting them, other than the ability to do the same things you've already been doing to get them in the first place slightly better. For example, there is an enemy called a Lifeberg. It is fast, deadly, and has a large pool of health, and when killed, rewards the player with upwards of 300e of supplies and fuel. In order to kill it, you need roughly 20000e of equipment. Equipment you will hardly need for anything else in the entirety of the game.
In the end, it plays, not like a game, but like a book, with the pages scattered across the metropolitian museum of art. The first time across, it's beautiful. The 8th time across, you see something you never saw before. But by the 50th time across, you just look forwards to the 500 pages ahead in despair.

I sailed deep into the dark. 6 crew on a ship that could hold but 10.
We went out in search of Mt. Palmerston, to deliver a package for someone I didn't trust, but could funnel me enough money or supplies to keep us alive a bit longer.
We pushed further and further. Round piles of rocks named and unnamed. Stopped briefly at ports without so much as a drop of fuel for sale, or a meal to be found. Our terror grew.
I was only surprised that it took me so long for one of my crew to go mad. I tried to talk her down, but she ended up killing two before she hit the deck herself. A bullet between the eyes at the start might've saved us all in the end.
We found Mt. Palmerston shorttly thereafter, but it was an empty victory. We dropped the crate and were paid nothing. That waited for us in Fallen London out on the far side of the zee.
With a skeleton crew, we could only limp along at half speed, dodging creatures and pirates. Running silently, without a single light to burn away the blackness that surrounded and threatened to pull us down, down, down...
Soon, the terror became all-consuming. It was impossible to think clearly. The only thought that came through was Home. So went on.
We were a third of the way across the zee when a tentacle silently swept one of my crew under the flat, waveless water. He went without a shout, said not a word and was gone. There were just two of us left.
Our fuel ran dry a few hours later. What other way was there to keep going? But to burn it all. And we did. Our supplies went right into the furnace and fueled the boilers. It was our only hope to push on a little further.
Not too long after, we ran out of supplies.
Soon, my hunger grew. What other way was there to get home but to burn and to eat? I thought about this as the pangs ravaged my stomach. Weakness and fear consumed me as I wanted to consume something. And in the end, I did.
With that, my crew was gone.
My food fueled my ship, and my crew fueled me. Two thirds of the way home, the engines stopped. The tanks were dry, the hold empty. There was no way to fill my plate.
I sank down. All the way down. My ship went adrift above me, and the darkness closed in. It was cold and black and how I always feared it would be in the end.
9/10 - Buy it.

The term "unplayable" is one that is thrown around frequently in such a way that the word often loses meaning. But in this case, I think that it is an apt description of my experience with Batman The Telltale Series. We all know that QTEs are an essential part of Telltale's method of storytelling and that is what you buy the game for, essentially.
I saw a few videos on the internet that displayed how combat would work and I was excited to give it a try. To my frustration, though, when I bought this game as a birthday gift to myself, I got stuck on a section for 10 minutes that is supposed to last 30 seconds, the very first fight sequence.
See, the game has a frame rate issue for certain computers. I tried to look into the issue, spent 6 hours of my day trying to fix it, but nothing I did would matter. See, the game gives you 1 second to react to a QTE (which doesn't sound very long, but it is). The problem is, the instructions on the screen are late. You have to have already pressed the associated button prior to the instructions for it to be registered. It's undoubtedly to do with the framerate issues.
I've run it at it's lowest settings, I have called with NVIDIA to fix the issue and nothing seems to change the simple fact that this game simply refuses to run well. So, I've given up. I am refunding my game. I do not recommend this title until Telltale fixes the issues.
EDIT: Never mind. I have changed the settings on my own, finding out how to do it after 6 hours of talking with experts didn't get me the advice I needed. Playing the game like this is much more enjoyable and I'd like to change my tune to recommend it. Edits pending for more information about the game as I progress.

DAY 15, DUSK: I'm getting really low on food. I only have thin clothes, my trusty hatchet and a few granola bars to get me through the run i'm going to attempt. This is gonna be a leap of faith ; Tomorrow, I'll venture into the freezing forest in search of food. I'm enjoying a last cozy night in my cabin, slowly falling asleep next to a fire with an empty belly.
DAY 16, MORNING: I got lucky ; I woke up to an unexpectedly warm dawn. Fully rested and ready to go, I leave the safety of my cabin to venture into he woods, filled with courage.
Hours later, the weather gets colder and forces me to stop to warm up next to a fire. I find a spot behind a hill to start the fire and protect me from the chilling wind. I eat my last food supplies, then decide to climb the hill.
What I see on the other side is pretty interesting : a frozen pond. A wolf. And the best part : a frozen deer carcass being eaten by the wolf. Quick, I snatch a flare from my bag, light it, then run straight at the wolf, yelling with the courage of a starving man. The wolf turns around, but starts to back away when he sees me. When i get closer, I throw the flare at him, and that's it: he runs away on all four, scared. The snow stopped falling, the sun is going down, and my surrounding is incredibly silent. I might freeze to death if I harvest this meat, but a moan from my belly convinces me to proceed with this choice.
DAY 16 , DUSK: Oh god. I'm in for trouble now. As I finish harvesting all the frozen meat from the deer, a strong wind starts, followed a few minutes later by such strong snowfall that I can barely see 5 meters in front of me. I'm stuck in a blizzard. My low quality clothing instantly shows it's innapropriateness to the situation: I start being cold. I take out a storm lantern from my bag and light it ; It's warmth is going to be insanely useful. Exhausted from my day of traveling and starvation, I start walking back to my cabin, one slow step at a time.
I'm not going to make it. This reality strikes me hard an hour later, when I can no longer feel my arms and legs, frozen like I've never been in my life. I was following my footsteps back to my house, but they have long vanished. I'm getting slower and slower. At some point, I just drop on my knees. I start recalling my best life moments. I remember my wife, Laury, and pull out a photo from my bag with my icy fingers. It depicts her and my son, playful, with a smile on their faces. A tremendous spark of courage strikes me to the core. I can not die in this frozen hell. I get up and walk with renewed courage back to my cabin.
DAY 17, 2 AM: I stumble upon a hollow tree. My know my cabin is near this landmark. I'm almost there.
My vision gets blurry, but I see the faint outlines of my cabin in front of me. It takes me every last bit of willpower I have to get back inside, but I make it. As soon as I close the door behind me, I drop on the floor, uncouscious.
DAY 17, 1 PM: I wake up, frozen to the core, hungry and thirsty. I'm shaking uncontrolably. I grab some Fir firewood and light a fire. I then cook my meat and quench my thirst with some warm green tea. I might be more dead than alive, but...
I made it another day.

The game has lots of potential and the addition of a substantial single-player mode with the official expansion should have elevated Blood Bowl II to the level of "essential" for anyone even remotely interested in Blood Bowl or fantasy sports in general.
Sadly, the AI remains atrocious. Nine games into my new campaign in the Eternal League mode, I have played against 3 different elven teams (2 high elves, 1 dark elves) and have yet to see them even attempt a single pass. The AI seems entirely incapable of handling passes, resorting with each and every team, regardless of composition or skills/attributes, to playing "the cage", and even that rather poorly.
It is both pathetic and utterly disappointing watching snotlings and halfings trying to form a cage. It has no logic and I'm pretty positive that the (entirely unimpressive) AI of the first Blood Bowl was not nearly this incompetent. I know I haven't improved that much (and how could I, playing against such a lacking AI).
Speaking of passing, I have yet to see a single attempt on the part of the big guys of those "special" teams (Ogres, Halflings and Goblins) try to toss one of their stunty, dodgy team-mates. There's no passing whatsoever on the part of the AI. No attempt to position multiple dodgy, agile runners downfield (I had seen this time and again in BB 1), so as to have options for a pass next turn.
Moreover, the AI seems entirely unable to properly take advantage of special weapons: even when losing the toss, the AI keeps ALL special weapons in the team (when there are numerous regular reserves), risking (and suffering, due to its aforementioned incompetence) an early touchdown, whereupon, it loses ALL special weapons for no particular gain.
The only thing that the AI does passably is bash a weaker team, and then it has to be substantially weaker. In fact, the easiest way (and major exploit) is to send a weaker units (say, ST 2) alone towards the opposite side you wish to move, and the AI will promptly surround it with far more players that it would need to bash the living daylights out of your guy: it is not rare to see 4 enemies surrounding a catcher, completely oblivious to the fact that their defense is being overrun on the other end of the field: no, let's bash that ST 2 guy (and not even attempt a foul to get him off the field for good, at the very least).
So, no passing, no tossing team-mates, no proper use of special weapons, no defense unless the AI fields, say, Orcs or Chaos unless an utterly inexperienced player side that is weaker on 1 vs. 1.
And so, the potential is squandered: because there is true potential here; the teams are beautiful, the core rules (as far as I can tell, I'm no BB expert by any means) are here and despite the rather questionable (and by now entirely established) policy of breaking the game in two parts, it has several teams that can play rather differently, plus special teams for those willing to try their hand against very demanding setups or even seemingly impossible odds. The animations are delightful and, although the spectators are unimpressive copies of the same 4-5 models, the overall atmosphere is good. Plus, it's a game with dice, so there's always room for a couple of double skulls to thwart even the best plan.
There's just no AI to support all this content, and unless you can find time to get into a multiplayer league (and then face the demands of having to sit down, uninterrupted, for a good hour each time), you're left with a rather flat experience: a goblin managed to seriously injure my star human blitzer (their single armor break in the entire game, and that's Nuffle for you),  practically forcing me to retire him, and I did not mind at all: without serious opposition, such an event is not a proper loss, merely a setback or, even worse, a welcome development that helps even the field, ever so slight, for the insufferably incompetent AI.
So, sadly, I cannot recommend Blood Bowl II, in its current state. Maybe Cyanide manage to fix (or, more properly, code in) the AI, but I'm not optimistic. I was waiting for a passable AI in BB1 for months, and it never materialized. Hopefully they will prove me wrong and give me a reason to revisit this review and recommend the game.
I sincerely hope they do.

BioShock is one of the greatest games of all time, and if you haven't played it yet, then maybe this review could convince you to play it.

This game is about the main character Windir, whom you get accused of murder and have to prove you innocence. It's mainly about exploring your locations, talking to NPC's, gathering evidences, finding and using items to unlock new and previously locked rooms and area. It has an intruging story that kept me lingering and not much of a combat system (which isn't a minus), but has a very confusing and uninformative use of items to progress the story.
At the start it's interesting enough to read all the documents and uncover clues to find out who framed you, but then it becomes a nightmare of finding objects and find where you are supposed to use them, some of which I had no idea how you where supposed to find out the solution without a walkthough.
There is not nearly enough tips in the game as of how to use certain items, for example, how are you supposed to know Djinni is able to spy on people if you put its crystal in a nearby "cup" or "bucket"? How are you supposed to know which object corresponds to which crystal in the corridor of elements to get the tome of elements? How are you supposed to know which documents you are supposed to use on different people to get to the next point in the game? There's a plethora of items to use and not much information to let you know when or where to use it and with whom.
Pros:
+ Windir's story, the plot is very good
+ Crime investigation
+ Combat system is very simplistic and not often used, which is nice for a investigation styled RPG
+ Lack of a love story, it's short and abrupt which isn't very expected
Cons:
- Really hard puzzles & quests (time-consuming to find the correct person/place/object you're supposed to interact with and how)
- A lot of backtracking
TL;DR:
6.5/10
For an RPG Maker made game it's very well done, one of the better RPG Maker games I've played, and I've played quite a few of them. It's mostly a criminal investigation style game with some rare instances where you have to use combat, mostly just interactions. Complicated use of items to progress the story so if you really wanna get this game done and over with fast (less than 10 hours) I'd strongly suggest using a guide.

This game is great and has so much potential!
The steam distcription is very apt: it is very challenging but the dev has managed to very nicely splice together the 'godlike' town builder with essential tower defense. I recommend you definitely watch the tutorial linked in the game's main menu. For the current unstable 29 build there is plenty to do and I am having a great time. Be careful though, this game is unforgiving; which is why it is so fun and replayable. Don't get me wrong there is plenty to do but after ~10 hours of learning the ropes you begin to hit the limit of building new stuff (if you've made it that long with one village!). This is where the difficulty lends itself to replayability (for the current build and beyond). As soon as everything begins to fall apart you get that sense of newgame+ going into the next village (comprable to They are Billions or Banished). Each time you push the limits, expand even farther, and begin to grasp the min-max of logistics. Lastly, I really like the dev's implementation of your god powers. Not only do you have direct powers to affect the land, etc. but the source of these powers also fuels your villagers' magic buildings. I found this to be a great balance of mechanics.
Tl;Dr: Great, challenging little town builder that has tremendous potential going forward. It has been early access for awhile but it is mostly one dev who has been busting butt adding to the game so don't let that hold you back! The $10 tag is worth it, but getting it for $5 during the winter sale feels like a steal.

Big thumbs up to this game and the developers behind it. From what I can tell, this game is a true masterpiece, and not just because of the art direction.
I want to sing the praises of the game play. It's reminiscent of 90s platformers such as Megaman, Contra and Super Mario, borrowing some of the best elements from each. The gameplay is fair and engaging. You really don't want to stop playing until you beat a level or boss, and even after then, you'll feel compelled to at least see what's next.
People are talking about this game like it's the most difficult game ever made. It isn't. There are challenges, sure, but considering there's even an easy mode, I don't see how anyone should complain about the difficulty. Having said that, I do worry about how difficult the final stages/bosses are going to be. So far, the rollercoaster boss has given me the most grief (although would have been much less grief if I'd purchased different weapons). The Mausoleum stages I wish were a bit more difficult tbh.
Finally, I have to commend the art assets. They aren't lazily reused time and again throughout the game. Each level/boss is completely fresh and super creative. That level of dedication and work is unseen in big publisher AAA games where every job that can be outsourced is until the game comes out a lazy hackneyed mess. Thank god for independant game developers. Give them your money. Buy this game at full price. I did and I do not regret it.

The question is should you buy Five Nights at Freddy’s?
Yes
Five Nights at Freddy’s is a first-person horror game developed by Scott Cawthon.  The game revolves around you as a security guard and five animatronics who will attempt to get into your office.  The object of the game is, of course, to keep them from getting in using your video cameras and the doors.  There is a setback, you only have a limited amount of power and failure to limit your power usage wisely results in a jump scare.
The gameplay is fairly simple and quickly gets repetitive.  You slide your mouse to the bottom of the screen to pull up your cameras.  From there you can select different rooms to view excluding the kitchen, whose camera is disabled for some reason.  Sliding the mouse down will exit out of the camera view and put you back into the office where you can open/close the doors and flicker the lights on either side of you.  While simple and repetitive, this gameplay choice surprisingly enhances the game as it gives the player a sense of hopelessness at they can’t move or try and hide from the animatronics.  The animatronics themselves are reminiscent of the Chuck E Cheese animatronics and have different attack patterns.  For example, Foxy requires you to view the camera in♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥constantly or he will rush to your door resulting in a jump scare and a game over.
The jump scares are affective in scaring the player, but the game as a whole is enough to fill anyone with dread.  Once the infamous phone guy hangs up you’re left in a startlingly silent environment for a few seconds before you begin to hear strange sounds.  Random laughs, pots and pans clattering, and strange whistling sounds can be heard and are enough to put anyone on the edge of their seats.  The atmosphere is brilliantly crafted, creating a desolate environment that fits the story it tells.
The greatest thing about FNAF is its story.  While most horror games have no story or shove its story in your face, FNAF forces you to root around if you want to learn more.  At the beginning of the first four nights a man, lovingly referred to as Phone Guy, will leave you a voice message that both instructs you on how to play, and tells small tidbits of the restaurant itself.  After that, however, you are on your own for the rest.  Posters of news clippings will change telling you more about the lore of the place, but most else is left to the imagination.
In the end, this game is worth the five bucks you shell out to buy it.  Not content to just be youtube bait, this game goes above and beyond what is considered to be a good horror game.  Simple gameplay, actually scary antagonists and environments, and a story that gets more interesting the more you dig into it.  The game is not perfect, the gameplay does get repetitive and the animatronics do loose some fear points as you get used to them.  However with the games that have been released to us as of late, it is refreshing to see a unique and enjoyable experience from a game that should not have delivered so much with so little.

Nightmares turn into reality for a small boy who wakes up in this pitch-black world of LIMBO. Uncertain of his sister's fate, he wanders forth into the unknown.
The black and white setting puts this boy in the darkest of places as he tries to survive long enough to find his sister. The graphics of the game are simple but make the dark and evil scene come to life. Running on Windows, Mac, and Linux LIMBO is available for everyone that enjoys the challenge that this game has to offer. LIMBO runs well on fast or slow computers, with a frame rate between 30 and 60.
The sound effects in LIMBO are amazing, this includes water, footsteps, etc.. The errie atmospheric soundtrack is incredible, and it will send goosebumps up your spine as you play through LIMBO.
The protagonist's story is unknown, but his speechless, glowing eyes tell a tale of sorrow and despair. His animations are well done and the gameplay along side makes for the amazing puzzels and terrain navigation that his small feeble body must endure. He is not a fighter but he is a trickster, as he leads enemies into their own traps and disables other traps by using the limp dead bodies of his enemies as a way to set off trip wires. The environment of LIMBO is just as dangerous as the enemies. As you wander you will come across large spikes, spinning blades, rotating rooms, endless pits, etc.. The game is made up of over twenty chapters, and each has unique ways of completion.
LIMBO is an amazing remake of a world that would scare even the most brave man and woman. The graphics, sounds, animations, controls, and everything else has come together to make a game for anyone that would love a dark mystery.
LIMBO has definitely deserved its overwhelmingly positive reviews.

BioShock is one of the greatest games of all time, and if you haven't played it yet, then maybe this review could convince you to play it.
The atmosphere and the setting is just so incredibly original and creepy. The game takes place in the underwater-city of Rapture, which used to be a rich utopia but then went to hell. Now horrible creatures have arised and you must stop them with the help of a strange man named Atlas.
The villian and characters in this game are so good. You meet horrible people, creatures called Big Daddy's and Little Sisters, and a man called Atlas. Great voice-acting makes for an amazing story with an incredibly shocking plot-twist that left my jaw, and I am sure many others, drop to the floor.
So if I still haven't convinced you yet, then how about this. The combat is so incredibly smooth and has a ton of variety. There are, of course, the normal guns like a shotgun, pistol machine gun, etc. But the real fun is where the plasmids are. Plasmids are almost like magic where you can shoot different abilities like fire, lightning bolt, or even one where you can hack robots/turrets, makes you rethink your approach.
Overall, BioShock is not only one of the best games of "last-gen", but is one of my favorite games ever made. Absolutely no reason on why you shouldn't play this fantastic game.

An excellent example of how creativity can build an amazing game out of an engine renown for bad RPGs like RPG maker. Combat is almost nonexistant, and frankly what little combat there is i found greatly dragged down the pace of the game.
This is a murder mystery. Prepare to spend hours combing through every drawer, trashcan, and NPC you can find trying to find clues and puzzle pieces to keep the story going. At the beginning you are a prisoner charged with the crime of killing the king. To prove your innocence you set out a fugitive running around the castle trying to piece together information about the other possible killers and figuring out what happenned. The world is really built up and if you're willing to take the time and read all the books there is some really good stories in here. You get a really good idea through reading about the warring factions and groups, possible murder suspects and some of the waves the political struggle goes through. The grammer can have issues but untimately i got really into the story and the world, and i think it helps a lot that for 90% of the game there are no combat scenarios. Most of the game is through puzzle solving that makes use of the books and information you have similar to how a point and click game works. It's not what i normally expect seeing the RPGmaker tag.
Admittedly some of the solutions are extremely contrived. At one point I needed an item from a cloaked wizard, who said he would help me if i found out what happenned to a girl named Indra. Turns out INdra hangs out in a cell in the prison, but when you talk to her she doesn't actually say her name. You just go back to the hooded guy and your character says he met with Indra in the jaul cell, but she never said her name and i can't tell where else we would have that information. Little things like that pop up everynow and again and it makes a walkthrough extremely neccessary to play the game (taking a bit of the fun out of it IMO). Also towards the end the game starts to really drag on as you encounter a barn and a labrynth with monster encounters. It's not a dealbreaker but it did annoy me that the appeal of the game - murder mystery puzzle solving - had been replaced by the most basic rpgmaker mechanics i had played so many times before.
All in all though it's still a very cool game that makes really good use of the rpgmaker toolkit to do something unique and pretty fun.

I love survival games, and picked this one up when it first came out.
It seemed to be exactly what I have always wanted, a game about surviving elements.  And how fortunate, its about cold, something I have a good deal of experience in.
I have lived in ND all my life, and it quite frequently gets below -40F/-40C, plus a windchill factor dipping temps to -60F in late winter. This creates very dangerous situations, and I have personally lost 2 REAL family members to separate winter exposure incendents, one of which died from exposure in less than 40 minutes.
The game is good, don't get me wrong, they have been headed down the wrong path IMO.
This is not an element survival game, as it is portrayed.  Rather, they have chosen to give what I perceive as unneeded opponents in the form of the wolves and later the bears.  These will attack you and end your game basically, either killing you right off or causing large amounts of damage.  I know the  Geomagnetic disaster made them bloodthirsty, but have a hard time believing that one wild wolf would make an attempt on a grown mans life unless cornered.
I really like setting traps and trying to make a living in the woods, its definitly my favorite part of the game.  some people complain about not being able to transport a dead animal into a lodge for processing, with this I disagree.  MAYBE if  you build a sled, as not many of you reading this could drag a whole dead wolf 500 yards through the snow in your bluejeans, much less a deer.  A smart bushman would start a fire very near his kill to stay warm while he worked.
By the way what kind of deer is that supposed to be? Pretty small for a north woods deer of any specie, possibly a Blacktail? I would expect a whitetail, and accept a mule deer.  Its pretty confusing since most deer species take on dark colors in the winter as to better blend in and conserve warmth. In the game the "deer" has a bright red coat as it would wear in the summer. all deer seem to have antlers, which is a male only trait. Also the antlers are shaped like an elk, an entirely different deer specie, close to twice the size of the portrayed "deer".
Mostly I am dissapointed in the lack of exposure mechanic, I had been hoping for a moisture dynamic.
In the real cold, the amount of moisture in the clothes your wearing will decide if you live or die.  Most people know that you can go hypothermic in fairly mild conditions if you get wet and are continually exposed to wind and temps below 50F.  Getting sweaty while running or chopping wood dampens your cloths from the inside, and when its below 0F it won't take long before your core temp drops dramatically.  Put your foot down an icehole sometime and walk back to shore with your jeans frozen solid and you will know the pain of moisture in the winter. I feel they really missed out here, as clothes could be dried by the fire as another activity, stimulating players to realize that if its warm inside you can take your clothes off and save them from degrading.(storing items on corpses greatly increases shelf life)
Speaking of moisture in the winter, what happens to soda cans left to below freezing? This is litterally what convinced me to write this review. Ever since this game has been out up untill today, I have found soda cans outside In loot bins and on bodys.  anyone whe has ever left a coke in freezer knows whats next, BOOM!. There would not be unexploded unfrozen soda cans though.
To sum it all up, I just wish there was more focus on the cold.  In the real cold, everything is harder, and if you really landed in this place with the small amount of gear you begin the game with, you would almost certainly die in less than 6 hours.  I am fine with that fact, its the challenge I had hoped for.  What I miss is the real powerfull dynamic of the cold, where are the equipment failures from exposure to frost? Why doesent your water freeze if its in a bottle outside on your back or whatever? Why if i take my boots off and run outside does it only remove the warmth bonus and not have any other adverse affect? You would not make it 50 meters with no shoes in the snow.
But really the soda cans....

Played Labyronia I and II and having played this, I enjoyed the story plot that ties in all three games together.
This game differs drastically from the other two games in that you aren't exactly geared towards fighting monsters to level up. Rather, you are mostly on a hunt-seek to solve a mystery. Much like modern click and search games, this is like that, but in JRPG format, where you move everywhere, click everywhere, and try different actions with different characters. This may not be for everyone considering the amount of patience and memorization you have to have to perform certains actions. IE: immense backtracking to get an item back you didn't realize you needed or remembering which note/diary to pull up in front of a character. What was nice is that any monsters you killed previously does not respawn. With  the amount of backtracking at the later parts of the game, I appreciated this fact so I didn't have to re-kill all the monsters as I went back and forth.
About the gameplay, it is somewhat linear in that you can progress in slightly different paths, but they all converge down to the same ending when you reach the end of that part. IE: you can complete one side quest before the other. Fight scenes are pretty rudimentary RPG mechanics. Not the best, but not the worse either. Some of the puzzles can stump you for awhile. I enjoyed solving them and even had to use a guide to figure out a few.
One downside to the game is the vast amount of items you have. As noted earlier, you need to have a good memory or you will repeatedly scroll through your items trying to figure out which item goes to whom. I played the game without pausing too much inbetween so I had a decent rememberance of each item, but if you play the first few hours and then come back after a week or longer, you may struggle trying to remember everything. For a mystery RPG, there is a LOT of things to be found and to use. A few might even say too many, but considering the story plot, it does kind of make sense as to why there are so many items.
Overall, it's a nice game to play. I did end up using the guide for the last 1/4 of the game, but I was progressing pretty quickly in the game in that I don't think I'd reach 10 hours of gameplay. 7.5/

Legend of Mysteria is an RPGMaker game developed by Labyrinthine and released Oct 9, 2015.
Legend of Mysteria is a prequel to the Labyronia RPG games. You play as Windir (an air mage) who has been framed for murdering Dinyon
. I dare say 90% of this game is puzzle solving, and 10% of this game is reloading saves and trying your RNG against bosses, and weather to use items or not.
Unlike the Labyronia games, this game emphasizes story telling and puzzle solving.
However everytime you actually get into battle you realize just how annoying it would have been to battle more often. This time there is no combat given for battling... but thankfully once you defeat a foe it does not respawn or come back when you leave the screen. There are also zero random encounters.
As I've already said most of the game is completing puzzles, I played for about 2 or 3 hours before getting discouraged and looking up a guide.
I'm not very good at puzzle solving in general, but this was the first RPG maker game I've ever played which emphasized on story telling and puzzle solving rather then combat level grinding.
I can definitely say this much: Labyrinthine always tries in each game made. The driving factor seems to be for creating a world, and I can respect that.
There's also a clear sense of effort and work put into each of Labyrinthine's games.
The only problem is that they're stunted and held back by being constrained to the RPGmaker model... Most people have seen all the sprites in other RPG maker games "We've danced this dance".
I hope that this series becomes a springboard for the developer to create something new outside of RPG maker.
In conclusion to answer the question "should you play this or not": Have you played many RPG maker games? Do you like puzzles? Do you like reading? If so this game will work for you.
The final factor or motivator I can think of would be for people going for steam trading cards, or 100% achievers... Thanks to Karinms guide the achievements and game can be played for a minimalist amount of time.... however those motivations are at your own discretion.
Clearly, I was motivated by the story and achievements. (Seeing as I got discouraged and followed a guide after the first hour. For what it's worth I can say I cleared maybe a third of the game on my own! I could figure out a lot without the guide... and didn't even go in the same order, but yeah, no, I'm just trying to salvage my pride.)

Would I recommend this game?
Would I recommend this game?
Yes. But only if you're ready.
Without spoiling too much, my suggestion to you is that you prepare yourself mentally/emotionally. It's quite a ride. After awhile, you may become unsure as to whether the person in question is who he is or if he's...someone else...
This game came with some expectations. I tried not to let my experience with The Stanley Parable cloud it too much. I knew it was from the same creator. So I had a feeling any expectation I could possibly contrive would be blown out of the water anyway. However, whatever it was that I was expecting from this game, it ended up being not at all what I'd imagined. The trailer is an excellent foreshadower. You get curious. It gives a (very) vague idea of what the game will be about. But you look back at it after a playthrough, and you realize that even though it advertised the game perfectly well, it also somehow managed to not reveal the game in any way. Like...you can pick out all the pieces the trailer used, but then you realize that the pieces it used were but small dots within a vast and intricate bigger picture. That was cool.
All I can really say is wow. I have been changed. By a simple, narrative walkthrough. There's not much to click on. Not much to explore. The textures have that same, simple-yet-elegant-and-kind-of-soothing feel to them as Stanley. The music is terribly beautiful. I bought the soundtrack as soon as I finished the game. It and the game itself manage to be calming at times and extremely unsettling at others, all while maintaining an ethereal, dreamlike quality. There are so many emotions in this simple little story, told through corridors and...well, not much else, really...that by the end I wasn't really sure what I was feeling - or what I was supposed to be feeling - at that moment.
If you're hoping for catharsis, I can promise you you'll either find it or you won't. I don't think there's an in-between for this one. It just depends on how you interpret, what choices you make, and what experiences you have had that have led you to this exact moment in your life. I found it. But not in the way I thought I would when I started the game.
Just...prepare yourself. You're about to go on a journey you won't forget anytime soon.
10/10

The most damning thing about Cuphead is that every time you die - and you will - you know it's your fault.
Cuphead is a love-letter to both 1930s-era animation - Silly Symphonies and Happy Harmonies, before Warner Bros. changed the game with Bugs and Daffy and the rest of the Looney Tunes. The entire game is rendered with art that would be totally at home in those cartoons, lovingly animated and filtered with the best film grain overlay I think I've ever seen. The music is pure 1930s and early 40s, with a lovely little opening ditty explaining the bare bones of the story and a nice sleazy blues tune for King Dice, the Devil's right hand man.
The story is simple: Cuphead and Mugman lost their souls playing dice with the devil, and now have to collect the souls of debtors to earn back their own. It's not much more complicated than that, and it's told in storybook form between the game's four worlds. I haven't beaten it yet, but it has all the charm of one of those old cartoons, and about as much logic.
The game, of course, is also a love letter to the hard as balls platformers and shooters many of us were raised on. It does not hold your hand. A screen of very easy tutorial is all you get, and it's all you need. Apart from buying a small selection of upgrades and power-ups, the five basic moves you learn in the tutorial are all you need to carry you thruogh the game: shoot, EX shot, jump, dash, parry, and stand still. Shooting things builds your EX meter (a hand of cards), which you can use for powerful shots or super moves you learn in bonus stages. You jump and dash to avoid enemies and shots, and you can parry pink shots/enemies/objects, which builds a full card of meter. You have three hit points. That is it. The rest of the game is boss fights and the occasional platform level, peppered with a few shooter levels that trade dashing for shrinking.
The game is hard as balls, but it never feels unfair. The hitboxes are fair, the RNG doesn't stick you in a no-win situation unless you're careless with your own movement, and it's not a bullet hell memorization-fest. The controls are tight and responsive, and Cuphead and Mugman are maneuverable enough to reasonably dodge most anything thrown at them. It's hard, but satisfying. You will die. A lot. There are no lives and no game overs, but you do have to start over from the beginning of a level or boss when you die. None of them take more than 2 or 3 minutes from start to finish, however, or at least they don't for me. You'll spend a lot longer learning the boss's patterns and what strategies work best against each part of the boss, but when you win it's very satisfying.
I can't reccommend this game enough, with the caveat that you have to have the patience for a really challenging game.

This game is a harkening back to all the beloved mascot 3D platformers that came before it. The influence of Banjo-Kazooie, the Super Mario series, a bit of Conker's Bad Fur Day, and a healthy dose of Psychonauts to name a few is sincerely noticeable. Also noticeable is a soundtrack that soars with the whimsy of Mario Galaxy, the cutsie charm of Banjo, and something entirely own with the likes of several guest musicians including Grant Kirkhope, of Banjo and Conker fame. And what also sticks with you is the constant barrage of clever and adorable details that didn't need to exist to make this game stand on its own, but was lovingly crafted regardless. Though it stumbles once in my opinion, I couldn't recommend this game possibly more. If you're on the fence and reading this for some reason: Buy. This. Game.
The cuteness is unlike any other, entirely its own brand of adorable lovability and unending charmfullness.
However, there are a few moments that were especially damning for this beloved game, and that is one of its levels: Alpine Skyline. This level is a bit of a callback to Banjo-Kazooie's Click-Clock Woods, a 4-part level with seasons differentiating it. Alpine Skyline by contrast is divided much more subtley by various themes such as visual puns like Lava Cake being a several story tall row of increasingly smaller piles of lava, like a super-heated wedding cake. The level is devoid of linear pathways in a more find-it-yourself fourway. It allows for freedom but is devoid of the game's typical charm and cutesy  style. It's a gorgeous level that feels very empty due to the lack of direction present in all other chapters. No major supporting character was present to offer the level of memorability that Mafia or The Snatcher had. Throw on top of this the gameplay extending Finale that was just a bit absurd in the way that it tests patience more than any other. Frankly, Alpine Skyline was an unnecessary level that could have been replaced by something far more memorable. But with such a shining star of a game, a knick in the paint isn't that bad overall.
Despite that rant, though, A Hat in Time is a modern classic of 3D platforming and a wonderful addition to a childlike longing for the happier times. A world of unending intrigue, love, and charm is something we all need from time to time. I'd recommend this to anyone who loves to have fun and would like to tap into their inner child.

There is art here, despite what many would say isn't possible with games, from Roger Ebert to game designers like Hideo Kojima. But it's in BioShock--it's in the gorgeously realized, watery halls of Rapture. It's in a Little Sister's expression of thanks when you choose to save her, or the utter silence if you harvest instead. It's in the way the characters develop, in the testimonials of the recording boxes you pick up along the way. It's in the way the narrative is structured, and the way it blends so seamlessly with the action. Irrational had a clear vision with this game, something pulled off with remarkable precision in every department. They didn't just deliver something that's fun to play, a criterion so often cited as the benchmark of what makes a game worthwhile. BioShock stands as a monolithic example of the convergence of entertaining gameplay and an irresistibly sinister, engrossing storyline that encompasses a host of multifaceted characters. This is an essential gaming experience.

Review for Batman Ep1.
Note: download the patch and run the game in Windows 7 mode.
TLDR;
A must buy now that it has been fixed into a playable state. You will be rewarded by experiencing a completely new Batman story, starting afresh just a couple of years after Bruce Wayne has donned the cawl of the caped crusader. This leaves open many threads for where you can make Batman boldly go where no bat has gone before.
I would've given this game a negative review for the poor performance that it showed. I even asked for a refund. But I was too hasty in my judgement. Telltale fixed the game within a week. And, yes, in some cutscenes, the framerate still chugs, but that's tolerable compared to how it was upon release. I was so butthurt, you could say, that I even tweeted Telltale a sad and sobby tweet like: "Why have you abandoned us PC players?" but if you're a PC player, you know that that was a long time coming. A lot of AAA devs nowadays don't give a rat's a$$ about PC optimization (and telltale games tend to have some minor glitches upon release that never really tend to get fixed, but they always run at a solid 60 fps). So, this time when this particular batman game had such a pathetic release, i was pi$$ed and I got really upset, thinking that now even Telltale (who btw I love very much as a dev team, as you can see from my game library, I've got many of their games, even Jurrassic Park, which isn't such a bad game, it's avg at best) had started to not give 2 faqs about PC. So, unlike when other AAA devs faq us over, I genuinely felt hurt when I saw this from Telltale, which is why my reaction to this was so over the top.
Anyways, the game got patched, people said play it on Win7 mode (why is that even an option Telltale in your new game engine? If you can see that people are recommending one mode over the other, why not just remove the choice, so that people don't experience poor optimization? But I digress), and so I decided to take a risk and buy the game once again (Props to you btw, Valve for allowing us to pay by card and the Steam wallet at the same time, that's a really awesome feature, I hate on you quite often for cen$orship in steam reviews{and other things}, but you hold a special place in my heart along with Telltale).
And my risk payed off. You're rewarded by a by the numbers Telltale game. And I mean that in a good way. A good and strong opening chapter to a new series. And it has a particularly good story btw. I won't reveal much, but you're given decisions which would change the image of Batman completely. Villains could be allies, can you trust your own goodness? And so on. You can be as brutal as Ben Affleck's potrayal of Batman, or as "nice" as Christian Bale's. I myself was sort of a mix between Chris Bale's and Kevin Conroy's Batman. A fear mongerer but kind, restrained, resolute, visibleand hopeful. I scare criminals like Bale's Batman, but I don't harm them; and I'm forming a friendship with Gordon like Conroy's Batman.
The no kill policy was very important to me.
Anyways, as you may have read in other reviews, the frst chapter opens up many threads for continuation, and this seems to be Telltale games at their best form, akin to The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us. I look forward to tough decisions in the future. Oh yeah, one other thing that I noticed your choices as Batman and Bruce Wayne matter very much (i.e. your choices make a true difference). The people of Gotham are still wondering what to think of you, are you a symbol of hope in  a city of despair, or have you  given in to the animalisitic side of you and are just a brutal vigilante and nothing more. And another thing, the QTEs, Telltale has made them very forgiving, so even if you miss something,  it'll still happen. The framerate chugs only a couple of times, like in one cutscene where a hologram of Gotham pops up, the FPS goes down to 10-15 fps. But the comic-book style of Telltale's games makes it less jarring on the eyes. But when this new engine works, it works. Animations are much smoother, the graphics look better than what they used to be, and so on.
The detective mode definitely is a very welcome tool in Batman. It's good to see his detective side as well.
All in all a very pleasant introduction to what appears to be a great series.

With the release of the Legendary edition, this game is finally worth the price they are asking for it. If you love Blood Bowl, this is a great adaptation. It takes a bit longer than playing a game on FUMBBL, but looks much, much better and I personally prefer the interface of BB2 over that of FUMBBL.
