Overall though I feel this is the best digital Blood Bowl experience available right now.
For those wondering what Blood Bowl is:
It is a turn based board game that relies on 6 sided dice(and sometimes an 8 sided die) to determine the success or failure of certain critical actions, its main mechanics are built around risk minimalization. Sports is mostly just a theme to 'dress up' hardcore turned based stratedgy and character progression elements. The game and its teams are designed to be slightly unfair and unbalanced, because of this the team you pick determines the difficulty level of the game, as well as the skill of your opponent.
Because the game is luck based, try to roll as few dice as you can, because every time you roll a die you risk a turnover, conversly try and set up your players in such a way that your opponent needs to roll as many dice as possible in order to do what they want to do.

First of all I actually like this game a lot, which is why I am giving it a bad review. Let me explain.
I really like this type of game, or rather these types of games. Rise to Ruins is, at its core, a mash up of city builders, survival games, tower defense, and God games. It offers a decent number of buildings construct and some require others to be built first which creates a good sense of progression.  If you are playing with monsters active, which you should be, you will need to create defensive towers to help the villagers or else they are all going to die pretty quickly. Everything you costs resources that need to be collected by villagers or energy which you can gain from various sources around the map.
Monsters are a serious threat if you are caught off guard and without a clear plan. They start off few and weak but quickly turn into swarms. Having a good maze of walls and defensive towers for monsters to navigate will become essential pretty quickly, and that is a good thing. Usually games of this type tend to be slow and leave the player with nothing to do for long stretches, not so much here.
The problems I have with the game all stem from the incredibly stupid AI. The villagers seem to be easily confused and will just stop building for no reason. Some structures require materials that have to be produced in order to be built. This means that when you attempt to build a structure but do not have the needed materials it will get as far as possible but stop until you provide the needed materials. Usually the construction will then complete according to whatever number it is in the que. Usually.
sometimes the game just fails to bother with a construction project, at all. This is particularly boggling when it is a project that DOES NOT REQUIRE any special materials. You can send a project to the front of the que, but that does not mean they will bother with it. The villagers will, instead, just keep building whatever they feel like building. This can be damning when you are attempting to rush the production of defenses.
Another issue concerning villager is that death by dehydration is far too common. After creating several ways for the villagers to stay hydrated, including bottling facilities so they can take some liquid goodness with them, I STILL have frequent deaths from dehydration. If it is my fault I sure as hell can not see what I am doing wrong. I have plenty of water and yet my villagers insist on ignoring it and dying. If it is my fault then the devs need to add a note for the tutorial that makes it clear what is needed to prevent this.
EDIT: It turns out the water issue was my fault. I was simply not producing enough water and it has been brought to my attention that water and food values carry different wrights, meaning that you need more water than food.
Monster AI can be a little daft as well, with monsters absolutely refusing to attack a wall if there is an opening somewhere else. This is forgivable, however, considering the difficulty of managing the hordes as is. You WILL have to face hordes of enemies too, make no mistake. Zombies, spectres, flame elementals and more will simply spawn and charge your villagers most nights. I found this to be a fun, if somewhat frustrating, mechanic that had me spending the days preparing for the night while also trying to meet the needs of my villagers.
The issues that the game currently has are not game breaking but can turn a good time sour quickly when you suddenly have construction projects that are mysteriously unable to complete of you have 10-20 villagers die of dehydration in a single day despite having over 100 water that no one is even drinking.
I have faith that the devs will smooth out these issuews and I will gladly change this review to the entirely positive review I wan to give. Oh, also more keys for goodness sake ;)

In Medieval Kingdom Wars you will fight in the midst of the middle ages as an important ruling power in those times, but as you will discover there is much more to it than that as you will siege castles, control your servants and expand your ever-growing empire. Although there Is still much work to be done even in its current stage  it’s already very detailed and will grow to one of the most genre defining medieval strategy games on the market.
Your main purpose is as a minor lord in a large kingdom to expand yourself through diplomacy, warfare and trade. However as this game is still in Alpha the “Warfare” part is the most prominent, this means that you’re going to be sieging a lot which is in this case the most important part of the game. Before getting into all the other parts of the game I would like to address the sheer time and effort that has been put into the game. I honestly admire the incredibly amount of care the developers have taken with the game and I hope that one day many more can also treat their products the same as these developers have. Even in early alpha the developers have already done so much to make the game run and work like they want it to which I think is incredible.
With that said that doesn’t mean the game doesn’t have problems which I will also elaborate on. The most important thing to keep in mind with this is that this is very early alpha so in this case I’m going to label them improvements.
You, a minor lord controlling a small area in a certain kingdom are supposed to grow your territory by trading, and brutally clubbing your enemies into submission. However because these features are not all available only clubbing your enemies is possible which is also very fun.
The games 3D map you watch in the campaign map view is absolutely stunning, not only does it look very pretty it’s also incredibly realistic which really drives the point of immersion to the player because in a medieval game that is very important. Looking at the map really surprised me as to how much effort and care had been taken of it which is something you don’t often see in an early access title. You might think that that goes at the cost of gameplay now perhaps there are more bugs than if all the money had been spent on fixing those however I think the tradeoff was worth it.
You as a player build your armies with taxes you collect from your citizens, with these armies you can select them and assign them a task to do, at the moment this is practically just stabbing your foes. Now while I do think that this system can be improved with perhaps a right-click movement option however for the time it suffices.
I think that personally the option to go with a small lord in a larger kingdom was perfect for this medieval era, as an entire empire wasn’t controlled by a single man or woman. This also shows how much the developers care for a realistic depiction of medieval times. Now although it’s not perfect I do appreciate this a lot as again I can see the amount of care the developers have for the game.
Because field battles are not implemented and trade is non-existent this is practically the primary component of the game: Besieging your enemies and your enemies besieging you. Even though it’s only early access this part is done terrifically well. Instead of brining your campaign map resources into a siege battle you gain your resources at the location itself because that’s actually how it happened, the only thing armies carried around was food who’s just going to take a cart of iron to war?
When you are sieging you arrive on site and start building your siege camp, practically a poorly built castle to defend yourself in case the defenders decide to come out and attack you. This is done by exploiting the natural resources like felling trees, building iron and stone mines; slaughtering the local wildlife or importing your own to slaughter. This kind of depiction of sieging, which is by far the most realistic one I have ever seen, is absolutely stunning but mostly very immersive as you start to look at the enemy’s gates for weaknesses that you can exploit to fight your way into the enemy city just like a medieval engineer would.
Inside your Siege camp you can build many different kind of structures, perhaps you are willing to focus on bombarding your enemies with trebuchets or just blindly storming the gate with a battering ram; or why not both? You can build a large variety already for research or just training troops which require the natural resources I talked about earlier. You also have to provide for the food of your troops, sadly this is only in a way of recruiting your troops with a certain amount of food; you gain food automatically and slaughtering animals for it is just nice for quickly building up your forces. Now this part is definitely not without flaw as often upgrades don’t seem to have affect or walls that you paid for with a lot of resources don’t get built. Now this is not incredibly often happening but it can be a bit annoying as the enemy can now march into your encampment right through the wall that was supposed to be constructed 6 days ago.
After a long time of building up and perhaps defending against the current occupiers of the city you are finally ready to end the siege and end the enemy’s reign. Out of all the parts of sieging an enemy this is probably the most least developed one however it still does its job, siege towers function as ladders to your enemy’s encampment and battering rams break open doors however some other parts of combat are a bit more clunky. For example archers can fire through floors because the enemy is in range! However they still function and still fire their arrows. Combat is still unsatisfying as your troops converge into a large mixing bowl of 4 different colours as you watch your amount of troops to see if you are winning, at least in medieval times you could see your soldiers get sliced in half and see them dying on the ground. Certain other features like mantlets, large shields on wheels to protect soldiers from arrows,  don’t quite work like they’re supposed to as often archers just fire over them.
Overall I really enjoy the sieging part however many things are still to be added or fixed however for an early alpha this is incredible.
While in real medieval times being sieged was quite different from sieging in the wonderful world of medieval simulators it is not. I can see that the developers have just taken the blueprint of the sieging part and loosely translated it to a defending side, this is most likely due to the lack of time to implement many new things however it is noticeable. Practically everything is the same like sieging except that your wood now comes from the houses of your inhabitants, which is incredibly historically accurate I love it, and you need to focus much more on defending and breaking the siege. The only problem so far is that there is no real pressure to do so. A real city that was being besieged would have to find a way to break the siege as soon as possible because with no access to their farms outside they just had to rely on the grains and other food types they had stored, however in game land this is not the case as you can just magically create pigs from your local barn; which for game purposes is fine but perhaps dwindling food resources would be nice.
Another issue is archers standing on walls and towers only sort of stand there, as they don’t actually form to the wall but stand in random formations spread out over the area which could be on the wall, on the floor and inside a tower.

The visual art style has a certain charm to it, original and unqiue art designs influenced by the early animation days. It adds to the novelty of the game and sticks out from the others. However, desipite its cartoonish designs,  it's a pretty challanging game and so far i'm impressed by how it gives an enjoyable experience even while losing several times.
The controls can be getting used to beginners new to the genre but feels inspired by other games like contra and metal slug. The music and audio also adds to the vintage cartoon style and overall it deserves the high ratings it deserves. For 20 bucks I say its well worth it.

''Rewrite medieval history through bloody siege combat and grand strategy. Rule, build, and wage war as one of the minor lords of medieval Europe… Medieval Kingdom Wars redefines Medieval Grand Strategy.''


Before reviewing a game, some might say it’s wise to have a butchers at its Steam page. It’s a great way to see how the game markets itself. When I opened the page for new RTS/grand strategy title “Medieval Kingdom Wars”, you can imagine my shock when it claims to be “redefining” the medieval grand strategy genre – a bold claim to make when you’re going toe-to-toe with the likes of Crusader Kings and Total War.
Scroll down past the flashy screenshots and the “very positive” user review rating, and you might be shocked to hear that the game is made by Reverie World Studios. “Why would I be shocked?” you ask. Well they’ve got a bit of a reputation for putting out games that are somewhat substandard. I purchased “Dawn Of Fantasy” in 2011 for £29.99, only to find that the game was a buggy, unpolished mess – trying to be both medieval and fantasy RTS rolled into one.
It seems that their next few titles (Kingdom Wars 1 & 2) followed in the same vein. In fact, I seem to recall that Kingdom Wars was a rehash Dawn of Fantasy, which had a dire rating on Steam. I was therefore flabbergasted to find out that they had released a third, very similar looking game in June of this year. Shall we take a look at how it fares in a tough-to-enter RTS/grand strategy market?


Let’s start with the good – of which there is a fair amount. The overall theme is the most coherent of any Reverie World Studios production thus far. The grand strategy map and large battlefields of Europe are seemingly etched out by hand – with a littering of props and nuances in the terrain that add to the game’s atmosphere. The game also has a fairly comprehensive tutorial that provides a loosely story-based approach to teaching you the ropes.
Medieval Kingdom Wars’ graphics are okay; not amazing, but neither are they terrible. They have a kind of gritty feel that is in-keeping with the time period – devoid of any bright colours as you may expect from war-torn medieval Europe.
This is all linked together by a fantastic soundtrack that makes you feel as though you’re in a medieval town. The rhythmic dialogue is generally acted well, further adding to the immersion in a medieval setting. Battle sounds are clear and well-selected for the period – ensuring the player knows what’s going on without confusion.
My final good point would be the interesting way that the developers present icons over buildings. When selected, the building’s construction options are displayed in a lancet window styling above – a nice touch to keep in with the theme of the game. This kind of attention to detail is sadly overlooked by many developers these days, who tend to opt for a clinically clean and personality-less style; but not here!


Unfortunately for all the good in Medieval Kingdom Wars, there is quite a lot of bad to balance it out. My biggest, overarching criticism of the game is that it’s far too similar to its predecessors. Reverie World Studios appear to have re-skinned their already existing games and given it a slightly different title – that to me screams lazy developer, and perhaps one to not be trusted so easily.
It can take the player up to an hour to perform a siege – rendering the game a non-starter for the casual player. Once in battle you’ll have to put up with clunky unit animations and to be honest, some very bland strategic gameplay. Tactics in Medieval Kingdom Wars comes down to hurling projectiles at a wall or gatehouse until it crumbles, before flooding the area with as many units as you can. For a game that claims to rival the likes of the Total War series, this is quite a poor effort at RTS battlefield tactics.
The game also purports to let the player “create” sprawling cities, where the choices you make when building will affect the entire game world, on a strategic map level. This is somewhat untrue however, as the player doesn’t have total freedom to place buildings – rather they’re built upon pre-determined locations. This eliminates strategy from city defence building, especially in siege-play where building placement could be crucial – thinking of classic RTS’s such as Age of Empires.
The grand strategy element of Medieval Kingdom Wars is also somewhat lacking. There is little direction in the story, although it must be said that the level of freedom afforded to the player here, suggests a kind of sandbox vibe for the grand strategy portion of the game. This area of Medieval Kingdom Wars is quite overbearing and can come across as brutal – especially due to the fact it just throws you in and hopes for the best.


When I was offered review of this game, I was excited to see if Reverie World Studios had turned over a new leaf – if they’d cast off their slapdash game design ways of the past and really gone hammer and tongs to create a fun and engaging medieval RTS. Sadly, it appears that they’ve stuck to the same concepts and low quality of previous titles. This said, the game does garner some merits, such as the fantastic soundtrack and audio design, as well as the atmosphere created by level design.
In defence of the developers though, the price of the game is modest at £14.99. I also noticed that Kingdom Wars 2 was quite cheap, with the first instalment being free-to-play. It seems that they’ve thought about what their games are worth and decided to give something back to the community – perhaps a developer to watch for the future.

For the first few hours of this game, unless you consult a guide, you will have no idea what you're doing. And that's okay. You will lose your first captain fairly quickly. But when a captain dies, the next one can inherit certain aspects of their life, ranging from weapons to money to heirlooms. Soon you'll have some notion of what's going on.
From an artistic standpoint, Sunless Sea is appealing. You will encounter a variety of islands and environments, discovering lore along the way, all set to a fitting soundtrack.
From a gameplay perspective, there are things that can be improved. You will spend most of your time sailing from island to island, trading, documenting, and trying not to be killed by zee monsters. Fuel and supplies are a near constant worry, because if either runs out while you're at zee, your ship is practically gone. Spending time at zee will also increase Terror, another important stat. It will take some time before you are even able to purchase a bigger ship; unless you know what you're doing, gold is scarce.
There is hope, though. You can choose to acquire a merchant ship, which has significant cargo space for efficient trading. Or you can choose the heavier battle ships to hunt monsters.
There's no doubt that you will die at least once before you're able to hold your own against the dark zee. But if you're persistant enough (or foolish enough), you can probably find some way to not lose your mind.

Not recommended in the slightest. I was really looking forward to a great new destruction derby racing game with sweet physics and lots of tuning options. You know, like it was in the early alpha. You could mod your car, have specific stats for everything, buy parts used and new, repair the parts that were broken and a lot more. Since the publishing deal with THQ Nordic the game has been incredibly dumbed down and a lot of the cool features have been taken away. The new menu system is also horrible compared to the original that gave you everything in one screen, instead of having to jump back and forth in various menus. At least it's not as much of a mess as it was after the first "dumbed down" update.
In all honesty, I was still okay with the menus and the dumbed down tuning of cars since the gameplay and overall look of the game itself was fun. However, now it feels like the graphics have gotten a huge downgrade and the gameplay itself isn't as fun as it used to be. The cars seem like they are always glued to the track and just generally don't feel as realistic as they should be.
The worst part, the absolute WORST part, the part that made me write this review, was the fact that apparently you can't even flip your car off the track at certain points anymore. You can't flip your car. In a destruction derby game. When I pushed my opponent in high speed, we both flipped and were flung in a glorious arc towards the woods... and then the game snapped us immediately back on the track, without losing any speed and not giving me the option to watch the wreckage, which honestly is the high point of games like this, at least to me. It turns out there was a spectator standing somewhere between the flimsy wooden fence and the trees and you aren't allowed to hit them, which is what caused the reset. This only begs another question: why would there be a bystander in a banger race in such a place? It adds nothing to the game. Have them all sit at the stands or at least have a "no spectators" option to take them out. Things like this just take away from the experience.
I am willing to change this review if the old tuning mechanism is added later as a patch (not a paid DLC) and the insta-reset is taken out of the game completely.

Updated: April 2017
It's a year since I last reviewed Sunless Sea, and given the release of Zubmariner, I thought it was time for an update.
Clearly with 180 hours play time (at the time of writing), I love this game and I definitely recommend it to others. It has been a great experience and I still have so many endings to explore and secrets to uncover. I find immersing myself (pun intended) in this world comes so easily and I can lose hours without realising it.
Part of my love for the game comes from NOT playing it as a rogue-like. Manual save is the way to go with this game. It takes so long to achieve the victory conditions for each captain that starting from scratch because of one bad decision is soul-destroying. So do yourself a favour - just use the manual save. The game is much better for it as it allows you the freedom to take chances, to push yourself further and to do the outright stupid at times. I felt that I missed so much of the game while playing perma-death because I was afraid of losing it all. With manual save I can experience everything.
My feelings on the game are pretty much the same as below, but I wanted to add that the Zubmariner expansion is so well done. It fits into the game as though it belonged there the entire time. It is so well integrated that I can't remember a time before the DLC's introduction, and it's a worthwhile addition to the game. If you find the atmosphere and story in any way gripping, then Zubmariner is a great way to expand the range of the game without it feeling tacked on or forced.
I get that this game isn't everyone's cup of tea and some people find it too text-based, but it's right up my street and is now by far my most-played game on Steam.
Updated: February 2016
I love this game. I found it had a very steep learning curve but once I learned the ropes I discovered a wonderfully layered world with brilliant stories. I have sunk (heh) 80+ hours of gameplay into the world of Sunless Sea and I'm still learning and still discovering. I'm pursuing a different ambition and able to take the opposite options to what I chose last time around and there are lots of little details that I didn't pick up before. The more time I spend playing, the more I fall in love with it.
The story and atmosphere are the strongest aspects of the game, in my opinion. Each island has its own unique story, peeled away layer by layer with each visit. Islands which appear innocuous at first have hidden secrets. I felt genuine anxiety watching my fuel and supply gauges continue to drop miles from the nearest friendly port, knowing that having to detour to avoid a single zeebeast could cost me everything. All of your officers have their own motivations for joining you and while it's costly to help them, you gain huge benefits in the long run, as well as more richly flavoured story.
I would consider the combat the weakest point of the game. Unless you need a specific item drop it's almost always safer and more economical to avoid combat altogether. Perhaps this is intentional as it's more realistic, but anyone hoping for a game filled with epic zee-battles with either be disappointed or frequently dead.
No previous knowledge from Fallen London is required, although I did find myself consulting forums and the wiki to get the background of some stories as information is fed rather piecemeal to give a slow reveal. This does give you motivation to continue returning to islands which don't, at first, appear to have much interesting happening on them.
It took about 60 hours of gameplay for me to finally succeed in permadeath mode, although others have done it in considerably less. I felt that towards the end I was shying away from dangerous encounters a lot for fear of losing my captain and I think I missed a lot because of that. I'm using manual save now and I feel a lot freer to make mistakes and to take chances, although I don't feel quite the same tension as before.
Special shout-out to the soundtrack, which is amazing. It's melancholic and joyful and frightening in all the right ways. You can listen to it for free a limited number of times on Bandcamp if you want to check it out.

Metal Slug (Japanese: メタルスラッグ Hepburn: Metaru Suraggu?) is a series primarily of run and gun video games created by SNK. Spin-off games include a third-person shooter and a tower defense game. Originally created for Neo-Geo arcade machines and game consoles, the original games have also been ported to other consoles, with several later games created for various other platforms. The games focus on the Peregrine Falcon Squad, a small group of soldiers who fight against a rebel army, aliens and various other forces intent on world domination.
The gameplay of the series is characteristic of run and gun games: large numbers of enemies and a player character with extremely powerful weapons. In most run and guns, contact with an enemy leads to annihilation.[citation needed] In this series, however, contact results in the opportunity to perform a melee attack and the opportunity for the enemy to perform a melee attack of his own, if he has one. The player's melee attack is also much stronger than most shots. This leads to the players ability to run in and use melee attacks to take down a number of enemies, and the ability to quickly defeat enemies that can take plenty of damage, such as the mummies in Metal Slug 2.
The player starts with only a simple handgun; as the game progresses, the player may pick up new weapons. The player can only use one weapon at a time. When a new weapon is found, it replaces the previous one. Similarly, when ammunition runs out, the player reverts to using the handgun, which has unlimited ammunition. A new system was implemented with Metal Slug 6 allowing players to carry and switch between the handgun and two other weapons.
The SV-001 (SV being an abbreviation for "Super Vehicle") or 'Metal Slug' is the main vehicle of the Metal Slug franchise. It is a small, cartoonish silver-gray tank. The tank is armed with one cannon and twin vulcan cannons. The vehicle can jump and crouch. Crouching opens a hatch on the top of the tank through which grenades can be thrown. The grenades are independent of the cannon's ammunition system. The vehicle can run over infantry and perform a suicide attack, with the driver jumping clear and the tank ramming into and exploding upon the target. The vehicle can take three direct hits before it is destroyed. The enemy chaser variant has a shield that must be destroyed before the vehicle can be destroyed. It is propelled by caterpillar treads. Over time, these specifications changed into any vehicle armed with a vulcan cannon and a cannon variant suited to the role of the vehicle, and propelled suitably for that vehicle's environment. In Metal Slug 6 (and the home version of Metal Slug X, 3, 4, 5), the playable character Tarma can lock the vulcan cannons into one position and fire continuously.
Metal Slug games typically have 6 levels. The exceptions are Metal Slug 3 and Metal Slug 5 which have 5 and Metal Slug 7 which has 7. In several of the arcade and console versions, the game would have the blood censored, showing white blood instead of red. However, there is a code to disable this censor.

Metal Slug is the classic arcade run and gun that has always hung its hat on its fantastic and over the top animations. If you've played one Metal Slug, you've played them all and they're all worth playing several times. This is the one that started them all and its a thirty minute joy ride for one or two players simultaneous. The Steam version has online multiplayer, but unless you bring along a friend, there's no one playing.
If there is a plot to the game, I'd say an evil dictator has conquered a land and you alone must liberate it, slaughtering hundreds of soldiers along the way. There's blood, guts, gore as you shoot enemies dead, in half or even light them on fire. Oh but its more than just troops you'll be wrecking, its a slew of vehicles like tanks, helicopters, bulldozers, metal walls, planes and various other metal monstrosities.
The game play is a bit sluggish, but that's the price you pay for such great animation. You can fire in four directions and crouch when shooting, but who needs that when you can just shoot enemies dead. To fire downward, you'll need to jump and this is the formula for some of the bosses, leap and fire down. If an enemy is next to you, then you'll knife them. Its a nice little detail. Other than your primary gun, you've got a limited supply of grenades. Metal Slug is a game about endurance, how long can you shoot for, because there's no auto fire outside of specific weapons.
Along the way, you'll rescue blonde cave men prisoners-of-war that will reward you with items worth points, extra ammunition and more importantly, weapons. There are a few weapons, but they all have a lot of impact. Flamethrowers will char soldiers. Shotguns will rip them in half. A heavy machine gun has a lot of firepower. Rockets will somewhat seek out enemies.
At least once per level, you'll get your own Metal Slug tank that diversifies the action. In this tank you have two turrets, one replaces your bomb and can only fire to the right. The other is a standard gun that swivels depending how long you hold the direction. Its unique and can take a lot of punishment. When the tank is about to explode it warns you to jump out or you'll die.
Oh but even if a tank doesn't get you, the enemy bullets will. They come in from all directions and while the first level is easy enough, the challenge ramps up accordingly. Soldiers will parachute in, jump in from water, run in to knife you.
This version of Metal Slug brings a modernization of achievements, video options and controls for keyboard or the 360 controller. I have a feeling that this is emulation rather than a true PC port, because the game will slow down just like the real Neo Geo version when appropriate.
While the game is tough, freeplay makes it forgiving and if you're looking for a challenge, there are four levels of difficulty. For anyone looking to have their name in fame, you'll find an online leader board.
So if you've played one Metal Slug, you've played them all, what makes this one different? This one is a straight up army action game before the series went too far over the top fighting snowmen, turning into zombies spitting blood and being frozen into a snowman. It also has one protagonist even if they all seem to play the same.
Other than that, there's just different level design. Later Metal Slugs let you chose different paths while this one puts you on a straight path headed for the boss. You'll trudge through city streets and see people running for their lives. Packs of dogs will run by. You'll crush parked cars in your tank. One level has you climbing an ice mountain. A building will collapse on you and you'll crawl out. Another level has you battling next to a cliff with tanks rolling over the edge to try and crush you.
I've mentioned the amazing animation, but the graphics in general are stellar. They have their own style that makes the game stand out from others in the genre. Its a blend of quirky, cartoon and realism. Its such a good style that the other Metal Slug games kept the graphics. The music and sound effects also do a lot to add to an already incredible game.
While there are better Metal Slugs out there, even the worst of the series is still far better than most games out there. Its worth playing for the first time or the one hundredth.

Prepare for an experience that strums (and maybe break) your heartstrings, with so many possibilities.  This game takes the basic fact of psychology that our brains don't like empty voids or logical gaps and would rather have an irrational explaination for something we don't understand.  For example, when you look at a connect the dots picture, normally you can see what it is before you even connect them.  It's how our minds work.  This game takes that premise and turns it on its head.
After playing this game, it really opened my eyes that, sometimes, although "helping people" feels great, isn't that selfish in it's own way?  Is it really possible for a person to be truly "selfless"?  We evolved as a social species, and this kind of experience really makes you think about the ramifications of a "well intended act".
This is a great alternative to your run-of-the-mill shooters.  Thought-provoking, deep, and insightful, I would highly recommend this game to anyone and everyone, although that in itself would be counterintutitive to the premise and purpose of the story, which we are only given a fraction of.  The rest is up to our irrational wanting to "bridge the gaps" and refuse the fact that sometimes...a rose is just a rose,

I loved The Stanley Parable and very much wanted to feel the same about The Beginner's Guide, but it just didn't do anything for me. Where TSP was immediately understandable to anyone who'd ever played a game, I don't feel that TBG's story is relatable to anyone who either isn't a content creator or who hasn't experienced a specific sort of anxiety. Most stories are capable of overcoming that boundary and still impacting people who can't personally related, but something about the narrative structure and abstract nature of TBG prevented that from happening. Though occasionally interesting, the plot can't support the game on its own.
Unfortunately, TBG has very little to stand on once its narrative fails. The game can barely be called that - most of the scenes consist of walking around hallyways and boxes with no opportunity for meaningful interaction or failure. What choices there are can be briefly interesting, but don't appear to change anything notable beyond the very short term. The exploration and experimentation that sustained TSP simply aren't here.
Recommended only either for $3 or less or (potentially) for people who've published work. Expect 60-100 minutes of playtime.

SUPERHOT- the game where time moves only when you do. Well, actually it's the game where time moves slightly slower than normal when you're not moving, but I guess that the former makes for a better tagline. The idea behind SUPERHOT would be a novel concept, indeed, if the game contained anything other than that (minus a Mario Party style minigame that you can play on the home menu for funsies.) For you see, the game seems to believe that the gimmick alone is enough to sell and be entertaining. Sadly, it is not.
To the game's credit, there were elements that I, personally, found enjoyable. The starting levels do a good job of showing off your character's capabilities and limits. This powerful opening is why you'll find more than your fair share of let's plays and first impression reviews of the game singing nothing but praises all over the internet. The environments are detailed and interactive, with the ability to pick up various props and hurl them toward your enemies to disarm and stun them. The physics have that classic video game-y (is that a real adjective?) feel to them, as killing people causes them to flail around helplessly as they swiftly become intimate new friends with the flooring. It doesn't take long for the tranquil stream of positives to be overflown with a torrent of negatives
To start off with, the story. I can see what the developers were trying to accomplish, with the commentary on video game culture. You play as an overweight, awkward, lonely gamer (that hit a little to close to home) who finds a popular new game that all the cool kids are playing. As he plays it, strange things begin to happen, as the game begins to harrass him through his computer. The setup is fine, albeit cliche, but my main gripe is through the presentation of the story. The game is told, through the most part through text conversations between you and your friend and an evil A.I. thing. In order to text them, you must mindlessly smash your keyboard as words show up on your computer (kind of like what I'm doing right now.) It doesn't take long for the gameplay to grow tedious, as weapons have little variety, enemies do little to no strategy other than to run at you, arms flailing, and there isn't any real variety to the levels, other than kill all the other guys or don't let the other guys kill you. Sometimes both. As I mentioned above, the whole tagline is that time only moves when you do, but as I also mentioned earlier, that is a bit of a lie. you could stand still to strategize the best way to dispach your foes, but if you do, don't be suprised if you get killed by a bullet from behind that you didn't see coming, because enemies don't make any noise other than the occasional gunshot or the dialogue I make up in my head ("Hey, Phil, did you check out that sporting event last thursday?" "We can continue this later, Ronald, I'm busy getting myself slashed in half by this guy.") Eventually, the game introduces a new function. By befriending the killer A.I., you get the power to switch bodies with your opponent, and cause your old head (to an extent, your opponent's head) to explode. While this can prove handy to get out of certain situations, you could always take the easier route and just shoot them. This brings me to my next point, shooting. For the beginning of the game, this was never a problem, but later on I got rather annoyed with the kickback of the guns. Due to the fact that time doesn't move very fast in this game, it takes around five to ten seconds to be able to fire again while standing still. It will take faster if you walk back and forth, but then enemies will have no trouble killing you. You end up having to stand there, waiting to shoot, gazing upon your opposer's fine, glassy features. The same goes for your enemy, but then an intense firefight just turns into a game of When Will I Shoot? as you constantly stop running toward your enemy to make sure that they aren't seconds away from making you significantly less alive than you were 3 seconds ago. All and all, after a while the game just starts to feel long and redundant, not unlike this paragraph.
Now, don't think that this game is a lost cause or anything like that. I believe that a few patches will do more than enought to turn this game into a fabulous first person shooter with a great mechanic, but at the moment, my advice is to hold tight and wait for the game to update, if the devs decide to. Which hopefully they will. Please?

We find ourselves with the third delivery of the Medieval Kingdom saga with a Reverie World Studios that surprises us, the purest strategy that you can imagine, manages cities, raises entire empires. A game that once again gives a lot to offer to the genre of strategy and that can undoubtedly revolutionize it if it is so desired. Will you serve the crown with honor or will you die like a simple pagan?
•As soon as we find this game in steam, we can see that it is available in a total of 6 languages, among which are the main ones spoken globally, which are English and Spanish.
The artwork that has the game is incredible, they have a great prolixity and are pleasing to the eye, because it has a very strong color palette and that sticks with the environment/theme of the time.
•To start the game the tutorial is more than good, and i will consider it a positive point because the topics that are explained within it are very well expressed, but there are many topics that are crucial for the game that has not yet been come to see in it (As the management of the economy on the map, diplomacy, among others).
•You can do things in so many different ways that you can not play an equal game 2 times so it seems more than correct that they have put 9 game slots. [Claps for this point].
•We find a total, incredibly, of 14 eligible factions to play. All the factions have an introduction and a different story that adapt them in their place of the time.
•The system of mechanics within the game can make us agree a lot to the Total War Series, but I have to say that the one in this title is much more complicated and challenging when it comes to learning. I say this both in the organization of the economy and in the management of battles.
•The system of improvements / technologies of the game is fantastic and innovative, as you progress in the game you will get different objects with which you can perform these investigations (The objects are usually given after a battle).
•The developers are constantly getting updates every 1 or 2 weeks, and best of all, they listen to what the community has to say in order to have a better game.
•The map editor is very complete and gives a lot of potential to people with experience to make thousands of maps of sieges or incredible battles.
•The game has very good hopes with the hierarchy system (Although it is not yet implemented), to serve your king until he is one of the best vassals he has, and who knows, until you can replace him.
•Its price is more than good, and I think it should be more expensive, and it makes up for it with all its content.
•The requirements you ask for to play it are not high and can be accessible to a large part of the public.
•The soundtrack is fantastic, you will feel all the time in a thirteenth century tavern with a bard who is about to recite his poetry.
•The system of construction or training of units is like a deck of cards that opens to you so that you can choose freely, it is something very simple but at the same time it is ingenious.
•The quality of the translations is good, but the problem is not quality but quantity. There are many lines of dialogue, texts or pictures that are not translated, and some of the texts that are not translated are fundamental parts that require greater understanding. An example of this is the technological or improvement branch. (All this I comment from the translation to Spanish).
•The HUD is quite annoying, although the vast majority of them can hide, we will always find something that hinders the gameplay.
•Some achievements are buged and even if you complete them in your game they will not appear.
•Most factions start with the same amounts and kinds of units, and with the same amount of gold. This can be understood because in the history of games we will always start as a noble so we can situate ourselves with the same situation in different places. (I will put it as a negative point until this is officially clarified).
•There is no faction that has special units of its kingdom, or that its units have a different clothes from the others. Where are the cataphracts or the warriors of the highlands wearing their kilts?
•There are no naval battles, the only battles available are on land.
•The policy almost does not exist in this game (I know that it is currently in development), a faction can attack you as if nothing and your "king" will not respond in any way for it.
•A very funny bug that I found and can give you a significant advantage over the enemy is that by clicking on a city that is not yours, you will "discover" at random a certain number of enemy troops. What happens is that by clicking on the city again, thanks to the random effect, we can see other troops that had not been shown previously because the game reveals troops randomly with each click. (I hope you could explain me well).
•In each game and regardless of what faction you are, the marshal and the administrator (which is on the bottom right) will be of the French nation.
•The lord of your city (you), like the lord of the city next to you (of the same faction), like that of the city at the other end of your empire, are all the same. There is only 1 representative character for each faction in the game.
•The texts that appear at the top of the screen are REALLY annoying, please do something to change them, move them or simply remove them. (Or at least more than the messages appear that have a relationship with the player)
•Sometimes it is very difficult to achieve what you want to touch, the hitbox of absolutely everything (even the buttons on the HUD) are wrong.
•Playing with the Holy Roman Empire or playing with England is experienced the same, there is nothing special that tells you and reminds you: I am playing with this or that.
•Something I do not really understand how a city like Paris has a fence instead of having real walls? It can happen in less developed cities or founded a short time ago but in Paris could have put at least a part that represented the wall of King Philippe Auguste. (Wall built in 1190)
•Speaking of something logical, you being kings would not seem strange that a man of his court begins to forcibly take the castles from all your other vassals?. I would consider him a rebel.
I could really continue to talk much more about the positive or negative points of the game but as this particular one has interested me I prefer to leave some suggestions to the developers:
•Improve the HUD considerably in some parts, as in the technology window that is "transparent", and easily gets confused with the background.
•Continue to work in the political system because the game is badly needed, or at least minimize the number of attacks you receive simultaneously from everyone.
•Have the possibility to fight naval battles.
•Put special units for each of the factions.
•That the Italian spear units are distinguished from the spear units of England. Not specifically these units or nations, generally in the game.
•The possibility of starting as a King, as a man with many lands or as a poor man.
•Put colors on top of the name of the cities according to who they belong to, in order to distinguish them more. For example: All cities in England with the box of the name in red.
•Make a tutorial that understands all aspects of the game.
•Continue reading the suggestions of the community and do not leave this project aside.
It's a title with a lot of potential and will certainly go in history as the beast that was difficult to master but in the end it surprised everyone. If it's on offer, you can't leave it.

This game showed promise, to be a interesting city survival management game with god elements.
However, in the latest designs and apparently in future plans, the developer has made it clear he is uninterested in maintaining any sort of lore. Personally telling me that "I never cared much about the lore". Meanwhile without the lore holding it together, I find the game vastly lacking. It is a it is a weak city builder, a weak tower defense and a weak god game. I played it because I found the idea of surviving in an apocalyptic world where you are most likely to die to be an interesting premise.
From filling the game with knock off names, from popular culture (Star Trek, Game of Thrones, and Celebrities), even stealing Elder Scrolls 'Catjeet' (Khajiit). Having magical beings that can somehow manage to survive the hordes of zombies, while you 'god' fail to direct your village to survival.
In the end, I find that this is a amateur game from an amateur programmer. In some ways it shows promise, but the lack of direction or focus from the game developer has lead to a scattered game design, and concept.

There are tons of reviews on this game already, but I have still decided to add my 2 cents into this pile of rapture. I agree that this game has an amazing atmosphere. Visuals, music, sound effects, voice acting - all of these are implemented amazingly. But I don't like to talk about positive aspects (especially because almost every review on steam extols this game to heaven), I would like to talk about drawbacks of this game.
First of all, story telling. I am not a fan of means to tell the story that this game uses. Namely, through documents/e-mails that you find during your adventure, although this method to tell the story is used in almost every horror game on the market. I don't like it because such documents are usually scattered in random order, and to understand what they mean you must find them all and read them after that in one particular order.
Second thing, that I think should be improved is gameplay itself. In this regard Outlast is a generic horror game - corridor, hide, run. All enemy encounters are almost the same. There are two types of them - there you must hide, and there you must run. I presume developers might diversify these parts of the game somehow.
So, let's conclude. This is a very, VERY good game, but still with some insignificant minuses, although nothing fatal. Highly recommended for all, who like GOOD HORROR games.
P.S. I know that "Red Barrels" are working on the second chapter. And if they manage to maintain all positive aspects of the game and get rid of negative ones, it will be almost perfect game. Time will tell.

This is a really, really _fun_ game to play.
Pros:
* Level design is whimsical and inventive.
* Music is really well done, and transitions between states is very smooth and intuitive.
* Combat is good, though the "double-jump then seek-attack" combo can be hard to get 100% of the time.
* Dying outside a boss fight is usually fairly forgiving.
* Boss fights are tough, w/o being impossible.
Cons:
* Levels are mostly platform-based, so lots of practice is required before you can do the trickier moves reliably.
* Game doesn't explain that many optional areas of the 1st zone's levels are inaccessible w/o hats obtained from further zones.
TL;DR: If you like whimsical level design and your reflexes aren't worse than mine (and mine suck), you should get it.

I don't normally review games but I have decided to review this one. First things first, this game is sad and unfullfilling. It felt like I was reading an interesting book, a deep thought driven journey that ends right before the characters resolve any of their issues. And that is what this game is, it's not really a game you play; although you play tons of little half done games. This game brought insight into the world of game development, as it follows half the journey of a game developer. Now it is written and narrated like the Stanley Parable, but it is far far far from the Stanley Parable. This felt like reading a personal narrative without someone's permission with an unrealiable narrator. I felt like I learned something, like I was moved by some of the conclusions the narrator comes too. I felt wrong playing these games, as if I was delving myself too deep into someone's world. I felt at some points that this game was meaningless, at others I felt as if it was a game everyone should expirience. And I left the game sad and confused, because this game hit home at the pain of reality, and it hits hard. It strains on themes of struggle, depression, the need for external validation, the game shows the pain in living. But the game only shows hope if you know where to find it, I would like to think I found hope to be a reocurring theme but I see why some didn't.
You think something, you're lead to believe certain things, that everything has a meaning, that there is this brokeness, even inherit pain, but what you find is that all of it is true and untrue. I honestly don't recommend buying tis game full price, wait till it is on sale or watch it on YouTube.
It is more of an expirience than a game, and the expirience betrays your trust, several ties over. I like those games, if you do too, than I suggest gettig it on sale.

Metal Slug is a classic NEO GEO game brought to the PC crow through steam, but will you want to play this game ?
Story wise the game forces you to take down the evil General Morden and his army. There's not much story to speak of as the game is a simple platform run and gun.
The gameplay is what really makes people love Metal Slug and the first game in the series is no exception. The game works almost perfectly. It's incredibly fun to run and just shoot everything in sight and see everything explode is just awesome.
The game is quite short, but there is a ton of replay value. It took me 40 minutes to finish the entire campaign, but I loved the game so much I went back and finished it two more times. There is also a online mode where you can play alongside your friends.
The game however has one slight issue and that is the game runs quite poorly. I noticed quite a few stutters while playing. Apart from that I didn't notice anything game breaking, but the stutter was  a surprise since the other two Metal Slug games on steam ran perfectly.
The game has the perfect difficulty setting for all sorts of players. Ranging from easy to flat out impossible. You want it the game has it.
I highly suggest giving Metal Slug a shot, it's one of the funnest games I have played in a while and I highly suggest playing it.
Final Rating:
8/10 - Worth Buying

Through our whole journey there is some narrating done by the creator himself. Which, in itself, is a pretty interesting idea, if you ask me. The thought process of a game developer.
But... seriously now.
The whole game does nothing else than just tell you the "story" of how depressed the creator is. And let me tell you all about why this is bull. I do not see why in the world would anyone spend YEARS making random games that are solely about the author having a deep hatred towards creating games. Like... why continue doing it, then? Especially while it's just your hobby (at the time of creating the old games) and not, like, a job. Also, those games even seem like made in 2015, for the purpose of this game, instead of being from 2009, 2010, etc. Either that, or the person who made them should get some mental treatment, and fast.
It's not even a game, really. There is LITEARLLY no choice, no options, just a straight-forward path of you walking from point A to point B to hear another line of narration. You'll get the exact same experience just watching a playthrough on YouTube. I also spent 80% of my time being bored to death, which qualifies to me as a terrible game design, regardless of whether there is or there is not some sudden twist in the end (there is not).
The game tries to be way too "artsy". It tries so hard to push some message through, but it's just not working. That's not how you make games, and neither interactive stories. And please, save all the "YOU ARE TOO CLOSE-MINDED TO UNDERSTAND IT" for yourself. All I'm doing is warning people not to waste their money.
I think it would be something cool to release on the developer's site for free, for those who were curious (if the story was even real), but not as a standalone game. Nope. I, too, expected The Stanley Parable 2 and avoided any information about the game to avoid any spoilers... oh well.
This is also my first negative review on Steam, so let that tell you something.

Like its predecessor, 'System Shock 2', 'Bioshock' is not a fluid experience. Whilst 'System Shock 2' is infamous for being an unforgiving and disorientatingly deep game, 'Bioshock' becomes too easy. It is possible to completely break the combat with the right combination of plasmids, tonics, and weapon upgrades (which are far too abundant). The game attempts to merge the 'Half-Life' shooting system with the roleplaying elements of 'System Shock 2' and sadly both styles do not mix. The 'Half-Life' model is intended to be balanced and dynamic, whilst adding customisation to this ruins that balance and narrows the players choice.
The 'moral choice' system remains pointless, since rescuing Little Sisters gives you plenty of Adam already. There is no need or reason to harvest them unless you get some sick pleasure out of seeing little children being evicerated - in which case, you deserve the awful ending you get for following that path. Not that the other ending is much better. In fact, the last section of the game is awful.
Which is a shame because whilst the gameplay is flawed, the story and enviroment are strong enough to warrant a reccomendation. The beautifully rendered enviroment tells a story in itself, and the audio logs add a welcome 'second layer' to the narrative. Just like its follow-up, 'Biosock Infinite', the best parts of the game are usually spent roaming the enviroment absorbing it all. The opening sequence may be one of the best in gaming (play the demo if you think I'm exaggerating) - which makes it all the more infuriating that the ending is such an ill-fitting anti-climax.

This could be an amazing td/rts but why do some developers still insist on using JRE? It's bloated, the garbage collection while revolutionary in 2002 is wonky at best and it handles memory usage in general, terribly because every interaction with the os is third hand.
The dev while I think he or she are/is awesome, pass this off as bloated AI but, after playing the game, I simply disagree. To qualify that statement just play Anno 1404 or even stronghold (a really old game) both of which were well ahead of their times' respectively in terms of graphics and AI, and the quality of the gaming experience are ones that still hold up today, despite their obvious vintage, and exhibit AI qualities I would consider to be far more rewarding and advanced than RtR.
I have played the game and I do not think the AI justifies the overheads, this is not dwarf fortress, you are asking me for money to fund your hobby in advance.
Furthermore, it seems to be plagued with identical issues in terms of performance Mincraft was a decade ago. Notch knew the JRE was limited, do you?
To cut a long story short, there are many other great platforms to launch this game on, many of which are free and offer significantly better performance so people like me can focus on the gameplay rather than the flaws, please look at them and stop romanticising about JAVA. Use it for JSP or SQL, it's a bad platform for anything other than old school motorola games or server side scripting, please.
Otherwise, good game.
And let me re-iterate. This is no joke, Java is simply a bad platform to make games with. You simply have to examine how sub-optimally it handles memory usage and uses handshakes with the kernel rather than native injection.
Again, it's a great game on a bad platform.
Raybarg, to answer your question fully, I do think this game has potential, but the developers choices force me to give it a negative review. "But why?", you may say. Well. I can appreciate the dev has built the AI from the ground up and to be quite frank, that's ambitious. But nothing alters the fact the capability of JRE will consistently be significantly lower than the developers expectations. It's like an invisible barrier the game will never overcome.
To put that into perspective play Witcher 3 for ten minutes. How amazing does that game look and how interactive and real does the AI feel? Do you think that level of depth is achievable on Java? I can tell you the answer, an the answer is NO.
"But we are talking about AI", you may argue. The developer has suggested the AI is more complex than the likes of Rimworld or Prison Architect but like I summarised, I simply disagree. The difference being Rimworld AI works beautifully, and triple speed doesn't stop a computer dead. I don't own an incapable computer and therefore I do not expect it to be brought to it's knees performing even the most rudimentary operations. But that is not because this is a BAD GAME, that is because the developer is using JAVA.

If you want an exercise in frustration, this is the game for you.
It's so well made as far as concept, interface and performance, but it's so picky with how you do things that its too irritating to recommend.
Everything is a balance, and if something goes wrong, even a little, hours of work goes down the tubes in a matter of moments. This wouldn't be a problem because a hard game can still be recommended, but how things go wrong is not obvious:
There's a delay in cause-and-effect, so any mistakes that are made just seem like random events at first. For instance,
if you need some more citizens, you build a home with redirected labour. But redirecting labour ends up stopping production of something else and that's enough to crash a population.
It's also not obvious where labour is going because the "gather resource" marker is always obstructed. Also, when looking at what a citizen is doing, the designers really needed to make "show paths" on instead of a second button click.
The biggest difficulty is that you're forced to design small towns so that citizens can get to resources. However, the UI bundles all your statistics into a global amount. And when disasters start to happen, it's always localised at first. A way to easily see the flow of different traffic would be great, as well as a "heat map" that would show how different towns are doing. Maybe even a mini-townhall that could show statistics about its area when it's in view.
So in the end, a game that at first seems like a creative town builder is really a puzzle game in disguise that has only 1 solution in mind.
So in it's vanilla form, I can't really recommend this. Perhaps some mods will help this game reach its full potential.

EA Review -
-Short-
If you want to support the game, I strongly recommend purchasing it; However, while it is a shining example of how a game should be developed, and is very promising (I cringe saying that word in any review), it is still lacking some core features at the moment (Diplomacy and Trading), that may temporarily make the game less appealing for those who want a more finished game.
- Long -
I usually am very critical of most EA games after getting burned over and over. This one however, I feel very happy about supporting. Instead of devs that act like gods lording over their peasant customers, these devs -actually- use the EA system as it was intended, engaging their customers, finding bugs and actually addressing them, and actually -are- working on their product in a rapid and efficient pace. This is obviously made by people who are gamers who love their craft, and not just businessmen.
As a huge fan of the Mount and Blade system, I found this to scratch a long waiting itch for another game even remotely similar, the game's system of building armies, conquering cities, building cities, and the continous RTS/RPG/grand strategy style is very satisfying for those interested in the genre. That being said though, I am -dying- for the diplomacy and trade systems to be implemented. That's what is really holding this game back from being great, but as I said, the devs are working rapidly and it's in the oven.
As for graphics, don't expect the best, to me it feels like the style of  artwork from the original Diablo (although more modern), the gritty dark textures and colors, which I feel are fitting due to the dark ages being a really crappy time to live in, it feels like the dark ages. The maps are pretty, but the characters are a bit blocky in design.
Pros -
Excellent replayability
Satisfying Grand Strategy Game
EA - Devs are a shining example of how to handle EA
Artwork - Gritty Gothic style art adds to immersion
Cons -
Graphics - Slightly dated, but I feel artwork makes up for it (This often intensional and I feel a good thing, as excellent graphics in large battles usually lead to massive framerate drops and crashing)
Unit Clunkyness - Right now, Archers sometimes decide to Leeroy Jenkins infantry (believe this is being worked on)
Diplomacy and Trade are not yet implemented.

This game makes me think of several really old games, such as Beasts & Bumpkins, Dungeon Keeper and a touch of Black & White.
It's a more intricate system in some ways and simler in some:
The resource management being pretty direct - Resource A, Refined Resource A, A-type products and as you go higher, resource B and refined resource B becomes involved.
Enemies have special attributes, some spread plague, others poison, some strike with fire and ice. Not overwhelming but making you look around to see what dangers are evolving.
The god-mode is the hardest part to get a grip on since all things are mana/energy based and it can be a tough ride getting enough to be as active as one is in direct god-simulators. It's not a focus, it's one of your tools in my opinion.
I find it an enjoyable experience to explore and there is a fair bit of content for an early access title - I'd say some might feel it's an instant miss, but most would likely need to try this out for 3-5 hours to really get a feel for the game since it's easy to be troubled at the start and then "AAAA-HAAAA! THIS works for ME!" My own restart #14 proved a lot easier than it's predeccesors since I finally figured out a way to balance monster presence taht suited my gameplay, for example.
Made for a rather rewarding experience.
Fingers crossed that dev will not tire anytime soon and keep adding to this game for many years to come, it feels like a diamond being processed.

Prepare to lose a lot when you start. Banished is a nice little village managing game that requires careful planning on the part of the player to avoid mass die-offs of the populace. It is enjoyable, especially for the price. However, the game suffers from two major maladies:
1. Before you attain all seeds and livestock and have a sizeable population, there comes a tipping point after which the game is no longer challenging. Early on, it is a struggle to get your people through the first few winters. You must manage  your villagers very carefully, since any misstep could result in total collapse of the village. Once you have some crops growing, a few hunting cabins and gatherers's huts, it is all but assured that your village will never fail. Severe mismanagement can still result in the deaths of large portions of your population, but only if you don't know what you're doing.
2. The game's mechanics tend to break down after you've gotten into the later stages of your community's development when your village has a large population and most of the seeds and livestock. For example, when you try to create multiple city centers on a large map, it is possible that the villagers will end up spending most of the day walking to their assigned job, causing massive inefficiency and probably resulting in a mass die-off of some sort.
Pretty fun, though.

Medieval Kingdom Wars has taken top priority on my gaming list in the last week since purchasing. While browsing through the Steam store, searching for my next gaming addiction, I came across the title which was in my price range and looked promising. After downloading and playing MKW for a few hours, I was pleasantly surprised. The tutorial gave me a clear understanding of managing the basic battle/ field economy functions, and after a few short tries on campaign mode, I mastered the art of each micro battle. I use the term micro not in the sense of small, but in the sense that there is a huge world out there, and each battle is a small piece of the larger pie. The pie, being Great Britain along with the rest of Europe to conquer, pillage, destroy, and govern.

What makes this game so enjoyable? First off, the realization of having all of Europe to dominate, and starting off in your small corner of the world with one town, is a feeling that there is much work that needs to be done. Each battle won is a step in having more citizens to tax, more resources to build armies, and an expanding Empire that grows ever daunting. While there is a huge world map bustling with lively feeling AI Lords with their own agendas, each battle that takes place feels like a traditional, well rounded, tower defense/ castle builder/ RTS. The individual battles are sparked by AI Lords attacking your territories/towns for conquest, or you attacking their territories/towns. There is a convenient auto-resolve button that bases win/loose on varying levels of armies, or you can spend anywhere between 15 min- 2+ hours duking it out the old fashion way.
The battles are centered around an easy to manage economy, and quickly pumping out mass numbers of soldiers/ siege weapons. Building barracks, archery range, production buildings, and the likes, is a no-nonsense process that maximizes your time to efficiently focus on the important fighting aspects. One feature which I’m particularly impressed with is after spending a set amount of resources, the walls/towers have a pre-set layout which constructs themselves. No need to micro manage your villagers on defense buildings while the enemy destroys you. The building structures also have pre-set tile layouts, which make organization and management of field economy hassle-free to keep up with. The serf/workers even auto-seek resources with a single command, without getting sidetracked and wandering off.
The developers frequently drop in and out of the game to answer any questions or comments the gamers may have. They are very friendly and attentive, which clearly shows how much love and care is being put into their project. As a traditional Age of Empires, Stronghold, Cossacks, series player, I am truly impressed. Reverie World Studios has taken the best of all worlds, and worked out the kinks to create a fresh and enjoyable medieval battle simulator. With the current price for Early Access, and the vast living virtual world, you cannot go wrong with Medieval Kingdom Wars.

The long dark is an engaging, convincing and challenging survival game that fills a niche I have been looking at for a long time. Not only is the interface intuitive, but the conditions and responses from the characters you can play as are releastic and interesting. There is a huge number of ways to die, which in my eyes is actually a good thing, including: freezing, starving, dying of thirst, being mauled to death by wolves, getting food poisoning, and injuries such as broken legs and sprained ankles are great at helping you along to one of these fates.
A few people call this game a walking simulator, but that definitely comes down to how you play the game. There are three 'difficulty' modes which affects the way the environment responds to you. If you choose the 'stalker' difficulty, you may find yourself reluctant to leave whatever shelter you may have come across, for fear of being attacked by a wolf, or freezing in the harsh winds at -30°C. However, on the 'pilgrim' setting weather is gentler, and animals actively try to run away from you. Personally, I would love to see another difficulty setting or a modular menu, so that I could have extreme weather and tame animals, or dangerous animals and gentle weather. The game is still in alpha and so I hope this will happen.
On a similar note, I have found the devs to be very productive so far in the creation of this game, I have witnessed changes that came as a result of community suggestions, and the changelogs are always very informative. Overall I am very happy with the current state of the game and must praise Hinterland for the work they have carried out. I am greatly looking forwards to future updates, and I am excited to play the complete game once it is released.

The true horror of Sunless Sea is the grind. It has several fun stories and strives for horror, but those make up maybe a tenth of what you will be doing in the game.
I want to love this game. It has lovely influences, and on rare occasion, lovely player-driven moments. I just wish it would focus on that. Instead, I suggest you keep a show or book handy during most of your playtime, and you should definitely abuse manual saves. I realized this far too late.
The writing is better than average for a videogame, but you shouldn't play this game for the writing. You'll spend most of your time watching a ship move at a glacial pace across the map on a leg of one of your necessary trade routes. Without money, you are very much at sea, and that will end poorly. So you'll grind. You'll find your preferred trade route, and move goods from one port to the next for a profit that might be grand in the real world, but isn't here.
As an additional note, the best stories come from making poor decisions. This makes sense to some degree (danger and insanity tend to make things a bit more thrilling), but suffering through these options often means you're already set for death. And then you start all over again and spend several hours getting to an actually interesting moment.

SUPERHOT- the game where time moves only when you do. Well, actually it's the game where time moves slightly slower than normal when you're not moving, but I guess that the former makes for a better tagline. The idea behind SUPERHOT would be a novel concept, indeed, if the game contained anything other than that (minus a Mario Party style minigame that you can play on the home menu for funsies.) For you see, the game seems to believe that the gimmick alone is enough to sell and be entertaining. Sadly, it is not.
To the game's credit, there were elements that I, personally, found enjoyable. The starting levels do a good job of showing off your character's capabilities and limits. This powerful opening is why you'll find more than your fair share of let's plays and first impression reviews of the game singing nothing but praises all over the internet. The environments are detailed and interactive, with the ability to pick up various props and hurl them toward your enemies to disarm and stun them. The physics have that classic video game-y (is that a real adjective?) feel to them, as killing people causes them to flail around helplessly as they swiftly become intimate new friends with the flooring. It doesn't take long for the tranquil stream of positives to be overflown with a torrent of negatives
To start off with, the story. I can see what the developers were trying to accomplish, with the commentary on video game culture. You play as an overweight, awkward, lonely gamer (that hit a little to close to home) who finds a popular new game that all the cool kids are playing. As he plays it, strange things begin to happen, as the game begins to harrass him through his computer. The setup is fine, albeit cliche, but my main gripe is through the presentation of the story. The game is told, through the most part through text conversations between you and your friend and an evil A.I. thing. In order to text them, you must mindlessly smash your keyboard as words show up on your computer (kind of like what I'm doing right now.) It doesn't take long for the gameplay to grow tedious, as weapons have little variety, enemies do little to no strategy other than to run at you, arms flailing, and there isn't any real variety to the levels, other than kill all the other guys or don't let the other guys kill you. Sometimes both. As I mentioned above, the whole tagline is that time only moves when you do, but as I also mentioned earlier, that is a bit of a lie. you could stand still to strategize the best way to dispach your foes, but if you do, don't be suprised if you get killed by a bullet from behind that you didn't see coming, because enemies don't make any noise other than the occasional gunshot or the dialogue I make up in my head ("Hey, Phil, did you check out that sporting event last thursday?" "We can continue this later, Ronald, I'm busy getting myself slashed in half by this guy.") Eventually, the game introduces a new function. By befriending the killer A.I., you get the power to switch bodies with your opponent, and cause your old head (to an extent, your opponent's head) to explode. While this can prove handy to get out of certain situations, you could always take the easier route and just shoot them. This brings me to my next point, shooting. For the beginning of the game, this was never a problem, but later on I got rather annoyed with the kickback of the guns. Due to the fact that time doesn't move very fast in this game, it takes around five to ten seconds to be able to fire again while standing still. It will take faster if you walk back and forth, but then enemies will have no trouble killing you. You end up having to stand there, waiting to shoot, gazing upon your opposer's fine, glassy features. The same goes for your enemy, but then an intense firefight just turns into a game of When Will I Shoot? as you constantly stop running toward your enemy to make sure that they aren't seconds away from making you significantly less alive than you were 3 seconds ago. All and all, after a while the game just starts to feel long and redundant, not unlike this paragraph.
Now, don't think that this game is a lost cause or anything like that. I believe that a few patches will do more than enought to turn this game into a fabulous first person shooter with a great mechanic, but at the moment, my advice is to hold tight and wait for the game to update, if the devs decide to. Which hopefully they will. Please?
