Usually a review is supposed to help people decide if they should buy this game. But most of the reviews I read are more like a movie review that is meant for people who watched the movie. So this will contain spoilers. Stop reading after "About the game" if you want to try the story with fresh eyes.
While "playing" I was very torn between recommend and not recommend. The ending made my decision easy though.
About the game:
The gameplay is nothing like the Stanley Parable if you wonder. In fact there is no gameplay. Yes you can play the little game sequences but the narrator will not let do much else. It is more like a movie where I have to keep "W" pressed so the movie continues. You choices (few there are) are meaningless. I think it is neither a game nor some showcase about game design...it is statement. See it as a movie where you can walk around the set.
Spoilers start here-----------------------------------
About the story:
I'd like to preface this with the fact that everything in this game might not be true. I could be a fantasy. But the narrator really tries to convey the notion that this is actually true and Coda exists or did exist. This of course opens Wreden (the dev) up to much critisism over his behaviour, which did influence my gaming experience quite a lot.
In the first few minutes I thought I knew what was going to happen. We will see a person (Coda) deteoriate through "playing" his games until he commits suicide (or at least tries). And this game is supposed to be like a monument and the admission that Wreden did not or could not help him.
This is not how it is going to end. Coda just cuts off contact with Wreden because he felt violated. Coda just made games for himself, Wreden thought he is in some dark place and tries to "help" him by showing his games to others. To get Coda some praise and feedback. He did that without his consent. Coda feels like Wreden is just projecting his own issues onto him and his games. Coda made games like others write diaries. For himself. That is why he breaks off contact. Wreden instead makes the "Beginners Guide" to somehow apologize and try to reconnect with Coda. And he does exactly what Coda does not want him to do.
This is a very ♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing to do. After playing it I felt like I had invaded someones deepest private thoughts. Stuff other people might tell their therapists. I felt disgusted because Coda clearly wanted to keep these games for himself. It is like Wreden was reading his diary on Youtube.
I feel like I just had to sit trough 90mins of someone rationalizing an act (well two) he feels guilty about. I am not a therapist. I don't usually enjoy this. With friends I will listen and try get to the bottom of there arguments and feelings or I just tell them to stop. Or I tell them I disagree. But here you can not. You have to listen and thats it. Wreden can feel good about himself and his public apology...we can't even say no or not accept it or probe his arguments further. Well we can write reviews.
Wether or not the story is true. I feel like I was convinced to do something wrong. If this story is true. My moral disgust outweighs any artistic merit. If the story is fantasy, why? Do I as a gamer really need to replay a morally wrong act. We all done bad things. No I think this is story is real or Wreden at least wants us to feel like it is real. Then I am back with moral disgust.
Do not get me wrong. Some of the games and narrators interpretation are emotionally quite powerful but after the end, I feel like I should not have done it. Have you ever snooped on someone elses phone and felt kinda dirty afterwards? Thats how I feel and I am angry that Wreden made me do it. The narrator will mislead you.

Lots of people giving this game Negative reviews are giving it from the fact it has an extremely short campaign. Yes it is 2 hours long to complete, and some think its rubbish, but after putting time into the game, looking for all the secrets, going through every single additional content there is, I can say that 2 hours of playtime is not even close to finishing the game.
The campaign is short yet really clever, you can't say much in reviews for it without going into spoilers, but I'll just put it there that is very mysterious, and the fact they made a campaign that plays really well for this type of game is really something worth praising. There are also secrets in most levels, all which give you little messages and questions with more questions. Some of the extra content really puts thought onto these questions.
The part where most negative reviews is from the campaign, believe it or not though, there is more content, you need to finish the campaign to unlock it. The two main are "Challenges" which gives Speedrun challenges, a certain weapon only challenge or even a AD2013 challenge which plays the game out again except in the form of the 2013 version of the game. The 2nd is my favorite which is "Endless", and it is what it is said, just endless waves of enemies, its really fun and some how addicting even though all you are doing is shooting Red guys over and over, and that is what makes the game so great, is its simplicity mixed with some innovative ideas.
The other additional content is nice, you get some ASCII art and videos, a made up chat room which is really funny to watch for the 15 minutes it goes on for before it repeats, a Timberman game which is just Timberman with ASCII code as its art style and some other little extras.
Now saying all these positives there are something this game really needs. Yes after a while you will get bored and sadly the maps, though great aren't really enough of them, there are only 9 endless maps, which aren't too big, this is where a massive requirement of Workshop support comes in, it really needs it to keep its community alive.
Another negative is the fact there is no Leaderboard in Endless mode, I really want to share my top scores against other players, and there is KILLSTAGRAM (which is technically SUPERHOT's own Instragram which is quite nice :D) but I think an actual in-game leaderboard would be a bit better alongside KILLSTAGRAM.
Luckily for all these negatives the developer has promised that they will be constantly adding new content in the future, and they have been really good with communicating with the community, for instance they did recently add Trading Cards due to the community really wanting the addition of it, and they have said that STEAM Workshop support should hopefully happen soon.
All in all I really do recommend this game, yes the asking price of £18/$25 can look a little bit over the top for the insanely short campaign, but with all the additional content and a developer constantly adding new content, with the game also being very innovating, it really does feel fair.
TL;DR
+ Really Innovativing Idea.
+ Lots of additional content.
+ Really addicting for such a simple idea.
+ Developers adding content and listening to community.
+ You can feel like Neo from The Matrix now :D
+ Lovely Art Style for both in-game and the art.
+ Short but superb story.
/ No Leaderboards :(
/ Lack of STEAM Workshop support.
- Price feels a bit steep if you are not into Endless and Challenges.
Overall - 9/10

I played this game for around 13 hours before writing this review.
The game is comprised of three parts. The most obvious one is Base Building. You have your villagers, they gather resources, build buildings, defend themselves against monsters and have their own set of needs and demands that must be met. This part closely resembles RimWorld, with the difference that you have no information whatsoever how everything works. Rise to Ruins seems like a game that wants players to sink their teeth into numbers, try build orders and ressource assignments, fail miserably and do better the next time around. Resources are stone, wood, and crystals, food and water all renewable in one way or another. You can dig yourself into mountains, assign prioorities to buildings and establish work orders. I can't stress the resemblance with RimWorld enough here. But compared to that, everything seems simpler, less polished. Of course I played Rise to Ruins in Alpha. It's difficult to establish several bases and explore the map, not because of the threat of monster attacks, but because it takes villagers forever to do just about anything. The AI isn't perfect yet either, with some of your villagers just standing around confused sometimes, eventually dying of hunger or thirst.
The second part is Tower Defense. Villagers probably aren't meant to hold up against hordes of monsters on their own, just now (Alpha) there are almost as much towers to choose from than any other building. Again, as of now, you have no wiki, no statistics. Yout don't know if it's better to build a more expensive tower or upgrade the cheap one you build already. Heck, you don't even know how the pathfinding of monsters work. Do they attack walls, or do they follow your "maze" ( I haven't gotten to the point where I could have built an actual TD maze yet)? It's for you to find out.
The third part is a kind of God Simulation. Those of us who remember Black & White won't fail to see the simliraties. Almost everything in the world can be turned into magic power that can be used to fuel magic towers, grow your crops or damage the monsters. I have to point out that this part especially isn't balanced out yet. At all. You can basically force grab all mosters on the map and turn them into even more mana in a big cooking pot. On the other hand, there are four offensive spells which all do about the same amount of damage/mana but neither of them is worth it.
What do I think about this game? It looks very promising. The think-try-fail-rethink concept already works. Too little information, inconvienient controls and (sometimes) seemingly unbalanced gameplay are an issue. For a game like this, those things are exactly what defines it's playability and long-term motivation. Rise to Ruins offers TD meets RimWorld meets Black & White. The combination has a lot of potential to make for a great game. Let's see if the developers can deliver.

I've been eagerly awaiting Studio MDHR's Cuphead for quite a long time and it's finally here.  It isn't every day a run and gun comes out, much less one with a cool jazz/ragtime/band soundtrack and retro cartoon animation art style.  While it didn't turn out to be exactly what I expected, it's a solid game and a welcome addition to the genre.
The story is simple.  Cuphead and Mugman lose a bet with the devil and the price is their souls.  They beg for their lives and the devil says he may pardon them if they collect other souls for him.  The remainder of the game is spent working as the devil's debt collector.  As one might imagine, the debtors put up a fight when confronted.
The vast majority of stages in the game consist of boss battles.  Bosses generally have a few attacks for each phase of their fights.  Which attacks they use seems to be based on RNG, but they're all possible to dodge once you've learned the patterns.  Cuphead has the ability to shoot, swap weapons, parry pink objects/projectiles, dash, and use a special attack.  The special attack charges while doing damage and performing successful parries.  Using special attacks, parrying, and avoiding damage will earn you points towards a higher letter grade in each stage.  Some of the boss fights are done in a horizontal shmup style.  Cuphead flies an airplane during those fights and his abilities vary somewhat.  In addition to the standard boss stages there are also some platforming stages.  I had expected there to be more of these, and that they would be smoothly intertwined with boss fights.  They are standalone and optional, but happen to be the primary source of in game currency.  Coins can be used to buy alternate attacks and passive abilities.  Out of a self imposed challenge I went through my first playthrough without buying anything, so I can confirm that you really don't need any items other than the default pea shooter.
Things will probably be a bit easier if you do decide to buy items.  There are a handful of alternate weapons including a short range spread, homing shots, charge shots, and bouncing shots.  The passive abilities are useful as well, especially the ones that grant automatic special recharging and brief invincibility while dashing.  A total of two weapons, one passive, and one special attack can be equipped at any given time.  Selected items can only be changed on the overworld/map screen.  There is also a menu that displays grades for each boss fight/stage which is convenient.
While there are many positive things to say about Cuphead, there are a small number of negatives as well. An astounding amount of work must have been put into the game's visual style, but sadly there were a few moments where I felt that some of the details ended up being a hindrance.  Specifically, there were times when objects in the foreground obscured the play area making it unnecessarily difficult to dodge some attacks.  There is also one attack that I can consistently avoid, but I'm doing it completely based off of memorized timing and still have no idea what it is I'm dodging.  Who knows, maybe it's just a lack of observational skills on my part.  Other than that, I also found myself feeling that the post special attack invincibility could have been a little more generous.  If you don't carefully time special attacks it's easy to put yourself in a situation where you'll almost certainly take damage when the animation finishes.
Overall Cuphead is great.  While it doesn't do anything particularly innovative in the gameplay department, it stays true to its genre.  That said, Cuphead is completely groundbreaking in the presentation department.  I don't think I've seen a game of this style look or sound so good since the Metal Slug series.  The run and gun genre is old and sadly doesn't see many new releases.  I hope Cuphead inspires people to make more games of this style.  It took me a little less than nine hours to complete the game on “regular” difficulty with “A” ranks in every stage and about three more hours to complete the game again on "expert" difficulty.  Players that don't care to strive for better ranks or play on higher difficulty levels may feel the game is short.  I found the amount of content to be fine considering most classic run and guns can be completed in 30-45 minutes by a skilled player.  I'd definitely recommend Cuphead, especially to people that enjoy Contra, Gunstar Heroes, and Metal Slug.

The writing is better than average for a videogame, but you shouldn't play this game for the writing. You'll spend most of your time watching a ship move at a glacial pace across the map on a leg of one of your necessary trade routes. Without money, you are very much at sea, and that will end poorly. So you'll grind. You'll find your preferred trade route, and move goods from one port to the next for a profit that might be grand in the real world, but isn't here.
As an additional note, the best stories come from making poor decisions. This makes sense to some degree (danger and insanity tend to make things a bit more thrilling), but suffering through these options often means you're already set for death. And then you start all over again and spend several hours getting to an actually interesting moment.

This is a bit of a challenging review to write.  While I love the concept behind Sunless Sea a lot, and it definitely nails it when it comes to tone and atmosphere, but the game itself has some fundamental flaws that erode its fun factor a lot.
The good: Graphically, it is a rather beautiful game, depicting its underground sea in an almost painterly way.  It captures the rich, dark, almost Lovecraftian tone of it's world perfectly; and the artwork it uses to represent the characters and creatures populating that world are great too.  It's writing its fantastic, fo rthe most part, and make me wish there was a straightup novel I could buy that would let me dive more deeply into its mythos.  The gameplay itself is a rather simple top-down view of your ship, but it is effective, fun, and evocative of older sailing titles from the 90's like Sid Meyer's Pirates.
The bad: The game is designed around perma-death, and while that is actually a feature that drew me to the title in the first place, it doesn't really work here.  You are going to die... a lot... and unless you managed to advance to the point in the game where you can pass things along to an heir, which is NOT an easy task, that means you have to start all over again.  By the fifth or sixth attempt, it grows really repetitive to have to re-find the same officers, have the same conversations, re-encounter at the same obstacles at the same ports, and re-read the same blocks of text (no matter how brilliantly written).  In the end, after my ninth captain went down with his beautiful customized ship, I just didn't have it in me to start in a crappy little boat all over again.
The bottom line: I'm still recommending you buy this game, if you can get it on sale, so that you can experience the good stuff it does have to offer... but be aware that it does have some flaws that will become increasingly hard to overlook.  3 out of 5.

As an Early Access game perspective, some pros include; frequent development updates, accessible developers and developer communication, nice graphics and a long game campaign. Some cons of Early Access include; the occasional graphic glitch, some awkward/not the most straight forward tech tree (at this point 40% of the tech tree research options are still locked owing to EA) and not the best/complete tutorial. A safe bet in my books if ever there was one.

Going into A Hat in Time I honestly wasn't too sure what to expect, I had heard comparisons to everything from Super Mario Sunshine, to Yooka-Laylee and Banjo Kazooie and everything in between. The only thing I knew I'd be getting was a platformer from a kickstarted indie developer.
With that being said A Hat in Time has surpassed all of my expectations and has been one of the few new games I've not only purchased in recent years, but enjoyed enough to want more, and more.
This review will discuss aspects of the story, characters, levels, etc. and thus will contain mild spoilers. If you've watched trailers and/or played the Beta none of this should come as a surprise, but nontheless here is your obligatory:
- MILD SPOILER WARNING -
The Story: (everything discussed is seen in the trailer)
A Hat in Time is about a young girl (Hat Girl) trying to find her way home. Suddenly while in orbit above "Mafia Town" a member of the Mafia breaks his way into Hat Girl's starship in an attempt to force her to pay a tax. While rather simplistic and certainly a callback to other popular platformers' style of handling story such as the Super Mario series this direction also feels fresh and charming.
With such a simple goal as 'get your Time Pieces back so you can go home' A Hat in Time really frees the player to have as open-ended of an adventure on the planet as they want in the meantime.
As is customary with games in this genre though, there isn't much to talk about here. Story is never the selling point of games in this genre and A Hat in Time focusing on letting you make your own story out of what they've provided should only encourage gamers to pick it up.
Characters:
It's no surprise to anyone that's watched the trailers or played the Beta that Gears for Breakfast has gone out of their way to make likeable, and very memorable characters for their game.
- If you're one of the people that hasn't watched trailers or seen anything, let me assure you, they're fantastic -
The protagonist, Hat Girl, is "heckin'-cute", or adorable as I'd simply put it and helps give the game a very unique charm. Other minor characters such as the Mafia are given just as much attention and they really help make the areas you explore feel alive. This is a great improvement off of other titles in the genre which just feel like you're jumping across random platforms suspended in space (like many newer Mario titles would have you do).
I won't give a breakdown of each character, as I'd like to keep spoilers to a minimum, but I can assure you there is plenty of charm hidden in this gem of a game.
Levels:
Here I'll mostly discuss what the levels bring to the table as I'm not quite qualified to speak on behalf of level design (although I did enjoy how they were all layed out). So here goes:
A Hat in Time is broken up into five 'Chapters', each Chapter being a different portion of the planet your starship is in orbit above. Chapter 1, Mafia Town is a large town built on a tropical island paradise.  Chapter 2, Battle of the Birds takes place within a film studio (and movie sets). Chapter 3, The Subcon Forest is (as you'd guess) set within a forest. Chapter 4, Alpine Skyline is a very beautiful level set atop lofty mountain peaks (and totally open to free roaming might I add). Chapter 5 I will leave as a surprise, mostly because I didn't expect it to be anything like it was and I'd like to allow you a similar opportunity to be surprised.
Overall, I have no idea if any of this would help someone to pick up the game, but these are my thoughts on these three aspects of the game after beating it. I haven't 100%'d the game as of yet, at the time of writing I've beaten the game with the minimum of 26 time pieces (with 40 total to collect in the game - although I hear there's also rumors of free DLC going around, I'll have to look into that), so I may come back to edit this if my opinion on anything changes between now and when I 100% finish. Throughout my playthrough I was graced with wonderful platforming that was not too challenging (even with a keyboard and mouse - no controller needed here folks!), a good difficulty that straddled the line between easy and hard, never too easy but challenging at times, and a wonderful overall experience. A Hat in Time is the kind of game I used to expect from 'AAA' companies before they became consumed by greed and I wish the best to Gears for Breakfast. I genuinely enjoyed A Hat in Time and I will more than likely continue to for a long time. From what I've heard the game is also open to modders so I likely won't get bored of this title for quite a long time.
After all is said and done my final rating is:
(Minimum % rating): 10/10
Now that I have finished I can say that I stand behind my initial rating: 10/10.
I hope this review helped you!

This game is really, truly, great.
Despite still being in development, it feels (and looks) more polished than many games that are fully released. It has an excellent atmosphere, including wonderfully stylized art, and highly detailed range of environmental sounds. When the light is fading and the wind starts howling, I feel cold, even in my hot summery apartment.
There is an element of luck to the game with randomized item spawns, and an unfortunate tendency (in gameplay) towards taking the same, safe path every play through. For example, it is really REALLY hard not to set up shop in the farm house every time, because it is so disproportionately advantageous to do so. That said, it is also quite fun to deliberate roam and range.
As the crafting system grows, this game will improve even more. As it stands the crafting system is fun, but very slow (getting and curing that many guts takes just... ages), and quite small.
I'm greatly looking forward to the Story Mode, and all the other additions and updates I'm hoping they include as development continues.
Overall? I can say this: even if this game weren't in development and getting better as time passes, I would still feel confident and happy in paying the $20 for it as it stands.

This game is a piece of art. Its hauntingly sparse greyscale-and-silhouette landscape, and corresponding minimalist soundtrack, evoke an unending and inescapable dream world... one with plenty of nightmare elements as giant spiders, bear traps, savagely hostile others, giant saws, deep water, machine guns, zombifying brain worms, and the ever-present dark compete to kill you. Despite the game's stately-slow pace, it is capable of making your heart pound as you suddenly and unexpectedly find yourself in mortal danger. It's not without a light side, as the death animations—impeccably rendered according to a detailed 2D physics model—are often able to make you chuckle despite the gruesome end you just met.
Controls are dead simple, limited to running, jumping, swinging on ropes, and pushing and pulling objects. Puzzles are neither easy nor insanely difficult, and are offered in a no-explanation, learn-by-dying fashion. The game's secrets (literally eggs) and limited-death-run achievements offer some replay value (a full run of the game takes about 40 minutes if you're familiar with the puzzles). Mostly, this game is just about the experience of LIMBO... and it delivers incredibly.

To start it off, if you know nothing about this game, and were brought to the Steam Page off the recommendation from a friend or the internet, I highly recommend you stop reading here and just go experience it for yourself. (Remainder is Spoiler Free, but this really is best done blind).
That being said, The Beginners Guide is an interesting game. I almost don’t even want to call it game, because the interaction with the environment is so limited. For the most part you’re just moving from area to area with expository narration from the games developer, Davey Wrenden. His voice work is adequate for the most part, however at times he comes across as board or uninterested. It pays off in the more dramatic moments. There are brief moments where you can select dialogue trees, however you don’t really seem to have any choice or feedback in the results. In the end what you’re left with is something between a movie, a video game, and someone telling you a story. If you’re looking for deep or immersive gameplay, you’re not going to find it here, but if you’re interested in a story (one that hasn’t really been told before), then you should check this out.
Now whether or not you agree with this message of this story I can’t guarantee. Wrenden can come across as extremely pretentious, obnoxious, and self-righteous (and yes, at times that is obviously the intention, however it branches beyond those times). I’m not even sure I agree with it yet. What I can guarantee is that playing through this will elicit a strong emotional reaction, be it anger, sadness, confusion etc. The ending is not a happy one that ties everything up, but will leave you thinking. That emotional elicitation, and that thought, I believe is well worth the admission.
Speaking in terms of value, the game takes about 90 minutes to go through. Repeat playthroughs can be done (I’ve done it with friends, which opens up some discussion) which can change the experience per say, but the game proper will be entirely the same each time. This isn’t The Stanley Parable (for better or for worse). After some time passes I’ll probably do a third playthrough to re-evaluate my thoughts.
In short, I can easily recommend that if you’re even thinking about playing this game, you should do it, and make sure to play it all the way through. Whether you love or hate it, you aren’t going to forget it.

Metal Slug is a rarity. This is one of those once-in-a-forever franchises that'll never be duplicated, perfectly cloned, or perhaps even improved upon. To accurately explain just how unique this series is, I have to start with Nazca Corporation. As you might already know, Nazca developed the first four* Metal Slug games. Before they started work on the Neo Geo, they were originally a part of Irem.
A number of Irem titles have a unique style of pixel-graphics. Aside from making for highly-detailed sprites, backgrounds, and effects, this technique allows for a lot of manipulation. So when you see a wall crumble, a ship explode, or an enemy get torn to ribbons, you can actually see the pixels pull away from each other. It's difficult to describe, but it looks incredible in motion and lends a lot of flavor to the action. Some examples that immediately come to mind are
,
, and
aka
.
Metal Slug is a showcase for Nazca's pixel-wizardry. Not only does each stage look incredible, but the game goes above and beyond in terms of personality. Every character in the game is loaded with animations and creativity, most notably the enemy soldier. This is the most common foe in the series, and Nazca put more effort into making these adversaries more memorable than entire games. These games also perfectly blend humor and violence, At no point does the tone ever shift to a point where the player starts feeling uncomfortable. Although, the designers do know when to play around with emotions, such as when a destroyed enemy helicopter drops a letter. Sure it's just bonus points to you, but for that soldier, it was probably a letter from a loved-one. It was still sealed, so maybe he was going to read it after the battle.
All of this would be irrelevant if the actual games weren't any good. Needless to say, this isn't the case. Metal Slug is a master-class in Run & Gun game-design. The controls are loose enough so that you can freely rush through enemy territory, but they're also subdued and accurate for when you need to prioritize survival over everything. Like most other shooters, the heroes of MS die in one hit. Being able to shift between situations of wildly varying intensity is massively important. Nazca accomplishes this goal via one running speed, mid-air controllable jumps, grenades, and the ability to shoot in multiple directions. In these games (aside from later post-Nazca entries) there aren't any special moves like slides, dodge-rolls, or parries. You have to read every moment, consider every possibility, and make the movements that keep you out of danger.
The phrase "doing a lot with very little" is one I just love to throw around, and it definitely applies to Metal Slug 1. This is a short game, and it doesn't have the enemy and stage variety of its sequels. However, this game has enough presence of mind to play with ideas, employ the same foes in different fashion, and create moments that remain exciting even on replays. The tight mechanices and game-design allow you plenty of room to focus on improving. Every time you die, you'll know exactly how it happened, and you can quickly mull over where it all went wrong, in the brief seconds before your next life appears on-screen.
Metal Slug also establishes a lot of the rules of the series. Not only do the heroes die in a single hit, but there aren't any extra lives. In fact, since all POWs are lost upon death, you pretty much have to adopt a "1-life" mindset if you're playing for score. In arcade games, we tend to look at lives as resources. I know when I reach the final boss of a 2D shooter, I do an inventory of all of the lives & bombs in-stock. I know what I can afford to expend, in order to guarantee that clear. This approach simply doesn't work for Metal Slug. These three lives represent three chances, you have to protect them...well..like they're your own. Obviously that's extremely difficult due to the armies you have to contend with, but over-time you work everything out.
Honestly though, even if you approach this series with the mindset of "I don't want to worry about 1CCs, 1LCs, or any of that other stuff" you can still have a lot of fun. The moment-to-moment combat is just so visceral it's a reward in itself when heavy-machinegun fire chews through half a dozen soldiers, or a shotgun blast rends a tank into nothingness. Simply playing these games, without a specific goal in mind, is just flat-out glorious entertainment.
While it's easy to say that the sequels are better, there's a level of simplicity and charm that absolutely fits Metal Slug 1. Feel free to revisit it whenever you have the opportunity. Oh but just one thing, while I have all the praise in the world for these games, I don't have anything nice to say about Dotemu.
*I count Metal Slug X as a separate entry.

A Hat in Time is fantastic! The game consists of different worlds, similar to Mario 64 or Mario Sunshine. Each world is entirely unique. The main goal of the game is to collect time pieces (stars). Along the way you will meet a colorful cast of characters, discover new game mechanics, and collect different hats which give you different abilities.
The platforming is the main focus of this game and when it works, it shines. Sometimes I do feel like I have to fight with it a bit though.
The game is a little short as well, however, what it lacks in quantity, it makes up for in quality. Every single goal and world is wonderfully crafted. The plot and subplots are easy to follow but are interesting enough to stay invested.
A Hat in Time hammers hard on the nostalgia, but it still seems new. While other 3D platformers seem to lack ingenuity, A Hat in Time is exploding at the seems with great fresh content.
I give A Hat in Time 8/10.

WaveLand is a game based on Super Smash Bros. Melee's game exploit known as wavedashing. In this game, you wavedash,the act of dodging towards the ground and then gaining momentum from it. It is your main method of movement. In this game, you will also come across wall jumping as an ability and a shine-stall, which lets you stall in the air and reflect projectiles. The game can prove to be very challenging and have extremely tight situations. My biggest gripe with the game is how it handles time. If you fail to beat a level in a certain amount of time, you will be unable to progress to the Nightmare levels which are required to beat the game. This does make it quite annoying to progress but overall, it can be done eventually.
Overall, the game is good and I'd recommend to people who enjoy quick but difficult games like Super Meat Boy.

This game is simply amazing.
Once you get past figuring out what the hell you're looking at, it opens up much more to do.
The main purpose is to build and expand on your village while fending off monsters. All while doing this, managing your resources and trying to defend adds the extra spice to this game. The progression in this game is not boring, and the amount of options you have when building is great. The whole thing with essence too makes the game so much better. It allows you to change the weather, help the village with gathering resources, using magic, etc. I also like how there is a limit so you have to strategize on how to use it efficiently (as with everything else in the game).
On top of this...
-The developer is very open to the community and works a lot on this. You can tell how much effort is put in just by seeing how much interaction the developer has with the community.
-The music is well picked/made, and is not really annoying.
-The pixel graphics are satisfying.
-The timing on everything syncs well and captures you back into the game. This allows you to enjoy the game more, without stuff getting too stale too soon.
As for the cons, the UI can be pretty intimidating at the start and may make you want to back out-as it did with me, but don't let it scare you away. As I said earlier in the review, once you figure out what you're looking at, you realize the potential to everything in the game.
There's much more to add and I'm looking forward to it, and I'd say that my money was well spent on a game like this.

This is a recreation of the turn based sports board game. After a couple of years worth of patches this feels more complete. The main draw is the multiplayer mode which has strategic depth on and off the field but is exceptionally unforgiving. It is harder to recommend for offline play so maybe when on sale if you have no interest in playing online.
The game suffered criticism at launch for having far less content than the original Blood Bowl game. If you are a fan of Games Workshop you will know that they are in the business of flogging DLC whenever possible. Obviously it would be better if they didn’t but it is the reality. However I think the base game is good enough value without any extras. It has a good selection of competitive teams. They are missing an undead team, out of the box, as well as the more unusual teams so if you know you want to play with one of these it will cost extra. A try before you buy mode would have been welcome.
For newcomers the game has a 16 hour single player campaign with a human team which was enjoyable with it’s tongue in cheek look into the world of sport in the ultra violent Warhammer universe. However it doesn’t teach much beyond the basics of the game and the AI doesn’t play well. Off the field you level up your players with a pool of 40+ skills that you will want to memorise to play competitively. This offers surprising tactical depth but the game doesn’t really cover the main strategies or why they work.
The design and UI is much improved from the first game. There is a need for a lot of information and it could always be clearer for the more complicated rules. The graphics are really nice and benefit a lot from the great Warhammer style.
This was designed as a board game and it plays very differently from modern multiplayer games. It is slow paced, games can last an hour or more and you have no interaction during your opponent’s turn. Everything is based on dice rolls and you will be rolling a lot so expect bad luck at almost every turn. This is fine playing at a table, having a laugh at misfortune with your friend, but can make for frustrating competitive play. Many of the teams are based on bashing to injure the opponents players which can lead to really unfair games if a team clears 3+ players or boring slugfests where you both try to gain a player advantage. Most teams have very optimised build orders which make some skills, players and teams feel underpowered. Passing is hard on all beginner teams and is never guaranteed. Despite these flaws you will have to make many tactical decisions which can make for really exciting moments and stories.
There is nothing quite like it in the niche of competitive turn based sports strategy games but don’t expect a quick or easy multiplayer game.

Metal Slug is a rarity. This is one of those once-in-a-forever franchises that'll never be duplicated, perfectly cloned, or perhaps even improved upon. To accurately explain just how unique this series is, I have to start with Nazca Corporation. As you might already know, Nazca developed the first four* Metal Slug games. Before they started work on the Neo Geo, they were originally a part of Irem.
A number of Irem titles have a unique style of pixel-graphics. Aside from making for highly-detailed sprites, backgrounds, and effects, this technique allows for a lot of manipulation. So when you see a wall crumble, a ship explode, or an enemy get torn to ribbons, you can actually see the pixels pull away from each other. It's difficult to describe, but it looks incredible in motion and lends a lot of flavor to the action. Some examples that immediately come to mind are
,
, and
aka
.
Metal Slug is a showcase for Nazca's pixel-wizardry. Not only does each stage look incredible, but the game goes above and beyond in terms of personality. Every character in the game is loaded with animations and creativity, most notably the enemy soldier. This is the most common foe in the series, and Nazca put more effort into making these adversaries more memorable than entire games. These games also perfectly blend humor and violence, At no point does the tone ever shift to a point where the player starts feeling uncomfortable. Although, the designers do know when to play around with emotions, such as when a destroyed enemy helicopter drops a letter. Sure it's just bonus points to you, but for that soldier, it was probably a letter from a loved-one. It was still sealed, so maybe he was going to read it after the battle.
All of this would be irrelevant if the actual games weren't any good. Needless to say, this isn't the case. Metal Slug is a master-class in Run & Gun game-design. The controls are loose enough so that you can freely rush through enemy territory, but they're also subdued and accurate for when you need to prioritize survival over everything. Like most other shooters, the heroes of MS die in one hit. Being able to shift between situations of wildly varying intensity is massively important. Nazca accomplishes this goal via one running speed, mid-air controllable jumps, grenades, and the ability to shoot in multiple directions. In these games (aside from later post-Nazca entries) there aren't any special moves like slides, dodge-rolls, or parries. You have to read every moment, consider every possibility, and make the movements that keep you out of danger.
The phrase "doing a lot with very little" is one I just love to throw around, and it definitely applies to Metal Slug 1. This is a short game, and it doesn't have the enemy and stage variety of its sequels. However, this game has enough presence of mind to play with ideas, employ the same foes in different fashion, and create moments that remain exciting even on replays. The tight mechanices and game-design allow you plenty of room to focus on improving. Every time you die, you'll know exactly how it happened, and you can quickly mull over where it all went wrong, in the brief seconds before your next life appears on-screen.
Metal Slug also establishes a lot of the rules of the series. Not only do the heroes die in a single hit, but there aren't any extra lives. In fact, since all POWs are lost upon death, you pretty much have to adopt a "1-life" mindset if you're playing for score. In arcade games, we tend to look at lives as resources. I know when I reach the final boss of a 2D shooter, I do an inventory of all of the lives & bombs in-stock. I know what I can afford to expend, in order to guarantee that clear. This approach simply doesn't work for Metal Slug. These three lives represent three chances, you have to protect them...well..like they're your own. Obviously that's extremely difficult due to the armies you have to contend with, but over-time you work everything out.
Honestly though, even if you approach this series with the mindset of "I don't want to worry about 1CCs, 1LCs, or any of that other stuff" you can still have a lot of fun. The moment-to-moment combat is just so visceral it's a reward in itself when heavy-machinegun fire chews through half a dozen soldiers, or a shotgun blast rends a tank into nothingness. Simply playing these games, without a specific goal in mind, is just flat-out glorious entertainment.
While it's easy to say that the sequels are better, there's a level of simplicity and charm that absolutely fits Metal Slug 1. Feel free to revisit it whenever you have the opportunity. Oh but just one thing, while I have all the praise in the world for these games, I don't have anything nice to say about Dotemu.
*I count Metal Slug X as a separate entry.

The long dark is an engaging, convincing and challenging survival game that fills a niche I have been looking at for a long time. Not only is the interface intuitive, but the conditions and responses from the characters you can play as are releastic and interesting. There is a huge number of ways to die, which in my eyes is actually a good thing, including: freezing, starving, dying of thirst, being mauled to death by wolves, getting food poisoning, and injuries such as broken legs and sprained ankles are great at helping you along to one of these fates.
A few people call this game a walking simulator, but that definitely comes down to how you play the game. There are three 'difficulty' modes which affects the way the environment responds to you. If you choose the 'stalker' difficulty, you may find yourself reluctant to leave whatever shelter you may have come across, for fear of being attacked by a wolf, or freezing in the harsh winds at -30°C. However, on the 'pilgrim' setting weather is gentler, and animals actively try to run away from you. Personally, I would love to see another difficulty setting or a modular menu, so that I could have extreme weather and tame animals, or dangerous animals and gentle weather. The game is still in alpha and so I hope this will happen.
On a similar note, I have found the devs to be very productive so far in the creation of this game, I have witnessed changes that came as a result of community suggestions, and the changelogs are always very informative. Overall I am very happy with the current state of the game and must praise Hinterland for the work they have carried out. I am greatly looking forwards to future updates, and I am excited to play the complete game once it is released.

Bioshock was one of those games that initially didn't grab my attention. I would occasionally see it come up either on the internet or in conversation, but i never gave it any serious thought. However, upon purchasing a Bioshock bundle here on Steam, I thought I'd try it out and see what all the fuss is about.
And man does this game deliver.
The underwater city of rapture, althought hardly seen in it's entirety, is magnificantly crafted and the eerie setting of the entire game always had me on edge from start to finish. The story's gripping action, drama, and plot twists kept me playing for hours. the combat system is ingenious and innovative, with plasmids (elemental powers gained throughout the game) and a wide array of weapons. Although I initially thought this to have more of a scare factor, the game quickly moved past that and became one of solely action, which in the long run kept me more enticed and not anxious about something popping out of the corner (although that happened quite a few times). The Big Daddies and Little Sisters were also a really creative add-on, making the game more exciting as I frantically try to avoid one of those heavy beasts ramming me down.
Overall, Bioshock is a wonderful and thought provoking game, it explores the dark and dirty recesses of human ingenuity and shows just how far down us humans can go before greed consumes us all. The only flaw i have to give for this game is the fact that at times the story lags a bit, and recurring enemies can be a bit of an annoyance. But that's hardly an issue at all when looking at the big picture.

I remember when BioShock was almost upon us in 2007. The spiritual successor to
made by the same people who made System Shock 2? I had to own this. I had read the reviews again and again, watched every trailer and ordered my collector's edition with the Big Daddy model that managed to arrive at my house undamaged and then the big day arrived. I installed it, fought with the SecuROM DRM and was immediately having sound and graphical problems because this was 2007, the time Windows Vista was making lives a misery for people around the world, drivers for sound cards were generally crap and games made for Windows Vista sometimes didn't work well with XP and vice versa.
But now it is officially the future and going back to this game on a nice beefy PC was an amazing experience, I had forgotten how good this game was and how close to System Shock 2 it was and, if you like that game then you will most certainly like this.
BioShock is a First-Person Shooter with horror and stealth elements set in the year 1960. You are on a flight to an unknown destination when all of a sudden, the plane ends up crashing somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean and you are the only survivor. You make your way to a lighthouse in the distance only to find, not sanctuary and rescue from the near-death experience you just survived, but the gateway to a mysterious underwater city built by one of the most libertarian antagonists you will probably ever see in a video game.
When you arrive, the city is in a state of chaos and decay. The majority of its residents are dead and the few that have survived have either gone insane or are just trying to survive and find a way to leave. A lack of maintenance is causing the city to slowly fall apart and flood. You will have to find some way of getting back to the world above.
You are not completely defenceless however, you soon learn of a mysterious substance called ADAM and how it can be used to alter an individuals genetic code from scratch. Plasmids are powers which you can acquire that will give you many different abilities such as the ability to set foes on fire, freeze them on the spot in ice, throw heavy things with telekinesis and even summon a swarm of killer insects!
From the very beginning, the game does a phenomenal job of creating an amazing world for the player to explore with a really nicely done Art Deco style and presentation. The game also feels very reminiscent of the Fallout series. The music and some of the artwork you'll see will definitely make you feel a little Wasteland nostalgia deep inside.
Every game so far made by Ken Levine has had a brilliant story to it and BioShock is no different. Like System Shock 2, you'll find Accu-Vox voice recorders lying around the environments you explore that are made by the citizens of the city. They will tell most of the story and give you key information about what exactly happened to the residents in the city, how it all started to collapse and how to progress through the dangerous world ahead.
The first hour or so of the game is quite linear, guiding you around perfectly crafted set-pieces and environments to get you used to what exactly is going on, what everything is and does and who your friends and foes are. The game opens up fairly quickly with non-linear levels and the player is then free to explore any area they can get access to. The environments are nicely varied and very detailed too; you will explore many different locations along your journey such as theatres, parks, hospitals and gardens and you are free to go back to any area you have previously been to.
The game is extremely atmospheric. A large part of the game's atmosphere comes from its amazing lighting and sound score. The sombre music and orchestral stings do an amazing job of creating a unique sense of fear and tension that had not been seen any any game before it.  The water effects were also, for the time, an incredible accomplishment and something that had not been seen since Half-Life 2. Different objects have different levels of buoyancy, water leaks from the ceiling and walls, doors that are holding back water from a collapsed walkway are bulging and warping due to the pressure and it all adds up to a constant lingering reminder of where you are and what is happening to the city. The game also includes a fair amount of superbly crafted jump scares and is good with messing with your head right until the very end of the game.
BioShock's game mechanics largely copy System Shock 2's albeit with a few corners cut off; the game doesn't have a deep role-playing system like System Shock 2. Shock 2 has a full RPG system with character statistics and skills and those skills were needed to determine what you were good at doing. In BioShock, you can hack any machine, use any gun and use and plasmid right from the beginning. The only thing that comes close to any sort of RPG element comes from the equippable plasmids and tonics you find and earn. You have a limited amount of slots for them which means choosing what you want to be able to use against your enemies at will require some forward thinking.
BioShock also allows for the use of different ammo types in weapons, you have your standard kind of ammo that's quite plentiful but not really good or bad against any specific thing but guns can have armour-piercing rounds for tough opponents, anti-personnel rounds for dealing quickly with squishy human type enemies, proximity mines for sealing off passageways and many other kinds of things. You will need to choose the right ammo type for the right opponent in order to conserve that precious ammo.
And now, it's time to talk about the faults, yes it has faults but they are somewhat minor. Hacking, whilst always useful, is the most bizarre and tedious mini-game that they could've made. You have to reveal tiles on a grid that conceal different sections of pipes and then re-arrange those pieces of pipes to form a system that can get a slowly progressing body of water along from its starting point to its finishing point whist avoiding security and alarm nodes which are also hidden under those tiles. It can be fun at times but after the 50th time you do it, you may find it becoming tedious. You have the option to just pay money to hack things anyway if you're feeling lazy. The game also pauses whilst you hack so if a camera is just out of reach, you can jump, hit the hack button and hack away whilst seemingly floating in mid-air!
Also, they went and added some more plasmids and tonics as downloadable content but they fell into the trap of breaking immersion by telling you in game that those new goodies are "downloaded" when you go to buy them and thinking the player wants access to them with as little effort as possible, therefore setting the price of these new goodies to just 1 ADAM each! It wouldn't have taken much effort to sensibly price them to match their original counterparts. A slightly missed opportunity to make your plasmid buying decisions a tiny bit more demanding.
The final area of the game is a pain, having to go through a tedious section with really slow pacing is probably the lowest point of the game. The boss fights for the game are, for the most part, exactly like fighting normal enemies but they just have more hit-points. The game also wants to hold your hand all the way through. It will constantly remind you to press keys to reload and press keys if you are stuck and need a hint.
BioShock is an incredible game to play and I'm glad I went through it again as I was reminded just how much of a good game it was. It's an artistic and technological masterpiece that has aged really well and is a blast to play from start to finish. Just be sure to go through the options, turn off Vita (Respawn) Chambers that eliminate all challenge and play on at least Normal difficulty to have one whale of a time!

Even with the abundance of references to Melee both from players and the game itself, I actually felt it played a lot like a spiritual successor to Dustforce, another speedrunning platformer which is amazing, obviously with a few key differences.  I've played my own large share of many Smash Bros. games, but I was never interested in the intricacies of high level movement.  Given all of the time spent in those games and a large number of other platformers, speedrun-ny or otherwise, this game still feels like it has a life all its own, even when it flaunts its inspiration.
Built from love, loads of fun, and a bargain price tag.  Instant recommendation if you have any interest in it.

TL;DR WaveLand is lovely, challenging, and a successful loveletter to Melee movement
Below is a somewhat wordy review:
Concept: I have a deep love of Super Smash Brothers Melee, and Logan Foster brings the unique spacing manuever "Wavedashing" into a world of platforming. After experiencing Melee movement and microspacing I found myself desiring these options in other games as well, so I had high hopes and bought WaveLand on release.
Gameplay: Within minutes I approved of the game's physics and movement. Mr. Foster tuned his level design splendidly with the beast he had constructed. The input buffering and hitboxes all feel precise. The potential for optimization and speed in WaveLand is massive and addicting. Several times I could not make myself leave  a level until I was #1 on the leaderboard. After introducing the concept, no time is wasted in ramping up the difficulty, and similar to Melee, WaveLand might be treacherous for the casual gamer. Those hungering for a challenge will have their appetite sated. In game currency is entirely for aesthetic customization, but obtaining coins and solving hubworld puzzles is fun and satisfying in its own right.
Story: Messages are scattered  throughout the world alluding to the overarching plot of the game. The story is sparse and slightly cryptic, and is certainly not the focus of WaveLand.
Visuals: I'd lay money that WaveLand was created in Gamemaker, which typically means the visual quality is largely tied to the skill of the pixel artist/animator. In WaveLand's case, everything looks clean and clear. There was not a single time that my eyes were confused about any part of the game. Everything is immediately recognizable which allows a player to react and maintain speed even in the first time through the area. Environmental art keeps things fresh and imaginative between worlds while remaining unobtrusive.

Sound: All sound effects are distinguishable and appropriate. WaveLand's soundtrack is mixed nicely with the feel of the game. It functions mainly as slighty hype background music, but there are some inquisitive and atmospheric touches in the hubworlds.
Closing comments: WaveLand is fully aware of itself. Most game elements function as above average placeholders and take a backseat to the core mechanics. This game is about speed, efficiency, and near frame perfect inputs a la Dustforce. While the roots are strongly in Melee, the mechanics come into their own with a few intelligent tweaks.  I must praise Mr. Foster specifically for his level design, difficulty curve, and overall awareness. The later levels fully respect and employ the difficulty that is called for when you make wavedashing your core mechanic. We should all keep our eyes out for his upcoming projects in the future! Congratulations to Logan Foster on a well-made game. Your love for Melee movement is shared by many, and is palpable in Waveland.

There is good and bad.
Personally I love this game. It is by far the most realistic survival game I have ever seen. Do get it, you'll like it, but be aware of the following;
The good:
- intense and gripping, never gets boring
- MEGA FUN
- realistic
- solar storms deserve somebody to make a apocalypse story about them, hello? No electricity, colder (like an extra -20) winter and mad animals. And more, no wifi! What's more epic than that? P.S., you think that's an easy apocalypse to survive compared to zombies? Play this game then say!!
- dev team are releasing about an update a week, you heard me, an update a week?! :)
- they definitely wont abandon this game, trust me, they wont
- you can't jump. Unrealistic, you may say at first, but oh, my friend, do you jump over rocks and up mountains, or do you climb?
- its hard
The bad;
- the devs are really anti making shelters and living outside, in other words, a building HAS to be your home in the current state
- you can't chop wood off trees! Hello? You're in a forest! You've got to go find wood on the ground or rip up furniture (for the record, you can burn wood from live trees, it's just less productive)
- if you're waiting for story mode skip a few years in a time machine, cos I don't think they ever want to make that, it's sandbox only now my friends!
- wolves don't attack humans, I'm aware that they state that obvious error in the description and that the geo storm has disrupted their brains (true), but to make them aggressive (false).
- bears should be more dangerous (my opinion)
- this game says "no zombies, just you against the elements...", but has anyone else noticed? The wolves, ARE, the zombies!
- you are not rewarded for your knowledge of the wilderness, cannot use knowledge to know what wood is best for a bow or what plants are edible. It's just really a test of your patience, but still fun
- things break unnecessarily quick. Every time you hack up a log you lose 2% on your hatchet out of a total of 100. All in all, that makes a 30-year lifespan tool live for about three months in game, don't get me started on the clothes...
- not very interactive, you don't "start a fire" literally, you click a button that says you are and on chance it may or may not be done. A randomiser hooked up to a switch.
- the game is waaaaay too number-y. Everything has a percentage of damage and a percentage of success and a number of HP. What weirdo can tell in real life how much percentage left of his knife he has left? Or what direct treatments for his wounds should be. The game should include an option where you click to say observe your tool and give an estimate when it will break. Or instead of have a bar of hunger, just say "I'm hungry". It should be a lot more environmentally immersive, not numerically, thats all I'm saying.
- no lighters, do people in Canada just not smoke?
But ultimately, great game! Just if any of that *minority* bad effect you, then consider it. I'm just being truthful on my opinion.

I got a lot of enjoyment out of the team creation aspect of this game - taking a personalized team of pun-based Orks from squishy greenhorns to granite-jawed vets felt great, and reminded me in some ways of playing the Xcom franchise. If there is any aspect of this game to draw enjoyment from, it's this.
Everything else about this game, however, is garbage. It can be compared, pretty reasonably, to a convoluted slot machine with lots of cardboard cutout action and deceptively inconsequential decisions to keep it mildly interesting.
There is almost no tactical involvement in this game whatsoever. Nearly everything comes down to a dice roll, leaving pretty much all of your tactical decisions in the hands of an intensely capricious RNGsus who WILL ruin your day at every opportunity. An irritatingly high number of insanely great plays are reverted or negated based entirely on a single dice roll, or some nonsense turn where the enemy pulls off multiple nye-impossible rolls, or kills/removes half of your team from play while your team is failing to pull off a single block. It feels cheap; in fact I would go so far as to say that it never doesn't feel cheap. All of the challenge in this game comes from rolling the dice. Not strategically placing your players or successfully securing tackles. Rolling dice...
At least in Xcom the dice are actually under the hood. In Blood Bowl it feels as though the entire car is made of dice.
What I'm trying to say is, if you're looking for an experience which requires the strategic acumen of Xcom - or any other game which requires coherent thought rather than luck to win - this probably isn't for you.
If you, however, enjoy fantasy-based NFL dressup simulators with slot-machine style gameplay, then I would recommend purchasing this game at its next large sale - and only if you have friends who want to play it as well, because playing against the computer is probably one of the worst experiences I've had playing a game in my entire life.
I'm not even going to go into the whole money-grabbing DLC nonsense that this company is notorious for, since I'm sure other raters have already reamed them thoroughly for it, but that is among the other reasons this title gets a solid thumbs down.

Next, about what makes a game scary. As I mentioned, it was fairly scary for the first 30 minutes or so, mostly because your fear is fueled by your imagination and fear of unknown. Good ambience, eery sounds, doors closing on their own and the magnificent library walkthrough. It is really scary and unexpected when Chris Walker grabs you from behind the first time and then you see disturbing glimpses with priest as you come to. Afterwards, you move forward by collecting two things and activating the third one, while evading monster of the week. As you realize that and that you can respawn immediately at the convenient safespot even when caught, all tension goes out of the window. The main character is even scarier than the mutants, surely he must have some lizard genes. Not only can you take quite a few hits from formidable enemies, you regenerate almost immediately. Fingers cut off? Not a problem. The "cat and mouse" game, mentioned by some other reviewers, would be more properly described as avoid the annoying guard game, because the cat is not really looking for you. If you sit still and observe their path for a while, you could evade them completely without any fear. If you start early, you can outrun anyone in the game. And they don't chase you beyond a particular point, also into the holes and vents. This is for normal difficulty, but likely true for others.
Now, a bit about the characters. In the trading cards, you don't see many. That's because that's all there is to them. They can't show the last couple of guys, because spoilers - the Pyro is just an ordinary patient, who happened to burn a room. The guy I mentioned, Chris Walker is huge, but not particularly scary and moves slow when not chasing you. You see him in the first half an hour, which destroys the scare of further encounters and it is bad, because he is the one you'll be meeting the most throughout the game. The game throws some patients at you, who aren't scary at all, even the first time. The doctor's level was a bit refreshing, as you didn't have to collect two things to unlock the third and actually had to think how to progress. It also had a bit more of the story. I really enjoyed my encounters with the twins, their dialogues and was looking forward to an eventual confrontation, which, to my disappointment, never came. It is as thougn the devs designed very good villains with potentially good background stories, but then scrapped them due to lack of time or budget. The main character is alright, and it is apparent that a lot of effort went into designing his animations.
All in all, Outlast could be considered a B-grade cinematic, consolised experience with lots of gore. The levels are well crafted, but linear. The tension wears off really early due to how game works. Some enemies are good, but there aren't many. It gets repetetive and boring, especially with the tasks you have to perform. The ending is something else. It is not a bad game, but is strangely overhyped. That is what got my hopes up, and eventually led to disappointment.

Starting with the TLDR version...
I love the game and am growing to like it more as I play it more!
More specifically, first the bad...
- lots of lack of completeness to many parts. This list? The stadiums are all full of exactly the same audience of humans and a random Orc. Push someone off the pitch and they are beaten up by the same 3 humans. The cheerleaders are an army of plastic, poorly animated humans. You will get annoyed by the announcer comments during the match. Each position/race has one block animation which will get boring quickly....
But... These are all non game-affecting niggles.
- the campaign is an over-long tutorial. It is really pretty boring - but it does try to explain all the intricacies of the game (and there are many!)
- The game is absolutely designed as multiplayer. This is where it shines.
The AI in single player is ok and makes you feel good about winning games, after a few matches it does get predictable... But...
- There are many great routes to enjoy the multiplayer aspect. The private leagues are great to run and very configurable (not intuitive to set up, but then works well).
- The Cyanide Open Ladder (COL) is easy to join, match-making is pretty quick with opponents chosen close in "maturity" to yours and the players (at least those I have encountered) were nice, fun and fair and I have had a blast!
- I have not joined a public league so cannot really comment, but it looks similar to the private leagues but with more players and a more regular game time (eg committing to a match a week).
- Races are being added regularly - there are already a very good selection and although as DLC they are expensive (at full price...), those released after you buy the game are free (at least for the first 4 after original game release). The races offer good variation of tactics and all are good if played to their strengths.
- You cannot save matches during the game. This means you have to commit to a whole match and I am sure is a reason for some concede results and in Multiplayer with no way to pause, can cause difficulties (a match can take between 30-60 mins)
- The game itself is very well presented, the interface is clear, smooth and informative.  It does not hide from being a dice game at its core and that is also fine - dice are rolled in front of you.
- Sometimes it feels like rolls are rigged against you, but this is not the case! (And can't be if everyone feels "done over" by bad luck even in the same game!). The reality is that this is a game about managing risk and making too many rolls increases the risk of failing rolls.
- Player graphics are great, not particularly varied between players, which is a shame, but that would only make the loss of a highly customised player even more painful, so perhaps no bad thing!
- Game play is smooth and exciting - each turn very relevant and tactical to the match - it is no Real Time Sports Sim, and for me that is a good thing!
- Team management is fun, quick and relevant - the skills each player can learn are clear and impactful
In Conclusion...
The game is exciting, fun, has a learning curve which takes some learning, but is very rewarding.

Sunless Sea is a very original and interesting game with a unique setting. In it, you choose who you are from a select few backgrounds and victory conditions, then you embark into the titular sea to explore and achieve whatever goal you set for yourself. Think FTL, but instead of jumping from event to event you actually steer your ship there and can sail around the map at your leisure.
All of this sounds good on paper, until you have to start managing your resources most of which cost money. the early game will see experienced players shooting back and forth between the main hub (London) and various select locations that can be farmed for money. Money will get you new ships and improvements like any other game, but the problem comes when this money farming grind starts to spill over into the mid game and even the end game. next thing you know ten hours have gone by and your still running sunlit mirror boxes back and forth for cash because your nice new ship consumes more fuel and supply. Only on occasion do you find the time to explore other parts of the map or continue a story line for one of your officers.
And then, when on your 20th journey to the money farm, you die. Why? No idea, because after 20 times you stop actually reading the text for the event.
Sunless Sea is a game I want to recommend, but the grind is pushing past the level of most japanese games. What I can say is that it's a game that needs a sequel, because there's a lot of great stuff going for it, and even more stuff that needs improvement.

Metal Slug (MS) is a 2-D side-scrolling platformer game developed by the company DotEmu with emphasis on action-oriented run & gun gameplay.
+ Remastered version from the year 1996 resolving some technical faults of the original.

o Level of difficulty and number of continues are adjustable.

DotEmu has done a solid job on the emulation of the game to the PC. MS is a nostalgia trip that takes the player through one of the best 2-D run & gun games of the '90s.

Ever wished you could live out your World War II combat fantasies in lush war-torn European locales? Now you can! Destroy enviornments and crawl around in an adorable tank in this SNK classic. Featuring some of the best backgrounds in the series, and fun platforming to match, Metal Slug is the first of four releases by Nazca that make Metal Slug one of the best video game trilogies out there.
Unfortunately the features outside of the game don't fare as well. Once again SNKPlaymore has chosen to ship Metal Slug to PC with DotEmu, which worked great for 3, questionably for X, and fared much worse with 1. Frame drops during mission intros and endings, plenty of places ingame where lots of things onscreen at once cause slowdown.
Problems extend into the game's menu. Keeping the original intro is great, and having game art on the menus is better. However, there still is no gallery mode following the absence of one in X despite 3 having one. The Nazca games have wonderful art direction, and many people would love to further appreciate the art of the series by having access to an ingame gallery.
It's not Metal Slug 3, and it certainly isn't worth the same price as 3, but Metal Slug is worth a buy if you want a piece of 2D gaming history.

After a mega popular public beta a couple of years back and a succesful kickstarter, Superhot has hit Steam. The main gimmick of time moving at 1/100th its normal speed when the player is still, along with the new feature in this release of being able to swap bodies with enemies makes this game more of a first-person tactical puzzler than a shooter. The story revolves around a meta-narrative of the player becoming enthralled by the game, and eventually in a true Neuromancer-y and cyberpunk style merging their mind with machine and losing control to the game. It's got little to do with the actual gameplay, but I think it was a great effort and it was an interesting way for this game to go - though that is as a guy who likes cognitive science and cyberpunk literature, so milegae may vary.
I enjoyed the story campaign for Superhot, but that's not where the meat of the game is. Actually, the story mode that the player will have to go through for the first couple of hours can be considered to be a long tutorial to the player before the real challenge of the game; the various challenge maps which necessitate the repetition of those levels with various handicaps or accomplishments, and Endless Mode, in which the player uses their skills to dodge, swap bodies, and rack up kills on a variety of challenge maps. Is this worth £18? I think so, and I'd challenge anyone who claims the game is 2 hours long to actually get into the meat of the content in the challenge and endless modes.
The level designs are heavily inspired by various setpieces encountered in action cinema; story mode has the player effectively playing out the action scenes in locales like labs, boardrooms, and museums. The 'coolnes' factor of these encounters is enough to make me go back again and again. After looking back at my replay at the end of the level, I really do get a sensation of being in an action film through playing Superhot's story levels that I don't get elsewhere.
Every run through is enjoyable. Every battle feels great. It's one of those games which really drives you to outperform yourself and refine your approach and strategy; beneath what appears to be a single gimmicky concept lies a plethora of choice and strategy. Taking twitch reflexes out of the equation elevates the gunplay to a matter of rational computation. As you stare down the barrel of a raised gun, you weigh the possibility of swapping bodies and the safety from death against the possibility of tackling the enemy for their gun and thus averting the need to wait for the swapping ability's cooldown. Alternatively, you could jump to the side. Or you could swap bodies with the enemy on the other side of the room. If this were a conventional shooter, chances are that none of this would cross your head - but Superhot allows the player to think, decide, and act throughout the battle.
It turns a 20 second encounter into what I can only say as a rewarding and awesome series of dodges, shots, and swaps; unlike Hotline Miami, I never feel like my failures are because of the game and not something in my approach. I can always improve, alter my strategy to that enemy placed over there, and choose a different series of actions entirely. That all seems vapid, but I have to say it to stress how fun and replayable this game is, and how I think its critics miss the mark.

I HAVE MIXED FEELINGS ABOUT SUPER HOT.
It's an intro in TO cyberpunk. It gives players of any skill level a unique action-puzzle experience that ends up being a blend of The Matrix meets MKultra if M.K. stood for Manchurian Killer.
It's better as an arcade game, and you'll unlock that mode following the completion of the short story campaign. I thought it was a tensionless, droll experience up until about the point where the story began to end, when the levels become much more difficult (when it became fun).
There's a lot to get into in too many words, so here was my experience.
Spoilers will not be tagged, but I'll try to avoid blatantly spelling it out.
Super Hot is all about glamour and if you're a playful gamer, you'll have plenty to do. The campaign is presented very well, but I always felt three steps ahead of the cyberpunk story. It ended at about the point where I thought it should've continued on, but damn it was it ever presented in a visually exciting way. I went on to discover all the game's secrets and that's where the story started to really lose me.
"You aren't actually going to reveal anything, I get it, Super Hot." And then Super Hot's mysterious Red Voice continued on and on with its attitude. I continued to find the secrets because it did answer some of its questions, only for it to conclude with a reward for my dedication, and while I appreciate that it fits back in with the hypnosis/brainwashing angle, I felt as insulted by the game as if it asked me if I wanted to buy more energy, like a freemium game would.
The "secrets" were ultimately unecessary, since like I said, the majority of the ""secret"" """"answers"""" were questions that I'm confident most players solved themselves in the campaign.
What a strange path the story took though. I was really into it up until the point where it was clear that the secrets were bunk, and then it got all capitalist on me and threw the punk part of the cyberpunk out the window with the coupon.
Still, tho, the game's themes and presentation are intertwined, and I actually do like Killstagram because it ties back into the boldness of their compulsion to make you part of their viral marketing, and even the warez angle feeds into the viral edginess. That stuff is fantastic. Moreover, Killstagram feeds into the playfulness and how much fun you can have by learning that juggling guns and banking thrown objects off walls is the most hilarious and cool looking fun you can have. The story is an intro to cyberpunk and posthuman themes though, and its style and tone are its own. I just wish they excluded the "secrets" which ruined it pretty handily.
