TLDR;
The artwork is fantastic, has the Telltale feel along with it giving that Batman/comic book touch. The story has set itself up rather well and has left me wanting more. The detective mode gives a little more than the usual telltale gameplay we have seen before. The quick time events actually feel powerful and badass compared to spamming "E" to open a door.
Basically the game is great, I'd say wait for all 5 episodes to come out though unless you want to suffer the wait.
TLDR;
As someone who wants to get into comics and one of them being Batman, this has been a great taster of what I should expect. It starts off with year 1 of the Batman comics and as of the first episode it has done an excellent job of easing me into the Batman world. Telltale has done a great job with giving the Arkam world a dark gritty feel, it definitely feels like a Batman game.
Story
Telltale have done a great job of giving the background story while also setting up for what is to come. There are some difficult choices you have to make in the first episode, if they matter then I can see it leading to great things story wise. Telltale have given the player a choice of how you want to play Batman, you can stay in the shadows or you can be a little more gritty. Getting to play Bruce Wayne on top of Batman gives a dynamic edge to the story, playing through his perspective will bring another level to the story. Overall the game has been written incredibly well and the voice actors so far have been great.
Gameplay
As much as I love Telltale games, I never assume there will be groundbreaking gameplay. However, the quick time events feel good in cutscenes, there is a "link mode" both in combat and a detective mode where you solve crime scenes in the surrounding environments. Overall, I feel like Telltale has put in more thought into the world out of the cutscenes, which is rather refreshing. The first episode itself felt a tad short, It was a little over an hour so I hope the following episodes are lengthier.
Performance
This has been very controversial. I had no issues launching the game, nor did I get a black screen. I can see how this can be frustrating but on the day of launch Telltale released a patch and there have been fixes posted on the discussion forums and guides have been created by the community. I get a solid 60fps and I will post specs to those who are interested in that sort of thing, but Telltale games are never very demanding.
I feel like after playing the first episode I'm left wanting more. It feels like a great setup, and had nice little twists along the way to keep me glued to my seat. I'm excited for the rest of the game. I think Telltale have made a great choice with telling this story(one game released previously had me questioning where they were going with releases *cough*) There are many ways that Telltale have given to introduce me to the Batman lore, through the story itself and the codex in the Batcave.

If you love resource management and infrastructure planning, in medieval times, Banished is the game for you! This game reminds me a lot of
(the old one from 1994), even some of the music tracks seem either inspired or
homaged. Though, this is where the games part similarities, whereas The Settlers had enemies, knights and a sense of "goal" when defeating the opponents on the map, Banished is only about building a city...
There are some enemies, but all of them the silent type, like diseases, tornadoes, fires, pests and plagues. Your worst enemy is yourself. Rapidly over-populating or over-expanding can quickly lead to lack of resources, and with out food and firewood your poor inhabitants will both starve and freeze to death...
Poor infrastructure is also your enemy. That and a bad map seed. While writing this review I'm 58 hours into the game, this is the 5th or 6th city I'm building, not counting the 20+ map seeds I looked over. But this time I got it right. I planned half of the city before un-pausing the game...
Anywho, this game seriously lacks progression. I've built my city, it's self-sustaining now, all I really do is maintenance... and this is only year 101... What I'm missing from this game is: fog of war/map shroud, enemies to defeat, land to conquer, horse carriage for faster transport, structures and technology to research and develop, multiplayer... list goes on... But! For resource management and infrastructure planning this game is great! If you're a little bit OCDC like me, you'll love/hate this game!

I recommend going through the turorial and playing 3-5 exhibition games on Blood Bowl Chaos Edition. Then play a campaign on Blood Bowl 2. BB2 is so much more enjoyable. Having not been a product of the table top version of the game, BB2 allows for so much more development on the fly than BBCE. The main difference is that in BBCE any failed attempt results in a turnover. In BB2 you are allowed to fail in an attempt and then you can adjust your team and strategize to accomodate failures in that same round. I recommend practicing in BBCE because it will make you appreciate the strategic elements of blood bowl as you dont have the safety net of taking a chance in a situation and making up for it in the same round; In BBCE nearly every move you make has dire consequences. So, if you are a masochist who likes to gamble with nearly every chance taken, play BBCE. If you are like Maverick in Top Gun and you like being able to adjust on the fly, and possibly salvage a situation, play BB2.....I loved the concept of Blood Bowl, but BBCE just felt like a chore. I have really enjoyed playing this game. There isn't really anything else like this out there.
It's sort of a cross between Pirates and a choose your own adventure. It's roguelike and pretty hard (at least till you have played a few captains, and kind of worked out what you need to be doing to stay alive).
The setting as I understand it is that London fell underground and is now called Fallen London. You are a ship captain, leaving the safety of Fallen London to explore the surrounding sea underground (hence the title Sunless Sea). The tone of the game is quite dark and similar to Lovecraft.
You start off with a Steam Ship carrying fuel (for powering the ship and also to power the ships light). Without the light on you become insane faster, but the light burns fuel faster meaning fuel will be used faster. The other major resource is supplies. It represents the food for you and your crew, run out of supplies and you all starve. So yeah the game is bleak.
You don't make huge amounts of cash to buy new supplies or fuel, so it's difficult starting out to balance what you need. Trade routes aren't too profitable in the early game, and the sea does randomise itself to a degree for each captain.
If you progress far enough though you can buy a house, write a will, and leave other benefits to your successor increasing their chance of success next time. (last time I played, I returned to London only to find that my partner and our child had both died wiping out my next bloodline. I think I had upset one of the gods of the sea...)
Overall the game has a great atmosphere. If you like rogue like games, and don't mind a little reading you should really enjoy this.

It's been a long time since I've played a strategy game, mainly because none of them have really caught my attention, or kept it, since the days when Command & Conquer was good.
Medieval Kingdom Wars has been the first to catch my interests since then. I knew very little going into it, but was blown away by the attention to detail on historical accuracy. It is not often you see this in modern games.
The world is immersive and huge. Whether I am viewing the regional map or down in the combat, it just feels as though the land and sea stretches out in all directions for miles. The amount of detail brings the world to life, even with all of the dying going on... City building only adds to the sheer size of it all!
The combat is balanced, but challenging! Many past strategy games I've played never fulfilled a challenge once the game mechanics and AI capabilities were figured out, but MKW has challenged me to stay focused, otherwise it is easy to have victory slip away from you. It has supplied me with a challenge I find myself needing to attack a little more fiercely in my next session of play.
The art is fantastic, no matter where it is placed in the game. The loading screens are very detailed, depicting scenes of battle or beautiful scenery, and the overall graphic design of the gameplay world is beautiful, even in the darkest, bloodiest trenches of war-torn lands.
I've noticed a large amount of updates from the Devs, which is a great sign for any early release project! It means they really care about this project, and are improving this Early Access frequently! I'm excited to see what comes of it.
Also... Is that a map editor I see? Now THAT I will be having a lot of fun with. When I was a kid, I used to purposely seek out games that had map editors so I could create my own worlds and scenarios. Map Editors are a dying breed, and I'm so happy the Devs included one in this early access!
I'm looking forward to more updates and gameplay!

I have experienced very few games like Sunless Sea: a game that is both casual, and completely engrossing.
After booting up the game, the player finds themselves in the town of Fallen London, a once great city which was unfortuitously dragged into a massive underground ocean by angry bats during the reign of Queen Victoria. From there, you are given a bout, some crew, a few strange coins, and a mission: explore, bring glory to the empire, die where someone will find you.
One could roam the oceans doing menial tasks for the hierarchy to scrape up a few coins, or, one could side with the Great Khanate, trading their honor for riches.
Alternatively, you can be Captain Crusty Cumswallow, scourge of the low-zees, fighting off overlarge sharks, moustachieod fish, defenseless merchants, and the wrath of the gods whilst smuggling pornagraphy and human souls in the hopes of one day putting your feet up in your zeeside mansion.
In this game, you really feel the choices you make, and you can reap their benefits of suffer cruel punishment for the smallest actions, which can be a no-go for some people, but for me I found that it accuratly portrays the fragility of life on the Zee, in the dark, with no friends. The only true negative I can think of about this game is it's lack of replayablity, as every character will eventually carry out most of the same missions with most of the same officers, which averages out to a mostly the same experience.
I would highly recommend people who enjoy exploration and adventure, but wouldn't cry if you character of 12 hours goes insane and is murdered by what crew he hasnt eaten yet.

I like Metal Slug games. I just don't recommend any of them.
✓ Good ol' button smashing arcade goodness
✓ Decent replayability value
✓ It's Metal Slug! RUN AND GUN, DIE AND REPEAT
✗ 30 minutes long (I'm not joking, look at my playtime and achievements)
✗ You can only play as Marco
✗ Missions are average at best (detailed below)
✗ The final boss is incredibly disappointing
✗ Noticeable choppiness during intense action, despite the game being constantly at 60fps
This is the first game in the series so no wonder it falls short in many aspects, but honestly, why didn't DotEmu port this first and then the others? If you play MS3, MSX and then MS1, you'll miss a lot of stuff and the game will feel bland and boring.
Not only there's a single character (Marco), this Metal Slug easily has the shortest and easiest campaign so far (despite playing in Hard). There is no air combat, submarine combat or air combat, just the typical "tank" in pretty much every mission. The enemies are all the same (soldiers) throughout the entire game and there are no novelties (there are zombies in MGSX) or anything noteworthy... it's just run and gun, die over and over again, get to the final boss and next level.
I mean, that's the formula for every Metal Slug ever, but everything just feels so average in this one. So far it's the most boring one, and just like I say in every one of my Metal Slug reviews: don't buy it unless you played it as a kid or the disappointment will be even bigger.

This is one of the best survival games ever made, and potentially one of the best computer games out there right now.
Why is this game so good?
1) As a player, you have to really be on the ball to *make* it; the realism is amazing. One major mistake and you might be dead.
2) As sound effects go, Hinterland Games has done a perfect job of giving every single item, action, and event its own unique and lively sound; it enhances the gameplay experience hugely.
3) Can't say enough about the awesome weather.
4) Every single resource is precious and item valuation is top notch - a can of tomato soup can save you; a toque can give you an edge in warmth so you can stay outside just a little longer; a hunting knife enables you to extract meat (but where are you gonna find a knife??).
5) The gameplay system is on its way to stardom; it's only in alpha right now, yet is worthy of multiple playthroughs.
Examples of awesome gameplay:
1) I needed to get some wood to heat up snow to make water and while I was out, a huge blizzard rolled in and I didn't know the way back. I had to check my footprints in the snow to see where I had come from in order to find shelter.
2) I got mauled by a bear...and survived!...bearly. It took about 2 days of R&R to get back to full strength, which took a lot of food and time and left me in an impoverished state. I almost didn't make it through, but I did.
3) Nearly out of food, I went fishing with my last supplies. Both of my fishing hooks broke, and I was a goner. Bad luck, in addition to making mistakes, is death.
There are tons of improvements and enhancements to be made for The Long Dark, but without a doubt Hinterland Games has opened its doors with a gem. Just look at the *overwhelmingly positive* trail of reviews for a game still in alpha. If you like intense survival strategy, this is not a game to miss.

Way overhyped for unknown reasons.
I was really scared for 30 or so minutes into it, but then the impression wore off quickly and towards the endgame I was more worried about finding all journal scraps ( :( ) than getting spooked. Not to mention the ending is ridiculous and defiles the whole build-up leading to it.
First off, it's extremely linear, you could call it a corridor runner. The levels are well designed, that's a plus, but most of time you'll be walking or running on a pre-defined path, occasionally pressing a button to jump or climnb over an obstacle. The quality is cinematic and the video and sound quality are good. If you're after that type of experience, you will enjoy it better than me.
Next, about what makes a game scary. As I mentioned, it was fairly scary for the first 30 minutes or so, mostly because your fear is fueled by your imagination and fear of unknown. Good ambience, eery sounds, doors closing on their own and the magnificent library walkthrough. It is really scary and unexpected when Chris Walker grabs you from behind the first time and then you see disturbing glimpses with priest as you come to. Afterwards, you move forward by collecting two things and activating the third one, while evading monster of the week. As you realize that and that you can respawn immediately at the convenient safespot even when caught, all tension goes out of the window. The main character is even scarier than the mutants, surely he must have some lizard genes. Not only can you take quite a few hits from formidable enemies, you regenerate almost immediately. Fingers cut off? Not a problem. The "cat and mouse" game, mentioned by some other reviewers, would be more properly described as avoid the annoying guard game, because the cat is not really looking for you. If you sit still and observe their path for a while, you could evade them completely without any fear. If you start early, you can outrun anyone in the game. And they don't chase you beyond a particular point, also into the holes and vents. This is for normal difficulty, but likely true for others.
Now, a bit about the characters. In the trading cards, you don't see many. That's because that's all there is to them. They can't show the last couple of guys, because spoilers - the Pyro is just an ordinary patient, who happened to burn a room. The guy I mentioned, Chris Walker is huge, but not particularly scary and moves slow when not chasing you. You see him in the first half an hour, which destroys the scare of further encounters and it is bad, because he is the one you'll be meeting the most throughout the game. The game throws some patients at you, who aren't scary at all, even the first time. The doctor's level was a bit refreshing, as you didn't have to collect two things to unlock the third and actually had to think how to progress. It also had a bit more of the story. I really enjoyed my encounters with the twins, their dialogues and was looking forward to an eventual confrontation, which, to my disappointment, never came. It is as thougn the devs designed very good villains with potentially good background stories, but then scrapped them due to lack of time or budget. The main character is alright, and it is apparent that a lot of effort went into designing his animations.
All in all, Outlast could be considered a B-grade cinematic, consolised experience with lots of gore. The levels are well crafted, but linear. The tension wears off really early due to how game works. Some enemies are good, but there aren't many. It gets repetetive and boring, especially with the tasks you have to perform. The ending is something else. It is not a bad game, but is strangely overhyped. That is what got my hopes up, and eventually led to disappointment.

I recommend this game!
First things first though. It's a steep climb to start. Playing Rise to Ruins is about learning to balance and prioritize what is important at the moment. And many players will fall, slip and lose their balance.
If you don't have the patience to dig in and look at what the game is doing and saying, this may not be the game for you.
You have to manage your village and distribute your villagers properly accross a multitude of jobs. You have to have food and water to last through the tough seasons, and there are tough seasons. You have to have shelter to protect your villagers from heat and cold, the hot summer and the cold winter can kill by themselves if things get out of hand. And you have to protect your village from the monsters that come when it's dark. But you are a god, and can guide and act through divine miracles... ok, spells. When telling them what to build and where comes up short, the magic you can use can fill in the gap. But that's another layer, resources harvested and monsters slain yeild free floating essense that you can harvest. The happiness of your villagers will refill your essense directly, keep them happy and safe and it will fill faster.
Individually, all your tools, the buildings, the defenses and your spells are not terribly strong. There is no overwhelming single button or single building solution. Especially the villagers, without your guiding hand, would be helpless. Learn to use your tools and the map around you however, and you can shape the world to your will. This game is about the satisfaction of learning to craft a thriving settlement. All the tools are there, but they expect you to learn them and master them. Rise to Ruins is not giving itself away, but is more than happy to be earned.
There are multiple difficulties. Peaceful, Traditional, Survival and Nightmare are the main settings. Custom lets you set the difficulty factors before the map starts, and the options are broad and potentially crushing if you're into that. Then there is Sandbox which lets you change settings and even the map on the fly. There is also a reasonably good map editing tool to make your own field of play and a small community of map builders as well.
The music is a nice background to the gameplay as well and lets you cycle through to the songs you like.
The graphics are simple but I find them both charming and suitable. Although there is a wealth of particles, so if particles are your thing, WELL. Have I got a game for you. There are also small little quirks in this game that give it a fun charm as well, from moments like seeing the ridiculous names that villagers and dogs get, to things like a villager leveling up after mating (Someone really upped their game that night).
Disclaimer: This game is cpu intensive as you start to get into the meat of it. Its the calculations of wide range map alterations like the 'earthquake spell' and the constant decision making of the horde of villagers that will bog the computer down. If You're playing on a toaster, your enjoyment will be hindered. :(
If you got this far, thanks for reading, I've enjoyed this game quite a bit and I wish it continued success.

The first Metal Slug, initially released in 1996 is the game that set the bar for run'n'gun games. It had everything to succeed, gorgeous 2D graphics and animation, accessible controls, smooth and packed action, various enemy types and well crafted level design to make use of the enemy types and renew the gameplay. It was an instant classic, seducing the heart of players mainly in the Arcades since not so many people owned a Neo Geo, and Metal Slug was so popular that you would find Arcade machines of it almost everywhere. The possibility to play in 2 player cooperation also contributed to the fun and appeal of the game.
Metal Slug set the blueprints for the formula that would be perfected in Metal Slug X (a revamped version of Metal Slug 2), and brought to an entirely new level in Metal Slug 3. In comparison to those, the first Metal Slug is easier, much shorter, less epic, offers far less variety in enemy types and backgrounds, so for someone with limited buying power I would recommend the aforementioned games instead. And for everyone that already has the two others, Metal Slug 1 is indeed worthy to sit in the collection as it is a great game in itself. If Metal Slug X and 3 were not out yet, I would say that Metal Slug 1 is essential!
The port and content are very similar to the previous Metal Slug games from DotEMU, meaning that the player can choose the amount of starting credit (including unlimited), choose whether to play through the whole campaign or start from a specific mission, has leaderboards for all difficulty settings, and most importantly allows for local and online coop. All kinds of controllers are recognized, which is nice considering that many games are so lazy they only recognize the XBox type controllers. The previous Metal Slug ports had slight sound issues that could pop up, I have not encountered any problem in this version yet but some people did. Also, not sure if it is because of the port or being the first game in the series and still perfunctory, but there are some occasional slight input issues: when trying to perform multiple actions at the same time, like throw a grenade and shoot, one of the actions just seems to be ignored unlike in the other Metal Slug games.
I personally use the HQ4X filter described in this guide, it was written for Metal Slug X but since the engine and file organization are similar, everything works just fine.
So overall I recommend this game to those that already have the most important Metal Slug games (2 and X) and want more content to their Metal Slug collection. Otherwise, wait for the inevitable price drop.
In any case, do not miss out on the Metal Slug series as it is gorgeous and fun, and surprisingly robust to the test of time, unlike many old games that now feel dated or clunky.
What next would I want from the Metal Slug series? Metal Slug 6 is the next in line with epic story and original new content. This is the one I want to see most. Then Metal Slug XX (a revamped Metal Slug 7). However Metal Slug 5 and to a lesser extent Metal Slug 4 could come next as they were also released on Neo Geo and their port would probably be easier. In any case, more content is better as this whole series is fun to play.

The Stanley Parable is one of my favorite games, so I was excited when I heard about this game but wasn't brainwashed into thinking I would love it. To be honest, I wasn't loving the game for the first half hour or so. It was interesting because it felt like listening to a professor critique someone's art in video game form. But it also felt like I was listening to some forum user rant about how they love some amateur artist's art and how that person is the greatest artist ever.
However, when the level with the fake written messages was shown, my mind was changed. I could relate to almost every message written, and the commentary during this level nearly brought me to tears. I've struggled with loneliness and social anxiety for the majority of my life, and making games is the only way I've been able to cope with it. Seeing that other people feel this way too and use games to cope with it was very comforting. From this point on, the game seemed much more focused and personal.
If you enjoy games that grab you and have a strong emotional impact, buy this game. I felt as if something had shifted in my mind after I played this...like I had made a decision to overcome my anxiety and not let it control me like it may have for Coda. I want to make games and let the world see my art, and I don't want my axiety to stop me from doing that.
Please keep making games, Davey. They are like water in a desert to me.

This review is based on Episode 1 and will change as necessary when the new episodes are released.
Another Telltale point&click choose-your-own-adventure game, this time starring Batman!
In spite of the people not recommending this on account of a few day 1 bugs, this is a masterfully crafted story that gets Batman right on many levels. More importantly, it gets Batman right through various filters. Be it Frank Miller's Batman breaking bones because he gets a thrill out of it and is too dangerously close to the edge, Paul Dini's Batman who understands how close to the edge he truly is, or a decidedly more stable version of our caped and coweled detective, YOU DECIDE!
But most importantly of all, this game has you playing the role not just of Batman, but of Bruce Wayne, focusing heavily on a day in the life of the richest man in Gotham when he's wearing a business suit instead of body armor. Many of the relationships that Bruce engages in are tantalizing alternate looks and what-if scenarios, including relationships that deal with the internal politics of Gotham itself on the level of, as was stated in Batman Begins, The Prince of Gotham. This story actually manages to capture that feeling and I applaud Telltale for taking that rout with it.
In many ways this is par for the course for Telltale games. The writing is rock solid, the multiple choice options are varied enough to give you an option that works for you, and the characters all have beautiful chemistry with each other. Combine the stellar writing with marvelous facial animation and top-tier voice acting, this is far closer to a Batman comic than the Arkham games ever were.
This game does have its flaws, however. At timese the walking animations are laughably robotic and Bruce has this obnoxious habit of referring to Alfred as "Al."
There are, however, plot twists aplenty, and if you like the Telltale format thus far you'll thoroughly enjoy Batman - The Telltale Series.

I've played many many RPGs in my day. Starting with Wizardry games on the PC when I was young and onto Final Fantasy, playing the newer ones as they came out. I was a PlayStation girl so I played the Personas, Xenogears, Grandias, Shadow Hearts - okay, listing them all would take too long and is off the topic. But I want you to know how well-versed I am in this genre. :)
Legend of Mysteria is the first RPG I've played on Steam that was obviously made using one of the generic RPGmakers and isn't a "big hit" game. I thought I'd give something different a chance. And I'm extremely glad I did.
Now, it's listed as a turn-based RPG but it's really all about an involving story where you do some serious detective work. In all the hours I played, I fought only a little over 10 battles - half of those, bosses. There is no leveling in this game whatsoever. You have to find different equipment to bolster your stats. And you play as a mage so the trick is figuring out what your enemy is weak against and then finding a staff or accessories that allow you to cast the elemental spell that will annihilate your target the quickest.
The meat of the game is interviewing everyone you can. Everyone thinks you're a murderer so you have to find the real culprit and clear your name. Of course, being that people view you as a killer, you must disguise yourself. You begin in a tower full of all different types of mages. You'll need to switch robes often to fit in with whatever group you're spying on. You also get different dialog choices here and there so think carefully before answering. Searching everywhere and everything is a must since you need those different colored robes, and reading notes and diaries on all the mages will help you find clues and point you towards those who might be willing to help you in your cause.
I would say this game is difficult. The times I had to turn to a walkthrough, I would sit there reading it thinking "who in the world would know this is what you're supposed to do?" But the story was so interesting that I had to see it to its end. What you do during the entire game affects what will happen at the very end. It's just very neat.
So in conclusion, this is not your typical RPG. It's frustrating at times and... no leveling? I'm  a girl who loves to level for hours so I can swat the last boss like a bug. In this game, I actually had to strategize my fights and manage my healing potions with care. :p  However, I loved Legend of Mysteria. I was never bored, the characters were interesting and detailed, and I really approved of the music selections they chose from the RPGmaker. The fact that I'm even writing this review at all says a lot because I don't really want to be doing this. I want to be playing! I just wanted you to know how much fun I had with this unique adventure. :)

I want to focus on why I LOVE Blood Bowl 2 as a mostly solo (anonymous//pub multi) player even though this game's true strength is in its playable, competitive multi-player mode...
I am a cancer surviving Old Fart who has played all kinds of games since likely before you were born... No big deal, just saying... Here'e a quick run-down of how I eventually came to become a member of the Blood Bowl community, (For the record, I am starting at BB2. Community member generational associations, while intensely version-specific, seem to be more indicative of crediblity/insight and commitment than whether folks love BB or not in a Big Picture context).
At any rate, I had BB2 on my Steam Wishlist for the LONGEST time. I watched it and debated with myself about this purchase through sale after sale, never pushing myself over the line to put it in my shopping cart. In June, I hit my 5-year post treatment milestone of being a Cancer Survivor, so I was primed for something new and different when the Summer Sale hit. While the BB2 sale bundle itself was compelling, it was the provocative first rumbling of what the BB2 Legendary Edition would be that pushed me over the line. AND AM I GLAD I BOUGHT IT!!!!
Honestly, my resigned thinking was that BB2 "as is" would be interesting, but the features that excited me were "to be" in the upcoming Legendary Edition. Once bought, however, I figured that it would be counter-productive to let this title just sit on my Steam list and no be installed and played even though I was pretty sure that the Legenary Edition would be a "soloist" dream edition. Well, holy moly was I wrong. I LOVE the current BB2 edition and am SO looking forward to the Legendary Edition. Maybe you will be too. To check out that possibility, here is a bit of my context upon approaching Blood Bowl 2...
"In my youth", I was a multi-sport athlete -- Fall, (American) football; Winter, wrestling; and Spring, the King of Sport, lacrosse (I grew up in the suburbs of Balitmore, MD and went to college on a lacrosse/football scholarship). Of course that did not get me anywhere, really, other than to the orthopedic surgeon and chiropractor due to repeated injuries, etc. but it did teach me a LOT about "play-based, positional" sports strategy where both skill and luck-of-the-moment exist in a yin-yang dynamic. I also played a lot of chess. I like how computer implementation can turn "traditional" board games into "dynamic/mutable" games that are chess-like but have an RNG-based risk aspect to them that "pure board" games, like chess, intentional (and physically) do not allow.
All this said, once I _finally_ broke down and purchased Blood Bowl 2 during the Summer Sale I HAVE BEEN HAVING A BLAST since "frame 1" of the launch of this game. I laugh a lot at the spot-on parody of "professional" sports programming from Jim and Bob. I am only a few games into the "tutorial" campaign of single player mode, so I am decidedly no expert. But what I can say is that EVERYTHING about the gameplay has been awesome already, so the upcoming multi-featured BB2 Legendary Edition is sure to be pure adrenaline eye- and brain-candy fun.
This coming weekend, August 4-7, there is a Beta weekend for current owners and Legendary Edition pre-order folk. I am SO looking forward to it. However, to date, I have only ever played solo/tutorial campaign mode. It scares the proverbial willies out of me to contemplate that the only way I will be able to try out the upcoming Legenardy Edition will be to go "mana a mama" with a fellow human player, but I'll do my best. I figure there will many other solo/new players as well, so "no harm, no foul" I suppose. It is not that I won't have fun... I just don't want to p__s a decent experienced player off by subjecting them to play far worse than they are used to.
Long term, I believe I will play enough BB2LE to join and play in multiplayer league/tournatment communities... but from what I have exerienced so far with BB2 and what is on the list of features for BB2LE, I believe the BB franchise will be a welcoming place for solo/campaign players as well as its well-established multi-player leagues, etc.
So, bottom line... even if you don't anticipate real-time, multi-player being the core of your interest in Blood Bowl, I can resoundingly say as a mostly-solo/co-op style player, Blood Bowl 2 is a great sports/chess-like game.
I am so looking forward to the August 4-7 beta weekend! :D
P.S. If there are any less-than-pro/serious players out there who would like to try to hook-up for a casual fun game during the upcoming beta, please do not hesitate to friend/ping me.
:-)
Seriously, if you are like me and have thought about it, now is a good  time to be checking out Blood Bowl 2 in anticipation of its upcoming Legendary Edition.

To begin Blood Bowl is a tactical turn-based game. Think of it sort of like american football Xcom set in the Warhammer universe. You'll be cursing Nuffle when you roll double skulls, and praising him when you pull off some crazy plays. Players earn Star Player Points for doing different actions (basically XP) and you level them up and give them skills. And then you watch them lose -1 in attributes or even die.
For anyone wanting to get into Blood Bowl BB2 is pretty approachable, at least in comparison to the first game. The UI is a lot better than the first game's. The base game's campaign with the Reikland Reavers is okay I guess. It has some gimmicky stuff I don't really care for, and it introduces mechanics here and there as you go along which I guess is easier? I learned by just doing standard games so I can't really comment. Either way you can do single-player leagues if you're nervous about online matches. And there's cKnoor on youtube / twitch who does videos, sites like fumbbl and bbtactics, and the community here on steam has guides and are generally pretty helpful.
As far as my thoughts on BB2 itself I think it's solid. I played BB1 but waited on BB2. It wasn't doing the teams as dlc that bothered me, but doing day 1 dlc of either Wood Elves or Lizardmen was crap. And seeing BB2 be played it did have a bit of a rocky start. Still, it's a good game. The UI itself is really nice compared to BB1. Numbers on tackle zones, dodge percentages, etc., are all great to have. And with Legendary coming out soon it's a definite recommendation from me. If you're reading this at the time Legendary is still up for pre-order you do get instant access to the base game and dlc while you wait for the teams and features Legendary will bring. For 45 USD, or 40 at the time of the pre-order discount which is what I paid, it's a good deal. Even more so on sale. And if you're just new BB2 Legendary is a nice entry point. There's no reason to get the base game only now.
Pro-tip: press ctrl for turning on player names and skill icons. And press c for changing the camera.
Now I just gotta wait on my favorite team, the Amazons, to come in Legendary Edition and I'm good to go.

With development on it starting way back in 2010, StudioMDHR's Cuphead is finally here. Officially announced in 2014, its been a hotly anticipated game for me and boy did it deliver.
Punishingly hard at times but incredibly satisfying once you master the many bosses and levels it has to offer, Cuphead will both frustrate and please you. Thankfully, the game offers unlimited lives and you don't lose upgrades or coins upon death.
The story is pretty simple, seeing as its inspired by 30's cartoons. Cuphead and his pal Mugman go to play dice but ultimately lose to the Devil and thus are forced to collect souls for him in the hopes of him sparing their soul. Given powers via a magical potion gifted by their friend, they set off to save their very souls.
Cuphead, apart from playing at 60fps, genuinely feels like you are playing a cartoon from the 1930's. Full of vibrant colours, fast-paced and hectic music, and some truly imaginative enemy design, the game is bloody gorgeous. I felt like I was playing out a classic Max Fleischer or Disney cartoon, waiting for Betty Boop, Popeye, or Mickey & friends to pop out at any minute.
With animations and colouring done completely by hand, its not hard to see why Cuphead took so long in development. Every single boss feels unique and has their own pattern to learn, with multiple phases to work through, getting intense the closer you get to the climax.
The game even shows you how close you are to the end of a fight, as if to taunt you for getting so close (or nowhere at all). The screen can get incredibly busy at times with all the enemies and projectiles flying at you, causing you to die if you lose focus for even a second.
Its not all bosses though, there are a handful of run and gun levels, featuring classic platformer elements. These are optional but by doing these you can collect gold coins to then purchase different weapons (especially Chaser, that upgrade will make your experience easier, trust me) and charms, such as one that auto-parries when you jump or briefly makes you invincible upon dashing.
Super arts can also be acquired, requiring all 5 special meters to be charged, these vary in effect going from a ton of damage or brief invincibility.
You also have flying sections where you control a plane that can shrink in size to dodge more easily but deal less damage, and later on, you can use bombs to deal more damage but have to be much closer to do so. These flying sections in particular were the hardest fights for me, having to dodge in all directions while having flying projectiles to deal with is really not my forte, but I eventually managed.
The music, both in terms of theme and the actual sound quality of it, could be placed over one of the classic cartoons and it would not sound out of place. Particularly the King Dice song that plays between islands, I loved that damn piece.
There are three islands that you'll be working your way through, but to move on to the next one you have to beat all the bosses, either in the simple mode or the regular mode, but to fight the final boss you do have to beat them on regular. So keep that salt handy, because it will flow.
Initially, you have a mere three hit points with no means of restoring health during levels. You can get an upgrade that bumps it up to four but as you can only equip one charm at a time, its up to you whether you want that one extra hit point or something like brief invincibility.
Co-op is local only, which is unfortunate. Keep in mind though that this makes bosses even more frantic as both of you have to dodge attacks, and, while you can revive each other, you still have to manage to stay alive to do so and reach their ghost in time.
I should note that when it comes to platformers, I am pretty bad for the most part. This took me much longer than I expected to actually beat but once I did, I felt like a great weight had been taken off me, Cuphead lured me in with its gorgeous art style and music, then kicked my♥♥♥♥♥until I finally beat it.
Both a work of art and a phenomenal game, Cuphead has already secured its place in my top 10 this year.

LASTING IMPRESSIONS
Five Nights at Freddy's
GENRE
Horror/Point-And-Click
STORY
Five Nights at Freddy's follows the story of Mike Schmidt, the new night guard for the vintage pizzeria starring the animatronic characters Freddy Fazbear, Chica the Chicken, Bonnie the Bunny, and Foxy the Pirate Fox. Upon starting his first night, Mike is informed by the previous night guard of his duties; check the cameras, make sure everything stays in place, and don't get murdered by the animatronics.  You know, the usual. Mike must now survive five(seven) nights in the building making sure to not run out of power, not get murdered by haunted robots, and get his paycheck.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay is fairly basic; easy to learn, hard to master. As your job is to guard the building, you must constantly check the cameras. This will allow you to know where the animatronics are, and keep some of them in place. Along with the camera you have the doors and the lights. The doors are used to keep any and all animatronics at bay should they decide your office would be a nice place to sneak into. The lights will let you know if Bonnie or Chica are outside of their respective doors, so that you may promptly close it right in their faces. Be careful not to forget that this pizzeria has fallen on hard times, and is running on a battery of sorts. All appliances run on this battery, and if you run out of power; it's over.
FINAL THOUGHTS
Five Nights at Freddy's is the first horror game I've ever played. In my first couple play sessions I was spooked solid. The game left me on edge, paranoid, and gave me a cold feeling inside. Sadly, the feeling didn't last. After a couple more play sessions it wasn't scary, it was frustrating. It had devolved from a horrific version of Night Trap to Night Guard Simulator 2014. I could only get enjoyment out of it by playing it with friends in a skype call. While I still enjoyed the whole look of the game and got quite engrossed the lore behind it all, I couldn't slog my way through all the nights. Five Nights at Freddy's did not leave a lasting impression, but I'll give it props for trying.

I have experienced very few games like Sunless Sea: a game that is both casual, and completely engrossing.
After booting up the game, the player finds themselves in the town of Fallen London, a once great city which was unfortuitously dragged into a massive underground ocean by angry bats during the reign of Queen Victoria. From there, you are given a bout, some crew, a few strange coins, and a mission: explore, bring glory to the empire, die where someone will find you.
One could roam the oceans doing menial tasks for the hierarchy to scrape up a few coins, or, one could side with the Great Khanate, trading their honor for riches.
Alternatively, you can be Captain Crusty Cumswallow, scourge of the low-zees, fighting off overlarge sharks, moustachieod fish, defenseless merchants, and the wrath of the gods whilst smuggling pornagraphy and human souls in the hopes of one day putting your feet up in your zeeside mansion.
In this game, you really feel the choices you make, and you can reap their benefits of suffer cruel punishment for the smallest actions, which can be a no-go for some people, but for me I found that it accuratly portrays the fragility of life on the Zee, in the dark, with no friends. The only true negative I can think of about this game is it's lack of replayablity, as every character will eventually carry out most of the same missions with most of the same officers, which averages out to a mostly the same experience.
I would highly recommend people who enjoy exploration and adventure, but wouldn't cry if you character of 12 hours goes insane and is murdered by what crew he hasnt eaten yet.

An absolutely great game even in Alpha. The easy difiiculty is exactly as prescribed, "pensive exploration," where the middle difficulty is dangerous and tough. I haven't even tried the hardest yet. Keep a pen and paper handy to draw a map of your area, you will get lost when the weather comes in. Once you get established in a shelter with some wood and food, don't venture without proper equipment and a plan. The game makes sense and there is a purpose to everything. For example, a deer was frozen. I couldn't harvest it without a knife. Then it dawned on me to light a fire nearby and defrost it. At 50% thawed, I could harvest by hand. Simple but genius.
Recommendations for the developers to consider:
Mechanism to siphon fuel from the abandoned cars
Be able to craft a knife
Tune the game so that durable tools like the hatchet do not degrade so quickly
Binoculars would be a nice touch
Ax to chop down a whole tree would be good but would likely be very difficult and would consume many calories
Rub sticks for a fire by hand (make that very hard - last resort type stuff)
Duct tape
Some birds sound tropical
Handguns would be good to add variety instead of just the rifle
Bugs:
Just two so far - a soda can was hovering in mid-air in a house and when I chopped up a table the dishes hovered after the table was harvested.

There is good and bad.
Personally I love this game. It is by far the most realistic survival game I have ever seen. Do get it, you'll like it, but be aware of the following;
The good:
- intense and gripping, never gets boring
- MEGA FUN
- realistic
- solar storms deserve somebody to make a apocalypse story about them, hello? No electricity, colder (like an extra -20) winter and mad animals. And more, no wifi! What's more epic than that? P.S., you think that's an easy apocalypse to survive compared to zombies? Play this game then say!!
- dev team are releasing about an update a week, you heard me, an update a week?! :)
- they definitely wont abandon this game, trust me, they wont
- you can't jump. Unrealistic, you may say at first, but oh, my friend, do you jump over rocks and up mountains, or do you climb?
- its hard
The bad;
- the devs are really anti making shelters and living outside, in other words, a building HAS to be your home in the current state
- you can't chop wood off trees! Hello? You're in a forest! You've got to go find wood on the ground or rip up furniture (for the record, you can burn wood from live trees, it's just less productive)
- if you're waiting for story mode skip a few years in a time machine, cos I don't think they ever want to make that, it's sandbox only now my friends!
- wolves don't attack humans, I'm aware that they state that obvious error in the description and that the geo storm has disrupted their brains (true), but to make them aggressive (false).
- bears should be more dangerous (my opinion)
- this game says "no zombies, just you against the elements...", but has anyone else noticed? The wolves, ARE, the zombies!
- you are not rewarded for your knowledge of the wilderness, cannot use knowledge to know what wood is best for a bow or what plants are edible. It's just really a test of your patience, but still fun
- things break unnecessarily quick. Every time you hack up a log you lose 2% on your hatchet out of a total of 100. All in all, that makes a 30-year lifespan tool live for about three months in game, don't get me started on the clothes...
- not very interactive, you don't "start a fire" literally, you click a button that says you are and on chance it may or may not be done. A randomiser hooked up to a switch.
- the game is waaaaay too number-y. Everything has a percentage of damage and a percentage of success and a number of HP. What weirdo can tell in real life how much percentage left of his knife he has left? Or what direct treatments for his wounds should be. The game should include an option where you click to say observe your tool and give an estimate when it will break. Or instead of have a bar of hunger, just say "I'm hungry". It should be a lot more environmentally immersive, not numerically, thats all I'm saying.
- no lighters, do people in Canada just not smoke?
But ultimately, great game! Just if any of that *minority* bad effect you, then consider it. I'm just being truthful on my opinion.

Blood and Bacon is a lighthearted single player or cooperative first/third person shooter set on a farm with zombie pigs. The gameplay is similar to Killing Floor, Left 4 Dead, and Serious Sam. The goal of the default game mode is to survive increasingly difficult waves of enemies each level. The levels vary by enemy type, ultra violent bonus revenge rounds, and occasional boss battles. The ultimate goal of the game is to purge the farm of undead pigs while unlocking new weapons, hats, and characters.
-101 levels of increasing difficulty
-Various unlockable weapons, powerups, and cheat options
-Steam achievements/Trading Cards
-Excellent controller support
-Free content updates by developer
-Easter eggs and other secrets
-Creative over the top gore
-High entertainment to price ratio
-Only one map
-Charming, but dated graphics
-Repetitive enemy types and bosses
-Normal difficulty might not be challenging for some players
This game is a fantastic value at $0.99 and I highly recommend it to anybody who enjoys games like Killing Floor or any FPS featuring hundreds of enemies. Blood and Bacon offers a lot of entertainment for the price of admission, but don't expect next generation graphics or a fully developed storyline. It costs less than a weapon skin from games like that and it's already more entertaining than a similarly priced candy bar.

I rate the game Just Cause 2 4/5. Good.
While this game improves upon nearly every aspect of the first Just Cause its most fun moments come not from the main plot but from tooling around the game's massive, open-world environments on your own. However, like the first game, Just Cause 2 often feels like it has many more sights to see than interesting things to actually do and this is the game's biggest weakness. The main plot (which is not very interesting in itself) can be over and done long before you see even half of this game's massive open world, which is a real shame because this game really is quite beautiful. You can see and do stuff after the main plot is over though but in that situation it seems odd that you are still hanging around, causing the poor country even more trouble while not seeing much about the country actually change as a result of your efforts.
Like in Far Cry 3, when your faction takes an area over I want the enemy soldiers to no longer be present there in the future. I want to see other major changes taking place also as a result of your faction having gained control along with many more additional side quests which spring up as a result of those changes. Just Cause 2 doesn't do this and Just Cause 2 also doesn't seem to really give a hoot about ethics. Steal anyone's car, shoot anyone, run over innocent bystanders, whatever. The game doesn't punish you in any way other than your actions drawing more of the attention of the enemy military. So yes, the game punishes you for hurting people but only in the short term. Just Cause 2 unfortunately does not really keep track of how evil you act and give you any lasting plot-oriented or quest/faction altering repercussions. If you act evil in general, maybe the factions you are helping should start acting more evil due to your example and vice versa...or something like that.
So far as its quests are concerned, when playing this game I found I often found myself missing Skyrim's tendency to have a quest or two associated with every single geographic location in the game. This game features fairly large geographic areas which may easily go unexplored (unless, of course, you like working for factions which are thinly disguised Islamic terrorists or doing quests for drug dealers. I honestly didn't have any problem working for the socialists, but then that's me. This game tries hard to beat Grand Theft Auto at its own game but never quite succeeds at being extremely funny and still doesn't really have any GTA style radiostations nor does it really have any interesting music to listen to. Most of the humor comes from the sheer craziness of the stunts you can pull off and the ludicrousness of the game's action. You can here little radio propaganda pod-casts occasionally from the government over your character's pda smart phone thing but podcasts these are few and far between.
This game really needs some more, seemingly random, personal quests in it like Skyrim had. This game needs some quests from seemingly random people you meet on the street or in the villages. Instead, all quests are directly related to things the game's main factions want you to do and are given to you only by the different faction leaders. This faction-focussed quest structure combined with the relative dearth of quests severely limits how deep or interactive the game world seems to be. This lack of quests/objectives leading to a lack of interactivity with the world is my biggest issue with this game and to make matters worse, the various factions and your choices regarding which faction to side with doesn't seem to have any great affect on how the game world turns out after the game's conclusion resulting in a fairly shallow experience in terms of plot and in terms of the affect you have on the world and a lack of any emotional catharsis.
The multiplayer mod looks like it had potential at one time but now what few rooms do still have people in them are also full of unusual game modifications, oddly re-worked control schemes which may interfere with your existing controls and still nothing much of interest to actually do besides finding and irritating other players. Almost tragically, the multiplayer mod has about as little to do (if not less) as the single player game.
But despite its various flaws there is also a whole lot to like. This game has
+Beautiful graphics. Truly this is the most beautiful third-person perspective game I have ever played. There's wonderful day/night cycle and the game has weather and wonderfully realistic looking clouds/sky. The tropics look muggy. The desert looks hot (with heat distortions in the air) and the mountaintops look very chilly with frost clinging to all surfaces. Just remember to turn decals off to prevent a memory leak which can result in the game crashing and kicking you back to your desktop.
+Varied and lush environments (even the desert islands have a lot of interesting stuff happening in them, full of people seeming to interact with one another and interesting sights.
+Good vehicular interactivity. Every vehicle in this game can be stolen and driven/flown. Everything from tiny, underpowered motor scooters to large passenger planes can be piloted. Flying helicopters and airplanes is pretty easy. This leads to some amazingly funny and absurd situations, like having a running gun battle with the military while trying to flee in a 3 wheeled taxi.
+Wonderful destructability. While entire large buildings cannot be usually destroyed smaller structures can often be destroyed. Tires on vehicles can also be destroyed.
+Excellent controls though with a keyboard and mouse there may be a bit of a harsh learning curve. Unlike in the first Just Cause, your grappling hook is actually a lot of fun and is really useful. I used it almost constantly.
+Fun use of the game's physics engine to cause even more crazy situations. Vehicles can be attached to one another with your grappling hook. Indeed, pieces of debris can be attached to your vehicle. Even enemies and pedestrians can be attached to your vehicle. Enemies can be attached to each other.
+Good though fairly repetitive sound effects with loud, cracking explosions. Despite the fact that it sounds like the same explosion over and over it's still a very satisfying sound.
+A truly expansive virtual environment to explore. While perhaps not as massive an area as the first Just Cause game this is a lot more geographic variety to be had (this game could have used more easter eggs and references to other games/movies though to liven up the mood even further). It's just too bad that the game doesn't really reward you very much for doing all the exploring which you will have to do to see the game's whole environment.
Overall this game is a lot of fun to play but oddly, I wish it had been even more ambitious than it was. There's just so much to see and not enough to do.

Relaxingly brutal city-builder/strategy game. You build a society up from the bare basics and then they become too huge and die off in a terrible catastrophe. Again and again. You develop strategies to deal with it, ways to increase productivity, but then you want to add in little challenges, which inevitably causes society to collapse and people to starve to death in the streets. Totally uneducated society? Sure, why not? Society in the cold mountains? Heck yeah. Society without any religious structures? Sure, that should work fine. (It does.)
The music is peaceful, and the seasons add to that sense of peace while your society is collapsing in a spiral of death and despair. You bide the time while hundreds of people die in a single winter. I made up a game where the oldest person closest to Town Hall is the mayor. It's fun to find that person and watch them die.
This game instills a strong sense of Nihilism, and a peaceful acceptance that things are probably messed up from the beginning but you won't know until it's far too late.
And I utterly love it.

This game was something I had heard a lot about online and from friends, but I kept intentional ignorance on everything about the game so that I would be able to play it without knowing what to expect. Little did I know that that ignorance was going to make me feel more paranoid and helpless than I ever have in my entire life. I won't type review cliche of explaining the story, I'll just review gameplay and try my best not to spoil anything as far as gameplay goes.
Pros:
* Entering it with ignorance creates a truly horrifying experience.
* Produces a lot of paranoia while playing.
* Feeling helpless during gameplay makes it so much scarier.
* The simplistic character and level design (as well as simple game mechanics) really make the game seem scarier.
Cons:
* Once you've been scared a few times, you pick up on how to detect when something bad is going to happen, making the game feel redundant if you get too familiar.
* Can also be too easy if you establish a rhythm for checking the cameras and doors.
End result:
Without picking it apart too much, I give it a solid 8/10. It produces a lot of unexpected scares, but they do seem to be repetitive after a few hours of gameplay, and the game doesn't produce a lot of replay value, either. However, during the first playthrough, the ignorance of what you're doing and how to make it through the night creates a terrifying environment that is an adrenaline rush full of paranoia, suspension, and helplessness.

Having never played any iteration of Blood Bowl, I checked it out because I like both Warhammer and strategy games. I spent a good amount of time familiarizing myself with the various teams before setting into the campaign. It was fun right up until the Turnover rule is introduced to you. This is a gamebreakingly bad mechanic. In a split second, all the excitement of having battled tooth and claw with a Greenskin eam followed by a hardy Dwarf team was sapped away in turn1 against the High Elf team when you're notified "True Blood Bowl" includes a mechanice whwere the first one of your players to fail an action results in an immediate end of turn. Each team having 11 players on the field, it makes no sense whatsoever that everyone stops what they're doing because one idiot tripped(no, I'm serious, your characters can trip while running, resulting in a turnover) You can turnover on your very first attempt to do anything in your turn resulting in all 11 players doing NOTHING. This takes an otherwise very fun and challenging strategy game and breaks it to unplayability. I almost bought all the dlc today, that's how much I was enjoying this up to that moment. Now I feel like even had I gotten it free, I'd be salty about the amount of time wasted to come to this conclusion. And there are no custom settings to shut it off either. I never knew, or really cared enough, to find out why Blood Bowl wasn't played by more Warhammer people despite the fact the tabletop has been around so long. Now I know. They had this great thing and they shot it in the face with this one Turnover rule that someone, somewhere thinks is great.
TLDR: You vs "RNGesus" no level of skill and tactics will equal the role pure luck plays in success/failure.

Alright. A few things. First; I have no previous Bloodbowl experience. I didn't play the boardgame, I didn't play the first game on pc, hell, I barely have any real Warhammer experience other than Total War. So, this is a review probably for people like me.
I bought Bloodbowl 2 out of sheer curiosity. I love X-Com. A lot. The games are fantastic and they have been since their inception (even if the earlier games were maybe a bit too hard for my taste. I want a game, not another abusive relationship) Bloodbowl 2 brings some of these same strategic playstyles and game features to a more light-hearted (offline) place: Football. I f***king hate sports, to be honest. But Bloodbowl is pretty effing fun. I have done some campaign and I have done a lot of offline play but it was most fun when I was playing it online with someone who understood the game as well as I did (meaning, meh. pretty little). S**t was fun. Really fun. I won't get into the dumb micro-transactions or the over priced races because I just want people to see the core gameplay for what it is. It's a really, really interesting take on the rules of football and the lore of Warhammer. If you like X-Com and you don't want to see your crew die quite as much, this might be your jam. I've loved every second. It's easy to pick up and play for a couple games and then set down. Or, if you're awful like me, you'll probably go offline so no one knows you're on and just binge the game for an eight hour night. Your call.
Plus, the game is pretty cheap right now. I bought it for $10 but even the $20 asking price is well worth the package.

This is one of the best survival games ever made, and potentially one of the best computer games out there right now.
Why is this game so good?
1) As a player, you have to really be on the ball to *make* it; the realism is amazing. One major mistake and you might be dead.
2) As sound effects go, Hinterland Games has done a perfect job of giving every single item, action, and event its own unique and lively sound; it enhances the gameplay experience hugely.
3) Can't say enough about the awesome weather.
4) Every single resource is precious and item valuation is top notch - a can of tomato soup can save you; a toque can give you an edge in warmth so you can stay outside just a little longer; a hunting knife enables you to extract meat (but where are you gonna find a knife??).
5) The gameplay system is on its way to stardom; it's only in alpha right now, yet is worthy of multiple playthroughs.
Examples of awesome gameplay:
1) I needed to get some wood to heat up snow to make water and while I was out, a huge blizzard rolled in and I didn't know the way back. I had to check my footprints in the snow to see where I had come from in order to find shelter.
2) I got mauled by a bear...and survived!...bearly. It took about 2 days of R&R to get back to full strength, which took a lot of food and time and left me in an impoverished state. I almost didn't make it through, but I did.
3) Nearly out of food, I went fishing with my last supplies. Both of my fishing hooks broke, and I was a goner. Bad luck, in addition to making mistakes, is death.
There are tons of improvements and enhancements to be made for The Long Dark, but without a doubt Hinterland Games has opened its doors with a gem. Just look at the *overwhelmingly positive* trail of reviews for a game still in alpha. If you like intense survival strategy, this is not a game to miss.

This game is a truly excellent experience, and one that should not be missed. It has deep, challenging (but rewarding) gameplay, and the story and setting are very finely crafted. One of my new favorite games, and one that deserves the hype that it gets...mostly.
The only issue I have with it is the moral choice system and the ending. If you haven't played this yet, be warned, you'll constantly be presented with a moral choice throughout the game. But there are only two endings, one for those who were complete saints, and one for everyone else, regardless of whether you did one bad thing or were a complete psychopath. So there is no point to alternating your attitude, and it's better to decide to either be pure good or pure evil at the start. In order to get the most out of it, you should just make the same choice throughout, which rather undermines the whole point of having a constant moral choice throughout the game. A major mar on an otherwise near flawless experience.

WARNING: This is a review for InDev 28c and this games updates a lot so maybe my review will be obsolete in the future. That being said I will write it half review half starting guide for the ones who are interested in the game.
As a side note I play this a lot in offline so my hours on record are alot more than what it says in Steam.
1º The game is hard, and by that I mean
. You will be bound to fail the first time, do not despair. The final goal of the game is ruin your rising village (hence the name Rise to Ruins). Some might complain about starving and dehydrating, yeah thats a common issue there, unless you build first the
... so in order to survive more days you need to perfect your early building planning.
2º This games is a half tower defense for the time being. So the monsters will be quite strong in later stages of the game and if you do not plan correctly like building and improving the towers, and narrowing your entrance with walls you will have a very hard time defending your village. The monsters have resistances and vulnerabilities, so a varied tower building and improving is highly encouraged. Remember the ultimate goal of this game is Ruin your village.
Aside tower defenses you have the oportunity to have
(Villager Job who specializes on fending off monsters and patrolling) and
(An entity made of essence that will defend your village and can be upgraded) both of them have a specific defense building that let us recruit them. I must note the guards and golems sometimes go full Leroy Jenkins on a monster horde, my personal preference is golems over guards but I saw fulfilling maps with a good guard regiment.
3º There are 2 main modes (aside difficulties)
(With a shared pool called Limbo for Villagers and Resources, and also monsters if you send them to that place, consider cleaning the limbo from monsters when you start a new village in a same World unless you want surprises) and
that is basically independent villages that will only be affected by what happens inside that gameplay.
4º There are two RNG events
they can hit you consecutively, and range from an eclise to an earthquake (and a lot more) so be prepared for them while you play. And the appearence of "allied forces" that is
(Pet Dogs) who are neutral mobs and
potential villagers so they will be hostile with every monster mob (rescue them). The hit-rate of the harmful RNG is influenced by the size of your village, that also influences the appearence of the "allied forces" so in early game you will be mostly safe unless you are hated by the RNG gods.
5º Jobs, as I said before ther is Guard Job, but there are a lot more, every Job has its own building, yeah you will not full all the places in that job but you can change the job of the villagers if for some reason you lack manpower in that aspect. That being said the villagers sometimes fail to do their jobs due to 2 main reasons, aggro towards monsters and confussion and mainly due to the powers, and this takes us to the next point.
6º Powers, right now they are limited. They are fuelled with
aka Mana this resource will recharge slowly and also with the drops from the living beings and monsters. This powers let you interact with the world. That being said some are lackluster and some are essencial to the survavility of the village. But still they need improvement.
-------------
Side Notes:
-The game runs in Java, so despite having that pixel look it needs a moderate specs computer. Because its JAVA!!
-The developer is quite active in the forums and he will answer your questions and troubleshooting he also makes roadmaps for future updates. Like for the version 29 the inclusion of a Shop system and overhaul of Storages and Farms.
With all that said, I hope you will be interested in the game.

Limbo is one of the games that will stay with me for a very long time. And that's saying something for a game you will finish in a few hours. It's not because the story is epic. It's not because the gameplay is out of this world. The mechanics are good, but nothing you haven't seen before in other games. And still this game made a big impression on me.
The reason that a game with only left+right+jump controls and one contextual 'use' button accomplishes this is atmosphere. The protagonist is thrown in one of the drabiest of places one can imagine and the player is given the same feeling since there is no information what-so-ever. You're as helpless and alone as the poor little boy on the screen.
Limbo is a seemingly simple platformer with intricate little puzzles. At times you will think you're stuck, because let's face it; There's not much the little boy can perform. And yet, for the oberservant player there are various visual and aural clues to get you further.
I can heartily recommend this game to anyone that has at least average timing abilities or doesn't suffer from a serious depression.

A very notice open-world third person shooter with a bunch of story and a lot of explosions. The typical Just Cause formula.
There's simply nothing bad you can say about this game, it's fun, challenging enough to not get boring easily, it becomes a sandbox after the main story ends and there's a crapton of collectables.
Gameplay:
The game starts out relatively fast paced, the tutorial is fluently designed to work with the game, but features like using the grapling hook to pull down enemies from high points, i.e. watchtowers, or connecting them to the ingame world, i.e. surroundings or vehicles, are simply sandbox gimmicks: Fun to use every now and then, but essentially you'll forget about them in the heat of combat.
Graphics:
I can't say too much about this part, as my computer forces me to play on low-ish settings, even then the graphics are simply stunning, with little details such as Rico's clothes "looking" wet after coming out of water. Especially explosions look amazing.
AI:
Could be better, but it's pretty advanced. Whenever available, any AI combatants will use any stationary turrets in their surroundings. A great example of this is the gangs fighting military forces (the military wins most of the time), after which the military forces generally use the gang-vehicle's stationary turret. Although their aim on moving targets could certainly improve.
Controls:
Of course, controls are customizeable but are easily learned nonetheless, the game supports controller input as well. I do really dislike the default map button assignment, which is F1 for some reason, playing on a laptop would force me to hit Fn and F1 all the time, but I simply changed it to M, which makes more sense imo.
Vehicles each control differently but are generally very steerable, I suggest using a controller for driving cars. Helicopters are the easiest to steer in my oppinion, while (jet-)planes are hardest.
Misc.:
After the main story, the so called "Mercenary-Mode" is being activated, in which you can freely roam the island and clear settlements to reach 100% progression, which is a nice challenge. What you have to do in each settlement is the same all the time: collect any special parts lying around and destroy all government equipment, such as fuel tanks, water towers or generators. Even though it sounds repetitive, it somehow doesn't get boring at all.
Overall this game is worth the money you spend on it, the multiplayer mod (which is available for free in the steam store) has improved a lot in recent times (such as synchronity and all that).

So recently I just 100% the game (minus the achievements), and I can safely say that this was one of the best games I played this year.
The movement of the game is very fluid and is a blast to experiment with; you can take huge shortcuts and take shortcuts if you learn to master how to utilize your tools to the fullest potential. The game also has a very cute artstyle and sense of humor. The game never truely takes itself seriously and that benefits the whole  lighthearted feeling of the game. The artstyle, while a bit rough, is charming and works well.
The only problems  I really had with the game involved HOW the story progressed and a couple of issues I ran into during my playthrough. The main antagonist of the story and the way the story moves felt a bit disorganized as I never really saw the villain as all that important or relevant until the very end of the game. The bugs that I ran into have (to my knowledge) been patched out by the developers, so this shouldnt effect as many others and their playthroughs any more.

Alright. A few things. First; I have no previous Bloodbowl experience. I didn't play the boardgame, I didn't play the first game on pc, hell, I barely have any real Warhammer experience other than Total War. So, this is a review probably for people like me.
I bought Bloodbowl 2 out of sheer curiosity. I love X-Com. A lot. The games are fantastic and they have been since their inception (even if the earlier games were maybe a bit too hard for my taste. I want a game, not another abusive relationship) Bloodbowl 2 brings some of these same strategic playstyles and game features to a more light-hearted (offline) place: Football. I f***king hate sports, to be honest. But Bloodbowl is pretty effing fun. I have done some campaign and I have done a lot of offline play but it was most fun when I was playing it online with someone who understood the game as well as I did (meaning, meh. pretty little). S**t was fun. Really fun. I won't get into the dumb micro-transactions or the over priced races because I just want people to see the core gameplay for what it is. It's a really, really interesting take on the rules of football and the lore of Warhammer. If you like X-Com and you don't want to see your crew die quite as much, this might be your jam. I've loved every second. It's easy to pick up and play for a couple games and then set down. Or, if you're awful like me, you'll probably go offline so no one knows you're on and just binge the game for an eight hour night. Your call.
Plus, the game is pretty cheap right now. I bought it for $10 but even the $20 asking price is well worth the package.

OK, hear me out.  The game is good.  You get Batman in all of his Bat-glory and you get another incredible Telltale story.  But I feel obligated to tell you about a couple of issues before you make your buying decision.
Only about 10% of the game includes any actual gameplay, which consists primarily of quick time events.  Being under 2 hours long, this is more like a movie than a game.  A $25 movie.  Of course, this $25 will be of much greater value when the other episodes are released.
The other issue is the lack of consequence.  In previous Telltale games, your decisions had significant and often shocking impact on the story and characters.  In this game, I don't think any of my decisions actually changed a single thing.  A few characters "remembered" what I did, but the game really let me get away with anything.  There were even multiple times when I hit the wrong button during quick time events and nothing bad happened at all.  ("I am Batman" is no excuse.  But nice try.)
In my video I said I had a great time playing and it's true.  I did.  It was fun.  But I got the game for free.  It’s hard for me to say if it’s worth the $25 at the moment.  I’m hoping the coming episodes will be more compelling and give everyone something to rave about.
EDIT:  It sounds like a lot of poeple are having crashes and framerate issues.  The game runs fine on my PC, but my PC is quite the beast.  This may be another reason for you to hold off on purchasing for now.
