I went in expecting a lot honestly. Maybe my expectations were too high. I'm not saying that the game's bad in its story; as a matter of fact it is quite engaging:
Pros
1. Being Bruce Wayne; almost all batman related games focus solely on being batman and it's understandable but I must admit that getting the chance to finally play as Bruce Wayne and see the world he sees is truly a refreshing experience.
2. Being a detective: The Arkham series did a good job with the detective mode where you could analyze evidence to form conclusions and it's good to see it expanded here with a less futuristic detective vision which requires you to get your hands dirty on the crime scene to piece things together. The fact that you can also make mistakes and draw wrong conclusions makes it all the better.
3. Politics: Being batman isn't just about putting on the suit and beating the crap out of bad guys; it's about being Bruce Wayne as well and knowing what it means to be the richest most powerful man in Gotham and the choices that you are presented with are almost...adrenaline pumping. You can choose to be the most righteous incorruptable hero you always envisioned batman to be or to play it close to the chest and know how to make use of your chess pieces carefully when dealing with people.
Unfortunately, coupled with these were problems that were simply too glaring to leave out:
1. Performance: First I had to tweak with the game for about an hour before I finally managed to get it to start up, not to mention that despite my 2GB 750 GTX NVIDIA video card and 8 GBs of RAM the game still significantly lagged even though there really isn't much action going on, which brings me to the second point.
2. The action: I understand what it means to play a Telltale game; there is less focus on the action and more on the story and by god they delivered on the story. But when you're talking about Batman, all fights being QTEs just doesn't feel right.
3. The length: With the game being just a bit over 10 bucks I didn't expect it to be awfully long but when you can finish a narrative game like this in just over an hour it leaves you wanting (especially when you realize you spent almost just as long trying to make the game to work). I've bought games for less than a buck that were longer than this. To its credit though, the game does have a lot of branching paths so at least the short story is replayable.
4. Crashing finale: When the preview for the next episode ends up freezing your hardware, it's simply a turn off...
Final thoughts: I would recommend this game on a sale but not at its full price and I really hope they patch the crash and start up issues soon.

Much like in the beta, the finished version of the game is really only enjoyable if you edit your save file from the get-go to jump up your stats and money. Otherwise, have fun grinding for several days before you have even the meager beginnings to start doing anything, and once you try to do anything, have fun barely having a 50% chance of success on anything you do.
Once edited, it's more enjoyable, because you can actually make decisions and expect them to succeed, and you skip all the interminable grinding. Or most of it, anyway.
Because even once you've got ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of money, a solid ship, the stats needed to act on stuff and a cargo hold full of various items for quests... you still need pure random chance to actually trigger the events when you hit a port and poke around. Don't get the event? Have fun going sailing again for another, interminable while until you get the alert that says you can take another shot at it.
And if you WEREN'T cheating your way to money, you'd have to do grinding in between each attempt in order to stay topped up on fuel, supplies and hull-repair.
The writing isn't fundamentally bad, but too often it tries to be prose rather than informative.
There's also the fighting is also pretty bad, since it basically consists entirely of just backpedalling while hurling salvos into enemies. There is literally no more tactics or skill to it and whether you win or not is completely down to stats and two or three consumables you can use to up your odds. Since the game has forwards and back-mounted weapons, rather than broadsides, there isn't even any space for basic naval stuff like crossing the T.

This is a single player story-driven naval RPG. You sail your ship between ports and explore dialogue trees at each port. There is some random variation in the map and story each game but not a lot, making this more like a scripted RPG than a roguelike. Death is permanent but you have the option of retaining a single item and attribute between replays.
The ship moves slowly making travel times tedius. I'd suggest installing CheatEngine or some other tool that will let you play the game in fast-forward when travelling between ports since the travel time isn't particularly interesting. This will remedy the most-often-cited complaint about the game.
The other common complaint is the user interface which is occasionally quite poor. In several places, you can only buy or trade one item at a time, requiring several clicks per trade. There are also situations where you'll need to fill your hold with 50 or more of such items, and you'll be cursing the user interface at these times.
Don't let these problems turn you off the game, though. Most of the game is very good -- it's an immersive world filled with excellent writing.

I wrote it off as 'too old' compared to the newer game, but a friend convinced me to give it another go.  On the second play though I gave it a bit longer to set the hook, and thoroughly enjoyed it.
The gameplay is good but, much like with Bioshock: Infinite, the story was the game's strongest asset.  If you've played through Inifite, or intend to, playing through the first game will illuminate elements of Infininte, as well as the DLC which follows.

The game (so far) is your standard fare of guiding a village of hopeless morons to prosperity and true strength, to the point you're literally no longer really needed, only there's god powers.
Since the game is VASTLY incomplete, I will say this game is absolutely worth the asking price, and it's REALLY fun.
However there are some thing it suffers from.
1. Survival difficulty is too difficult, and really only because A. the god spells mostly all suck total garbage in mostly every single way, and B. there's not enough structures yet to allow you some nice freedom without being inhibited and handicapped negatively, like by how the second farm type can't feed 125 people, even with literally 9 of them fully staffed.
2. Maps do apparently have a mostly-different difficulty curve associated with each and every one, making it essentially mandatory to start somewhere easy, unless you're just a badanoos at this game, and have the skill to survive in tougher areas without the benefit of just going back to another village to prepare for another try in a seperate, or the same region you'd failed in.
3. Spells such as Holy Golem, Dissolve, Earthquake, and Storm either cost too much to be useful, don't last long enough, or aren't effective enough.
Holy Golem can't 1v1 a zombie with 250 health if it has 300. This it kinda pathetic, since it's SUPPOSED to be a sort of divine god unit that can help turn a battle. It literally can get killed by 3 headless, since it degens health for some reason, which unequipped villagers can kill without problem.
Dissolve literally will never refund it's cost. It's supposed to remove corpses and resources from the map while giving you mana, or Influence, but it never has ever atleast gained me as much as it costs to cast the spell. However it DOES have a use as clearing corpses into essence for the purpose of fuelling essence collectors.
Earthquake and Storm take 3/4 of your influence/mana to cast, but neither can even destroy an enemy spawner. It seems like Earthquake should be designed to do this, since it's a large AoE spell with the highest cost, tied with Storm, which seems like a good way to thin a herd of enemies before nightfall, sicne it can easily kill most units instantly, or damn-near instantly.
4. Other spells, like Flame nad Meteor have VERY limited uses that can be on some vague benefit to you at all. Resurrect, which revives dead villagers if you click their ghost during ONLY Dawn or Dusk, which their ghost sometimes just never even appears, say they die in the morning, has a high cost, and roughly a 1/5 chance of just creating a zombie, instead of reviving the dead villager.
Flame is really only vaguely useful against low-health monsters like Headless, but like I said earlier, literally every can kill then in a 2 headless versus one of anything type of fight. The burning damage effect only affects buildings after 4 casts of this spell, which is less than 1/4 of the mana/influence bar, but the total damage of that many, is just pathetic, even if applied to enemies like Slimes or decent-health zombies.
Meteor can one-shot most units if they're not inside the hitbox of another unit or building. However they deal a slightly better amount of damage in an aoe, and can burn enemies after 4 casts in one location, but has as much killing power if not more than Earthquake or Storm if you use the entire mana/influence bar.
Burning damage is OP against your own villagers, so using them to help in battles is utterly pointless, and you'll most likely just kill your own people alongside the enemy, and every single person is needed entirely in Survival difficulty.
5. Monsters will prioritize dogs, gates, buildings, and then villagers usually when attacking at night, maknig Guards almost useless. Guards are also made worse when they equip leather and copper gear instead of iron, vastly limiting their possible effectiveness. Honestly I have literally no idea why monsters even drop leather armor, and copper swords. They're literally worse than iron gear, which you can start making literally as soon as day 4 if you rush for it, which is when monsters start ot appear on the map, while night 5, is when they start to attack and is rather tiny numbers, but by then, you can have a full guard with small amounts of iron gear anyways, so it makes leather/copper gear really quite irrelevant from the very moment you can ever get it, like literally.
6. Worse of all, builders randomly chat with one another, delaying them doing their jobs, which causes builder amounts under 25 or even 20 if you're patient unlike me, to be required, or else it'll take literally all day to complete one single level 1 bow tower. And btw, this chatting happens whenever a building is almost done, but ofcourse every builder who worked on this structure does NOT just go ahead and finish the structure up, but rather, they all WAIT until the last guy comes over to finish the building.
This is actually horrifically stupid by every concievable and possible term. It's so stupid, it almost hurts. Builders, should either continually work on a project until it's done, and then maybe chat for ten seconds or so, nothing more, or they should not chat ever and go to other projects until it's time to go home where they'd chat with whomever they share their home with.
That, or CHAT DURING WORK LIKE NORMAL PEOPLE WOULD.
The above 6 things, are all things I really don't like about this game. Still gonna play it however because the game is still good in spite of those points and also the obviously early point in it's development.

Ok just as a heads up, I got this game off of a giveaway, I never would have noticed it otherwise. However, while this may just seem like a cute little indie game that you'll pick up once then be done with, that was quite the opposite of what I have experienced.
So to start off, this game a has a HUGE learning curve. You'll probably do ok until winter, only having a couple monsters attack, and a couple people die. That period soon ends. My first play through I was all over, struggled until winter, then died a horrible death. However, through that play through, gave me so much insight onto the game, my second play through went far better.
The gameplay mechanics are fun, the heat, weather, light mechanics are all well done and provide nice modifiers to the game. The screen can get cluttered at times, but looks fairly clean until mid-late game. I’m a little iffy on the almost micro-management feature where you designate what to harvest, because I kept catching myself not having anything harvested. While being a little annoying at the start, you grow accustomed to it, and helps in the long run. Trying to manage resources was ok, kept getting annoyed that I didn’t have enough workers, boards, cut stones, etc. but I learned. (as I said this game has a HUGE learning curve)
The defensive mechanics were a little confusing to start, I didn’t know which golems were best, or how many turrets, walls, moats, that I needed. I learned through time, but would appreciate a clear stat sheet. trying to expand without getting horrible destroyed by monsters was fun, and always changing.
So in conclusion, I would HIGHLY recommend this game. It has its weak points, but that is to be expected with early access. The mechanics were fun, learning how each aspect worked was amazing, and kept me coming back for more. I learned to love the soundtrack, even though it would be playing the most chill music while all of my villagers were getting killed. They have an active discord, which has helped me learn a lot of the mechanics, and how to streamline my game. I love the feel of this game and would recommend it to all of my friends.

LIMBO is an indie horror puzzle sidescroller where the main character enters the limbo in search of his sister. The game uses a simple design of using a gradient of only black and white colors, and objects are shown by their silhouettes. Also, for most of the game, there are no background music, but sound effects such as water dropping, or crank spinning are amplified. These techniques successfully create the creepy, suspenseful feeling which immerses the player to the game. As for the puzzle element, they are very well designed to match the setting and mood of the game. This game was a bit short but was an amazing experience. I highly recommend this game to anyone.

Don't let the survival genre intimidate you into overlooking this really marvelous game -the scalability of The Long Dark's three difficulty settings allow any kind of gamer to enter its icy northern landscapes and find an adventure.
The primary strength of the game is in its straightforwardness - from the subtley cel-shaded art design to the easily understood menus and interface, this is a game that wants you to play it, learn it, and enjoy it. Unlike say, The Forest or DayZ, The Long Dark does not pose a steep learning curve for a survival game. Your needs -food, water, shelter, and ammunition- are revealed in a logical, step-by-step manner. At first, you survive off of the junk food you steal from abandoned homes and offices, as this is the easiest thing to do. But eventually these staples of modern life begin to run out and you're forced to hunt for food. The game instructs you in desperation inch by inch, rather than forcing it on you from the beginning. The same can be said for the shelter mechanics -at first you will spend most of your time in doors - but as you begin to hunt, you'll find yourself outdoors more frequently, and will thus have to learn how to keep warm while sleeping on snow overnight.
The game also has a wide scale of difficulty -from the Pilgrim (Easy) setting, to the moderately difficult Voyager mode and the very challenging Stalker mode (hmm, I wonder why they named it Stalker?!) However, I should emphasize that all of these modes will pose a challenge. So even if a more skilled player chooses go with Pilgrim or Voyager, the game mechanics will still demand that the player remain engaged in their quest for survival. The sense of immersion never breaks, and it never feels too easy.
One aspect of the game that I find to be really special are the snowstorms - while there are wild animals who will attack you provoked (or unprovoked, it's up to the animal, really!) the real danger is in the oppressive weather. Gusts of swirling snow fly horizontally across open plains, freezing your body and slowing you down. It's a really fantastic innovation that enhances the sense of immersion.
Because this game is in Early Access, not all the features are present -the Story Mode is being held back, I assume, so that everyone can enjoy it as a complete whole. But what is here is the open-ended Sandbox mode, which is very strong, with a lot of long-term promise. More importantly, it introduces you to the gameplay mechanics that will make you a pro when the Story Mode comes out.
Unlike most Early Access developers, Hinterland has been very engaged and are routinely updating and patching. They actively seek our feedback and are responsive to it. This is clearly a group of creative professionals who are commited to making the best game possible.
My one specific quibble is the varying performance of the game -as an Early Access title, I understand it's continually being optimized -but it makes it difficult to give it a 10/10 when its performance fluctuates between patches. Sometimes it delivers a solid 30+ fps, but it just as equally dips. Considering how they've routinely optimized the game's performance during its time in Early Access, I expect this will only improve.
Overall this is a fantastic game, and especially recommended for those who are new to the survival genre but still fit for a fight.

I'd recommend this to anyone looking for a hardcore but "casul" game, but I'd also recommend waiting for a steam sale being the price 24.99$ is a bit high for this.

SiNKR is inspired by simple indie puzzle games like Hook, but it pushes the concept a lot further. Unlike some of those indie puzzle games where you can't really make a mistake (all you have to do is find the piece that moves and move it, then find the next one), in SiNKR you really have to think to find out in which order to move which piece to end up with all the right pieces at the right places.
The puzzles are well designed and it has a nice progression in difficulty, with many new concepts added along the way. The game isn't long, it took me about an hour to complete, but for the price it's definitely worth it!

To everyone thinking about buying this because they liked The Stanley Parable:
The Beginner's guide is also a narrated walking simulator, but that's where the similarities end. The narrative is not influenced by what the player does, nor is it funny or the least bit interesting (to me).
The creator of TSP leads you through a series of very short ... instances, which are supposedly the unfinished works of "this friend of his", as he goes on about creative process and "his friend's" emotional/psychological problems and whatnot. Mostly, you'll just walk around a bit and when you've seen what little there is to be seen, you'll wait for him to stop talking and load the next half-finished demo level of a very weird, but mediocre intended-as-art "game".
I feel like I just paid money to listen to a guy vent, but shouldn't it be the other way around?
Forgive me for being presumptuous, but if you are not the type to find (or even look for) deeper meaning in abstract pieces of "art", you will probably not enjoy The Beginner's Guide either.

If you're considering buying this game, you're probably looking for cosmic horror lovecraft cthulhu thriller stuff, or possibly a capitalism simulator where you can be a merchant sea-captain. In actual fact, whatever you select for your ambition and background, you are a two-bit spy for the London admiralty, who visits faraway ports and takes notes for money. If you want to feel like you're actually making money in a way that makes sense for a sailing captain, you must accept smuggling jobs from a certain npc. While the world is strange and unhospitable to human life, the tone of the game is not the tone of a cosmic horror or thriller game. Instead, droll humor, blandly presented weirdness, and affectionate references to victorian culture combine to make the tone of Sunless Sea closer to a rather macabre Alice in Wonderland. I enjoy sunless sea, but I cannot recommend it to the sort of person I would expect to consider purchasing it.

In Outlast, you take on the role of Miles Upshur, a freelance journalist who received an anonymous tip regarding unethical activity at a presumed decommissioned mental asylum. Since you are a journalist, you bring along a camera to record any evidence of wrongdoing you may find. The camera also serves to provide you with night vision and acts as your flashlight for getting through dark areas although this requires batteries to function. Thankfully the game has plenty of them lying around in areas off the beaten path.
Gameplay is a mix of stealth and sprint as you have absolutely no weaponry whatsoever and discovery by enemies will result in a chase or instant death. Depending on your style of play, you may opt for simply “running for it” whenever possible as the game has plenty of places to hide if you get enough distance from your pursuer as well as avenues of escape (vents and narrow spaces) that you can squeeze through to get away. The AI is pretty decent and will catch you if you do dumb things like hide under tables or inside lockers within their visible range (or if you just do a bad job hiding in general)
Probably my favorite part of this game was encountering the various talkative enemies such as the twins and the “doctor”. Each of their plotlines had entertaining dialogue and the overall spooky asylum theme tied in especially well with them. The developers also don’t hold back with the overall goriness and you might find yourself wincing at a few scenes (especially in the DLC). I did find the ending to be a bit of a cop-out but I’ll let you decide that one for yourself.
All in all, this game is a great addition to any horror genre lover’s library.

Rise to Ruins begins with an overhead map of the game’s continent, from which you select a region in which you want to settle your first village. These locations differ in available resources and, I think, climate, so choose carefully. (You can found multiple villages in different regions, but you only have a limited pool of villagers, shared between them all.)
After you’ve chosen a region the game takes you to the region map, from which you’ll play the game proper. There’s no real tutorial at the moment, but the game gives you some help in the form of pop-up tips. These are a bit lacking, though. For example, I had no food growth and no food, but nothing in any of the tips told me I should build anything until it was too late, and even then I didn’t know the best place to build it. An in-game tutorial would really help; the youtube tutorial video notwithstanding. Still, although you should be able to work out the very basics pretty easily, it’s a steep learning curve when things go wrong and you don’t know why. The Steam Discussions are a useful resource.
Anyway, you choose a section of promising looking land — water, rocks, trees, and wild food, if you can find it, are all good — and build a camp. That then lets you build other buildings, too, and before long you’re harvesting resources and growing your camp into a little village community.

What can I say that's not already been said?  The game has a very simple design, and absolutely NO INSTRUCTIONS.  That's not a bad thing, because you are thrust into puzzle after puzzle and have to figure out how things work.  Sometimes they don't work exactly as you expect; that's part of the game.  Figuring things out.  Learning by trying.  Clicking things and seeing what happens.  Some levels introduce new mechanics, and then the next levels put them together with what you already know in strange and unexpected ways.
The main joy for Me in this game (and in life) is figuring things out.  There seem to be some videos on YouTube showing exactly how to play the game and get through every puzzle.  I didn't watch any of them and downvoted the link to them on Steam.  I certainly don't recommend them to anyone.  But I guess if you're just an achievement wrhoe who doesn't care about actually achieving anything in real life, those videos could be handy.
It is completely mouse-constrolled; I don't think I touched the keyboard at all during the game.  As I said, there are NO INSTRUCTIONS.  The icons in the game menus aren't even labeled.  They are, for the most part, pretty obvious -- but sometimes you do what you do in the game: click and see what happens.
The game offers very little replay value for people without Alzheimer's.  However, it could be enjoyable to come back to every now and then to relax and keep your mind sharp.  The music is nice, the background is pretty, and the sound effects aren't jarring.  For the price, this game is outstanding.  The author appears to be very active in the forums and quite responsive to customer problems.  And perhaps most importantly of all for someone like Me, it's available on Linux.

SiNKR by developer Robert Wahler constitutes a good minimalist puzzle game. From truly great level designs to soothing music scores, SiNKR excels at incorporating the constituent elements of its genre into the fabric of its gameplay. Offering a relaxed experience with no timers or move counters, SiNKR allows players to lavish their full attention onto the puzzle facing them. SiNKR also nails the difficulty progression of its levels, starting out slow but quickly working its way to simultaneously being complicated and fun. At its current price of $1, SiNKR is a great value and is definitely worth playing.
SiNKR opens very slowly, allowing players time to adjust to the game’s mechanics. The gameplay is revealed to center around moving pucks into holes using hooks. The hooks only move in one direction and cannot return to their original positions once they have been reeled in close to the holes, which serves as the operative limiting factor that makes the game challenging. Some holes take more than one puck to fill, while all hooks are able to collect more than one puck at any given moment. While those with completionist tendencies do not need to worry about succeeding in a certain finite number of moves, all players must be strategic or else they will have to redo the puzzles.
The aspect of the puzzler that really shines is its great, handcrafted level design. SiNKR really succeeds in striking a balance between stimulating and frustrating players. Whenever players figure out a creative solution to a level, they are immediately gratified by the effort that they put in. SiNKR feels smart and really encourages exploration within its individual levels.
The game mechanics become more sophisticated as players progress through the levels. While they begin by just being able to pull on hooks, soon players gain the abilities to horizontally or vertically flip the side of the hook and to connect hooks together. Linking hooks allows players to advance their hooks to parts of the levels previously inaccessible due to their original positioning, adding initially unexpected flavor to SiNKR. The game never allows for a mechanic to become stale or monotonous, instead introducing new ones before players have the chance to grow disinterested.
The music that is played in the background of each level really enhances the gaming experience. It encapsulates the tranquil yet thought-provoking feel that is at the essence of the SiNKR. The ambient music fits perfectly with the niche that SiNKR fills, really elevating the game.
Even though SiNKR only takes between one and two hours to complete, it is really worth investing in. The thought put into each level is readily apparent, making players utilize visual as opposed to textual learning to become accustomed to new gameplay mechanics. Full controller support and touch screen compatibility only further enhance a great game. SiNKR is worth picking up, and that is reflected in its score of 8/10.

This game is pretty much a must buy. Being pretty much broke, I rarely choose to devote any money to gaming anymore. However, after following this game for four years I couldn't let it slip by.
Gameplay:
The game is hard. Taking me nearly 10 hours to complete the game on the standard mode. Do not purchase unless you're looking for a game that really challenges you. Some of the stages and bosses took nearly 20-30 minutes of grinding down to complete. Now when I say grinding, I don't mean grinding for gear or loot of any sort; I mean grinding mastery over the varied mechanics that the 30+ bosses throw at you. The bosses are themed and creative with wild mechanics. Most of the game when encountering a new boss it seems nearly impossible that I would be able to best it, but after 3-4 run throughs you begin to see the patterns. While you can't memorize them, because they continuously change, you can predict to some degree where safety might be.
The Run-N-Gun levels are just as hard and in many cases harder than the bosses. The third world's fish level in particular took me nearly an hour alone to complete. But they add such fun platforming to the game that breaks up the boss rush feel of the game so well that doing them over and over sometimes feels like a break.
Visuals and Audio.
Little can be said about the visuals and audio. They are in a tier of their own.
Controls
I have a few minor issues with the controls. I found myself adjusting them quickly to use the controller a little better. Part of me wonders why this game doesn't have the ability to use the second control stick rather than the silly "Lock" button. I rarely if ever used the "Lock" button, but in the very few times the “Lock” button might have been helpful I tended to need to evade or dodge so much that locking my character's movement would have been death. If the second control stick had been used as a way to aim more carefully it would have been much more effective.
Overall that is a rather small issue. The game controls rather tight, especially after I switch the Fire button to right trigger and dash to left.
Replayability
I’ve already spent some time playing the new Expert mode which unlocks after completing the game. Getting S ratings for bosses is a tough challenge that keeps me coming back to the game. Also two player mode is incredibly fun and more than twice as difficult as single player. What this game lacks will surely be coming in form of DLC, which normally would upset me, but for this game it feels complete, I’m satisfied, but I still want more. Overall if you’re a most talented gamer expect this game to offer you at least 5 hours of solid gameplay, and the majority of gamers will probably take 10-15 hours to complete the normal mode.
Pros
-Excellent boss design
-Beautiful art and sound
-Great simple story
-Many cons likely to be fixed in updates or DLC
Cons
-No online multiplayer
-Leaves you wanting more (half a pro?)
-Some weird controller choices.
9.5/10

I bought Banished, because I expected a solid, well-crafted mediveal city-building game with beautiful graphics and while I can't say, that it didn't deliver what it promised, I wouldn't recommend buying it.
First off, this isn't a bad game and I'd rather leave a neutral than a negative review.
Normally I like simulations and building games. I love Simcity, I like Anno, I loved CitySkylines and so many more, so I've really been happy when I heared about Banished and it's medival flare (Since most city-building games - even the last parts of the ANNO-series play in the present or further) and went for it, when it still was in early access. At first I really thought I'd spend thousands of hours in this game, however it became boring sooner than I ever have imagined and I can't really explain why.
Most of these sandbox-like games heavily depend of grinding. I normally have no problem with grinding. I spent days or weeks digging stone in minecraft, smelting and crafting it in order to build a nice castle and I never bothered. In Banished, however, this grinding just feels dull and exhausting. Maybe I was just bad in this game, didn't know how to run a city properly, but I spent more than half of this game watching my screen and waiting. Waiting for the next spring to come. Waiting for my people to gather enough resources to build another house. Waiting for the next house to be build and so on. I never really took any risk, I rather played save and slowly, always watching food and resources, medical care and happiness. it might have been my slow playstile that made me ask rather sooner than later "What am I waiting for?". There was no real fun in building another house, watching another year to pass by, sitting and idling in front of my monitor.
Maybe it is just me, and maybe I would've loved this game if there was a little bit more action (like dangerous wildlife or some sort of combat), but I always felt that Banished lacked this little something that makes me to push forward, to archieve something, other building games have.

Dead Hungry Diner is a charming, casual game with strategic elements that has you working a restaurant, fulfilling orders from zombies, werewolves, vampires and other such monsters. Its an easy to play game that involves a bit of strategy to make the most efficient use of your time as you pick up two orders before delivering them, rather than one at a time. There’s a familiar formula here that offers a new twist outside of its monster gimmick in the way that your customers get hostile when seated next to the wrong patron. If you can endure the early first restaurant, the game gets better, more enjoyable and engaging rather than frustrating.
There are fifty levels, each broken into nighttime shifts that tick by as waves of new customers enter. It starts enough with tables for two or one. Customers arrive solo or tandem. You click on the next party in the cue and either seat them or push them to the back of the line. Once they’re seated, you wait as they take their order which appears as a bucket on their table. This means that they want a bucket of brains. What else would zombies and even vampires want?
You click on their order and then click on the brain tree, yes brain tree. Brains grow on trees. You see your selectable male or female character follow your commands in the order that you made them. After waiting a brief moment, brains will be served, where you then click on the table that they go to, but with only one thing on the menu, there’s no way to bring it to the wrong table. After they chow down, they raise a pair of golden moneybags where you take the money. If you’re quick enough, they leave a mess for you to wipe down by clicking and earn more of a tip for doing so. After that a pair of ravens show up to pick the table clean I suppose.
When you seat monster types at a table, the table will then give you a bonus for every monster of the same type that sits there afterward and it adds up. You need to be quick though, waiting in line causes blood to boil, which is why you’ll need to use special abilities like love to cheer them up and a rain check that forces them to return later. You can soon unlock super speed and a zombie substitution that turns a party into zombies rather than something else. There’s a lot to keep track of.
I would appreciate diverse upgrades such as the ability to serve the table behind you, because even if all you need to do is turn around, the game will run your character around to the opposite side. This is just a game mechanic, but visually, it makes little sense.
There is a lot of charm and story that adds to the gameplay, while weighing down the speed of the game. You’ll meet a mysterious cloaked figure that sells you power ups and new abilities. These upgrades can make your character move quicker and reduce the cool down wait between ability usages. You can even purchase ways to keep Frankie awake.
Who is Frankie? He’s your big green bouncer that breaks up werewolf scuffles that murder your patrons. As I’ve mentioned before, the werewolves become the bane of your business and the game in general. They hate vampires and lose their temper quick, before they take it out on other patrons. This costs you two parties as they’re both ejected or one kills the other. They ruin the flow and only add stress, when a game should be fun. To compensate for the werewolves hating the vampires, they love skeletons, because yes dogs love bones. A fight can lose a level for you, even if you need to wait until the end of a shift to see.
It turns into a maddening, frantic and stressful rush as the werewolves get introduced early in the game and start attacking other patrons. These werewolves and their high demand make me question if I want to keep playing after each level. It derails the game, but it does ease up if you can endure to larger bigger restaurants that have more tables to keep the troublemakers apart.
At some point a witch will show up to destroy the your patrons and you need to click each one before she fires her wicked spell. Under normal circumstances, witches in media would side with monsters, but since most witches are bad, this one is just as nasty. While you are running a business on brain trees, it would be nice to one day serve humans, but I suppose that encroaches on a different game’s territory.
The click heavy controls feel cumbersome and inefficient with a game that you need efficiency. With all of the frantic clicks, I think its better suited for a touch screen rather than a mouse. Several times I’d miss a click or perhaps it just never registered and it ruined the flow I had going. There are no hot keys, making it even less efficient.
You can get one of three star ratings for each level. A passing grade means that you’ll unlock the next level.One of the good things about the game is that you can see the stars build up in the top right corner. Like with most casual or mobile games, you can replay any level to get a better score. Its a nice system that seems standardized by now.
As you progress through the game, there are five restaurants each with ten levels. The bigger the restaurant, the more tables you get. Each restaurant starts with a few tables in shambles that make it easier, but before you know it, the diner is fully operational by the final level. Having more tables makes the game far less frustrating, because you can have a werewolf section and a non werewolf section.
Dead Hungry Diner is a fun diversion that gets deeper in bite sized chunks the further you progress. I can recommend it more for a touch screen than a mouse, but its still enjoyable after a bout of frustration early on.
Eventhough it is early acces, it has quite alot content and it is most enjoyable. I am having high hopes for the final product. Definitely worth of 15€

There are many positive things to say about this game. Things like the atmosphere and the sounds, or the way the chapters are presented as a single continuous adventure.
The big problem is that this is a puzzle game, and it is a badly executed one. Puzzle games are ideally iterative where you are introduced to a tool and then you use the tool, and eventually forced to apply the tool in creative ways. Think of it like a really good math course. This is present through most of the game, but in the last quarter it starts to fade. When I did give up and look for a solution, I didn't react with wonder and awe for the puzzle creators, or curse at my stupidity about why I didn't think of something, or how I could have missed the clues, despite these being my normal reactions. No, instead I was frustrated by a feeling of arbitrariness, where in the end even the goal becomes unclear.
This game started with a feeling of dread and that was fine because it was intentional, but it ended as a grind. I completed this just in case there was something in this to redeem the previously mentioned failing. There is not. Play ICO instead.

This is a very nice Village Builder + Tower Defense game.

+ the resource economy/infrastructure is understandable
+ assigning villagers to specific tasks is easy
+ the combat is easily viewable

+ farms don't produce (unless the weather gets warm enough) in the winter, I like this because its life-like, and forces planning
+ that 8-bit nostalgia
+ once you understand how to defend your village within the first year, each new village start gets a little easier
Cons:
- steep learning curve
- villagers can easily die to food, water, and zombie related issues
- the game has a lot of moving parts and is susceptible to huge lag spikes
-- during auto saves
-- during the start of the night-time cycle, because all the enemies are moving
-- when you play long enough to have a large enough village population and too many enemies left in the map
---*my issue started at 150 pop village with 400ish enemy mobs on the map
- graphics, 8-bit, if you want a really nice 3D village builder with pretty buildings and terrain, this is not for you
Worth playing.

Full Review (for my original Quick First Look just scroll down):
Legend of Mysteria is a spin-off from the Labyronia RPG series and story wise a prequel. While there are a lot of familiar characters and the main area of the game is the so called Mysteria Tower, the story can be enjoyed on it's own, without any prior knowledge. However if you have played Labyronia RPG 1 and 2, Legend of Mysteria will give some nice additional insights. The main storyline, the murder of a high rank mage called Dinyon and Windir (the player character) trying to clear his name, while being accused of being the man behind the dirty deed, is a very well put together detective story that will keep you guessing until pretty late who the true culprit is.
As I have already said in my First Look, gameplay wise is where the biggest different lies between Legend of Mysteria and the original Labyronia RPG games. While all 3 titles share their RPG Maker VX Ace foundation, the later are more traditional CRPG games with a quite a heavy focus on battles. Legend of Mysteria on the other hand plays more like a classic Point & Click adventure with hardly any battles at all and even then, there is no real RPG style character progression, XP system etc. This game is about exploring your locations, talking to NPC, gathering evidence, finding and using items to unlock new and previously locked rooms and areas. At this point it needs to be noted that even though I have played a lot of adventures in my gaming career (including most LucasArts Games and even more Sierra Games), I did get stuck quite a lot. This is not due to strange tasks to be done, but rather the fact the due to the absence of a quest log, the player should really start writing (I mean really writing with pen & paper!!) down notes. Thankfully to a kind player, there is a full walkthrough in the community guides section!

Quick First Look:
Legend of Mysteria RPG is a spin-off from the Labyronia RPG series; actually according to the title screen it should be called "Labyronia Tales Legend of Mysteria". Hence anybody who is familiar with the main series, will feel right at home, as there many characters one would have already met and familiar locations, only at a different time and with new content. This should not scare of newcomers, since it is an independent story that doesn't require any prior knowledge.
Gameplay is where the Legend of Mysteria RPG seems to have changed the most, at least from what I have seen so far. It actually feels way more like a classic adventure game with RPG elements. In the beginning the player character, a mage called Windir, gets innocently accused of attacking and possibly murdering another Mage called Dinyon. Now it is time to find the real culprit and clear Windir's name. This all happens in traditional adventure game style, that is talking to NPCs, doing favors for them and finding ways to access new areas.
What about the battles, you might be asking by now? There are battles, but unlike in Labyronia RPG 1 + 2, it actually will take some time until you will have your first encounters. Despite appearing to be easier now, simple attack spamming still won't get you anywhere - just don't forget that Windir is a mage!
In conclusion I can easily recommend this game to fans of Labyronia RPG, because it is more Labyronia, even though it kinda feels different now. There are many characters appearing from the main series as well as well-known locations featuring additional content (new areas). However this should not turn off newcomers, as no prior knowledge is required to make sense of what is going on.
NOTE: I will update this quick first look with a full fledged review, once I have finished the game.

TL;DR: NOT RECOMMENDED, not worth 25$ at the time this review was posted. Wait for 15$ or preferably less on a sale.
Superhot, as a game concept, is really good. A first person shooter where time only passes when you move. This trick lets you weave in and out of enemies and bullets, letting you do a lot of movements and actions that let you feel like a pro stuntman. A small variety of weapons and throwable objects give you plenty of options to choose when dealing with oncoming bullets. Do you jump and dodge? Take cover? Do you block the bullet with an object? Cause the enemy to do friendly fire? You are free to deal with situations as you see fit, so you can express a lot of your personal style in your actions. A well integrated replay feature lets you share your choices with the world.
If that was all that were in the game, similar to the 2013 prototype, along with plenty of levels and a point beyond "just killing red dudes", there'd be no complaints.
Frustratingly though, it feels like the developers spent more time over the past two years making useless content and coming up with a dumb narrative and making it all fit in with some 90s IRC/hacker aesthetic. This wouldn't be such a big deal if it wasn't constantly bashing you on the head with this to the point where it gets in the way of your game.
A lot of levels are large but enemies spawn in only a small area, making most of the space functionally useless. Only a few enemies spawn at a time, so a lot of the time you are just waiting for enemies to spawn and come to you, wasting a lot of time over the course of the game. Enemies don't have any variable action, most of the time they stand and shoot at you, or run up to you for a melee attack. There is no variety in enemy type, only the weapon they carry differs.
This is all bundled up with the lousy text menu interface, 99% of which is empty content. The menu has all these tantalizing options like "Apps" and "Games".....but there's nothing there of substance. They contribute nothing to the game, and nothing gets added to them later. Add in a snarky narrative of "the system" and I really feel like I'm being made fun of by the game (and by extension, the developers) for trying to play it.
Wouldn't it have been great to have some more variety in the gameplay? At times you can really get into a killing flow as you progress through one of the areas, but the moment you acheive that high, the enemies stop spawning and the level is over. What if the level kept going? What if there were more interactive objects? Switches? Keys? Anything? The 2013 tech demo gave you at least a tiny sense of progression when you killed the CEO and jumped out the window to your doom, only for your death to be averted at the last moment. Here, there's no twist or change of course. Levels and battles are isolated affairs. Any sort of experience you may have had is wiped away immediately, and it's just on to the next repetitive encounter. In the end, you just feel "What's the point?"
If that is what the devs were aiming for, then I simply don't find it fun. Superhot COULD be a great game, but at this time there is little actual content to it. It's unfortunate the developers chose this path in the past two years of development, but it is what it is. Don't buy it at 25$.

Most of these sandbox-like games heavily depend of grinding. I normally have no problem with grinding. I never really took any risk, I rather played save and slowly, always watching food and resources, medical care and happiness. it might have been my slow playstile that made me ask rather sooner than later "What am I waiting for?". Obligatory line:  This is the most innovative shooter I've played in years!
There, now that I've done as the game clearly orders me to (literally), I can get to the actual review.
SUPERHOT (no, I dont know why it's always capitalized, just roll with it) is basically "Bullet Time: The Game".  The core mechanic is that time only moves when you do.  When you're just turning your view around, it'll move kinda slowly, but when you're actually MOVING, it'll be real-time. But the instant you stop... back to time-stop.  When combined with the fact that bullets dont move at the speed they do IRL... and are slowed down just enough that even in real-time, you can follow their path (they are still very quick though), you can watch enemy shots, and dodge out of the way, just like in the Matrix!  But if that were the only mechanic this offered, it wouldnt be nearly as interesting.
Needless to say, the other core mechanic is, well, the weapons.  There are only a few of these... pistol, shotgun, machinegun, katana, bat.  Not much, you say?  Believe me, it's enough.  Learning all of the properties of these weapons is key, not just for using them yourself, but for dealing with enemies.  With the game's bright, stark graphics, it's super easy to see at a glance what each enemy is carrying, and plan accordingly.  But shooting and slashing isnt your only trick.  You can also fling weapons or objects at enemies; hit them with one, and they'll be stunned, and their weapon will go flying... and you can grab it right out of the air, if you are in position.  Then let 'em have it!  Just as fun as it sounds.
That's not all though:  The game's other mechanic is the HotSwitch, the ability to instantly, and from any distance, switch into the body of any enemy you can see.  Did a guy with a shotgun just fire an unavoidable wall of bullets at you?  Take him over before they hit.  The only downside is that when you take someone over, the weapon they are holding will break; but you can bypass this by smacking them with an object so they drop it, taking them over, and then grabbing the gun that'll be hanging in the air right next to you.
Oh, and you can slash, or even SHOOT, enemy bullets out of the air.
Combine all of these things, and, well... it cant get much more awesome than this.
Be warned though:  This is NOT a story-focused game.  Oh, it has one, and it's interesting, but it's very short.  This is more of an arcade-style score-attack game, as the meat of the game's content... and there's alot of it... is in the "endless" mode.  Dont think this makes the game not worth the cost though, because it is.
Also:  This game is HARD.  You're going to die.  A lot.  Enemies are extremely numerous, fast, aggressive, smart, and can grab weapons off of the ground. And you have to really pay attention, as they just... keep... coming.  You have to constantly check the doors for the tell-tale red glow that signifies an enemy about to spawn from one (and they can act *instantly* after they spawn, so dont think you have a safe moment while they're doing so!). But this just makes all of your awesome actions even more amazing, when you're successful against them.  But yeah, if you're after a challenge... you'll find it here.
Really, I cant recommend this one enough.  An FPS that rewards careful, tactical play, yet still requires LOTS of real skill to do well in, with awesome mechanics that let you do ridiculously awesome moves, and never any true unfairness... really, it doesnt get much better than this.  I'll be playing this one alot, myself.
Oh, and one more thing:  After any run, you can view, edit, and even upload a real-time replay of everything that just happened.  I honestly just never get tired of watching these.

Cuphead brings a classic form of animation into a videogame with absolutely no compromises. The first game that did that was South Park: The Stick of Truth, but that's kind of like comparing NES to PS4. Cutout animation serves its purpose for South Park, but the beautiful hand drawn animation style from the 30s is no easy thing to recreate, especially in video game form. Cuphead succeeds in doing just that, and it's an absolute joy to look at.
The game itself is tough as nails, but never unfair. It is balanced both for casuals, who can enjoy just trying to beat each stage, and for hardcore players, who have mostly reasonable goals to aim for in order to perfect each stage.
The music and aural presentation is wonderful as well, but for me, it always comes back to the animation. 2D hand drawn animation is basically dead in modern movies and television. I mourn for it. Cuphead has revived it, at least for a moment, and it feels nothing short of miraculous.

A lot of people seem to prefer the original Blood Bowl to the sequel, I couldn't be more opposite. Blood Bowl 2 is an improvement in every way, especially in it's accessibility. Everything is set out far more tactfully than the prior release its menus being much easier to navigate and it now has a great campaign mode to teach new players the rules of the game and to help ease them into the mechanics. It also helps that the game has received a significant graphical overhaul, it's a damn fine looking game in comparison to the rather ugly original. One thing that is a bit of a negative is the fact that a number of teams are locked behind a DLC pay wall, I purchased the wood elves at release and I belive that both they and the lizardmen should have been included with the base game as they launched at the same time but I seem to have acquired most of the other later released DLC teams for free, so definitely no complaints there.
As for the game itself. Blood Bowl 2 is tactical, turn based, fantasy football with teams composed of creatures and armies from Warhammer fantasy battle and a video game adaptation of the popular tabletop Blood Bowl game that launched in 1987. Blood Bowl's formula is extremely addictive once you get the hang of it and settle on a team that fits your play style, teams can be set up to play a number of ways, utilising a variation of strategies with each team tending to favour particular strategies over others. Dwarves for example are great at caging up units around the ball, blocking enemies and charging in formation, essentially playing the long game, elves and skaven on the other hand focus on running, passing dodging and generally focusing on the sport itself, whereas teams like orks and chaos tend to favour getting up close and personal and physically demolishing the opposing team with bashier, combat focused gameplay. Teams are composed of various players that focus on differing aspects of the game such as throwers, catchers, runners and blockers and most teams have a "big guy" a larger than life unit that often has a number of flaws that prevent them being too overpowered, but some incredible skills that, when they work, can be utterly devestating. Before Blood Bowl got the video game treatment the closest thing I had ever really played video game wise was Mutant League Football on the Megadrive, which didn't really play the same but had very similar aesthetics, likely inspired by the tabletop version of Blood Bowl.
Blood Bowl 2 has a great sardonic sense of humour, the commentators Bob and Jim (an ogre and a vampire respectively) banter over much of the game, commentating the matches and making small talk during the menus, both are voiced well and give the game a great sense of character, never failing to spout something amusing. All of the teams have a very tongue in cheek design about them that matches this tone, orks especially have some amusing quirks, their big guy, the troll wearing a sign with the words "do not feed dat" crudely scribbled on it and boasts an ability that allows him to throw goblins across the pitch. The teams certainly are made up of an assortment of colourful characters and figuring out how they all work together and stack up against each other is great fun. As Blood Bowl 2 is essentially a virtual tabletop game it utilises RNG (random number generator) dice rolls, these can be somewhat frustrating due to the nature of the game as a poor roll can completely flip a thus far successful strategy on it's head, costing you the entire game, it can even result in your players being injured or killed, which admittedly can be a little rage inducing, I fully admit to launching the nearest object to hand across the room after losing a particularly long game that went into extra time due to nuffle's dice deciding to screw me over at the last minute. The key thing to remember here is that Blood Bowl is absurd and terrible things happening to your team is part of the fun, it's chaotic in nature and not to be taken seriously, opposing players will be suffering the same bad luck with dice rolls as you, so though you may have one seriously bad game the next one may end up going entirely in your favour, randomness is what Blood Bowl is all about.
So, on to the important question, do I recommend Blood Bowl 2? The answer absolutely is yes. Blood Bowl 2 is a great title either played alone or with friends supporting both online gameplay and a local hotseat option, this version in particular is great for newcomers as it manages to convey the rules much better than it's predecessor, but I'd also say it's the optimal virtual version of Blood Bowl, so experienced players should give it a look too. If fantasy football with monsters and fantasy creatures is your thing and you enjoy turn based strategy then this is definitely a game you should look into. So pick up some dice and pray to nuffle that you don't lose your entire team in their first game, Blood Bowl after all is not for the faint of heart.

A computer game largely based on a table top miniatures game first published in 1986 and various versions since. Tolkein's The Lord of the Rings meets the NFL basically-Games Workshop's Warhammer Fantasy Battles combined with American Football (and other sports). Fun. Addictive. Brutal. Rewarding.
Recommended if you get it on sale (60% off) as not all races are included. The table top gives you two races (teams), this game gives you eight. This is a battle-not a sports-game. It is the restructuring of war in a fantasy world into sport contests but with extreme widespread corruption. Not competitive, as certain teams are available only by paying more.
I have played a lot of table top games, historical, fantasy and science fiction games; grand strategy/campaign level wargames and skirmish battle games; Warhammer Fantasy Battles, Warhammer Ancient Battles and Warhammer 40,00 but never Blood Bowl. This pc Blood Bowl II version has me considering buying the table top game.
There are several aspects of the game I like: the chess like/battle like match game play and the team managing. It gives a nice feel to playing a series of games and there are numerous leagues both AI controlled and player versus player. You can create online leagues, solo (versus AI) leagues, of several types; and you can have mutiple teams in various leagues.
I have no problem with the use of dice in this strategy game. You manage risk. The game has a good balance between strategy and variables like many wargames.
The combination of Warhammer lore and modern sports is funny and odd.  I see the game as mocking a lack of concern about violence.
If you like turn-based strategy or tabletop miniatures games I think you will have fun with this game. I'm not sure on the current price point however.

The short life of Captain Abraham Adams. Set to sea with a crew of ten (including a cook with poor hygiene and a chronically lazy ferret). His aim? Glory and gold. And wouldn't you know, he actually did ok for a while! Made a slim profit from sailing into the darkness and discovering new ports for the admiralty and ferrying pilgrims to their final rest. He even had time to find romance and have a child and this only gave him more impetus to succeed in his efforts. It was therefore desperation which led him to accept a commission to smuggle contraband to a new destination far beyond his normal range of operations. With a hold laden with supplies and an engine greedily devouring fuel, Captain Adams set sail knowing that whatever happened he could not risk returning until the illicit cargo had been delivered lest he run afoul of the port authorities. Due to the vague directions given, Captain Adams had little real idea of his course but was optimistic that he would find his way. He was a fool. Adams became hopelessly lost and struggled to keep his crew in high spirits. Perhaps if he had simply turned back when the fuel ran out and risked the wrath of the law then they would have been spared the horrors that lay ahead. But greed often overpowers wisdom. To keep the engines running long enough to find a port Captain Adams ordered that their food be thrown into the engine but this was only a temporary measure. When the food ran out and the engines sputtered and coughed their last there was only one desperate course of action left. Captain Adams prayed fervently to anyone, anything that could hear and his prayer's were answered in the worst possible way. His humble ship finally found harbour in an ancient and very much abandoned temple far beyond any known lands. After several more frantic attempts to appease whatever was watching over his crew, Captain Adams was rewarded with one last fuel reserve. Adams needed no further prompting and forced his starving men back onto their floating prison to make one final effort to find a port. With the lamp dimmed to preserve fuel the superstitious crew began to cave to terror, despair and insanity. With no food Captain Adams pragmatically ordered that the dead be butchered and eaten, if anyone ever asked: they went overboard. Adams asserted that a safe harbour would be found soon and pressed them on but his crew had stopped believing. When the engine at last died with land no closer the last of the crew finally unleashed their fury upon the man who had signed their death warrants. And so Captain Abraham Adams and his crew sunk below the black waters unmissed and unmourned just another victim of the Sunless Sea. The moral of the story? When a one-eyed man brandishing a knife asks you to deliver something it is in your best interests to reply with a polite but firm "Go ♥♥♥♥ yourself!". But yeah, in short, "Lose your mind. Eat your crew. Die." is a highly accurate description of this game.
10/10 Would be toyed with by cruel sea gods again.

The best FPS game I've ever played, and I've tried HL2. Everything about it - everything - is brilliant. Rapture is magnificent, one of the great settings ever devised in gaming. It is a glorioius masterpiece gone mad, turning into one of the creepiest gaming experiences I've ever played.
The combat is fantastic. The sheer variety of styles available to you is simply staggering. 8 different guns, 8 different plasmids, hacked turrets, hacked security drones...it's amazing how many choices you have in the way you fight.
Of course, the real selling point is the story. It is a philosophical masterpiece with a stunning twist in the middle that practically knocked me off of my feet. The depth and complexity involved is incredible. There's a ludicrous amount of content available for you to find, whether it's through in-game dialogue, audio logs, incidental dialogue from splicers, or simple exploration of the rooms.
The only disappointing part of the game is the boss battle at the end of it, which is disappointingly generic and easy. But it's a minor quibble when put up against the mastery that makes up the rest of the game. A 10 of 10 game if I've ever played one, and you owe it to yourself to play it.

If you find yourself here, chances are you already know whether or not this game is for you. If you like to solve increasingly tricky puzzles to ambient music, then you are certainly in the right place.
This game is fairly intuitive to understand. It introduces concepts one at a time, increasing the difficulty with each new piece after it does before introducing something new. I had a chance to see this game before, and got to level 45 before stopping to review.
It works really well if your screen has touch support, even supporting multi-touch on Windows 10 (careful there). While it does have great controller support, I recommend using mouse/touch to make things a little easier. It might be possible to improve controller support by holding a "modifier" key (one of the triggers, for example) to change what the directional pad targets when selecting. Two modifiers with two joysticks should cover all the different types (I think six "categories" would be enough). Even so, the later stages can get rather busy, so mouse/touch is strongly encouraged.
Overall, SINKR is a wonderful game worth much more than it costs. I strongly recommend picking it up and playing it. According to the developer it takes roughly an hour to complete. For under a dollar, what's to lose?

This game is a perfect example of what happens when a dev team makes a really good game and then decides to get greedy and make a freemium sequel. In order to get any characters except for the first 4, you have to log in a solid 20+ hours across several days to get the currency you need for them from daily missions, or simply do what they want and buy premium currency. Along with that, the daily missions suck♥♥♥♥♥ You'd expect things like "deal x amount of damage within 10 seconds in a match" or "kill x enemies with y character" but nope, the only daily missions are "beat x maps of this theme" It's utterly stupid. On top of that, in the first dungeon defenders game, it actually mattered that you leveled each character up, got good equipment, and played your towers correctly. Now none of that really matters. All of your characters level up together now, which makes leveling up completely pointless at all. And then to actually do anything you have to "level up further" through ascension which is actually completely stupid. On top of that, the level cap for you and items is 50  (although I've never seen an item above lvl 46), and in order for any equipment to do jack♥♥♥♥♥♥it needs to be upgraded, and all new equipment starts from 0. This game is an absolutely♥♥♥♥♥♥poor sequel to the first game, which was actually really good. Now, it's just a greedy company trying to get money.
Oh, and one last note: the devs don't know how to balance for♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the game is absolutely FILLED with bugs and optimized horribly. I shouldn't be teleporting across my PRIVATE TAVERN when I'm BY MYSELF. Having lag when playing alone is horrendous. Oh, and the dev teams attitude towards patches sucks too. They literally will say "we know x bug exists, but we'll address that in the next patch." That's a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor attitude towards the literal stability of the game.
Last thing I want to mention: the campaign is really ♥♥♥♥ing easy and doesn't require all the extra ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t I mentioned earlier. The campaign doesn't need you to upgrade your equipment 30+ levels to do anything, and it's easy enough to where the "balance" the devs try to make doesn't hurt you. The campaign itself is fun. Really fun. And it's worth going through some lag to play. I'd give the campaign experience an 8/10. The problem is that the campaign is like 15% of the game itself, where the rest of it is post game ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that requires ungodly ammounts of grinding. If you're interested in this game at all, then I definitely recommend trying it and playing the campaign, because it's worth it. This game is boring as hell. You're basically going to sit watching villagers chop wood for hours and not be able to do anything else because you are unable to expand.
The reason being is that your population will basically never grow. Villagers won't reproduce unless they're assigned to doing nothing. Plus, after you do make a baby, it takes about three game days for it to grow up and enter the labor force, which turns out is quite a long time.
Every building requires a dedicated workforce. You start with 40 villagers, so fine. You will have enough free villagers to assign them to work in your first buildings—say, a lumber mill. But the more you build—which you will want to do because you're going to want a population that is well fed and watered and well armed—the more you get spread thin. So then if you lose a villager to fighting zombies, you may well have lost the only person that smelts ore for all you know or who makes arrows for the ballistae.
You also don't really get nomads adding to your population from the outside. As game events go, notifications of nomads in the area are few and far between. Plus, after day four or so, it's unlikely they'll even be able to make it to your base because there will be so many graveyards and monster spawns on the map that they'll probably be killed en route with nothing you can do about it.
Plus, there's a fairly ungenerous building cap that requires you to continually expand your city center before you can add more buildings. Meaning more waiting and boredom while you watch your dwindling number of villagers chop wood. Your villagers are also very dumb. They will go all the way across town to chop wood instead of chopping the wood you've assigned right next to them/the building you told them to build. Also, don't try and build more than one structure at a time because they are so addlebrained that they will start one structure, get halfway through completing it, then go to the next one and start it until it's halfway done, then go back to the first one. So, more waiting.
So bored. Do not recommend.

A good city builder is often the kind of game you can relax with. It's like an ant farm or a fish tank, you have a certain level of input, but from there you just watch nature take its course. Banished is a deceptively relaxing game, with its pastoral themes and gentle, lilting soundtrack. Beneath the inviting exterior however is a persistent test of your planning abilities, one that can have you sweating before you know it.
"Banished" refers to the tiny group of country folk you start the game with, a group of exiles in a wild, untamed land. From a humble start you help them assemble food, shelter, and comfort for themselves against the harsh winters. This is a personal-level game, similar to Tropico or Children of the Nile, where you can follow each individual resident from their house to their work and back. You'll also find elements of the Anno games, with each home and structure having its own inventory of goods that must be balanced against the consumption of the ever-growing population.
This is where the game can make you panic, because I wasn't kidding about the harsh winters. Your people need food, firewood, clothes, tools, medicine, and other goods and services to survive and prosper, and their needs change by season. When winter comes you'll see a run on the food and firewood stores that can quickly leave people starving and freezing if you haven't adequately prepared. Shortfalls can be extremely hard to recover from, because farms are planted and harvested by seasons, orchards take years to grow from saplings, and your livestock ages as your residents do.
Once you master the balance of goods for your populace, the rest of the challenge is up to you. Banished gives you access to all the buildings right up front, only gating them behind required quantities of the basic building materials. You can have your people farming, fishing, herding, hunting, gathering, brewing, trading, and so on in just a few years, and then aside from the seeds and livestock you have to trade for, you'll have seen everything. From that point on the challenge is entirely in balancing your resources as your village expands indefinitely. The margins get thinner and thinner and curveballs like nomads joining your community en masse can throw off your plans, but the basic rules of expansion do not change.
The magic of the game is that you'll play for a few hours, set up a perfectly functional town with all the buildings and services, put it down... and then find yourself coming back to expand again and again. The quaint graphics and simple mechanics make it a delight to simply keep building out further and further. There are no scenarios or campaigns, just you and the random maps to fill, and even without anything pushing you forward to fill them you might find yourself inclined to do just that. Banished ended up being one of the more addictive city builders I've played, making up for simplicity with more than enough charm.

So, first of all, yes, story mode took me around 2,5 hours to complete. That's fairly short for that price, so if you're only interested in that, then it may not be worth your money. But, after spending twice as that, for me it has much more to offer after finishing the story.  There are various challenges and endless modes, both are really fun to do and unlock progressively - the more you play and beat the target score/time/pass the level, the more content you have. This so far keeps me entertained and still makes me play more and improve. For 15 euro I paid for this game, I think I already got my money worth by those 5 hours spent. This is a long review, so I will include a short summary just at the end of it as TL;DR version.
Gameplay-wise, this is not your everyday shooter. As you may already know from trailers, time only moves when you move (or generally, perform any action). Some of the story levels felt more like a puzzle - getting the spawn patterns right, knowing which corner to watch for, avoiding those nasty gunshots from ever hitting you. The more you play, the more game mechanics you discover. At very first, I did not know that you can have your time slowed while jumping, but this apparently is a thing and can help with avoiding bullets a lot while still closing the gap to any weapons you need. Melee weapons are a blast, with katana being the strongest (in my opinion) - I personally like to throw it for instakills, slice red guys with almost no hit delay whatsoever (with gunshots, most of guns have a delay between shots to make sure you just don't spam the trigger). I also saw katana blocking bullets, but so far I mostly failed with that one by destroying a weapon I wanted to grab by accidentally throwing katana into it (whoops !). AI is spot-on, although it just shoots in your general direction and may cause some friendly fire on the way, but I find it more as a feature than a flaw.
It's hard to say more about gameplay  without spoiling too much for the player, so let's get to visuals and performance, both are really great. I'm running the game on fairly low-spec laptop (with Geforce 630m crippling it the most) in 1024x768, and manage to mantain 30fps+ at most moments, while having the graphics at low quality, but that only impacts the shadow quality and Anti-Aliasing, and game still looks great with artstyle of mostly white and red colours used. Just beware, as the game seems to be built with Unity engine, there are some issues with that, which are engine-specific - it seems like changing resolution to one with non-native aspect ratio (4:3, 5:4 etc. if you're running a 16:9 monitor), makes it so there are black borders on the side that are catching any Steam in-game elements to stay in there even if they are not visible, and also making the video smaller overall. I could get used to this, but I figure some people may not, so just be aware of this.
SUMMARY
-great, innovative gameplay (time moves only when you move, kind of player-centred)
-flashy, white and red artstyle with text comments about what's going on flashing in front of gameplay (may be obstructive at times, but overall it's spot on IMO), a small epilepsy warning here, as this text is the most "flashy" element in the game.
-just OK sound, nothing out of this world, nothing that could break game experience
-very good performance with some Unity engine-specific issues here and there
-big replay value with challenges and endless modes
Is it worth the money ? If you considered all the stuff mentioned here and still want to just finish story mode and be done with it, then I may not think so. But I think some of those "story mode only" people may still get enough of an impression to still get going with rest of the content this game has to offer. If along what you have seen by trailers and read in reviews is enough for you to think, that you may or will enjoy this game, definitely buy it. You will not regret it.
Oh, and lastly:
SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT.
