superhot is a first person shooter whose main differential to other games in the genre is tying the running of time to your movements, meaning that the moment you stop moving, the enemies and the bullets already fired will essentially stop too (i say essentially because they still move, although on veeeeeeeeery slow motion).
the game follows the "one shot one kill" school of design, meaning that there isn't a life bar or regenerating health i.e. the moment you get hit by one bullet, no matter on which part of your body, you will die, the same applying to the enemies.
the arsenal of weapons is not particularly impressive, being composed of 1. melee weapons: a katana sword, something resembling a baseball bat and your fists (the only instance where you will need more than one hit to kill an enemy) and 2. some shooter staples: a pistol, a rifle, and a shotgun, but it gets the job done. additionally, you can throw various items found throughout the levels, as well as all the weapons, which will either kill the enemy (in the case of the katana sword) or stun them for a period of time (the other ones).
around the middle of the game you will receive the ability to change bodies with any enemy, which will allow you to do some cool things, e.g. waiting for an enemy to fire against you, stop moving (thus essentially freezing the bullets during their trajectory) and then changing bodies with the enemy, which will lead you to safety while the red dude that fired at you gets shattered by the very bullets he fired mere moments earlier).
there are not different kinds of enemies (i.e. you won't encounter blue, yellow or green dudes that are harder to fight or have more health), meaning you will be fighting red dudes from the first to the very last stage; difficulty increases, then, come from the different situations you are put in and the number of enemies you will face on a given level, as well as their weapons.
each level is fairly short, meaning that after you have died enough time to more or less master a level you will be able to beat it in a matter of seconds.
visually, the game is essentially monochromatic, with white being the dominating color, although pale blues and greys are also present; at first it reminded me of the visuals on mirror's edge, but it doesn't have the strong, vivid colors that dice's game uses to break the "monotony". i like this clean approach, but to some it may get tiresome and uninteresting.
the campaign is fairly short, but the single player is expanded by a challenge mode (where you play through the game with a set of predetermined conditions, e.g. playing with the katana only, playing the game with each gun having only on bullet) and by a mode that seems to be essentially an endless wave kind of thing (admittedly, though, i haven't put much time on this one).
there is also a little story, told through chat sessions, some small levels and interventions made by the system (as well as featuring some meta elements), but it seemed kind of secondary to me.
all in all, it's a nice game with an interesting, unique mechanic that i would say deserves to be played, even if you wish to wait for a steam sale to buy it cheaper.

Looking through the reviews of both Blood Bowl Legendary/Chaos and Blood Bowl 2, the biggest criticisms I've seen is that the RNG is unfair. I'm sorry to break it to you guys, but that's the focus of the game. The game's core isn't about devising complicated, bullet-proof strategies that outwit and destroy less strategic players. The game is centered on risk and chance, and the fun about chance is that you can fail a 99% chance to win. The Blood Bowl series does what it does: It's a tabletop based on dice. We aren't in League of Legends where we know the damage and risks of everything we do, where gameplay boils down to individual skill. The smartest player can have their bulky orc get killed by a scrawny skink, and the newest player can score a touchdown because all the enemy's team were stunned by an event. The strategy comes from how much you want to be safe and how much you want to push your luck. But sometimes, the dice aren't in your favor and there's nothing you can do about it.
This is the fun of the game, coming from someone who has played a few hours of Blood Bowl: Legendary and some hours of Blood Bowl 2. I think Blood Bowl is a relaxed series. From a newbish standpoint, meta-gaming seems toned down and anyone can win a game. It allows us to be more immersed in the game itself than in just "winning". Blood Bowl isn't a game we should look at seriously as some huge e-sport like MOBAs and other popular games, because then it starts to lose its charm. This is a silly game with a lot of cool customization and mechanics. I know Blood Bowl 2 has some flaws over the original games, such as a lesser single-player mode, but I just play online exclusively as I find playing with others much more enjoyable. If this game is on sale, along with its expensive DLC, grab it! You'll have some fun with it.
The next time your goblin gets eaten by your troll, don't roll your eyes and call the game unfair. Know that you took that risk, and the wonderful thing about chance is that no matter the odds, anything can go.

Let me preface this review by stating:
1. I used to love the old 'Lunar Lander' flash games when I was younger.
2. I love Kerbal Space Program
3. I just got a Steam Controller and have been using it exclusively to get the hang of it.
With 23 hours in, I liked this game. However, I was under the assumption that it was an early access title.
It's not, and that's what turned my review from positive to negative.
The three statements above meant that the control schemes weren't a blocker for me.
- The landing portions aren't too difficult between practice and having a controller - thrust is stronger with the duration of button press, so to mitigate it just tap the button faster or hold it down longer.
- The system navigation is Kerbal-lite, but at rediculous speeds - the speed limit is 6 AU per hour, or roughly 82% the speed of light to go from planet to planet
The map is procedurally generated, but that's not a good thing here. My first run I ended up 38,000 parsecs from Earth at good old Proxima Centauri. For those who aren't aware, Proxima Centauri is literally the closest star to the Sun at 1.3 parsecs.
The surfaces seem to be procedurally generated as well, but it mostly worked out okay for me. Except when I had to land on a 80 degree wall to explore some ruins...
Most planets are interchangeable and forgettable. I found a few that piqued my curiosity, planets that were hollowed out or had massive chunks missing. I wanted to know more, what caused it? Some space dragon hinted at in the lore? A civilization that blew itself up? Nope, nothing on those. No ruins, wreckage or resources
The races, quests, and items are all the same, but you'll run into them at different times and places depending on your map seed.
Dialog with other races is lackluster. I did get hooked into one quest, just to have the Meorcl randomly steal the quest item from me. No way to get it back, maybe a second was procedurally generated, but it closed down two quests. The save system prevents save-scumming which is both a good and bad depending on what kind of player you are.
There a lot of little bugs and features that I'd love to see addressed, but the last update seems to be back in August.
Optimization being a big one. During lander scenes I get 20 FPS, yet I can run Fallout 4 at max settings?
This game has a great concept and lots of potential, but I don't think the devs will get it there.
Don't buy this game at full price, don't buy it at half price.

I find this game hard to recommend. On one hand it's trying for a Star Control 2-esque universe with it's races and galatic history. The problem is the core of the game of maintaining your ship and advancing toward home, doesn't feel fun.
Going anywhere takes resources in terms of ship/lander hull and fuel. If you botch your landing, you may not even break even for the resources you are trying to collect. It seems to encourage you to not take chances, and not to stray from the shortest path to reach home. Avoiding all the fun parts of the game feels like the right way to play the game.
I end up wanting to explore the galaxy, doing quests, exploring the backstory of the races in this universe. But this is at odds with the ship maintenance, and crew injury systems, which want you to consider every move you make and conserve your ship and crew.
To round out the package is a very rudimentary combat system, with basically no ship loadout/upgrade options, the game ends up feeling sparse and repetitive. At the asking price of $40 USD I would definately not recommend this. Buying this on sale for 50% off I'm not sure I would consider myself satisfied with my purchase.
There is something to this game that I can see being fun. But it doesn't come together.

MM BRAINS! While no innovator of the genre or GOTY candidate, Dead Hungry Diner is a relatively fun indie arcadey game which manages to be a competent casual Diner Dash clone. While not much at the core of this game is different from its predecesors except for a ghoulish Plants vs. Zombies-esque theme, it does everything it promises to deliver extremely well. Due to how well the game is executed, I see no reason to not recommend this game to fans of the time-management games or as an introduction to those who haven't.
OVERVIEW: To describe the game in a single sentence, the objective is to seat impatient customers, take their order, gather a brain-matter-like meal, serve it, collect your tip, and clean their table all while managing to keep them happy and not eat each other. As an arcadey title, it's a nice game to play when you only have a few minutes to play a game. At the same time, it's addicting enough to make you not want to stop. The game starts easy and progressively adds more elements - such as different monsters - to complicate your simple task as you progress worlds. As your progress, new abilities are unlocked to aid in your venture such as cheering up customers, making them more patient, and increasing your waitresses speed. At the end of a 90-120 second stage, your performance is evaluated based on your ability to serve customers quickly, chain together like-kind actions (ie cleaning multiple tables one-after-another), and place customers at tables that monsters of the same class previously ate at. Afterall, no respecting Zombie would want to eat at a table a werewolf left his hind furs at! While absolute perfection is not necessary, witty use of abilities, knowledge of chaining actions, and placing monsters at correct tables will be necessary to achieve a 3-start rating. However, a 3-star rating is only a concern if you're achievement hunting.
Dead Hungry Diner does have a dozen-or-so achievements (and one hidden) to keep you trudging along. The achievements are pretty generic (such as obtain 1000 starts) and will take multiple playthroughs to get 100%. In addition, it does have Steam Trading Card drops that should give you a perfect understanding of what the game is about while obtaining them. Finally, the game has multiple playstyles including a survive-until-death mode and an uncaptivating story mode that will add a little charm.
SOUND & ART: As I mentioned prior, the game has a well-polished Plants vs. Zombies inspired look. While the game has only a full-screen and (I think) 1024x768 resolution, the graphics do look decent - albeit a bit blurry on a 1920x1024 monitor. On the other hand, the games' repetitive music is probably worth muting after 15 minutes and throwing on a Helloween album for a better experience. The interface is very basic, but does the job it needs to do with little complaints.
RATING: 6/10. Note that: I'm a "5/10 is an average game" kind of guy where a 5/10 means 50% of games are worse. This game is above average, but definitely nothing special. Due to the game being fun, playable, and polished, it'd be an injustice to not recommend this game or to consider it worse than average. While I'm beating the dead horse by once again saying it's been done before, it has been done before. But Dead Hungry Diner has has been done well in a charming way.
PRICE: I was able to pick this title up as an "undesired title" in a Game Bundle (I believe Blink) for around $0.50. By undesired, I mean I had very little interest in it prior and probably wouldn't have gotten it unless it was from a bundle or free. Seeing as the trading cards were worth significantly more than the game, I chose to keep it and grab the trading cards while I slept. So mind you, 8 or so hours of my gameplay was just the game sitting open unplayed. I'd say the game is worth $0.50-$1.00 if you're craving some Diner Dash, but I personally wouldn't drop $6.99 on it myself. Despite having little interest in the game, I did have enough fun with it to warrant a buy if you can get it for under $1, but avoid it otherwise.

I'm not sure why everyone calls Sunless Sea a roguelike. It's randomized to a lesser extent than any roguelike, and you do tend to die a fair bit, but Sunless Sea should really be in a class of its own.
What really stands out in this game is the writing and its ability to draw you into the world of Fallen London (never knew what that was until I started this game, but now I do); a fictional world where London has been drawn into an underworld surrounded by an ocean called the Unterzee. Each life, you play a captain of a ship who sails (zails) the sea looking for adventure and to complete an Ambition which you choose at the beginning of the game. Fierce monsters, pirates, superstition, fear and scarcity of food are your biggest enemies; every port you zail to brings new stories (and there are plenty) for you to experience and unlock. It's like reading a victorian gothic novel, except, you know, you play it.
Highly recommended for those who love to read.

Yes, Limbo knows exactly what it is, and it is artsy because it is trying to be artsy and all of that. But out of all the games that do this, Limbo is one of the best. I can think of no game that gives you a better sense of pure melancholy isolation. The minimalist, wordless, antidescriptive design is the first thing to show this to you: nobody is there with you, nobody to tell you your goal, nobody to tell you even how to play. The game teaches itself wonderfully, and then proceeds to take you on a journey where the journey itself is the reward. The twisted, uninviting landscape is a joy to look at and speaks of a  world with an unseen grandeur in size and scope, frozen in time and trapped in a state of pure, emotionless... well, limbo. This game will take you places, literally. You will feel as though you have traveled a very great distance by the end, only to discover... a somewhat abrupt and slightly shallow ending, one of my only complaints. It is still a satisfying resolution to the plot. Not to mention that the game plays really well. It is a very smooth platformer with robust puzzles and controls that feel really good. The visual effects and motions applied to the camera are also spectacular and feel larger-than-life.
If you're looking to disappear from the world for three or four hours (I highly recommend playing the game in one sitting) and travel into a fantastical, but mysterious illusionary world, Limbo will give you a fantastic experience and make you feel alone more than any other game I've played.

SiNKR is one of those puzzle games that rewards you for really thinking to get the answer, instead of attempting mindless trail and error.
The way to play is really straightforward, move the shaped orbs by moving them with hooks and simple contraptions to specified goals. And where the game shines is in the sum of all the simple mechanics put together. Bruteforcing the answer will only get you so far, as most of the moves you make are irreversible. And because of that inherent commitment for each movement I was sometimes left staring at the screen thinking what hook I should move next or where the orbs should end up at. Which makes the"oh, that is what I'm supposed to do" moment all the more satisfying.
My only pet peeve would be the fact that when making a wrong move you have to restart the puzzle again. But then again, I understand there really is no other way to punish for making a wrong move. If I was able to undo / redo endlessly the last movements, the game would swap from really thinking for an answer to mindless trail and error.
I might have to also point out that it didn't sink right away that circles could go inside square goals, another "tutorial" for this would be nice. But once you get the hang of it, you are in for a good experience.
What should I say? It is $1 (and while you may be reading this, maybe even cheaper), it trains your brain, it is entertaining, and doesn't need a single word of dialogue to tell you what is going on. There is really no way you can go wrong for something so underpriced, just give it a shot.
A bus ticket is more expensive than this game (that might someday get a mobile version you can play while riding that bus).

So, first of all, yes, story mode took me around 2,5 hours to complete. That's fairly short for that price, so if you're only interested in that, then it may not be worth your money. But, after spending twice as that, for me it has much more to offer after finishing the story.  There are various challenges and endless modes, both are really fun to do and unlock progressively - the more you play and beat the target score/time/pass the level, the more content you have. This so far keeps me entertained and still makes me play more and improve. For 15 euro I paid for this game, I think I already got my money worth by those 5 hours spent. This is a long review, so I will include a short summary just at the end of it as TL;DR version.
Gameplay-wise, this is not your everyday shooter. As you may already know from trailers, time only moves when you move (or generally, perform any action). Some of the story levels felt more like a puzzle - getting the spawn patterns right, knowing which corner to watch for, avoiding those nasty gunshots from ever hitting you. The more you play, the more game mechanics you discover. At very first, I did not know that you can have your time slowed while jumping, but this apparently is a thing and can help with avoiding bullets a lot while still closing the gap to any weapons you need. Melee weapons are a blast, with katana being the strongest (in my opinion) - I personally like to throw it for instakills, slice red guys with almost no hit delay whatsoever (with gunshots, most of guns have a delay between shots to make sure you just don't spam the trigger). I also saw katana blocking bullets, but so far I mostly failed with that one by destroying a weapon I wanted to grab by accidentally throwing katana into it (whoops !). AI is spot-on, although it just shoots in your general direction and may cause some friendly fire on the way, but I find it more as a feature than a flaw.
It's hard to say more about gameplay  without spoiling too much for the player, so let's get to visuals and performance, both are really great. I'm running the game on fairly low-spec laptop (with Geforce 630m crippling it the most) in 1024x768, and manage to mantain 30fps+ at most moments, while having the graphics at low quality, but that only impacts the shadow quality and Anti-Aliasing, and game still looks great with artstyle of mostly white and red colours used. Just beware, as the game seems to be built with Unity engine, there are some issues with that, which are engine-specific - it seems like changing resolution to one with non-native aspect ratio (4:3, 5:4 etc. if you're running a 16:9 monitor), makes it so there are black borders on the side that are catching any Steam in-game elements to stay in there even if they are not visible, and also making the video smaller overall. I could get used to this, but I figure some people may not, so just be aware of this.
SUMMARY
-great, innovative gameplay (time moves only when you move, kind of player-centred)
-flashy, white and red artstyle with text comments about what's going on flashing in front of gameplay (may be obstructive at times, but overall it's spot on IMO), a small epilepsy warning here, as this text is the most "flashy" element in the game.
-just OK sound, nothing out of this world, nothing that could break game experience
-very good performance with some Unity engine-specific issues here and there
-big replay value with challenges and endless modes
Is it worth the money ? If you considered all the stuff mentioned here and still want to just finish story mode and be done with it, then I may not think so. But I think some of those "story mode only" people may still get enough of an impression to still get going with rest of the content this game has to offer. If along what you have seen by trailers and read in reviews is enough for you to think, that you may or will enjoy this game, definitely buy it. You will not regret it.
Oh, and lastly:
SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT.

Where SiNKR shines for me, is in how the designer built puzzles around a small set of core pieces.  By combining them in interesting ways, each puzzle feels fresh and poses a new challenge, rather than repeating the same action over and over.
Learning the mechanics actually reminds me of the way The Witness teaches the player its puzzle language.  While the scope is smaller, the experience felt very similar to me.
Highly recommended!

superhot is a first person shooter whose main differential to other games in the genre is tying the running of time to your movements, meaning that the moment you stop moving, the enemies and the bullets already fired will essentially stop too (i say essentially because they still move, although on veeeeeeeeery slow motion).
the game follows the "one shot one kill" school of design, meaning that there isn't a life bar or regenerating health i.e. the moment you get hit by one bullet, no matter on which part of your body, you will die, the same applying to the enemies.
the arsenal of weapons is not particularly impressive, being composed of 1. melee weapons: a katana sword, something resembling a baseball bat and your fists (the only instance where you will need more than one hit to kill an enemy) and 2. some shooter staples: a pistol, a rifle, and a shotgun, but it gets the job done. additionally, you can throw various items found throughout the levels, as well as all the weapons, which will either kill the enemy (in the case of the katana sword) or stun them for a period of time (the other ones).
around the middle of the game you will receive the ability to change bodies with any enemy, which will allow you to do some cool things, e.g. waiting for an enemy to fire against you, stop moving (thus essentially freezing the bullets during their trajectory) and then changing bodies with the enemy, which will lead you to safety while the red dude that fired at you gets shattered by the very bullets he fired mere moments earlier).
there are not different kinds of enemies (i.e. you won't encounter blue, yellow or green dudes that are harder to fight or have more health), meaning you will be fighting red dudes from the first to the very last stage; difficulty increases, then, come from the different situations you are put in and the number of enemies you will face on a given level, as well as their weapons.
each level is fairly short, meaning that after you have died enough time to more or less master a level you will be able to beat it in a matter of seconds.
visually, the game is essentially monochromatic, with white being the dominating color, although pale blues and greys are also present; at first it reminded me of the visuals on mirror's edge, but it doesn't have the strong, vivid colors that dice's game uses to break the "monotony". i like this clean approach, but to some it may get tiresome and uninteresting.
the campaign is fairly short, but the single player is expanded by a challenge mode (where you play through the game with a set of predetermined conditions, e.g. playing with the katana only, playing the game with each gun having only on bullet) and by a mode that seems to be essentially an endless wave kind of thing (admittedly, though, i haven't put much time on this one).
there is also a little story, told through chat sessions, some small levels and interventions made by the system (as well as featuring some meta elements), but it seemed kind of secondary to me.
all in all, it's a nice game with an interesting, unique mechanic that i would say deserves to be played, even if you wish to wait for a steam sale to buy it cheaper.

Amazing. Some of my favorite games (Oxyd, Cyberbox, The Incredible Machine and Lemmings) have one thing in common: They all are rule based manipulation puzzles. SiNKR is right up there with all of them. Using a deceptively simple mechanic, SiNKR provides 60 increasingly challenging puzzles to entertain you with. With each puzzle you learn something new that will then be built upon in the remaining puzzles. In addition to the challenging puzzles, they are presented in a minimalist environment with a pleasing soundtrack that dovetails well with the sounds created by the mechanic itself. There is also no hidden information, which is a technique that I prefer. On some puzzles, you can figure out the solution before making your first move. On later puzzles, you can try to do this...but I found I always overlooked one or two things and had to fail a few times before having the critical "A-Ha" moment to help me solve a particular puzzle. All in all, just a great game. I look forward to seeing what this developer comes up with next. (I want to add that I played the entire game in the final beta form just prior to launch. I spent about 2.5 hours playing it on Tuesday and Wednesday.)

Banished is a deceptively quiet game.  You sink slowly but steadily into immersion.  The next thing you know the whole day is gone.
Graphics are unassuming and charming.  Music can be a bit tedious, but then looping sounds can always be tedious. Ambient sounds could use some work but I do like the fact that they diminish with reasonable distance.
I also like that the background story is minimal.  I usually like a lot of story detail but in this case less is best.
The way the game actually plays is just fun.  Anticipation and build up to events is very engrossing.  Also its re-play value is high.  I find myself returning to Banished over and over again.
Finally, this game has a robust modding community.  And that says something in itself.  Banished is a fun game that grows on you.  I highly recommend adding this game to your library.

Controls 6/10 (not a fan of using sliders to adjust how my game is running, but realistically I don't know how else they would have done it, so it earns a 6 here instead of what I wanted to give, a 4/10).

The games graphics are great, it runs smoothly on my 3.4GHz i3-2130, 8GB RAM, GeForce GT 640 with Very Low-Medium settings and low res terrain. The music is good and fits the Medieval theme well.
THERE IS NO WINDOWED MODE. This is a blow to my overall opinion of the game as Windowed mode is important for many people including those with disabilities that prevent them from utilizing programs necessary to use the computer, and those with only a single monitor who wish to chat or watch streams on the same screen.
I played through the Tutorial, though not much was explained very well. Many times I was left to wander the screen trying to locate whatever objective the game wanted me to accomplish because it wasn't clearly pointed out. Only on a few occasions did the game actually inform me to attack something and show me what it is I'm attacking, and even then I was felt that I wasn't actually hitting the targets I selected. Much of this is due to my unfamiliarity with the game, but during a Tutorial that should be taken into account.
I was also unable to find any "select all units" buttons, nor any keybindings at all even though they are clearly in use. This includes the ability to change keybindings, it just isn't there. WASD and your right click controls the camera, but if you are selecting any units right click no longer responds to the camera and is locked to moving units. You are then forced to use WASD, which could pose a problem for one-handed gamers. To deselect a unit you must left click off of it onto the battlefield, or simply select another unit/building without holding Shift. Dragging to select multiple units does exist, however it seems to only select the foot soldiers and none of the siege weapons that are necessary to taking enemy kingdoms. You are forced to Shift-click these units individually if you want to group them together.
The gameplay itself is fun once you get familiar with the controls. You need to manage resources such as food, wood, stone, iron and people by building homes and giving them jobs. This game is effing terrible, just straight away. It is. This review is not about the game mechanics, they work well, though I still have my doubts about loaded dice. So lets start from the beginning.
The single player campaign is a joke. Its about getting  the Reikland Reavers to former glory. You have no options about team design or even how to play for the most part. Saying the single player campaign is bad is not enough, its a guided tutorial. After finishing it, you "can" play single against a ridiculous AI in single player tournaments. But its Blood Bowl right? Its about MP. I only played the official tournaments so far, and my XP in this is also just terrible. Maybe results differ when you are playing with people you know, but hey, I'm playing online because I have no one for table top playing in the first place. So all the reviews that state "yadayadayada.... play with some friends in your own league"...well you get my point
The interface, dont get me started. Its one of the most counter intuitiv designs I have come across in 30 years of gaming. For starters you start a MP match, you dont get to see the team rooster, but the picture of the team. You have to click one more tab. Also navigating your teams, its ALWAYS one or two clicks more that are needed. Message me if you disagree but I swear I will present you with the idea of a GUI that is more sleak and usefull within 3 secs. You always have to hit a button that presents you with a different view, than you will find what you are looking for with just another 2 clicks. Its just a click too far every single time,
To get a MP started you have to register in a league, so far so ok. If you want to play a game there, you just hit the "find and opponent" button. AAANNND thats about it. You dont see what your chances are to find an adequate opponent. You dont see a lobby how many players are online. You get a guestimate how long it will take to match you but that numbers are just made up. So you want to play, hit the button, than you wait. You cant get up to do something else, because you get punished by the game mechanics if you let a counter go to zero. YOu dont get notified if you found a match. Basically you sit there and stare at the screen. And wait. and wait. ....anything between an hour and 20 secs is possible.  wtf are we in the middle ages of IT?
The money, its all about the money right? 30 EUS for a game is ok, charging 30 EUS for all the DLC additionally is not.
No new animations, you dont even have to download something. YOU JUST PAY FOR BEING ALLOWED to start teams with another race.
They made promises to fix this with a legendary edition soon, but seriously? They are proud to announce to charge only "about" 50% of the legendary edition price to people who already own the original game with all DLCs. And thats not even sure.
So, summary here. Its Blood Bowl, You currently have to invest 60 EUS to get all of it. They want to charge you some 30 EUS more when legendary comes out and the game and interface just suck at this state, the community is mixed but partly toxic,
Would play again, but not because its a good game. Its Blood Bowl .

Thanks to Steam's sales I've finally been able to buy LIMBO. I really wanted to try this award-winning indie game since a long time. After finishing it, here's my little review:
GAMEPLAY: LIMBO is basically a mixture of platform and puzzle games. You only have a few options in technical terms but the levels are well designed and offer many variations in the gameplay. Your path is full of tricky traps. Observation and logic are your only friends in the limbo. Difficulty is well balanced and that's something essential for a successful platform/puzzle game.
VISUALS, MUSIC & ATMOSPHERE: The best aspect of the game in my opinion. The limbo is imagined as a dark, nerve-racking and blurry world. The black and white art design enables to emphasise the contrast between lights and shadows, between hopes and fears. Designed by Arnt Jensen, it is at the same time simple - only shapes are used to represent characters and objects - and elaborate, with the use of many light effects. The ambient soundtrack also fits very well with the global opressive atmosphere.
STORY: As the name of the game suposes, the story is very vague. The player is free to make up his own interpretation of the clues that the game has to offer. And I think that's a good point. Even is the game is very linear, it's up to you to read the ending in a positive or depressing way. It makes the game universal and very personal at the same time: everyone can identify with the lonely boy fighting his own fears, but we all experience this hardship in a different way.
____________________________
Both the peculiarity and the universality of LIMBO make it a success. Indeed the game is not too odd or to "indie" to reach a large audience. And providing a considerable freedom of interpretation, LIMBO can be enjoyed both as an entertaining platform game and as a philosophical experience.
PS: I can't wait for the next game by Playdead, INSIDE.

Got this game as part of a bundle, and it reminded me of the casual gameplay and gamestyle I've enjoyed on gaming websites like Kongregate and Newgrounds.
If you enjoy restaurant (diner) management games and casual playstyle, you will like this game.
The aesthetics are very nice and cute in this game, with art that reminded me a lot of Bardbarian. The music is fitting with the theme. The feedback is very good, and you can easily see where everything is.
The controls are very simple - you just use your mouse. The learning curve is minimal, however, the game does a good job of getting progressively more and more difficult, adding new layers of mechanics to deal with. The first few levels do a great job of preparing you for the rest of the game. Whenever new mechanics are introduced, you are given a short briefing on how to incorporate these into your gameplay.
I haven't paid much attention to the story, but it seems to be pretty decent (your two main characters attempt to feed supernatural entities so they don't have to prey on humans).
As for gameplay, it is fairly easy if you are familiar with restaurant management games. You don't have to cook or prepare anything here, you just have to seat different clients and get food to their tables before the happiness gauge falls to 0, causing them to leave.
You slowly unlock new game mechanics as you progress through the game. A few levels in, you will unlock a store where you can buy upgrades for your skills pre-game. Skills include: a speed buff (extremely useful), a happiness buff (you can apply it to a single table, or the entire queue waiting to be seated), a table swapping ability (only same-size), a turn-guest-into-zombie ability, and a raincheck spell, which causes the first person in the queue to reutrn at a later time.
You can swap people around in the queue to help you strategize. Once you seat a guest (you have tables seating 1 or 2 guests, and guests come in singles or pairs {singles can still sit alone at a 2-person table}), you will have to wait a few seconds before they place a bucket on the table. You then take the bucket (you can hold two at a time) and bring it to the brain tree. After a few seconds, the bucket will be set in front of the tree with food inside. Next, you pick up the bucket and give it to any applicable table (indicated by 1 or 2 on the bucket). When the guests are done eating, they will have their hands up with money bags - once you pick up the tab, you must click again to have the table cleaned (by ravens).
Later on, a supernatural huntress is introduced - she will periodically spawn and attempt to hex/kill your guests. This will initiate a mini-phase, where you must click on the guests that have been hexed in order to shield them from the attack; any guests not saved in time will be killed.
Another mechanic is introduced where certain customer types will not like being seated next to others (so far, werewolves hate being seated next to vampires {but not vice versa}). If you keep them seated next to each other and the werewolves have not yet been fed, they may eventually start a fight - you will have to click the fight to have your bouncer step in and remove them.
The zombie ability is useful since you can use it on a werewolf or vampire to turn them into a neutral creature. You will later have a new guest (skeleton girl) who is loved by werewolves, negating the negative effect of being seated next to vampires. The table swapping ability is also useful in a pinch if a fight is about to break out.
Overall, there is a good variety of game mechanics if you are interested in this type of game. The game remains fairly challenging and is nice as a time filler. Take a look if you are interested.
Recommend.

When Diner Dash first released in 2004, it not only became a casual classic but almost single handedly created the time management game sub-genre. Among the copycats that have since began to pop up in endless droves is Dead Hungry Diner, which takes the idea of Diner Dash and seeks to give it a Halloween themed twisted, replacing the customers with hungry monsters and the plates of spaghetti and burgers with brains (well, fruits that looks a good deal like them). This all sounds well in line with a typical DD knock-off, able to entertain even while being fairly derivative in its niche of the casual game market, but Black Market Games wanted to go one further and throw in their own unique mechanics into the mix. Essentially, it wasn't broke, and they tried to fix it.
DHD shares a lot in common with its Playfirst cousin. Customers/monsters line up hungry for a meal, and you must manage them in a timely fashion, seating, feeding, and collecting the checks while racking up combos and frequent seating bonuses before the day ends. This is all fine, if done to death by a million other games already. Ironically, it's when DHD tries to differentiate itself from the pack that all its problems arise.
First, it cripples your ability to quickly seat customers by requiring you to first move them up to the front of the line. It's only one extra step, but quickly becomes hugely frustrating as more and more line up and you have to shift through them to get to who you want to seat. Second, it segregates different customers by the type of monster they are, forcing you to reorganize your seating arrangement so opposing monsters won't fight with each other and have to be thrown out. Interesting on paper? Yes, but in practice it turns what should be a light diversion into a stressful experience, requiring far too much advance planning and trial and error to succeed.
I like what Black Market Games was going for, and applaud them for attempting to innovate in a genre that desperately needs it, but they went about it in a way that makes Dead Hungry Diner more of a chore to play than anything else. I'm rather confused as to why they chose to alter the parts of a tried and true formula that they did, as the changes seem to have little logic behind them or practical purpose for existing. It's a shame, but one can hope they get it right the next time (because casual games never die, they just redo themselves). I honestly didn't think it was possible to screw up Diner Dash, but I guess there's a first for everything.

So I just finished Limbo, a short but very unique Puzzle Platformer, probably the best Puzzle Platformer I've played since Braid. The art style to the game is very black and grey giving it a very noir, dark feel, the lack of music throughout huge parts of the game really gives it some ambience, the only sounds you'll be hearing throughout a lot of the game is the atmosphere around you and your own movements, though you will get the ocasional bit of music which is just a continous background sound for the most part as to not take away from the atmosphere.
You really do feel a sense of loneliness and isolation when playing this game. Honestly, if there's a platformer out there that really puts you into a chilling atmosphere, it's this one, which is why I'd reccomend playing this game at night with the lights off.
The puzzles in the game are fairly challenging, not the most difficult I've ever seen, but they're challenging enough so that you have to use your brain cells and there will be a fair amount of trial and error....and death if there happens to be spinning gears involved to slice you into multiple pieces.
There are a lot of clever elements to Limbo; like a lot of puzzle games, as you progress new elements are added into the puzzles to make them more challenging, there's one which turns you upside down for example. There's another which is a white worm which will shoot into your brain and try to force you to walk to your death by walking you towards gaping holes etc. and you have to try to stop it from killing you.
Now there is actually a story to Limbo which I refuse to spoil for you as it was spoilt to me, it didn't really make a lot of sense, but if you don't know about that spoiler, then chances are you're going to be left wanting an explanation as the game ends very abrubtly, almost like a cliffhanger.
But what's interesting about this is that throughout the whole game, there is no explanation as to what the boy is doing and where he is going, no reason is given until the very end, until then you are essentially playing a storyless puzzle platformer.
I suppose this was done intentionally to surprise the player but seeing as I already knew the entire time why the boy was entering Limbo, I guess it wasn't a surprise for me which is a pity really, Braid on the other hand, I didn't see that one coming, I don't think anybody did. Braid had books at the beginning of every chapter so the story was more consistent throughout the game, Limbo on the other hand does not, if you don't know that there is a story or rather what the boy is actually doing in Limbo, then you won't know that until the very end of the game and even then, it is left open to interpretation by the player.
What I think is incredible is that approximately 70% of the game content that was developed for Limbo was scratched out of the final product because the developers felt that it did not fit well into the context of the game; a lot of developers I think would have left that content in there, but the developers here clearly wanted to make a great game that was short, had a unique art style, possessed a really strong eery, haunting atmosphere and had some clever puzzles which it does.
I just personally felt that the puzzles were not as challenging as they could have been, Braid was certainly a lot harder in that respect, I had to use a guide for Braid at times and I didn't for this, then again I was a lot younger back then.
8/10

Very rarely do I ever come across a game that is aout as painful to play as it is so creative and rich I want to play it anyway. Overall the game has an amazing world, very rich lore you could play for months and still learn a little something new, perfect atmosphere and great mechanics. However this game suffers from the horrible curse of being so hard to play its not so much fun but more of a challenge.
Good aspects:
-As I said the world is incredibly well thought out and populated with so many things
-The mechanics while not completely new are very tailored to this game and fit well
-Characters feel real and not: Hello I am the Tutorial quest
-The map and quests/events often change so you wont always get the same results
Now comes the other side of the game the negative. I dont mind a challenging game, FTL is challenging but just fair enough to keep you coming back for more. This game expects you to die and die often. More often than not 2 things will happen. 1. Run out of fuel and then the trouble starts usually leading to the end of the game. 2. the food runs out which leads to the end of the game. This game really had such marvolous potential but the fact of the matter is you only have so much space for fuel and food (not counting cargo if you want to make a profit) and if your a person who likes to explore and investigate a world vs just going from quest to quest you wont get much of a chance here.
Bad aspects:
-you only have so much space for fuel and food so you have to make choices
- it is REALLY hard to make money in this game
-when you die all your progress in the game resets (maps, money, treasure)
-the distance between islands is very long so exploring unknown places means you wont last long in a small boat
-the game promises to be lovecraftian and filled with horrors, but they arnt easy to find and not nearly as exciting or rewarding as you would think
-combat sucks unless you have very exspensive equipment
-unless you have acomplished very hard to do quests, you dont get to keep hardly anything from your last game
-the game punishes curiosity more than it rewards it
So here is my advice, if you want a game that takes hours to play, has tons of content and a facinating world this is a great game to buy. However if you want to have FUN or explore it, download Cheat Engine to solve the money problems. It does make the game more enjoyable.

Despite all the hate that its 'abandonware', which it could be, or it may not be, who really knows, but this game still is fun to pick up, run a few demolition derbies in, and have a laugh or two.
I wouldn't pay full sticker price though at the time, but if you already have it, its alot of fun.
What keeps me hoping about this game, is it reminds me of the old DOS game Destruction Derby, and it even uses the same kind of damage monitoring system (the triangles at the rear, sides and front that fade from green to red and eventually black) that the old game used. Never has a game since Destruction Derby has ever played up as well as DD did in its day. Few have tried, like Dirt Showdown was pretty entertaining, but just wasn't the same as it was more arcade and not a true to the dirt demolition derby.
So I continue to hope that this will see a release,
The Career mode and its features such as advanced vehicle tuning and parts selecting have been disabled as of the last release.
The damage modeling has gotten better, but some of the vehicles still unrealistically compress into a little ball. This just may be due to the limitations of the base models of the car itself. Handling is about what I'd like.
Also, I do like the new menus, they're much more easier to navigate than previous versions. I also got to test this game out with a Logitech G29 racing wheel, and it works great. If it wasn't for the unrealistic body compression, first person all the time would be alot of fun, heck even VR would be enjoyable for the demolition derby.
I feel that at least in the demolition derby aspect, the cars move unrealistically fast. In real life demolition derbies, cars are limited to 1st gear, and generally move at a slower speed. Adjusting how fast vehicles go may also help with the unrealistic body compression and damage. Also Grand Theft Auto 4 had some really nice damage modeling with "no crumple areas" where the actual frame of the car is more rigid and the body falls apart around it.
I get many enjoyable hours just in the demo derby part of the game, since there really isn't any decent demo derby games such as this.

Sunless Sea is an exploration and resource management game, with a VERY heavy focus on the writing and general atmosphere. The game is not fast paced, it is aimed at people who want to enjoy the exploration of it's giant map, the people that want to read for the majority of their time in game.
For this reason, Sunless Sea is inevitably love or hate. If you enjoy reading AND difficult resource management and route planning, you will love this game. These are not always things that go together however, so it is definitely not for everyone.
Personally I love this game. I enjoy the long treks into the sea, I enjoy writing down which items I need, and keeping track of where I can get them. I enjoy running the same trade routes to get the money I need for upgrades and quests. It is an excellent game, with very few flaws.
Outside of the game being very niche, the only other flaws are minor UI bugs; the objectives tab is pretty useless so expect to write things down in order to remember them, many other values are pretty unclear and there is sometimes clipping in item discription when reading rewards/costs of actions.
All in all, this is a great game for the kind of people it was made for, and will not be for everyone. If you're okay with dying to explore, learning from your mistakes, and taking in a vaste new world; I recommend you buy this game. You will easily get 100 hours of gameplay out of this if you learn the basics, and if you love it you will get even more.

This is a good game, but it is a broken game.
It is a exploration game that consists of captaining a ship through the Lovecraftian sea beside Fallen London.  The synopsis of the game is very accurate.  It's a bit heavy on resource management and there is quite a bit of pointless grinding, but it's really fun.  Exploring the sea is challenging, there are always these new shocks and surprises and the game keeps you on your toes.
But it's a broken game.  It's broken in that the death of your character can occur in random encounters.  You can build up a captain with 30 hours of sailing in between ports, have a nice powerful ship, and then- bam- random street encounter, he's dead, and all that progress is lost.  There's no way to judge the lethality of encounters, especially encounters in ports, before making a decision.  Hence, death and the loss of the character has this whimsical aspect to it.  It's like getting insta-killed by a monster you can't see.  So, a broken game.  I think the designers wanted something with the lethality of "Dark Souls," maybe.  Who knows?  They screwed up.
To play the game successfully, like with "Dark Souls," requires manipulating the game mechanics themselves.  Specifically, figuring out when the game auto-saves and using that to your advantage.  If you die at sea, alt-f4 the game, closing it, opening it again, and then reload the last autosave.
It's cheesy.  It's cheap.  It's borderline cheating, but that's how to fix the design flaws.  Once that's done, it's really fun.  So, a B+ game.  Good, but flawed.  With fixable flaws.

I wanted to like this game. Bought it because it was cheap, looked interesting, and everybody all over the internets are crapping themselves playing it, apparently.
I used up all my power quickly on the first night while listening to the jackass on the phone and got killed at like 2 or 3 AM because a big teddy bear appeared and I couldn't close the door. Loaded it up again and pretty much just sat there for 90% staring dead ahead (both in-game and irl) to conserve power, checked the cameras closest to my doors the remaining 10% of the time, and made sure to shut 'em in time if one of the robotic carebear ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s got close. Easy.
Second night was more frustrating. Every time I got to around 3 AM I got jumped by the purple ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ named Bonnie or whatever. I realize the whole game comes down to observing and responding to the patterns of these bigass pooh bear dolls before they jump you and make sweet animatronic love to your corpse, and I realize that if I stuck with it I could figure out these patterns and respond to them appropriately, and I ALSO realize that this is where a lot of the 'fear' that's supposed to drive this game is derived from.
The problem is that I can't find anything compelling enough about its presentation to bother with it.
It's far too formulaic; even if the animatronics have increasingly complex or unpredictable patterns of movement that increase the likelihood of sudden death and generic ho-hum jumpscares (the lamest form of 'horror'), EVERYTHING is rooted in repitition. The interactive element of the game is so sparse it almost feels like you're just clicking on random pictures in a slideshow until 'AHHH uneckspected soscary.gif' inevitably pops up. And they're the same pictures each time. ALL you can do is move the character's perspective left and right while you're in your office or whatever, open up the camera, and check all the security cameras one by one. Oh, and close and open doors and turn lights on and off. That's it.
In theory, the idea of restricting player control in the interest of generating fear is a good one; but it's implemented poorly here due to a lack of variety and a heavy reliance on cheap scares.

It's alien isolation without any additional mechanics or open endedness
IT's a walking and jumpscare simulator. On rails.
Story is not that bad and atmosphere is allright except for too much blood which became stale immediately.
Things may change as I play. It's not bad but if you're expecting some super good horror out of it - don't.
Sound and atmosphere are great, but the "cam corder horror" trope from movies is taken too literally and poorly implemented.
You see, the found footage plays on the idea, that someone found the footage and the unbelievable events happened for real. You are left scared at night thinking about the plausibility of the found footage.
In outlast, you are recording these events. You know you're in a game recording face footage. It is just retundant.
Mechanics wise, the camera is useful since it has nightvision and events recorded on camera get notes. And only nightvision consumes batteries.
This means you should never, ever be without camera. For what reason having no camera is even in the game is beyond me. This is a broken, retundant mechanic.
The game is advertised as horror but yet it plays on the weakness of horror with too many jumpscares. Only times the game truly has been scary thus far has been when you're in a big room that has lots of potential hiding places. You are scared that someone might come and hunt you.
There should be more creative moments like that to get you scared, not an autist peeking at you through a hole you're crawling in. It's just wasted potential.
This should've really been a movie. You are always on rails, everything is extremely linear and there's nothing to explore or search for. Every playthrough will be identical sadly.
The strenghts of video games as a medium is choice and interactivity. This game has very little of either. You just walk and walk from one scare to next and from one glowy item to next.
In the end it's not an horrible game and not nearly as bad or offencive as far cry 3 or call of duties or battlefields or gone homes. It's just a alien isolation with less features but it is still worth the experience.
If you hope devs make a good game in the future, buy it and play it.
If you want to experience it, just watch a let's play.
Either way it'll be the same.

I've enjoyed this game so far and I'm not entirely sure why there are so many reviews panning on its difficulty. The game sort of plays like a mix between Star Control and KSP. You've got the colorful alien interactions, 2d plane combat, and modular ship of Star Control and the physics, fuel management, and exploration of KSP. Be warned you will come to both love and hate this game in equal measures, but as far as the £23.99 price tag goes, there's no question it's worth it, grab some buddies and form a league, it's time for some Blood Bowl!

So I just finished Limbo, a short but very unique Puzzle Platformer, probably the best Puzzle Platformer I've played since Braid. The art style to the game is very black and grey giving it a very noir, dark feel, the lack of music throughout huge parts of the game really gives it some ambience, the only sounds you'll be hearing throughout a lot of the game is the atmosphere around you and your own movements, though you will get the ocasional bit of music which is just a continous background sound for the most part as to not take away from the atmosphere.
You really do feel a sense of loneliness and isolation when playing this game. Honestly, if there's a platformer out there that really puts you into a chilling atmosphere, it's this one, which is why I'd reccomend playing this game at night with the lights off.
The puzzles in the game are fairly challenging, not the most difficult I've ever seen, but they're challenging enough so that you have to use your brain cells and there will be a fair amount of trial and error....and death if there happens to be spinning gears involved to slice you into multiple pieces.
There are a lot of clever elements to Limbo; like a lot of puzzle games, as you progress new elements are added into the puzzles to make them more challenging, there's one which turns you upside down for example. There's another which is a white worm which will shoot into your brain and try to force you to walk to your death by walking you towards gaping holes etc. and you have to try to stop it from killing you.
Now there is actually a story to Limbo which I refuse to spoil for you as it was spoilt to me, it didn't really make a lot of sense, but if you don't know about that spoiler, then chances are you're going to be left wanting an explanation as the game ends very abrubtly, almost like a cliffhanger.
But what's interesting about this is that throughout the whole game, there is no explanation as to what the boy is doing and where he is going, no reason is given until the very end, until then you are essentially playing a storyless puzzle platformer.
I suppose this was done intentionally to surprise the player but seeing as I already knew the entire time why the boy was entering Limbo, I guess it wasn't a surprise for me which is a pity really, Braid on the other hand, I didn't see that one coming, I don't think anybody did. Braid had books at the beginning of every chapter so the story was more consistent throughout the game, Limbo on the other hand does not, if you don't know that there is a story or rather what the boy is actually doing in Limbo, then you won't know that until the very end of the game and even then, it is left open to interpretation by the player.
What I think is incredible is that approximately 70% of the game content that was developed for Limbo was scratched out of the final product because the developers felt that it did not fit well into the context of the game; a lot of developers I think would have left that content in there, but the developers here clearly wanted to make a great game that was short, had a unique art style, possessed a really strong eery, haunting atmosphere and had some clever puzzles which it does.
I just personally felt that the puzzles were not as challenging as they could have been, Braid was certainly a lot harder in that respect, I had to use a guide for Braid at times and I didn't for this, then again I was a lot younger back then.
8/10
Best Puzzle Platformer I've Played Since Braid.

Just Cause 2 is probably one of the best games I've played this year. It's got tons of action, tons of content, and an excellent (and huge) map to explore. And there's always something to do, be it completing missions for the different factions, doing some challenges, finding collectibles, or simply blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up. Oh, and it's got a storyline too.
It improves a lot from the original game; for starters, the grappling hook is now more versatile, not to mention it's no longer counted as an extra weapon (although it's more effective as one than in the first game!). You can also combine it with the parachute, which gives a new way to move across the map; it might be tricky at first, but once you get to know the hook/parachute combo, you'll be using it a lot. The gunplay feels good as well, and while the driving is tricky at first (especially in cars), once you get used to it, it's very good as well.
As for the environment, it's gorgeous. The Panau Islands are pretty varied; from dense jungles, to snowy mountains, river deltas, and even a huge desert! And they all look pretty good; the day and night cycle makes them even more beautiful, as it can create some fantastic  sunsets for you to enjoy. One of my favourite parts of the game was simply flying around in a helicopter doing some sightseeing. Another thing, the map itself is huge. Not only is there variety in environments, as I said, but there's many secrets to find as well, from collectibles, to some pretty cool easter eggs.
When it comes to story, well, just like the first game, it's something that you'd expect from a cheesy action movie. Nothing bad, mind you, simply lots of action all over the place. And it's great! Explosions everywhere, gunfights on top of moving cars; it's got everything. And the last mission, in particular, is probably the most over the top action sequence I've ever seen, and it's the best part of the game. Really, you must get there and see it, as I don't want to spoil the fun.
The game also has a cool soundtrack. Now, it's not like most open world games where you can listen to a radio station while driving; the soundtrack actually shows up during certain portions of the game, for example, when the military is chasing you, there's a pretty tense soundtrack playing. And the faction themes that play out after taking over a stronghold are also very good. The voice acting, well, it's interesting, for lack of a better word. I'm not sure if that's how accents from South East Asia are supposed to sound or not, but they did feel somewhat unique. And the dialogues from the main characters were also filled with cheesy one liners and such.
As I already mentioned earlier, it also offers lots of stuff to do. Besides the main storyline (which is actually somewhat short, if you focus entirely on it), there's settlements to complete by finding collectibles and destroying stuff; there's three factions you can help out, doing missions for them and taking over strongholds; there's different challenges to complete; and, as I said, you can simply take your time and fly around creating some chaos, which, by the way, is essential to unlock storyline missions.
Well, I don't know what more to write. All I can say is that I really enjoyed this game, and I hope that, if you get it, you enjoy it as much as I did.

In the wake of the survival-game fever that seems to have spread like wildfire over the last 1-2 years comes The Long Dark.  Set in the bleak and cold environment in the Canadian wilderness, you will have to stay warm, traverse the mountains and frozen landscapes, avoid the wildlife and scavenge to survive.  While The Long Dark boasts a vastly improved, stable experience when compared to many other survival games in early access, it unfortunately falls short (for the moment).  The reason I'm giving it a tentative thumbs up is because, as mentioned before, the experience itself is well optimised and stable for an early access game.  Updates are relatively frequent, and there is decent communication between devs and the community.  Here are the pros and cons -
+ THE GOOD +
- Well optimised experience
- Amazing atmosphere and artwork
- Immersive sound design
- An intuitive and easy to navigate UI
- THE BAD -
- After surviving a few days, you've pretty much seen all that the game has to offer
- Repetitive gameplay. You'll find yourself eating, travelling, eating, travelling, sleeping. Repeat.
- Limited map size.  Although it's pegged as a sandbox, it is a small sandbox at that.
- Lack of purpose after a few days.  There's simply nothing to do after a few days of surviving.
- Some bizarre survival mechanics.  You dehydrate if you don't drink 1L of water a day, which seems a little much.
*SUMMARY*
A solid, stable sandbox experience that unfortunately leaves you scratching your head after a few days, as there is nothing to do.  Sure, you could aim to craft that bow, or find that gun, or go fishing and become self sustainable - but all you're really doing is hopelessly extending your survival time in what ends up being a pretty bland world.
They took our money and ran.

HTTYD is a really cool setting, which I really love. Then you got a game based on that setting, how can you go wrong? Well...
1) The looks
Graphics aren't everything, for sure. But this game was released in 2014 and it looks like something made like 10 years ago. Compare this with another MMO, such as Final Fantasy 14. Released 4 years prior to School of Dragons, and boy does it look better.
2) Limitations
Of course, this is a free to play game, so it lives of microtransactions and paying memberships (which are optional). To unlock stuff, you need to buy gems which serve as ingame currency. But is it really necessary to actually charge gems if you want to DELETE a character? Oh, and you can only have one character unless you purchase additional slots.
3) Dragons
In the beginning, you get to choose which dragon you want. The dragon only follows you around and when it's grown up, you can ride it. I have no idea if that's only for looks, or if the dragons actually have different skillsets. As a non-paying player, you get to choose from four dragons. Four. So I guess the paying member gets a much larger variety, right? I couldn't check, because I didn't have enough gems to delete my character and start a new one, but if I remember correctly, a paying member gets an additional 2 dragons to choose from. And no, the nightshade is not one of them. Why not offer more variety?
Also, when choosing your dragon, there are a few options for customization, like colors. They don't seem to work, at least I couldn't change them. Maybe I chose a dragon that cannot be customized or I need to be a paying member to do so.
4) The controls
Oh boy. So, moving around on the ground is easy enough, if a bit stiff. You can't look around while moving, but at least you can control the character's orientation with the mouse. In flight, that's a different story. You control the flying direction solely with the keyboard. The steering feels very slippery and you constantly have to steer and counter-steer to keep the dragon on track as it keeps turning for a while longer after you released the button.
Climb and dive angles are limited, some flight school courses actually required you to do a steeper dive or climb than is actually possible.
Seriously, why not allow steering the dragon with the mouse? You could then use WASD for strafing.
Also, attacking or using skills in flight is terrible. You actually have to click on the skills to use them. You're in flight, trying to quickly attack something? First you must look and make sure the cursor is placed above the button.
5) Loading times
Every time you change to another area, you get a loading screen. Which is, of course, used as a canvas for advertising. At times, the game made me feel like I was walking through a forest of billboards.
6) Settings

That's it.

This game has more atmosphere than all the gas giants combined. At first, it's a little over whelming but once you get into the swing of things, exploring the Unterzee is incredibly fun.
The writing is brilliant. Seriously, the universe this game is set in needs a book or two. Half the time you've only got a picture to show what's happening, but you don't even need that. The writing is so vivid and immersive, as long as you have half an imagination, you'll easily lose yourself to it.
The thrill of discovering a new island in this game is something few games can match. The itch to explore this weird world is one that just can't be scratched. Every location has it's own story and mysteries to solve.
This game does have it's flaws however. The combat is pretty stupid and unintuitive. In my opinion, it should have just been left out and replaced with random events that occure whilst at sea. Enemy types aren't particularly interesting either. "Oh look, another pirate or swarm of bats" is a thought that often crossed my mind.
I was also disappointed by the map size. I wanted the sea to feel bigger. Other than when you first start out, you almost never run out of fuel or supplies. By the time I bought my second ship, I'd already been everywhere on the map and was just revisiting places to finish quest lines. This can make the game feel a little grindy. If travelling from place to place was more interesting and took longer, the sense of discovery and wonder would have been far greater.
All in all, this is a great game. It's a fantastic change of pace from other recent games and easily sets it's self apart. You're first proper play through where you don't die in the first 30 minutes will by far be some of the most interesting gameplay you'll have experienced in a while. And whilst it does lack in certain areas, all of the positives more than make up for it.

This game is a village simulator w/ a tower defense like twist. The game is fun for a few rounds, then gets boring. One/two rounds for learning the basics and the third for trying to survive as long as possible. The game is easy to learn. The game recently got very well optimized and sped up, which is really nice. The game doesn't slow down as much with the current patch.
The con's of this game, in my opinion, is the stale need to provide the bare necesities for the villagers to, in a way, start the game. It is the same start up every game. There should be openess to vast combinations of buildings people can try as soon as you start. Some can rush bow towers or rush way-maker, or toolsmith to arm citizens.
I really like this game but it is still satisfactory at best. (If it wants to be not early access.) I constantly revisit the game after an update to see what has changed.
If you want my opinions to make this game better (more replayable), you need to have even more building materials options, building upgrade options and strategically designed maps with different scarcities. (I really like the weathers btw, it felt more frequent after the update.) In an example scenario a player chooses a map with no rocks and lakes but with plenty of trees. The player builds a well and builds wooden fences, wooden towers, bows, wooden golems, etc. A map can have interactive previews that players can prepare beforehand (like df). Such as "50% fire element monsters" and players can build ice towers to counter them, or the map has no rocks so take some rocks or special blue prints to building stone buildings with wood.  A map can have region temperature, which it kind of does by seasons. In my opinion simple changes in maps and options of building materials can dramatically increase the replayabilities. Every game will feel new and different. As of now, the maps seem extremely random drawn meaning some maps have too much open area while others don't.
The game also need benchmarks and objectives (quests, goals, free steam icons). These are things imo very simple to accomplish and motivate players to play more. I would also like multiplayer and online play but these things are too far fetched and unnecessary.
The recent update with the marketplace, more frequent nomads, and treasure boxes tried to make the game feel fun and new but didn't really address the replayability issues. I think it simply made the game alot easier. The optimization improved alot I think I surpassed 128 population w/ at least 60 golems w/o issues. Started slowing down during the night time after 170 population and 70+ golems. Previsously I couldn't play past 80/90 population. (Props to you developers!) I'll be waiting for the next update to try out the changes. I thumbs up long lasting games. I think this can be one of my thumbs up review with a bit more changes.

I play a lot of city builder type of games. Mostly Dwarf Fortress. I've tried a few others like Banished, Towns and Gnomoria but they fell a little flat for me. I had Rise to Ruins on the wishlist for some time then bought it and let it sit there for months, untouched. I finally tried it this week (uh, the week I wrote the review). In my initial playthrough, I liked it. It has elements of these others games in it. It is relatively cheap so you get a good deal for the price. It isn't as deep as Dwarf Fortress but still a nice time killer.
Then time went by... It got boring real quick. I guess I can't complain. It's worth the price on sale but not much more. There isn't much depth here to hold my interest. I am used to Europa Universalis and Dwarf Fortress so maybe I'm overly critical when comparing it to games I keep gravitating back to.
I'm going to leave this review at "Recommend" but I am rating it to really be more of a 'so-so' game that you should buy if you like this genre and then, only on sale.
The Good
+ Inexpensive
+ Developer is active (not going to die in developement)
+ Pixel Graphics, UI and general look and feel are nice
+ Seems to run smoothly for an early access game (so far)
The Bad
- Nancy Pelosi is the name of one of the random nomads <shudders>
- Gameplay can get a little repetative once you get established
- Music could use a few more songs, they get old pretty fast but they arene't bad

What's to say about this game that every webcamming Youtuber hasn't said in the past few years. There really isn't a whole lot so I'll just be straight forward. Outlast is SCARY! It has a slightly different take on horror with some of it's mechanics, which is nice but, even to this day I still see the game as nothing but an Amnesia knock off. I'm sorry but Amnesia and Cry of Fear are still going to be my top favorite horror games that I've ever played, but back to Outlast.
Outlast definitely spooked me the first time I played it, but at times it felt a bit more suspenseful than scary, which if that's what they were going for they did a great job at it. It's definitely terrifying/exhilarating to be chased by crazy inmates or Chris Walker and it's definitely not fun to hide in the locker until an enemy goes away, while trying to conserve your battery life on your camera. Speaking of which, the first time I played this game I had a big issue when it came to finding batteries and trust me I explored as much as I could (which could be the reason for why my batteries died out so fast).
One big problem I had with this game came to the puzzle sections and it got disappointing of how simple they were. This is where they failed for trying to captivate what Amnesia did. In Amnesia you're required to collect objects and mix them with other objects and use them on other objects and to solve puzzles (it was basically a first-person point and click adventure), all while trying to reserve your oil and sneak past enemies. Outlast on the other hand requires you to sneak past enemies and press some buttons, flip a switch or collect some item and make it back to safety without getting killed. While the puzzles for the game are not innovative, surviving encounters with enemies definitely comes close to a whole new level of scariness for me. 1st) the hiding spaces that you have are pretty limited which isn't very fun to handle, 2nd) it's almost beyond pointless to turn off your night vision in the game, especially when you need to see enemies from a distance, 3rd) the sound design is exellent and 4th) there were a lot of times in this game for I literally thought I was not going to be able to progress past enemy because of how scared I was or because of their walking patterns being completely random/unpredictable. While that may sound like a good thing it really isn't, there was one time where I had to hide under a bed and I was completely trapped in this hallway because Chris freaking Walker kept walking past the hallway into a dead end every 15 seconds and gave me little time to escape, it was complete luck that I got out of that situation on un-hurt, which could be a fault in game design, but I'm going to put this on myself because I'm a pretty big wimp when it comes to this stuff despite the fact and Amnesia: The Dark Descent and Cry of Fear are both some of my most favortie games ever.
So in my opinion Outlast doesn't do everything perfectly, but in the end I still felt really scared which is what the game overall meant to do.
Basically, I enjoyed my time with Outlast and I'm pretty excited for Outlast 2!

TL;DR I would recommend this game in a few circumstances.  You liked the previous kingdom wars titles.  You like Total War, but would like to have real-time base building and strongholds you build up/defend.  Or you like to support up and coming indie developers who are making some quality products, even if it lacks a bit of finese.
Pros
This game follows its predescessors in the type of gameplay.   This title specifically adds more of a total war map where you can invade other kingdoms and the like.
The dev team have been very communicative and are taking our ideas seriously.   I've seen them implement recommendations and changes mere days after reading/talking about it.   I've seen ideas where they like it but the scope of work is far greater or is a feature that would be on lower priority was released down the road.
Gameplay is fun
Town building
Total War style fights with a good range of units
Updates frequently (at least once a week thus far)
Cons
Its still in the earliest stages of developement
Lacks finese of modern titles (AI rework occurring ~August, much content to be added, some models are too big so hard to select units that are too close during combat, lacking some basic features like "A" from starcraft so that units can attack as they come across enemies, etc)
Graphics aren't the best - if that matters to you
No free form building, game uses predesignated  plots to balance attacking force camp and hamlets/castles (was a different concept for myself but works out IMO)
Lack of trading/alliances currently (Potentially added in later content updates)
No low level API's in use (DX12, Vulkan, etc.  Next title please? :D )
Conclusion
If you're not into RTS/TOtal War, don't get this game.  If you don't like games that lack the finese of AAA titles, might not be the game for you.  But if you're like me and love finding diamonds in the rough, I'd say give this game 1 hour and 59 minutes of your time to see if you like it.
