What started for me as watching someone play through this game and laughing hysterically at their reactions would quickly turn into breath-stealing panic once I started playing the game myself. I knew from the start that Outlast was an intense horror game and I was excited to play it myself, but I didn't quite realize the level of immersiveness until I put on headphones. Instantly, I was placed in Miles' shoes with my camera in hand, creeping cautiously through corridors and around corners, praying my batteries wouldn't run out while I was lost in the darkness being chased by the mutated criminally insane and hearing his heartbeat and breathing react to the stresses of the various situations you find yourself in throughout the game environment. I would soon find my own heart beating in synch with his, my breath catching in my throat while my eyes were glued to the screen with paranoid alertness to the horrors that surrounded me. It would take pulling my headphones off and looking around my room to pull me back into reality and remember that it was just a game.....an incredible, horrific and well-done game.
So much can be said about this game that can sum up my approval, but I will limit it to as few as possible; with a storyline that isn't so obvious and characters that can be as unpredictable as youd'd expect real lunatics to be, the first-person perspective and protagonist reactions make this a game that truly transports you there and terrifies you to your core. I can only imagine what this would be like if played on the Oculus Rift....

Sunless Sea can honestly be compared to Dark Souls, in that every move you make must be carefully calculated in order to prevent disaster. Play your cards right, and with a bit of luck, you'll find success. Play your cards wrong, however, and you lose everything. Even with the occasional saving grace that you might have built up sailing around and talking to the right people, your odds of succeeding are always low.
Like Dark Souls, however, when you finally do succeed, the reward is gratifying. Finally finding your objective in the dark underzee, and managing to fight tooth and nail back to Fallen London for reward is be extremely satisfying. And soon, the hunger for adventure out in the zee returns.
The difference between these two games, though, is that whenever you fail in Dark Souls it is entirely your fault. You learn from your mistakes when you venture out again. In Sunless Sea, it's not always your own mistakes that lead to failure. As satisfying as it can be to finally find a location where your objective is, it's just as frustrating if your literal shots in the dark are fruitless. And the more often you return to Fallen London empty handed, the more difficult it is to keep your adventure going.
That being said, the story in the game is wonderful. You make it entirely your own. From giving your character a name and silhouette, to choosing an ultimate objective, to meeting new people and customizing your ship. And while I think there should be more basic ships that you can buy, the options are pretty varied. The atmosphere is set by the wonderful score, and the little pop-ups that determine the mood of your ship, shipmates, and you--the captain--and it adds beautifully to the entire experience.
So, while it can be frustratingly unfair at times, it's the kind of game that demands time and planning, and ultimately, warrants success.

Cuphead, from Studio MDHR is a run n' gun type platformer akin to the likes of megaman and the sort. The difference between this and a *WHOLE* lot of other games in the genre is just how outstandingly polished and fun to play it is. First off, the visuals, the animations were all hand-drawn and meant to replicate the classic era of cartoons around the 1930's. This matched with Beautiful watercolor backgrounds and a grainy, film-damaged aesthetic running throughout the entire game, it gives this game a charm that is found in no other. Every part of the aesthetics were perfectly planned out and executed with such a sheer amount of dedication that it baffles me. But if the game's terrible then you may as well watch a movie, right? Good news everyone, Cuphead plays fantastically as well. In my 11-hour playthrough (consisting of mostly deaths, More on that later) I've had the pleasure of experiencing cuphead's tight controls and fluid moveset. The Parry-Slap is very satisfying to use and can give the skilled player an upper hand in combat, and The dash is necessary for most of the game, much like in Megaman X. The downside being you can't dash cancel but I really didn't expect them to do it anyways. The difficulty of cuphead is bonkers. Like, Ball-bustingly-tear-your-hair-out kind of difficult. The difference between this and something like the "Difficulty" of dark souls is that any mistake the player makes is on them. Every boss in the game is achievable if you understand the pattern. There can be times that the game looks to go insane with how many obstacles are on screen at once, but there is really just a simple pattern for most fights that you need to follow, even when projectiles fill the screen, a keen eye will notice quite a few openings in attack patterns.
Now onto what little amount of bad things in this game: One main problem I had was the feeling of time wasted on some bosses. I spent a ton of time on some of these, mainly due to repeatedly dying. With having such high stakes in a game without any health regeneration items, 3-4 hits can really feel like not enough sometimes.
To sum it up, Cuphead is a beautiful demonstration of animation and game design. Masterfully crafted art style, music, and platforming put into a blender with Pac-man shaped eyes, and despite some flaws, still shattered my expectations to the point where it's now in the running for my game of the year. I highly recommend purchasing this game if you haven’t already. Solid 9/10

I wish there was a third button in the recommendations - "don't recommend, but not a bad game".
For me, the crux of the problem lay in my great expectations which Sunless Sea failed to fulfill. Now pair that with the price (I bought it during the summer sale for €11,40 and honestly, even that is a complete rip-off).

So there is no action (excluding the abhorrent "combat mechanism" during which you shoot against mountainous crabs - and I am expecting some action as a Victorian captain. There is also no fear. Like, none. I can't feel the darkness, I can't feel the terror - I can only feel the tedious terror of boredom as my steamship is "töff töffing" towards London yet again to deliver yet another Admiral's report.  Fear could add so much to this game, but it doesn't - because terror literally doesn't exist! If you "die", you are just given a new captain. That's all.
I would be content, were it a 3-euro mobile platform game, meant to be played shortly after take-off in a plane, only to abandon it to in-flight entertainment. But it is a 20-euro "indie explorer", which in the case of Sunless Sea equals a glorified roll and move.

In comparison to the pre-alpha state this game took a huge leap backwards:
- Server performances are getting worse with every update.
- Endgame is now divided in CHAOS tiers, where each new tier renders a category of your defense towers completely useless, which makes tower/strategy diversity in the endgame almost non-existant.
- Solo'ing is significantly easier than playing in a party. Player scaling is pretty damn rough, with 4 players being at x4 HP and x4 Damage. Since walls in a 4 man session don't scale up, you can expect your walls to expire 4 times faster than when you play alone.
- Patches right now consist mostly of nerfing "current meta" towers, rendering them useless and narrowing the diversity even further, instead of buffing up weaker towers and tweaking the monster's stat accordingly.
- Nerf>Bugfix: Still nothing has been done about those Orcs and Female Orcs phasing through/ignoring your walls.
Wouldn't really recommend it at its current state.

...is a jigsaw puzzle game. Complete multiple jigsaw puzzles of different sizes and difficulties from photographs of various birds.
You're offered a collection of 25 puzzles to complete, although you initially only have access to a few, branching out your selection from completing them. Each puzzle has a fixed quantity of pieces, but selection branches aren't based on difficulty and completing some won't unlock necessarily harder ones.
Gameplay is simple, you click and drag pieces that are floating in the moat surrounding the table, while right-clicking rotates the pieces 90°. When holding a piece, a small crab could appear underneath it. Catching and dragging the crab to the net serves as hint points, which can be used to view the picture again, rotate the held piece properly, or even show its placement on the table.
There's a nice selection of professional quality photographs, all themed on birds, showing one of more specimens on various waterfronts or landscapes. The pieces have different interlocks from one puzzles to another, some being traditional bumps, others being various shapes, hooks, or even birds and fishes. While these serve the same purpose, it gives an impression a variety to the various puzzles.
The hint system is nicely implemented. Instead of a plain hint button, it takes the form of a mini-game of crab catching and collecting changes the pace of the game, having you drop parts to catch them. The more useful the hints, the more crabs it will cost to use it. And if the crab becomes annoying as they constantly get in the way of your view, you can disable it completely.
Pieces do not lock with each other, but instead lock on the table at their designated position. That means you cannot assemble blocks of pieces that fit together to drag them at their proper location later. It also means that you can luck out by dragging and dropping a piece all over the place until it sticks. Also, on more than one occasion, I was trying a piece in a position and accidentally saw it jump to its designated location I wasn't even considering.
Because each photograph has a preset quantity of jigsaw pieces, you won't feel very compelled to try the same photograph twice, a missed opportunity of having various difficulties reusing the same photographs, therefore a missed replayability opportunity. It would make sense if the size was determined on the difficulty of the picture, but it isn't the case: some very varied pictures had large pieces, while other bland-looking ones had 100+ very similar-looking pieces.
It's a nice jigsaw puzzle game that may evoke childhood memories of doing cardboard jigsaw puzzles with your grandmother, but it doesn't do anything spectacularly well. Yet, if you're craving a jigsaw puzzle collection, I suppose
is an ok pick.

What started for me as watching someone play through this game and laughing hysterically at their reactions would quickly turn into breath-stealing panic once I started playing the game myself. I knew from the start that Outlast was an intense horror game and I was excited to play it myself, but I didn't quite realize the level of immersiveness until I put on headphones. Instantly, I was placed in Miles' shoes with my camera in hand, creeping cautiously through corridors and around corners, praying my batteries wouldn't run out while I was lost in the darkness being chased by the mutated criminally insane and hearing his heartbeat and breathing react to the stresses of the various situations you find yourself in throughout the game environment. I would soon find my own heart beating in synch with his, my breath catching in my throat while my eyes were glued to the screen with paranoid alertness to the horrors that surrounded me. It would take pulling my headphones off and looking around my room to pull me back into reality and remember that it was just a game.....an incredible, horrific and well-done game.
So much can be said about this game that can sum up my approval, but I will limit it to as few as possible; with a storyline that isn't so obvious and characters that can be as unpredictable as youd'd expect real lunatics to be, the first-person perspective and protagonist reactions make this a game that truly transports you there and terrifies you to your core. I can only imagine what this would be like if played on the Oculus Rift....
10/10 in my book, with the DLC included. Two different perspectives during the same timeline and both equally as disturbing. Love it.

This isn't just the first refund I've requested, it's also the first review I've ever left on any game I've purchased from the Steam platform.
"It tells the story of a person struggling to deal with something they do not understand." - - Read: It attempts to communicate an idea it doesn't quite know how to describe. It tries to make up for it's lack of ability to describe it by being equal parts excessively abstract, melodramatic, and baffling.
Occasionally a bit of the visual architecture or sound design is striking. But ultimately these serve primarily as a means to distract the player from the fact that it really doesn't know what it wants to say. A two hour exercise in patience waiting for an interesting "story rich" experience to form, and instead at the end you realize it was a two hour snooze-fest as you waited for the game to finish expressing it's singularly insipid, trite idea.
"Beginner's Guide" isn't a game for people who are interested in immersive or engaging stories. It's a half-baked, self-serving conceptual exercise. Instead of "Beginner's Guide", a more accurate title would be, "Vain High-Concept 'Art' Game".

As you can see for yourself the 3rd in a series of Jigsaw games made by this company.
They even have their own website
Jigsaws for me is all about having conversation with family, your loved ones, or as a conversation opener. Don't believe me? Go out, buy yourself a jigsaw and set it up on the dinner table and watch as your family start to drop their iphones and begin to tinker with the puzzle. Watch as invited dinner guests quickly gravitate to the open puzzle domain. These people are now vulnerable to being spoken too and often conversation follows.
On the other hand jigsaws to me are also a source of frustration as you shake the sofa violently for that missing piece, the dog looks guilty and you know he has eaten the damn thing as it fell from the table thinking it’s a foreign food scrap since your wife's cooking most of time tastes like paper, or your examining the front cover of the jigsaw box like you’re a doctor examining a x-ray about to perform a complicated heart transplant and have convinced yourself that the piece your holding needs to go into the place it’s not going, but just needs a bit of gentle persuasion with a closed pounding fist.
Unfortunately you will get none of those experiences with this game. The objective is to complete 25 jigsaw puzzles as the pieces float randomly around the edges. Annoyingly you have to collect crabs too and put them in a basket so you can earn points that give you three cheat options, which will reveal the picture for a few secs, correctly rotate the piece you are holding, or show you where the piece goes. Once you have used your cheat option, you have to collect crabs again to renew that ability.
UI isn't exactly friendly, backgrounds of the pictures are often blurred, and the crabs are just annoying gimmick that get in the way, thankfully you can turn them off. Other than that, it's exactly what it claims to be, a jigsaw game featuring bird pictures. What did you expect it to have? Boss fights?
Still in this day and age there are now animated jigsaw puzzles, puzzles with murder mysteries or intricate stories to them, and my favourite puzzle, find waldo. This offers none of that than 25 useless pictures about birds with no additional info about the picture or the bird.
However, since it is what it says it is and if your a bit of a jigsaw cuckoo then this may be one for you when it goes on sale.
Great game, would love more content though.

Nice and large-scale Roguelike:
"The Long Journey Home" (TLJH) ist a nice rogue like game with a fantastic art design and great sound design. The comparison to games like "Faster than light" comes in mind. The biggest difference: TLJH leaves several paths open to solve a solution. Be peaceful or be aggressive, be cooperative or be ignorant ... making choices is important. Nice fact: so to say no choice in dealing with aliens is game-ending, there is nearly always a way out.
Much more difficult are your choices concerning the exploring of planets: sooner or later you'll have to make a choice in exploring high-risk areas. The mini-games of exploring, which are already a small challenge for low-risk planets, then become a real challenge. And due to the persistent lack of ressources you'll definitely have to take a risk.
Conclusion: The aliens and therefore the storytelling is rich in variety and therefore the game is worth playing a couple of times despite constantly failing. The mini-games are challenging (sometimes unfair) and acceptable connection between exploring and storyline. Don't play this game, if you don't like rogue likes and have a low frustration threshold.

Can the game improve ? Yes , some improvements are needed to the UI and the campaign map . More information regarding your army that gets deployed , some details about the AI army. As said they are still working on the game and it definitely does not deserve the negative reviews it has received at the moment. Looking forward to future updates and simply can't wait ! I will update this review as the updates comes along !

Blood Bowl is the best one vs one turn based game ever made.
Think that's a bold claim? Just remember it's nearly 30 years old now and Jervis Johnson and the other chaps who invented it are amongst the finest games designers in the world. There aren't any other games that balance random dice with a wide tactical playbook so well.
Cyanide were a little slow on the uptake but they've made a nice job of it this time around and have proven themselves a competent developer. Good graphics and the model animations are superb: each player is full of expression and character. Finally now a we find a  much improved UI (compared to the first Blood Bowl game, which was pretty awful in all fairness).
I'm not going to comment too much on the DLC pricing, other people have done that discussion to death here and to be honest I'm really not that bothered about it... if you were going to play the tabletop game it'd be WAY more expensive than this, and they've done a nice job of each team.
As for single player, I never bothered with the campaign, but the few seasons I've played against the AI I have quite enjoyed. It makes the odd questionable move, and really isn't up the the standard you'd see from a half decent human player, but considering the complexity of the game, I feel Cyanide have done a fair job with the AI all in all.
Blood Bowl is all about the multiplayer though, and now they've sorted out the matchmaking somewhat (you'll still get some crazily unbalanced match fixings, but less so than at release I feel) it's a lot easier to pick up and play a game with people. The in match UI is well designed and once I'd gotten my head around the controls I found I made none of the blunders I did on Blood Bowl: Chaos Edition. The team management interface I find a little unintuitive and even after hours of play regularly find myself searching for the right button to press to select what I'm after: you won't have this problem with mouse and keyboard though.
Great game, if you're a Blood Bowl fan, make the upgrade, it's well worth it!
LEGENDARY EDITION UPDATE:
Yeah, it was cool to take the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Cyanide for being a bit slow on the uptake but I'm really happy with this game now.
Really, BB1 was cool but a bit of a mess and it's taken a long time to get this one to where it needs to be for serious players, but I want to say that the end result is magnificent. The graphics and animation are superb, the UI is a vast improvement now and works really nicely both Mouse/Keyboard and with a controller, the matchmaking is much improved. There are a host of options and game variations to keep things sweet. Two hundred hours plus of gameplay and the commentary still suprises me occasionally, and the voice acting is absolutely brilliant!
I'm also impressed that Cyanide took the criticism of their poor communication into consideration, as I think they are much improved on that side now. They've clearly listening to more experienced players on what to implement, and that shows.
The AI is still... hmm, needs improvement. But I'm a programmer and I know how hard it is to make a AI for a game this complex, but there are some glaring issues that I think could be fixed without too much effort.
But I rarely play single player anyway, and it's a multiplayer game so it's not a big issue really.
Well done, keep working on it and we'll keep playing :)

In BioShock you are a survivor of a plane crash in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. You are able to make your way to an island where a submarine is waiting to take you to into the great depths below where the mysterious underwater city of Rapture awaits. The city is trashed and genetic freaks called splicers roam around, attacking anything that gets in front of them. In order to survive you will have fight through these Splicers and other oddities keeping your eyes and ears open for clues into what has gone wrong, how you may be able to help or how you can escape.
One aspect that makes the storyline work so well is the way it is told. BioShock uses a real time method of telling the story through random radio reports, overheard conversations and audio recordings.
You can choose from a variety of different weapons, anywhere from pistols and shotguns to chemical throwers and grenade launchers. Each gun has different ammo that you can use. There are also many plasmids that you can use. You can electrify the water to kill everyone in it, set people on fire, freeze them and then smash them with a wrench, among other things.
The graphics in this game are good, out of date, but still good.
The sound of BioShock really puts you into the game. From the creepy things the splicers say to the background music, everything fits perfect.
BioShock builds a great atmosphere by using terrific graphics and sound to set a creepy mood. BioShock is truly a stunning game and worth to buy.

You're spurred out of your bed by a screeching alarm clock, begin to head to the kitchen to eat your two day old chinese food from the fridge, and instead are greeted by a beefy mustachioed man beating on the glass window to your spaceship. What's that, why does a spaceship have an openable window? Why is this man seemingly able to just be in space without a suit? WHO CARES!
This game is charming. Like, really charming. Each level is beautifully detailed in a style that reminds people of Elf in Tights 2: Sea Shanty of the Red Boat and they pull it off swimingly. There's a good amount of collectibles strewn about each level map, including balls of yarn to make new hats with different powers, special coins that your space child can gamble with to get new aesthetic changes and the usual platformer currency barfed all over the place for people to collect called pons. Pons can also be used for upgrades, particularly for pins, which you wear on your hat to gain extra effects.
Each world has chapters, which has a different objective based on the same map. After enough chapters are completed, there's a finale, which involves beating the snot out of people with protective raingear like an umbrella. There are also things called Time-Rifts, which are basically obstacle courses that you have to go through in a similar manner to Italian Tropical Janitor 3: Maximum Hydration on the gamecube.  Simple enough concept, sure, but this games music score, tight controls and whimsical feel are extremely happy, anti-depressive and really wrap up an extremely solid package of a game.
It is a short-ish game though, even if you want the 100%. The longest time sink in the game is probably getting every single color palette and hat skin from the slot machine on your ship. But the game is so buttery smooth in the gameplay department that it makes it all enjoyable and worth every last shekel. A Hat in Time is not a breakthrough of exciting new platforming standards, but it has mastered a lot of the tried and true elements of the classics.
A Hat in Time gets 4 Chinese Leftovers out of 5.

So here's my short opinion on School of Dragons.
I downloaded it with some friends because we were all curious about how a game based off this particular franchise would go. To be honest none of us really expected much. Upon downloading we were greeted by, if you have not already guessed from the other reviews, lots of loading screens. Loading screens aren't a bad thing...normally. But these are heavy and a bit sore on the eyes. The attempts to get you excited by all the new content fall flat when you cycle through the same 5 ads over and over for 10 minutes. They could be better designed but moving on.
The intro experience is a bit clunky but long story short you get to pick from a few dragon breeds and get your baby dragon. The colour customization is actually pretty solid and the dragon models are great for the level of graphics the game can handle. Excellent textures a fairly well contructed world and you're off to level up yourself and your baby dragon.
The game attempts to be educational and actually does a fairly decent job at being engaging about it...at first. You have some quests involving the scientific theory and although the game gets a bit 'please allow us to shove this information directly down your child's throat, you are very welcome' the sentiment does not go unnoted. You collect different minerals and see how they interact with dragonfire and check the results against your hypothesis. Actually kind of rad.
Too bad all the other science related quests are replaced with this Candy Crush Simulator that makes NO SENSE WHATSOVER. But I digress. I was fairly impressed at this point.
Then I tried to meet up with my friends.
After the initial dance of 'where are you' and 'meet me here' we finally made it to the same location. Only...my friends were not there. Ok, so there are different servers. No way to see which one you are on? No problem. We'll just exchange friend codes and teleport to each other. Only...you can only befriend someone on the same server as you.
Oh. Well then...challenge accepted. We spent the next hour switching from single player mode back to mmo mode until we found each other. Grand. Only there is a chance that when you leave the area you could swap servers. Graaaaaaand. No matter. We'll meet up later when our dragons can fly and explore together.
By the time our dragons could all fly, we had stumbled upon the most ridiculous series of bugs and paywalls imaginable.
Gems, in this game, just so happen to be truuuuuuly outrageous. They can be obtained for free, rarely and in small quantities. Otherwise you have to pay for them. That's fine, I don't need Gems right? Ho boy. You can't do anything without them.
Want another dragon? Gems. Saddle? Gems. Another go at a race? Gems. Open a chest you found? Gems. Start a clan? Gems.
Heck, some places you can't even get to without a membership. Not only that but if you don't have mum's credit card to get those sweet, outrageous beauties you can forget about playing at all. You're dragon can run out of energy. How do you fix that? Feeding them. How do you feed them? By fishing. Fishing bait costs gold which can be obtained through quests...which you need your dragon for. If your dragon is tired you can't do quests. Hazzah! I think you can recharge your dragon by paying gems though. So, yey.
Bugs include, quests that can only be completed by logging in on someone else's computer after attempting to light a campfire for two hours, quests that you never took, lead no where, and simply don't exist, and, my favorite, incomplete maps. INCOMPLETE MAPS.
There are literally places in this game where you can be flying over a mountain and suddenly it looks like the entire world is see through, like your minecraft server crashed or you're trying to play on your mum's flip phone again to prove you can. I was flying in the glitchy ocean (which should have a seziure warning on it btw because the shaders are bugged) and heading towards the island only to find a neat surprise. Its flat. Its literally a 2D render of the island the disappears when you pass go. I mean, come on. Don't make flying there an option if you're going to be lazy.
Half the trees are flat. There is a forest of 4 very sad, out of place trees in this one location that you have to go to for any quest involving chopping wood. MUST I GO ON?
And do you know what the worst part about this game is? It has freaking potential. It has such a good base but it feels like no one is working on it. I want to shut it down, give it to a team of college kids, and put it back up in a couple of months because it would probably be ACES and I would probably LOVE IT. Because flying on your own dragon is COOL and the setting is CHARMING but it all feels like an alpha game that someone ran out of energy for halfway through and still had to turn it in.
I hate this game and I want someone with some fire in their soul to take over the whole freaking project so I can sleep at night instead of sketching out ideas for a better system that does not wreek of being a quick cash grab. Ugh. Don't play it just go send some letters to the developers or find a kickstarter to fund. I don't know just don't download this until someone takes responsibility for this beautiful disaster.

Introduction
I am Tigerfrost. I would like to apologize for anything that is miss-spelled or any grammar issues. Thank you.
If you'd like to skip straight to Pro's & Con's, please move to the bottom of the page. Thank you.
How I Found Out About "Just Cause 2"
The same way I found out about a lot of games, from YouTube. I randomly came across a video that was showing someone driving a vehicle off of a tall snowy mountain. The crash and destruction effects made me fall in love. See, I've always loved destruction in games/movies/etc. So when I see something like that, I know I must own the game.
Unfair First Impressions
I've seen a lot of different unfair first impressions for this game. The first, and most simple being, the fact that someone may not have liked the original Just Cause game. Therefor it leads to an automatic thought that any sequel will be just as bad, or worse. I can understand this, but believe me, Just Cause 2 makes everything better.
Second, I've heard that the game can get low reviews and less players because of it's story. I know some people are looking for games for their story. However, not everyone is. You can have a game like Just Cause 2 where the story is bad but the gameplay is good, very good.
Third, because it's a third person shooter style of game. Which can turn some people away.
Review Of "Just Cause 2"
Just Cause 2 is a massive open world, sandbox, TPS game, that comes with a full story, side missions, bonus missions, and so many collectables that you'll die before finding all of them.
The world of Just Cause 2 is massive (Panau). One of biggest I have ever seen! Stretching across desert terrain and mountains, snowy mountains and terrain, jungle and marsh, ocean, urban areas, and military bases. One downside to the world of Just Cause 2 is that it may be very big, but it's not well populated with stuff. Meaning, all that jungle and desert, 90% of it will not have anything in it besides sand and trees. So you may find the world itself being very boring at times. However, the rest of the game makes up for that. In the world of Just Cause 2, there are urban areas to explore. Villages that may hold resources and ammo to big cities that contain higher costing vehicles & helicopters. Places like airports where you can obtain a passenger jet. There are military bases you can liberate by destroying & collecting all things within it. These bases could consist of ports, vehicle factories, little infantry camps, to big fortress type places.
You can get around the world of Just Cause 2 with many things. First of all, you can use your grappling hook to get to higher places, then you can use your parachute to glide down or travel across land faster. Not only is that the most basic of travel, there are vehicles...a lot. There are a little over 100 vehicles in Just Cause 2. Anything from ATV's, motorcycles, cars, trucks, boats, armored cars, planes, helicopters, etc. The list goes on. One thing that I do not care for in the vehicle department is the vehicle physics. The vehicle isn't really that responsive, or reliable. You can hit the movement key lightly and the vehicle will spin out, even at low speeds.
You can defend yourself with weapons like SMG's, shotguns, etc. There really aren't many weapons to use in the default game unless you purchase DLC. However, there is still so much content in the game, you don't actually need DLC so the DLC is just there for bonus weapons & vehicles. I would like it if Just Cause 2 had more weapons in the default game. With how big the world is, having more weapons gives you more options to do things with.
This isn't really the game that plays like a TPS game. You don't run up to a base and get behind cover then start attacking. The AI is kind of stupid, and the same time, they work well. There really isn't any stealth. The concept behind Just Cause 2 is that you drive in for fly in, kill everything, and walk away from a massive explosion.
As for the story and side missions. The story itself is generic and not really exciting, except for the final mission. There are only six missions I believe, maybe more. However, to unlock story missions you must gain chaos which can be obtained by destroying key points in military bases, fighting the military, collecting things, or completing side missions. There are a lot of side missions to choose from three different sub factions who you'll find fighting the military at times. The side missions themselves can actually be unique and fun, however the briefing itself is low. Every mission start, you'll stand there and the leader of the sub faction will drive by, tell you what you need to do, and then drive away. Not a word said.
Don't get me wrong, Just Cause 2 is a great game, it just may not be what you are looking for.
Content In Just Cause 2 (Bonus Missions & Collectables)
In the world of Just Cause 2, you have bonus missions alongside "side missions". These mainly consist of races, for all vehicle types.
Other then that, you have thousands of collectables. These can be little pickups for the sub factions, or little resource crates that boost your stats, like giving you weapon parts to upgrade your weapons, or armor parts to give you more health, etc.
To gain 100% in Just Cause 2 requires you to collect every piece of sub faction items and resources, also, destroying key military structures in an area. Each area you discover will give you a progress bar, when everything has been collected or destroyed, the progress bar will reach 100% and that area is clear. However, the PC version of Just Cause 2 experienced a bug where a few items & structures do not spawn in the game. Therefor it is impossible to beat the game 100% without a mod. The devs apparently do not care to fix this easily fixed problem.
Pro's & Con's (Overall Rating)
Just Cause 2 is an open world TPS that provides a wide variety of collectables and fun destruction. You can spend hours on the game before ever reaching 15% for full completion. Despite needing a mod to fully beat the game 100%. There has alos been a community mod released that allows people to play together in the world of Panau.
Pro's:
+Massive open world.
+Loads of collectables for hours of game time.
+Fun destruction system.
+Addicting "I must find everything" style.
+DLC is not required to play.
+Nice variety of vehicles.
Con's:
-Mod needed for full completion.
-Enemy will spam helicopters.
-Mostly boring empty world.
-Strange vehicle mechanics.
-Low leveled main story & side mission briefing.
Overall Rating: About A 12/15 (A Nice Game That's Worth A Pickup)

Ah, Blood Bowl.
A game in which bribery is rife and fouling is fine. A game in which a player must be carefully nurtured, thoughtfully assigned skills and then ruthlessly fired after a few seasons because he's inflating the team value. This is all assuming said player doesn't break his neck after being tripped by a particularly malevolent blade of grass. It's a game in which a medical professional's treatment options might either be accepting death or simply accepting death. It's a game in which you swap players through Nurgle's Rot and the Necromancer instead of swapping jerseys.
It's the world's greatest game when your Orc Blitzer gets up off the ground, runs over to grab the ball at an opponent's feet, evades a tackle and then throws a pass for a touchdown. It's the world's worst when half your team suffers from heat stroke in a must-win match. (How does a zombie suffer from heat exhaustion anyway?)
It's certainly a game for a niche audience. The game's complexity makes it a frustrating experience for new coaches. Expect a lot of "why can't I ...?" and "how do I …?" moments in the first dozen or so hours of play as the ruleset is filled with gotchas and exceptions. Since the game adheres closely to tabletop rules, The Living Rule Book is an essential read and new coaches would also do well to consult guides on
(one of gaming's great strategy sites) while leveling up players.
There are laughable suggestions Blood Bowl is completely random and devoid of strategy. It's not. The game's strategy involves risk-management, canny positioning and deep understanding of the complex skill system to tilt the odds in your favour.
Just as in any dice- or random number generator-heavy game, risk-management is essential. Make low-risk moves before attempting risky blocks or dodges. Gang up on opponents to improve the odds of success. Mark or foul dangerous opponents. Self-restraint will often be just as valuable as tactical acumen because sometimes the best move is not moving at all. And finally, plan for failure because Nuffle, god of dice and unintentional comedy, delights in tearing up your carefully laid plans.
Victory will be all the more satisfying considering the forces arrayed against coaches:  the opposing coach (AI or human), fate and time. The game's AI is mediocre but it offers enough of a test for new coaches. New or experienced, coaches must contend with fate as represented by the RNG. While the odds can be improved with tactics and carefully crafted player and team builds, time is an implacable foe. If the referee blows for time, it doesn't matter how close you are to the end zone.
Some would-be coaches will find it difficult to get past the fickleness of the RNG and the twiddling of thumbs while the opponent stalls and drags out matches that can't be won. Those who persevere will be rewarded with one of strategy gaming's great campaigns. There are few gaming experiences as enjoyable as taking a team of hapless butterfingered greenhorns and turning them into a battle-scarred team of champions over the course of several seasons.
Still, the initial reviews for this latest adaptation of Blood Bowl were mixed and understandably so. The playerbase was irritated at having to pay extra for teams which were bundled together in previous editions, annoyed at being nickled and dimed for customisation skins and just as annoyed over missing customisation options. The publisher responded by giving away most of the DLC teams to early customers and this placated some but not all.
It bears minding Blood Bowl 2 was developed by a small developer backed by a small publisher for a relatively small market. Of course, there's room for improvement and of course, the playerbase should push both developer and publisher to make those improvements but the question is, and has always been, whether the playerbase would be willing to fund ongoing development for a game that would benefit from continued attention.
There's no getting around the fact a game like this will never be made by the likes of EA, Ubisoft and Activision. In the unlikely event a major publisher did pick up the Blood Bowl license, it would be so altered to appeal to a larger audience that it would scarcely be recognisable.
(It would probably be a third-person shooter with unnecessary overlong cutscenes featuring Griff Oberwald attempting to avenge the death of his family at the hands of Varag Ghoul-Chewer.)
The game as it stands is really good for what it is -- a relatively faithful adaptation of a cult favourite tabletop game -- and with the recent announcement of the Legendary Edition, with its laundry list of fan-requested features, the future looks bright indeed for Blood Bowl fans.

In the wake of the survival-game fever that seems to have spread like wildfire over the last 1-2 years comes The Long Dark.  Set in the bleak and cold environment in the Canadian wilderness, you will have to stay warm, traverse the mountains and frozen landscapes, avoid the wildlife and scavenge to survive.  While The Long Dark boasts a vastly improved, stable experience when compared to many other survival games in early access, it unfortunately falls short (for the moment).  The reason I'm giving it a tentative thumbs up is because, as mentioned before, the experience itself is well optimised and stable for an early access game.  Updates are relatively frequent, and there is decent communication between devs and the community.  Here are the pros and cons -
+ THE GOOD +
- Well optimised experience
- Amazing atmosphere and artwork
- Immersive sound design
- An intuitive and easy to navigate UI
- THE BAD -
- After surviving a few days, you've pretty much seen all that the game has to offer
- Repetitive gameplay. You'll find yourself eating, travelling, eating, travelling, sleeping. Repeat.
- Limited map size.  Although it's pegged as a sandbox, it is a small sandbox at that.
- Lack of purpose after a few days.  There's simply nothing to do after a few days of surviving.
- Some bizarre survival mechanics.  You dehydrate if you don't drink 1L of water a day, which seems a little much.
*SUMMARY*
A solid, stable sandbox experience that unfortunately leaves you scratching your head after a few days, as there is nothing to do.  Sure, you could aim to craft that bow, or find that gun, or go fishing and become self sustainable - but all you're really doing is hopelessly extending your survival time in what ends up being a pretty bland world.

Cuphead brings a classic form of animation into a videogame with absolutely no compromises. The first game that did that was South Park: The Stick of Truth, but that's kind of like comparing NES to PS4. Cutout animation serves its purpose for South Park, but the beautiful hand drawn animation style from the 30s is no easy thing to recreate, especially in video game form. Cuphead succeeds in doing just that, and it's an absolute joy to look at.
The game itself is tough as nails, but never unfair. It is balanced both for casuals, who can enjoy just trying to beat each stage, and for hardcore players, who have mostly reasonable goals to aim for in order to perfect each stage.
The music and aural presentation is wonderful as well, but for me, it always comes back to the animation. 2D hand drawn animation is basically dead in modern movies and television. I mourn for it. Cuphead has revived it, at least for a moment, and it feels nothing short of miraculous.

I've only played traditional or whatever the normal mode is. Overall it's a decent game that seems to tie together a lot of elements from other similar games, making an attempt at covering a lot of aspects from those games that I enjoy.
Issues thus far. Game is EA, so obviously there are going to be issues. The dev is super responsive, my problem is that from some of his responses, some changes haven't come even though he commented about them a year ago. For example, if you accidentally dismantle a building, there's no obvious way to stop this. Researching it shows a comment from the dev stating this function is planned for InDev 18, the game is now on InDev 28.
This really ties into another issue, it's a combination of the game having a small playerbase and the dev probably being indie, there's no updated wiki to look up the game in its current state. The wiki link on the game's official site gives you a WIP page. Trying to look up information on the game leads to posts that span years, making it unreliable on whether or not it's still relevant.
I also have a pretty big issue with the way your buildable area expands. Your walls cut off your "sphere of influence" and you can't build beyond your them. This forces you to tear down walls in order to release your "SOI" in order to build beyond it. This makes it a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to expand. It's constant leapfrogging your sphere to expand and it gets rather repetitive.
As a final note, props to the dev for being super responsive. This however, leads to another con for me. The dev has indicated some game decisions that I don't really agree with.
For example, I'm in my second game on traditional, it took me some time figuring out how to get things going in my first attempt so I abandoned it after 20ish minutes to restart. My 2nd and current game started a bit hairy, but now I control like 40% of the map and it's just a slow grind at this point. I realize that I'm playing the easiest mode in probably an easy mapset, my issue is that I don't really feel like doing it all over again because of the time investment to build from the ground up again.
I know the dev has made responses as to speeding up the game, my problem is with his responses. The dev has indicated that he wants to add a spell to the game as a temporary buff to your villagers speed instead of just adding a game speed option. My problem with this is that a speed buff is pretty much irrelevant to the issue game speed, they're two entirely different things and the fact that the dev thought this was a response makes me doubt his decision making and the future of the game.
The lack of a game speed option is pretty much deterring me from wanting to try any other maps. Sure, it might be harder and the challenge might be a bit more interesting, but there's just too much sitting and waiting for your villagers to get anything done. Especially when you do get strong enough and start having to expand your base.
I'm 9.5 hours into the game and pretty much finished with it in my opinion. I got it on sale so I guess I got my money's worth, I'd recommend the game for a quick play, but for the type of game it is, that relies on replayability, I think it still needs a lot of work which might never come, so I can't really recommend it.

It was only yesterday that I realized that this is more a tower-defense game...
To learn the game mechanics I played a custom game, increased the day/night duration and deferred monster-spawning to day 15
That allowed me to build a nice town with a good working infrastructure. At around day 10 I started to take a closer look on defenses, and started building some defense towers. There are tons of defensive buildings compared to the regular buildings, but that’s ok. When monsters arrived at day 15 it was quite easy to handle at first, but within a very short time, they arrived in HORDES. Especially the spectres are dangerous, the others are merely lining up at the walls trying to get through, ready to get pierced by my towers. Only the spectres can walk through the walls, attacking towers or people within my walls.
During nighttime, when the monster waves move towards the town, I try to grab as many spectres and place them far far away on the map to reduce the risk of getting overrun. At the same time, I try to grab my golems to drop them near a building that heals them. So, during night it’s a bit stressful to make sure not to get overrun.
While realizing that this is more a tower-defense style game is not that bad, the fact that you cannot control your villagers is a bit disappointing. Somewhere I read 'like populous should have been' - yeah, back in the days of that classic you had control over a 'hero' or 'leader' that you could send towards the enemy population. That game needs that too - urgently!

If you like games in the style of Dwarf Fortress, Black&White or Populous, this will be perfect for you.
The possibility to directly interact with the world, pick up enemies and throw them into a divine smoothie maker is just one aspect of it. Feeding an ever-increasing population that also requires housing, water and protection from the elements and monsters is another thing on your list, so be prepared for a bit of a learning curve.

Even if you are more of a bleeding edge indev version addict, you can quickly report bugs and crashes in Discord, and the dev really puts his all into it and gets things fixed in a matter of minutes. Oh and it also has doggos now, so give it a whirl.

I don't mind a rogue-like game, or ironman type of game, as long as I can dial the difficulty WAY down.  Not the case in this game.
Your lander blows up constantly.  Your devices break down at least once-thrice per star system. The current settings for Story Mode should be called "Average", with an "Easy" mode below that and a "Storyline" mode below that.  I haven't dared to try the higher difficulties I assume they will be just much much much more murderous.  Also, I wish that you had a lot more expandability in your ship or lander devices. They could also consider having a greater variety of choices for your ship/lander at the start.

TL;DR: Very good exploration-roguelike game, which wont explain you everything. You have to figure out for yourself how the game works. Not a game for everyone but you should give it a chance if you really(!) like games like that.
The Long Journey Home, a game that's not easy to rate.
Let me start with a quote from Winston Churchill:
"I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat."
This sums the game up in a very good way.
You have three difficulties
- Story Mode
This is if you're new to the game the best mode to start. But it's still tough to beat.
- Adventure Mode
For  more experienced player. Hard times wait for you.
- Rogue Mode
The absolutely hardest mode and to beat this mode you must be very good in the game and have a near perfect seed.
The galaxy is generated in seeds. A seed is the code out of 10 letters/numbers that set the planets, encounters and so on. So you have a lot of possible galaxies to discover. If someone plays the seed: notmyfault he will always see the same galaxy like every other player with the same seed. So you can "share" interesting galaxies to friends.
The seed can create galaxies from easy to good to incredible hard or most likely impossible to beat. That's the RNG in the galaxy creation. Some like it, some not.
You choose 4 from 10 characters to start your mission. Every character brings one item to the mission. The use of some items are obvious, some not.
Every character is good in some things and others not. You get a hint in most of the descriptions which character has an advantage in some things. But you can manage to get home with every combination of chars. Some make it a little bit easy, some not.
The characters communicate via text and say some words to each other. Most people will not get connected to the crew and it's somewhat repetitive with those sentences. There is no voice acting. For myself i'm very fine with that and get a connection to my crew. I want to get them home alive.
You have the choice of three ships and three landers. Which one is the best for you is up to you. Every ship has advantages and disadvantages. It's up to you to find out which one fits you the most and which one is worth the risk to manouver trough the universe. You can upgrade ship and lander if you have luck and/or enough credits. Those upgrades will help you but they cost a lot.
The ships can be couloured with premade colours. They look a little bit like the coulours from the 80's especially Miami Vice to me and i love the colours.
There are missions in the game, you wont find every in a single seed. Some missions are offered to you, some you have to find by yourself. Each mission is doable but some are hard to do and for some you need specific character to solve the mission. You can start a seed over and over again if you found a mission that wasn't available because you didn't have the right chracter.
You meet in a seed always four from eight main alien races. The nine smaller alien races are normally in every seed but not always seen or found. Every Main race offers you specific things and have their own behaviour. If one race likes you another wont because you're friend with the others. It's up to you to find out how every race works, what they want, what they offer and what the like or dislike.
And here is another point of the game: It doesn't explain everything to you. You have to find out for yourself how the things work in the game. Some people dislike that, i love it. There are stories, mechanics and adventures to discover by yourself. Keep your eyes open and learn.
The controls are good, but a controller is highly recommended. You can play with mouse and keyboard but that is very hard.
You will do always the same things, jump from system to system, gather resources and try to keep ship and crew alive. I have to admit this is little bit repetitive and a lot of people don't like that. For myself im very okay with that. You will fail at the beginning very often with those minigames (landing on planet, manouvering trough space) but by time you will get better and get used to it.
You have to plan the way home, you can't jump from system to system, gather everything and think you will get home easy this way. You must look which resources you need, where you can get them and if the way is worth the risks.
Your ship will fall apart the further your flight goes. You can repair the systems at a few stations but this will cost a lot of credits. Which part will failure ist RNG based and every part that failed will affect your ship in a negative way. Some harder then the other. You can have "luck" with the parts or having a very bad time.
The graphics are beautiful. The game has it's very own style and i love this style. If you expect Ultra HD graphics and stuff like that, this game will disappoint you.
But the secret highlight in the game is the soundtrack. This soundtrack is so beautiful, you can listen to it and relax without doing anything in the game. If you buy the Captain's Edition you will recive the soundtrack and it wont disappoint most people.
At last: You don't get awards or something if you failed or survived in a seed. You just get knowledge of the things that awaits you so you can get further than before and what the races do or wont to for you or to you. That will disappoint a lot of people, i can understand that.
It's a very specific game that not everybody will like. It's hard, it's "simplistic" in some ways, it has not the AAA-graphics a lot of people wants, the game is somewhat repetititve, but it makes alot of fun if you get connected to the game.
If you want to discover a great universe, learn about the different races, missions and so on, this is a game for you. It's a real hard roguelike explorer game in some kind. You can't compare the game to FTL, that's not what the game wants. FTL gives you an idea of this game but there are a lot of differences. I would say give it a try and see what the game brings to you. Two hours gives a little hint how the game works.

I have played for 196+ hours and will probably play more just to finish the achievements, plus even more hours to keep the guide I wrote up to date as new content is added (but the new content never really changes the core gameplay) - but really, most of that is simply repeitive grinding.
On the balance, if you can get the game cheap then I think it's certainly worth looking at.  Otherwise, the lack of replayability may be an issue.

This is the best survival game I have ever played; not that that's saying much, as I haven't played many, with most of them being zombie-based. I don't think I've ever seen a game quite like this, in that it's just you in a wilderness with only your wits and some luck to keep you alive. Especially considering it's an alpha game with 6 zones and only sandbox, this game looks beautiful, sounds beautiful and can be both hauntingly beautiful and completely terrifying.
The difficulty settings are pretty fair; the easiest difficulty makes it easier to appreciate the cold beauty and deadly serenity  of the game, the middle is harsh but fair (sometimes), and I haven't even looked at the most difficult.
All in all, best $20 I have ever spent.

I mentioned in the review that the game crashed for me and the dev contacted me (see comments) within an hour or so. I know indie devs fear negative reviews like the plague, but it's still nice to get instant help. But seeing that the game was released into EA in october 2014, it kinda left me with a feeling that the dev is more concerned about the negative reviews than finishing the game. Now I just bought the game and haven't been observing the pace of the development, so I might be completely off with that (and I hope I am). I also took a quick glance at the steam forums and it seemed like the dev was actually active there too (which is surprisingly rare).
Thoughts about the actual gameplay after 10 hours:
+The pace of the game seems good. Doesn't require reflexes like a RTS would, but also doesn't make you just sit and wait too much.
+In general it shows potential and implies that it has depth and replay value.
+For the most part the UI is clear and easy to use.
+-The lack of in-game tutorial. There is a button for "Watch a tutorial video" and the game gives you some general tips along the way, but they help very little.
-The game offers too little information about things like how many buidlings you need to have in order to have your town survive (farms for food, wells or rain catchers for water etc).
-The time for pixel graphics has come and gone. It actually gets extremely blurry if you zoom in even a little bit (why does it even allow you to do this?).
-The villagers' AI is sometimes bugged and not knowing what their priority is in performing different tasks takes a lot of the fun out of the game.
-Some of the buttons on the UI (assigning villagers to different buildings for example) are WAY too small, considering the next point.
-The mouse pointer moves like it's on a rubber band. The delay ain't that bad, but just enough that it actually gets really annoying to try and aim at some of the smaller buttons.
It's these last two points that made my review negative. Feels like something that wouldn't bother a normal person, but some of the buttons are really small and the rubber banding mouse ain't helping.
And in case anyone gets to read this before the fanboys downvote this into oblivion (as they do to all negative reviews): I'm not saying not to buy it. But I am suggesting to keep an eye on the development for a while before doing so.

Now there's a save function, system settings stay the same after you restart the game, there are window resolution options though minimal, and the floating puzzle pieces on the pond are a little easier to click on.
When you start up a puzzle all progress is automatically saved when you exit. You can even start up a new puzzle and have the previous one you were working on stay intact.
If you want to make the game slightly tougher you can enable puzzle piece rotation as well though they still snap on to the mat like a magnet and you still can't put two puzzle pieces together outside of the magnets. For some reason though if you disable piece rotation the game won't remember what you rotated when you restart the game.
As you move puzzle pieces around on the mat, crabs will start appearing though only 2 can spawn at a time. Apparently you're supposed to drag them to the net on the side of the screen so you can use handicap abilities depending on how many crabs are in the net. You use 5 crabs to show a ghost image of the puzzle for a few seconds, 10 crabs to have a held puzzle piece correctly rotated if rotation is enabled, and 20 crabs to show where the piece you're currently holding is supposed to go to. If you exit the current puzzle the crab net will be emptied out.
There are varying puzzles that have exactly 60 pieces, 112 pieces, 153, 220, and one with 350 at the very end. There's no specific order you can complete them but finishing a puzzle unlocks the corresponding locked puzzles on the puzzle select screen.
From the technical side of things it's an improvement. Getting interested in this game is just going to be based on if you somehow actually got into the premise of the other Pixel Puzzles titles and/or if you fancy pseudo-jigsaw puzzles that magnetize on a mat with birds as the theme.

Word in advance: Though I'd recommend the game, there are a few major buts to be said about it.
A few years ago I first picked up Pixel Puzzles: Japan and, as a puzzle enthusiast, was glad to discover that it was both fun and well-designed. I've since picked up almost every other entry in the series, bar (at the time of this review) the Space version.
Like the rest of the series, Pixel Puzzles 2: Birds is basically a pc-game based off of the ages old jigsawpuzzles you might have played with as a kid. Each game gives you a set of themed puzzles of varying size along with one or more mini-games as a part of it.
There's a built-in cheat system where you have to pick up appearing crabs and deposit them in the net before you can choose one of three cheats (show image, correct rotation, pinpoint correct placement) depending on how many crabs you have.
Don't get me wrong, there are a lot of beautiful pictures among the puzzles, but this entry in the series stands out for one thing: not all photo's are optimal for the puzzle system, resulting in a near-mandatory use of the cheats (or if you want a perfect set of achievements, definitely mandatory). Take for example a 220 piece puzzle withlots of small by distance penguins on a brown-grey rock formation. It has so many near identical pieces that with the floating pieces that are a hallmark of the series that its next to impossible to fish out the ones you need.
Add to that the sheer annoyance that the crabs (which you can turn off thankfully) spawn more often than bullets in Touhou and you can see why its hard to really recommend this game.
Yes, it has a few good pictures. Yes, it still is fun. But the cheat-achievements, crabs, sometimes unstuitable (and penguin-abundant) pictures do make it a lesser entry in the series. Think well before buying.

Pixel Puzzle franchise. Recommended for those who literally like to put puzzles together, and I do mean piece by piece.
Pixel Puzzles 2: Birds
Features birds, of course, all kinds, everywhere - fenceposts to snow covered areas, big, small, entire colonies.  There is even an introduction puzzle found on the main screen.  25 puzzles in all ranging from 60 pieces to 350 pieces, with some odd shaped and bird themed puzzle pieces.  All the puzzles can be seen in the picture gallery once the puzzle is solved.  The game grid is more or less choose your path around the grid.
Puzzles: 60 piece - 6, 112 piece - 6, 153 piece- 4, 220 piece - 6, and 350 piece - 1.
The game board is surrounded by water where the puzzle pieces float and MOVE.  The pieces also must be rotated to gain the correct orientation (like in a physical puzzle.)  Fortunately there is an option for the player to choose the correct orientation permenantly (or until such time as the player chooses to turn it off).  I recommend having this feature on for the 220 piece and 350 piece puzzles due to the size of the pieces.
Best feature of this game: Crabs.  Now, now no laughing.  These helpful crustaceans can be picked off the puzzle board and put in a net.  When the player has collected enough a hint can be used.  "G" stands for "ghost" (cost 5 crabs).  This power-up shows the puzzle picture for approximately 10 seconds.  "Ctrl" (10 crabs) will cause that puzzle to have the correct orientation (unless the player rotates the piece).  "space bar" This helpful power up (20 crabs) shows exactly where that piece belongs in the puzzle, edge or middle.  Other functions: "T" make a tray to hold the pieces, "S" shuffle the pieces. "Z" zoom in on the puzzle board.  "C" change the puzzle board's background color.
There 33 achievements including ones like 'No More Crabs' and 'Ghost Power'.  Trading cards are available.

This game is a masterpiece on par with a lot of the 3d Mario games.  While I've only played Mario 64 and Galaxy, I'd still easily say I enjoy this game far more than them;  The hat system is great, and I love using each individual power, as well as using them one after another on certain occasions.  All the chapters have a unique theme: [SPOILERS START HERE] Mafia Town is an island with enemies that you can choose to fight, and a flying sub-island which contains the boss.  Battle of the Birds has the crowd-pleasing acts of DJ Grooves, and the wild west train acts of the Conductor.  Subcon Forest has the overall spooky atmosphere, the eerie (Not really eerie, more like run like hell or get frozen by a shadow of a person) mansion of Queen Vanessa, and the Snatcher's contracts.  Alpine Skylines has the four portions which are made up of platforming, be it over lava, over death pits, the inside of a windmill, or trying to not get slapped into hell by the pompadour birds.  [SPOILERS END HERE] While there are only a few main characters (Around 2 or 3), the plot is good, the player character is extremely loveable, and I found myself enjoying a large amount of the other characters, whether they're main characters or side characters.  (My personal favorite is Snatcher.)  The bugs are extremely hard to notice and rather insignifcant when they are found.
The boss fights are difficult, but not too hard;  They're going to pummel you sometimes, but that's until you figure out how to dodge the attacks, and a lot of the time it's a simple matter of leaping or diving at the right time.  Some of the bosses can be wacked all the time, but that's incredibly rare, or it's going to get you killed if you do try to.
The collectibles are fun to get and rewarding when you do get them, but besides the yarn, it's not going to give you anything more than cosmetics, so it's not too bad if you don't get them;  It's nice to get a lot of the cosmetics so you can give Hat Kid a look you're happy with. (My current favorite is lady bug hat flair for Sprint hat with the Blood Moon color scheme.)  The soundtrack is nice in the way that it sounds good and varies;  They're not going to give you a bloody orchestra for a train ride in the wild west, they're going to give you something fitting.
TL;DR This game is great in many ways and has very little flaws, so buy it if you like quality platformers with good soundtracks.

Game is highly overrated.  While it is an achievement by the development team and it is not a bad game by any definition, there are those who would say this game is on par with Mario.  They would be crazy.
The game lacks A LOT of polish.
The platforming is pretty medicore and quite often more annoying than rewarding. There is a lot of tight rope platforming where you cannot gauge where your character is in relation to the rope itself.  A lot of the level design is confusing and does not offer much in the way of visual cues to naturally guide you.  Instead you need to rely on a hat power up to point you in the right direction.
Boss fights carry on FAR to long, and while they are not terrible exactly, a lot of bosses rely on TONS of visual clutter to provide an artifical challenge rather than a tightly crafted one. In fact, looking back the most difficult stages were ones with tons of visual clutter (Penguine Parade, Owl boss fight.) The most challenging boss however is the camera, good luck beating him.
The controls feel way to loose. you will often find yourself running up a wall only to pull yourself up and over the platform and then falling to your death shortly after. Careful not to push that analog a bit to hard, hat girl will launch herself in that direction at tims and often to your death.  Something feels very off with your homing attack as well (Think sonics homing dash only slow and clumsy) then again the combat in general is pretty unfullfilling.
There are quite a lot of bugs as well. Power ups that don't work at times (umbrella safe fall), clipping issues in some instances and a few other minor issues as well.  While not game breaking, after a while it starts to get harder to ignore.
It may be unfair to be so harsh on a small development team and kick starter game.  Anyone who can put out a game of this calibur through kickstarter should be proud of their achievement.  However, I personally did not enjoy this game at all.  After 10 hours I put it down and uninstalled because I found myself more furstrated fighting with the controls and camera (and I've been platform gaming since the 80s) on top of zoning out mentallly while just aimlessly running around some of the levels.
I write this negative review because I bought it on the fact that everyone was overhyping this game and some even made the bold statement to say they enjoyed it more than Mario Odyessy.  Obviously that is their opinion and they are 100% entitled to feel that way but let me just say I almost completed 100% of Mario Odyessy but could not make it past 10 hours of this game.  I would strongly recommend you try this game before buying it as I feel this game comes no where close to Mario (which I would have never assumed it could if it wasn't for other reviewers).
Negative rant aside, I am positive Gears for Breakfast will only improve on this game and should contiue making games they love.

OVERALL:
I really wanted to like this game. I really did. Ultimately, it fell short of my expectations. It's a great concept, but the excecution is just very poor.
When I hear "roguelike," I expect a steep learning curve and highly skill-based gameplay. I also expect that the game will still be challenging and interesting even after several playthroughs. I expect victory to feel rewarding, much like in FTL, or Rogue Legacy, or Nethack. I expect each playthrough to be different.
Sunless Sea doesn't have any of these things. The learning curve isn't that steep, and survival is too easy once you get the hang of it. The quests are the same in each playthrough, and I found myself rapidly clicking through text that I'd seen several times already. The exact placement of various landmarks is somewhat random, but not enough to make an actual difference in gameplay. This game is absolutely not a roguelilke.
If you stay near coastal waters and avoid the obviously overpowered enemies (Lifebergs) the game is just too easy. I wasn't afraid of dying. Terror accumulation is only an issue if you sail in circles with your lights off. The few times I "lost," it was because I couldn't afford more fuel/food in port (also, I died of boredom once.) If I lose, I want it to be dramatic and terrifying! Where were the eldritch abominations from the depths? Where were the Lovecraftian monsters?
I have uninstalled this game, and I don't plan on reinstalling or recommending it unless the devs do an extensive overhaul.
PROS:
+ Interesting concept and premise
+ Good writing
+ Eerie, dark atmosphere
+ Graphics are simple but aesthetically pleasing, and fit the theme well
+ Good music
CONS:
- EXTREMELY slow-paced
- Gameplay is boring
- It takes forever to get anywhere
- Lots of "back-and-forth" style fetch quests
- If you die, you'll have to repeat the same quests over again - this gets VERY repetitive after the second or third death
- Once you get over the initial learning curve, the game is barely challenging
- The game feels basically the same in subsequent playthroughs
WHAT NEEDS TO CHANGE?
= Intermediate goals need to be better defined
= Subsequent playthroughs need to be less repetitive
= Needs to be challenging even to experienced players (and more difficult in general)
= More enemies, and better rewards for killing them
= Quests should be randomized somewhat
= Your ship should move a LOT faster
= Cut down on "go here then come back" quests
= Terror needs to accumulate faster and have more dire consequences
= There should be better rewards for taking risks (difficult quests, etc.)
= Locations should be randomized more! Do we have to start on the left side every time? Why not the lower-left corner?

Stay away until developers change this and add more content not based on text questing.

The narrative of the game is its strongest point, and the thing that keeps the game alive. Dying often does not immediately cut down on the replayability of the game, as many of the text-based narratives allow you to explore different options. As such replayability increases by not sticking to the same beaten path and trying out different backgrounds and directions to explore. After thirthy hours of play and a number of captains I still have two or three places left to explore, and the end-game is still open to me, which keeps the game interesting and fun to play for me. However, I cannot speak for what happens to the fun of replaying after a full first playtrough.
That being said, I personally advise against playing in hardmode after a certain point. The game has this hypnotizing atmosphere and quality, but that loses its charm once you have to go back to that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ship and engine after your previous captain died. The random number generator can really destroy the best planned route to the other side of the map, especially when your gambling with fuel and terror. The later ships don't mitigate this fact, as the increasing crew numbers offset your cargo capacity and food consumption: well-balanced or unpleasent surprise, up to the player I guess. There is a discrepency in the slow, relaxed way of discovering all the nararives and the possibility of the destruction of one's enthousiasm for the game in the roguelike hardmode of play. If frustration is your thing, be my guest, but I advice to leave this roguelike quality to games where it actually fits.
I recommend this game for its unique storytelling and atmosphere, and for that would definitly recommend people to buy it. Learn the game on hardmode, and saving once you have your first proper ship and 4000 credit engines is my advice on the way to truly get the most out of this game.
tl;dr:
+ Unique storytelling and atmosphere.
+ Well balanced economy and progression into late game.
- disconnect between roguelike and slow progress of text-based adventure: consider playing on casual to get most out of the game after a certain point in progression.

"The Long Dark is a thoughtful, exploration-survival experience that challenges solo players to think for themselves as they explore an expansive frozen wilderness in the aftermath of a geomagnetic disaster. There are no zombies -- only you, the cold, and all the threats Mother Nature can muster. " So all of this is true, and it is very refreshing to be playing a game with no zombies for once. The game is very deep and from what I can tell with a sort of crafting system that is meant to allow you to survive long term after you've scavenged the hell out of the landscape. You can hunt animals and fish for long term food, but you will be mostly scavenging buildings for food and water, which is your main concern in this game. There is also fatigue to worry about, which can just be managed by sleeping every night. I mean there's nothing else to do during the night since it gets so dark you can't really see anything. There's also a "cold" meter that will increase when you're outside and decrease when you're inside, basically. The game does a really good job with the atmosphere. Better than most horror games do. Everything seems so desolate, and you feel very alone. Yet you still often feellike some kind of monster is going to jump out and attack you, but it never does. Now I should mention that I have not gotten very far in this game. The reason is that this game has 1 fatal flaw that ruins it for me. Scavenging for things is so incredibly boring! Whenever you walk up to a container and click it you see a white bar and text under it that says "searching" and the white bar fills up slowly. Now this wouldn't be so bad if
. The game is just a way to incredibly boring with nothing ever happening, andyou're usually just starting at a white bar waiting for it to fill up. It is worth mentioning that this is an alpha version, though, and the developers are very dedicated and release regular updates. I hope this game becomes more interesting in the future because I feel like it's so close to being fun, but just falls short.

No ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t review. Straight to the chase. It's $10. Get it. Review: 40+ hours in. I've played Caesar III, Zeus, Pharoah, SimCity, Rollercoaster Tycoon, Gnomoria, The Guild II, and numerous other great management, defense, citybuilding games out there, even Banished (not recommended, see my review for it). I adore this genre and this game easily fits in with the best of them. It's very similar to Gnomoria but with an easier interface and on a larger scale.
I've mostly played this on Survival. Great balance between risks/dangers and development. You WILL build a beautiful village/city with 500+ individual semi-autonomous villagers even, but you will also HAVE to feed them, quench their thirst, gear them, and allocate them to their roles and tasks as efficiently as possible to thwart nightly monster raids.
That is, you will build a village and you will constantly be fighting for survival. Even at larger populations, you will still have to find a way to feed your village when your farms stop growing in the winter and enough clean water in the hot summer. Gear them up to fight off the monsters. Build defence towers from a limited pool of resources and building slots. Build walls to funnel the monsters through them.
It will be a real challenge and unlike Banished, there is a real risk.
Moreover, there's a world map with multiple locations to build villages. You can move resources and material from one village to another with your godly abilities.
Game's still in Early Access. Could use improvements and additions such as trade. Dev says he's working on them. We'll see. So far, beautiful game as it is. And for $10? Absolutely recommended. No second thoughts.
