A beautiful and well made town builder and management game.
Banished can take a little practice to get the hang of with to start with but when you get going you can build up a really large town able to sustain itself.
There's a good amount of resources to to collect and a wide variety food grow, gather and hunt.
There's no progression in the sense that you unlock new buildings or features, everything is available for you from the start so you can build up how you wish.
Your village can spiral out of control into disaster if you're not careful, especially near the beginning or if you're hit by a natural disaster. Such as lack of tools which bring all of your production down and makes even more chaos.
One thing to watch out for is the colonists can get a little greedy and take all available food when there's only a small amount in stock, leaving none for others and letting them starve.
The base game does lack buildings and you can soon feel as though you've built everything in a short time, there's plenty of mods to download but I would have liked to have seen more in the game.
Biggest problem with the game is the frame-rate when reaching 1,000+ population, for me it became unplayable so you will need to keep that in mind when building a village across the whole map.
Overall it's a great game and plenty of time can be spent, there's some nice achievements you can work towards if you like extra challenges/goals..
Definitely worth a buy if you like builders and/or management games.

Where to begin. It's Batman. It's TellTale. That's a pretty good mix for me.
Pros:
An interesting take on the Batman origin. While we have the standard alleyway shooting, the game delves much further into the past of not just Bruce, but of the whole Wayne family. This is something that is generally ignored in much of the comic mythos and let's just say we get what appears to be a rather interesting story twist that I'm looking forward to.
Of course, this being an early years Batman, we aren't going to run into many of the iconic villains, at least not in their recognized form since the whole escalation angle hasn't happened yet. Much like Batman Begins, local organized crime is the key focus of Batman's efforts and sets up the initial tensions felt between GCPD, Lieutenant Gordon and the political class in Gotham which Bruce in his civilian identity also gets caught up in. This game serves for a good opening Act of this Five Act Play.
Cons:
The game is quite short. As you can see from my play time, Episode 1 clocks in just under 2 hours. I felt this was a touch disappointing given the past games that TellTale has produced. There is also a minor complaint I have with the control scheme. While the QTE makes a return and I generally don't have much of a problem with that, what I don't like is the new Shift-Q and Shift-E commands. I feel this adds unnecessary keyboard complexity since the placement of the required keys is not the most comfortable to engage in on a regular basis and my off-hand is usually on the mouse. Combined with the short window for action, this makes for some tense moments a bit more annoying than they should be. Still, it's mostly a minor quibble.
Overall:
I'd give this episode as it stands now a weak recommend. I'm basing this mostly on TellTale's track record which, apart from Jurassic Park and the poker games, has been stellar in my eyes. Still, the short Episode 1 is a potential warning sign and, at this time, I would suggest putting this on your wishlist and revisiting the store page a few months from now when a few more episodes hit and the length can be better evaluated.

Pros: This is an open sand box game where you have a lot of freedom to make choices over how your settlers move forward. It is reminiscent of a wilderness version of the old (fill in the blank) Tycoon! games. If you liked those games, I would definitely recommend this game mostly because there aren't a lot of newer games in it's niche. I would recommend starting without natural disasters because at first struggling to move forward is hard enough (and slow enough) in this game without half your village burning to the ground. It's definitely fun once you learn the controls, but it wears off. The graphics seem good for a casual game, and the soundtrack sets a very immersive mood. The controls aren't that difficult to pick up on, and abundant descriptions help you learn as you go. Also the randomly generated geography is both entertaining and beautiful.
Cons:
There's a limit to how long you can play before you get annoyed/bored out of your skull. Commands take annoyingly long to complete. And when you have limited resources (Basically the entire time you play) you're basically watching people die while you wait a painfully long time for workers to collect/make a resource so that you can do something so that they won't die. Even in full fast-forward the game seems to take forever. It probably is a more realistic expectation, it just means that you spend the whole game scrolling around looking for something to do while you anxiously wait for something to finally finish.
Some of the game mechanics are annoying. The merchant ships never have anything that you want, and the few things that you would want (different livestock for example) never arrive. You're supposed to be able to help prevent natural disasters with different structures in the game, but they don't seem to help much (wells don't seem to do much against fires, the sick people wander around outside the hospital and get everybody sick) And it feels like nobody is ever productive. Most annoying of all, Resouce production is stupid slow.

Cuphead has been a game I've been fascinated with since my first time seeing it in 2015. Just a small snipet within a Microsoft games montage was enough to peak my fascination as its style was reminiscent of the old Tom & Jerry cartoons I watched as a kid and frankly allowed it to stand out in the crowd. Since then I've kept up with the game keeping it in the back of my head until the release date had been revealed, to which I pre-ordered it for the $20 its worth. So is it worth that much?
Short answer:
Yes, though if you'd rather look at the art over playing an unforgiving boss-rush game I'd point you towards lets plays over purchasing this game.
As for those wanting the full review, here you go:
To start off with easily the biggest selling point we have the art style. This is 60fps animation of rubberhose-era 1930s cartoons on top of watercolor backgrounds. Now don't get me wrong, many a game has tried making 1900s era characters within a rubberhose style (an example being Peacock from Skullgirls). But few have gone the extra mile that makes this game's style truely a masterpiece to the era with some quality of life things that they could've easily avoided. Instead of going for the sharp HD look it goes for a more bled coloration to give an SD look. It also has a film grain over it to give the simulation of film imperfections while you play. These may sound bad but it contributes to the idea of it being an early 1900s cartoon. Bosses are animated in 60 fps instead of the 24 they could've easily gotten away with. This makes quite a number of bosses visual treats to the eyes with the final boss of the game being the best example I can give to the overall quality this animation gets.
The main thing the style contributes to is the bosses. For one the limitless nature of 1930s cartoons gave many different possibilities to potential bosses and it really shows in this game. From living vegetables to humanoid frogs to balloon clowns to the devil himself, each boss feels unique to approach and watch. They also contribute the 1930s style of transformations into their bosses during phase changes to turn what was a simple fight to one careening into epicness. Almost every boss I've faced has gone through a transition from simple little bout to "fate of the world" levels of scale over the course of the fight.
You'd think that this kind of boss-rush style of game would be cheap or even... "unfair", but the animation and sound design lend hand in hand to keep this from being the case. Each attack and action has a tell animation. If the animation is difficult to make out, they usually give a loud noise to bring attention to it. Never once have I died to an attack or boss (outside of bugs) did I ever find my death unfair or cheap. Heck most of my deaths are usually due to attacks I couldn't predict the first time I faced it or simple user error. It seems people find this kind of difficult game too much, but I say it's like live, die, repeat where you live through the fight, die to something, then live once more with the knowledge of what killed you and an idea on how to approach it next time. So yeah, don't expect to beat the bosses on your first... I don't know 10 times? There's no way you'll be able to beat the boss using your limited knowledge in a short time span save for some of the early ones.
Now this is a boss rush style of game so the bosses make up around 75% of every stage you can go to, but the remaining 25% is platformers. Now you aren't forced to play the platforming stages to progress through the game, but doing so will allow you to acquire coins that you can use to buy charms and shot types for your character which can help you in later boss fights. There are a set number of coins in each platforming stage so you can't go back to a stage to "farm" coins. Do note however that while you can buy everything in the shop with the number of coins you can possibly get in the game, you cannot get all of the coins simply by doing the platforming stages...
So we have a great looking game that's difficult yet fair... any downsides?
Well I have two:
For one the developers have left co-op to local play. While this doesn't make or break the game, it is odd (at least for PC) that multiplayer is limited to local. This will be removed if they add online co-op in the future.
Another thing is that the game isn't perfect. I've ran into a few bugs in some of the fights that make it more difficult to face the boss. Instances of "phantom damage" facing the devil, pink pill stacks with the bird and the rare instance of a boss invulnerability bug I found within the aforementioned bird boss. Again these aren't deal breakers, but they are the only things I've seen from the bosses that can be remotely considered "unfair".
Aside from that this is an amazing game with great visuals, challenging gameplay, and all the love and care in the world.
Buy it if you're interested enough in the artstyle and or gameplay, but if you can't take the heat of this hard game then I'm afraid Cuphead isn't the game for you.

I'm very much a fan of rogue-like games.  And I really wanted to like TLJH, but sadly that didn't happen.
To start, please ignore reviews saying that the game is "too hard" for whatever reason.  It's not.  The lander missions are fine, unless you're particularly clumsy.  Keeping everything maintained is challenging, but doable if you're strategic.  It's par for the course for anyone who likes this genre of game.
What's wrong with the game is, sadly, that it just isn't fun.  It creates a vast universe, teeming with alien life and interesting worlds.  And you'll want to be off exploring that ... but you won't.  Nope, instead you'll be spending literally about 80% of your game time in lander missions grinding out the resources to keep your ship barely afloat.  Grinding, and grinding, and more grinding.  And worse, the lander minigame gets boring very quickly.
I suspect the devs wanted it to be a challenge to keep the ship running.  But it isn't, it's just time consuming.  And from what I've read on the forums, the devs aren't particulary interested in changing the game.  I feel this game has a lot of potential that just isn't realized.  If they ever allow modding, I'll pick this up again and try it out.  But as it is, I can't recommend it at all.

If you're reading anything about this game then chances are you're already pretty familiar with the series, since, unless you REALLY have a thing for birds, it's unlikely anyone would start with this over Japan, UndeadZ, or any of the later ones that have been released since. So you should already know more or less what you're getting into here - some puzzle pieces float in some water around the edges of the screen and you have to pick them up and assemble them into a picture in the middle. With each new entry, they try to add something a little different on top of the new theme (which is now birds, for some reason). This time, the extra feature is being able to rotate pieces. It doesn't sound like much, but that one small change makes a great big difference.
Previously you could just brute force your way through a puzzle if need be; pick up a piece, drop it in an empty space, repeat until you find the right one, profit. Now, while you could do that if you were absolutely desperate or determined, it pays instead to make a more calculated effort in your approach and take the time to look closely rather than hammer away mindlessly. It's an extra layer of complication that does mean puzzles can take a little longer to complete than in previous entries. But, thankfully, they've also added in a new range of abilities to compensate for this fact.
As you move, drop and rotate pieces around the board, crabs will randomly appear from under them and slowly scuttle around the play area, which can then be picked up and placed into a fishing cage at the side of the screen. For every 5, 10 or 20 you gather, you'll have access to a special ability - either briefly display the finished picture on the board, auto-correct the orientation of a held piece, or show the correct location to drop a held piece. Even though there never seems to be more than 2 crabs running around at any given time, there's never any shortage of them appearing. So even if it might be more time-consuming, the game is at least pretty forgiving in allowing the player to progress.
you want to use the abilities, that is. You can always chose to remove that element from play completely and just have a vanilla jigsaw puzzle if you'd prefer.
I do really like how flexible they are with each element they add to the games. if you want to have crabs, keep them. If you don't, get rid of them. The same also applies to the new rotation mechanic, which can be disabled at any time, though I kinda wish I had've realised that at the start of the game rather than the end, as it's tucked away in the options and is never expressly pointed out to you. In fact, the way the game communicates with you is a little sloppy overall, if I'm being honest. There is a How to Play section in the menu, but it's a jumble of information all thrown at you in a single image rather than introduced as you play. It would have been nice to tell us an automatic save feature has been added for each puzzle as well instead of having to discover it accidentally ourselves. Also, rather than pausing the action, pressing Esc spits you out of the puzzle and back into the menu screen, meanwhile a list of immovable options are on show at the left side of the screen throughout, which can sometimes get in the way of pieces floating underneath. Which seems an odd oversight for what has so far been a pretty competently made series.
The whole thing kind of feels like two steps forward and one step back. The new features are largely welcome, and they've finally managed to all but eliminate the sometimes awkward issue of picking up pieces by having more space for them to float in, but it feels like more could have been done, or some things just handled better. I don't know why birds were the main attraction this time around, either, or why it's only photographs. Maybe some artworks would have been nice? Or, instead of using images that were all taken from one guy, all seemingly from his one trip to a single island with a small variety of unspectacular birds, they could have had some more exotic examples; some birds of prey or paradise, a few emus running around, or even the common pigeon as a jokey finale or extra. The images used are pleasant enough and all, but the game could have been a far more flamboyant, engaging or enthralling experience for the player rather than just... nice.
It's difficult to know where to place this among the series as a whole. The tiny added extra of rotating pieces is actually something of a game-changer which potentially pushes it above the others, but then the subject matter may be a bit of a yawn for some and make it the weakest of the series yet. But if you enjoyed the other games and still want more, then you'll hardly go wrong with the many hours of casual, laid back fun on offer here. Though, all that said, you will get covered in much more poop here than the other games, so you might want to prepare yourself for that.

This is a fantastic experience. A amazing throw back to collectathon game play like Banjo-Kazooie and Super Mario 64. The game play is flawless and smooth, albeit a tad frustrating at times. Some levels are harder then others, especially late game. This game also has amazing potential for speedrunners.
The soundtrack for this game is just amazingly perfect. Each song is fitting for each level and location in the game, and sets the atmospheres of the levels well. There are even a bunch of remixes for said levels that you can unlock via slot machine rolls you can get from completing the "Time rifts" (AKA, challenge levels). Finding the Relics and mission objectives is rewarding as well, some of the challenges are pretty satisfying to complete.

When you play a main world pink rift, you can collect pictures to look at. The story in this game is simple... if somewhat non-sensical.
It dosn't make to much sence, but it's quirky and it's entertaining.
The voice Acting in this game is sublime, all the voices fit their respective characters and nothing feels out of place. Not much else to say about it really.

Full Disclosure: I received a beta copy of the game for free.
I really wanted to like the TLJH, but just couldn't. The gameplay is really just a few minigames stitched together. None of these minigames - lander exploration, mining, trading, diplomacy, fighting - are satisfying to play. Each one is tedious and expensive in terms of ship resources, encouraging you to avoid everything in order to maintain your ship.
TLJH's worst offense is that it punishes the player for exploration/experimentation. If you encounter for the first time a new event, item, location, species, etc., chances are that you will die and lose your progress. Several mechanics - illnesses, mining, diplomacy - along with LOTS of little things that can leave you penniless or crippled are explained poorly or never at all. This would be forgivable if it were possible to recover from the losses, but it RARELY is. 9 times out of ten, making the wrong dialogue choice, losing a crew member, losing the planetary lander, etc, spells doom for your run. The end result is a game that is simply tedious, frustrating, and not fun.
Even more frustrating is that the players explained a LOT of these issues to the devs during the open beta, and the devs routinely dismissed almost all criticism. I tried pointing out some of the things that were truly frustrating, saying that learning by losing a whole run usually isn't fun, but the devs always said that the "issues" weren't issues at all, and that all of those "features" I complained about were intentional.
Well, congrats, Daedalic. You made the boring, tedious, slogfest of a game that you wanted.

I strongly suggest watching the video for a much more detailed rundown!
First, the gameplay is solid from an RTS perspective. The base building, resource gathering, unit compositions and everything related around that idea is very well implemented, and though the balance isn't there yet (especially in terms of ramp up and resource production). Sadly, the UI is probably the most annoying part of this. From an RTS perspective this UI is horrible and actively hates giving you quick access and overview of a situation and units. From a visual perspective, i'm not a great fan of the visual fidelity (Gimme some AA Devs) but from an aesthetic point it looks pretty fitting and well put together, with solid cohesion. On the animation quality, the devs have a bunch of work left to do across the board.
From the Grand Strategy side, there is nothing implemented so if you plan on picking this up - Do it for the skirmish mode for now (which IS fun), or wait until the Grand Strategy part is implemented.
finally a note on performance and stability: It's okay after a few hot-fixes. I've not had any crashes as of update 0.11 during gameplay, but i must note that the game is filled with minor bugs all over the place.
Overall, i would either wait a few months until more of the game is properly implemented and we have a better overall picture, but if you enjoy medieval style RTS gameplay, it might be worth a stab at it already.

The narrative of the game is its strongest point, and the thing that keeps the game alive. Dying often does not immediately cut down on the replayability of the game, as many of the text-based narratives allow you to explore different options. As such replayability increases by not sticking to the same beaten path and trying out different backgrounds and directions to explore. After thirthy hours of play and a number of captains I still have two or three places left to explore, and the end-game is still open to me, which keeps the game interesting and fun to play for me. However, I cannot speak for what happens to the fun of replaying after a full first playtrough.
That being said, I personally advise against playing in hardmode after a certain point. The game has this hypnotizing atmosphere and quality, but that loses its charm once you have to go back to that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ship and engine after your previous captain died. The random number generator can really destroy the best planned route to the other side of the map, especially when your gambling with fuel and terror. The later ships don't mitigate this fact, as the increasing crew numbers offset your cargo capacity and food consumption: well-balanced or unpleasent surprise, up to the player I guess. There is a discrepency in the slow, relaxed way of discovering all the nararives and the possibility of the destruction of one's enthousiasm for the game in the roguelike hardmode of play. If frustration is your thing, be my guest, but I advice to leave this roguelike quality to games where it actually fits.
I recommend this game for its unique storytelling and atmosphere, and for that would definitly recommend people to buy it. Learn the game on hardmode, and saving once you have your first proper ship and 4000 credit engines is my advice on the way to truly get the most out of this game.
tl;dr:
+ Unique storytelling and atmosphere.
+ Well balanced economy and progression into late game.
- disconnect between roguelike and slow progress of text-based adventure: consider playing on casual to get most out of the game after a certain point in progression.

Axis Football 2016 does a few things right, but for American football fun you’ll be better served finding a copy of Madden 08 on Amazon.
Total size on my hard drive: 1.4 GB
+ Run mechanics. Well-implemented, with moves that are easy to execute.
+ Kicking mechanics. With the right timing, some long kicks are possible.
+ Good hot-route audibles.
+/- Graphics are acceptable, but not special. There is no crowd animation – not even animated 2D sprites.
+/- Decent but limited in-game announcer commentary.
- No referees = no penalties.
- No penalties means no challenges for incorrect plays (out of bounds, didn’t cross the down marker).
- Passing mechanics. Under-throw your receiver, and he’ll turn around and wait for it. Even if the opposing defense is there and in position to intercept, the defender will rarely if ever turn around for the ball.
- Not enough plays, especially on defense.
- No player draft when beginning franchise mode. Stock rosters are what you start with.
- Defensive plays don’t have the effect you’d expect. Blitzes apply very little pressure, meaning an extra receiver will be open – no doubt turned around and waiting for the under-thrown ball to arrive. Zone defenses are oddly effective against the run, and poor against the pass.
Overall, a project with a lot of promise, but a lot of work yet to be done. If you’re a fan of American-style football, worth trying at 80% off or more.

I have played a lot of FPS games that throw you into a war, but even as battle hardened as I was this game gave me PTSD for the first few days after I played it. you sit in cover as you see half your squad move up. then you see blood plumes and have your squad falling down from a machine gun.
all sadness aside though, this is as close to WW2 as you will get. <----thats right that a period, that means its final. there is bullet drop, but I find that you really never need to shoot farther than 250 to 300 feet, which makes acounting for it rare. You can run with a giant MG shooting like a commando, but you arnt going to hit nothing if you dont sit down and use it right, like deploying its bipod. there isnt a dot in the center of the screen, so you have to actualy use your sights in this game. tanks are not a one man show, you need more that one person in the tank with you. ok enogh with realisticness. this is a team work game, something rarely found in other FPS games. while battlefield is working to get ride of teamwork these guys do their best to encourage it.
A few things I dont like. I played this instead of BF1942 because I thought that with the gamespy shutdown the multiplayer would not work (which was a load of BS). and what it had that RO2 doesnt have is uncostomizable loadouts. I hate costomizable loadouts, its anything but realistic and it means you have to level up to get better stuff (another thing that BF1942 doesnt have) but you know mabey you like that, its just my preferance. but even with those changable loadouts, there isnt too much to change. a choice bettween 2 or 3 different main and secondary wepons and thats it, I can live with that.
BF1942 maps were very open usualy, however this game have very linear and small maps. its not a super bad thing, but I really enjoyed traveling across all of iwo jima from its airfields to the peak of Mt. Suribachi. all in all, its a game where if you get shot once, you are going to most likely die. if you dont die from the first shot, then there will probably be a second one coming as soon as you know that you were hit. it has action, horror, guns, strategy, and war all in one package. buy ASAP. it doesnt even take a super computer to run.

Wow... just wow.  What a triumph of game design.  This game is so minimalistic in its presentation, but the story it tells, the ideas that it presents, are so compelling that you can't help but trudge through that next seemingly endless expanse to the next part of the story.  To describe the game much more deeply would give away far too much.  And as someone who didn't know exactly what to expect beyond this-is-the-stanley-parable-guy going into it, I would hate to rob anyone of that experience and in all honesty it would rob one of the very essence of the game if I were to do so.  I will summarize it with this; I have never played another game that made me look at myself so deeply.  This is an experience that demands introspection and demands that you examine your relationships with others.  I had a sinking feeling in my gut the entire time I played, and for all the best reasons.  This is a work that transcends entertainment and I would suggest that the world would be a much better place if everyone played this game and genuinely took the ideas to heart.  Do support this developer, do play this game, and do your part to encourage the expansion of the idea of what games can be.

Pros: This is an open sand box game where you have a lot of freedom to make choices over how your settlers move forward. It is reminiscent of a wilderness version of the old (fill in the blank) Tycoon! games. If you liked those games, I would definitely recommend this game mostly because there aren't a lot of newer games in it's niche. I would recommend starting without natural disasters because at first struggling to move forward is hard enough (and slow enough) in this game without half your village burning to the ground. It's definitely fun once you learn the controls, but it wears off. The graphics seem good for a casual game, and the soundtrack sets a very immersive mood. The controls aren't that difficult to pick up on, and abundant descriptions help you learn as you go. Also the randomly generated geography is both entertaining and beautiful.
Cons:
There's a limit to how long you can play before you get annoyed/bored out of your skull. Commands take annoyingly long to complete. And when you have limited resources (Basically the entire time you play) you're basically watching people die while you wait a painfully long time for workers to collect/make a resource so that you can do something so that they won't die. Even in full fast-forward the game seems to take forever. It probably is a more realistic expectation, it just means that you spend the whole game scrolling around looking for something to do while you anxiously wait for something to finally finish.
Some of the game mechanics are annoying. The merchant ships never have anything that you want, and the few things that you would want (different livestock for example) never arrive. You're supposed to be able to help prevent natural disasters with different structures in the game, but they don't seem to help much (wells don't seem to do much against fires, the sick people wander around outside the hospital and get everybody sick) And it feels like nobody is ever productive. Most annoying of all, Resouce production is stupid slow.

This game requires study. It requires the player to appreciate this work as seriously as any monologue in a theatrical production.
This game requires introspection. It requires the player to have a good understanding of themselves as well as a willingness to engage their sense of empathy.
This game isn't about what it says on the tin. Though it lacks enemies, health bars and jumping puzzles, it invites the player to take what it presents and engage with it through interpretation.
This game requires an appreciation of art as a medium with which to communicate ideas. It requires the player to accept that whatever price you pay for this game should not affect your reaction to it.
In my view, this game is a simple experience with the potential for numerous intepretations and discussions. To call this a walking simulator would do it a major disservice. I think a more apt description would be a thinking simulator.

The Long Journey Home is a very good game.
The game has good music and good graphics. I have set the anti aliasing and the postprocessing setting to low to not overheat my graphics card. Steering the game with a game pad seems to be easier than with the mouse.
TLJH is a survival game like Don't Starve and a rogue like game like FTL: faster than light.
The player is the commander of the first human interstellar space ship during the first flight to Alpha Centauri, but something goes wrong, and the ship gets thrown throught the hyper space to the another end of the galaxy.
With some injured Crew and damaged systems on higher difficulty levels, the long journey home begins. Flying the first human spaceship makes the survival not easy. Doing jobs for aliens to earn credits and mining planets with the lander is important to survive.
The player can choose at the start of the game a 4 man crew out of 10 different crewmen with different abilities. I recommend Ash, who can make medicine of the different plants found on planets, and the woman, who is an engineer and can repair damaged ship modules. The other are free to choose. You can choose, who of the 4 crewman should be the lander pilot, before landing on a planet. Depending, who has been chosen als pilot, the results are different, when exploring alien ruins or a ship wreckage. An engineer for example has a better chance to open doors or disable a computer alarm.
The next choice at the start of the journey is to choose one of three different spacesphips and one of three different planetary landers. My favourite so far: The medium Ulysses spaceship and the light Pathfinder lander.
I haven't reached earth yet, but i hope, that i will make it.

A bit of a change from their previous games.
The puzzles themselves are much more difficult now. Puzzle pieces can be rotated now, and there are many more puzzles this time around. Only downside was the actual pictures themselves. The camera focuses on the birds themselves, but there is a lot of background noise in most of the photos, which leaves unfocused, blurry objects in the background. Some puzzles arent so bad, but some have so many blurry background objects that the puzzle can be annoyingly difficult. Most puzzles arent bad though.
Sounds wasnt bad, but it got annoying after awhile so I turned it off. I cant comment much else on it. Worth giving it a listen to see if youll like it.
The minigame didnt bother me. Was a vast improvement over the zombie minigame from their zombie puzzle game. Basically, as you bring pieces on the board, crabs appear. Drag the crabs into the net and after awhile you unlock some hints. 5 Crabs for a full view of the picture that will fade out after a few second. 10 I believe for a hint to the right rotation for the piece youre holding. 20 to find where the piece goes. Between the frequency of the crabs and the hints, even on the tough puzzles you shouldnt get stuck for very long.
Only bug I found was related to the settings being saved (an issue Ive had in the previous games as well). When Id load the game, it would go into fullscreen and volume for a few seconds before "remembering" my settings and adjusting.
Overall, its a nice addition to the game series. Its true to the previous games, sticking to the jigsaw puzzles, with some improvements to the minigame gimmick. Id have loved better picture selections, but these were quite nice. Worth grabbing, especially on sale, and especially if you just want a relaxing jigsaw puzzle to finish.

As a result of the update, and upon the developer's request, I'm revising the review. The original is at the bottom.
I'm very pleased that the developers have made updates to improve the gameplay experience. I've briefly played the game after the review, and I've noticed considerable improvement in some regards. Mostly in the resource economy, and the handling of the lander.
However, many of the issues I brought up were not changed. Picking up the game for the second time has only reminded me of them. The narrative parts of the game still feel stale. You know that a certain amount of time has elapsed when someone on the crew says something - a snippet of a conversation, with no context or reply. The threadbare communication of the game (ASK SELF) further contributes to a surreal feeling, and you are bleakly reminded of the limtations of the medium and genre of this title.
I wondered to myself at times what makes this roguelike a $40 title. Parallax scrolling on starbound-esque planets has been replaced with beatifully rendered 3d environments (don't stick around though), yet the narrative is dry, and each zone feels randomly generated with little depth.
I guess at the end of the day, I don't really know what the game is trying to do. There is no narrative, and the game is only as strategic as "gather all resources and occasionally take risks" can be. There are no RPG elements. It isn't realistic. First contact gets old quickly.
So I'm keeping the non-recommendation. Maybe I liked it more the way it was before -  it subverted my expectations, frustrated me, and surprised me with its bleak message about the futility of it all. There was substance to it, where now there is a padded experience with nothing behind the curtain but the vacuum of space.
Below is the original review:
The game was really hard. It was also obtuse at times.
The ship felt a hair away from breaking down permanently, and countless landings and asteroid hunts didn't ever resolve this. My crew was injured and I couldn't afford to help them. There were other mechanics, like combat, quests, and diplomacy, but I never got to those, because they were extremely risky (tended to kill me when I tried), and I rarely had enough resources to do anything other than mine resources.
The game's mechanics were also often very unintuitive. For example, trading and conversation with the aliens often left them mad at me for asking too many questions. When things were getting dire, I would try to take some risks to survive, and usually be screwed over, and rarely rewarded. In a game supposedly about diplomacy, danger, and exploration, I was quickly punished for curiousity and risk-taking (a "ludonarrative dissonance" if you will). Various items that looked like they might be multiple use (tool sets, or a giant medical bag) ended up being single use.
Many narrative beats that seemed important to me went unnoticed by the game. We barely survive a planet landing, or a fight, or make first contact, or land on the first planet outside our solar system, or anything of that nature, and the crew never even mention it. The dialogue that was present was a highlight of the game, especially when it worked with the game's story - like after meeting the traders, a crew member talks of distrust of them. It often repeated, which I found disappointing.
Overall, risk-taking felt overly punishing - it almost never paid off, the game felt more like a survival game than an exploration one. You watch your crew go from walking to limping to crawling, and if you're lucky, you get to earth before they all die. It's depressing, and the game is far too slowly paced for its gameplay - you shouldn't have to mine every resource from every accessible planet to barely limp along.
Maybe if some of the mini-games were more rewarding and easier, and risk-taking was seeded with more rewards, then the game would be more balanced towards the other mechanics, and wouldn't feel bogged down in resources scarcity. For now, I don't recommend this title.

Would you like to start hating penguins? Then this game is for you. The penguins themselves are not the problem.
The problem are some design choices in this game that seem to be done with the sole purpose of making the game more frustrating to play. Either that or the creators just never actually played tried playing their own game after that after adding them.
The most horrible of these is the background. Everybody would expect at least a uniform neutral color background (preferably selectable), but no, they went with a horrible pattern that makes anything put on it much harder to see. Sure you can change the color of the background, but the pattern is always the same and the colors are ugly and too vivid.
The next horrible thing is the fact that all the pieces are under water and they get a bluish tint which makes it impossible to see the actual color of a piece without actually picking it up. The pieces also float freely around in the water so a dropped piece doesn't stay where you dropped it and there is a big chance you will pick it again and again. Sure, there is a tray on which you can put the pieces on, but that's off the screen and doesn't change color with the background so it's practically useless.
The next horrible thing are the crabs. Little funny creatures that pop up under pieces you move around the table and give you bonuses that can help you with the game. Sounds good on paper, but in practice they are totally annoying as they pop up right under your mouse and you tend to grab them instead of the pieces so you can't just ignore them. Sometimes you even end up throwing away pieces while trying to get rid of the crabs. The bonus they provide isn't worth the hassle in most games, as you have to collect 20 of them to get the only useful powerup.
On the positive side, the photos that you have put together are rather beautiful and the design of the pieces is very interesting and not boring as it changes from game to game.
I can't recommend this game to you unless you are a really hardcore fan of jigsaw puzzle games that can get over all the frustrating stuff in this game.
UPDATE: Most of the issues I had with this game are now fixed.
Background is now of a (almost) uniform color and the colors aren't too bad.
Bluish tint on the pieces in water has been greatly reduced so it doesn't bother you that much anymore.
Crabs can be removed from a puzzle if not tha which is great because sometimes they are really annoying and sometime you need them.
I can now recommend this game. 8/10 must play for jigsaw puzzle lovers. You might still end up hating penguins but that's because some of the jigsaws are very hard and not because of bad design.

I've been playing TLJH for about 29 hours total at the time of this review. I bought it because I'm a big fan of Faster Than Light & this felt like it had the same spirit.
There are several aspects to the game, system navigation where your ship (displayed as an arrow) moves around the map being affected by gravity which is displayed as a grid system with flat and recessed lines to indicate gravity strength. You goal is fairly straight-forward. Mine planets for resources to repair / refuel your ship. Jump to the next star system. Get to jump points and progress to the next sector.
During this journey you will encounter various alien races, some of whom are pleasant to deal with and others who are a pain (Meorl) because they are psychic and you have no way to resist their whims until a specific storyline.
The 2nd aspect of the game involves your ship's landing craft which flies down to the planet's surface to mine resources or explore Ruins / Wrecks. Depending which crew member you send can affect the results. Some purchased items will help you immensely with winds (convection) for your lander and it makes the process MUCH simpler.
The 3rd aspect of the game is asteroid mining which involves flying your ship around various asteroids to blast 1-3 asteroids that have resources hidden within.
There is of course buying/selling in the game as you encounter star bases & jump gates, but after a few sales to the merchant they may simply become bored with you and you can't do any more selling to them. Thankfully there are items of value you find along your journey which help immensely to improve your vessel.
The game is very fun. But as with FTL you will struggle with random events such as "wear and tear" on your equipment or health events for your crew or the occasional space pirate race who wants to fight you. One sector may leave you feeling invincible while the next may leave you desperate for resources and jumping in fear of each approaching vessel.
My play time say it all.. Couldn't play alone.

The platforming of Mario with the charm of the Wind Waker and the scenario design from Paper Mario. What's not to love?
In all seriousness, this game has rapidly become my favorite platformer of all time. Mouse + keyboard controls are incredibly tight and almost never frustrating. The writing is hilarious, the characters are endearing, the scenarios are incredibly inventive and unlike anything I've ever seen before, and the sheer variety of creativity here is stunning. All of it is good. None of it is dull. I can say, without a word of hyperbole, that I enjoyed this game more than Mario Galaxy. It's that good.
With that said, there is a bit of controversy still surrounding the game. JonTron is in the game and has not been removed. His role is very small, as an optional NPC, and I understand the developer's trying to not create the massive spectacle that Playtonic Games went through when they removed JonTron, but I still don't see why they couldn't have just silently patched him out. There's plenty of silent, unvoiced NPCs in the game (and occasionally, even voiced characters have unvoiced, text only lines) - what difference would one more make? His inclusion is a blemish on an otherwise spotless game, but, in my opinion, is not enough to invalidate the work done by the rest of the development team. If no one told you about JonTron, you probably would never have known about him being in this game in the first place.
At the end of the day, A Hat In Time combines fluid, satisfying platforming with an inventive world that you'd want to stay in for hours. Sure, minor nitpicks exist - Mustache Girl should have showed up more, Mafia Town is too Mario Sunshine-y, etc. - but ultimately, all of that melts away as you just enjoy the game itself. This is a platformer that certainly deserves a spot up there with the greats, if it doesn't exceed them altogether. Absolutely worth your time, especially since two additional chapters are coming for free. And if this game is on sale, then it gets an unconditional recommendation from me.

As someone who plays Madden NFL and NCAA Football on console all the time, I think my expectations were set unreasonably high for this game. That being said, I think that, for the price, Axis Football 2016 probably isn't worth the money. I love having a football simulation game on my Mac that spoofs the NFL, and it's a great way to keep myself entertained for a while when I have nothing else to do, but I feel like the quality of this game—e.g. the graphics, the gameplay, the interface—is akin to that of the old NCAA Football 11 app for the iPhone, which came out in 2010...I spent $4.99 on that game. It's overly simplistic, the graphics are poor, the mechanics are both bizarre and confusing, and there aren't a ton of unique features. In a sense, it's a glorified flash game.
Again, it's my fault for expecting the complexities of a $60 console game to show up in a 1.3 GB $20 computer game, so keep that in mind when factoring this review into your decision-making process. I bought it on sale, so I don't regret spending $10 on boredom therapy, but if you're looking for a solid, deeper game with your $20 bill, this probably isn't for you.
Also, if you do decide to get the game, it's far better with a Steam controller, especially if you play Madden NFL or NCAA Football.

Since 2005, Madden has been the only football game available. Many people agree that NFL 2K5 was and still is the best football game made, but EA snatched up the exclusive rights to the NFL and has had an iron grip on the property since. As a long time player of the Madden games, I have yearned for some competition for the franchise as they really have no one to push them. While Axis Football 2016 will not dethrone Madden, it’s a heck of a good start.
Since EA holds the exclusive rights to the NFL, Axis is not allowed to use team or players names but they are allowed to have teams like the Chicago Grizzles and New England Volunteers. Luckily, the game is fully moddable and an NFL roster already exists. This also opens the door for legacy rosters which are not available in Madden.
As far as the actual gameplay goes, it is somewhat rudimentary. If you’re looking for Madden levels of fluidity and polish, you won’t find that here. This being the games’ second installment, it’s not that surprising that there are still areas to be improved upon, and the developer seems quite active on the forums and dedicated to making this series as good as possible. I really didn’t have a problem with the minor jank that the game may have, but I do hope that there are some future balancing changes. There are some easily exploitable plays on both offense (I got 26 receptions with one WR) and on defense (6 sacks with a MLB).
While I have my gripes with the game, these are all fixable, and really the game makes up for it in a big way: the passing game. When I talk about wanting competition for Madden and more innovation, the passing system in Axis is exactly what I’m talking about. Instead of having icons assigned to different receivers, you use the right thumbstick to direct where you want the ball to go. This system feels infinitely more natural than the standard icon passing since you can pass to a specific spot on the field and lead the receiver or throw it shorter if you want him to come back to the ball. This mechanic is just so intuitive and brilliant that I wouldn’t be surprised if Madden ripped it off.
Axis Football 2016 is by no means perfect, but for PC players who have been craving a proper football game this is a great start. It’s not even so much that I recommend Axis 2016 based on what it is, but rather on what the Axis franchise can become going forward. I would say that it’s worth getting the game just to support someone who is trying to innovate and do new things with a genre that has largely been stagnant for the past decade. Will Axis ever be as big as Madden? Probably not, but it doesn’t have to be either. There is enough of a solid foundation here that I am excited to see where this franchise goes if it keeps improving and listening to community feedback.

Sunless Sea is such an interesting concept but is hampered by some really poor decisions. There's a reason I call it Funless Sea.
The good part is that the developers have crafted a weird, wonderful world populated with interesting stories and artwork. The mood is great. The world is interesting. The stories are kind of cool and occasionally not just a little messed up in the head. The world is the same close to your base but in every game it gets more and more randomized the further you get. That's a wonderful gameplay idea and I give serious props to the devs for creating such a great universe.
Unfortunately, they didn't know what to do with it. People will talk about the decent writing, the dark mood, the truly unique world that was created when they praise this game. What they don't talk about is the gameplay and that's where this falls flat. There is no direction and there are really no aims in this game. You get in a ship and go...wherever. It doesn't really seem to matter. You'll find a rare workable trade route and do nothing but grind it as long as you can because money is hard to come by. You'll visit the same ports over and over getting nothing but port reports for a few echos (dollars) at a time when it takes tens of thousands to get a new ship. The pace of the ship is ponderous (and that's being kind). So underneath this interesting world the game devolves into a slow, dull grind. It's really a shame because even mediocre gameplay mechanics could have gone a long way here.
Yes, the pace is supposed to reflect the tension of your slowly deteriorating crew. To some respect it does that. But more often than not my head just wants to hit the keyboard from playing this. My time is more valauble than that. Most of the people I've talked to that have "enjoyed" the game used cheats to boost their gold to get somewhere in this bore-fest. I love good exploration games, but this feels aimless and pointless to me.
Not that I haven't give it a chance. I tried buying it and then returned it under the Steam policy. I tried again when they had a free weekend and really tried to like this game. But I just can't find the fun in it. Funless Sea - such a great world marred by such boring gameplay.
EDIT 1/1/2018
I've always thought that Sunless Sea should be a game I like. Exploration and story-telling are some of my favorite things. But the game mechanics just never clicked. So I bought this for $5 on sale and gave it one last shot....this time with mods to take away the ever-increasing terror, increase the speed of the boat and remove fuel and food requirements. If there was a mod to reduce these I would have downloaded that instead but there wasn't, so the elimination method was the option.
While the gameplay still isn't *great*, it's a heckuva lot more fun this way. I can actually make a bit of money without spending hours grinding because I can get to other ports. The sense of terror isn't quite there anymore but Darkest Dungeon did that aspect far, far better than Sunless Sea. The stories can be enjoyed without feeling like you're always on the brink of death and therefore won't have to repeat everything all the time. I'm cruising with the same character for 4 hours now and it's satifsying to build up my crew, my boat and see the Zee. I'm not going to change the rating on this review because the base mechanics are simply too punishing to make the the game fun. But with this mod it's actually something I'm looking forward to playing even more.

Bioshock I don't even know where to begin the good, the bad, the scary, the funny the impressiveness, the uninspiring.  This game has to be one of the best story’s I have ever played.  I went in not liking the game not wanting to play the game.  And even though it did take me about a month or two of casual gaming to achieve the ending because I did not want to play it.  The game play and story won me over.  This has to be one of the scariest, 80's hack and slash style movie, rolled into a first person shooter.  Now if you have read my other reviews you know I'm not a huge fan FPS's (first person shooters).  I do like to play video games so I play them and above all else I love video games with a fantastic story and this has one.  Bioshock is like the Twilight Zone meets Alfred Hitchcock and they had a baby.  Now I think it took me so long to get into the game because it starts off slow and you are leveling your character getting new ability’s, weapons, and getting the crap scared out of you by the slicers and the enviroment.  It takes you awhile to start to understand this game its set in the 1950's in an underwater city called Rapture.  If you are going to play it the biggest element to the game are the audio diaries.  They give you an inside look into the minds of the citizens of Rapture and explain how the city has evolved into its current state of commotion.  There are some essential lines in the game and one of the best is at the very begin as you ascend to the majestic city.
This honestly does set the tone for the rest of game.  Now if you are going to play this game beware there are three different endings.  Make up your mind at the begin which way to go kill, save, or do both on the little sisters those three options determine your ending.  The game is 14-20 hours long depending on your play level and style.   Now I can't stress the audio diaries enough they are essential for you to get the whole story out of this phenomenal game.  Just when you think you are like this is it this is the ending nope hold on to your hat.  I think that was a decisive turning occurrence for me to start apprenticing this game and seeing why it has a 96 meta critic score.   Now the downside the game crashed on me a few different times. (Windows 7 user)  So just save often.  The story little slow at first but it picks up.  Wallet has a cap.  Hacking certain machines not set up to well I thought. Bots not the brightest.  Now the last couple I'm nitpicking because honestly this game doesn't have a lot of flaws in my opinion other then being a first person shooter :)  Get it love and play it again and again.

At the time of writing, it's been more than two months since the last update, which was only a hotfix to the june update, which was five months ago. This after a promise from Bugbear for monthly content updates.
In Wreckfest's current state, it plays well and looks great. The feeling of driving heavy, slippery old junkers that was present in the Flatout series is still there. Sliding an iron behemoth from half a century ago through a dirt track feels just right, and shunting a car out of your way does suitable damage to both vehicles. Wreckfest plays and wrecks great. Its basic gameplay even better than any of the good Flatouts, and the deformation as far more graphically pleasing than Flatout's limited model-change-based deforming.
Gameplay is not the thing holding Wreckfest back. The issue with this game is its' lack of polished content. While there are around twenty levels included in the game currently(more if you count circuit variations), but there are only about seven completley finished tracks. The rest are in various states of completion, with some nigh-indistinguishable from a completed level and others having placeholder assets and misaligned roads. The car customization is pretty good on the one car that actually has customization parts, all others being static apart from their paint job. If there were more finished tracks and cars with actual parts to use, this would be a superb game. As it stands it is only a good example of how a lack of content can't be completley made up for with gameplay.
I still reccomend Wreckfest because it plays well and is a fun distraction from time to time, but unless a ton of people buy this game soon, I doubt we'll ever hear from Bugbear or this game ever again. Don't buy this for a deep, feature-rich experience like the Bugbear-era Flatout series. Buy it if you enjoy contextless screwing with a fun driving model and interesting deformation technology.

I always watched Telltale games on youtube, like a tv show, but when I heard the developer was making a Batman game, I had to get it.
Batman: The Telltale Series gives you control of Bruce Wayne and of course Batman. Something that hasn't really been done before in any Batman game.
The story is top notch and unique. A web of lies (or maybe truths) is affecting both Bruce Wayne and his alter ego. The supporting characters are believable, and all have a clear motive for their actions.
The soundtrack is amazing. In previous Batman games, the sounds is always grim and serious with low tones. In this one the music is hopeful and tense.
The gameplay like every Telltale game is minimal, but when you play a TT game, you aren't here for the gameplay. You are here for the experience.

This is the first Steam review I've written where I feel conflicted about giving a thumbs down. Let me explain why I don't recommend this game.
My first 50 hours in this game were okay--it was somewhat challenging and I sorta enjoyed it but, the game lacks depth. Once you figure out how to minimize disaster (diseased crops/livestock, sick citizens, etc.) there isn't much left to do. I moved on to using mods for the remaining hours I played. I tried all of the mods and many had neat additions but, they all failed to add real depth to the game-play. Additional types of crops and livestock don't add depth all they do is make it easier for me to keep the citizens happy.
On top of the game lacking depth (its #1 problem) it also has some very glitchy mechanics. I've had a newborn child end up living alone in a house (and somehow survived). Greedy citizens will steal all the resources they can and horde those resources (food/fuel) in their homes at the expense of neighbors who will starve and/or freeze to death. Resources can randomly teleport across the map which, can cause your workers to starve or freeze to death during the long journey to pick up that gliched out resource (in my case a piece of meat) from across the map.
The final nail in the coffin for this game is the horrible FPS drops it suffers when you build up a large population. People who are really into this game play it on pause because once you have a large population, if you try to play at 5x or 10x, you'll get 1-5 FPS/sec even with the best possible hardware.
In the end there was nothing that made me want to come back and play this game. I love City Builders but, this game pales in comparison to games like Anno 2070 and Cities: Skylines. I like the general idea of this game but, aside from building up an ever-larger population (which isn't even much of an option because of the game's♥♥♥♥♥♥optimization), there's really nothing to do after about the first 20 hours of game-play. This game doesn't have war/fighting, the trading is limited/lackluster and the random glitches/FPS drops can be infuriating. If you're looking for a City Builder with real depth check out Anno 2070 or Cities: Skylines.

Where to even start with this game? This game is targeted for a younger generation. Yes I'm 22 and I play it but that's because I'm a child at hart and I loved the movies. So this game you get to make a viking and live in Berk. You then get to go to the hatchery and pick out your very own dragon egg to hatch. The dragons can be customize (name and color) and there are several choices of dragons you can pick from when you start. So for a few hours after you start your dragon will be in its baby stage (which seems like forever). So that means it can only follow you around yes that means you dont get to do any flying just yet. It also means that there are some places you cant reach yet mainly places that you need your dragon to fly to. So you can run around and do quest and you get to learn the basics of science (the teachings aspect of the game targeted to a younger generation). You can also grow crops at your farm, or go fishing. When your dragon reaches level 5 it becomes a teen dragon (is that even a thing?) then when your dragon reaches level 10 you can fly. So it takes a little bit in order to be able to fly in the game. But after you have an adult dragon you are good to fly wherever you wish doing quest and help save Berk. You can also collect as many dragons as you want to hatch and have. They get stored in your private stables that you can add rooms too and pick which dragon you want active at the time. Over all it is very cute, I like that it uses dragons and such to teach science and its a deffinate recommendation!
I'm still hoping Linux support comes out soon, but it Wines well and the game is delightful.

One of the best city building sims I've ever played.
It seems, almost, too simple of a game...build farms, cut down trees, chip away at the stone, hunt some deer etc. Then, all of a sudden, your tools are broken, so you cannot harvest wood for warmth, cannot break stone or mine iron to make new tools, and then your townsfolk start dying off....
So, be prepared to start over, chances are your town will die off (due to starvation, lack of warmth, population has stopped growing, or simply due to illness). The replayability is decent enough, so starting over isn't a huge deal, and it has a learning curve (esecially the larger settlements).
The mod support adds so much to the vanilla game (Though I suggest starting off with the core game, as some mods can seem overwhelming to a beginner).
All in all, I highly suggest this game (especially if you enjoy this genre). I got it on sale, I suggest you do too (Let's face it, most of us get our games this way)

Please keep in mind that you should go into this game expecting to be treated to
, and not neccessarily a lot of gameplay. If you are looking for a good action oriented combat focused Batman game I highly suggest you check out Arkham Asylum/City/Origins/Knight.
(which is currently the only episode released)
+ The quick time event (QTE) combat scenes although few and far between are done exceptionally well and are a lot of fun even if they are just inputing a few buttons while watching an epic fight go down. To me these fight scenes were the best parts about this game, and I could go back and watch/play them again and again.
+ Amazing voice actors for essentially every character, I thought Batman's low voice while in his suit was especially menacing in this game and was pretty badass.
+ Great believable characters and dialogue
+ Quite a few dialogue options that do impact the story a bit which you get to witness near the end
+ The environments in this game were very well crafted, it truly did feel like I was in the Gotham / Batman universe.
+ The story was pretty good in the first episode. In all honestly, it felt like a good superhero TV drama with a heavy emphasis on mystery, crime solving, and diving into Bruce Wayne's mind while you take down a big mob boss who's up to no good. Not to spoil too much, Falcone (mob boss) claimes Bruce's parents were making shady deals with the mob, and Batman is trying to clear his name while doubting himself and what he stands for.
- There really wasn't enough action in Episode 1, there's basically a great scene at the very beginning and then there's nothing but talking for about 1-1.5hours...and then you get a great fight scene at the end.
- As said previously, the pacing felt a bit off. At times I felt a bit bored waiting for some action to take place
- I really wanted to have seen more villains. You mainly only see Catwoman and Falcone.
- Although I do realize this is an "Adventure" game, I did find myself wanting more actual gameplay or gameplay events as it did get a bit tiresome listening on while sitting on the sidelines waiting for something to happen.

This is what the new populous games SHOULD look like.  This is a god-game done right, with detailed monsters and worshipers.  It is not Black and White, in the sense that you do not compete for worship nor abuse your followers.  It is a simple concept, your villagers against the world and you are their god.
A lot of people might be worried about 'early access' these days, and rightfully so.  This is one of the games I can solidly say is a safe bet.  It has a strong development cycle and does not have any half-finished features implemented in the game.  It is a fully playable and enjoyable game.  A lot can be said for the developer as well, I posted a bug report with a corrupted save file and not only recieved a response within an hour, the game was patched shortly thereafter to resolve the problem.  Finally, since I still had a corrupted save, he fixed the save file so I could play again.  All of this within 6 hours of the intial bug report.  That sort of thing is common anymore, and it's refreshing to see such dedication.
It's a good game with a solid design and a reliable developer, that's worth a buy in my book.

This is similar to Pixel Puzzles 2:Anime but not quite as good. Reasons:
1. The background is not a solid colour but contains a pattern.  This sometimes makes it hard to see a pieces shape once placed.  Although you can change the colour, the texture remains in place, so if a "black" part of the texture is behind a black piece, it is very hard t see.
2. The pieces float in water which "tints" the colour of the pieces.  This makes it more difficult to match colour to colours of pieces already picked or placed.
3. For some reason my computer often slowed down while playing this game.  I'm not a tech, so I don't know if this was a memory leak or that background programs would kick in.  All I know is that I didn't have this issue with Anime.  When it happened, I pretty much had to stop as the "lag" would make it unplayable.
Still a good puzzle game and I'm a fan of the series.
